Alternatively, since it is to be asked, 'How much of the sutta to be expounded does the sutta known as the Netti expound?', it is said, 'The sutta is expounded according to the sutta.' Here, 'according to the sutta' means that whatever sutta was spoken by the Blessed One, the sutta known as the Netti expounds all that sutta by way of showing gratification and danger. Therefore, it is said, 'Indeed, there is no sutta that cannot be expounded by the Netti method' (Netti. Aṭṭha. Saṅgahavāravaṇṇanā).

“Yaṃ yaṃ bhagavatā desitaṃ suttaṃ nettisaṃvaṇṇanāya saṃvaṇṇitaṃ, sā saṃvaṇṇetabbā desanā ca viññeyyā, udāhu desitabbañcā”ti vattabbabhāvato “yā ceva desanā”tyādimāha. Yā ceva desanā pāḷi saṃvaṇṇitā, sā ca, tāya desanāya desitaṃ yaṃ dhammajātaṃ, tañca ubhayaṃ vimuttāyatanadesanāsīsena paricayaṃ karontehi ekantena viññeyyaṃ ubhayasseva anupādisesaparinibbānapariyosānānaṃ sampattīnaṃ hetubhāvato. “Tassa ubhayassa vijānane sādhetabbe sādhetabbassa vijānanassa hetubhūtā katamā anupubbī”ti pucchitabbabhāvato vuttaṃ “tatrā”tyādi. Tattha tatra vijānane sādhetabbe suttādinavaṅgassa sāsanassa atthapariyesanā atthavicāraṇā hāranayānaṃ ayaṃ anupubbī vijānanassa sādhetabbassa hetubhūtā anupubbī nāmāti attho. Atha vā tassa ubhayassa vijānane sādhetabbe suttādinavaṅgassa sāsanassa atthapariyesanāya atthavicāraṇāya ayaṃ anupubbī vijānanassa sādhetabbassa hetubhūtā anupubbī nāmāti. Atha vā vakkhamānāya hāranayānupubbiyā navavidhasuttantapariyesanā vijānanassa hetubhūtāti veditabbā. Tenākāreneva aṭṭhakathāyaṃ tidhā vuttāti.

Since it is to be asked, 'Regarding whatever sutta was taught by the Blessed One and expounded by the Netti's exposition, should the teaching to be expounded be understood, or also what is taught by it?', he states, beginning with 'both the teaching and...'. Both the teaching, the Pāli, that is expounded, and the body of Dhamma taught by that teaching, should be understood entirely by those who cultivate familiarity with the teaching culminating in the sphere of liberation, because both are causes for the attainments culminating in final Nibbāna without residue. Since it is to be asked, 'In achieving the understanding of both, what sequence is the cause for the understanding that is to be achieved?', it is said, 'herein...'. Herein, in the understanding to be achieved, this sequence—the search for and investigation of the meaning of the ninefold teaching beginning with the sutta, and of the modes and ways—is the sequence that is the cause of the understanding to be achieved; this is the meaning of 'sequence'. Alternatively, in achieving the understanding of both, this sequence—by means of the search for and investigation of the meaning of the ninefold teaching beginning with the sutta—is the sequence that is the cause of the understanding to be achieved. Alternatively, the search for the ninefold Suttanta through the sequence of modes and ways to be explained should be understood as the cause of understanding. For this reason, it is stated in three ways in the commentary.

Saṅgahavārassa atthavibhāvanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the meaning of the Section on Compilation is finished.

2. Uddesavāraatthavibhāvanā

2. The Exposition of the Meaning of the Summary Chapter.

1. Evaṃ [V 0.0161] saṅgahavārena saṅkhepato dassite hārādayo idāni vibhāgena dassetuṃ “tattha katame soḷasa hārā”tiādidesanā āraddhā[M 0.0019]. Atha vā soḷasahārādisamudāyā netti nāma mayā mahākaccānena niddiṭṭhāti vuttā, “katame te soḷasa hārā”ti pucchitabbattā vuttaṃ “tattha soḷasa hārā”tyādi. Tattha tatthāti tesu soḷasahārādīsu. Desanā hāro, vicayo hāro…pe… sāmāropano hāroti ime soḷasa hārāti daṭṭhabbā.

1. Thus, the hāras and so forth, having been briefly shown by the Saṅgahavāra, are now to be shown in detail; therefore, the exposition beginning with 'Therein, what are the sixteen hāras?' is commenced. Alternatively, since it is said, 'The Netti, which is the collection of the sixteen hāras and so forth, was pointed out by me, Mahākaccāna,' and since it is to be asked, 'What are those sixteen hāras?' it is said, 'Therein, the sixteen hāras,' and so on. Here, 'therein' refers to those sixteen hāras and so forth. The Teaching Mode, the Investigation Mode… up to the Application Mode—these should be seen as the sixteen hāras.

Tattha sabbasādhāraṇattā hārapadassa vacanattho paṭhamaṃ vattabbo. Kenaṭṭhena hārāti? Harīyanti etehīti hārā. Etehi saṃvaṇṇanāvisesehi saṃvaṇṇiyesu suttageyyādīsu aññāṇasaṃsayavipallāsā harīyanti, iti aññāṇādiharaṇakāraṇattā “etehī”ti padena niddiṭṭhā saṃvaṇṇanāvisesā hārā nāma, hara-dhātuyā ācariyassa vacībhedasaddo, taṃsamuṭṭhāpako cittuppādo ca mukhyattho, veneyyānaṃ saṃvaṇṇetabbasuttassa atthajānanādiñāṇasampayuttacittuppādo kāraṇūpacārattho, tassa upanissayapaccayabhūtānaṃ saṃvaṇṇanāvisesānaṃ upanissayapaccayasatti phalūpacārattho, iti-saddena sā upanissayapaccayasattiyeva parāmasīyati. Taṃsattisampannā saṃvaṇṇanāvisesā ṇa-paccayatthā honti. Esa nayo evarūpesu ṭhānesupi. Vitthāro aṭṭhakathāyaṃ (netti. aṭṭha. 1) vutto eva.

Here, the verbal meaning of the word 'hāra' should first be stated because it is common to all. In what sense is it 'hāra'? It is called 'hāra' because by these, ignorance and so forth are carried away. By these special expositions, ignorance, doubt, and distortion are carried away in the suttas, geyyas, and so forth that are expounded. Thus, because these special expositions indicated by the word 'etehi' are the cause of carrying away ignorance and so forth, they are called hāras. The primary meaning of the root 'hara' is the teacher's variation of speech and the arising of consciousness that produces it. The figurative meaning by way of cause is the arising of consciousness, associated with the knowledge of the meaning and so forth of the sutta to be expounded to the trainable ones. The figurative meaning by way of result is the power as a supporting condition of the special expositions, which serve as a basis for that arising of consciousness. By the word 'iti,' that very power as a supporting condition is referred to. Those special expositions, endowed with that power, have the sense of the ṇa-suffix. This is the method in such cases. The detailed explanation is given in the commentary (Netti-aṭṭhakathā 1).

Asādhāraṇato pana desīyati etāyāti desanā. Etāya saṃvaṇṇanāya saṃvaṇṇetabbasuttattho desīyati saṃvaṇṇīyati saṃvaṇṇanānusārena ñāpīyati, iti ñāpanakāraṇattā “etāyā”ti padena niddiṭṭhā visesasaṃvaṇṇanā desanā nāma, na pāḷidesanā, pāḷidesanāya saṃvaṇṇetabbasaṃvaṇṇanābhāvena sahacaraṇato vā desanā. Kiñcāpi aññe hārā desanāpāḷisaṅkhātassa suttassa atthasaṃvaṇṇanābhāvato desanāya sahacārino honti, ayaṃ pana hāro yebhuyyena yathārutavaseneva viññāyamānattā pāḷidesanāya saha caratīti vattabbataṃ arahati, na tathā pare. Na hi assādādīnavanissaraṇādisandassanalakkhaṇarahitā pāḷidesanā atthi, ayañca hāro assādādisandassanalakkhaṇoti.

However, specifically, it is called 'desanā' because 'it is taught by this.' By this exposition, the meaning of the sutta to be expounded is taught, expounded, and made known according to the exposition. Thus, because it is the cause of making known, the special exposition indicated by the word 'etāyā' is called 'desanā,' not the Pāli teaching. Or, it is 'desanā' from its association with the Pāli teaching, which is to be expounded, not an exposition itself. Although other hāras are associated with the teaching by virtue of being expositions of the meaning of the sutta designated as the 'Pāli teaching,' this hāra, however, deserves to be called one that accompanies the Pāli teaching because it is mostly understood just as it is heard, unlike the others. Indeed, there is no Pāli teaching devoid of the characteristic of showing gratification, danger, escape, and so forth, and this hāra has the characteristic of showing gratification and the like.

Viciyanti etenāti vicayo. Etena saṃvaṇṇanāvisesena sutte padapañhādayo viciyanti, iti [V 0.0162] vicāraṇakāraṇattā so saṃvaṇṇanāviseso [M 0.0020] vicayo nāma. Katvatthādhikaraṇatthāpi labbhanti. Saṃvaṇṇetabbasuttena padapañhādivicayanalakkhaṇo saṃvaṇṇanāviseso vicayo hāro.

It is called 'vicaya' because things are investigated by it. By this special exposition, words, questions, and so forth in the sutta are investigated. Thus, because it is the cause of investigation, that special exposition is called 'vicaya.' Meanings in the sense of agency and locus are also obtained. The special exposition, whose characteristic is the investigation of words, questions, and so forth with regard to the sutta to be expounded, is the Investigation Mode.

Yuttāyutti vicārīyati etāyāti yutti. Etāya visesasaṃvaṇṇanāya sabbesaṃ hārānaṃ bhūmigocarānaṃ yuttāyutti vicārīyati, iti vicāraṇakāraṇattā “etāyā”ti padena niddiṭṭhā visesasaṃvaṇṇanā yutti nāma. Idha uttarapadalopo daṭṭhabbo, yuttiyā vicāraṇā, vicāraṇīyabhāvena sahacaraṇato vā yutti. Sabbahārānaṃ bhūmigocarānaṃ yuttāyuttivicāraṇalakkhaṇo saṃvaṇṇanāviseso yutti hāro.

It is called 'yutti' because suitability and unsuitability are investigated by it. By this special exposition, the suitability and unsuitability of all hāras and their grounds and spheres are investigated. Thus, because it is the cause of investigation, the special exposition indicated by the word 'etāyā' is called 'yutti.' Here, the elision of the subsequent word should be understood: 'investigation of suitability,' or it is 'yutti' due to its association with the state of being what is to be investigated. The special exposition characterized by the investigation of the suitability and unsuitability of all hāras and their grounds and spheres, is the Yutti Mode.

Padati pavatteti phalaṃ etenāti padaṃ, kāraṇaṃ. Ṭhanti tiṭṭhanti ettha phalāni tadāyattavuttitāyāti ṭhānaṃ, kāraṇaṃ. Padañca taṃ ṭhānañcāti padaṭṭhānaṃ, āsannakāraṇaṃ. Sutte āgatadhammānaṃ padaṭṭhānaṃ vicārīyati etāyāti padaṭṭhānā, visesasaṃvaṇṇanā, vicāraṇalopova, sutte āgatadhammānaṃ padaṭṭhānānaṃ, tesañca padaṭṭhānānaṃ vicāraṇalakkhaṇo saṃvaṇṇanāviseso padaṭṭhāno hāro.

It is called 'pada' because 'it causes the result to proceed by it'; it is a cause. It is called 'ṭhāna' because 'results stand or exist here, their existence being dependent on it'; it is a cause. That 'pada' and that 'ṭhāna' together are 'padaṭṭhāna,' the proximate cause. 'By this, the proximate cause of the phenomena found in the sutta is investigated'; thus it is 'padaṭṭhānā,' a special exposition, with the elision of 'investigation.' The special exposition, characterized by the investigation of the proximate causes of the phenomena found in the sutta, and of those proximate causes, is the Padaṭṭhāna Mode.

Sutte avuttāpi samānalakkhaṇā dhammā lakkhīyanti etena saṃvaṇṇanāvisesenāti lakkhaṇo, sutte vuttena dhammena samānalakkhaṇānaṃ dhammānaṃ avuttānampi niddhāraṇalakkhaṇo saṃvaṇṇanāviseso lakkhaṇo hāro.

It is called 'lakkhaṇa' because, 'by this special exposition, even unstated phenomena with similar characteristics are discerned.' The special exposition characterized by the determination of unstated phenomena with characteristics similar to a phenomenon stated in the sutta, is the Lakkhaṇa Mode.

Sutte dassiyamānā nibbacanādayo cattāropi viyūhīyanti vibhāgena sampiṇḍīyanti ettha, etena vāti byūho, catunnaṃ nibbacanādīnaṃ byūho catubyūho. Nibbacanādhippāyabyañjanānañceva desanānidānassa ca pubbāparena saddhiṃ sandassanalakkhaṇo saṃvaṇṇanāviseso catubyūho hāro.

Here, or by this, things shown in the Sutta are both analyzed in detail and synthesized; thus it is called 'byūho' (arrangement). The arrangement of the four—etymology, intention, expression, and the basis of the teaching—is 'catubyūho' (fourfold arrangement). The special exposition characterized by the demonstration of etymology, intention, expression, and the basis of the teaching, together with what precedes and follows, is the Catubyūha Mode.

Desanāya gahitadhammena sabhāgā, visabhāgā ca dhammā āvaṭṭīyanti ettha, etena vāti āvaṭṭo, desanāya gahitadhammānaṃ sabhāgavisabhāgadhammavasena āvaṭṭanalakkhaṇo saṃvaṇṇanāviseso āvaṭṭo hāro.

Here, or by this, similar and dissimilar phenomena are drawn in by the phenomenon grasped in the teaching; thus, it is called 'āvaṭṭo' (inclusion). The special exposition characterized by the inclusion of phenomena grasped in the teaching by way of similar and dissimilar phenomena, is the Āvaṭṭa Mode.

Asādhāraṇāsādhāraṇānaṃ saṃkilesadhamme, vodānadhamme ca sādhāraṇāsādhāraṇato, padaṭṭhānato, bhūmito ca vibhajanalakkhaṇo saṃvaṇṇanāviseso vibhatti hāro.

The special exposition characterized by classifying common and uncommon defiling and purifying phenomena by way of what is common and uncommon, by proximate cause, and by plane, is the Vibhatti Mode.

Sutte [V 0.0163][M 0.0021] niddiṭṭhā dhammā paṭipakkhavasena parivattīyanti iminā, ettha vāti parivatto, sutte niddiṭṭhānaṃ dhammānaṃ paṭipakkhato parivattanalakkhaṇo saṃvaṇṇanāviseso parivattano hāro.

Here, or by this, the phenomena stated in the Sutta are transformed by way of opposition; hence, it is called 'parivatto' (transformation). The special exposition characterized by the transformation of the phenomena stated in the Sutta by way of opposition, is the Parivattana Mode.

Sutte vuttassa ekasseva atthassa vācakaṃ vividhaṃ vacanaṃ ettha saṃvaṇṇanāviseseti vivacanaṃ, vivacanameva vevacanaṃ, sutte vutte ekasmiṃ atthe anekapariyāyasaddayojanālakkhaṇo saṃvaṇṇanāviseso vevacano hāro.

Here, the various words expressing a single meaning stated in the Sutta are a special exposition; thus it is called 'vivacana.' 'Vivacana' is indeed 'vevacana.' The special exposition characterized by the application of many synonymous expressions to a single meaning stated in the Sutta, is the Vevacana Mode.

Sutte vuttā atthā pakārehi ñāpīyanti iminā, ettha vāti paññatti, ekekassa dhammassa anekāhi paññattīhi paññāpetabbākāralakkhaṇo saṃvaṇṇanāviseso paññatti hāro.

Here, or by this, the meanings stated in the Sutta are made known in various ways; hence, it is called 'paññatti' (designation). The special exposition characterized by the mode in which each phenomenon is to be designated by many designations, is the Paññatti Mode.

Suttāgatā dhammā paṭiccasamuppādādīsu otarīyanti anuppavesīyanti ettha, etena vāti otaraṇo, paṭiccasamuppādādimukhehi suttatthassa otaraṇalakkhaṇo saṃvaṇṇanāviseso otaraṇo hāro.

Here, or by this, the phenomena that have come into the Sutta descend and enter into dependent origination and the like; hence, it is called 'otaraṇo' (descent). The special exposition characterized by the descent of the Sutta's meaning through the openings of dependent origination and the like, is the Otaraṇa Mode.

Sutte padapadatthapañhārambhā sodhīyanti samādhīyanti ettha, etena vāti sodhano, sutte padapadatthapañhārambhānaṃ sodhanalakkhaṇo saṃvaṇṇanāviseso sodhano hāro.

Here, or by this, words, their meanings, and the undertaking of questions in the Sutta are purified and settled; hence, it is called 'sodhano' (purification). The special exposition characterized by the purification of words, their meanings, and the undertaking of questions in the Sutta, is the Sodhana Mode.

Sāmaññavisesabhūtā dhammā vinā vikappena adhiṭṭhīyanti anuppavattīyanti ettha, etena vāti adhiṭṭhāno, suttāgatānaṃ dhammānaṃ avikappanavasena sāmaññavisesaniddhāraṇalakkhaṇo saṃvaṇṇanāviseso adhiṭṭhāno hāro.

Here, or by this, general and specific phenomena are determined and made to proceed without conceptualization; hence, it is called 'adhiṭṭhāno' (determination). The special exposition characterized by the determination of the general and specific by way of non-conceptualization regarding phenomena presented in the Sutta, is the Adhiṭṭhāna Mode.

Yo hetu ceva paccayo ca phalaṃ parikaroti abhisaṅkharoti, iti so hetu ceva paccayo ca parikkhāro, yo saṃvaṇṇanāviseso taṃ parikkhāraṃ hetuñceva paccayañca ācikkhati, iti so saṃvaṇṇanāviseso parikkhāro nāma. Sutte āgatadhammānaṃ parikkhārasaṅkhāte hetupaccaye niddhāretvā saṃvaṇṇanālakkhaṇo saṃvaṇṇanāviseso parikkhāro hāro.

That which, being both a cause and a condition, prepares and forms the fruit, is thus the cause and condition, the 'accessory'. The special explanation that points out that accessory as both cause and condition is called the 'accessory' (parikkhāro). The special explanation, characterized by explanation, which determines the cause and condition designated as 'accessory' among the phenomena that have come in the Sutta, is the 'accessory' heading.

Sutte āgatadhammā padaṭṭhānādimukhena samāropīyanti ettha, etena vāti samāropano, sutte āgatadhammānaṃ padaṭṭhānavevacanabhāvapahānasamāropanavicāraṇalakkhaṇo saṃvaṇṇanāviseso samāropano hāro. Bhāvasādhanavasenāpi sabbattha vacanattho vattabboti tassāpi vasena yojetabbanti. Sesaṃ saṃvaṇṇanānusārena ñātabbanti.

The phenomena that have come into the Sutta are superimposed by way of proximate cause and so forth. Herein, or by this, it is called 'superimposition'. The special explanation characterized by the investigation of proximate cause, synonymy, nature, abandonment, and superimposition of the phenomena that have come into the Sutta, is the 'superimposition' heading. The meaning of the expression should be stated everywhere based on the way of establishing the nature. Therefore, it should also be connected according to that way. The rest should be understood according to the exposition.

“Tattha [V 0.0164][M 0.0022] katame soḷasa hārā desanā”tyādinā hārasarūpaṃ vuttaṃ, kimatthaṃ “tassānugīti”tyādi vuttanti? Anugītigāthāya sukhaggahaṇatthaṃ puna “tassānugīti desanā vicayo yutti”tyādi vuttaṃ. Tattha tassāti hāruddesassa. Anugītīti anu pacchā gāyanagāthā. Pañcadasoti pañcadasamo. Soḷasoti soḷasamo. Atthato asaṃkiṇṇāti desanādipadatthato lakkhaṇatthato saṅkarato rahitā. Tena vuttaṃ aṭṭhakathāyaṃ “so ca nesaṃ asaṅkaro lakkhaṇaniddese supākaṭo hotī”ti. Sesaṃ saṃvaṇṇanānusārena ñātabbanti. “Keci hārā kehici hārehi saṃkiṇṇā viya dissanti, kasmā asaṃkiṇṇāti ñātabba”nti vattabbattā vuttaṃ “etesañcevā”tiādi. Tattha etesañceva bhavatīti etesaṃ soḷasannaṃ hārānaṃ yathā yenākārena asaṅkaro hoti, tathā asaṅkarākārena bhavati. Ayati pavattati nayavibhattīti ayā, vitthārena ayāti vitthāratayā, ta-kāro missakadosāpagamatthāya āgato, nayavibhattivisesavacanaṃ. Nayena ñāyena vibhatti nayavibhatti, na pañcanayavibhattāhārānaṃ vitthārena pavattā ñāyavibhatti tathā asaṅkarākārena bhavati tasmiṃ asaṃkiṇṇāti ñātabbāti adhippāyo.

By the passage beginning, "Therein, what are the sixteen headings: Exposition...", the nature of the headings has been stated. For what purpose is "its recitation" and so forth mentioned? For the sake of easy comprehension of the recitation verse, it is again stated: "Its recitation, exposition, investigation, and rationale." Therein, "its" refers to the enumeration of the headings. "Anugīti" means a verse sung afterward. "Pañcadaso" means the fifteenth. "Soḷaso" means the sixteenth. By "unmixed in meaning" is meant that they are free from confusion regarding the meaning of the terms "exposition" and so on, and free from mixing in terms of characteristics. Hence, it is said in the commentary: "And their unmixed nature is very evident in the explanation of the characteristics." The rest should be understood according to the explanation. Because it must be said, "Some headings may appear mixed with others—why should they be understood as unmixed?", it is stated: "And of these, indeed..." and so on. Therein, "and of these it is" means that the unmixed state of these sixteen headings exists in the way they are unmixed. "Ayati pavattati nayavibhattīti ayā" means that which proceeds, a distinction of method. "Vitthārena ayāti vitthāratayā" means it proceeds extensively, thus extensiveness; the letter 'ta' is inserted to remove the fault of mixing; it is a term denoting a special distinction of method. "Nayavibhatti" means distinction by way of method. The intended meaning is that the methodical distinction that proceeds extensively, which is not of the headings that have fivefold methodical distinctions, exists in such an unmixed way, and in that state is understood to be unmixed.

2. Soḷasa hārā sarūpato vuttā, amhehi ca viññātā, “katame pañca nayā”ti vattabbabhāvato tathā pucchitvā sarūpato uddisituṃ “tattha katame pañca nayā”tyādi vuttaṃ. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana “evaṃ hāre uddisitvā idāni naye uddisituṃ ‘tattha katame’tiādi vutta”nti (netti. aṭṭha. 2) vuttaṃ. “Tattha nayanti saṃkilese, vodāne ca vibhāgato ñāpentīti nayā, nīyanti vā tāni ettha, etehi vāti nayā”tiādinā (netti. aṭṭha. 2) aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vitthārena vacanattho vutto. Nī-dhātuyā nandiyāvaṭṭādinayānusārena saṃkilese, vodāne ca ālambitvā pavatto ñāṇasampayuttacittuppādo mukhyattho, nandiyāvaṭṭādinayānaṃ upanissayapaccayasatti phalūpacārato gahitā, iti-saddo taṃ phalūpacārato gahitasattiṃ parāmasi, taṃsattisahitā nandiyāvaṭṭādinayā a-paccayatthā.

2. The sixteen headings have been stated in their own form, and we have understood them. Because it was necessary to ask, "What are the five modes?" and to point them out in their own form, it was said: "Therein, what are the five modes?" and so on. In the commentary, however, it is said: "Having thus enumerated the headings, now to enumerate the modes, 'Therein, what are...' and so on was said." The word meaning is explained in detail in the commentary with phrases like: "Here, 'modes' (nayā) refers to that which makes known defilements and purifications by way of distinction; or they are called 'modes' because they are led to by these, or by means of these." The primary meaning of the root 'nī' is the arising of consciousness associated with knowledge, proceeding by taking defilement and purification as objects, according to modes such as the cycle of delight. The power of the supporting condition for the modes like the cycle of delight is grasped metaphorically through the result. The word 'iti' refers to that power grasped metaphorically through the result. The modes like the cycle of delight, together with that power, have a meaning that is not a condition.

Taṇhāavijjāhi saṃkilesapakkhassa suttassa, samathavipassanāhi vodānapakkhassa suttassa catusaccayojanamukhena nayanalakkhaṇo saṃvaṇṇanāviseso [M 0.0023] nandiyāvaṭṭo nayo. Tattha catusaccanti taṇhā ca avijjā ca bhavamūlattā samudayasaccaṃ, avasesā tebhūmakā dhammā dukkhasaccaṃ, samathavipassanā maggasaccaṃ, tena pattabbā asaṅkhatadhātu nirodhasaccanti.

The special explanation characterized by leading the meaning of the Sutta, which pertains to the defilement side through craving and ignorance, and to the purification side through serenity and insight, by way of the application of the four truths, is the 'mode of the cycle of delight'. Therein, regarding the four truths: craving and ignorance, being the root of existence, are the truth of arising; the remaining phenomena of the three realms are the truth of suffering; serenity and insight are the truth of the path; and the unconditioned element attainable through them is the truth of cessation.

Tīhi avayavehi lobhādīhi saṃkilesapakkhe, tīhi avayavehi alobhādīhi ca vodānapakkhe [V 0.0165] pukkhalo sobhanoti tipukkhalo, akusalamūlehi saṃkilesapakkhassa, kusalamūlehi vodānapakkhassa suttatthassa catusaccayojanamukhena nayanalakkhaṇo saṃvaṇṇanāviseso tipukkhalo.

The individual (puggala) is excellent (sobhana) by way of the three factors—greed and so on—on the side of defilement, and by way of the three factors—non-greed and so on—on the side of purification; hence, it is called the 'threefold individual' (tipukkhala). The special explanation characterized by leading the meaning of the Sutta, which pertains to the defilement side through unwholesome roots and to the purification side through wholesome roots, by way of the application of the four truths, is the 'mode of the threefold individual'.

Sīhassa bhagavato vikkīḷitaṃ ettha nayeti sīhavikkīḷito, subhasaññādīhi vipallāsehi sakalasaṃkilesapakkhassa, saddhindriyādīhi vodānapakkhassa suttatthassa catusaccayojanamukhena nayanalakkhaṇo saṃvaṇṇanāviseso sīhavikkīḷitanayo.

The playful display of the Blessed One, the lion, leads here; hence, it is called the 'lion's play'. The special explanation characterized by leading the meaning of the Sutta, which pertains to the entire defilement side through perversions such as the perception of beauty and so on, and to the purification side through faculties such as faith and so on, by way of the application of the four truths, is the 'mode of the lion's play'.

Atthanayattayadisābhāvena kusalādidhammānaṃ ālocanaṃ disālocanaṃ. Tassa tassa atthanayassa yojanatthaṃ katesu suttassa atthavissajjanesu ye vodānādayo, saṃkilesikā ca tassa tassa nayassa disābhūtā dhammā suttato niddhāretvā kathitā, tesaṃ yathāvuttadhammānaṃ citteneva “ayaṃ paṭhamā disā, ayaṃ dutiyā disā”tiādinā ālocanaṃ disālocanaṃ.

The examination of wholesome and other phenomena by way of being the direction of the three modes of meaning is 'direction-examination'. In the explanations of the Sutta's meaning, made for the purpose of applying each mode of meaning, those phenomena—such as purification and defiling states—which are the directions for each mode, having been determined and stated from the Sutta, the mental examination of those phenomena as stated, saying 'this is the first direction, this is the second direction,' and so on, is 'direction-examination'.

Tathā ālocitānaṃ dhammānaṃ atthanayattayayojane samānayanato aṅkuso viyāti aṅkuso, tassa tassa nayassa disābhūtānaṃ kusalādidhammānaṃ samānayanaṃ aṅkuso nayo.

Because it brings together the phenomena thus examined in the application of the three modes of meaning, it is like a hook; hence, it is called 'hook'. The bringing together of wholesome and other phenomena that are the directional aspects of each mode is the 'hook mode'.

Lañjetīti lañjako. Yo nayo suttatthaṃ lañjeti pakāseti, iti lañjanato pakāsanato so nayo lañjako nāma, nayo ca so lañjako cāti nayalañjako. Nayalañjako paṭhamo nandiyāvaṭṭo nāma, nayalañjako dutiyo tipukkhalo nāma, nayalañjako tatiyo sīhavikkīḷito nāmāti yojetabbo.

That which marks is called the 'marker' (lañjako). The mode that marks and clarifies the meaning of the Sutta is called the 'marker mode' due to its marking and clarifying nature. It is both a mode and a marker; hence, it is called the 'mode-marker'. The first mode-marker is called the 'Nandiyāvaṭṭa', the second is called the 'Tipukkhala', and the third is called the 'Sīhavikkīḷita'—thus it should be connected.

Uggatānaṃ visesena uggatoti uttamo, taṃ uttamaṃ. Gatāti ñātā, matāti attho. “Matā”ti vā pāṭho. Sesamettha vuttanayānusārenapi saṃvaṇṇanānusārenapi jānitabbanti.

That which is supremely elevated among the elevated is called the 'highest' (uttamo); that is the highest. 'Gatā' means known; the meaning is 'understood'. Alternatively, 'matā' may be the reading. The rest here should be understood according to the method previously stated and according to the explanation.

Yathāvuttanayavisesasaṃvaṇṇanāya [M 0.0024] ṭīkāyaṃ –

In the sub-commentary on the explanation of the special modes as stated—

“Samūhādiṃ upādāya lokasaṅketasiddhā vohāramattatā sammutisabhāvo, pathavīphassādīnaṃ kakkhaḷaphusanādilakkhaṇaṃ paramatthasabhāvo. Ayañhettha saṅkhepo – yasmiṃ bhinne, itarāpohe vā cittena kate na tathā buddhi, idaṃ sammutisaccaṃ yathā ghaṭe, sasambhārajale ca, tabbipariyāyena paramatthasacca”nti –

The nature of convention is mere designation established by worldly convention, dependent on aggregates and so forth. The nature of the ultimate is the characteristic of hardness, contact, and so on, pertaining to the earth element, contact, and so on. Here is the summary: when something is broken, or when its other components are mentally removed, and the cognition is no longer thus, this is conventional truth—as with a pot, or water with its components. The opposite of that is ultimate truth.

Vacane [V 0.0166] ghaṭakathalaāpajalakaddamādisaṅkhātaṃ samūhādiṃ upādāya lokassa pubbe ghaṭakathalaāpajalakaddamādisaṅketasiddhā ghaṭakathalaāpajalakaddamādivohāramattatā sammutisabhāvo saṅketavasena avitathattā. Pathavīādīnaṃ kakkhaḷādilakkhaṇaṃ, phassādīnaṃ phusanādilakkhaṇaṃ paramatthasabhāvo. “Yadi evaṃ ghaṭādike abhinne vā āpādike vā anurūpena ūnabhāvena appavattamāne vā sati sammutibhāvo hotu, bhinne vā ūne vā kathaṃ sammutibhāvo bhaveyya, pathavīphassādīnampi bhijjamānattā, kakkhaḷaphusanādīnañca pathavīphassādīhi anaññattā kathaṃ paramatthasabhāvo bhaveyya, katamena saṅkhepena atthena sammutisabhāvo, paramatthasabhāvo ca amhehi jānitabbo”ti vattabbabhāvato “ayañhettha saṅkhepo”tiādimāha. Tattha etthāti etesu sammutisabhāvaparamatthasabhāvesu ayaṃ nayo vuccamāno saṅkhepo attho daṭṭhabbo.

In the discourse, by relying on aggregates designated as pots, potshards, water, mud, etc., the conventional nature is merely the verbal usage of pots, potshards, water, and mud, established by the world through prior agreement, and is not false in terms of convention. The ultimate nature is the characteristic of hardness, etc., in earth and other elements, and the characteristic of impinging, etc., in contact and other factors. “If, in this way, the conventional nature exists when pots and the like are unbroken, or when water and the like are not functioning in a correspondingly diminished state, how could the conventional nature exist when they are broken or diminished? Since earth, contact, and the like are also subject to breaking, and since hardness, impinging, and the like are not different from earth, contact, and the like, how could the ultimate nature exist? By what concise meaning should we understand the conventional nature and the ultimate nature?” Because this must be said, it is said, “Here is the summary,” and so on. Here, in this context, the meaning to be seen is this concise principle being explained regarding the conventional nature and the ultimate nature.

Yasmiṃ ghaṭādike bhinne sati tato ghaṭādito itaro kathalādibhāvo cittena pubbe katena yathā yena kathalādivohārena bhavati, yasmiṃ āpādike sambhārajalādike ūnabhāvena pavattamāne sati vā tato āpādito itaro kaddamādibhāvo cittena pubbe katena yathā yena kaddamādivohārena bhavati, tathā tena vohārena buddhi kathalādisabhāvajānanaṃ kaddamādisabhāvajānanaṃ bhavati, idaṃ abhinne ghaṭādikaṃ vā bhinne kathalādikaṃ vā anūne āpādikaṃ vā ūne kaddamādikaṃ vā sabbaṃ sammutisaccaṃ hotveva. “Kaddamasmiṃ bhinne, kaddamasmiṃ ūne vā sati itaro sammutisabhāvo”ti pucchitabbabhāvato “ghaṭe, sambhārajale cā”ti vuttaṃ.

When a pot or the like is broken, then from that pot, etc., the other state of being fragments or the like occurs, according to the usage of fragments and so on, due to the mind having previously formed the concept. When water or water with its ingredients, etc., exists in a diminished state, then from that water, etc., the other state of being mud or the like occurs, according to the usage of mud and so on, due to the mind having previously formed the concept. Thus, through such usage, the intellect’s knowing of the nature of fragments and the like or the nature of mud and the like arises. All this—whether an unbroken pot, etc., a broken state of fragments, etc., undiminished water, etc., or a diminished state of mud, etc.—is merely conventional truth. Since it should be asked, “When there is breakage or diminution in mud, what is the other conventional nature?” it is said, “In the case of a pot or a collection of water.”

Sammutisaccasabhāvo [M 0.0025] tumhehi vutto, amhehi ca ñāto, “katamo paramatthasaccasabhāvo”ti vattabbabhāvato “tabbipariyāyena paramatthasacca”nti vuttaṃ. Pathavīādīnaṃ kakkhaḷādilakkhaṇato itarassa phusanādilakkhaṇassa asambhavato, phassādīnañca phusanādilakkhaṇato itarassa kakkhaḷādilakkhaṇassa asambhavato pathavīphassādīnaṃ lakkhaḷaphusanādilakkhaṇaṃ paramatthasaccaṃ hotvevāti imasmiṃ saṅkhepatthe gahite koci virodho natthīti adhippāyoti.

The nature of conventional truth has been stated by you and known by us. Because it must be asked, “What is the nature of ultimate truth?”, it is said, “In contrast to that, it is ultimate truth.” Because for earth and so on, which has the characteristic of hardness and so on, another characteristic, such as that of impinging, is impossible; and for contact and so on, which has the characteristic of impinging and so on, another characteristic, such as that of hardness, is impossible, therefore the characteristic of hardness, impinging, and so on, of earth, contact, and so on, is indeed ultimate truth. When this concise meaning is grasped, there is no contradiction—this is the intention.

3. Pañca nayā sarūpato ācariyena uddiṭṭhā, amhehi ca viññātā, “yāni padāni aṭṭhārasa mūlapadāni uddiṭṭhāni, katamāni tānī”ti pucchitabbattā tāni sarūpato dassetuṃ “tattha katamāni aṭṭhārasa mūlapadāni”tyādimāha. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana “evaṃ nayepi uddisitvā idāni mūlapadāni uddisituṃ ‘tattha katamānī’tiādi āraddha”nti vuttaṃ. Tattha kusalāni [V 0.0167] nava padāni, akusalāni nava padāni aṭṭhārasa mūlapadānīti daṭṭhabbānīti yojanā. Mūlanti patiṭṭhahanti etehi nayā, patiṭṭhānavibhāgā cāti mūlāni, padanti patiṭṭhahanti ettha nayā, paṭṭhānavibhāgā, adhigamā cāti padāni, vuttappakāraṭṭhena mūlāni ca tāni padāni cāti mūlapadāni. Kucchite pāpadhamme salayantīti kusalāni, kuse rāgādayo lunantīti kusalāni, kusā viya lunantīti kusalāni, kusena ñāṇena lātabbāni pavattetabbānīti kusalāni. Kusalānaṃ paṭipakkhānīti akusalāni a-saddo cettha paṭipakkhatthoti.

3. The five methods have been taught by the teacher in their proper form, and we too have understood them. Since it is necessary to ask, “Which are those eighteen root terms that have been taught?” in order to present them properly, it is said, “Herein, which are the eighteen root terms?” and so on. In the commentary, however, it is stated, “Having thus taught the methods, now the root terms are taught, beginning with ‘Herein, which are…’” Herein, it should be understood that there are nine wholesome terms and nine unwholesome terms, making eighteen root terms. “Root” (mūla) means that the methods are established by them, and they are the basis for classification; therefore they are roots. “Terms” (pada) means that the methods, classifications, and attainments are established here; therefore, they are terms. Thus, they are called “root terms” (mūlapada) in the sense of being both roots and terms as described above. “Wholesome” (kusala) means they shake off vile, evil states; or they cut off defilements such as lust; or they cut like kusa grass; or they are to be attained and developed by sharp wisdom. “Unwholesome” (akusala) means they are the opposites of the wholesome; here, the prefix “a-” conveys the sense of opposition.

Nava padāni kusalāni, nava padāni akusalānīti gaṇanaparicchedato, jātibhedato ca uddiṭṭhāni, “katamāni tānī”ti pucchitabbattā nava padāni akusalāni paccāsattinyāyena sarūpato dassetuṃ “katamāni nava padāni akusalānī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana –

Nine wholesome terms, nine unwholesome terms—thus they are taught by way of enumeration and by way of kind. Since it must be asked, “Which are these?”, the nine unwholesome terms are stated, according to the principle of proximity, to show their own nature, as it is said: “Which are the nine unwholesome terms?”, and so on. But in the Commentary—

“Evaṃ gaṇanaparicchedato, jātibhedato ca mūlapadāni dassetvā idāni sarūpato dassento saṃkilesapakkhaṃyeva paṭhamaṃ uddisati ‘taṇhā’tiādinā”ti (netti. aṭṭha. 3) –

“Having shown the root terms by way of enumeration and distinction of genus, now, to show them by way of essence, he first points out the aspect of defilement with ‘craving’ and so on” (Netti. Aṭṭha. 3).

Vuttaṃ. Tattha rūpādike khandhe tasati paritasatīti taṇhā. Avindiyaṃ kāyaduccaritādiṃ vindatīti avijjā[M 0.0026], vindiyaṃ kāyasucaritādiṃ na vindatīti avijjā, vijjāya paṭipakkhāti vā avijjā. Lubbhanti tenāti lobho, lubbhatīti vā lobho, lubbhanaṃ vā lobho. Dosamohesupi eseva nayo. Asubhe rūpakkhandhādike “subha”nti pavattā saññā subhasaññā. Dukkhadukkhādike “sukha”nti pavattā saññā sukhasaññā. Anicce saṅkhāradhamme “nicca”nti pavattā saññā niccasaññā. Anattasabhāvesu cakkhādīsu khandhesu “attā”ti pavattā saññā attasaññā. Yatthāti yesu padesu sabbo akusalapakkho saṅgahaṃ samosaraṇaṃ gacchati, tāni padāni akusalānīti yojanā. Saṅgahaṃ gaṇanaṃ. Samosaraṇaṃ samāropanaṃ.

It is said. Herein, craving is the trembling and constant trembling with regard to the aggregates such as form. Ignorance is experiencing what should not be experienced, such as bodily misconduct; or ignorance is not experiencing what should be experienced, such as bodily good conduct; or ignorance is the opposite of knowledge. Greed is that by which one is attached, or it is the act of being attached, or it is attachment. The same principle applies to hatred and delusion. The perception that arises perceiving the form aggregate and the like—which are unattractive—as “beautiful” is the perception of beauty. The perception that arises perceiving suffering and the like—which are painful—as “pleasant” is the perception of pleasure. The perception that arises perceiving conditioned phenomena—which are impermanent—as “permanent” is the perception of permanence. The perception that arises perceiving the eye and the like, or the aggregates—which are of the nature of not-self—as “self” is the perception of self. “Where” (yatthā) means those terms where the entire unwholesome faction goes to a collection and convergence. “Those are unwholesome terms”—this is the interpretation. “Collection” (saṅgaha) means counting. “Convergence” (samosaraṇa) means assembling.

Paccanīkadhamme uddhaccādike nīvaraṇe sameti vūpasameti tadaṅgavikkhambhanavasenāti samatho. Saṅkhāre aniccādīhi vividhehi ākārehi passatīti vipassanā. Lobhassa paṭipakkho alobho. Dosassa paṭipakkho adoso. Mohassa paṭipakkho amoho. Etthāpi a-saddo paṭipakkhattho, na abhāvatthādikoti adhippāyo. Asubhe rūpakkhandhādike, cakkhādimhi vā “asubha”nti pavattā saññāpadhānacittuppādā asubhasaññā, visesato kāyānupassanāsatipaṭṭhānaṃ[V 0.0168]. Dukkhadukkhatādīsu “dukkha”nti pavattā saññāpadhānacittuppādā dukkhasaññā, visesato vedanānupassanāsatipaṭṭhānaṃ. Anicce khandhādike vipariṇāmadhamme “anicca”nti pavattā saññāpadhānacittuppādā aniccasaññā, visesato cittānupassanāsatipaṭṭhānaṃ. Anattasabhāve khandhe, cakkhādimhi vā “anattā”ti pavattā saññāpadhānacittuppādā anattasaññā, visesato dhammānupassanāsatipadhānaṃ. Paññāsatisīsena hi pavattā ayaṃ desanā. Tena vuttaṃ bhagavatā “kathañca, bhikkhave, satibalaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ? Catūsu satipaṭṭhānesu, ettha satibalaṃ daṭṭhabba”nti. Yatthāti yesu padesu sabbo kusalapakkho saṅgahaṃ samosaraṇaṃ gacchati, tāni padāni kusalānīti yojanā.

Calming is the subduing or pacifying of opposing states, such as restlessness and other hindrances, through temporary suppression; hence, it is called samatha. Insight is seeing formations in various ways, such as through impermanence; hence, it is called vipassanā. The opposite of greed is non-greed. The opposite of hatred is non-hatred. The opposite of delusion is non-delusion. Here, the prefix “a-” means opposition, not absence, etc.; this is the intention. The perception of unattractiveness (asubhasaññā) is the arising of perception-led thought that focuses on the unattractive in form, such as the body aggregate or the eye, etc.; specifically, it is the mindfulness of the body in the foundations of mindfulness. The perception of suffering (dukkhasaññā) is the arising of perception-led thought that focuses on suffering in states like pain and the nature of suffering, etc.; specifically, it is the mindfulness of feelings in the foundations of mindfulness. The perception of impermanence (aniccasaññā) is the arising of perception-led thought that focuses on impermanence in formations subject to change, like the aggregates; specifically, it is the mindfulness of the mind in the foundations of mindfulness. The perception of non-self (anattasaññā) is the arising of perception-led thought that focuses on not-self in the aggregates or in the eye, etc., which are without an inherent nature; specifically, it is the mindfulness of phenomena in the foundations of mindfulness. This teaching proceeds with wisdom and mindfulness as its guiding principles. Therefore, the Blessed One said: “And how, monks, is the strength of mindfulness to be seen? It is to be seen in the four foundations of mindfulness.” “Where” (yatthā) means those terms where all wholesome qualities come together in a collection and convergence. “These are wholesome terms”—this is the interpretation.

Uddānanti uddhaṃ dānaṃ rakkhaṇaṃ uddānaṃ, saṅgahavacananti attho. Uddāne avutte sati heṭṭhā vuttassa atthassa vippakiṇṇabhāvo dinno viya bhaveyya, tasmā vippakiṇṇabhāvassa nivāraṇatthaṃ uddānanti adhippāyo. Caturo ca vipallāsāti subhasukhaniccaattasaññā. Kilesā bhavanti ettha navapadesūti bhūmī, kilesānaṃ bhūmīti kilesabhūmī, kilesapavattanaṭṭhānāni nava padānīti vuttaṃ hoti.

Uddāna means a lifting up, a giving, and a protection; the meaning is a term of collection. If the summary were not given, the meaning of what was said below might become scattered. Therefore, the intention is to prevent this scattering by providing the summary. The four distortions are the perceptions of beauty, pleasure, permanence, and self. Defilements arise here in nine terms—this is the ground; the ground of defilements is kilesabhūmi, meaning it is said that there are nine terms which are the places where defilements operate.

Caturo [M 0.0027] satipaṭṭhānāti asubhadukkhaaniccaanattasaññā. Indriyabhūmīti saddhādīnaṃ vimuttiparipācanindriyānaṃ bhūmī pavattanaṭṭhānāni samosaraṇaṭṭhānāni.

The four foundations of mindfulness are the perceptions of unattractiveness, suffering, impermanence, and non-self. The ground of the faculties (indriyabhūmi) is the ground, the place of occurrence, and the meeting place for the faculties of faith and so on that ripen into liberation.

Navahi kusalapadehi kusalapakkhā yujjanti yojīyanti, navahi akusalapadehi akusalapakkhā yujjanti yojīyanti. Navahi kusalapadehi saha kusalapakkhā yujjanti yujjantā bhavanti, navahi akusalapadehi saha akusalapakkhā yujjanti yujjantā bhavantīti uddesavāre vuttāvaseso saṃvaṇṇanānusārena vijānitabbo.

By nine wholesome terms, the wholesome side is yoked and connected; by nine unwholesome terms, the unwholesome side is yoked and connected. The wholesome side is yoked and comes to be yoked with the nine wholesome terms; the unwholesome side is yoked and comes to be yoked with the nine unwholesome terms. The remainder of what was stated in the outline section should be understood in accordance with the detailed explanation.

Iti sattibalānurūpā racitā

Thus, it is composed in accordance with ability and strength.

Uddesavārassa atthavibhāvanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the meaning of the outline section is completed.

3. Niddesavāraatthavibhāvanā

3. Explanation of the Meaning of the Exposition Section

Soḷasahāraniddesavibhāvanā

The Explanation of the Exposition of the Sixteen Modes

4. Hārādīsu [V 0.0169] samudāyassa nettippakaraṇassa uddeso uddiṭṭho, amhehi ca ñāto, “katamo niddeso”ti pucchitabbattā uddiṭṭhe hārādayo niddisituṃ “tattha saṅkhepato nettī”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana “evaṃ uddiṭṭhe hārādayo niddisituṃ ‘tattha saṅkhepato’tiādi āraddha”nti (netti. aṭṭha. 4) vuttaṃ. Tattha tatthāti tasmiṃ “tattha katame soḷasa hārā? Desanā vicayo”tiādiuddesapāṭhe. Saṅkhepatoti samāsato. Nettīti nettippakaraṇaṃ. Kittitāti kathitā, idāni niddesato kathessāmīti vuttaṃ hoti.

4. The outline of the Nettippakaraṇa, a collection of the modes and so on, has been stated and is known by us. Since it should be asked, 'What is the exposition?', the passage beginning 'Therein, briefly, the guide...' is commenced in order to expound the modes and so on that have been stated. However, in the commentary, it is said: 'In order to expound the modes and so on that have been stated in this way, the passage beginning "Therein, briefly..." is commenced' (Netti-aṭṭha. 4). Therein, 'there' refers to that passage in the outline section, 'Therein, what are the sixteen modes? The teaching, the investigation,' etc. 'Briefly' means concisely. 'The guide' refers to the Nettippakaraṇa. 'Declared' means spoken of; it is said that now I will explain it by way of exposition.

1.

1.

“Assādādīnavatā, nissaraṇampi ca phalaṃ upāyo ca.

Gratification and danger, escape, fruit, and means.

Āṇattī ca bhagavato, yogīnaṃ desanāhāro”ti. –

And the Blessed One's command: this is the mode of teaching for practitioners.

Gāthāyaṃ yena saṃvaṇṇanāvisesena sutte āgatā assādopi ādīnavatā ādīnavopi nissaraṇampi phalampi upāyopi yogīnaṃ atthāya bhagavato āṇattipi ime dhammā dassitā saṃvaṇṇitā saṃvaṇṇanāvasena ñāpitā, so saṃvaṇṇanāviseso desanāhāro nāmāti atthayojanā.

In the verse, that particular mode of exposition by which these things that have come in the Sutta—gratification, danger, escape, fruit, means, and the Blessed One's command for the benefit of practitioners—are shown, described, and made known by way of exposition, is called the 'mode of teaching.' This is the connection of the meaning.

Vacanatthādayo [M 0.0028] aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vitthārato vuttāva, tasmā kiñcimattameva kathessāmi. Assādīyateti assādo, ko so? Sukhaṃ, somanassaṃ, iṭṭhārammaṇabhūtā pañcupādānakkhandhā ca. Assādeti etāyāti vā assādo, ko so? Taṇhā, vipallāsā ca. Vipallāsavasena hi ekacce sattā aniṭṭhampi ārammaṇaṃ iṭṭhākārena assādenti.

The meanings of the words and so on have already been explained in detail in the commentary; therefore, I will discuss only a little. 'It is enjoyed' (assādīyati), thus it is 'gratification' (assādo). What is that? It is pleasure, joy, and the five aggregates of clinging that have become agreeable objects. Or, 'one enjoys by this' (assādeti etāya), thus it is 'gratification' (assādo). What is that? It is craving and the distortions. For due to the distortions, some beings enjoy even a disagreeable object as if it were agreeable.

Ābhusaṃ kammena dīnaṃ dukkhādi hutvā vāti pavattatīti ādīnavo, dukkhādi. Atha vā ativiya ādīnaṃ kapaṇaṃ hutvā vāti pavattatīti ādīnavo, kapaṇamanusso, tathābhāvā ca tebhūmakā dhammā aniccatādiyogato.

Having become miserable and suffering, etc., through kamma, it proceeds exceedingly; thus, it is 'danger' (ādīnavo), which is suffering and the like. Or, having become extremely miserable and wretched, it proceeds; thus, it is 'danger' (ādīnavo), like a wretched person. And the phenomena of the three realms are of such a nature due to their connection with impermanence and so on.

Nissarati etenāti nissaraṇaṃ, ariyamaggo. Nissaratīti vā nissaraṇaṃ, nibbānaṃ. Pi-saddo [V 0.0170] sampiṇḍanattho. Nissaraṇabhedo aṭṭhakathāyaṃ (netti. aṭṭha. 4 hārasaṅkhepa) bahudhā vuttova.

'One escapes by this' (nissarati etena), thus it is 'escape' (nissaraṇaṃ); it is the Noble Path. Or, 'it escapes' (nissarati), thus it is 'escape' (nissaraṇaṃ); it is Nibbāna. The particle 'pi' has the meaning of inclusion. The various kinds of escape are extensively stated in the commentary (Netti-aṭṭha. 4, Hārasaṅkhepa).

Phalati pavattatīti phalaṃ, desanāya phalaṃ. Yadipi desanā phalanipphādikā na hoti, tathāpi bhagavato dhammadesanaṃ sutvā puññasambhārā sambhavanti, puññasambhārahetuto phalaṃ pavattaṃ, tasmā desanāya phalaṃ nāmāti. Katamaṃ taṃ? Devamanussesu āyuvaṇṇasukhabalayasaparivāraadhipateyyaupadhisampatticakkavattisiridevarajja- siricatusampatticakkasīlasamādhisampadā vijjābhiññā paṭisambhidā sāvakabodhipaccekabodhisammāsambodhiyo.

'It bears fruit, it proceeds' (phalati, pavattati), thus it is 'fruit' (phalaṃ); it is the fruit of the teaching. Although the teaching does not directly produce fruit, still, having heard the Blessed One’s Dhamma discourse, accumulations of merit arise, and fruit proceeds from the cause of these accumulations of merit. Therefore, it is called the fruit of the teaching. What is that? Among humans and devas: long life, beauty, happiness, strength, fame, retinue, sovereignty, the accomplishment of the substrata of existence, the glory of a universal monarch, the glory of divine kingship, the wheel of the four accomplishments, the accomplishment of virtue and concentration, knowledge, direct knowledges, analytical knowledges, the enlightenment of a disciple, the enlightenment of a Paccekabuddha, and perfect self-enlightenment.

Paccayasāmaggiṃ upagantvā ayati pavattati phalaṃ etenāti upāyo, ko so? Ariyamaggassa pubbabhāgapaṭipadā. Purimā paṭipadā hi pacchimāya paṭipadāya adhigamūpāyo, paramparāya magganibbānādhigamassa ca upāyo. Keci “maggopi upāyo”ti vadanti, tesaṃ matena nibbānameva nissaraṇanti vuttaṃ siyā. “Te pahāya tare oghanti idaṃ nissaraṇa”nti (netti. 5) pana ariyamaggassa nissaraṇabhāvaṃ vakkhati, tasmā kesañci vādo na gahetabbo.

'Having approached the collection of conditions, fruit proceeds in the future by this' (paccayasāmaggiṃ upagantvā ayati pavattati phalaṃ etena), thus it is 'means' (upāyo). What is that? It is the preliminary practice for the Noble Path. For the earlier practice is the means to attain the later practice and, sequentially, is the means to attain the Path and Nibbāna. Some say, 'The Path too is a means.' According to their view, it would be said that Nibbāna alone is escape. However, the text will state that the Noble Path is the escape with the words, 'Having abandoned them, one crosses the flood—this is escape' (Netti. 5). Therefore, the view of some should not be accepted.

Āṇattīti āṇārahassa bhagavato veneyyānaṃ hitasiddhiyā “evaṃ sammāpaṭipattiṃ paṭipajjāhi, micchāpaṭipattiṃ mā paṭipajjāhī”ti vidhānaṃ āṇāṭhapanaṃ āṇatti nāma.

'Command' (āṇatti) is the ordinance, the establishment of command, of the Blessed One, who is worthy of command, for the attainment of the welfare of those to be trained: 'Practice the right practice thus; do not practice the wrong practice.'

Yujjanti [M 0.0029] payujjanti catusaccakammaṭṭhānabhāvanāsūti yogino, veneyyā, tesaṃ yogīnaṃ atthāyāti vacanasesaṃ nīharitvā yojanā kātabbā. Sutte āgatānaṃ sabbesaṃ assādādīnaṃ ekadesāgatānampi nīharitvā sabbesaṃ vibhajanasaṃvaṇṇanāviseso desanāhāroti niddesato gahetabbo, so ca vibhajanākāro desanāhāravibhaṅge (netti. 5) āgamissatīti idha na dassitoti.

'They are yoked, they exert themselves in the development of the meditation subject of the four noble truths'—thus, they are 'practitioners' (yogino), those to be trained. The connection should be made by extracting the remainder of the statement, 'for the benefit of those practitioners.' Having extracted even a portion of all the gratifications and so on that have come in the Sutta, the particular mode of analytical exposition of all of them is to be understood by way of exposition as the 'mode of teaching.' And that mode of analysis will come in the Analysis of the Mode of Teaching (Netti. 5); therefore, it is not shown here.

Desanāhāraniddeso niddiṭṭho, amhehi ca ñāto, “katamo vicayahāraniddeso”ti pucchitabbattā –

The exposition of the mode of teaching has been expounded, and it is known by us. Since it should be asked, 'What is the exposition of the mode of investigation?' –

2.

2.

“Yaṃ pucchitañca vissajjitañca, suttassa yā ca anugīti.

What was asked and what was answered, and the subsequent recitation of the Sutta.

Suttassa yo pavicayo, hāro vicayoti niddiṭṭho”ti. –

The analysis of the Sutta—this mode is indicated as 'investigation.'

Gāthā [V 0.0171] vuttā. Tattha suttassa yaṃ pucchitañca yā pucchā vicayamānā ca suttassa yaṃ vissajjitañca yā vissajjanā vicayamānā ca suttassa yo padādivicayo, assādādivicayo ca atthi, te vuttappakārā vicayamānā pucchādayo yena saṃvaṇṇanāvisesena viciyanti, so saṃvaṇṇanāviseso vicayo hāroti niddiṭṭhoti atthayojanā kātabbā.

The verse has been stated. Therein, what was asked in the Sutta and the question being investigated, and what was answered in the Sutta and the answer being investigated, and the analysis of words and so on in the Sutta, and the analysis of gratification and so on, exist. That particular mode of exposition by which those questions and so on, being investigated in the manner stated, are investigated, is indicated as the 'mode of investigation'—thus should the meaning be connected.

Pucchīyate pucchitaṃ. Vissajjīyate vissajjitanti bhāvasādhanattho daṭṭhabbo, na kammasādhanattho. Tena vuttaṃ ṭīkāyaṃ “bhāvatthe toti āha – ‘vissajjitanti vissajjanā’”ti.

'It is asked' (pucchīyate) is 'what was asked' (pucchitaṃ). 'It is answered' (vissajjīyate) is 'what was answered' (vissajjitaṃ)—this should be understood as having the meaning of a verbal noun, not a past passive participle. Therefore, it is said in the subcommentary: 'He said "-ta" in the sense of the verbal noun – "vissajjitaṃ" means "vissajjanā" (the act of answering).'

“Suttassā”ti niyamitattā saṃvaṇṇanāvasena aṭṭhakathāyaṃ āgataṃ na gahetabbanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. So vicayo hāro aṭṭhakathāyaṃ (netti. aṭṭha. 4 hārasaṅkhepa) vuttova. Kathaṃ? –

Since 'of the Sutta' (suttassa) is specified, it should be understood that what has come in the commentary by way of exposition should not be taken. That mode of investigation is indeed stated in the commentary (Netti-aṭṭha. 4, Hārasaṅkhepa). How so? –

“Ayaṃ pucchā adiṭṭhajotanā diṭṭhasaṃsandanā vimaticchedanā anumatipucchā kathetukamyatāpucchā sattādhiṭṭhānā dhammādhiṭṭhānā ekādhiṭṭhānā anekādhiṭṭhānā sammutivisayā paramatthavisayā atītavisayā anāgatavisayā paccuppannavisayā”tiādinā pucchāvicayo veditabbo. “Idaṃ vissajjanaṃ ekaṃsabyākaraṇaṃ vibhajjabyākaraṇaṃ paṭipucchābyākaraṇaṃ ṭhapanaṃ sāvasesaṃ niravasesaṃ sauttaraṃ [M 0.0030] niruttaraṃ lokiyaṃ lokuttara”ntiādinā vissajjanavicayo.

This question is one that illuminates what was unseen, connects with what is seen, cuts off doubt, a question seeking agreement, a question arising from a desire to speak, based on beings, based on phenomena, based on a single basis, based on multiple bases, related to conventional truth, related to ultimate truth, related to the past, related to the future, related to the present—thus the investigation of questions should be understood. This answer is a direct explanation, an analytical explanation, an explanation by counter-question, a setting aside, with a remainder, without a remainder, surpassable, unsurpassable, worldly, transcendental—thus the investigation of answers.

“Ayaṃ pucchā iminā sameti, etena na sametī”ti pucchitatthaṃ ānetvā, vicayo pubbenāparaṃ saṃsanditvā ca vicayo pubbāparavicayo. “Ayaṃ anugīti vuttatthasaṅgahā avuttatthasaṅgahā tadubhayatthasaṅgahā kusalatthasaṅgahā akusalatthasaṅgahā”tiādinā anugītivicayo. Assādādīsu sukhavedanāya “iṭṭhārammaṇānubhavanalakkhaṇā”tiādinā, taṇhāya “ārammaṇaggahaṇalakkhaṇā”tiādinā, vipallāsānaṃ “viparītaggahaṇalakkhaṇā”tiādinā, avasiṭṭhānaṃ tebhūmakadhammānaṃ “yathāsakalakkhaṇā”tiādinā sabbesañca dvāvīsatiyā tikesu, dvācattālīsādhike ca dukasate labbhamānapadavasena taṃtaṃassādatthavisesaniddhāraṇaṃ assādavicayo.

Having brought forward the meaning of the question, 'This question accords with this, but does not accord with that,' the investigation that connects what precedes with what follows is the 'investigation of what precedes and follows.' This is the investigation of recitation, by way of 'This recitation includes the stated meaning, the unstated meaning, both meanings, the wholesome meaning, the unwholesome meaning,' and so on. Among the gratifications and so on, the investigation of gratification is the determination of the specific meaning of each gratification by way of the terms found in all twenty-two triads and the one hundred and forty-two dyads, such as for the feeling of happiness, 'characterized by experiencing desirable objects,' and so on; for craving, 'characterized by grasping objects,' and so on; for distortions, 'characterized by inverted grasping,' and so on; for the remaining phenomena of the three realms, 'characterized according to their own individual nature,' and so on.

Dukkhavedanāya “aniṭṭhānubhavanalakkhaṇā”tiādinā, dukkhasaccānaṃ “paṭisandhilakkhaṇā”tiādinā, aniccatādīnaṃ ādiantavantatāya aniccantikatāya ca [V 0.0172] “aniccā”tiādinā sabbesañca lokiyadhammānaṃ saṃkilesabhāgiyahānabhāgiyatādivasena ādīnavavuttiyā okāraniddhāraṇena ādīnavavicayo. Nissaraṇapade ariyamaggassa āgamanato kāyānupassanādipubbabhāgapaṭipadāvibhāgavisesaniddhāraṇavasena, nibbānassa yathāvuttapariyāyavibhāgavisesaniddhāraṇavasenāti evaṃ nissaraṇavicayo. Phalādīnaṃ taṃtaṃsuttadesanāya sādhetabbaphalassa tadupāyassa tattha tattha suttavidhivacanassa ca vibhāganiddhāraṇavasena vicayo veditabbo. Evaṃ padapucchāvissajjanapucchāpubbāparānugītīnaṃ, assādādīnañca visesaniddhāraṇavaseneva vicayalakkhaṇo “vicayo hāro”ti veditabboti –

For the feeling of suffering, 'characterized by experiencing the undesirable,' and so on; for the truths of suffering, 'characterized by rebirth-linking,' and so on; for impermanence and so on, 'impermanent,' and so on, due to having a beginning and an end and being of an impermanent nature—the investigation of danger is by way of determining the meaning of 'okāra' (fault) in the sense of danger for all worldly phenomena, by way of their being associated with defilements, associated with decline, and so on. In the section on escape, the investigation of escape is thus by way of determining the specific distinctions in the preliminary practices, such as mindfulness of the body, that lead to the arising of the Noble Path, and by way of determining the specific distinctions in the classification of Nibbāna as previously stated. The investigation of fruits and so on should be understood by way of determining the distinctions of the fruit to be attained by each Sutta teaching, its means, and the specific Sutta passages therein. Thus, the characteristic of investigation, which is the 'mode of investigation,' should be understood as being solely by way of determining the distinctions of words, questions, answers, prior and subsequent connections, recitations, and of gratifications and so on.

Evaṃ vuttova.

Thus it has been stated.

Vissajjanaviseso pana ṭīkāyaṃ vutto. Kathaṃ? –

However, the specific explanation is stated in the subcommentary. How?

“Cakkhu anicca”nti puṭṭhe “āma, cakkhu aniccamevā”ti ekantato vissajjanaṃ ekaṃsabyākaraṇaṃ, “aññindriyaṃ bhāvetabbaṃ, sacchikātabbañcā”ti [M 0.0031] puṭṭhe “maggapariyāpannaṃ bhāvetabbaṃ, phalapariyāpannaṃ sacchikātabba”nti vibhajitvā vissajjanaṃ vibhajjabyākaraṇaṃ, “aññindriyaṃ kusala”nti puṭṭhe “kiṃ anavajjaṭṭho kusalattho, udāhu sukhavipākaṭṭho”ti paṭipucchitvā vissajjanaṃ paṭipucchābyākaraṇaṃ, “sassato attā, asassato vā”ti vutte “abyākatameta”ntiādinā avissajjanaṃ ṭhapanaṃ, “kiṃ panete ‘kusalā’ti vā ‘dhammā’ti vā ekatthā, udāhu nānatthā”ti idaṃ pucchanaṃ sāvasesaṃ. Vissajjanassa pana sāvasesato veneyyajjhāsayavasena desanāyaṃ veditabbā. Apāṭihīrakaṃ sauttaraṃ sappāṭihīrakaṃ niruttaraṃ, sesaṃ vicayahāraniddese suviññeyyamevāti –

When asked, 'Is the eye impermanent?' replying definitively, 'Yes, the eye is indeed impermanent,' is a categorical answer. When asked, 'Should the faculty of final knowledge be developed and realized?' replying analytically, 'What pertains to the path should be developed; what pertains to the fruit should be realized,' is an analytical answer. When asked, 'Is the faculty of final knowledge wholesome?' replying after questioning, 'Is it wholesome in the sense of being blameless, or in the sense of resulting in happiness?' is an answer by counter-question. When it is said, 'Is the self eternal, or not eternal?' not replying, saying, 'This is undeclared,' is a setting aside. As for the question, 'Are these, whether called "wholesome" or "dhamma," the same in meaning, or different in meaning?' this is a question with a remainder. As for the answer, it should be understood that the teaching is given with a remainder depending on the disposition of the trainees. What is not to be rejected is answerable; what is to be rejected is unanswerable. The rest is easily understood in the exposition of the mode of investigation.

Vuttova. Saṃvaṇṇanāsu vutto attho anākulo pākaṭo yatipotehi viññāto, so sabbattha amhehi na vibhattoti daṭṭhabbo.

It has been said. The meaning stated in the commentaries is clear and unconfused, understood by monks and novices, and it should be seen that it has not been elaborated upon by us in all cases.

Vicayahāraniddeso niddiṭṭho, amhehi ca ñāto, “katamo yuttihāraniddeso”ti pucchitabbattā –

The exposition of the mode of investigation has been expounded and is known by us. Since the question should be asked, 'What is the exposition of the mode of suitability?'

3.

3.

“Sabbesaṃ [V 0.0173] hārānaṃ, yā bhūmī yo ca gocaro tesaṃ.

Of all the modes, that which is their ground and their domain,

Yuttāyuttaparikkhā, hāro yuttīti niddiṭṭho”ti. –

The examination of what is suitable and unsuitable—this mode is designated as suitability.

Gāthā vuttā. Tattha sabbesaṃ soḷasannaṃ hārānaṃ yā bhūmi pavattanaṭṭhānabhūtaṃ byañjanaṃ, yo gocaro suttattho ca atthi, tesaṃ bhūmisaṅkhātabyañjanagocarasaṅkhātasuttatthānaṃ yā yuttāyuttaparikkhā yuttāyuttīnaṃ vicāraṇā saṃvaṇṇanā katā, so yuttiayuttiparikkhāvicāraṇasaṅkhāto saṃvaṇṇanāviseso “yutti hāro”ti niddiṭṭhoti atthayojanā.

The verses have been spoken. Therein, for all sixteen modes, that which is the ground—the expression serving as the place of operation—and that which is the domain—the meaning of the sutta—exists. Of these expressions designated as the ground and sutta meanings designated as the domain, the examination of suitability and unsuitability, the consideration and elucidation of what is suitable and unsuitable, has been made. That specific elucidation, consisting of the examination and consideration of suitability and unsuitability, is designated as 'the mode of suitability.' Such is the connection of the meaning.

Tesaṃ hārānaṃ bhūmibhūtassa sutte āgatassa byañjanassa yuttibhāvo duvidho sabhāvaniruttibhāvo, adhippetatthavācakabhāvo ca. Gocarabhūtassa pana sutte āgatassa yuttibhāvo suttavinayadhammatāhi avilomanaṃ. Ayuttibhāvo vuttavipariyāyena gahetabbo.

The suitability of the expression found in the sutta, which serves as the ground for those modes, is twofold: its inherent etymological nature, and its capacity to express the intended meaning. However, the suitability of what is found in the sutta, which serves as the domain, is its non-contradiction with the principles of the Sutta and Vinaya. Unsuitability should be understood as the opposite of what has been stated.

Yuttihāraniddeso niddiṭṭho, amhehi ca ñāto, “katamo padaṭṭhānahāraniddeso”ti pucchitabbattā –

The exposition of the mode of suitability has been expounded and is known by us. Since the question should be asked, 'What is the exposition of the mode of proximate cause?'

4.

4.

“Dhammaṃ [M 0.0032] deseti jino, tassa ca dhammassa yaṃ padaṭṭhānaṃ.

The Conqueror teaches the Dhamma, and that which is the proximate cause of that Dhamma,

Iti yāva sabbadhammā, eso hāro padaṭṭhāno”ti. –

Thus, up to all states, this mode is the proximate cause.

Gāthā vuttā. Tattha dhammanti yaṃ kiñci kusalādidhammaṃ sutte jino deseti, tassa sutte jinena desitassa kusalādidhammassa yañca padaṭṭhānaṃ niddhāretabbaṃ, taṃ taṃ padaṭṭhānañcāti evaṃ vuttanayena yāva yattakā sabbe dhammā sutte jinena desitā, tattakānaṃ sabbesaṃ dhammānaṃ yañca padaṭṭhānaṃ niddhāretabbaṃ, tassa ca padaṭṭhānassa yañca padaṭṭhānaṃ niddhāretabbaṃ, taṃ taṃ padaṭṭhānañca, iti evaṃ vuttanayena yāva yattakā sabbe padaṭṭhānadhammā niddhāretabbāva, tattakāni sabbāni dhammapadaṭṭhānāni yathānurūpaṃ niddhāretvā yena saṃvaṇṇanāvisesena kathitāni, eso saṃvaṇṇanāviseso “padaṭṭhāno hāro”ti niddiṭṭhoti atthayojanā.

The verses have been spoken. Herein, 'dhamma' means whatever wholesome or other states the Conqueror teaches in the sutta. For that wholesome or other state taught by the Conqueror in the sutta, whatever proximate cause is to be ascertained, that proximate cause is also to be considered. In this way, to whatever extent all states are taught by the Conqueror in the sutta, for all those states, whatever proximate cause is to be ascertained, and for that proximate cause, whatever proximate cause is to be ascertained—that proximate cause is also to be considered. Thus, in this manner, to whatever extent all states that are proximate causes are invariably to be ascertained, all those proximate causes of states should be ascertained appropriately. By whatever special mode of elucidation they are spoken, that special mode of elucidation is designated 'the mode of proximate cause.' Such is the connection of the meaning.

Sutte desitakusaladhammassa yonisomanasikārasaddhammassavanasappurisūpanissayādi padaṭṭhānaṃ, sutte desitaakusaladhammassa ayonisomanasikāraasaddhammassavanaasappurisūpanissayādi padaṭṭhānaṃ, abyākatassa dhammassa yathārahaṃ kusalākusalābyākatā padaṭṭhānantiādinā niddhāretabbanti.

The proximate cause for wholesome states taught in the sutta is proper attention, listening to the true Dhamma, reliance on good people, and so on. The proximate cause for unwholesome states taught in the sutta is improper attention, listening to false Dhamma, reliance on bad people, and so on. The proximate cause for indeterminate states should be determined accordingly as wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate, and so forth.

Padaṭṭhānahāraniddeso [V 0.0174] niddiṭṭho, amhehi ca ñāto, “katamo lakkhaṇahāraniddeso”ti pucchitabbattā –

The exposition of the mode of proximate cause has been expounded and is known by us. Since the question should be asked, 'What is the exposition of the mode of characteristic?'

5.

5.

“Vuttamhi ekadhamme, ye dhammā ekalakkhaṇā keci.

When one state is stated, whatever states have a single characteristic,

Vuttā bhavanti sabbe, so hāro lakkhaṇo nāmā”ti. –

All these are spoken of; that mode is called characteristic.

Gāthā vuttā. Tattha ekadhamme sutte bhagavatā vuttamhi, aṭṭhakathāyaṃ niddhārite vā sati tena dhammena ye keci dhammā ekalakkhaṇā bhavanti, sabbe te dhammā sutte sarūpato avuttāpi samānalakkhaṇatāya saṃvaṇṇetabbabhāvena ānetvā yena saṃvaṇṇanāvisesena vuttā bhavanti, so saṃvaṇṇanāviseso “lakkhaṇo nāma hāro”ti niddiṭṭhoti atthayojanā.

The verses have been spoken. Therein, when one state is spoken of by the Blessed One in the sutta, or when it is ascertained in the commentary, whatever states share a single characteristic with that state, even if not explicitly mentioned in the sutta, they are brought in as something to be elucidated due to their shared characteristic, and by whatever specific mode of elucidation they are spoken of. That specific mode of elucidation is designated as 'the method called characteristic.' Such is the connection of the meaning.

Ekaṃ samānaṃ lakkhaṇaṃ etesanti ekalakkhaṇā, samānalakkhaṇā, sahacāritāya vā samānakiccatāya vā samānahetutāya vā samānaphalatāya vā samānārammaṇatāya vā avuttāpi niddhāritāti. Kathaṃ[M 0.0033]? – “Nānattakāyānānattasaññino (dī. ni. 3.341, 357, 359; a. ni. 9.24), nānattasaññānaṃ amanasikārā”tiādīsu sahacāritāya saññāya sahagatā dhammā niddhāritā. “Dadaṃ mittāni ganthatī”tiādīsu (saṃ. ni. 1.246; su. ni. 189) samānakiccatā, piyavacanaatthacariyā samānatthatāpi niddhāritā, “phassapaccayā vedanā”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 3.126; saṃ. ni. 2.1; mahāva. 1; vibha. 225; udā. 1; netti. 24) samānahetutāya saññādayopi niddhāritā, “avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 3.126; saṃ. ni. 2.1; mahāva. 1; vibha. 225; udā. 1; netti. 24) samānaphalatāya taṇhupādānādayopi niddhāritā, “rūpaṃ assādeti abhinandati, taṃ ārabbha rāgo uppajjatī”tiādīsu (paṭṭhā. 1.1.424) samānārammaṇatāya taṃsampayuttā vedanādayopi niddhāritā, niddhāretvā vattabbāti atthoti. Vitthāro vibhaṅgavāre (netti. 23) āgamissati.

They have one common characteristic, hence they are called 'single-characteristic' or 'shared-characteristic,' and are ascertained through association, similar function, similar cause, similar result, or similar object, even if not explicitly stated. How so? In passages like, 'Diverse bodies, diverse perceptions (D. III, 341, 357, 359; A. IX, 24), by not attending to diverse perceptions,' the states accompanied by perception are ascertained through association. In statements like, 'Giving binds friends (S. I, 246; Sn. 189),' similar function is ascertained, and kind speech and beneficial conduct, which have a similar purpose, are also ascertained. In phrases such as, 'Contact conditions feeling (M. III, 126; S. II, 1; Mhv. 1; Vibh. 225; Ud. 1; Netti. 24),' perception and other states are also ascertained through their similar cause. In teachings like, 'Ignorance conditions formations (M. III, 126; S. II, 1; Mhv. 1; Vibh. 225; Ud. 1; Netti. 24),' craving, clinging, and other states are also ascertained through their similar result. In passages like, 'One delights in form, takes pleasure in it, and lust arises dependent on it (Paṭṭhā. 1.1.424),' the associated feelings and other states are also ascertained through their similar object. The meaning is that they should be spoken of after being ascertained. The detailed explanation will appear in the section on analysis (Netti. 23).

Lakkhaṇo hāro niddiṭṭho, amhehi ca ñāto, “katamo catubyūho hāro”ti pucchitabbattā –

The method of characteristic has been expounded and is known by us. Since the question should be asked, 'What is the method of the fourfold array?'

6.

6.

“Neruttamadhippāyo[V 0.0175], byañjanamatha desanānidānañca;

Pubbāparānusandhī, eso hāro catubyūho”ti. –

Etymology, intention, expression, and the occasion of the teaching; and the connection of what precedes and follows: this method is the fourfold array.

Gāthā vuttā. Tattha neruttaṃ suttapadanibbacanañca buddhānaṃ tassa tassa suttassa desakānaṃ, sāvakānaṃ vā adhippāyo ca atthabyañjanena byañjanamukhena desanānidānañca pubbāparena anusandhi ca ete niruttādayo yena saṃvaṇṇanāvisesena vibhāvīyanti, eso saṃvaṇṇanāviseso “catubyūho hāro”ti niddiṭṭho. Desanāpavattinimittaṃ desakassa ajjhāsayādi desanānidānaṃ nāma. Catubyūhahārassa bahuvisayattā vibhaṅge (netti. 25 ādayo) lakkhaṇasampattiṃ katvā kathayissāma.

The verses have been spoken. Therein, etymology, which is the analysis of sutta passages; the intention of the Buddhas or their disciples who taught each sutta; the expression, by way of its meaning and phrasing; the occasion of the teaching; and the connection with what precedes and follows—these, etymology and so forth, are elucidated by a specific mode of elucidation. That specific mode of elucidation is designated as 'the method of the fourfold array.' The occasion of the teaching is the inclination of the teacher and so forth, which is the cause for the teaching to proceed. Due to the extensive scope of the method of the fourfold array, we will explain it by establishing its characteristics in the Vibhaṅga (Netti. 25 onwards).

Catubyūhahāraniddeso niddiṭṭho, amhehi ca ñāto, “katamo āvaṭṭahāraniddeso”ti pucchitabbattā –

The exposition of the method of the fourfold array has been expounded and is known by us. Since the question should be asked, 'What is the exposition of the method of turning?'

7.

7.

“Ekamhi padaṭṭhāne, pariyesati sesakaṃ padaṭṭhānaṃ;

Āvaṭṭati paṭipakkhe, āvaṭṭo nāma so hāro”ti. –

In one proximate cause, one seeks the remaining proximate cause; it turns towards the opposite—that method is called turning.

Gāthā vuttā. Tattha parakkamadhātuādīnaṃ padaṭṭhāne ekamhi ārambhadhātuādike desanāruḷhe sati visabhāgatāya vā sesakaṃ padaṭṭhānaṃ pariyesati[M 0.0034], desanāya sarūpato aggahaṇena vā sesakaṃ padaṭṭhānaṃ pariyesati, yena saṃvaṇṇanāvisesena pariyesitvā yojento desanaṃ pamādādīnaṃ padaṭṭhānabhūte kosajjādike paṭipakkhe āvaṭṭati āvaṭṭāpeti, so saṃvaṇṇanāviseso “āvaṭṭo hāro nāmā”ti niddiṭṭhoti atthayojanā.

The verses have been spoken. Therein, when the teaching has arisen regarding one proximate cause, such as the element of initiative, among the proximate causes of the element of effort and so forth, one seeks the remaining proximate cause due to dissimilarity, or one seeks the remaining proximate cause due to not grasping the teaching in its true form. By whatever specific mode of elucidation, having sought and applied it, one turns or causes the teaching to turn towards the opposite, such as sloth and the like, which are the proximate causes of negligence and so forth. That specific mode of elucidation is designated as 'the method called turning.' Such is the connection of the meaning.

“Paṭipakkhe”ti idaṃ nidassanamattaṃ, sesepi sabhāge āvaṭṭanato. Na hi ārambhadhātuādike desanāruḷhe sati tappaṭipakkhe kosajjādikeyeva desanaṃ āvaṭṭeti, atha kho avasesavīriyārambhādikepi desanaṃ āvaṭṭetīti.

The word 'opposite' here is merely an example, since it also turns towards similar instances. For when the teaching has arisen regarding the element of initiative and so forth, it does not turn the teaching only towards its opposite, such as sloth and so forth, but also turns the teaching towards the remaining qualities like energy and effort and so forth.

Āvaṭṭahāraniddeso niddiṭṭho, amhehi ca ñāto, “katamo vibhattihāraniddeso”ti pucchitabbattā –

The exposition of the method of turning has been expounded and is known by us. Since the question should be asked, 'What is the exposition of the method of classification?'

8.

8.

“Dhammañca [V 0.0176] padaṭṭhānaṃ, bhūmiñca vibhajate ayaṃ hāro.

This method classifies the Dhamma, the proximate cause, and the ground.

Sādhāraṇe asādhāraṇe ca neyyo vibhattī”ti. –

In the common and the uncommon, the classification should be understood.

Gāthā vuttā. Tattha kusalādivasena anekavidhaṃ sabhāvadhammañca dānasīlādipadaṭṭhānañca “dassanabhūmi bhāvanābhūmī”ti evamādikaṃ bhūmiñca sādhāraṇe ca asādhāraṇe ca yena saṃvaṇṇanāvisesena vibhajate, so saṃvaṇṇanāviseso “vibhatti hāro”ti neyyoti atthayojanā.

The verse has been spoken. Herein, the various kinds of natural states, such as the wholesome and so on; the proximate causes, such as generosity and virtue; as well as the grounds, such as 'the ground of seeing and the ground of development,' and so forth, are classified in terms of the common and the uncommon by a specific mode of elucidation. That specific mode of elucidation is to be understood as 'the method of classification.' Such is the connection of the meaning.

“Imasmiṃ sutte vuttā kusalā vāsanābhāgiyā, imasmiṃ sutte vuttā kusalā nibbedhabhāgiyā”tyādinā, “imasmiṃ sutte vuttā akusalā kilesabhāgiyā”tyādinā dhammañca, “idaṃ sīlaṃ imassa mahaggatavisesassa padaṭṭhānaṃ, idaṃ sīlaṃ idaṃ jhānaṃ imassa lokuttarassa padaṭṭhāna”ntyādinā padaṭṭhānañca, “dassanapahātabbassa puthujjano bhūmi, bhāvanāpahātabbassa sotāpannādayo bhūmi”tyādinā bhūmiñca, “kāmarāgabyāpādā puthujjanasotāpannānaṃ sādhāraṇā”tyādinā sādhāraṇe ca, “kāmarāgabyāpādā anāgāmiarahantānaṃ asādhāraṇā”tyādinā asādhāraṇe ca yena vibhajati, so vibhatti hāro nāmātiādinā (netti. 33-34) vitthāretvā vibhajanākāro gahetabbo.

"In this discourse, wholesome qualities conducive to wholesome tendencies are spoken of; in this discourse, wholesome qualities conducive to penetration are spoken of," and so on; "In this discourse, unwholesome qualities connected with defilements are spoken of," and so on—this is the Dhamma. "This virtue is the proximate cause for this exalted distinction; this virtue, this meditation, is the proximate cause for this supramundane state," and so on—this is the proximate cause. "The ordinary person is the ground for what is to be abandoned by seeing; stream-enterers and so on are the ground for what is to be abandoned by development," and so on—this is the ground. "Sensual desire and ill will are common to ordinary persons and stream-enterers," and so on—this is the common. "Sensual desire and ill will are not common to non-returners and arahants," and so on—this is the uncommon. The method by which one classifies in this way is called the 'method of classification,' and so on (Netti. 33-34). The mode of classification should be understood in detail.

Vibhattihāraniddeso [M 0.0035] niddiṭṭho, amhehi ca ñāto, “katamo parivattanahāraniddeso”ti pucchitabbattā –

The exposition of the method of classification has been explained, and it is known to us; since the question must be asked, 'What is the exposition of the method of turning about?'

9.

9.

“Kusalākusale dhamme, niddiṭṭhe bhāvite pahīne ca.

Wholesome and unwholesome states, designated, developed, and abandoned.

Parivattati paṭipakkhe, hāro parivattano nāmā”ti. –

It turns about the opposing side; thus, the method is called 'turning about'.

Gāthā vuttā. Tattha sutte bhāvite bhāvitabbe kusale anavajjadhamme niddiṭṭhe kathite, saṃvaṇṇite vā pahīne pahātabbe akusale sāvajjadhamme niddiṭṭhe kathite, saṃvaṇṇite vā tesaṃ dhammānaṃ paṭipakkhe viparītadhamme yena saṃvaṇṇanāvisesena parivattati parivatteti, so saṃvaṇṇanāviseso “parivattano hāro nāmā”ti veditabboti atthayojanā.

The verse has been spoken. Therein, when in a sutta wholesome, blameless states that are developed or to be developed have been indicated, spoken of, or described, or when unwholesome, blameworthy states that are abandoned or to be abandoned have been indicated, spoken of, or described, the specific mode of elucidation by which one turns, or causes to turn, towards their opposing, contrary states is to be understood as 'the method of turning about.' Such is the connection of the meaning.

“Sammādiṭṭhissa purisapuggalassa micchādiṭṭhi nijjiṇṇā bhavatī”tiādinā ca “yassa vā pāṇātipātā paṭiviratassa pāṇātipāto pahīno”tiādinā ca “bhuñjitabbā kāmā [V 0.0177] …pe… kāmehi veramaṇī tesaṃ adhammo”tiādinā ca paṭipakkhe parivattanabhāvaṃ vibhaṅgavāre (netti. 35 ādayo) vakkhatīti na vitthāritā.

"To a person with right view, wrong view is eliminated," and so on; "For one who abstains from killing living beings, killing is abandoned," and so on; "Pleasures should be enjoyed... abstaining from pleasures is their unrighteousness," and so on. The state of turning about in opposition will be explained in the Vibhaṅga section (Netti. 35 onwards), thus it is not elaborated upon here.

Parivattanahāraniddeso niddiṭṭho, amhehi ca ñāto, “katamo vevacanahāraniddeso”ti pucchitabbattā –

The exposition of the method of turning about has been explained, and it is known to us; since the question must be asked, 'What is the exposition of the method of synonyms?'

10.

10.

“Vevacanāni bahūni tu, sutte vuttāni ekadhammassa.

Many indeed are the synonyms, spoken in the Sutta about one phenomenon.

Yo jānāti suttavidū, vevacano nāma so hāro”ti. –

He who knows the suttas—that method is called 'synonymy'.

Gāthā vuttā. Tattha ekadhammassa padatthassa sutte vuttāni tu vuttāni eva, bahūni tu bahūni eva vevacanāni yena saṃvaṇṇanāvisesena yo suttavidū jānāti, jānitvā ekasmiṃyeva padatthe yojeti, tassa suttaviduno so saṃvaṇṇanāviseso “vevacano nāma hāro”ti niddiṭṭhoti atthayojanā.

The verse has been spoken. Therein, for the meaning of a single term, what is spoken in the sutta is indeed spoken, and many indeed are the synonyms. By whatever distinction of exposition the knower of the suttas understands, and having understood, applies them to just one meaning—for that knower of the suttas, that distinction of exposition is pointed out as 'the manner of synonyms,' thus is the meaning to be construed.
