Ettha ca yo so-saddā asamānatthā ca hontīti “yo suttavidū”ti vatvā “so saṃvaṇṇanāviseso”ti vuttanti. “Bhagavā”ti padassa [M 0.0036] ekasmiṃyeva atthe bhagavati “arahaṃ sammāsambuddho vijjācaraṇasampanno sugato lokavidū anuttaro purisadammasārathi satthā devamanussānaṃ buddho bhagavā, phalanipphattigato vesārajjappatto adhigatapaṭisambhido catuyogavippahīno agatigamanavītivatto uddhaṭasallo niruḷhavaṇo madditakaṇṭako nibbāpitapariyuṭṭhāno bandhanātīto ganthaviniveṭhano ajjhāsayavītivatto bhinnandhakāro cakkhumā lokadhammasamatikkanto anurodhavirodhavippayutto iṭṭhāniṭṭhesu dhammesu asaṅkhepagato bandhanātivatto ṭhapitasaṅgāmo abhikkantataro ukkādharo ālokakaro pajjotakaro tamonudo raṇañjaho aparimāṇavaṇṇo appameyyavaṇṇo asaṅkheyyavaṇṇo ābhaṅkaro pabhaṅkaro dhammobhāsapajjotakaro”ti (netti. 38) evamādīni bahūni vevacanāni yojitāni. Vitthāro vibhaṅgavāre (netti. 37 ādayo) āgamissati.

Here, because the words 'yo' and 'so' have different referents, it is said 'he who knows the suttas' and then 'that distinction of exposition.' To the word 'Bhagavā,' regarding the Blessed One, who has one meaning, many such synonyms are applied: 'Arahant, Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, accomplished in knowledge and conduct, Well-Gone One, Knower of the World, unsurpassed trainer of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, Buddha, Blessed One, one who has attained the fruit, one who has attained confidence, one who has achieved analytical knowledge, one who has abandoned the four yokes, one who has gone beyond wrong destinations, one whose dart has been removed, one whose wound has healed over, one whose thorns have been crushed, one whose fever has been extinguished, one who has transcended bonds, one who has unraveled knots, one who has gone beyond inclinations, one whose darkness has been shattered, one who has vision, one who has transcended worldly conditions, one who is freed from attraction and aversion, one who is not constricted by desirable and undesirable things, one who has gone beyond bonds, one whose battle has been laid aside, a very superior one, a torch-holder, a light-maker, a lamp-maker, a dispeller of darkness, one who has abandoned strife, one of immeasurable praise, one of incalculable praise, one of innumerable praise, a light-maker, a radiance-maker, a maker of the illumination and lamp of the Dhamma.' (Netti. 38) The detailed explanation will come in the Vibhaṅga section (Netti. 37 onwards).

Vevacanahāraniddeso niddiṭṭho, amhehi ca ñāto, “katamo paññattihāraniddeso”ti pucchitabbattā –

The exposition of the manner of synonyms has been set forth, and it is known to us; since the question must be asked, 'What is the exposition of the manner of designation?'

11.

11.

“Ekaṃ [V 0.0178] bhagavā dhammaṃ, paññattīhi vividhāhi deseti.

The Blessed One teaches one Dhamma with various designations.

So ākāro ñeyyo, paññattī nāma so hāro”ti. –

That mode is to be known; that manner is called 'designation'.

Gāthā vuttā. Tattha bhagavā ekaṃ khandhādidhammaṃ vividhāhi nikkhepappabhavapaññattādīhi paññattīhi yena paññāpetabbākārena deseti, so paññāpetabbākāro yena saṃvaṇṇanāvisesena vibhāvito, so saṃvaṇṇanāviseso “paññatti hāro nāmā”ti ñeyyoti atthayojanā.

The verse has been spoken. Therein, the Blessed One teaches a single phenomenon such as the aggregates with various designations such as designation by way of assigning and by way of origin. By whatever mode of designation he teaches, that mode of designation, by whatever distinction of exposition it is elucidated, that distinction of exposition is to be known as 'the manner of designation,' thus is the meaning to be construed.

Tattha vividhāhi paññattīhi nikkhepapaññattipabhavapaññattipariññāpaññattipahānapaññatti- bhāvanāpaññattisacchikiriyāpaññattinirodhapaññattinibbidāpaññattīti evamādipaññattīhi ekapadatthasseva paññāpetabbākāravibhāvanālakkhaṇo saṃvaṇṇanāviseso paññatti hāro nāmāti.

Here, with various designations, such as designation by way of assigning, designation by way of origin, designation by way of full understanding, designation by way of abandoning, designation by way of cultivation, designation by way of realization, designation by way of cessation, and designation by way of disenchantment—thus, with designations such as these, the characteristic of elucidating the mode of designation of a single meaning is the distinction of exposition called 'the manner of designation'.

Tattha “idaṃ dukkha”nti ayaṃ paññatti pañcannaṃ khandhānaṃ, channaṃ dhātūnaṃ, aṭṭhārasannaṃ dhātūnaṃ, dvādasannaṃ āyatanānaṃ, dasannaṃ indriyānaṃ nikkhepapaññatti.

Therein, “This is suffering” is a designation for the five aggregates, the six elements, the eighteen elements, the twelve sense bases, and the ten faculties; this is a designation by way of assigning.

“Kabaḷīkāre ce, bhikkhave, āhāre atthi rāgo, atthi nandī, atthi taṇhā, patiṭṭhitaṃ tattha viññāṇaṃ viruḷhaṃ. Yattha patiṭṭhitaṃ viññāṇaṃ viruḷhaṃ, atthi tattha [M 0.0037] nāmarūpassa avakkanti. Yattha atthi nāmarūpassa avakkanti, atthi tattha saṅkhārānaṃ vuddhī”ti (saṃ. ni. 2.64; kathā. 296) evamādi pabhavapaññatti dukkhassa ca samudayassa cāti.

"Monks, if there is passion for nutriment in the form of morsels, if there is delight, if there is craving, consciousness is established there and grows. Where consciousness is established and grows, there is the descent of name-and-form. Where there is the descent of name-and-form, there is the increase of formations." (SN 12.64; Vibh 136) Thus and so on is the designation by way of origin for suffering and its origin.

“Kabaḷīkāre ce, bhikkhave, āhāre natthi rāgo, natthi nandī, natthi taṇhā”ti (saṃ. ni. 2.64; kathā. 296) evamādi pariññāpaññatti dukkhassa, “pahānapaññatti samudayassa, bhāvanāpaññatti maggassa, sacchikiriyāpaññatti nirodhassā”ti ca “nikkhepapaññatti sutamayiyā paññāya, sacchikiriyāpaññatti anaññātaññassāmītindriyassa, pavattanāpaññatti dhammacakkassā”ti evamādivitthāro vibhaṅge (netti. 39 ādayo) āgamissatīti.

"If, monks, there is no passion, no delight, no craving for nutriment in the form of morsels..." (SN 12.64; Vibh 136) — thus and so forth is the designation of full understanding regarding suffering. "The designation of abandoning applies to the origin, the designation of development applies to the path, the designation of realization applies to cessation," and "the designation by way of assigning pertains to wisdom born of learning, the designation of realization pertains to the faculty of 'I shall know what has not yet been known,' the designation of setting in motion pertains to the wheel of Dhamma." Such detailed explanations will come in the Vibhaṅga (Netti. 39 onwards).

Paṇṇattihāraniddeso niddiṭṭho, amhehi ca ñāto, “katamo otaraṇahāraniddeso”ti pucchitabbattā –

The exposition of the manner of designation has been set forth, and it is known to us; since the question must be asked, 'What is the exposition of the manner of descent?'

12.

12.

“Yo [V 0.0179] ca paṭiccuppādo, indriyakhandhā ca dhātuāyatanā.

Whatever is dependent origination, the faculties and aggregates, and the elements and sense bases.

Etehi otarati yo, otaraṇo nāma so hāro”ti. –

That which descends by these—that manner is called 'descent'.

Gāthā vuttā. Tattha yo paṭiccasamuppādo ca ye indriyakhandhā ca yāni dhātuāyatanāni ca yena saṃvaṇṇanāvisesena niddhāritāni, etehi paṭiccasamuppādādindriyakhandhadhātāyatanehi, sutte āgatapadatthamukhena niddhāriyamānehi ca yo saṃvaṇṇanāviseso otarati ogāhati paṭiccasamuppādādike tattha vācakavasena, tattha ñāpakavasena vā anupavisati, so saṃvaṇṇanāviseso otaraṇo hāro nāmāti atthayojanā.

The verse has been spoken. Therein, whatever dependent origination, and whatever faculties and aggregates, and whatever elements and sense bases are determined by whatever distinction of exposition—by these, that is, by dependent origination and so on, faculties and aggregates, elements and sense bases, and by what is determined through the meaning of the words that occur in the Sutta—whatever distinction of exposition descends, penetrates, or enters into dependent origination and so on, whether by way of expression or by way of indication, that distinction of exposition is called 'the manner of descent,' thus is the meaning to be construed.

Tattha indriyakhandhāti indriyāni ca khandhā cāti indriyakhandhā. Dhātuāyatanāti dhātuyo ca āyatanāni ca dhātuāyatanā. Kathaṃ otaraṇo? “Uddhaṃ adho sabbadhi vippamutto”tiādi (netti. 42) pāṭho.

Here, 'faculties-and-aggregates' means faculties and aggregates; thus, 'faculties-and-aggregates.' 'Elements-and-sense-bases' means elements and sense bases; thus, 'elements-and-sense-bases.' How is it the manner of descent? It is the passage 'Released above, below, everywhere' (Netti. 42) and so on.

Uddhanti rūpadhātu ca arūpadhātu ca. Adhoti kāmadhātu. Sabbadhi vippamuttoti tedhātuke ayaṃ asekkhāvimutti. Tāniyeva asekkhāni pañcindriyāni, ayaṃ indriyehi otaraṇā.

'Above' means the form realm and the formless realm. 'Below' means the desire realm. 'Released everywhere' means this is the liberation of the non-trainee in the triple world. These very five faculties of the non-trainee—this is descent by way of the faculties.

Tāniyeva [M 0.0038] asekkhāni pañcindriyāni vijjā, vijjuppādā avijjānirodho…pe… dukkhakkhandhassa nirodho hoti, ayaṃ paṭiccasamuppādehi otaraṇā.

These very five faculties of the non-trainee are knowledge; from the arising of knowledge comes the cessation of ignorance... and so on... there is the cessation of this whole mass of suffering. This is descent by way of dependent origination.

Tāniyeva asekkhāni pañcindriyāni tīhi khandhehi saṅgahitāni sīlakkhandhena samādhikkhandhena paññākkhandhena, ayaṃ khandhehi otaraṇā.

These very five faculties of the non-trainee are included in the three aggregates: the aggregate of virtue, the aggregate of concentration, and the aggregate of wisdom. This is descent by way of the aggregates.

Tāniyeva asekkhāni pañcindriyāni saṅkhārapariyāpannāni ye saṅkhārā anāsavā, no ca bhavaṅgā, te saṅkhārā dhammadhātusaṅgahitā, ayaṃ dhātūhi otaraṇā.

These very five faculties of the non-trainee are included in formations—those formations that are without taints, and not the life-continuum, are included in the element of phenomena. This is the descent by way of elements.

Sā dhammadhātu dhammāyatanapariyāpannā, yaṃ āyatanaṃ anāsavaṃ, no ca bhavaṅgaṃ, ayaṃ āyatanehi otaraṇāti evamādīhi vibhaṅge (netti. 42 ādayo) āgamissatīti.

That element of phenomena is included in the sense base of phenomena, which is the sense base that is without taints, and not the life-continuum. This is the descent by way of the sense bases. Such detailed explanations will come in the Vibhaṅga (Netti. 42 onwards).

Otaraṇahāraniddeso [V 0.0180] niddiṭṭho, amhehi ca ñāto, “katamo sodhanahāraniddeso”ti pucchitabbattā –

The exposition of the manner of descent has been set forth, and it is known by us. Because the question should be asked, 'What is the exposition of the manner of purification?'

13.

13.

“Vissajjitamhi pañhe, gāthāyaṃ pucchitā yamārabbha.

When a question has been answered, concerning which a verse was asked,

Suddhāsuddhaparikkhā, hāro so sodhano nāmā”ti. –

the examination of pure and impure—that manner is called 'purification'.

Gāthā vuttā. Tattha tissaṃ gāthāyaṃ āruḷhe pañhe ñātumicchite atthe bhagavatā vissajjanagāthāyaṃ vissajjitamhi yaṃ suttatthaṃ ārabbha adhikicca sā gāthā pucchitā pucchanatthāya ṭhapitā, tassa suttatthassa yena saṃvaṇṇanāvisesena suddhāsuddhaparikkhā vicāraṇā bhave, so saṃvaṇṇanāviseso sodhano hāro nāmāti atthayojanā.

The verse has been spoken. Therein, when a question that arose in a verse, the meaning of which was desired to be known, was answered by the Blessed One in an answering verse—concerning that sutta-meaning for which that verse was asked and established for the purpose of questioning, the distinction of exposition by which an examination and analysis of its purity and impurity occurs—that distinction of exposition is called 'the manner of purification.' Thus is the meaning to be construed.

Kathaṃ? “Avijjāya nivuto loko”ti padaṃ sodhitaṃ, ārambho na sodhito. “Vivicchā pamādā nappakāsatī”ti padaṃ sodhitaṃ, ārambho na sodhito. “Jappābhilepanaṃ brūmī”ti padaṃ sodhitaṃ, ārambho na sodhito. “Dukkhamassa mahabbhaya”nti padañca sodhitaṃ, ārambho ca sodhitoti. Evaṃ padādīnaṃ sodhitāsodhitabhāvavicāro hāro sodhano nāma. Vitthārato pana vibhaṅge (netti. 45 ādayo) āgamissatīti.

How? The phrase 'The world is shrouded by ignorance' has been purified, but its commencement has not been purified. The phrase 'Through heedlessness, it does not shine forth from perplexity' has been purified, but its commencement has not been purified. The phrase 'I call craving an ointment' has been purified, but its commencement has not been purified. And the phrase 'Suffering is its great fear' has been purified, and its commencement has also been purified. Thus, the consideration of whether phrases and so on have been purified or not is called the mode of purification. But a detailed explanation will be found in the Vibhaṅga (beginning at Netti. 45).

Sodhanahāraniddeso [M 0.0039] niddiṭṭho, amhehi ca ñāto, “katamo adhiṭṭhānahāraniddeso”ti pucchitabbattā –

The exposition of the mode of purification has been set forth, and it is known by us. Because the question should be asked, 'What is the exposition of the mode of determination?'

14.

14.

“Ekattatāya dhammā, yepi ca vemattatāya niddiṭṭhā.

Phenomena by way of unity, and also those that are set forth by way of diversity.

Te na vikappayitabbā, eso hāro adhiṭṭhāno”ti. –

They should not be conceptually proliferated; this is the mode of determination.

Gāthā vuttā. Tattha ye dukkhasaccādayo dhammā ekattatāya sāmaññenapi ca vemattatāya visesenapi niddiṭṭhā, yena saṃvaṇṇanāvisesena niddiṭṭhā dukkhasaccādayo dhammā na vikappayitabbā sāmaññavisesakappanāya vohārabhāvena anavaṭṭhānato, kāladisāvisesādīnaṃ viya apekkhāsiddhito ca, eso saṃvaṇṇanāviseso adhiṭṭhāno hāroti atthayojanā.

The verses were spoken. Herein, those phenomena such as the truths of suffering and so forth, which are set forth by way of unity as generality and by way of diversity as particularity—those phenomena such as the truths of suffering and so forth, set forth by that particular mode of exposition, should not be conceptually proliferated by conceiving of generality and particularity, because of their instability as conventional expressions, and because they are established by dependence, like distinctions of time, direction, and so forth. That particular mode of exposition is called the mode of determination: such is the connection of meaning.

Tattha [V 0.0181] ekattatāyāti ekassa samānassa bhāvo ekattaṃ, ekattameva ekattatā, tāya. Ekasaddo cettha samānatthavācako, na saṅkhyāvācakoti. Vemattatāyāti visiṭṭhā mattā vimattā, vimattā eva vemattaṃ, vemattassa bhāvo vemattatā, tāya. Yathā hi “ajja sve”ti vuccamānā kālavisesā anavaṭṭhitā bhavanti, “purimā disā, pacchimā disā”ti vuccamānā disāvisesā, evaṃ sāmaññavisesā ca atthassa sabhāvāti. Tathā hi “idaṃ dukkha”nti vuccamānaṃ jātiādiṃ apekkhāya sāmaññaṃ samānampi saccāpekkhāya viseso hoti. Esa nayo samudayasaccādīsupīti. “Dukkha”nti ekattatā. “Jāti dukkhā, jarā dukkhā, maraṇaṃ dukkha”nti evamādi vemattatā. “Dukkhasamudayo”ti ekattatā, “taṇhā ponobhavikā nandīrāgasahagatā”ti evamādi vemattatāti evamādi vitthāro vibhaṅge (netti. 46 ādayo) āgamissatīti.

Herein, `ekattatāya` (by way of unity) is explained: the state of being one or the same is `ekattaṃ` (oneness); oneness itself is `ekattatā` (the state of unity). In this context, the word `eka` conveys sameness, not a numerical count. `Vemattatāya` (by way of diversity) is explained: a distinguished measure is `vimattā`; `vimattā` itself is `vemattaṃ`; the state of `vemattaṃ` is `vemattatā` (the state of diversity). For just as distinctions of time, when spoken of as 'today' or 'tomorrow', are unfixed, and distinctions of direction, when spoken of as 'the eastern direction' or 'the western direction', so too are generality and particularity the inherent nature of the meaning. Thus, when 'this is suffering' is stated, with reference to birth and so on, it is a generality; yet even though it is common, with reference to the truth, it becomes a particularity. This same principle applies to the truth of the origin of suffering and the others. 'Suffering' is unity. 'Birth is suffering, aging is suffering, death is suffering,' and so on—this is diversity. 'The origin of suffering' is unity; 'craving that leads to renewed existence, accompanied by delight and lust,' and so on—this is diversity. A more detailed account will be found in the Vibhaṅga (Netti. 46 onwards).

Adhiṭṭhānahāraniddeso niddiṭṭho, amhehi ca ñāto, “katamo parikkhārahāraniddeso”ti pucchitabbattā –

The exposition of the mode of determination has been set forth, and it is known by us. Because the question should be asked, 'What is the exposition of the mode of requisites?'

15.

15.

“Ye dhammā yaṃ dhammaṃ, janayantippaccayā paramparato.

Those phenomena which generate a certain phenomenon by way of conditions, successively.

Hetumavakaḍḍhayitvā, eso hāro parikkhāro”ti. –

Having drawn out the cause, this is the mode of requisites.

Gāthā vuttā. Tattha avijjādikā ye paccayadhammā saṅkhārādikaṃ yaṃ phaladhammaṃ paccayā sahajātapaccayena paramparato paramparapaccayabhāvena janayanti, tassa saṅkhārādiphalassa paccayaṃ parikkhārabhūtaṃ purimuppannaṃ avijjādikaṃ asādhāraṇaṃ [M 0.0040] janakaṃ hetuṃ, ayonisomanasikārādikaṃ sādhāraṇaṃ paccayahetuñca avakaḍḍhayitvā suttato niddhāretvā yo saṃvaṇṇanāviseso parikkhārasaṃvaṇṇanābhāvena pavatto, eso saṃvaṇṇanāviseso parikkhāro hāro nāmāti atthayojanā. Avijjādayo hi avijjādīnaṃ asādhāraṇahetū bhavanti, ayonisomanasikārādayo sādhāraṇapaccayā. Tenāha – “asādhāraṇalakkhaṇo hetu, sādhāraṇalakkhaṇo paccayo”ti, “avijjā avijjāya hetu, ayonisomanasikāro paccayo”tiādikaṃ (netti. 49) vibhaṅgavacanañca.

The verses were spoken. Therein, those conditioning phenomena such as ignorance and so forth, which generate a certain resultant phenomenon such as formations and so forth, by way of conditions, by way of the co-nascence condition, and successively by way of the successive condition—having drawn out and determined from the sutta the pre-arisen ignorance and so forth, which is the unique generative root-cause, being a requisite, and unwise attention and so forth, which is the common causal condition—that particular mode of exposition which proceeds by way of describing the requisites, that particular mode of exposition is called the mode of requisites: such is the connection of meaning. For ignorance and so forth are unique root-causes for ignorance and so forth, and unwise attention and so forth are common conditions. Therefore, it is said: 'The characteristic of the root-cause is uniqueness, the characteristic of the condition is commonality,' and 'ignorance is the root-cause of ignorance, unwise attention is the condition,' etc., as well as the statements in the Vibhaṅga (Netti. 49).

Parikkhārahāraniddeso niddiṭṭho, amhehi ca ñāto, “katamo samāropanahāraniddeso”ti pucchitabbattā –

The exposition of the mode of requisites has been set forth, and it is known by us. Because the question should be asked, 'What is the exposition of the mode of superimposition?'

16.

16.

“Ye [V 0.0182] dhammā yaṃmūlā, ye cekatthā pakāsitā muninā.

Those phenomena which have a certain root, and those that are declared by the Sage as having one meaning.

Te samāropayitabbā, esa samāropano hāro”ti. –

They should be superimposed; this is the mode of superimposition.

Gāthā vuttā. Tattha ye sīlādayo dhammā yaṃmūlā yesaṃ samādhiādīnaṃ mūlā, te sīlādayo dhammā tesaṃ samādhiādīnaṃ padaṭṭhānabhāvena saṃvaṇṇanāvisesena samāropayitabbā, ye ca rāgavirāgacetovimuttisekkhaphalakāmadhātusamatikkamanādisaddā anāgāmiphalatthatāya ekatthā samānatthāti buddhamuninā pakāsitā, te rāga…pe… tikkamanādisaddā aññamaññavevacanabhāvena samāropayitabbā, eso saṃvaṇṇanāviseso samāropano hāro nāmāti atthayojanā.

The verses were spoken. Herein, those qualities such as virtue and so forth, which are the roots, the roots of concentration and so forth—those qualities such as virtue and so forth should be superimposed by way of a particular mode of exposition as the proximate cause for those concentrations and so forth. And those terms such as 'mind-liberation through dispassion from passion,' 'the fruit of a trainee,' 'transcendence of the sense-sphere,' and so forth, which are declared by the Buddha, the Sage, as having one meaning, as being synonymous with the state of the non-returner's fruit—those terms such as 'passion'… up to 'transcendence' should be superimposed upon one another by way of being synonyms. That particular mode of exposition is called the mode of superimposition: such is the connection of meaning.

Ettha ca sīlādikkhandhattayassa pariyāyantaravibhāvanāpāripūrī kathitā, bhāvanāpāripūrī ca pahātabbassa pahānena hotīti bhāvanāsamāropanapahānasamāropanāpi dassitāti catubbidho samāropano padaṭṭhānasamāropano, vevacanasamāropano, bhāvanāsamāropano, pahānasamāropanoti.

Here, the complete exposition of the threefold aggregate of virtue and so forth by way of alternative classifications has been stated, and the fulfillment of development. And since the fulfillment of development occurs through the abandonment of what should be abandoned, the superimposition of development and the superimposition of abandonment have also been shown. Thus, the fourfold superimposition is: the superimposition of the proximate cause, the superimposition of synonyms, the superimposition of development, and the superimposition of abandonment.

Tattha kāyikasucaritaṃ, vācasikasucaritañca sīlakkhandho, manosucarite anabhijjhā, abyāpādo ca samādhikkhandho, sammādiṭṭhi paññākkhandho. Sīlakkhandho samādhikkhandhassa padaṭṭhānaṃ, samādhikkhandho paññākkhandhassa padaṭṭhānaṃ. Sīlakkhandho, samādhikkhandho ca samathassa padaṭṭhānaṃ, paññākkhandho [M 0.0041] vipassanāya padaṭṭhānaṃ. Samatho rāgavirāgacetovimuttiyā padaṭṭhānaṃ, vipassanā avijjāvirāgapaññāvimuttiyā padaṭṭhānanti evamādi padaṭṭhānasamāropano. Rāgavirāgā cetovimutti sekkhaphalaṃ, avijjāvirāgā paññāvimutti asekkhaphalaṃ, idaṃ vevacanaṃ. Rāgavirāgā cetovimutti anāgāmiphalaṃ, avijjāvirāgā paññāvimutti aggaphalaṃ arahattaṃ, idaṃ vevacanaṃ. Rāgavirāgā cetovimutti kāmadhātusamatikkamanaṃ, avijjāvirāgā cetovimutti tedhātusamatikkamanaṃ, idaṃ vevacanaṃ. Paññindriyaṃ, paññābalaṃ, adhipaññāsikkhā, paññākkhandhoti evamādi vevacananti evamādi vevacanasamāropano. Kāye kāyānupassino viharato cattāro satipaṭṭhānā bhāvanāpāripūriṃ gacchanti, catūsu satipaṭṭhānesu bhāviyamānesu cattāro sammappadhānā bhāvanāpāripūriṃ gacchanti, catūsu sammappadhānesu bhāviyamānesu cattāro iddhipādā bhāvanāpāripūriṃ gacchantīti evamādi bhāvanāsamāropano. Kāye kāyānupassī viharanto asubhe “subha”nti vipallāsaṃ pajahati, kabaḷīkāro cassa āhāro pariññaṃ gacchati, kāmupādānena ca anupādāno bhavati, kāmayogena ca visaṃyutto bhavati, abhijjhākāyaganthena ca vippayujjati, kāmāsavena ca anāsavo bhavati, kāmoghañca uttiṇṇo bhavati, rāgasallena ca visallo bhavati, rūpūpikā cassa viññāṇaṭṭhiti pariññaṃ gacchati[V 0.0183], rūpadhātuyaṃ cassa rāgo pahīno bhavati, na ca chandāgatiṃ gacchati, vedanāsūti evamādi pahānasamāropanoti evamādi samāropano hāro niyuttoti.

Herein, bodily good conduct and verbal good conduct are the aggregate of virtue; in mental good conduct, non-covetousness and non-ill will are the aggregate of concentration, and right view is the aggregate of wisdom. The aggregate of virtue is the proximate cause for the aggregate of concentration; the aggregate of concentration is the proximate cause for the aggregate of wisdom. The aggregate of virtue and the aggregate of concentration are the proximate cause for serenity; the aggregate of wisdom is the proximate cause for insight. Serenity is the proximate cause for the liberation of mind through dispassion for lust; insight is the proximate cause for the liberation by wisdom through dispassion for ignorance—thus is the superimposition of the proximate cause. The liberation of mind through dispassion for lust is the fruit of a trainee; the liberation by wisdom through dispassion for ignorance is the fruit of one beyond training—this is a synonym. The liberation of mind through dispassion for lust is the fruit of non-returning; the liberation by wisdom through dispassion for ignorance is the supreme fruit, arahantship—this is a synonym. The liberation of mind through dispassion for lust is the transcending of the sense-sphere realm; the liberation by wisdom through dispassion for ignorance is the transcending of the three realms—this is a synonym. The faculty of wisdom, the power of wisdom, the training in higher wisdom, and the aggregate of wisdom—thus are the synonyms—thus is the superimposition of synonyms. For one who dwells contemplating the body in the body, the four establishments of mindfulness go to the fulfillment of development. When the four establishments of mindfulness are developed, the four right strivings go to the fulfillment of development. When the four right strivings are developed, the four bases of spiritual power go to the fulfillment of development—thus is the superimposition of development. One who dwells contemplating the body in the body abandons the perversion of perceiving the unattractive as attractive. And for them, material food comes to be fully understood. And they are without the clinging to sensual pleasures. And they are disjoined from the yoke of sensuality. And they are dissociated from the bodily tie of covetousness. And they are untainted by the taint of sensuality. And they have crossed over the flood of sensuality. And they are without the dart of lust. And for them, the station of consciousness based on form comes to be fully understood. And for them, lust for the form realm is abandoned. And they do not fall into a course of partiality due to desire. And so on for feelings—thus is the superimposition of abandonment. Thus is the mode of superimposition applied.

Iti sattibalānurūpā racitā.

Thus, it is composed in accordance with my ability and strength.

Soḷasahāraniddesavibhāvanā niṭṭhitā.

The Elucidation of the Exposition of the Sixteen Modes is complete.

Nayaniddesavibhāvanā

The Elucidation of the Exposition of the Methods

17. Hāraniddesā niddiṭṭhā, amhehi ca ñātā, “katame nayaniddesā”ti pucchitabbattā “taṇhañcā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Atha vā evaṃ uddesakkameneva hāre niddisitvā idāni naye niddisituṃ “taṇhañcā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha yo saṃvaṇṇanāviseso sutte āgataṃ taṇhañca avijjañca atthato niddhāraṇavasena gahitaṃ taṇhañca avijjañca saṃkilesapakkhaṃ neti, sutte āgatena [M 0.0042] samathena, sutte āgatāya vipassanāya atthato niddhāraṇavasena vā gahitena samathena, gahitāya vipassanāya vodānapakkhaṃ neti, nayanto ca saccehi yojetvā neti, ayaṃ saṃvaṇṇanāviseso so nandiyāvaṭṭo nayo nāmāti atthayojanā.

17. The expositions of the Modes have been set forth and understood by us. Since the question, 'What are the expositions of the Methods?' is to be asked, 'Craving and...' and so on is stated. Alternatively, having thus set forth the Modes by way of enumeration, now, in order to set forth the Methods, 'Craving and...' and so on is stated. Herein, the special explanation is this: that which leads craving and ignorance—which have come in the Sutta and are grasped by way of determining their meaning—to the side of defilement; and which leads serenity and insight—which have come in the Sutta, or which are grasped by way of determining their meaning—to the side of purification; and which, in leading, yokes them with the truths—this special explanation is called the Nandiyāvaṭṭa method. Such is the application of the meaning.

Ettha ca atthanayassa bhūmi, saṃvaṇṇanā ca gāthāyaṃ “nayo”ti vuttā, tasmā “saṃvaṇṇanāviseso”ti vuttaṃ. Na hi atthanayo saṃvaṇṇanā, catusaccapaṭivedhassa anurūpo pubbabhāge anugāhaṇanayo atthanayova. Tassa pana atthanayassa yā saṃvaṇṇanā ugghaṭitaññuādīnaṃ vasena taṇhādimukhena nayabhūmiracanā pavattā, tassa saṃvaṇṇanāva nayavohāro katoti vitthārato hārasampāte (netti. 78-79) āgamissati.

Here, the ground of the method of meaning and the explanation are called 'method' in the verse; therefore, it is said to be 'a special explanation.' For the method of meaning is not the explanation; the method of preliminary support, suitable for the penetration of the four truths, is indeed the method of meaning. However, the explanation of that method of meaning, which proceeds through the composition of the ground of method by way of craving and so on, in the manner of the quick-witted and others—that very explanation is termed the application of method. This will be discussed in detail in the Compendium of Modes (Netti. 78-79).

Nandiyāvaṭṭanayaniddeso niddiṭṭho, amhehi ca ñāto, “katamo tipukkhalanayaniddeso”ti pucchitabbattā –

The exposition of the Nandiyāvaṭṭa method has been set forth and understood by us. Since the question to be asked is, 'What is the exposition of the Tipukkhalā method?'—

18.

18.

“Yo akusale samūlehi, neti kusale ca kusalamūlehi.

“Whoever leads the unwholesome with their roots, and the wholesome with wholesome roots;

Bhūtaṃ tathaṃ avitathaṃ, tipukkhalaṃ taṃ nayaṃ āhū”ti. –

That method which is real, true, and unerring, they call Tipukkhalā.”—

Gāthā vuttā. Tattha yo saṃvaṇṇanāviseso akusale samūlehi attano akusalassa tīhi lobhādīhi [V 0.0184] mūlehi saṃkilesapakkhaṃ neti, kusale ca kusalamūlehi tīhi alobhādīhi vodānapakkhaṃ neti, nayanto ca bhūtaṃ kusalākusalaṃ neti, na abhūtaṃ māyāmarīciādayo viya, tathaṃ kusalākusalaṃ neti, na ghaṭādayo viya sammutisaccamattaṃ, avitathaṃ kusalākusalaṃ neti, na vitathaṃ. Kusalākusalānaṃ sabhāvato vijjamānattā bhūtā paramatthasaccattā tathā, akusalassa iṭṭhavipākatābhāvato, kusalassa ca aniṭṭhavipākatābhāvato vipāke sati avisaṃvādakattā avitathā bhavanti, kusalākusalā hi etesaṃ tiṇṇaṃ “bhūtaṃ, tathaṃ, avitatha”nti padānaṃ kusalākusalavisesanatā daṭṭhabbā.

The verse has been spoken. Herein, the special explanation is this: that which leads the unwholesome to the side of defilement with its own three unwholesome roots, namely greed and so on; and leads the wholesome to the side of purification with its three wholesome roots, namely non-greed and so on; and in leading, it leads the wholesome and unwholesome, which are real, not unreal like illusions or mirages; it leads the wholesome and unwholesome, which are true, not merely conventional truth like pots and so on; it leads the wholesome and unwholesome, which are unerring, not erroneous. Because the wholesome and unwholesome exist by their own nature, they are real; because they are ultimate truth, they are true; and because the unwholesome does not have a desirable result and the wholesome does not have an undesirable result, they are unerring when there is a result, due to their non-deceptive nature. Indeed, the wholesome and unwholesome should be understood as qualifying these three terms: 'real,' 'true,' and 'unerring.'

Atha vā akusalamūlehi akusalāni, kusalamūlehi ca kusalāni nayanto ayaṃ nayo bhūtaṃ tathaṃ avitathaṃ neti cattāri saccāni niddhāretvā [M 0.0043] yojeti. Dukkhādīni hi bādhakādibhāvato aññathābhāvābhāvena bhūtāni, saccasabhāvattā tathāni, avisaṃvādanato avitathāni. Vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā – “cattārimāni, bhikkhave, tathāni avitathāni anaññathānī”ti saṃ. ni. 5.1090; paṭi. ma. 2.8). Akusalādisuttatthassa catusaccayojanamukhena nayanalakkhaṇaṃ taṃ saṃvaṇṇanāvisesaṃ tipukkhalaṃ nayanti āhūti atthayojanā.

Alternatively, this method, in leading from unwholesome roots to unwholesome states and from wholesome roots to wholesome states, leads to the four truths, which are real, true, and unerring, by determining and yoking them. For suffering and the like are real because of their nature of oppressing and so on, and because of the impossibility of their being otherwise; they are true because of their nature as truths; and they are unerring because they are not deceptive. As the Blessed One has said: 'Bhikkhus, these four are true, unerring, and not otherwise' (SN 56.20). The characteristic of this method is to lead the meaning of a discourse on the unwholesome and so on by way of yoking it with the four truths—this special explanation they call the Tipukkhalā method. Such is the application of the meaning.

Tattha tīhi hetūhi pukkhalo sobhanoti tipukkhalo akusalādiko atthanayo saṃvaṇṇanāvisesoti ṭhānūpacārato tipukkhalanayo nāmāti. Vitthāro pana hārasampāte (netti. 87-88) āgamissati.

Herein, 'one is excellent (pukkhalo) for three reasons' is tipukkhalo. The method of meaning concerning the unwholesome and so on is a special explanation, and by way of figurative usage, it is called the Tipukkhalā method. The detailed explanation, however, will come in the Compendium of Modes (Netti. 87-88).

Tipukkhalanayaniddeso niddiṭṭho, amhehi ca ñāto, “katamo sīhavikkīḷitanayaniddeso”ti pucchitabbattā –

The exposition of the Tipukkhalā method has been set forth and understood by us. Since the question to be asked is, 'What is the exposition of the Sīhavikkīḷita method?'—

19.

19.

“Yo neti vipallāsehi, kilese indriyehi saddhamme.

“Whoever leads defilements by distortions, and the true Dhamma by faculties;

Etaṃ nayaṃ nayavidū, sīhavikkīḷitaṃ āhū”ti. –

This method those skilled in method call the Sīhavikkīḷita.”—

Gāthā vuttā. Tattha yo saṃvaṇṇanāviseso sutte vuttehi vipallāsehi kilese saṃkilesapakkhaṃ neti, sutte vuttehi indriyehi saddhamme vodānapakkhaṃ neti, etaṃ saṃvaṇṇanāvisesaṃ nayavidū saddhammanayakovidā, atthanayakusalā eva vā sīhavikkīḷitaṃ nayanti āhūti atthayojanā.

The verse has been spoken. Herein, the special explanation is this: that which leads defilements to the side of defilement by the distortions mentioned in the Sutta, and leads the true Dhamma to the side of purification by the faculties mentioned in the Sutta—this special explanation, those skilled in method, those expert in the method of the true Dhamma, or those adept in the method of meaning, call the Sīhavikkīḷita method. Such is the application of the meaning.

Tattha vipallāsehīti asubhe subhaṃ, dukkhe sukhaṃ, anicce niccaṃ, anattani attāti catūhi [V 0.0185] vipallāsehi. Indriyehīti saddhādīhi indriyehi. Saddhammeti paṭipattipaṭivedhasaddhamme. Sesamettha vuttanayameva. Vitthāro pana hārasampāte (netti. 86-87) āgamissatīti.

Herein, 'by distortions' means by the four distortions: perceiving the unattractive as attractive, the painful as pleasant, the impermanent as permanent, and what is not-self as self. 'By faculties' means by the faculties beginning with faith. 'The true Dhamma' means the true Dhamma of practice and penetration. The rest here is just as stated in the method. The detailed explanation, however, will come in the Compendium of Modes (Netti. 86-87).

Sīhavikkīḷitanayaniddeso niddiṭṭho, amhehi ca ñāto, “katamo disālocananayaniddeso”ti pucchitabbattā –

The exposition of the Sīhavikkīḷita method has been set forth and understood by us. Since the question to be asked is, 'What is the exposition of the Disālocana method?'—

20.

20.

“Veyyākaraṇesu [M 0.0044] hi ye, kusalākusalā tahiṃ tahiṃ vuttā.

‘For in the explications, whatever wholesome and unwholesome states are stated here and there;

Manasā volokayate, taṃ khu disālocanaṃ āhū”ti. –

one surveys them with the mind—that indeed they call the Surveying of Directions.’

Gāthā vuttā. “Sīhalocanaṃ āhū”ti pāṭho likhito, so pana na therassa pāṭhoti daṭṭhabbo bhinnalakkhaṇattā. Tattha tahiṃ tahiṃ veyyākaraṇesu ye kusalākusalā nayassa disābhūtā dhammā vuttā, te kusalākusale nayassa disābhūtadhamme abahi abbhantaraṃ citte eva yaṃ olokanaṃ karoti, taṃ olokanaṃ khu olokanaṃ eva disālocananti āhūti atthayojanā.

The verse has been spoken. The reading 'Sīhalocanaṃ āhū' is written, but it should be understood that this is not the Elder's reading, because of its different characteristics. Herein, whatever wholesome and unwholesome phenomena are stated in the various explications as being the directions of the method—whatever surveying one does of those wholesome and unwholesome phenomena, which are the directions of the method, within one's own mind and not externally—that very surveying, indeed, they call the Surveying of Directions. Such is the interpretation of the meaning.

Tattha veyyākaraṇesūti tassa tassa atthanayassa yojanatthaṃ katesu suttassa atthavissajjanesu. Kusalāti vodāniyā. Akusalāti saṃkilesikā. Vuttāti suttato niddhāretvā kathitā. Olokayateti te kusalādidhamme citteneva “ayaṃ paṭhamā disā, ayaṃ dutiyā disā”tiādinā tassa tassa nayassa disābhāvena upaparikkhati, vicāretīti attho. Khūti avadhāraṇatthe nipāto, tena disālocananayo koci atthaviseso na hotīti dassetīti.

Here, 'in the explications' means in the expositions of the meaning of the Sutta, which are made for the purpose of connecting with the meaning of each method. 'Wholesome' means purifying. 'Unwholesome' means defiling. 'Stated' means stated after having determined it from the Sutta. 'Surveys' means that one examines those wholesome and other phenomena with the mind itself, investigating them as the directions of that particular method, saying 'this is the first direction, this is the second direction,' and so on; this is the meaning. 'Indeed' (khu) is a particle in the sense of emphasis. By this, it is shown that the Disālocana method is not some special meaning.

21. Disālocananayaniddeso niddiṭṭho. Amhehi ca ñāto. “Katamo aṅkusanayaniddeso”ti pucchitabbattā “oloketvā”tiādigāthā vuttā. Tattha taṃtaṃnayadisābhūte sabbe kusalākusale disālocanena oloketvā ukkhipiya suttato uddharitvā yaṃ samāneti yaṃ samānayanaṃ karoti, ayaṃ samānayanasaṅkhāto nayo aṅkuso nayo nāmāti atthayojanā.

21. The exposition of the Disālocana method has been set forth and understood by us. Since it should be asked, 'What is the exposition of the Aṅkusa method?', the verse beginning with 'having surveyed' was spoken. Herein, having surveyed by the Disālocana method all wholesome and unwholesome phenomena that are the directions of the respective methods, and having lifted them up and extracted them from the Sutta, whatever one brings together, whatever act of bringing together one performs—this method, known as bringing together, is called the Aṅkusa method. Such is the interpretation of the meaning.

Ettha ca aṅkuso nāma hatthīnaṃ icchitaṭṭhānaṃ ānayanakāraṇabhūto vajirādimayo tikkhaggo ujuvaṅkabhūto dabbasambhāraviseso, ayampi nayo aṅkuso viyāti atthena aṅkuso. Etena hi nayena icchitaṃ suttatthaṃ nayatīti. Mukhyato pana aṅke vijjhanaṭṭhāne uddhaṭo asati anto pavisatīti aṅkuso. Aṅkasaddūpapadaupubbaasadhātu apaccayoti. Ayampi nayo kocipi atthaviseso na hotīti.

Here, the term 'aṅkusa' refers to a sharp-pointed, straight or crooked tool made of iron or similar material, a special implement that is the cause for bringing elephants to desired locations. This method is also like an aṅkusa, and thus it is called aṅkusa in meaning. For by this method, one leads to the desired meaning of the Sutta. Primarily, however, it is an `aṅkusa` because when not extracted, it enters inside at the piercing spot (`aṅka`). The word is formed from the root `as` preceded by the prefix `u`, with the word `aṅka` as a pre-verb, and the suffix `a`. This method also is not some special meaning.

Soḷasa [V 0.0186][M 0.0045] hāraniddesā ceva pañca nayaniddesā ca ācariyena niddiṭṭhā. Amhehi ca ñātā, “saṃvaṇṇetabbasutte kiṃ soḷasa hārā paṭhamaṃ yojetabbā, udāhu nayā”ti pucchitabbattā –

The sixteen expositions of the Modes and the five expositions of the Methods have been set forth by the Teacher and understood by us. Since the question should be asked, 'In the Sutta to be explained, should the sixteen Modes be applied first, or the Methods?'—

22.

22.

“Soḷasa hārā paṭhamaṃ, disālocanato disā viloketvā.

‘The sixteen Modes first, having surveyed the directions by the Disālocana method;

Saṅkhipiya aṅkusena hi, nayehi tihi niddise sutta”nti. –

and indeed having summarized by the Aṅkusa, one should explain the Sutta by the three methods.’

Gāthamāha. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana “evaṃ hāre, naye ca niddisitvā idāni nesaṃ yojanakkamaṃ dassento ‘soḷasa hārā paṭhama’ntiādimāhā”ti (netti. aṭṭha. 22) vuttaṃ. Tattha soḷasa hārā byañjanapariyeṭṭhibhāvato saṃvaṇṇetabbasutte saṃvaṇṇanābhāvena paṭhamaṃ yojetabbā, yojentena niddiṭṭhā hārānukkameneva yojetabbā, na uppaṭipāṭiyā. Hārasaṃvaṇṇanānukkamena saṃvaṇṇetabbaṃ paṭhamaṃ saṃvaṇṇetvā pacchā disālocanena oloketvā aṅkusanayena netvā tīhi atthanayehi niddiseti adhippāyo.

He spoke the verse. In the commentary, however, it is said: 'Thus, having set forth the Modes and the Methods, now, showing their order of application, he spoke the verse beginning 'the sixteen Modes first' and so on' (Netti. Aṭṭha. 22). Herein, the sixteen Modes, being concerned with the investigation of the literal meaning, should be applied first in the Sutta to be explained, as they constitute the explanation. When applying them, they should be applied in the order of the indicated Modes, not in reverse order. The intention is that what is to be explained should first be explained in the order of the explanation of the Modes; then, having surveyed by the Disālocana method, and having led by the Aṅkusa method, one should explain by the three methods of meaning.

Iti sattibalānurūpā racitā

Thus, composed in accordance with my ability and strength,

Nayaniddesavibhāvanā niṭṭhitā.

The Elucidation of the Exposition of the Methods is concluded.

Dvādasapadavibhāvanā

The Elucidation of the Twelve Terms

Nettivisayaṃ sāsanavarasaṅkhātaṃ saṃvaṇṇetabbasuttaṃ yesaṃ byañjanapadānaṃ, atthapadānañca vasena “dvādasa padāni sutta”nti saṅgahavāre vuttaṃ, “katamāni tānī”ti pucchitabbattā sarūpato niddisituṃ –

Regarding the discourse to be expounded—the domain of the Netti, known as the supreme teaching—it was said in the summary section that 'the discourse is twelve terms,' by way of terms of expression and terms of meaning. Since it should be asked, 'What are they?', in order to point them out in their essential nature:—

23.

23.

“Akkharaṃ padaṃ byañjanaṃ, nirutti tatheva niddeso.

‘Letter, word, expression, language, and likewise designation.

Ākārachaṭṭhavacanaṃ, ettāva byañjanaṃ sabbaṃ.

Mode is the sixth term; this much is the whole of expression.

24.

24.

Saṅkāsanā pakāsanā, vivaraṇā vibhajanuttānīkammapaññatti.

Manifestation, clarification, exposition, analysis, making plain, and designation.

Etehi chahi padehi, attho kammañca niddiṭṭha”nti. –

By these six terms, both meaning and action are indicated.’

Gāthādvayaṃ [V 0.0187][M 0.0046] vuttaṃ. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana “idāni yesaṃ byañjanapadānaṃ, atthapadānañca vasena ‘dvādasa padāni ‘sutta’nti vuttaṃ, tāni padāni niddisituṃ ‘akkharapada’ntiādimāhā”ti (netti. aṭṭha. 23) vuttaṃ.

These two verses have been stated. However, in the Commentary, it is stated: 'Now, in order to indicate those terms—by way of which, as terms of expression and terms of meaning, it was said 'twelve terms are the discourse'—he spoke the verse beginning with 'letter, word'' (Netti. Aṭṭha. 23).

Tattha kenaṭṭhena akkharanti? Akkharaṭṭhena asañcaraṇaṭṭhena. Akārādivaṇṇo hi akārādito ikārādipariyāyaṃ nakkharati, na sañcarati, na saṅkamati. Tenāha aṭṭhakathāyaṃ “apariyosite pade vaṇṇo akkharaṃ pariyāyavasena akkharaṇato asañcaraṇato”ti (netti. aṭṭha. 23). Apariyosite padeti ca vibhatyantabhāvaṃ appatte dviticatukkharavantesu padesu ekadvitikkharamatteyeva akkharaṃ nāma, pariyosite padaṃyeva, na akkharanti adhippāyo. Padaṃ pana pavesanato atthavasena pariyāyaṃ sañcarantaṃ viya hoti, na evaṃ akārādivaṇṇo avevacanattā. “Mā evaṃ maññasī”tiādīsu vā ekakkharapadā mā-kārādi akkharaṃ nāma, vibhatyantaṃ padaṃ pana padameva hoti.

Here, in what sense is it called `akkhara`? In the sense of being imperishable and in the sense of not moving. For the letter 'a' and so on does not perish, move, or pass over into 'i' and other variations. Therefore, the commentary states: 'In an incomplete word, a letter is an `akkhara` because of its imperishability and non-movement' (Netti. Aṭṭha. 23). The phrase 'in an incomplete word' means that in words of two, three, or four syllables, before they have attained the state of ending in an inflection, only a single, double, or triple syllable is called an `akkhara`, while a complete word is simply a word, not an `akkhara`—this is the intention. A word, however, by virtue of its entry into meaning, as it were, moves by way of meaning, unlike the letter 'a' and so on, which is not an utterance. In phrases like 'mā evaṃ maññasī' ('do not think thus'), the one-syllable word 'mā' and so on is called an `akkhara`, whereas a word with an inflectional ending is simply a word.

Pajjati attho etenāti padaṃ. Taṃ nāmākhyātopasagganipātappabhedena catubbidhaṃ. Tattha dabbapadhānaṃ “phasso vedanā citta”nti evamādikaṃ nāmapadaṃ. Tattha hi dabbamāvibhūtarūpaṃ, kiriyā anāvibhūtarūpā. Kiriyāpadhānaṃ “phusati vedayati vijānātī”ti evamādikaṃ ākhyātapadaṃ nāma. Tattha hi phusanādikiriyā āvibhūtarūpā, dabbamanāvibhūtarūpaṃ. Kiriyāvisesabodhahetubhūtaṃ pa-upa-itievamādikaṃ upasaggapadaṃ nāma. “Cirappavāsiṃ (dha. pa. 219) upavuttha”nti (a. ni. 3.71; su. ni. 405) evamādīsu hi pa-upādisaddā vasanādikiriyāya viyogādivisiṭṭhataṃ dīpenti. Vacanattho pana nāmapadaākhyātapadadvayaṃ upagantvā tassa padadvayassa atthaṃ sajjantīti upasaggāti daṭṭhabbo. Kiriyāya ceva dabbassa ca sarūpavisesapakāsanahetubhūtaṃ “evaṃ, itī”ti evamādikaṃ nipātapadaṃ assapi saṃvaṇṇanāyapi icchitattā, akkharena pana kathaṃ gahitoti ce? Akkharehi suyyamānehi suṇantānaṃ visesavidhānassa katattā padapariyosāne padatthasampaṭipatti hoti. Tasmā akkharenapi atthākāro gahitovāti veditabbo. Tena vuttaṃ – “akkharehi saṅkāseti, padehi pakāseti, akkharehi ca padehi ca ugghaṭetī”ti (netti. 9) ca.

Meaning goes by means of this, thus it is a 'pada' (word). It is of four kinds: noun, verb, prefix, and particle. Among these, the noun-term is predominant in expressing substance, such as 'contact, feeling, consciousness,' and so on. Here, substance is clearly evident, while action is not clearly evident. The verb-term is predominant in expressing action, such as 'touches, feels, knows,' and so on. Here, the action of touching, etc., is clearly evident, while substance is not clearly evident. The prefix-term, such as 'pa-', 'upa-', 'ati-,' etc., serves as the cause for understanding distinctions in action. For example, in phrases like 'cirappavāsiṃ (Dhp. 219)' and 'upavuttha (AN 3.71; Snp. 405),' the prefixes 'pa-' and 'upa-' highlight the specific nature of separation or dwelling in the action of staying, etc. The meaning of a prefix, however, should be understood as joining with both noun and verb terms and connecting to the meaning of those two terms. The particle-term, such as 'evaṃ,' 'iti,' etc., serves as the cause for revealing specific forms of both action and substance. Since an explanation of this is also desired, if it is asked how meaning is grasped by a syllable, the answer is that because a particular arrangement is made for those who hear syllables being heard, comprehension of the word's meaning occurs at the conclusion of the word. Therefore, it should be understood that the form of meaning is grasped even through syllables. Hence, it is said: 'He indicates through syllables, he expresses through words, and he reveals through both syllables and words' (Netti. 9).

Vivaraṇā [M 0.0047] vitthāraṇā. Vibhajanā ca uttānīkammañca paññatti ca vibhajanuttānīkammapaññattīti samāhāre ayaṃ dvandasamāso. Tattha vibhāgakaraṇaṃ vibhajanaṃ nāma. Byañjanākārehi yo atthākāro niddisiyamāno, so atthākāro vivaraṇavibhajanāti dvīhi atthapadehi [V 0.0188] niddisito. Pākaṭakaraṇaṃ uttānīkammaṃ nāma. Pakārehi ñāpanaṃ paññatti. Niruttiniddesasaṅkhātehi byañjanapadehi pakāsiyamāno yo atthākāro atthi, so atthākāro uttānīkammapaññattīhi paṭiniddisito. Etehi saṅkāsanādīhi chahi atthapadehi attho suttattho gahito, kammañca ugghaṭanādikammañca niddiṭṭhanti attho. Yena suttatthena ugghaṭitaññuno cittasantānassa sambodhanakiriyāsaṅkhātassa ugghaṭanakammassa nibbatti bhave, so suttattho saṅkāsanāpakāsanākāro hoti. Yena suttatthena vipañcitaññuno cittasantānassa bodhanakiriyāsaṅkhātassa vipañcanakammassa nibbatti, so suttattho vivaraṇāvibhajanākāro hoti. Yena suttatthena neyyassa cittasantānassa pabodhanakiriyāsaṅkhātassa nayakammassa nibbatti, so suttattho uttānīkammapaññattākāro hotīti daṭṭhabbo. Tenāha aṭṭhakathācariyo “suttatthena hi desanāya pavattiyamānena ugghaṭitaññuādiveneyyānaṃ cittasantānassa pabodhanakiriyānibbatti, so ca suttattho saṅkāsanādiākāro”ti (netti. aṭṭha. 24).

Exposition, elaboration. Analysis and making plain, and designation—this is a dvandva compound, a combination of terms. Herein, the act of dividing is called analysis. The form of meaning that is pointed out through modes of expression, that form of meaning is indicated by the two meaning-terms: exposition and analysis. The act of making evident is called making plain. Making known through modes is designation. The form of meaning that is revealed by the terms of expression, namely linguistic interpretation and designation, that form of meaning is represented by making plain and designation. Through these six meaning-terms—manifestation and so on—the meaning of the discourse is grasped, and both the act and the work of opening up, etc., are indicated. The meaning of the discourse by which the work of opening up—an activity of awakening—arises in the mental continuum of one with quick understanding, that meaning of the discourse takes the form of manifestation and clarification. The meaning of the discourse by which the work of elaboration—an activity of awakening—arises in the mental continuum of one with detailed understanding, that meaning of the discourse takes the form of exposition and analysis. The meaning of the discourse by which the work of guidance—an activity of awakening—arises in the mental continuum of one who needs guidance, that meaning of the discourse takes the form of making plain and designation. Thus, the commentary teacher said: "For when the meaning of the discourse is being presented in the teaching, the awakening activity arises in the mental continuum of those who are to be trained, beginning with those of quick understanding. And that meaning of the discourse takes the form of manifestation and so on" (Netti. Aṭṭha. 24).

“Yathāvuttehi tīhi atthanayehi ceva chahi atthapadehi ca ayuttopi attho kiṃ koci atthi, udāhu sabbo attho yutto evā”ti pucchitabbattā –

Because it should be asked: "Is there any meaning that is discordant with the three methods of meaning and six terms of meaning as stated, or is all meaning concordant?"—

25.

25.

“Tīṇi ca nayā anūnā, atthassa ca chappadāni gaṇitāni.

"The three methods are not deficient, and the six terms of meaning are enumerated.

Navahi padehi bhagavato, vacanassattho samāyutto”ti. –

By nine terms, the meaning of the Blessed One's teaching is connected."

Gāthamāha. Tattha tīṇīti liṅgavipallāsaniddeso, tayoti pana pakatiliṅganiddeso vattabbo. Gaṇitā anūnā tayo atthassa nayā ca gaṇitāni anūnāni cha atthassa padāni ca niddiṭṭhāni, niddiṭṭhehi ca atthapadehi bhagavato vacanassa sabbo attho samāyuttova ayutto koci attho natthīti yojanā kātabbā. Atthassāti suttatthassa. Nayāti nettiatthanayā. Padānīti nettiatthapadāni.

He speaks a verse. Herein, `tīṇi` is an exposition with a change of gender, while `tayo` is an exposition with the natural gender (which is to be supplied). Counted and not deficient are the three methods of meaning, and counted and not deficient are the six terms of meaning that have been indicated. And with the indicated terms of meaning, the entire meaning of the Blessed One’s statement is connected—no meaning is unconnected. Thus should the connection be made. 'Of the meaning' refers to the meaning of the discourse. 'Methods' refers to the methods of meaning in the Netti. 'Terms' refers to the terms of meaning in the Netti.

26. Ye [M 0.0048] hārādayo niddiṭṭhā, te hārādayo sampiṇḍetvā nettippakaraṇassa padatthe sukhaggahaṇatthaṃ gaṇanavasena paricchinditvā dassento “atthassā”tiādimāha. Tattha atthassa samūhassa avayavabhūtāni navabhedāni atthapadāni suttabyañjanassa atthassa pariyeṭṭhisaṅkhātāya saṃvaṇṇanāya gaṇanato catuvīsati byañjanapadāni honti, atthapadabyañjanapadabhūtaṃ ubhayaṃ saṅkhepayato sampiṇḍayato tettiṃsā tettiṃsavidhā ettikā tettiṃsavidhāva nettīti yojanā.

26. Showing how the previously indicated `hārā`s and so on are collected and classified by way of enumeration for the easy comprehension of the meaning of the terms in the Nettippakaraṇa, he said, beginning with 'atthassā'. Herein, there are nine kinds of meaning-terms (atthapadāni), which are parts of the collection of meanings; by counting in the explanation which is called the search for the meaning of the discourse's expression, there are twenty-four expression-terms (byañjanapadāni). When both, consisting of meaning-terms and expression-terms, are summarized and collected, they are thirty-three. Thus, the interpretation is that the Netti is thirty-threefold; that is, it is only thirty-threefold.

Tattha [V 0.0189] navappadānīti tayo atthanayā, cha atthapadāni ca. Catubbīsāti soḷasa hārā, cha byañjanapadāni, dve disālocananayaaṅkusanayā cāti evaṃ tettiṃsavidhā ca netti nāma, ito vinimutto añño koci nettipadattho natthīti attho daṭṭhabbo.

Herein, the 'nine terms' refers to the three methods of meaning and the six meaning-terms. The 'twenty-four' refers to the sixteen `hārā`s, six expression-terms, and the two methods of directional analysis and the goad. Thus, the Netti is called thirty-threefold, and it should be understood that there is no other subject matter of the Netti beyond this.

“Evaṃ tettiṃsapadatthāya nettiyā hāranayānaṃ katamo desanāhāravicayahāro”tiādi desanākkameneva siddho, evaṃ siddhe satipi “soḷasa hārā paṭhama”nti ārambho “sabbepime hārā ceva nayā ca iminā dassitakkameneva saṃvaṇṇetabbesu suttesu saṃvaṇṇanāvasena yojetabbā, na uppaṭipāṭiyā”ti imamatthaṃ dīpeti. Dīpanavacanasavanānusārena ñāpeti, tasmā evaṃ kamo dassito, assādādīnavanissaraṇāni dhammadesanāya nissayāni, phalañca dhammadesanāya phalaṃ, upāyo ca dhammadesanāya upāyo, āṇatti ca dhammadesanāya sarīraṃ. Desanāhārassa tāsaṃ assādādīnavanissaraṇaphalupāyāṇattīnaṃ vibhāvanasabhāvattā.

The question, "Among the Netti with its thirty-three terms, which of the `hārā`s and methods are the Teaching `Hāra`, the Investigation `Hāra`?" etc., is established by the order of the teaching itself. Even when this is established, the statement "the sixteen `hārā`s first" is a beginning that elucidates this meaning: "All these `hārā`s and methods should be applied by way of explanation in the discourses to be explained, in the order shown, and not in reverse." This meaning is indicated and made known according to the instruction in the Dīpanavacana. Therefore, this sequence is shown. Allure, drawbacks, and escape are the foundations for the Dhamma-teaching; the fruit is the fruit of the Dhamma-teaching; the method is the method of the Dhamma-teaching; and the command is the body of the Dhamma-teaching. This is because the Teaching `Hāra` has the nature of making clear these—allure, drawbacks, escape, fruit, method, and command.

Niddhāraṇena vināpi pakatiyā sabbasaṃvaṇṇetabbasuttesu anarūpāti suviññeyyattā, saṃvaṇṇanāvisesānaṃ vicayahārādīnaṃ nissayabhāvato ca paṭhamaṃ desanāhāro dassito.

The Teaching `Hāra` is presented first because, even without explicit determination, it is easily understood that it is suitable for all discourses that are to be explained in the normal way, and because it serves as a foundation for the special features of the explanation, such as the Investigation `Hāra`.

Padapucchāvissajjanāpucchāpadānugītīhi saddhiṃ desanāhārapadatthānaṃ assādādīnaṃ pavicayabhāvato desanāhārānantaraṃ vicayo hāro.

The Investigation `Hāra` follows the Teaching `Hāra` because it involves the investigation of the allurements and so on, which are the meanings of the terms of the Teaching `Hāra`, along with word-questions, answers, questions on terms, and recitation following the terms.

Vicayahārena pavicitānaṃ atthānaṃ yuttāyuttivicāraṇabhāvato vicayahārānantaraṃ yutti hāro.

Following the Investigation `Hāra`, the Coherence `Hāra` comes next, because it considers the suitability or unsuitability of the meanings investigated by the Investigation `Hāra`.

Padaṭṭhānahārassa yuttāyuttānaṃyeva atthānaṃ upapattianurūpaṃ kāraṇaparamparāya niddhāraṇattā yuttihārānantaraṃ padaṭṭhānahāro.

After the Coherence `Hāra`, the Basis `Hāra` follows because it ascertains the suitable and unsuitable meanings through a sequence of causes in accordance with their origination.

Yuttāyuttānaṃ [M 0.0049] kāraṇaparamparāya pariggahitasabhāvānaṃyeva ca dhammānaṃ avuttānampi samānalakkhaṇatāya gahaṇalakkhaṇattāya padaṭṭhānahārānantaraṃ lakkhaṇahāro.

After the Basis `Hāra`, the Characteristics `Hāra` comes next, because it has the characteristic of grasping, by reason of their similar characteristics, even unstated phenomena, as well as those phenomena whose nature has been comprehended through a series of causes, whether suitable or unsuitable.

Lakkhaṇahārena atthato suttantarato niddhāritānampi dhammānaṃ nibbacanādīni vattabbāni, na sutte sarūpato āgatadhammānaṃyevāti dassanatthaṃ lakkhaṇahārānantaraṃ catubyūho hāro. Evañhi niravasesato atthāvabodho hoti.

To show that explanations and so on should be stated even for those phenomena determined by the Characteristics `Hāra` from the meaning and from other discourses, not merely for those phenomena that appear in the suttas in their own form, the Fourfold Array `Hāra` follows the Characteristics `Hāra`. For in this way, understanding of the meaning becomes complete without remainder.

Catubyūhena [V 0.0190] hārena vuttehi nibbacanādhippāyanidānehi saddhiṃ sutte padatthānaṃ suttantarasaṃsandanasaṅkhāte pubbāparavicāre dassite tesaṃ suttapadatthānaṃ sabhāgavisabhāgadhammantarāvaṭṭanaṃ sukhena sakkā dassetunti catubyūhahārānantaraṃ āvaṭṭo hāro. Suttantarasaṃsandanassa hi sabhāgavisabhāgadhammantarāvaṭṭanayassa upāyabhāvato “ārambhatha nikkamathā”tiādigāthāya (saṃ. ni. 1.185; netti. 29; peṭako. 38) ārambhananikkamanabuddhasāsanayogadhunanehi vīriyasamādhipaññindriyāni niddhāretvā tesu ārambhananikkamanabuddhasāsanayogadhunanesu ananuyogassa mūlaṃ pamādoti suttantare dassito pamādo āvaṭṭitoti.

When the examination of what precedes and follows, called the collation with other discourses, has been shown for the meanings of terms in a sutta, along with their bases, intentions, and grounds as stated by the Fourfold Array `Hāra`, then it is possible to easily demonstrate how those meanings of the sutta terms revolve among similar and dissimilar phenomena. Therefore, after the Fourfold Array `Hāra`, comes the Revolving `Hāra`. For the collation with other discourses is a means for revolving around similar and dissimilar phenomena. As in the verse beginning, “Begin, depart,” etc. (SN 1.185; Netti 29; Peṭ 38), by beginning, departing, engaging in the Buddha’s teaching, and shaking off, the faculties of energy, concentration, and wisdom are determined. In the context of beginning, departing, engaging in the Buddha’s teaching, and shaking off, negligence is the root of non-application. Thus, negligence, as shown in another sutta, is what revolves.

Āvaṭṭena hārena sabhāgavisabhāgadhammāvaṭṭanena payojite sādhāraṇāsādhāraṇavasena saṃkilesavodānadhammānaṃ padaṭṭhānato ceva bhūmito ca vibhāgo sakkā sukhena yojetunti āvaṭṭahārānantaraṃ vibhatti hāro.

When the Revolving `Hāra` is applied by means of the revolving of similar and dissimilar phenomena, then a classification of defilement and purification phenomena, in terms of common and uncommon, and in terms of their bases and grounds, can easily be made. Thus, after the Revolving `Hāra`, comes the Classification `Hāra`.

Vibhattihārena saṃkilesavodānadhammānaṃ vibhāge kate saṃvaṇṇetabbasutte āgatā dhammā akasirena paṭipakkhato parivattetuṃ sakkāti vibhattihārānantaraṃ parivattanahāro. Vibhattihārena hi “sammādiṭṭhissa purisapuggalassa micchādiṭṭhi nijjiṇṇā hotī”ti (netti. 35) paṭivibhattasabhāve eva dhamme parivattanahāravibhaṅge udāharīyissati.

When a classification of the phenomena of defilement and purification has been made by the Method of Classification, the phenomena that have come in the sutta to be commented upon can easily be turned around from their opposites. Thus, after the Method of Classification, comes the Method of Transformation. For, in the analysis of the Method of Transformation, a phenomenon whose nature has been precisely distinguished by the Method of Classification, such as 'For a person of right view, wrong view is rejected' (Netti. 35), will be cited as an example.

Parivattanahārena paṭipakkhato parivattitāpi dhammā pariyāyavacanehi bodhetabbā, na saṃvaṇṇetabbasutte āgatadhammāyevāti dassanatthaṃ parivattanahārānantaraṃ vevacanahāro.

Even phenomena that have been turned around from their opposites by the Method of Transformation should be made known through synonymous expressions, not merely those phenomena that have come in the sutta to be commented upon. To show this, the Method of Synonyms follows the Method of Transformation.

Vevacanahārena [M 0.0050] pariyāyato pakāsitānaṃ dhammānaṃ pabhedato paññattivasena vibhajanaṃ sukhena sakkā ñātunti vevacanahārānantaraṃ paññatti hāro.

When phenomena have been revealed in various ways by the Method of Synonyms, their division by way of designation according to classification can easily be understood. Thus, after the Method of Synonyms, comes the Method of Designation.

Paññattihārena pabhavapariññādipaññattivibhāgamukhena paṭiccasamuppādasaccādidhammavibhāge kate sutte āgatadhammānaṃ paṭiccasamuppādādimukhena avataraṇaṃ sakkā dassetunti paññattihārānantaraṃ otaraṇo hāro.

When a division of phenomena such as dependent origination and the truths has been made by the Method of Designation, through the classification of designations such as the full understanding of origin, it is possible to show the entry of the phenomena that have come in the sutta through the means of dependent origination and so forth. Thus, after the Method of Designation, comes the Method of Entry.

Otaraṇena hārena dhātāyatanādīsu otāritānaṃ saṃvaṇṇetabbasutte padatthānaṃ pucchārambhasodhanaṃ sakkā sukhena sampādetunti otaraṇahārānantaraṃ sodhano hāro.

By the Method of Entry, the clarification of the initial questions regarding the meanings of terms in the sutta to be commented upon, which have been entered into elements, sense bases, and so on, can easily be accomplished. Thus, after the Method of Entry, comes the Method of Purification.

Sodhanena [V 0.0191] hārena saṃvaṇṇetabbasutte padapadatthesu visodhitesu tattha tattha ekattatāya vā vemattatāya vā labbhamānasāmaññavisesabhāvo sukaro hotīti dassetuṃ sodhanahārānantaraṃ adhiṭṭhāno hāro.

When the meanings of the words and phrases in the sutta to be commented upon have been thoroughly purified by the Method of Purification, it becomes easy to show the common and distinctive characteristics obtained in various places, whether by way of unity or diversity. To demonstrate this, after the Method of Purification, comes the Method of Determination.

Sāmaññavisesabhūtesu sādhāraṇāsādhāraṇesu dhammesu adhiṭṭhānena hārena paveditesu parikkhārasaṅkhātassa sādhāraṇāsādhāraṇarūpassa paccayaheturāsissa pabhedo suviññeyyoti adhiṭṭhānahārānantaraṃ parikkhāro hāro.

When common and uncommon phenomena, which are of the nature of common and distinctive, have been revealed by the Method of Determination, then the distinction of the aggregate of conditions and causes, which is of a common and uncommon nature and is called requisites, is easily understood. Thus, after the Method of Determination, comes the Method of Requisites.

Asādhāraṇe, sādhāraṇe ca kāraṇe parikkhārena hārena dassite tassa attano phalesu kāraṇākāro, tesaṃ hetuphalānaṃ pabhedato desanākāro, bhāvetabbapahātabbadhammānaṃ bhāvanāpahānāni ca niddhāretvā vuccamānāni sammā saṃvaṇṇetabbasuttassa atthaṃ tathattāvabodhāya saṃvattantīti parikkhārahārānantaraṃ samāropano hāro dassito hoti. Idaṃ hārānaṃ dassanānukkamakāraṇaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ.

When common and uncommon causes have been shown by the Method of Requisites, then the manner of the cause in its own results, the manner of teaching by distinguishing those causes and results, and the development and abandonment of phenomena to be developed and abandoned, when determined and spoken of, rightly conduce to the realization of the true meaning of the sutta to be commented upon. Thus, after the Method of Requisites, the Method of Application is shown. This should be seen as the reason for the sequence of showing the methods.

Uddeso ugghaṭitaññuno upakārāya saṃvattati yathā, evaṃ nandiyāvaṭṭanayo ugghaṭitaññuno upakārāya saṃvattati, tasmā paṭhamaṃ nandiyāvaṭṭanayo dassito. Niddeso vipañcitaññuno upakārāya saṃvattati yathā, evaṃ tipukkhalanayo vipañcitaññuno upakārāya saṃvattati, tasmā nandiyāvaṭṭanayānantaraṃ tipukkhalanayo. Paṭiniddeso neyyassa upakārāya saṃvattati yathā, evaṃ sīhavikkīḷitanayo neyyassa upakārāya saṃvattati[M 0.0051]. Tasmā tipukkhalānantaraṃ sīhavikkīḷitanayo dassitoti tiṇṇaṃ atthanayānaṃ dassanānukkamo veditabbo. Atthanayānaṃ disābhūtāya bhūmiyā āloketvā tesaṃ tassā disāya bhūmiyā samānayanaṃ hoti. Na hi sakkā anoloketvā samānetunti disālocananayaṃ dassetvā aṅkusanayo dassito. Potthakāruḷhāvachekā sabbāsu disāsu hatthigamanaṭṭhānaṃ oloketvā aṅkusena icchitaṭṭhānaṃ samānayanti. Keci acchekā anoloketvā vinayanti. Tesaṃ nayanamattameva, na samānayanaṃ. Evameva paṇḍitā suttatthaṃ vaṇṇentā manasāva oloketvāva nayā netabbāti daṭṭhabbā.

Just as the summary conduces to the benefit of those with quick understanding, so too does the Nandiyāvaṭṭa Method conduce to the benefit of those with quick understanding. Therefore, the Nandiyāvaṭṭa Method is shown first. Just as the detailed explanation conduces to the benefit of those with developed understanding, so too does the Tipukkhalana Method conduce to the benefit of those with developed understanding. Therefore, the Tipukkhalana Method follows the Nandiyāvaṭṭa Method. Just as the counter-explanation conduces to the benefit of those requiring guidance, so too does the Sīhavikkīḷita Method conduce to the benefit of those requiring guidance. Therefore, the Sīhavikkīḷita Method is shown after the Tipukkhalana Method. Thus, the sequence of showing the three methods of meaning should be understood. Having illuminated the ground that serves as the direction for the methods of meaning, their application is then brought into harmony with that ground and those directions. For it is impossible to harmonize without first examining. Thus, the Method of Examining Directions is shown, followed by the Method of the Goad. Skilled elephant trainers, mounted on their elephants, examine the ground in all directions where the elephants are to go, and then guide them to the desired place using the goad. Some unskilled trainers, however, drive them without examination. For them, there is only driving, not proper guidance. Similarly, the wise, when explaining the meaning of the suttas, should guide the meaning only after careful mental examination. This should be understood.

Samuṭṭhānasaṃvaṇṇanā adhippāyasaṃvaṇṇanā padatthasaṃvaṇṇanā vidhianuvādasaṃvaṇṇanā nigamanasaṃvaṇṇanāti vā, payojanasaṃvaṇṇanā piṇḍatthasaṃvaṇṇanā anusandhisaṃvaṇṇanā codanāsaṃvaṇṇanā parihārasaṃvaṇṇanāti vā, upogghāṭasaṃvaṇṇanā padaviggahasaṃvaṇṇanā padatthacālanasaṃvaṇṇanā [V 0.0192] paccupaṭṭhānasaṃvaṇṇanāti vā, tathā ekanāḷikākathā caturassakathā nisinnavattikākathāti vā āgatā.

The explanation of origin, the explanation of intention, the explanation of word meaning, the explanation of method and re-statement, and the explanation of conclusion; or the explanation of purpose, the explanation of summary meaning, the explanation of connection, the explanation of objection, and the explanation of refutation; or the explanation of introduction, the explanation of word analysis, the explanation of stirring up word meanings, and the explanation of manifestation; or likewise, the Ekanāḷikā Talk, the Caturassa Talk, and the Nisinnavattikā Talk—these have come.

Tattha samuṭṭhānaṃ nidānameva. Vidhianuvādo visesavacanameva. Upogghāṭo nidānameva. Cālanā codanāyeva. Paccupaṭṭhānaṃ parihārova.

Therein, the arising is simply the origin. The method and re-statement is simply a specific statement. The introduction is simply the origin. The stirring is simply the objection. The manifestation is simply the refutation.

Pāḷiṃ vatvā ekekapadassa atthakathanasaṅkhātā saṃvaṇṇanā ekanāḷikākathā nāma.

Having recited the Pāli, the explanation designated as the meaning of each word is called the Ekanāḷikā Talk.

Paṭipakkhaṃ dassetvā paṭipakkhassa upamaṃ dassetvā sapakkhaṃ dassetvā sapakkhassa upamaṃ dassetvā kathanasaṅkhātā saṃvaṇṇanā caturassakathā nāma.

The explanation that proceeds by showing the opposing side, a simile for the opposing side, one's own side, and a simile for one's own side, is called the Caturassa Talk.

Visabhāgadhammavaseneva pariyosānaṃ gantvā puna sabhāgadhammavaseneva pariyosānagamanasaṅkhātā saṃvaṇṇanā nisinnavattikākathā nāma.

The explanation designated as ending by way of dissimilar phenomena and then again ending by way of similar phenomena is called the Nisinnavattikā Talk.

Tā sabbā saṃvaṇṇanāyopi desanāhārādīsu nettisaṃvaṇṇanāsu antogadhāyeva. Tenāha “yattakā hi suttassa saṃvaṇṇanāvisesā, sabbe te nettiupadesāyattā”ti. Evaṃ ettāvatā etaparamatā daṭṭhabbā[M 0.0052]. Hetuphalabhūmiupanisāsabhāgavisabhāgalakkhaṇanayādayo pana aṭṭhakathāyaṃ (netti. aṭṭha. 4 dvādasapada) vitthārato vuttāti na vitthārayissāmīti.

All these explanations are included within the Netti explanations, such as the Method of Teaching and so on. Therefore, it is said: 'Whatever distinctions there are in the explanations of the sutta, all are dependent on the instructions of the Netti.' Thus, this much should be seen as its supremacy. However, causes, results, grounds, preconditions, similar and dissimilar characteristics, methods, and so on, are explained in detail in the commentary (Netti. Aṭṭha. 4, twelve topics), therefore, I will not elaborate further.

Iti sattibalānurūpā racitā

Thus, it is composed in accordance with one's own power and strength.

Niddesavāraatthavibhāvanā niṭṭhitā.

The elucidation of the meaning of the Section on Exposition is completed.

4. Paṭiniddesavāraatthavibhāvanā

4. Elucidation of the Meaning of the Section on Counter-Exposition.

1. Desanāhāravibhaṅgavibhāvanā

1. Elucidation of the Analysis of the Method of Teaching.

5. Evaṃ [V 0.0193] hārādayo sarūpato ācariyena uddesato uddiṭṭhā, niddesato ca niddiṭṭhā, amhehi ca ñātā, atha kasmā puna “tattha katamo desanāhāro”tiādiko āraddhoti ce? Veneyyānaṃ tividhattā. Veneyyā hi atitikkhapañño nātitikkhapañño mandapaññoti tividhā honti. Tesañhi atitikkhapaññassānurūpaṃ hārādayo uddesato uddiṭṭhā, nātitikkhapaññassa anurūpaṃ niddesato niddiṭṭhā, idāni mandapaññassānurūpaṃ hārādayo vibhajitvā dassetuṃ “tattha katamo desanāhāro”tiādiko vibhaṅgavāro āraddho. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana “evaṃ hārādayosukhaggahaṇatthaṃ gāthābandhavasena sarūpato niddisitvā idāni tesu hāre tāva paṭiniddesavasena vibhajituṃ ‘tattha katamo desanāhāro’tiādi āraddha”nti (netti. aṭṭha. 5) vuttaṃ.

5. Thus, the methods and so on have been presented by the teacher in their essential nature by way of summary and explained by way of exposition, and are also known by us. Then why is it that the section beginning with 'Herein, what is the teaching method?' is commenced? Because of the threefold nature of the trainees. For the trainees are of three kinds: those of very sharp wisdom, those of moderately sharp wisdom, and those of dull wisdom. For those of very sharp wisdom, the methods and so on have been presented by way of summary. For those of moderately sharp wisdom, they have been explained by way of exposition. Now, to show the methods and so on by analyzing them in detail suitable for those of dull wisdom, the section of analysis beginning with 'Herein, what is the teaching method?' has been commenced. In the commentary, however, it is said: 'Having thus explained the methods and so on in their essential nature for the sake of easy comprehension, in the form of connected verses, now, to analyze them by way of counter-exposition, the section beginning with 'Herein, what is the teaching method?' has been commenced' (Netti-aṭṭhakathā 5).

Tattha ye hārādayo uddesaniddesesu niddiṭṭhā, tattha hārādīsu katamo desanāhāroti ce? Yā “assādādīnavatā”tiādigāthā (netti. 4) vuttā, sā ayaṃ gāthā niddesavasena desanāhāro nāma, tassa “assādādīnavatā”tiādi (netti. 4) niddesassa idāni mayā vuccamāno “ayaṃ desanāhāro kiṃ desayatī”tiādiko vitthārasaṃvaṇṇanāviseso desanāhāravibhaṅgo nāmāti yojanā. “Ayaṃ desanāhāro kiṃ desayatī”ti pucchitabbattā pucchaṃ ṭhapetvā “imaṃ desayatī”ti niyametvā dassetuṃ “ayaṃ desanāhāro kiṃ desayati? Assādaṃ ādīnava”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha ayaṃ desanāhāro kiṃ desayatīti ce[M 0.0053]? Assādaṃ desayati saṃvaṇṇeti vitthāreti, ādīnavaṃ desayati…pe… vitthāreti, nissaraṇaṃ desayati…pe… vitthāreti, phalaṃ desayati…pe… vitthāreti, upāyaṃ desayati…pe… vitthāreti, āṇattiṃ desayati saṃvaṇṇeti vitthāretīti yojano.

Among those modes and so on mentioned in the summary and exposition—if asked, among those modes, which is the teaching mode? The verse beginning with 'assādādīnavatā' (Netti. 4) is, by way of exposition, called the teaching mode. Now, the detailed exposition and special explanation of that exposition beginning with 'assādādīnavatā' (Netti. 4), which I am about to explain—such as, 'What does this teaching mode teach?'—is called the analysis of the teaching mode. Because the question 'What does this teaching mode teach?' should be asked, having set aside the question and determined, 'It teaches this,' in order to show this, it is stated: 'What does this teaching mode teach? It teaches gratification, danger...' and so on. Here, if asked, 'What does this teaching mode teach?' It teaches, expounds, and elaborates on gratification. It teaches danger... and so on... elaborates. It teaches escape... and so on... elaborates. It teaches the fruit... and so on... elaborates. It teaches the means... and so on... elaborates. It teaches, expounds, and elaborates on the injunction—this is the connection.

Ettha ca “ayaṃ desanāhāro”ti saddo pubbāparāpekkhoti daṭṭhabbo. “‘Assādādīnavatā’tiādigāthāyaṃ (netti. 4) dassitā ime assādādayo kattha saṃvaṇṇetabbe pāḷidhamme āgatā”ti pucchitabbattā “dhammaṃ vo, bhikkhave, desessāmī”tiādi vuttaṃ. “‘Assādādīnavatā’tiādigāthāyaṃ (netti. 4) dassitā ime assādādayo kattha saṃvaṇṇetabbe pāḷidhamme āgatā”ti pucchitabbattā “dhammaṃ vo, bhikkhave, desessāmi ādikalyāṇaṃ [V 0.0194] majjhekalyāṇaṃ pariyosānakalyāṇaṃ sātthaṃ sabyañjanaṃ kevalaparipuṇṇaṃ parisuddhaṃ brahmacariyaṃ pakāsessāmī”ti paṭiññātabbe pāḷidhamme saṃvaṇṇetabbe ye assādādayo āgatā, te ayaṃ desanāhāro desayatīti adhippāyo.

Here, the term 'this teaching mode' should be seen as related to what precedes and follows. Because it should be asked, 'Where in the Pali Dhamma, which is to be expounded, do these gratifications and so on, shown in the verse beginning with 'assādādīnavatā' (Netti. 4), occur?' thus it was said, 'Monks, I will teach you the Dhamma...' and so on. Because it should be asked, 'Where in the Pali Dhamma, which is to be expounded, do these gratifications and so on, shown in the verse beginning with 'assādādīnavatā' (Netti. 4), occur?' the intended meaning is that this teaching mode teaches those gratifications and so on that occur in the Pali Dhamma that is to be declared: 'Monks, I will proclaim the Dhamma—beautiful in the beginning, beautiful in the middle, beautiful in the end—with its meaning and phrasing, entirely perfect and pure, the holy life.'

Tattha dhammasaddo pariyattisaccasamādhipaññāpakatipuññāpattiñeyyādīsu bahūsu atthesu pavatto, tathāpi idha pariyattidhammeyeva pavattoti daṭṭhabbo. Atthuddeso pana aṭṭhakathāyaṃ (netti. aṭṭha. 5) vutto, tasmā idha mayā na vutto. Vo-kāropi upayogakaraṇapadapūraṇasampadānatthesu dissati ca, tathāpi idha sampadānatthevāti daṭṭhabbo. Bhikkhanti yācanti sīlakkhandhādayo, paccaye vā kāyaviññattiyāti bhikkhū, saṃsāre bhayaṃ ikkhanti paccavekkhantīti vā bhikkhū. Bhikkhaveti te bhikkhū ālapati, kimatthāyāti attano mukhābhimukhaṃ katvā dhammassavane atiussāhane niyojetuṃ ālapatīti veditabbo.

Here, the term 'Dhamma' is used in many senses, such as in the texts, truth, concentration, wisdom, nature, merit, offence, the knowable, and so on. Yet here, it should be understood as referring specifically to the Dhamma texts. The explanation of the meaning is given in the commentary (Netti. Aṭṭha. 5), so I have not given it here. The particle 'vo' is seen in various senses—such as indicating use, instrumentality, filling out a word, or dative case—but here it should be understood solely in the sense of the dative. 'Bhikkhu' refers to those who beg for the virtue-aggregates and so on, or who beg for requisites by bodily intimation. Alternatively, it refers to those who perceive danger in the cycle of existence and reflect upon it. 'Bhikkhave' is how he addresses those bhikkhus. It should be understood as addressing them in order to make them face him and to urge them to listen to the Dhamma with great enthusiasm.

Dhammaṃ desessāmīti nāhaṃ issaratāya tumhe aññaṃ kiñci kāreyyāmi, dhammaṃyeva desessāmi, desento ca na aññesaṃ dhammaṃ sutvā sutamayañāṇānusārena desessāmi, anāvaraṇañāṇena sabbañeyyadhammesu paccakkhakāritāya idāni mayāyeva pavattiyamānaṃ dhammaṃ ahaṃ desessāmīti paṭijānāti. Ādimhi kalyāṇaṃ ādikalyāṇaṃ, ādi kalyāṇametassāti vā ādikalyāṇaṃ. Sesesupi eseva nayo. Ādikalyāṇādayo cettha atthakalyāṇādivasena vuttāti daṭṭhabbā. Tenāha – “sīlena [M 0.0054] ādikalyāṇaṃ, samādhinā majjhekalyāṇaṃ, paññāya pariyosānakalyāṇaṃ. Buddhasubuddhatāya vā ādikalyāṇaṃ, dhammasudhammatāya majjhekalyāṇaṃ, saṅghasuppaṭipattiyā pariyosānakalyāṇaṃ. Atha vā ugghaṭitaññuvinayanena ādikalyāṇaṃ, vipañcitaññuvinayanena majjhekalyāṇaṃ, neyyapuggalavinayanena pariyosānakalyāṇaṃ. Ayamevattho idhādhippeto”ti (netti. aṭṭha. 5).

I will teach the Dhamma—not because I claim authority over you or seek to impose anything else upon you. I will teach only the Dhamma. And in teaching, I will not teach the Dhamma by relying on knowledge derived from hearing others' teachings, but through unobstructed knowledge, having directly realized all knowable things, I declare that I will teach the Dhamma that is now being set forth by me. At the beginning, it is beautiful—the beautiful beginning; or that which has a beautiful beginning is the beautiful beginning. The same applies to the rest. Here, the beautiful beginning and so on should be understood as being spoken in terms of the beauty of the meaning and so forth. Therefore, it is said: 'Virtue is the beautiful beginning, concentration is the beautiful middle, wisdom is the beautiful end. Or, the Buddha’s supreme awakening is the beautiful beginning, the Dhamma’s perfect teaching is the beautiful middle, the Saṅgha’s good practice is the beautiful end. Alternatively, the discipline for those who are quick to understand is the beautiful beginning, the discipline for those who can be led after elaboration is the beautiful middle, the discipline for those who need to be trained is the beautiful end. This is the intended meaning here.' (Netti. Aṭṭha. 5)
