Arīyati ñāyatīti attho, ara-dhātuyā nippariyāyato ñāṇappadhāno ārammaṇikacittuppādo attho, ṭhānūpacārato atthassa ñātabbassa ārammaṇapaccayasatti attho, iti-saddena sāyeva satti parāmasīyati, ārammaṇapaccayasattisahito ārammaṇapaccayasaṅkhāto ñātabbo attho ta-paccayassa atthoti dhātupaccayānaṃ atthaviseso daṭṭhabbo. Asati bhavatīti vā attho, saha atthena yo dhammo vattatīti so dhammo sāttho, atthena samannāgato vā dhammo sāttho, saṅkāsanādichaatthapadasamāyogato vā sāttho. Ayamevattho idhādhippeto nettivisayattā. Sampannaṃ byañjanaṃ yassa dhammassāti sabyañjano. Sithiladhanitadīgharassagarulahusambandhavavatthitavimuttaniggahitasampannattā[V 0.0195], akārantādiitthiliṅgādiekavacanādisampannattā, pamādalekhādirahitattā ca avayavo sampanno taṃsamūhattā dhammo sampannabyañjano nāma, akkharādichabyañjanapadasamāyogā vā sabyañjano. Ayamevattho idhādhippeto. Imasmiṃ ayaṃ ūno, so netabbo pakkhipitabboti upanetabbābhāvato kevalaparipuṇṇo, sīlakkhandhasamādhikkhandhapaññākkhandha- vimuttikkhandhavimuttiñāṇadassanakkhandhapāripūriyā vā kevalaparipuṇṇo. Idhāyaṃ atireko, so apanetabboti vatvā apanetabbābhāvato parisuddho, caturoghanittharaṇatthāya, lokāmisanirapekkhatāya pavattiyamānattā vā parisuddho. Seṭṭhattā brahmacariyaṃ, brahmānaṃ vā seṭṭhānaṃ ariyānaṃ cariyaṃ brahmacariyaṃ, pabbajjabrahmacariyamaggabrahmacariyasāsanabrahmacariyādīsu sāsanabrahmacariyaṃ pakāsayissāmi, paridīpayissāmīti attho.

The meaning is that it is attained, it is known. Or, the meaning is the mind-arising predominant in knowledge, which is directly related to the root 'ara' and has an object. Or, the meaning is the power of the object condition of the meaning to be known, by way of proximity to a basis. With the word 'iti,' that very power is referred to. The meaning to be known, which is characterized as an object condition and accompanied by the power of the object condition, is the meaning of the suffix 'ta'; thus, the specific meaning of roots and suffixes should be understood. Or, the meaning is that it exists with meaning. The Dhamma that operates together with the meaning is meaningful; the Dhamma endowed with meaning is meaningful; or it is meaningful due to the combination of words such as explanation and others, which express its meaning. This is the intended meaning here because it is the scope of the Guide. That Dhamma which is complete in expression is called 'well-expressed.' It is complete in syllables due to being endowed with laxness, aspiration, length, shortness, heaviness, lightness, connection, established, released, and restrained sounds; it is complete due to having singular endings like the feminine gender and singular number, etc.; and its parts are complete due to being free from faults like negligence in writing, and because it is a collection of these, the Dhamma is called 'well-expressed.' Alternatively, it is well-expressed due to the combination of syllables, words, and other expressions. This is the intended meaning here. In this, what is lacking should be supplied, and thus it is entirely perfect because there is nothing to be added; it is entirely perfect due to the perfection of the aggregates of virtue, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation. Here, what is excessive should be removed, and thus it is purified because there is nothing to be discarded; it is purified because it operates for the sake of overcoming the four floods, or because it proceeds without concern for worldly gains. It is the supreme holy life; the holy life of the noble ones, who are supreme like Brahma, is the holy life; I will declare and illuminate the holy life of the teaching among the holy lives of renunciation, the path, and the dispensation—this is the meaning.

“Dhammaṃ vo, bhikkhave, desessāmi…pe… pakāsessāmī”ti paṭiññātabbe pāḷidhamme āgate assādādayo desanāhāro desayati saṃvaṇṇeti [M 0.0055] vitthāretīti ācariyena sāmaññavaseneva vuttaṃ, tasmā desanāhāro idha pāḷiyaṃ āgataṃ imaṃ assādaṃ desayati, idha pāḷiyaṃ āgataṃ imaṃ ādīnavaṃ desayatītiādi viseso na viññātabbo, “kathaṃ viññātabbo”ti pucchitabbattā “idha pāḷiyaṃ āgato ayaṃ assādo, idha pāḷiyaṃ āgato ayaṃ ādīnavo”ti visesaṃ niyametvā upalakkhaṇanayena dassetuṃ “tattha katamo assādo? Kāmaṃ kāmayamānassā”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha tatthāti tassaṃ “assādādīnavatā”tiādigāthāyaṃ niddiṭṭhesu visayavisayibhedesu assādesu katamo assādo tattha tesu pāḷidhammesu kattha pāḷiyaṃ āgatoti pucchitvā –

'I will teach you the Dhamma, monks... I will explain it.' When the Pali Dhamma is presented, the teaching mode teaches, expounds, and elaborates on gratifications and so on. This is stated by the teacher in a general way. Therefore, the specific distinction that the teaching mode teaches this gratification that occurs in the Pali text, or teaches this danger that occurs in the Pali text, and so on, should not be understood. Because it should be asked, 'How should it be understood?' to show the distinction by determining, 'Here in the Pali text, this is the gratification; here in the Pali text, this is the danger,' by way of defining characteristics, the section beginning with 'There, what is the gratification? For one who desires sense pleasures...' has been commenced. There—'there' meaning in that verse beginning with 'assādādīnavatā'—among the gratifications indicated in the distinctions of object and subject, which is the gratification? Having asked, 'Where in those Pali teachings, in which Pali text, does it occur?'—

“Kāmaṃ kāmayamānassa, tassa cetaṃ samijjhati;

Addhā pītimano hoti, laddhā macco yadicchatī”ti. (su. ni. 772; mahāni. 1) –

"For one desiring a sensual pleasure, should that wish of his be fulfilled, surely he is glad at heart, a mortal having obtained what he desires."

Idha pāḷigāthāyaṃ yo visayabhūto assādo āgato, so ayaṃ assādetabbo assādo desanāhārassa visayoti. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana –

Here, in the Pāli verse, the gratification that has appeared as the objective field, that very gratification to be savored, is the object of the Teaching Mode. But in the commentary—

“Evaṃ bhagavatā desito, pakāsito ca sāsanadhammo yesaṃ assādādīnaṃ dassanavasena pavatto, te assādādayo desanāhārassa visayabhūtā yattha yattha pāṭhe savisesaṃ [V 0.0196] vuttā, tato tato niddhāretvā udāharaṇavasena idhānetvā dassetuṃ ‘tattha katamo assādo’tiādi āraddha”nti (netti. aṭṭha. 5) vuttaṃ.

"Thus, the Dhamma of the Dispensation has been taught and revealed by the Blessed One, which proceeds by way of seeing gratification and so forth. Those gratifications and so forth, having become the objective field of the Teaching Mode, wherever they are specifically stated in the text, from there, having extracted them and brought them here by way of example in order to show them, the section beginning ‘Therein, what is gratification?’ has been commenced, it is said."

Tattha assādīyateti assādo, assādetabbo vatthukāmo. Kāmīyateti kāmo, vatthukāmo ca. Taṃ kāmayatīti kāmayamāno, satto. Tassa pītiyā yuttaṃ mano etassāti pītimano. Manati jānātītiādivacanatthena macco. Kāmaṃ kāmitabbaṃ vatthu kāmayamānassa tassa sattassa etaṃ kāmitabbaṃ vatthu sace samijjhati, evaṃ sati so satto addhā pītimano hoti. Yo macco yaṃ vatthuṃ icchati, taṃ vatthuṃ so macco laddhā addhā pītimano hotīti gāthāyattho daṭṭhabbo.

Therein, ‘it is savored’ (assādīyati), thus it is gratification (assādo); the sensual pleasure as object (vatthukāmo) is to be savored. ‘It is desired’ (kāmīyati), thus it is desire (kāmo), and also the sensual pleasure as object (vatthukāmo). ‘He desires that’ (taṃ kāmayati), thus he is one who desires (kāmayamāno), a being (satto). ‘His mind is endowed with joy’ (tassa pītiyā yuttaṃ mano etassa), thus he is joyful-minded (pītimano). By the meaning of such words as ‘he thinks’ (manati) and ‘he knows’ (jānāti), he is a mortal (macco). If that desirable object is fulfilled for that being who desires it, then that being surely becomes joyful-minded. A mortal who desires a certain object, having obtained that object, surely becomes joyful-minded—this is the meaning of the verse to be understood.

“Kāmaṃ [M 0.0056] …pe… pītimano hotī”ti ettakameva avatvā “laddhā macco yadicchatī”ti vuttattā lobhanīyaṃ vatthuṃyeva laddhā pītimano na hoti, atha kho patthetabbaṃ pūjetabbanti sabbaṃ laddhā macco pītimano ca hotīti atirekattho daṭṭhabbo.

Not having stated only this much, ‘Sensual pleasure… becomes joyful-minded,’ but because it is said, ‘a mortal, having obtained what he desires,’ a mortal does not become joyful-minded merely by obtaining a covetable object. Rather, having obtained everything that is to be wished for and to be honored, a mortal becomes joyful-minded—this additional meaning is to be understood.

Visayabhūto assādetabbo assādo idha pāḷiyaṃ gāthāyaṃ āgatoti ācariyena vibhatto, amhehi ca ñāto, “dukkhadomanassādibhedesu ādīnavesu katamo ādīnavo kattha pāḷidhamme āgato”ti pucchitabbattā “tattha katamo ādīnavo? Tassa ce kāmayānassā”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha tatthāti tassaṃ “assādādīnavatā”tiādigāthāyaṃ niddiṭṭhesu dukkhadomanassādīsu ādīnavesu katamo ādīnavo tattha tesu pāḷidhammesu kattha pāḷiyaṃ āgatoti pucchitvā –

The gratification to be savored, which has become the objective field, has appeared here in the Pāli verse—thus it has been analyzed by the teacher and is known by us. Because it should be asked, ‘Among the drawbacks divided into suffering, displeasure, and so forth, which drawback has appeared where in the Pāli Dhamma?’, the section beginning, ‘Therein, what is the drawback? And if for that one desiring…’ has been commenced. Therein, that is: in that verse beginning ‘gratification, its drawback,’ among the specified drawbacks such as suffering and displeasure, having asked, ‘which drawback has appeared where in the Pāli, among those Pāli Dhammas?’—

“Tassa ce kāmayānassa, chandajātassa jantuno;

Te kāmā parihāyanti, sallaviddhova ruppatī”ti. (su. ni. 773; mahāni. 2) –

"And if for that being who desires, for whom desire has arisen, those sensual pleasures decline, he is afflicted as if pierced by a dart."

Idha pāḷigāthāyaṃ yo domanassasaṅkhāto ādīnavo āgato, so ayaṃ domanassasaṅkhāto ādīnavo desanāhārassa visayoti.

Here in this Pāli verse, the drawback designated as displeasure that has appeared—that very drawback designated as displeasure is the object of the Teaching Mode.

Gāthāyaṃ pana kāmayati icchatīti kāmayāno. Atha vā yāyati gacchatīti yāno, kāmena yāno kāmayāno, tassa. Chando jāto yassa so chandajāto, tassa. Vijjhīyateti viddho[V 0.0197], sallati pavisatīti sallo, sallena viddho sallaviddho. Kāmaṃ kāmayānassa chandajātassa jantuno ye kāmā labhitabbā, te kāmā kenaci antarāyena yadā parihāyanti, tadā so jantu ruppati. Kīdisova ruppati? Ayomayasallaviddho migo ruppati iva, parihīnakāmo jantu ruppatīti daṭṭhabbo. Ettha ca “ruppatī”tivacanena domanassuppatti dassitāti daṭṭhabbā.

Now, in the verse: ‘he desires’ (kāmayati) means ‘he wishes’ (icchati), thus he is one who desires (kāmayāno). Or alternatively, ‘he goes’ (yāyati) means ‘he goes’ (gacchati), thus he is one who goes (yāno); one who goes by desire (kāmena yāno) is one who desires (kāmayāno); of him. ‘Desire has arisen for him’ (chando jāto yassa so), thus he is one for whom desire has arisen (chandajāto); of him. ‘It is pierced’ (vijjhīyati), thus it is pierced (viddho); ‘it penetrates’ (sallati), thus it is a dart (sallo); pierced by a dart (sallena viddho) is sallaviddho. For the being who desires sensual pleasure, for whom desire has arisen, when those sensual pleasures that are to be obtained decline due to some obstacle, then that being is afflicted. How is he afflicted? Just as a deer pierced by an iron dart is afflicted, so is the being deprived of sensual pleasures afflicted—this is to be understood. And here, by the word ‘is afflicted’ (ruppati), the arising of displeasure is shown—this is to be understood.

Domanassabhūto ādīnavo idha pāḷiyaṃ āgatoti ācariyena vibhatto, amhehi ca ñāto, “magganibbānavasena duvidhesu nissaraṇesu katamaṃ nissaraṇaṃ kattha pāḷiyaṃ āgata”nti pucchitabbattā “tattha katamaṃ nissaraṇaṃ? Yo kāme parivajjetī”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha tatthāti tassaṃ [M 0.0057] “assādādīnavatā”tiādigāthāyaṃ niddiṭṭhesu magganibbānavasena duvidhesu nissaraṇesu katamaṃ nissaraṇaṃ tattha tesu pāḷidhammesu kattha pāḷidhamme āgatanti pucchitvā –

The drawback that has become displeasure has appeared here in the Pāli—thus it has been analyzed by the teacher and is known by us. Because it should be asked, ‘Among the two kinds of escape, namely by way of the path and Nibbāna, which escape has appeared where in the Pāli?’, the section beginning, ‘Therein, what is the escape? He who avoids sensual pleasures…’ has been commenced. Therein, that is: in that verse beginning ‘gratification, its drawback,’ among the two kinds of escape specified by way of the path and Nibbāna, having asked, ‘which escape has appeared where in the Pāli Dhamma, among those Pāli Dhammas?’—

“Yo kāme parivajjeti, sappasseva padā siro;

Somaṃ visattikaṃ loke, sato samativattatī”ti. (su. ni. 774; mahāni. 3) –

"He who avoids sensual pleasures as one avoids a snake's head with the foot—he, being mindful, transcends this entanglement in the world."

Idha pāḷigāthāyaṃ yaṃ samativattanakaraṇaṃ maggasaṅkhātaṃ nissaraṇaṃ āgataṃ, taṃ idaṃ maggasaṅkhātaṃ samativattanakaraṇaṃ nissaraṇaṃ desanāhārassa visayanti.

Here in this Pāli verse, the escape designated as the path, which is the means for transcending, has appeared; this very escape designated as the path, the means for transcending, is the object of the Teaching Mode.

Gāthāyaṃ yoti jhānalābhī vā ariyo vā. Kāmeti vuttappakāro vatthukāmo. Tesu pavattachandarāgassa vikkhambhanena vā samucchindanena vā parivajjeti. Kiṃ parivajjeti iva vajjeti? Sappassa siro siraṃ cakkhumā puriso disvā padā pādena parivajjeti iva, evaṃ parivajjeti. Sato satisampanno so puggalo loke rūpādīsu visattikaṃ imaṃ taṇhaṃ yena maggena samativattati saṃ suṭṭhu atikkamitvā vattati, idaṃ maggasaṅkhātaṃ samativattanakaraṇaṃ ekadesaṃ nissaraṇaṃ nāmāti yojetabbaṃ. “Pādā”ti vattabbe ākārassa rassaṃ katvā “padā”ti vuttaṃ. Pādāti ca pādena yathā “amohabhāvā amohabhāvenā”ti. Tena vuttaṃ “attano pādenā”ti (netti. aṭṭha. 5).

In the verse, ‘he’ (yo) means one who has attained jhāna or a noble one. ‘Sensual pleasures’ (kāme) means the sensual pleasure as object of the type stated. He avoids them by suppressing or by eradicating the desire and lust that has arisen in regard to them. How does he avoid them? Just as a clear-sighted person, having seen a snake’s head, avoids it with his foot, so does he avoid them. That person, being mindful and endowed with mindfulness, by which path he transcends—that is, he thoroughly overcomes and abides—this craving, this entanglement in the world regarding forms and so forth, this means for transcending designated as the path is called a partial escape—this is how it should be construed. When ‘pādā’ should be said, the long vowel ‘ā’ is made short, and ‘padā’ is said. And ‘pādā’ is used for the instrumental ‘pādena’ (with the foot), just as ‘amohabhāvā’ is used for ‘amohabhāvena.’ Therefore it is said, ‘with his own foot’.

Ekadeso visayasaṅkhāto assādo idha pāḷiyaṃ āgatoti ācariyena vibhatto, amhehi ca ñāto, “ekadeso visayisaṅkhāto assādo kattha pāḷiyaṃ āgato”ti pucchitabbattā “tattha [V 0.0198] katamo assādo? Khettaṃ vatthu”ntiādi āraddhaṃ. Atha vā “tattha katamo assādo? Khettaṃ vatthu”ntiādi kasmā evaṃ āraddhaṃ, nanu “tattha katamo assādo? Kāmaṃ kāmayamānassā”tiādinā assādo vibhatto? Saccaṃ, assādo pana duvidho visayavisayivasena, tasmiṃ visayasaṅkhāto assādo pubbe vibhatto, idāni visayisaṅkhātaṃ assādaṃ vibhajituṃ “tattha katamo assādo? Khettaṃ vatthu”ntiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha tatthāti tassaṃ “assādādīnavatā”tiādigāthāyaṃ niddiṭṭhesu visayavisayibhedesu assādesu katamo assādo tattha tesu pāḷidhammesu kattha pāḷiyaṃ āgatoti pucchitvā –

The gratification designated as object, which is one aspect, has appeared here in the Pāli—thus it has been analyzed by the teacher and is known by us. Because it should be asked, ‘Where in the Pāli has the gratification designated as subject, which is one aspect, appeared?’, the section beginning, ‘Therein, what is the gratification? A field, a plot of land…’ has been commenced. Or else, why has the section beginning, ‘Therein, what is the gratification? A field, a plot of land…’ been commenced in this way? Was not gratification already analyzed by the section beginning, ‘Therein, what is the gratification? For one desiring a sensual pleasure…’? True, but gratification is twofold, by way of object and subject. Among these, the gratification designated as object was analyzed previously. Now, to analyze the gratification designated as subject, the section beginning, ‘Therein, what is the gratification? A field, a plot of land…’ has been commenced. Therein, that is: in that verse beginning ‘gratification, its drawback,’ among the gratifications specified by the distinction of object and subject, having asked, ‘which gratification has appeared where in the Pāli, among those Pāli Dhammas?’—

“Khettaṃ vatthuṃ [M 0.0058] hiraññaṃ vā, gavāssaṃ dāsaporisaṃ;

Thiyo bandhū puthū kāme, yo naro anugijjhatī”ti. (su. ni. 775; mahāni. 4) –

"A field, a plot of land, or gold, cattle and horses, slaves and servants; women, relatives, and the many sensual pleasures—the man who is greedy for these…"

Idha pāḷigāthāyaṃ yo anugijjhanasaṅkhāto assādo āgato, so ayaṃ anugijjhanasaṅkhāto visayiassādo desanāhārassa visayoti.

Here in this Pāli verse, the gratification designated as greed has appeared; this very gratification designated as greed, which is the subject’s gratification, is the object of the Teaching Mode.

Gāthāyaṃ khettanti khipīyanti bījāni ettha ṭhāneti khettaṃ. Khipantānaṃ janānaṃ khipanakiriyā khipa-dhātuyā mukhyattho, khipanakiriyājanako cittuppādo phalūpacārattho, tassa cittuppādassa upanissayapaccayabhūtassa kedārassa viruḷhāpanasatti phalūpacārattho, iti-saddena sā viruḷhāpanasattiyeva parāmasīyati, tassā sattiyā patiṭṭhaṃ kedārasaṅkhātaṃ ṭhānaṃ ta-paccayattho. Esa nayo tīsu piṭakesu evarūpesu ca vacanatthesu yathārahaṃ nīharitvā gahetabbo. Vapanti patiṭṭhahanti etthāti vatthu. Aparaṇṇādīnaṃ patiṭṭhahanaṃ vapa-dhātuyā mukhyattho, ṭhānassa patiṭṭhāpanasatti phalūpacārattho, iti-saddena sā patiṭṭhāpanasatti parāmasīyati. Tassā sattiyā patiṭṭhaṭṭhānaṃ ta-paccayattho. Khettaṃ pana pubbaṇṇavirūhanaṭṭhānaṃ, vatthu aparaṇṇavirūhanaṭṭhānaṃ.

In the verse, khetta (field) means the place where seeds are scattered. For the people who scatter, the primary meaning of the root khip is the act of scattering. The mental state that generates the act of scattering is a secondary meaning. The power of the field to cause growth, which is a decisive support condition for that mental state, is a secondary meaning. By the word 'iti,' that very power to cause growth is referred to. The place designated as the field, which is the basis of that power, is the meaning of the suffix ta. This method should be extracted and applied appropriately in the three Piṭakas and in similar word-meanings. 'They sow' and 'are established' in this place, hence it is a vatthu (plot of land). For later crops and so forth, the primary meaning of the root vap is the act of being established. The power of the place to cause establishment is a secondary meaning. By the word 'iti,' that power of establishment is referred to. The place which is the basis of that power is the meaning of the suffix ta. A field, however, is the place for the growth of early crops, while a plot of land is the place for the growth of later crops.

Hinoti pavattati pītisomanassanti hi, kiṃ taṃ? Pītisomanassaṃ, rāti pavatteti jātarūpanti raṃ, kiṃ taṃ? Jātarūpaṃ, hiṃ ranti hiraṃ, dutiyātappurisasamāso. Ñāpeti tosetīti ñaṃ, kiṃ taṃ? Jātarūpaṃ. Hiraṃ hutvā ñaṃ hiraññaṃ, pavattamānaṃ pītisomanassaṃ pavattetvā jane visesena tosetīti attho gahetabbo. Vā-saddo vuttāvuttatthasamuccayattho. Gacchanti visesenāti gāvo, rattindivaṃ asanti bhakkhanti visesenāti assā, gāvo ca assā ca gavāssaṃ. Dātabbaṃ paṭhamaṃ dentīti dā, asanti bhakkhantīti asā, datvā asā dāsā[V 0.0199], sāmikānaṃ dātabbaṃ paṭhamaṃ datvā pacchā asanti bhakkhantīti attho. Sāmikehi vā dinnaṃ asanti bhakkhantīti dāsā, dukkhena kasirena asanti pavattantīti vā dāsā,. Mātāpitūnaṃ hadayaṃ purentīti purisā, puraṃ hitaṃ vā isanti gavesantīti purisā. Buddhapaccekabuddhacakkavattibhāvaṃ pureti kammanti puraṃ, kiṃ taṃ? Balavakammaṃ, puraṃ isanti sīlenāti vā purisā. Purisā eva hi sammāsambuddhapaccekabuddhacakkavattibhāvaṃ gacchanti. “Puri uccaṭṭhāne sentīti vā purisā. Purisā [M 0.0059] hi mātūnaṃ pituṭṭhāne ṭhitā”ti ime vacanatthā vuttappakārā yuttāyeva atthasambhavato. Dāsā ca purisā ca dāsaporisaṃ, majjhe vuddhi. Ettha ca dāsaggahaṇena dāsīpi gahitā. Dāsā dukkaṭajanā, purisā sukhitajanāti viseso daṭṭhabbo. Ṭhanti patiṭṭhahanti ettha mātugāme puttadhītāti thiyo. Narasaddassa viggahattho heṭṭhā vuttova.

It produces joy and happiness, hence 'hi'; what is that? Joy and happiness. It produces gold, hence 'raṃ'; what is that? Gold. From 'hi' and 'raṃ' comes 'hiraṃ'—a tatpurisa compound of the second type. It pleases and satisfies, hence 'ñaṃ'; what is that? Gold. Having become 'hiraṃ', it is 'ñaṃ', hence 'hiraññaṃ'; the meaning to be understood is that it pleases people especially by producing ongoing joy and happiness. The particle 'vā' serves to combine stated and unstated meanings. They go especially—these are cows. They eat day and night especially—these are horses. Cows and horses together are 'gavāssaṃ.' They give what is to be given first, hence 'dā'; they eat, hence 'asā'; having given, they eat, hence 'dāsā' (servants). The meaning is that they first give what is to be given to their masters, and then eat. Or, they eat what is given by their masters, hence they are 'dāsā.' Or, they live on with difficulty and hardship, hence they are 'dāsā.' They fill the hearts of their parents—these are 'purisā' (men). Or, they seek what is beneficial for the city, hence 'purisā.' The kamma that fulfills the state of a Buddha, a Paccekabuddha, or a wheel-turning monarch is 'puraṃ'; what is that? Powerful kamma. Or, they seek the city through virtue—these are 'purisā.' Indeed, men attain the state of a fully enlightened Buddha, a Paccekabuddha, or a wheel-turning monarch. 'Or, they lie or dwell in high places—these are 'purisā.' For men stand in the place of fathers to mothers'—these meanings, as stated, are appropriate due to their coherence with the meaning. Servants and men together are 'dāsaporisaṃ,' with strengthening in the middle. Here, by the term 'dāsā,' female servants are also included. Servants are unfortunate people, men are fortunate people—this distinction should be noted. They stand and are established here in the family as mothers of sons and daughters, hence 'thiyo' (women). The etymological analysis of the word 'nara' has been stated below.

Ekadeso domanassasaṅkhāto ādīnavo idha pāḷigāthāyaṃ āgatoti ācariyena vibhatto, amhehi ca ñāto, “dukkhasaṅkhāto ādīnavo kattha pāḷiyaṃ āgato”ti pucchitabbattā “tattha katamo ādīnavo? Abalā naṃ balīyantī”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Atha vā “tattha katamo ādīnavo? Abalā naṃ balīyantī”tiādi kasmā evaṃ āraddhaṃ, nanu “tattha katamo ādīnavo? Tassa ce kāmayānassā”tiādinā ādīnavo vibhattoti? Saccaṃ, ādīnavo pana bahuvidho dukkhadomanassādivasena, tasmiṃ bahuvidhe ādīnave ekadeso domanassasaṅkhāto ādīnavo pubbe vibhatto, idāni dukkhasaṅkhātaṃ ādīnavaṃ vibhajituṃ “tattha katamo ādīnavo? Abalā naṃ balīyantī”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha tatthāti tassaṃ “assādādīnavatā”tiādigāthāyaṃ niddiṭṭhesu dukkhadomanassādīsu ādīnavesu katamo ādīnavo tattha tesu pāḷidhammesu kattha pāḷidhamme āgatoti pucchitvā –

A portion of the danger, designated as mental distress, is mentioned here in the Pāli verse, as explained by the teacher, and is known to us. Since the question should be asked, 'Where in the Pāli texts is the danger designated as suffering mentioned?', therefore, the passage beginning 'Therein, what is the danger? The weak overpower him...' is introduced. Alternatively, why is it begun thus with, 'Therein, what is the danger? The weak overpower him...'? Was not the danger explained previously with, 'Therein, what is the danger? If for one who desires them...'? Indeed, danger is manifold, consisting of suffering, mental distress, and so forth. Within that manifold danger, a portion designated as mental distress was previously explained. Now, to analyze the danger designated as suffering, it is begun with, 'Therein, what is the danger? The weak overpower him...'. Here, 'therein' refers to that verse beginning 'allure and danger...'; among the dangers such as suffering and mental distress that are mentioned, the question is asked: 'Which danger? In which Pāli teaching is it mentioned?' Having asked this—

“Abalā naṃ balīyanti, maddantenaṃ parissayā;

Tato naṃ dukkhamanveti, nāvaṃ bhinnamivodaka”nti. (su. ni. 776; mahāni. 5) –

The weak overpower him,

he is crushed by dangers;

then suffering follows him,

like water entering a broken boat.

Idha pāḷigāthāyaṃ yo dukkhasaṅkhāto ekadeso ādīnavo āgato, so ayaṃ dukkhasaṅkhāto ekadeso ādīnavo desanāhārassa visayoti.

Here, in this Pāli verse, the portion of danger that has appeared, designated as suffering—this portion of danger designated as suffering is the subject matter of the discourse-method.

Gāthāyaṃ natthi balaṃ etesaṃ kilesānanti abalā. Kasmā kilesā abalā hontīti? Kusalehi pahātabbattā. Naranti khettādikāme anugijjhantaṃ naraṃ, saddhābalādivirahato vā abalaṃ [V 0.0200] taṃ naraṃ balīyanti abhibhavanti. Kiñcāpi kilesā kusalehi pahātabbattā abalā honti, tathāpi kāmamanugijjhantaṃ saddhābalādivirahitaṃ abhibhavituṃ samatthā bhavanti. Maddantenaṃ parissayāti kāmagiddhaṃ kāme pariyesantaṃ, kāmaṃ rakkhantañca [M 0.0060] enaṃ naraṃ pari samantato paripīḷetvā ayanti pavattantīti parissayā, sīhabyagghādayo ceva kāyaduccaritādayo ca maddanti. Tato tehi parissayehi abhibhūtaṃ naṃ naraṃ jātiādidukkhaṃ anveti anugacchati. Kimiva anveti? Udakaṃ bhinnanāvaṃ anveti iva, evaṃ anvetīti attho.

In this verse, 'there is no strength in these defilements', hence they are 'weak' (abalā). Why are defilements weak? Because they are to be abandoned by wholesome qualities. They overpower (balīyanti) the man (naraṃ)—that is, the man who is engrossed in fields and other sensual pleasures, or that weak (abalaṃ) man who lacks the strength of faith and so on. Although defilements are weak because they are to be abandoned by wholesome qualities, nevertheless, they are capable of overpowering the man who is engrossed in sensual pleasures and lacks the strength of faith and so on. Regarding 'dangers crush him': 'dangers' (parissayā) are so called because they proceed, pressing down completely from all around, upon that man who is greedy for sensual pleasures, who seeks and guards them. Lions, tigers, and so on, and bodily misconduct and so on, are what crush him. Then, overwhelmed by these dangers, the suffering of birth and so on follows that man. How does it follow? Just as water follows a broken boat, so it follows—this is the meaning.

Ekadesaṃ maggasaṅkhātaṃ nissaraṇaṃ idha pāḷigāthāyaṃ āgatanti ācariyena vibhattaṃ, amheti ca viññātaṃ, “nibbānasaṅkhātaṃ ekadesaṃ nissaraṇaṃ kattha pāḷidhamme āgata”nti pucchitabbattā “tattha katamaṃ nissaraṇaṃ? Tasmā jantu sadā sato”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Atha vā “tattha katamaṃ nissaraṇaṃ? Tasmā jantu sadā sato”tiādi kasmā evaṃ āraddhaṃ, nanu “tattha katamaṃ nissaraṇaṃ? Yo kāme parivajjetī”tiādinā nissaraṇaṃ vibhattanti? Saccaṃ, nissaraṇaṃ pana duvidhaṃ magganibbānavasena, tattha duvidhe nissaraṇe maggasaṅkhātaṃ nissaraṇaṃ pubbe vibhattaṃ, idāni nibbānasaṅkhātaṃ nissaraṇaṃ vibhajituṃ “tattha katamaṃ nissaraṇaṃ? Tasmā jantu sadā sato”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha tatthāti tassaṃ “assādādīnavatā”tiādigāthāyaṃ niddiṭṭhesu magganibbānesu nissaraṇesu ekadesaṃ nibbānasaṅkhātaṃ nissaraṇaṃ tattha tesu pāḷidhammesu kattha pāḷidhamme āgatanti pucchitvā –

A portion, the escape designated as the path, has appeared here in the Pāli verse, as has been analyzed by the teacher and is understood by us. Since the question should be asked, 'Where in the Pāli teachings does the portion which is the escape designated as Nibbāna appear?', the passage beginning 'Therein, what is the escape? Therefore, a being, ever mindful...' is introduced. Alternatively, why is the passage beginning 'Therein, what is the escape? Therefore, a being, ever mindful...' introduced in this way? Was not the escape already analyzed with the passage beginning 'Therein, what is the escape? One who avoids sensual pleasures...'? True, but the escape is twofold, by way of the path and Nibbāna. Among these two kinds of escape, the escape designated as the path was analyzed previously. Now, to analyze the escape designated as Nibbāna, the passage beginning 'Therein, what is the escape? Therefore, a being, ever mindful...' is introduced. Here, 'therein' refers to that verse beginning 'allure and danger...'; among the escapes of path and Nibbāna mentioned therein, regarding the portion which is the escape designated as Nibbāna, the question is asked: 'Among those Pāli teachings, in which Pāli teaching does it appear?' Having asked this—

“Tasmā jantu sadā sato, kāmāni parivajjaye;

Te pahāya tare oghaṃ, nāvaṃ sitvāva pāragū”ti. –

Therefore, always mindful, a living being should avoid sensual desires;

having abandoned them, one should cross the flood,

like one who has gone to the far shore, having bailed out the boat.

Idha pāḷigāthāyaṃ yaṃ nibbānasaṅkhātaṃ nissaraṇaṃ āgataṃ, idaṃ nissaraṇaṃ desanāhārassa visayanti.

Here, in this Pāli verse, the escape designated as Nibbāna which has appeared—this escape is the subject matter of the discourse-method.

Gāthāyaṃ tasmāti yasmā kāmagiddhaṃ naraṃ dukkhaṃ anveti, tasmā jantu sadā sabbakāle pubbarattāpararatte jāgariyānuyogena sato satisampanno hutvā kāmāni kilesakāme vikkhambhanavasena vā samucchedavasena vā parivajjaye parijaheyya. Te kāme ariyamaggena pahāya catubbidhaṃ oghaṃ tareyya tarituṃ sakkuṇeyya. Ko tarati iva tareyya? Nāvāsāmiko nāvaṃ yaṃ pavisantaṃ udakaṃ sitvā bahi siñcitvā lahukāya nāvāya appakasirena taritvā pāragū pāraṃ gacchati iva, evaṃ attani pavattaṃ kilesūdakaṃ siñcitvā ariyamaggena nīharitvā lahukena attabhāvena anupādisesāya [V 0.0201] nibbānadhātuyā nibbānena pāraṃ nibbānaṃ santiṃ [M 0.0061] gaccheyyāti attho. Idaṃ nibbānaṃ kasmā nissaraṇaṃ hoti? Sabbasaṅkhatanissaraṇato nissaraṇaṃ nāma.

In the verse, 'therefore' means: because suffering follows a person greedy for sensual pleasures, therefore a being should always, at all times—in the early and late parts of the night—by applying wakefulness, being mindful and possessed of mindfulness, avoid and abandon sensual pleasures, that is, the defilements of sensuality, either by way of suppression or by way of eradication. Having abandoned these sensual pleasures through the Noble Path, one should cross, one would be able to cross, the fourfold flood. As who crosses, should one cross? Just as the owner of a boat, having bailed out the water that entered the boat and poured it outside, crosses with little trouble in a light boat and reaches the far shore; even so, having bailed out the water of defilements that has arisen in oneself and removed it through the Noble Path, with a lightened personal existence one would reach the far shore, Nibbāna, which is peace, by means of Nibbāna, the Nibbāna-element with no residue remaining. This is the meaning. Why is this Nibbāna called an escape? It is called an escape because it is the escape from all things conditioned.

Idaṃ nissaraṇaṃ idha pāḷidhamme āgatanti ācariyena vibhattaṃ, amhehi ca viññātaṃ, “katamaṃ phalaṃ kattha pāḷidhamme āgata”nti pucchitabbattā “tattha katamaṃ phalaṃ? Dhammo have rakkhati dhammacāri”ntiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha tatthāti tassaṃ “assādādīnavatā”tiādigāthāyaṃ niddiṭṭhesu rakkhananipphādanamaccutaraṇādīsu phalesu katamaṃ phalaṃ tattha tesu pāḷidhammesu kattha pāḷidhamme āgatanti pucchitvā –

'This escape has come here in the Pāli Dhamma'—this has been analyzed by the teacher and understood by us. Because it should be asked, 'Which fruit has come where in the Pāli Dhamma?', the section beginning 'Therein, which fruit? Indeed, the Dhamma protects one who lives by the Dhamma,' and so on, is introduced. 'Therein' means: having asked, 'Among the fruits indicated in that verse beginning with 'the allure and danger'—such as protection, accomplishment, and crossing over death—which fruit, therein, among those Pāli Dhammas, has come where in the Pāli Dhamma?'—

“Dhammo have rakkhati dhammacāriṃ, chattaṃ mahantaṃ yatha vassakāle;

Esānisaṃso dhamme suciṇṇe, na duggatiṃ gacchati dhammacārī”ti. (su. ni. 102, 103) –

Indeed, the Dhamma protects one who practices the Dhamma,

like a great umbrella in the rainy season.

This is the benefit of Dhamma well practiced;

a practitioner of the Dhamma does not go to a bad destination.

Idha pāḷigāthāyaṃ yaṃ anatthehi dhammassa rakkhanaphalaṃ āgataṃ, rakkhāvahanassa abbhudayassa yañca nipphādanaṃ phalaṃ āgataṃ, idaṃ rakkhananipphādanaṃ phalaṃ desanāhārassa visayanti.

Here, in this Pāli verse, the fruit that is the Dhamma's protection from harm has come, and also the fruit that is the accomplishment of prosperity which brings protection has come. This fruit of protection and accomplishment is the subject of the Desanāhāra.

Gāthāyaṃ dhammoti yena puggalena yo dānādippabhedo puññadhammo nibbattito, so dhammo. Dhammacāriṃ dhammanibbattakaṃ taṃ puggalaṃ anatthehi rakkhati. Kimiva? Vassakāle deve vassante sati mahantaṃ kusalena dhāretabbaṃ chattaṃ dhārentaṃ kusalaṃ taṃ janaṃ vassatemanato rakkhati yathā, evaṃ rakkhitabbo dhammopi attasammāpaṇidhānena appamatto hutvā suṭṭhu dhammaṃ rakkhantaṃyeva rakkhati, tādiso dhammacārīyeva duggatiṃ na gacchati. Eso ānisaṃso suciṇṇe suciṇṇassa dhamme dhammassa ānisaṃsoti attho.

In the verse, 'Dhamma' is that meritorious Dhamma, of the variety of giving and so on, that has been produced by a person. That Dhamma protects the Dhamma-farer, that person who produced the Dhamma, from harm. Like what? Just as, in the rainy season when it is raining, a large umbrella, skillfully held, protects the person holding it from being drenched by the rain; even so, the Dhamma, which should itself be protected, protects only one who protects the Dhamma well, being heedful with right application of self. Only such a Dhamma-farer does not go to a bad destination. 'This is the benefit in the well-practiced' means it is the benefit of the Dhamma that has been well-practiced.

Ekadesaṃ phalaṃ idha pāḷidhamme āgatanti ācariyena vibhattaṃ, amhehi ca ñātaṃ, “katamo upāyo kattha pāḷiyaṃ āgato”ti pucchitabbattā “tattha katamo upāyo? Sabbe saṅkhārā aniccā”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha tatthāti tassaṃ “assādādīnavatā”tiādigāthāyaṃ niddiṭṭhesu vipassanāpubbaṅgamanibbidādīsu upāyesu katamo upāyo tattha tesu pāḷidhammesu kattha pāḷidhamme āgatoti pucchitvā –

'A portion of the fruit has come here in the Pāli Dhamma'—this has been analyzed by the teacher and is known by us. Because it should be asked, 'Which means has come where in the Pāli?', the section beginning, 'Therein, which means? All formations are impermanent,' and so on, is introduced. 'Therein' means: having asked, 'Among the means indicated in that verse beginning with 'the allure and danger'—such as disenchantment which has insight as its forerunner—which means, therein, among those Pāli Dhammas, has come where in the Pāli Dhamma?'—

“Sabbe [V 0.0202][M 0.0062] saṅkhārā ‘aniccā’ti…pe…;

Sabbe dhammā ‘anattā’ti, yadā paññāya passatī”ti. (dha. pa. 277-279) –

All formations are impermanent…;

All phenomena are not-self—

when one sees this with wisdom…

Idha pāḷigāthāsu yo vipassanāpubbaṅgamanibbidāñāṇasaṅkhāto visuddhiyā adhigamahetubhāvato maggo āgato, ayaṃ upāyo desanāhārassa visayoti.

Here, in these Pāli verses, the path—which is known as the knowledge of disenchantment with insight as its forerunner, being the cause for the attainment of purity—has come. This means is the subject of the Desanāhāra.

Gāthāsu sabbe niravasesā kammacittotuāhārehi saṅkharitā saṅkhatasaṅkhārā hutvā abhāvaṭṭhena aniccā iti yadā paññāya passati, atha anicce dukkhasabhāve nibbindati, eso vipassanāpubbaṅgamo nibbindanañāṇasaṅkhāto dhammo visuddhiyā maggoti. “Sabbe saṅkhārā aniccā”tiādīsu saṅkhārānaṃ saṅkhatadhammabhāvo paccayākāravibhaṅgaṭṭhakathāyaṃ (vibha. aṭṭha. 226 saṅkhārapadaniddesa) vuttova, taṃ vibhaṅgaṭṭhakathaṃ anoloketvā ekacce ācariyā “vipassanāñāṇārammaṇattā tebhūmakadhammāyevā”ti vadanti, evaṃ sati maggaphaladhammānaṃ niccādibhāvo bhaveyya, tasmā vibhaṅgaṭṭhakathānurūpova attho daṭṭhabbo. Dukkhāti dukkhadukkhavipariṇāmadukkhasaṅkhāradukkhabhāvena dukkhā. Anattāti niccasārasukhasāraattasārarahitattā asārakaṭṭhena anattā, avasavattanaṭṭhena vā anattā.

In the verses, all without exception, being conditioned by kamma, mind, temperature, and nutriment, and having become conditioned formations, are impermanent in the sense of their ceasing to be. When one sees this with wisdom, then one becomes disenchanted with that which is impermanent and of a suffering nature. This Dhamma, called the knowledge of disenchantment which has insight as its forerunner, is the path to purity. In the phrases, 'All formations are impermanent,' and so on, the nature of formations as conditioned phenomena is stated in the Commentary to the Vibhaṅga. Without referring to that Commentary to the Vibhaṅga, some teachers say, 'They are only phenomena of the three realms because they are the object of insight knowledge.' If that were so, the path and fruition states would have the nature of permanence, and so on. Therefore, the meaning should be understood in accordance with the Commentary to the Vibhaṅga. 'Suffering' means suffering in the sense of pain, suffering due to change, and suffering inherent in formations. 'Not-self' means not-self in the sense of being essenceless, as it is devoid of a permanent essence, a pleasant essence, or a self-essence; or not-self in the sense of being uncontrollable.

Ekadeso upāyo idha pāḷidhamme āgatoti ācariyena vibhatto, amhehi ca ñāto, “katamā āṇatti kattha pāḷidhamme āgatā”ti pucchitabbattā “tattha katamā āṇatti? Cakkhumā visamānīvā”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha tatthāti tassaṃ “assādādīnavatā”tiādigāthāyaṃ niddiṭṭhāsu pāpaduccaritaparivajjanāṇattikalyāṇasucaritacaraṇāṇattiādīsu katamāṇatti tattha tesu pāḷidhammesu kattha pāḷidhamme āgatāti pucchitvā –

'A portion of the means has come here in the Pāli Dhamma'—this has been analyzed by the teacher and is known by us. Because it should be asked, 'Which injunction has come where in the Pāli Dhamma?', the section beginning, 'Therein, which injunction? As one with eyes avoids uneven paths,' and so on, is introduced. 'Therein' means: among the injunctions indicated in that verse beginning with 'the allure and danger'—such as the injunction to avoid evil and bad conduct and the injunction to practice good and wholesome conduct—having asked, 'Which injunction, therein, among those Pāli Dhammas, has come where in the Pāli Dhamma?'—

“Cakkhumā visamānīva, vijjamāne parakkame;

Paṇḍito jīvalokasmiṃ, pāpāni parivajjaye”ti. (udā. 43) –

As one with eyes avoids uneven paths,

so too, where exertion is possible,

a wise person in the world of the living

should avoid evil deeds.

Idha pāḷidhamme yā pāpaduccaritaparivajjanāṇatti āgatā, ayaṃ pāpaduccaritaparivajjanāṇatti desanāhārassa visayāti.

Here in the Pāli Dhamma, the injunction that has come concerning the avoidance of evil and bad conduct—this injunction concerning the avoidance of evil and bad conduct is the subject of the Desanāhāra.

Gāthāyaṃ cakkhumā puriso vijjamāne parakkame āvahitaṃ sarīraṃ āvahantova hutvā visamāni [V 0.0203] bhūmippadesāni vā visame hatthiādayo vā [M 0.0063] parivajjeti iva, evaṃ jīvalokasmiṃ paṇḍito pāpāni lāmakāni duccaritāni parivajjeti. Āṇatti nāma āṇārahassa dhammarājassa bhagavato āṇā, sā bahuvidhā, tasmā “kareyya kalyāṇa”ntiādigāthāyaṃ sucaritacaraṇā āṇatti.

In the verse: just as a person with eyes, where exertion is possible, bearing their body carefully, avoids uneven regions of ground or dangerous things such as elephants; even so, in the world of the living, a wise person avoids evil, base, and bad deeds. An injunction is the command of the Blessed One, the King of Dhamma, who is worthy of commanding. It is of many kinds; therefore, in the verse beginning, 'One should do good,' the practice of good conduct is an injunction.

“Upetha saraṇaṃ buddhaṃ, dhammaṃ saṅghañca tādinaṃ;

Samādiyatha sīlāni, taṃ vo atthāya hehitī”ti. (therīgā. 249-250, 289-290) –

Go for refuge to the Buddha, the Such-like One,

and to the Dhamma and the Sangha;

undertake the precepts—

that will be for your welfare.

Ādīsu gāthāsu saraṇagamanāṇattisīlasamādānāṇattiādi āgatāti.

In verses such as the preceding one, the injunction to go for refuge, the injunction to undertake the precepts, and so on, have come.

“Suññato lokaṃ avekkhassū”tiādi kasmā evaṃ āraddhaṃ, nanu “tattha katamaṃ phalaṃ? Dhammo have”tiādinā, “tattha katamo upāyo? Sabbe saṅkhārā”tiādinā, “tattha katamā āṇatti? Cakkhumā”tiādinā ca phalūpāyāṇattiyo vibhattāti? Saccaṃ, visuṃ visuṃ pana suttesu āgatā phalūpāyāṇattiyo vibhattā, idāni ekato āgatā phalūpāyāṇattiyo vibhajituṃ “suññato lokaṃ avekkhassū”tiādi āraddhaṃ.

Why is the passage beginning, 'Look upon the world as empty,' and so on, introduced in this way? Have not the fruit, means, and injunctions already been analyzed by means of the passages beginning, 'Therein, which fruit? The Dhamma, indeed…,' 'Therein, which means? All formations…,' and 'Therein, which injunction? One with eyes…,' respectively? True, but the fruits, means, and injunctions that have come separately in various suttas have been analyzed. Now, in order to analyze the fruits, means, and injunctions that have come together in one place, the passage beginning, 'Look upon the world as empty,' is introduced.

Tattha suññato lokaṃ avekkhassūti sabbampi saṅkhāralokaṃ attato suññoti avasavattitāsallakkhaṇavasena vā tucchabhāvasamanupassanavasena vā passāti idaṃ bhagavato vacanaṃ vidhānabhāvato āṇatti nāma. Niccasārasukhasāraattasārādirahitattā “mogharājā”ti ālapati, saddhāsīlasutacāgādirahitattā vā mogho.

Here, 'Look upon the world as empty' means seeing the entire conditioned world as empty of self—either through the characteristic of being uncontrollable or through perceiving its insubstantial nature. This statement of the Blessed One, being a directive, is called the instruction. Because it lacks the substance of permanence, happiness, self, and so on, he addresses him as 'Mogharāja.' Or, because one lacks faith, virtue, learning, generosity, and so on, one is 'empty' (mogha).

“Sadā sato”ti puggalavasena vuttāya satiyā suññatādassanassa sampajānahetubhāvato satiyeva upāyo, na satimāti ettha satīti adhippāyo.

'Ever mindful'—mindfulness, spoken of in terms of a person, being the cause of clear comprehension in seeing emptiness, is itself the means, not merely the mindful person. Here, 'mindfulness' is the intended meaning.

Attānudiṭṭhiṃ ūhaccāti ettha attānudiṭṭhi nāma “rūpaṃ attā, rūpavā attā, rūpasmiṃ attā, attani rūpa”ntiādippakārā vīsativatthukā diṭṭhi. Maggena ūhacca samucchinditvā evaṃ vuttavidhinā maccutaro maccuno visayātikkanto siyā bhaveyya. Ettha yaṃ maccuvisayaṃ taraṇaṃ atikkamanaṃ, tassa atikkamanassa yañca pubbabhāgapaṭipadāsampajjanaṃ, idaṃ bhagavato desanāya [V 0.0204] phalaṃ desanāhārassa visayanti adhippāyo. Pubbe visuṃ visuṃ phalūpāyāṇattiyo vibhattāpi –

'Having uprooted the view of self'—here, the view of self is the twenty-faceted view, such as 'form is self,' 'self possesses form,' 'self is in form,' 'form is in self,' and so on. Having uprooted and completely cut it off with the path, one may thus, by the method described, become a transcender of death, one who has gone beyond the realm of death. Here, the intended meaning is that this transcendence of the realm of death, this crossing beyond it, and the attainment of the preliminary practice for that transcendence—this is the fruit of the Blessed One’s teaching, the subject of the teaching's discourse. Though the fruit, means, and instruction were previously distinguished separately—

“Suññato [M 0.0064] lokaṃ avekkhassu, mogharāja sadā sato;

Attānudiṭṭhiṃ ūhacca, evaṃ maccutaro siyā”ti. (su. ni. 1125; mahāni. 186; cūḷani. piṅgiyamāṇavapucchā 144, mogharājamāṇavapucchāniddesa 88) –

'View the world as empty, Mogharāja, ever mindful; having uprooted the view of self, thus one may transcend death.' (Snp 1119; Mahāni 186; Cūḷani Piṅgiyamāṇavapucchā 144, Mogharājamāṇavapucchāniddesa 88)

Ekagāthāyaṃ puna ekato vibhajanato phalādīsu ekato dassitesu sabbattha suttesu vā sabbattha gāthāsu vā phalādayo dassetabbā assādādayo viya katthaci niddhāretvāti viseso vijānitabbo. Tenāha aṭṭhakathācariyo “yathā pana…pe… ekato udāharaṇaṃ katanti daṭṭhabba”nti (netti. aṭṭha. 5).

Again, since in a single verse they are analyzed together and the fruits and so on are shown together, this distinction should be known: that just as the allurements and so on are determined in some place, so the fruits and so on are to be pointed out in all discourses or all verses. Therefore, the commentary teacher said, 'Just as... an example is given together... this should be seen.' (Netti-aṭṭha 5)

6. Desanāhārassa visayabhūtā assādādayo “idha pāḷidhamme ayaṃ assādo āgato, idha pāḷidhamme ayaṃ ādīnavo āgato”tiādinā visesato nidassanavasena sarūpato ācariyena vibhattā, te assādādayo tiṇṇaṃ ugghaṭitaññuādīnaṃ puggalānaṃ sāmaññato bhagavā kiṃ nu kho deseti, udāhu ekassa puggalassa yathālābhaṃ kiṃ nu desetīti anuyogassa sambhavato imassa puggalassa imaṃ deseti, imassa puggalassa imaṃ desetīti puggalabhedena assādādayo vibhajitvā dassetuṃ “tattha bhagavā ugghaṭitaññussā”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha tatthāti tesu assādādīsu. Nissaraṇaṃ ugghaṭitaññussa puggalassa bhagavā deseti, ādīnavañca nissaraṇañca ime dve vipañcitaññussa puggalassa bhagavā deseti, assādañca ādīnavañca nissaraṇañca ime tayo neyyassa puggalassa bhagavā desetīti yojanattho daṭṭhabbo.

6. The allurements and so on, which are the subject of the teaching's discourse, have been explained in detail by the teacher by way of example, distinguishing their nature as follows: 'Here in the Pāli teaching, this allure has come; here in the Pāli teaching, this danger has come,' and so on. Because an inquiry might arise as to whether the Blessed One teaches these allurements and so on generally to the three types of individuals beginning with the one who understands quickly, or whether he teaches something to each individual according to their capacity, the passage 'Therein, the Blessed One teaches to the one who understands quickly,' and so on, is begun in order to show the allurements and so on by distinguishing them according to the types of individuals, saying, 'He teaches this to this individual, he teaches that to that individual.' 'Therein, therein' means among these allurements and so on. The Blessed One teaches the escape to the individual who understands quickly. The Blessed One teaches the danger and the escape, these two, to the individual who understands after elaboration. The Blessed One teaches the allure, the danger, and the escape, these three, to the individual who needs guidance. This is the application of the meaning to be understood.

Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana “evaṃ assādādayo udāharaṇavasena sarūpato dassetvā idāni tattha puggalavibhāgena desanāvibhāgaṃ dassetuṃ ‘tattha bhagavā’tiādi vutta”nti vuttaṃ.

In the commentary, however, it is said: 'Having thus shown the allurements and so forth by way of examples as to their nature, now to show the division of the teaching by way of classifying individuals therein, it is said, "Therein, the Blessed One," etc.'

Tattha ugghaṭitaññussāti ugghaṭīyate paṭivijjhīyate, ṭhapīyate vā sappabhedo vitthāro atthoti ugghaṭito, jānātīti ñū, ugghaṭitaṃ atthaṃ ñū ugghaṭitaññū, uddesamatteneva sappabhedaṃ savitthāraṃ [V 0.0205] paṭivijjhitabbaṃ atthaṃ paṭivijjhatīti attho. Yo puggalo uddeseneva uddiṭṭhamatteneva atthaṃ ñatvā atthasiddhippatto hoti, so ugghaṭitaññū nāma.

Therein, 'to one of quick understanding' means: the meaning, detailed and extensive, is revealed, penetrated, or established; this is what is meant by 'revealed' (ugghaṭita). One who knows is a 'knower' (ñū); one who knows the revealed meaning is 'one of quick understanding' (ugghaṭitaññū). The meaning is that one penetrates the meaning, which should be understood in detail and extensively, merely by a brief indication. The person who, having known the meaning just by a brief indication, attains the accomplishment of the meaning—that one is called 'one of quick understanding'.

Vipañcīyate [M 0.0065] vittharīyate atthoti vipañcito, taṃ jānātīti vipañcitaññū. Yo puggalo niddesena niddiṭṭhamattameva atthaṃ ñatvā atthasiddhippatto, so vipañcitaññū nāma.

The meaning is analyzed, it is expanded, therefore it is called 'analyzed' (vipañcita); one who knows that is called 'one who understands after elaboration' (vipañcitaññū). That person who, having understood the meaning only to the extent that it is indicated in the explanation, attains the accomplishment of the meaning, is called 'one who understands after elaboration'.

Paṭiniddesena attho netabbo pāpetabboti neyyo. Yo puggalo paṭiniddesena vā paṭilomena vā vibhattaṃ eva atthaṃ ñatvā atthasiddhippatto, so neyyo nāma. Nissaraṇadesanāyeva ugghaṭitaññussa paṭivedhābhisamayo siddho hoti, ādīnavadesanāya ceva nissaraṇadesanāya ca vipañcitaññussa paṭivedhābhisamayo siddho hoti, assādadesanāya ca ādīnavadesanāya ca nissaraṇadesanāya ca neyyassa paṭivedhābhisamayo siddho hotīti adhippāyo idha gahetabbo.

The meaning is to be led or conveyed by way of detailed explanation; thus, 'one who needs guidance' (neyya). The person who, having understood a meaning only when it is explained in detail or inversely, achieves the accomplishment of that meaning, is called 'one who needs guidance'. For one of quick understanding, penetration and realization are accomplished through the teaching of escape alone. For one who understands after elaboration, penetration and realization are accomplished through the teaching of drawbacks and the teaching of escape. For one who needs guidance, penetration and realization are accomplished through the teaching of gratification, the teaching of drawbacks, and the teaching of escape. This is the meaning to be grasped here.

Padaparamo panettha paṭivedhābhisamayabhajanābhāvato na gahito. Tasmiñca aggahite assādo, ādīnavo, nissaraṇaṃ, assādādīnavā, assādanissaraṇāni, ādīnavanissaraṇāni, assādādīnavanissaraṇāni cāti sattasu paṭṭhānanayesu tatiyachaṭṭhasattamāva gahitā, avasesā cattāro nayā na gahitā. Veneyyavinayanābhāvato hi gahaṇāgahaṇaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Veneyyavinayañca veneyyānaṃ santāne ariyamaggassuppādanaṃ, na sāsanavinayanamattaṃ, ariyamagguppādanañca yathāvuttehi eva tīhi padaṭṭhānanayehi sijjhatīti itare nayā idha na vuttā.

Here, the 'word-paramount' (padaparama) is not included because they have no share in penetration and realization. And when that type is not included, of the seven modes of establishing the teaching—gratification, drawback, escape; gratification and drawback; gratification and escape; drawback and escape; and gratification, drawback, and escape—only the third, sixth, and seventh are included; the remaining four modes are not included. For the inclusion and non-inclusion should be understood as being due to the training, or lack thereof, of those who are to be trained. And the training of those to be trained means the production of the noble path in the mental continuum of those to be trained, not merely the discipline of the teaching. And the production of the noble path is accomplished precisely by these three modes of establishing the teaching as stated. Therefore, the other modes are not mentioned here.

Yasmā pana peṭake (peṭako. 23) –

But since in the Peṭakopadesa (Peṭ 23) it is said:

“Tattha katamo assādo ca ādīnavo ca?

‘Yāni karoti puriso, tāni passati attani;

Kalyāṇakārī kalyāṇaṃ, pāpakārī ca pāpaka’nti.

'Here, what is the gratification and what is the drawback? "Whatever deeds a person does, those they see in themselves; the doer of good sees good, and the doer of evil, evil."'

“Tattha yaṃ kalyāṇakārī kalyāṇaṃ paccanubhoti, ayaṃ assādo. Yaṃ pāpakārī pāpaṃ paccanubhoti, ayaṃ ādīnavo.

'Here, that the doer of good experiences good is the gratification. That the doer of evil experiences evil is the drawback.'

“Aṭṭhime, bhikkhave, lokadhammā. Katame aṭṭha? ‘Lābho’tiādi (a. ni. 8.6). Tattha lābho yaso sukhaṃ pasaṃsā, ayaṃ assādo. Alābho ayaso dukkhaṃ nindā, ayaṃ ādīnavo.

'Monks, there are these eight worldly conditions. Which eight? "Gain," and so on (AN 8.6). Here, gain, fame, happiness, and praise—this is the gratification. Loss, disrepute, pain, and censure—this is the drawback.'

“Tattha [V 0.0206] katamo assādo ca nissaraṇañca?

'Here, what is the gratification and the escape?'

‘Sukho [M 0.0066] vipāko puññānaṃ, adhippāyo ca ijjhati;

Khippañca paramaṃ santiṃ, nibbānamadhigacchatī’ti. –

'The fruit of merit is happiness, and one's aspiration is fulfilled; and quickly one attains the supreme peace, Nibbāna.'

Ayaṃ assādo ca nissaraṇañca.

This is the gratification and the escape.

“Dvattiṃsimāni, bhikkhave, mahāpurisassa mahāpurisalakkhaṇāni, yehi samannāgatassa mahāpurisassa dveyeva gatiyo bhavanti…pe… vivaṭacchadoti sabbaṃ lakkhaṇasuttaṃ (dī. ni. 3.199) ayaṃ assādo ca nissaraṇañca.

'Monks, there are these thirty-two marks of a great man, which, when possessed by a great man, lead to only two destinies... up to "one who has removed the covering"—the entire Discourse on the Marks (DN 30). This is the gratification and the escape.'

“Tattha katamo ādīnavo ca nissaraṇañca?

'Here, what is the drawback and the escape?'

‘Bhārā have pañcakkhandhā, bhārahāro ca puggalo;

Bhārādānaṃ dukhaṃ loke, bhāranikkhepanaṃ sukhaṃ.

'The five aggregates are truly a burden, and the person is the bearer of the burden. Taking up the burden is suffering in the world, laying down the burden is bliss.'

‘Nikkhipitvā garuṃ bhāraṃ, aññaṃ bhāraṃ anādiya;

Samūlaṃ taṇhamabbuyha, nicchāto parinibbuto’ti. (saṃ. ni. 3.22) –

'Having cast off the heavy burden, not taking up another, having uprooted craving with its root, without craving, one is fully extinguished.' (SN 22.22)

Ayaṃ ādīnavo ca nissaraṇañca.

This is the drawback and the escape.

“Tattha katamo assādo ca ādīnavo ca nissaraṇañca?

'Here, what is the gratification, the drawback, and the escape?'

‘Kāmā hi citrā madhurā manoramā, virūparūpena mathenti cittaṃ;

Tasmā ahaṃ pabbajitomhi rāja, apaṇṇakaṃ sāmaññameva seyyo’ti. (ma. ni. 2.307; theragā. 787; peṭako. 23) –

Sensual pleasures are indeed varied, sweet, and delightful; they churn the mind with their diverse forms. Therefore, O king, I have gone forth; the ascetic life is unquestionably better.

Ayaṃ assādo ca ādīnavo ca nissaraṇañcā”ti vuttaṃ, tasmā tepi nayā idha niddhāretvā veditabbā. Phalādīsupi ayaṃ nayo labbhatiyeva.

This is the gratification, the drawback, and the escape—so it is said. Therefore, these methods should also be determined and known here. This same method is indeed found in the case of fruits and so forth.

Yasmā [V 0.0207] peṭake (saṃ. ni. 1.23, 192; peṭako. 22; mi. pa. 2.1.9) – “tattha katamaṃ phalañca upāyo ca? ‘Sīle patiṭṭhāya naro sappañño’ti gāthā, idaṃ phalañca upāyo ca.

Since in the Peṭakopadesa it is said: “Therein, what is the fruit and what are the means? The verse, ‘Established in virtue, a wise person…,’ this is both the fruit and the means.”

“Tattha katamaṃ phalañca āṇatti ca?

Therein, what is the fruit and what is the command?

‘Sace bhāyatha dukkhassa, sace vo dukkhamappiyaṃ;

Mākattha pāpakaṃ kammaṃ, āvi vā yadi vā raho’ti. (udā. 44) –

‘If you fear suffering, if suffering is displeasing to you, do not perform an evil action, either openly or in secret.’

Idaṃ [M 0.0067] phalañca āṇatti ca.

This is both the fruit and the command.

“Tattha katamo upāyo ca āṇatti ca?

Therein, what are the means and the command?

‘Kumbhūpamaṃ kāyamimaṃ viditvā, nagarūpamaṃ cittamidaṃ ṭhapetvā;

Yodhetha māraṃ paññāvudhena, jitañca rakkhe anivesano siyā’ti. (dha. pa. 40) –

‘Knowing this body to be like a pot, establishing this mind like a fortified city, one should fight Māra with the weapon of wisdom. One should guard what has been conquered and be without attachment.’

Ayaṃ upāyo ca āṇatti cā”ti vuttaṃ, tasmā evaṃ phalādīnaṃ dukkhavasenāpi udāharaṇaṃ veditabbaṃ.

“This is both the means and the command,” so it is said. Therefore, the example concerning fruits and so forth should also be understood in terms of suffering.

“Ugghaṭitaññuādīnaṃ tiṇṇaṃ puggalānaṃ imassa puggalassa imaṃ deseti, imassa puggalassa imaṃ desetī”ti yehi puggalehi assādādayo yathārahaṃ ācariyena vibhattā, te puggalā yāhi paṭipadāhi bhinnā, tā paṭipadā kittikā bhavanti, tāhi bhinnā puggalā ca kittikāti vicāraṇāya sambhavato tā paṭipadā, te ca puggalā ettakāti gaṇanato dassetuṃ “tattha catasso paṭipadā”tiādi āraddhaṃ.

With regard to the three types of individuals—the one of quick understanding and so on—for whom it is said, 'To this individual this is taught, to that individual that is taught,' and for whom gratifications and so forth have been suitably distinguished by the teacher: those individuals are distinguished by certain paths. Since an investigation is possible as to how many those paths are, and how many are the individuals distinguished by them, in order to show by enumeration that those paths and individuals are of such a number, the passage beginning, 'Therein, there are four paths,' was introduced.

Tattha tatthāti tesu ugghaṭitaññuādīsu puggalesu. Ye puggalā yāhi paṭipadāhi bhinnā, tā paṭipadā catasso bhavanti, te ca puggalā cattāroti yojanā kātabbā. Katamā catasso? Dukkhāpaṭipadā dandhābhiññā, dukkhāpaṭipadā khippābhiññā, sukhāpaṭipadā dandhābhiññā, sukhāpaṭipadā khippābhiññā cāti catasso. Katame cattāro? Taṇhācarito mando [V 0.0208] puggalo, taṇhācarito udatto puggalo, diṭṭhicarito mando puggalo, diṭṭhicarito udatto puggalo cāti cattāro.

Therein, 'therein' refers to those individuals, the one of quick understanding and so on. The connection should be made thus: the paths by which those individuals are distinguished are four, and those individuals are four. Which four paths? The painful practice with slow direct knowledge, the painful practice with quick direct knowledge, the pleasant practice with slow direct knowledge, and the pleasant practice with quick direct knowledge. Which four individuals? The dull person of craving temperament, the sharp person of craving temperament, the dull person of speculative-view temperament, and the sharp person of speculative-view temperament.

Paṭipadābhiññāhi kato vibhāgopi paṭipadāhi kato vibhāgo nāma hoti avinābhāvatoti manasi katvā “catasso paṭipadābhiññā”ti avatvā “catasso paṭipadā”ti vuttā. Tā panetā samathavasenāpi bhinnā, vipassanāvasenāpi bhinnā. Kathaṃ samathavasena? Pathavīkasiṇādīsu sabbapaṭhamaṃ “pathavī pathavī”tiādinā pavattamanasikārato paṭṭhāya yāva jhānassa upacāraṃ uppajjati, tāva pavattā paññā samathabhāvanā “paṭipadā”ti vuccati. Upacārato pana paṭṭhāya yāva appanā, tāva [M 0.0068] pavattā paññā “abhiññā”ti vuccati heṭṭhimapaññāto adhigatapaññābhāvato.

Even the division made by paths and direct knowledges is called a division made by paths, because they are inseparable. Bearing this in mind, instead of saying “four paths and direct knowledges,” it is said “four paths.” These, however, are also distinguished by way of serenity and by way of insight. How by way of serenity? In the earth kasiṇa, etc., from the initial attention, “earth, earth,” etc., up to the arising of access concentration of jhāna, the wisdom that arises during that period, which is serenity development, is called the “path.” But from access concentration up to absorption, the wisdom that arises during that period is called “direct knowledge,” because it is wisdom attained beyond the lower wisdom.

Sā ca paṭipadā kassaci dukkhā kicchā hoti nīvaraṇādipaccanīkadhammasamudācāraggahaṇatāya, kassaci tadabhāvato sukhā akicchā hoti, abhiññāpi kassaci dandhā asīghappavatti hoti avisadañāṇatāya, kassaci khippā sīghappavatti hoti visadañāṇatāyāti.

And that path is painful and difficult for some, due to the prevalence and grasping of opposing states such as the hindrances; while for others, due to the absence of those states, it is pleasant and effortless. Direct knowledge also is slow for some, being of sluggish progress due to unclear knowledge, while for others it is quick, being of swift progress due to clear knowledge.

Kathaṃ vipassanāvasena? Yo rūpārūpamukhena vipassanaṃ abhinivisanto cattāri mahābhūtāni pariggahetvā upādārūpaṃ pariggaṇhāti, arūpaṃ pariggaṇhāti, rūpārūpaṃ pana pariggaṇhanto dukkhena kasirena kilamanto pariggahaetauṃ sakkoti, tassa dukkhāpaṭipadā nāma hoti. Pariggahitarūpārūpassa vipassanāparivāse maggapātubhāvadandhatāya dandhābhiññā nāma hoti. Tabbipariyāyena itarā dve honti. Vipassanāvasena pana bhinnāyeva paṭipadābhiññāyo idha daṭṭhabbā abhisamayādhikārattā, aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana “evaṃ yesaṃ puggalānaṃ vasena desanāvibhāgo dassito, te puggale paṭipadāvibhāgena vibhajitvā dassetuṃ ‘catasso paṭipadā’tiādi vutta”nti (netti. aṭṭha. 6) vuttaṃ. Yojanānayo vuttanayānusāreneva veditabbo.

How is this in terms of insight? One who, applying oneself to insight through the portal of form and formlessness, having comprehended the four great elements, comprehends derived form and formlessness. But while comprehending form and formlessness, one is able to comprehend only with difficulty, hardship, and weariness—this is called the painful practice. For one who has comprehended form and formlessness, the slowness of the path's manifestation in the cultivation of insight is called slow direct knowledge. The other two are to be understood in the opposite way. However, the paths and direct knowledges distinguished by way of insight should be understood here, as this is the section on realization. In the commentary, however, it is said: “Thus, the classification of teaching has been shown according to individuals. To explain these individuals by classifying the practice, it is said, ‘four practices,’ etc.” The method of exposition should be understood in accordance with the stated way.

Catūhi paṭipadābhiññāhi cattāro puggalā sabbeva aniyamato vaṭṭadukkhato kiṃ nu kho niyyanti, udāhu “imāya paṭipadābhiññāya ayaṃ puggalo niyyāti, imāya paṭipadābhiññāya ayaṃ puggalo niyyātī”ti niyamato ca niyyātīti vicāraṇāya sambhavato “ayaṃ puggalo imehi nissayehi upanissayapaccayaṃ labhitvā imāya paṭipadābhiññāya vaṭṭadukkhato niyyātī”ti niyametvā dassetuṃ “taṇhācarito mando”tiādi vuttaṃ.

Do all four individuals, by means of the four paths and direct knowledges, escape from the suffering of the cycle of rebirths without a fixed rule, or do they escape according to a fixed rule, such that 'this individual escapes by this path and direct knowledge, that individual escapes by that path and direct knowledge'? Since such an investigation is possible, in order to show determinately that 'this individual, having obtained the decisive support condition by means of these supports, escapes from the suffering of the cycle of rebirths by this path and direct knowledge,' the passage beginning 'The dull person of craving temperament...' was stated.

Tattha [V 0.0209] taṇhācarito mando puggalo satipaṭṭhānehi nissayehi upanissayapaccayaṃ labhitvā satindriyena satindriyādhikena ariyamaggena dukkhāpaṭipadādandhābhiññāya vaṭṭadukkhato niyyāti, taṇhācarito udatto puggalo jhānehi nissayehi upanissayapaccayaṃ labhitvā samādhindriyena samādhindriyādhikena ariyamaggena dukkhāpaṭipadākhippābhiññāya vaṭṭadukkhato niyyāti[M 0.0069], diṭṭhicarito mando puggalo sammappadhānehi nissayehi upanissayapaccayaṃ labhitvā vīriyindriyena vīriyindriyādhikena ariyamaggena sukhāpaṭipadādandhābhiññāya vaṭṭadukkhato niyyāti, diṭṭhicarito udatto puggalo saccehi nissayehi upanissayapaccayaṃ labhitvā paññindriyena paññindriyādhikena ariyamaggena sukhāpaṭipadākhippābhiññāya vaṭṭadukkhato niyyātīti yojanā kātabbā. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana –

Therein, the dull person of craving temperament, having obtained the decisive support condition by means of the foundations of mindfulness as supports, is liberated from the suffering of the cycle of rebirths by the Noble Path in which the faculty of mindfulness is predominant, through the painful practice with slow direct knowledge. The sharp person of craving temperament, having obtained the decisive support condition by means of the jhānas as supports, is liberated from the suffering of the cycle of rebirths by the Noble Path in which the faculty of concentration is predominant, through the painful practice with swift direct knowledge. The dull person of speculative-view temperament, having obtained the decisive support condition by means of the right strivings as supports, is liberated from the suffering of the cycle of rebirths by the Noble Path in which the faculty of energy is predominant, through the pleasant practice with slow direct knowledge. The sharp person of speculative-view temperament, having obtained the decisive support condition by means of the truths as supports, is liberated from the suffering of the cycle of rebirths by the Noble Path in which the faculty of wisdom is predominant, through the pleasant practice with swift direct knowledge. The connection should be made thus. But in the commentary:

“Cattāro puggalāti yathāvuttapaṭipadāvibhāgeneva cattāro paṭipannakapuggalā, taṃ pana paṭipadāvibhāgaṃ saddhiṃ hetupāyaphalehi dassetuṃ ‘taṇhācarito’tiādi vutta”nti (netti. aṭṭha. 6) –

‘Four individuals’ means the four individuals undertaking the practice, according to the aforesaid division of practices. However, in order to show that division of practices together with its cause, means, and fruit, the passage beginning ‘The person of craving temperament…’ was stated.”

Vuttaṃ. Tattha taṇhācaritoti taṇhāya nibbattitaṃ caritaṃ etassa puggalassāti taṇhācarito. Mandoti mandiyāya avijjāya samannāgatoti mando, mohādhikapuggalo. Udattoti udaatto, uḷārapaññoti attho. Uḷāraṃ phalaṃ detīti udo, ko so? Pavicayo, attani nibbattoti atto, udo atto yassa puggalassāti udattoti vacanattho kātabbo.

It is said. Therein, 'a person of craving temperament' (`taṇhācarito`) is one whose temperament (`carita`) is produced by craving (`taṇhā`). 'Dull' (`mando`) means endowed with dullness and ignorance; a person in whom delusion is predominant. 'Sharp' (`udatto`) means 'elevated,' that is, of outstanding wisdom. The meaning of the word `udatto` should be construed thus: `uda` is so called because it gives an outstanding (`uḷāra`) fruit—what is that? Investigation. `atta` is so called because it is produced in oneself (`attani`). A person who possesses this `uda` and `atta` is an `udatto`.

Paṭhamāya paṭipadāya hetu nāma taṇhācaritatā, mandapaññatā ca, upāyo satindriyaṃ, sabbāsampi phalaṃ niyyānameva. Dutiyāya paṭipadāya hetu nāma taṇhācaritatā, udattapaññatā ca, upāyo vīriyindriyaṃ. Tatiyāya paṭipadāya hetu nāma diṭṭhicaritatā, mandapaññatā ca, upāyo samādhindriyaṃ. Catutthiyā paṭipadāya hetu nāma diṭṭhicaritatā, udattapaññatā ca, upāyo paññindriyanti hetupāyaphalāni daṭṭhabbāni.

For the first practice, the cause is a craving temperament and dull-wittedness, the means is the faculty of mindfulness, and the fruit for all of them is simply liberation. For the second practice, the cause is a craving temperament and keen-wittedness, the means is the faculty of energy. For the third practice, the cause is a view-based temperament and dull-wittedness, the means is the faculty of concentration. For the fourth practice, the cause is a view-based temperament and keen-wittedness, the means is the faculty of wisdom—thus, the causes, means, and fruits should be understood.

Ettha ca diṭṭhicarito udatto puggalo ugghaṭitaññū nāma, diṭṭhicarito mando ceva taṇhācarito udatto ca vipañcitaññū nāma, taṇhācarito mando puggalo neyyo nāma, tasmā “tattha bhagavā ugghaṭitaññussa puggalassa nissaraṇaṃ desayatī”tiādinā nayena ugghaṭitaññuādiveneyyattayassa bhedadassanena nissaraṇaṃ desayati, “ādīnavañca nissaraṇañca desayati, assādañca ādīnavañca nissaraṇañca desayatī”ti desanāvibhāgo dassito. “Tattha catasso [V 0.0210] paṭipadā”tiādinā paṭipadābhedadassanena “taṇhācarito mando puggalo, taṇhācarito udatto [M 0.0070] puggalo, diṭṭhicarito mando puggalo, diṭṭhicarito udatto puggalo”ti catudhā bhinnaṃ taṇhācaritamandādikaṃ puggalacatukkaṃ dassitanti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Here, a person with a view-based temperament who is keen-witted is called a ‘person of instantaneous understanding’ (ugghaṭitaññū). A person with a view-based temperament who is dull-witted, and also a person with a craving temperament who is keen-witted, is called a ‘person of elucidated understanding’ (vipañcitaññū). A person with a craving temperament who is dull-witted is called a ‘person to be guided’ (neyyo). Therefore, by way of the teaching beginning, ‘There the Blessed One teaches liberation to the person of instantaneous understanding,’ and so on, he teaches liberation by showing the distinction among the three types of persons to be guided, beginning with the one of instantaneous understanding. The division of the teaching is shown as: ‘He teaches the danger and the liberation,’ and ‘He teaches the gratification, the danger, and the liberation.’ In the section beginning ‘There are four practices,’ by showing the distinction of practices, it should be seen that the fourfold division of individuals—the dull-witted person with a craving temperament, the keen-witted person with a craving temperament, the dull-witted person with a view-based temperament, and the keen-witted person with a view-based temperament—is presented.

Idāni catūhi paṭipadābhiññāhi catudhā bhinnaṃ taṇhācaritamandacatukkaṃ atthanayayojanāya dutiyāya visayaṃ katvā dassetuṃ “ubho taṇhācaritā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha taṇhāya samādhipaṭipakkhattā taṇhācaritā mandaudattā ubho puggalā samathapubbaṅgamāya vipassanāya upanissayaṃ labhitvā rāgavirāgāya maggapaññāya niyyanti cetovimuttiyā sekkhaphalabhāvāya. Sammādiṭṭhisahiteneva sammāsamādhinā niyyānaṃ bhavati, na sammāsamādhinā eva, tasmā diṭṭhicaritā mandaudattā ubho puggalā vipassanāpubbaṅgamena samathena avijjāvirāgāya maggapaññāya niyyanti paññāvimuttiyā asekkhaphalabhāvāyāti cattāropi puggalā duvidhāyeva bhavantīti vuttaṃ hoti.

Now, in order to show the fourfold division of the four types of individuals—those with a craving temperament who are dull-witted, etc.—as differentiated by the four practices and direct knowledges, by making it the object of the second method of interpretation, the passage beginning ‘both with a craving temperament’ was stated. Here, because craving is an opponent of concentration, both types of individuals with a craving temperament—the dull-witted and the keen-witted—having gained decisive support for insight with serenity as its forerunner, are liberated by path-wisdom for the fading away of passion, by way of mental liberation, for the attainment of the fruit of a trainee. Liberation occurs by means of right concentration accompanied by right view, not by right concentration alone. Therefore, both types of individuals with a view-based temperament—the dull-witted and the keen-witted—are liberated by serenity with insight as its forerunner and by path-wisdom for the fading away of ignorance, by way of liberation by wisdom, for the attainment of the fruit of a non-trainee. Thus, it is said that all four individuals are of two kinds.

Rāgavirāgāyāti rañjatīti rāgo, so virajjati etāyāti virāgā, rāgassa virāgā rāgavirāgā, tāya rāgavirāgāya. Cetoti cittappabhedena ca samādhi vuccati yathā “cittaṃ paññañca bhāvaya”nti (saṃ. ni. 1.23, 192; mi. pa. 2.1.9.). Paṭippassaddhivasena paṭipakkhato vimuccatīti vimutti, cetasā cittena samādhinā vimuccatīti cetovimutti, ceto eva vā vimutti cetovimutti, anāgāmiphalasamādhi. Anāgāmipuggalo hi samādhismiṃ paripūrakāritāya cetovimuttiyā niyyāti. Avijjāvirāgāyāti avindiyaṃ kāyaduccaritādiṃ vindatīti avijjā, vindiyaṃ vā kāyasucaritādiṃ na vindatīti avijjā niruttinayena. Virajjati etāyāti virāgā, avijjāya virāgā avijjāvirāgā, tāya avijjāvirāgāya. Pakārehi jānātīti paññā, vimuccatīti vimutti, paññāya vimuccatīti paññāvimutti, paññā eva vā vimutti paññāvimutti, arahattaphalapaññā, tāya paññāvimuttiyā.

‘For the fading away of passion’ (rāgavirāgāya): ‘It colors,’ thus ‘passion’ (rāgo). ‘It fades away by means of this,’ thus ‘fading away’ (virāgā). ‘The fading away of passion’ is ‘the fading away of passion’ (rāgavirāgā). ‘By means of that fading away of passion.’ ‘Mind’ (ceto) is also said to be concentration by way of the divisions of mind, as in ‘Develop mind and wisdom.’ ‘It is liberated from the opposing factors by way of tranquilization,’ thus ‘liberation’ (vimutti). ‘It is liberated by the mind, by concentration,’ thus ‘mental liberation’ (cetovimutti). Or, ‘mind itself is liberation,’ thus ‘mental liberation,’ which is the concentration of the non-returner’s fruition. For the non-returner is liberated by mental liberation because he has perfected concentration. ‘For the fading away of ignorance’ (avijjāvirāgāya): ‘It finds unwholesome bodily conduct, etc., which should not be found,’ thus ‘ignorance’ (avijjā). Or, according to the method of etymology, ‘it does not find wholesome bodily conduct, etc., which should be found,’ thus ‘ignorance.’ ‘It fades away by means of this,’ thus ‘fading away’ (virāgā). ‘The fading away of ignorance’ is ‘the fading away of ignorance’ (avijjāvirāgā). ‘By means of that fading away of ignorance.’ ‘It knows by means of aspects,’ thus ‘wisdom’ (paññā). ‘It is liberated,’ thus ‘liberation’ (vimutti). ‘It is liberated by wisdom,’ thus ‘liberation by wisdom’ (paññāvimutti). Or, ‘wisdom itself is liberation,’ thus ‘liberation by wisdom,’ which is the wisdom of arahantship’s fruition. ‘By means of that liberation by wisdom.’

“Tesu katame puggalā kena atthanayena hātabbā”ti vattabbato “tattha ye samathapubbaṅgamāhī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha tatthāti tesu “ubho taṇhācaritā”tiādinā vibhattesu puggalesu ye ubho taṇhācaritā mandaudattā puggalā samatha…pe… niyyanti, te ubho taṇhācaritā [M 0.0071] mandaudattā puggalā nandiyāvaṭṭena nayena hātabbā gametabbā netabbā. Ye ubho diṭṭhicaritā mandaudattā puggalā vipassanā…pe… samathena niyyanti, te ubho diṭṭhicaritā [V 0.0211] mandaudattā puggalā sīhavikkīḷitena nayena hātabbā gametabbā netabbāti attho.

Since it is to be said, ‘Among them, which individuals should be understood by which method of interpretation?’ the passage beginning ‘Here, those who have serenity as their forerunner’ was stated. Here, ‘here’ (tattha) means: Among those individuals classified by the phrase beginning ‘both with a craving temperament,’ those two types of individuals with a craving temperament—the dull-witted and the keen-witted—who are liberated by serenity… (etc.)… should be understood, grasped, and led by the method of the ‘delightful turning’ (nandiyāvaṭṭena nayena). Those two types of individuals with a view-based temperament—the dull-witted and the keen-witted—who are liberated by insight… (etc.)… by serenity, those two types of individuals with a view-based temperament—the dull-witted and the keen-witted—should be understood, grasped, and led by the method of the ‘lion’s play’ (sīhavikkīḷitena nayena)—this is the meaning.

7. “Tattha catasso paṭipadā”tiādinā desanāhārena dukkhāpaṭipadābhedena taṇhācaritamandādibhedo puggalo vibhatto, amhehi ca ñāto, “tassa vibhattānantaraṃ svāyaṃ desanāhāro kattha saṃvaṇṇetabbe dhamme kenaci ākārena sambhavatī”ti pucchitabbabhāvato “svāyaṃ hāro kattha sambhavatī”tiādimāha. Navamakkhaṇasampannassa satthā yaṃ dhammaṃ deseti, tasmiṃ saṃvaṇṇetabbe dhamme yā vīmaṃsādikā sutamayādikā tisso paññā vibhattā, tāhi paññāhi ye ugghaṭitaññuādayo tayo puggalā vibhattā, iti vibhattākārena ayaṃ desanāhāro satthārā desetabbe dhamme sambhavatīti daṭṭhabbo.

7. By the mode of exposition beginning ‘There are four practices,’ the individual differentiated by way of the painful practice, etc., and by way of the dull-witted person with a craving temperament, etc., is known to us. Since it should be asked, ‘Immediately after that differentiation, where does this mode of exposition occur in the Dhamma to be explained, and in what manner?’ the passage beginning ‘Where does this mode occur?’ was stated. In the Dhamma which the Teacher, endowed with the nine excellent qualities, teaches—in that Dhamma to be explained—the three kinds of wisdom, beginning with investigation and beginning with learning, are differentiated. By means of those wisdoms, the three types of individuals, beginning with the person of instantaneous understanding, are differentiated. Thus, this mode of exposition should be seen as occurring in the Dhamma to be taught by the Teacher, in the manner of these differentiations.

Tattha svāyaṃ hāroti desanāhārena paṭipadāvibhāgena veneyyapuggalavibhāgo dassito, so ayaṃ desanāhāro. Kattha sambhavatīti kattha saṃvaṇṇetabbe dhamme saṃvaṇṇanābhāvena sambhavatīti. Yassāti yo so veneyyo paccantajādīhi aṭṭhahi akkhaṇehi vimutto, savanadhāraṇādīhi ca sampattīhi samannāgato, tassa veneyyassa. Satthāti sadevakaṃ lokaṃ sāsati anusāsatīti satthā. Dhammanti desitaṃ saṃvaṇṇetabbaṃ dhammaṃ. Desayatīti saṅkhepanayavitthāranayehi bhāsati. Aññataroti bhagavato sāvakesu evaṃ dhammaṃ desetuṃ samattho sāvako. Garuṭṭhāniyoti gāravassa ṭhānabhūtehi sīlasutacāgādiguṇavisesehi yutto mānito saddahitabbavacano. Sabrahmacārīti samaṃ, saha vā brahmaṃ satthusāsanaṃ carati paṭipajjatīti sabrahmacārī. Saddhaṃ labhati “yo satthā dhammaṃ deseti, so satthā sammāsambuddho hotī”ti satthari, “svākkhāto vatāyaṃ dhammo sāttho sabyañjano ekantaparipuṇṇo ekantaparisuddho atthāvaho hitāvaho sukhāvaho jhānamaggaphalanibbattako, amhehi ca saddahitabbo”ti desite dhamme ca acalasaddhaṃ labhati, saddahanaṃ attano santāne punappunaṃ uppādeti. Tathā [M 0.0072] “yo sāvako dhammaṃ deseti, so sāvako saṅkhepato vā vitthārato vā dhammaṃ desetuṃ samattho vata garuṭṭhāniyo sabrahmacārī mānito saddahitabbavacano”ti desake sāvake ca “tādisena sāvakena desito yo dhammo, so dhammo sāttho sabyañjano ekantaparipuṇṇo ekantaparisuddho atthāvaho hitāvaho sukhāvaho jhānamaggaphalanibbattako, amhehi ca saddahitabbo”ti sāvakena desitadhamme ca saddhaṃ saddahanaṃ attano santāne punappunaṃ uppādetīti attho.

Herein, this is the section: the classification of individuals to be trained is shown by means of the exposition of the teaching and the analysis of the path. This is the exposition of the teaching. Where does it arise? It arises as the act of praising the Dhamma where the Dhamma is to be praised. "Of whom"—that individual to be trained, freed from the eight inopportune moments such as being born in the borderlands, and endowed with attainments like hearing and retention, for that trainable one. "The Teacher"—one who instructs and guides the world together with its devas. "The Dhamma"—the Dhamma that has been taught and is to be praised. "He teaches"—he speaks concisely or in detail. "A certain disciple"—a disciple of the Blessed One capable of teaching the Dhamma in such a way. "Esteemed"—worthy of respect due to qualities such as virtue, learning, generosity, and other distinctions; one who is respected and whose words are to be trusted. "A fellow practitioner"—one who practices the holy life equally or together with others under the Teacher’s dispensation. "He gains faith"—he gains unwavering faith in the Teacher, thinking, "The Teacher who teaches the Dhamma is indeed the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One."
