And in the Dhamma that has been taught, thinking, "This Dhamma is well-proclaimed, with meaning and fine expression, perfectly complete, perfectly pure, bringing benefit, welfare, and happiness, giving rise to jhāna, path, fruit, and Nibbāna—and is to be trusted by us." He repeatedly generates faith in his own mind-stream. Similarly, regarding the disciple who teaches the Dhamma, he thinks, "This disciple, capable of teaching the Dhamma concisely or in detail, is indeed esteemed, a fellow practitioner who is respected and whose words are to be trusted." And regarding the Dhamma taught by such a disciple, he thinks, "The Dhamma taught by such a disciple is well-proclaimed, with meaning and fine expression, perfectly complete, perfectly pure, bringing benefit, welfare, and happiness, giving rise to jhāna, path, fruit, and Nibbāna—and is to be trusted by us." He repeatedly generates faith in his own mind-stream—this is the meaning.

Tatthāti tasmiṃ saddahitabbe satthārā desitadhamme ceva sāvakena desitadhamme ca saddahantassa veneyyassa [V 0.0212] yā vīmaṃsā, vīmaṃsantassa yā ussāhanā, ussahantassa yā tulanā, tulayantassa yā upaparikkhā, sā ayaṃ vīmaṃsādikā paññā saddhānusārena pavattanato sutamayī paññā nāma. Tattha vīmaṃsanaṃ vimaṃsā, pāḷiyā, pāḷiatthassa ca vīmaṃsā. Vīmaṃsatīti vā vīmaṃsā, padaṃ padantarena, padatthaṃ padatthantarena vicāraṇakā paññā. Yathā cettha, evaṃ ussāhanādīsupi bhāvasādhanakattusādhanāni kātabbāni. Ussāhanā ca ussāhena upatthambhikā dhammassa dhāraṇaparicayasādhikā paññā ca, na vīriyaṃ, ettha ca yā sutamatteyeva pavattā, vīmaṃsādibhāvaṃ appattā nivattā, sā sutamayī paññā na hoti. Yā ca sutvā vīmaṃsitvā ussāhanādibhāvaṃ appattā nivattā, yā ca sutvā vīmaṃsitvā ussahitvā tulanādibhāvaṃ appattā nivattā, yā ca sutvā vīmaṃsitvā ussahitvā tulayitvā upaparikkhanabhāvaṃ appattā nivattā, sāpi paññā na sutamayī paññā hotīti daṭṭhabbā. Yā pana sutvā saddahantassa vīmaṃsā, vīmaṃsantassa ussāhanā, ussahantassa tulanā, tulayantassa upaparikkhā hoti, ayaṃ sutamayī paññā nāma hotīti daṭṭhabbā.

Herein, 'in that' refers to the investigation (vīmaṃsā) that arises for the trainable person who has faith in the Dhamma taught by the Teacher and the Dhamma taught by a disciple, which is to be trusted; the encouragement (ussāhanā) of one who investigates; the weighing (tulanā) of one who is encouraged; the scrutiny (upaparikkhā) of one who weighs—this wisdom, beginning with investigation, proceeding in accordance with faith, is called wisdom born of hearing. Here, investigation (vīmaṃsanā) is the investigation of the Pāli text and the meaning of the Pāli text. Or, investigation (vīmaṃsā) is that wisdom which scrutinizes a word with another word, and the meaning of a word with the meaning of another word. Just as here, so too in the case of encouragement and so on, the derivations of the agent and the state should be understood. And encouragement is wisdom that supports through effort, aiding in retention and familiarity with the Dhamma—it is not mere energy. And here, whatever arises merely from hearing, and stops without reaching the state of investigation and so on, that is not wisdom born of hearing. And that which, having heard and investigated, stops without reaching the state of encouragement and so on; and that which, having heard, investigated, and been encouraged, stops without reaching the state of weighing and so on; and that which, having heard, investigated, been encouraged, and weighed, stops without reaching the state of scrutiny—that wisdom also should be understood as not being wisdom born of hearing. But that which, for one who has heard and has faith, is investigation; for one who investigates, is encouragement; for one who is encouraged, is weighing; for one who weighs, is scrutiny—this is what should be understood as being called wisdom born of hearing.

Sutamayī paññā ācariyena vibhattā, amhehi ca ñātā, “katamā cintāmayī paññā”ti vattabbabhāvato sutamayiyā paññāya vibhajanānantaraṃ cintāmayiṃ paññaṃ vibhajituṃ “tathā sutena nissayenā”tiādimāha. Tattha sutanti suyyate pariyattidhammoti suto, savanaṃ pariyattidhammassāti vā sutaṃ, duvidhampi sutaṃ. Nissayena upanissāyāti attho. Itthambhūtalakkhaṇe cetaṃ “sutena nissayenā”ti karaṇavacanaṃ. Ettha pana “idaṃ pāṇātipātādiviramanaṃ sīlanaṭṭhena sīlaṃ, ayaṃ ekaggatā samādahanaṭṭhena samādhi[M 0.0073], imāni bhūtupādāni ruppanaṭṭhena rūpāni, ime phassādayo namanaṭṭhena nāmāni, ime rūpādayo pañca dhammā rāsaṭṭhena khandhā”ti tesaṃ tesaṃ dhammānaṃ pīḷanādisabhāvassa vīmaṃsanābhūtā paññā vīmaṃsā nāma. Tesaṃyeva sīlasamādhiādīnaṃ sīlati patiṭṭhahati etthāti sīlantiādivacanatthaṃ pucchitvā sabhāgalakkhaṇarasapaccupaṭṭhānapadaṭṭhānānaṃ tuletvā viya gahaṇapaññā tulanaṃ nāma. Tesaṃyeva sīlasamādhiādīnaṃ dhammānaṃ sabhāvalakkhaṇaṃ avijahitvā aniccatādukkhatādinamanaruppanādisappaccayasaṅkhatādiākāre vitakketvā upaparikkhaṇapaññā eva upaparikkhā nāmāti visesato daṭṭhabbo. Sutadhammassa dhāraṇaparicayavasena pavattanato sutamayī paññā ussāhanā jātā viya na cintāmayī paññā cintitassa dhāraṇaparicayavasena appavattanatoti “ussāhanā”ti na vuttaṃ.

The wisdom born of hearing has been explained by the teacher and understood by us. Since it should be stated, "What is the wisdom born of reflection?", after the analysis of the wisdom born of hearing, in order to analyze the wisdom born of reflection, he said, "Thus, based on what is heard," and so on. Here, 'suta' (what is heard) means the Dhamma of the Canon that is heard, or the act of hearing the Dhamma of the Canon; both are 'suta'. 'Nissayena' means by way of strong support. This is an instrumental case (karaṇavacana) in the sense of 'characteristic of being such'. Here, for example: "This abstention from killing living beings is virtue (sīla) in the sense of restraining; this one-pointedness is concentration (samādhi) in the sense of composing the mind; these primary and derived material phenomena are form (rūpa) in the sense of being afflicted; these contacts and other factors are name (nāma) in the sense of bending; these five aggregates—form and so on—are aggregates (khandha) in the sense of being a heap." The wisdom that investigates the nature of these phenomena, such as being oppressed, is called investigation (vīmaṃsā). Further, by questioning the meaning of terms like "virtue" (sīla)—as in "it is established here (sīlati patiṭṭhahati ettha)"—the wisdom of grasping as if by weighing the characteristics, functions, manifestations, and proximate causes is called weighing (tulana). Moreover, without abandoning the intrinsic nature of these very phenomena—virtue, concentration, and so on—the wisdom that scrutinizes by reflecting on them in modes such as impermanence and suffering, bending and being afflicted, being conditioned and constructed, is called scrutiny (upaparikkhā). This should be understood distinctly. Encouragement is part of the wisdom born of hearing because it proceeds by way of retaining and becoming familiar with the heard Dhamma; but wisdom born of reflection does not proceed by way of retaining and becoming familiar with what is reflected upon. Therefore, 'encouragement' is not mentioned.

Sutamayī paññā ceva cintāmayī paññā ca ācariyena vibhattā, amhehi ca ñātā, “katamā bhāvanāmayī paññā”ti vattabbabhāvato kāraṇabhūtānaṃ dvinnaṃ sutamayicintāmayipaññānaṃ dassanānantaraṃ [V 0.0213] phalabhūtaṃ bhāvanāmayiṃ paññaṃ vibhajanto “imāhi dvīhī”tiādimāha. Tattha imāhi dvīhi paññāhīti sutamayicintāmayipaññāhi kāraṇabhūtāhi. Sutamayipaññāya vā cintāmayipaññāya vā ubhayattha vā ṭhitoyeva yogāvacaro vipassanaṃ ārabhatīti. Manasikārasampayuttassāti rūpārūpesu pariggahādivasena saṅkhāresu aniccatādivasena manasikārena sammā pakārehi yuttappayuttassa. Diṭṭhivisuddhikaṅkhāvitaraṇavisuddhimaggāmaggañāṇadassanavisuddhi- paṭipadāñāṇadassanavisuddhisampādanena vipassanaṃ ussukkantassa yogāvacarassa santāne ñāṇadassanavisuddhisaṅkhātaṃ yaṃ ariyamaggañāṇaṃ nibbānārammaṇadassanabhūmiyaṃ vā bhāvanābhūmiyaṃ vā uppajjati, ayaṃ bhāvanāmayī paññāti attho daṭṭhabbo. Yadipi paṭhamamaggañāṇaṃ paṭhamaṃ nibbānadassanato “dassana”nti vuttaṃ, bhāvanāvasena pana pavattanato “bhāvanāmayī paññā”ti veditabbaṃ. Dassanabhūmīti paṭhamamaggaphalāni, sesāni “bhāvanābhūmī”ti vuccanti.

The wisdom born of hearing and the wisdom born of reflection have been distinguished by the teacher and are known to us. Since it should be stated, "What is the wisdom born of development?", after showing the two—the wisdom born of hearing and the wisdom born of reflection—which serve as causes, he, while distinguishing the wisdom born of development, which is the result, said "by these two" and so on. Here, "by these two wisdoms" means by the wisdom born of hearing and the wisdom born of reflection, which are causal. The meditator, established in either the wisdom born of hearing, the wisdom born of reflection, or both, begins insight meditation. "Associated with proper attention" means for one who is properly engaged and connected by way of attention, by way of comprehending material and immaterial phenomena and so on, and by way of impermanence and so on in formations. For a meditator striving for insight by accomplishing purification of view, purification of overcoming doubt, purification by knowledge and vision of what is and is not the path, and purification by knowledge and vision of the way, the noble path-knowledge—designated as the purification of knowledge and vision—arises in their mental continuum, taking Nibbāna as its object in the sphere of seeing or the sphere of development. This is the wisdom born of development, and its meaning should be understood. Although the first path-knowledge is called "seeing" because it is the first seeing of Nibbāna, it should be understood as "wisdom born of development" because it proceeds through cultivation. The sphere of seeing refers to the first path and its fruition, while the remaining ones are called the sphere of development.

8. Amhākācariya tumhehi “yassa satthā vā”tiādinā sutamayipaññādikā vibhattā, evaṃ sati sutena vinā cintāmayī paññā nāma na bhaveyya, mahābodhisattānaṃ pana sutena vinā cintāmayī paññā hotvevāti codanaṃ manasi katvā tasmiṃ saṅgahetvā pakārantarena vibhajituṃ “paratoghosā”tiādimāha.

8. Our Teacher has analyzed wisdom born of learning and the like by means of the phrase 'whose teacher or' and so on. This being the case, without learning, there would be no such thing as wisdom born of reflection. However, having taken to mind the objection that for great bodhisattvas wisdom born of reflection does indeed exist even without learning, and having included that point, he speaks, beginning with 'from another's utterance,' in order to analyze it in another way.

Tattha [M 0.0074] paratoghosāti parato pavatto desanāghoso paccayo etissāti paratoghosā. Paccattasamuṭṭhitāti pati visuṃ attaniyeva samuṭṭhitā. Yonisomanasikārāti tesaṃ tesaṃ cintetabbānaṃ rūpādīnaṃ dhammānaṃ ruppananamanādisabhāvapariggaṇhanādinā upāyena pavattamanasikārā cintāmayī paññā nāma, iminā sāvakāpi sāmaññato gahitā, tathāpi ugghaṭitaññuādīnaṃyeva vuttattā sāvakā idha gahitā, tasmā purimanayo yuttataro. Paratoti dhammadesakato pavattena dhammadesanāghosena hetunā yaṃ ñāṇaṃ uppajjati, paccattasamuṭṭhitena, yonisomanasikārena ca hetunā yaṃ ñāṇaṃ uppajjati, ayaṃ bhāvanāvasena pavattanato bhāvanāmayī paññā nāma, iminā sāvakāpi sāmaññato gahitā, tathāpi ugghaṭitaññuādīnaṃyeva vuttattā sāvakā idha gahitā, tasmā purimanayo yuttataro. Paratoti dhammadesakato pavattena dhammadesanāghosena hetunā yaṃ ñāṇaṃ uppajjati, paccattasamuṭṭhitena, yonisomanasikārena ca hetunā yaṃ ñāṇaṃ uppajjati, ayaṃ bhāvanāvasena pavattanato bhāvanāmayī paññā nāmāti vibhajitvā paṇḍitehi ñeyyāti vitthārena gambhīratthaṃ ñātuṃ icchantehi “evaṃ paṭipadāvibhāgenā”tiādinā (netti. aṭṭha. 9) aṭṭhakathāvacanena jānitabbo.

Here, 'from another's utterance' means that the sound of the teaching proceeding from another is its condition; hence it is called 'from another's utterance.' 'Arisen internally' means arisen separately and distinctly within oneself. Regarding wise attention: wisdom born of reflection is the mental application that proceeds by the method of grasping the intrinsic nature, such as being afflicted, bending, and so on, of those various things to be contemplated, such as form. By this, disciples are also generally included; nevertheless, because it is stated specifically for those of quick understanding and others, disciples are included here. Therefore, the former method is more suitable. The knowledge that arises from the cause of the sound of the Dhamma teaching proceeding from a Dhamma teacher, and the knowledge that arises from the cause of what has arisen internally and of wise attention—this is called wisdom born of cultivation because it proceeds by way of cultivation. By this, disciples are also generally included; nevertheless, because it is stated specifically for those of quick understanding and others, disciples are included here. Therefore, the former method is more suitable. The knowledge that arises from the cause of the sound of the Dhamma teaching proceeding from a Dhamma teacher, and the knowledge that arises from the cause of what has arisen internally and of wise attention—this is called wisdom born of cultivation because it proceeds by way of cultivation. Having analyzed it thus, it should be understood by the wise. For those who wish to know the profound meaning in detail, it should be known through the commentary passage beginning with 'Thus, by the distinction of the path' (Netti. Aṭṭha. 9).

Sutamayipaññādikā [V 0.0214] tisso paññā ācariyena nānānayehi vibhattā, amhehi ca ñātā, “tāsu yassa ekā vā dve vā paññā atthi, so puggalo konāmo, yassa ekāpi natthi, so puggalo konāmo”ti pucchitabbabhāvato yassa ayaṃ paññā, imā vā atthi, so puggalo itthannāmo, yassa natthi, so puggalo itthannāmoti paṭipadāpaññāppabhedena puggalaṃ vibhajituṃ “yassa imā”tiādi vuttaṃ.

The three kinds of wisdom, beginning with wisdom born of learning, have been analyzed by the Teacher in various ways and are known by us. Since the question should be asked, 'Among these, for one who has one or two kinds of wisdom, what is that person's name? For one who has not even one, what is that person's name?', it is said, beginning with 'for whom these,' in order to classify persons by the distinction of wisdom related to the path: 'For one who has this wisdom, or these, that person has such-and-such a name; for one who has none, that person has such-and-such a name.'

Tattha yassa atitikkhapaññassa sutamayī paññā ceva cintāmayī paññā ca imā dve paññā atthi, ayaṃ atitikkhapañño uddesamatteneva jānanato ugghaṭitaññū nāma. Yassa nātitikkhapaññassa uddesaniddesehi sutamayī paññā atthi, cintāmayī paññā natthi, ayaṃ nātitikkhapañño uddesaniddesehi jānanato vipañcitaññū nāma. Yassa mandapaññassa uddesaniddesehi neva sutamayī paññā atthi, na cintāmayī paññā ca, ayaṃ mandapañño [M 0.0075] uddesaniddesapaṭiniddesehi jānanato niravasesavitthāradesanāya netabbato neyyo nāmāti. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana “idāni yadatthaṃ imā paññā uddhaṭā, tameva veneyyapuggalavibhāgaṃ yojetvā dassetuṃ ‘yassā’tiādi vutta”ntiādi (netti. aṭṭha. 8) vuttaṃ.

Here, for one whose wisdom is very sharp, both wisdom born of learning and wisdom born of reflection exist—this person, because they understand merely upon a brief statement, is called one who understands quickly (ugghaṭitaññū). For one whose wisdom is not very sharp, wisdom born of learning exists through a brief statement and an exposition, but wisdom born of reflection does not—this person, because they understand through a brief statement and an exposition, is called one who understands after elaboration (vipañcitaññū). For one whose wisdom is dull, neither wisdom born of learning nor wisdom born of reflection exists through a brief statement and an exposition—this person, because they understand through a brief statement, an exposition, and a counter-exposition, and must be led by a complete and extensive teaching, is called one who is to be guided (neyya). In the commentary, however, it is said: 'Now, in order to show the classification of persons to be trained by connecting it to the purpose for which these kinds of wisdom have been introduced, it is said, beginning with 'for whom...'' (Netti. Aṭṭha. 8).

9. “Tattha bhagavā ugghaṭitaññussā”tiādinā desanaṃ vibhāveti, “tattha catasso paṭipadā”tiādinā paṭipadāvibhāgehi, “svāyaṃ hāro”tiādinā ñāṇavibhāgehi ca desanābhājanaṃ veneyyattayaṃ ācariyena vibhattaṃ, amhehi ca ñātaṃ, “yāya desanāpāḷiyā desanāhāraṃ yojetuṃ pubbe ‘dhammaṃ vo, bhikkhave, desessāmī’tiādinā desanāhārassa visayabhāvena yā pāḷidesanā nikkhittā, sā pāḷidesanā desanāhārena niddhāritesu assādādīsu atthesu kimatthaṃ desayatī”ti pucchitabbattā “imaṃ atthaṃ desayatī”ti niyametvā dassetuṃ “sāyaṃ dhammadesanā”tiādi āraddhaṃ.

9. By elucidating the teaching with 'Therein, the Blessed One for one who understands quickly...' and so on; by the classifications of the paths, beginning with 'Therein are four paths...'; and by the classifications of knowledge, beginning with 'This is the method of conveyance...', the triad of trainees, the recipients of the teaching, has been distinguished by the Teacher and is known by us. Since the question should be asked: 'For what purpose does that Pāli teaching—which was previously set forth as the object of the teaching framework with 'I will teach you the Dhamma, monks,' and so on, in order to apply the teaching framework to that Pāli teaching—teach regarding the meanings, such as gratification, which have been determined by the teaching framework?'—therefore, to show by defining that 'it teaches this meaning,' the passage beginning with 'This Dhamma teaching...' is commenced.

Tattha sāyaṃ dhammadesanāti yā dhammadesanā ādikalyāṇādikā pubbe desanāhārassa visayabhāvena nikkhittā, sāyaṃ dhammadesanā assādādīsu kimatthaṃ desayatīti kathetukāmatāya pucchati, pucchitvā “cattāri saccāni desayatī”ti vissajjeti, tāni sarūpato dassetuṃ “dukkhaṃ samudayaṃ nirodhaṃ magga”nti vuttaṃ. Pavattipavattakanivattinivattanupāyabhāvena aviparītabhāvato “saccānī”ti vuttāni.

Here, 'this Dhamma teaching' refers to the Dhamma teaching that is good in the beginning and so on, which was previously set forth as the object of the teaching framework. With the desire to explain, it asks, 'For what purpose does this Dhamma teaching teach regarding gratification and so on?' Having asked, it replies, 'It teaches the four truths.' To show them according to their own nature, it is said, 'suffering, origin, cessation, path.' They are called 'truths' because of their unfailing nature as occurrence, that which causes occurrence, cessation, and the means to cessation.

Yassaṃ desanāyaṃ saccāni desanāhārena niddhāritāni, sā desanā cattāri saccāni desayatīti [V 0.0215] yuttaṃ hotu. Yassaṃ desanāyaṃ assādādayo niddhāritā, sā desanā cattāri saccāni desayatīti na sakkā vattuṃ. Heṭṭhā ca assādādayo niddhāritā, tasmā “assādādayo”tipi vattabbanti codanaṃ manasi katvā “ādīnavo phalañca dukkha”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Desanāhārena saṃvaṇṇanānayena desanāyaṃ niddhārito ādīnavo ceva phalañca dukkhasaccaṃ hoti, assādo samudayasaccaṃ, nissaraṇaṃ nirodhasaccaṃ, upāyo ceva āṇatti ca maggasaccaṃ hoti, tasmā “cattāri saccāni desayatī”ti vattabbamevāti.

Let it be fitting to say that a teaching expounds the four truths in a case where the truths are determined by the teaching framework. In a case where gratification and so on are determined, it cannot be said that the teaching expounds the four truths. And previously, gratification and so on were determined; therefore, having taken to mind the objection that 'it should also be stated as "gratification and so on,"' it is said, beginning with 'Danger and fruit are suffering.' By the teaching framework, through the method of description, in the teaching, what is determined as danger and as fruit becomes the truth of suffering; gratification becomes the truth of origin; escape becomes the truth of cessation; and the means and the instruction become the truth of the path. Therefore, it should indeed be said that 'it expounds the four truths.'

Taṇhāvajjā [M 0.0076] tebhūmakadhammā dukkhaṃ, te ca aniccādīhi pīḷitattā ādīnavāyeva. Phalanti desanāya phalaṃ lokiyaṃ, na lokuttaraṃ, tasmā dukkhanti vattabbameva. Assādoti taṇhāssādassa gahitattā “assādo samudayo”ti ca vattabbaṃ. Assādekadeso dukkhameva, assādekadeso dukkhañceva samudayo ca. Saha vipassanāya ariyamaggo ca bhagavato āṇatti ca desanāya phalādhigamassa upāyabhāvato “upāyo, āṇatti ca maggo”ti vuttaṃ, nissaraṇekadesopi maggoti daṭṭhabbo. “Imāni cattāri saccāni yā desanā visesato desayati, katamā sā”ti pucchitabbattā visesaṃ niyametvā dassetuṃ “imāni cattāri saccāni idaṃ dhammacakka”nti vuttaṃ. Idaṃ vuccamānaṃ dhammacakkaṃ imāni cattāri saccāni visesato desayatīti yojanā kātabbā.

The phenomena of the three planes, excluding craving, are suffering. And because they are afflicted by impermanence and so on, they are indeed a danger. Regarding 'fruit': the fruit of the teaching is worldly, not supramundane; therefore, it should indeed be called suffering. Regarding 'gratification': because the gratification of craving is taken, it should also be said, 'gratification is the origin.' One part of gratification is suffering itself; another part of gratification is both suffering and the origin. Because the Noble Path together with insight and the instruction of the Blessed One are the means for attaining the fruit of the teaching, it is said, 'The means and the instruction are the path.' A part of escape should also be regarded as the path. Because it should be asked, 'Which teaching particularly declares these four truths?'—to establish and show the specific case, it is said, 'These four truths—this is the Dhamma Wheel.' The connection should be made thus: 'This Dhamma Wheel, which is being spoken of, particularly declares these four truths.'

“Yā desanā imāni cattāri saccāni visesato desayati, tassā desanāya dhammacakkabhāvaṃ kiṃ bhagavā āhā”ti vattabbabhāvato “yathāha bhagavā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha “jātipi dukkhā”tiādivacanato (mahāva. 14) taṇhāvajjaṃ jātiādikaṃ tebhūmakadhammajātaṃ dukkhassa adhiṭṭhānabhāvena, dukkhadukkhādibhāvena ca “dukkha”nti vuttaṃ. Meti mayā pavattitanti yojanā. Bhikkhaveti savane ussāhaṃ janetuṃ ālapati. Bārāṇasiyanti bārāṇasīnagarassa avidūre. Isipataneti sīlakkhandhādīnaṃ isanato gavesanato “isī”ti voharitānaṃ paccekabuddhānaṃ patanaṭṭhāne. Migadāyeti migānaṃ abhayadānaṭṭhāne kārite assameva.

Since it should be stated, 'Regarding the teaching that distinctly explains these four truths, what did the Blessed One say about its being the Dhamma Wheel?', therefore, 'As the Blessed One said,' etc., is stated. Herein, from the statement 'Birth is suffering' and so forth (Mahāvagga 14), the collection of phenomena of the three planes, beginning with birth, excluding craving, is called 'suffering' because it is the basis for suffering and because of its nature as suffering-as-suffering, and so on. 'Me' is to be connected with 'was set in motion by me.' 'Bhikkhus'—he addresses them to arouse enthusiasm for listening. 'At Bārāṇasī'—not far from the city of Bārāṇasī. 'At Isipatana'—at the place where Paccekabuddhas, called 'seers' (isī) because of their seeking (isanato) and searching for the aggregates of virtue, etc., alight (patana). 'At Migadāya'—in the hermitage established as a sanctuary for deer.

Anuttaranti uttaritarābhāvena anuttaraṃ anatisayaṃ. Dhammacakkanti satipaṭṭhānādike sabhāvadhāraṇādinā atthena dhammo ceva pavattanaṭṭhena cakkañcāti dhammacakkaṃ. Appaṭivattiyanti appaṭisedhanīyaṃ. Kasmā? Janakassa bhagavato dhammissarattā sammāsambuddhattā, jaññassa ca anuttarattā koṇḍaññādīnañceva aṭṭhārasabrahmakoṭiyā ca catusaccapaṭivedhasādhanato ca. “Kena appaṭivattiya”nti pucchitabbattā “samaṇena vā”tiādimāha. Tattha samaṇenāti pabbajjamattūpagatena[V 0.0216]. Brāhmaṇenāti jātibrāhmaṇena. Paramatthānañhi samaṇabrāhmaṇānaṃ paṭisedhane cittuppādānuppajjanampi natthi. Devenāti chakāmāvacaradevena. Brahmunāti rūpabrahmā gahitā. “Samaṇena vā [M 0.0077] …pe… brahmunā”ti ettakameva avatvā“kenacī”ti vuttavacanena avasesakhattiyagahapatiparisajanā saṅgahitā. Tasmā khattiyabrāhmaṇagahapatisamaṇacātumahārājikatāvatiṃsamārabrahmaparisā aṭṭhavidhāpi paṭisedhetuṃ asamatthāyevāti veditabbā. Lokasminti sattasamūhe dhammacakkādhāre.

Unsurpassed: because of the absence of anything more excellent, it is unsurpassed, without superior. The Wheel of Dhamma: it is the Dhamma itself by way of its intrinsic nature, such as the foundations of mindfulness, and it is a wheel by way of the meaning of setting it in motion—thus, the Wheel of Dhamma. Irreversible: it is unopposable. Why? Because the Blessed One, its originator, is the sovereign of the Dhamma and the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One; and because of the unsurpassed nature of that which is to be known, and because it brings about the penetration of the four truths for Koṇḍañña and others, as well as for eighteen koṭis of Brahmās. Since it should be asked, 'By whom is it irreversible?', he states, 'by an ascetic or...' and so on. Here, 'by an ascetic' refers to one who has merely undertaken the going forth. 'By a brahmin' means one born a brahmin. For, in those who are ascetics and brahmins in the ultimate sense, not even the arising of a thought to oppose it occurs. 'By a deva' refers to the devas of the six sense-sphere heavens. 'By a Brahmā' includes the Brahmās of the form realm. By the phrase 'by anyone,' stated without limiting it to 'by an ascetic or... by a Brahmā,' the remaining groups—khattiyas, householders, and assemblies—are included. Therefore, it should be understood that even the eightfold assembly—khattiyas, brahmins, householders, ascetics, the Four Great Kings, the Tāvatiṃsa devas, Māra, and the Brahmā assemblies—is incapable of opposing it. 'In the world' means among the multitude of beings, the basis of the Wheel of Dhamma.

“Dvādasa padāni sutta”nti gāthānurūpaṃ dhammacakkasutte padāni vibhajanto “tattha aparimāṇā”tiādimāha. Tattha tatthāti dhammacakkadesanāyaṃ (saṃ. ni. 5.1081; mahāva. 13 ādayo; paṭi. ma. 2.30). “Aparimāṇā akkharā aparimāṇā padā”ti avatvā “aparimāṇā padā aparimāṇā akkharā”ti uppaṭipāṭivacanehi yebhuyyena padasaṅgahitānīti dasseti. Padā, akkharā, byañjanāti ca liṅgavipallāsānīti daṭṭhabbāni. Etasseva atthassāti vattabbākārassa catusaccasaṅkhātassa atthasseva saṅkāsanā pakāsanā pakāsanākāro paññattākāroti ākāravantaākārasambandhe sāmivacanaṃ. Saṅkāsanākāroti ca saṅkāsanīyassa atthassa ākāro. Esa nayo sesesupi. Itipīti iti iminā pakārenapi, iminā pakārenapi idaṃ jātiādikaṃ dukkhaṃ ariyasaccanti veditabbaṃ.

“The discourse has twelve phrases”: analyzing the phrases in the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta in accordance with the verse, he begins with “therein, immeasurable…” and so on. Here, “therein” refers to the exposition of the Wheel of Dhamma (Saṃyutta Nikāya 5.1081; Mahāvagga 13, and elsewhere; Paṭisambhidāmagga 2.30). By stating it in reverse order—“immeasurable phrases, immeasurable syllables”—instead of saying “immeasurable syllables, immeasurable phrases,” he indicates that they are for the most part included as phrases. “Phrases, syllables, and expressions” should be understood as having interchangeable genders. The genitive case in `etasseva atthassa` (of this very meaning) expresses the relationship between the meaning and its aspects; it refers to the clarification, manifestation, mode of manifestation, and mode of designation of the meaning itself, which is designated as the Four Noble Truths and is the manner in which it is to be expressed. “The mode of clarification” refers to the aspect of the meaning to be clarified. The same principle applies to the rest. “Thus also”: in this way too, in this manner too, this suffering consisting of birth and so on should be understood as the Noble Truth.

Ayanti kāmataṇhādibhedā ayaṃ taṇhā. Dukkhasamudayoti dukkhanibbattanassa hetubhāvato dukkhasamudayo. Ayanti sabbasaṅkhatato nissaṭā ayaṃ asaṅkhatā dhātu. Dukkhanirodhoti jātiādippabhedassa dukkhassa anuppādananirodhapaccayattā dukkhanirodho. Ayanti sammādiṭṭhādiko aṭṭhaṅgiko ariyo maggo. Dukkhanirodhabhūtaṃ nibbānaṃ ārammaṇakaraṇavasena gatattā, dukkhanirodhappattiyā paṭipadābhāvato ca dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadā. Sesaṃ vuttanayameva.

‘This’ means this craving, which is of various kinds, such as craving for sensual pleasures. ‘The origin of suffering’ is so called because it is the cause for the production of suffering. ‘This’ means this unconditioned element, which is free from all conditioned things. ‘The cessation of suffering’ is so called because it is the condition for the non-arising and cessation of suffering in its various forms, such as birth. ‘This’ means this Noble Eightfold Path, beginning with right view. It is called ‘the practice leading to the cessation of suffering’ because it goes to the cessation of suffering, which is Nibbāna, by way of making it an object, and because it is the practice for the attainment of the cessation of suffering. The rest is as previously explained.

“Tattha aparimāṇā”tiādinā byañjanapadaatthapadāni vibhajitvā tesaṃ aññamaññaṃ visayivisayabhāvena sambandhabhāvaṃ dassetuṃ “tattha bhagavā akkharehi saṅkāsetī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Atha vā bhagavā kiṃ sāmaññehi akkharādīhi saṅkāseti vā pakāseti vā, udāhu yathārahaṃ saṅkāseti pakāsetītiādivicāraṇāya sambhavato visayavisayibhāvena sambandhabhāvaṃ niyametvā dassetuṃ “tattha bhagavā akkharehi saṅkāsetī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha “akkharehi saṅkāsetī”ti kasmā evaṃ vuttaṃ, nanu “dukkhasacca”ntiādīsu [M 0.0078] padeneva dukkhasaccatthattādiko saṅkāsitabboti? Saccaṃ, padāvayavassa pana akkharassa gahaṇamukheneva akkharasamudāyassapi padassa [V 0.0217] gahaṇaṃ hoti, pade gahite ca dukkhasaccatthādikāvabodho hotveva, evaṃ sati padeneva sijjhanato akkharo visuṃ na gahetabboti? Na, dukkhasaccatthādikāvabodhassa visesuppattibhāvato. Du-iti akkharena hi anekupaddavādhiṭṭhānabhāvena kucchitattho gahito, kha-iti akkharena dhuvasubhasukhattabhāvavirahena tucchatthoti evamādikāvabodhassa visesuppatti bhavati. Tena vuttaṃ “padatthagahaṇassa visesādhānaṃ jāyatī”ti (netti. aṭṭha. 9). Padapariyosāne vākyapariyosānābhāvato akkharehi saṃkhittena dīpiyamāno attho padehi pakāsitovāti vuttaṃ “padehi pakāsetī”ti. Vākyapariyosāne pana saṅkāsito pakāsito attho vivarito vivaṭo katovāti vuttaṃ. “Byañjanehi vivaratī”ti. Pakārehi ca vākyabhede kate so attho vibhatto nāmāti vuttaṃ “ākārehi vibhajatī”ti. Vākyāvayavānaṃ padānaṃ paccekaṃ nibbacanavibhāge kate so attho pākaṭo katovāti vuttaṃ “niruttīhi uttānīkarotī”ti. Katanibbacanehi vākyāvayavehi vitthāravasena niravasesato desitehi veneyyasattānaṃ citte parisamantato tosanaṃ hoti, paññātejanañcāti āha “niddesehi paññapetī”ti.

By means of 'Therein, immeasurable,' and so on, having analyzed the terms of expression and the terms of meaning to show their mutual relationship as subject and object, it is said, 'Therein, the Blessed One illuminates with syllables,' and so on. Alternatively, does the Blessed One illuminate or reveal generally with mere syllables and so on, or does He illuminate and reveal as appropriate? To establish the relationship between subject and object by determining this through investigation, it is said, 'Therein, the Blessed One illuminates with syllables,' and so on. Therein, why is it said, 'illuminates with syllables'? Is it not the case that in expressions like 'the truth of suffering,' the meaning of the truth of suffering and so on should be illuminated by the word itself? True, but by grasping the syllable as a component of the word, the collection of syllables forming the word is also grasped. When the word is grasped, the understanding of the meaning of the truth of suffering and so on certainly arises. In that case, since the word itself accomplishes this, should the syllable not be grasped separately? No, because a specific kind of understanding arises. For instance, with the syllable 'du,' the meaning of wretchedness is grasped due to its being the basis for manifold troubles. With the syllable 'kha,' the meaning of emptiness is grasped due to the absence of permanence, beauty, and happiness. Thus, a specific kind of understanding arises. Therefore, it is said, 'A special contribution to the grasping of the word's meaning occurs' (Netti. Aṭṭha. 9). Because a sentence does not end at the conclusion of a word, the meaning, though concisely indicated by syllables, is said to be manifested by words—thus it is said, 'He manifests with words.' At the conclusion of a sentence, however, the illuminated and manifested meaning is made clear and laid open—thus it is said, 'He elaborates with expressions.' When the divisions of the sentence are made by modes, that meaning is distinguished—thus it is said, 'He distinguishes with modes.' When the individual derivations of the components of the sentence, the words, are analyzed, that meaning is made manifest—thus it is said, 'He makes plain with linguistic analysis.' When the components of the sentence, with their etymologies explained, are taught exhaustively and in detail, the minds of those capable of being guided are thoroughly satisfied, and wisdom is stimulated—thus it is said, 'He makes known with expositions.'

“Bhagavā akkharehi saṅkāsetī”tiādīsu “bhagavā evā”ti vā “akkharehi evā”ti vā avadhāraṇe yojite “sāvako na saṅkāseti, padādīhi na saṅkāsetī”ti attho bhaveyya, sāvako ca saṅkāseti, padādīhi ca saṅkāseti. Kattha avadhāraṇaṃ yojetabbanti ce? “Bhagavā akkharehi saṅkāsetiyevā”ti avadhāraṇaṃ yojetabbaṃ. Evañhi sati sāvakena saṅkāsito vā padādīhi saṅkāsito vā attho saṅgahito hoti. Atthapadānañca akkharādinānāvisayatā siddhā hoti. Tena ekānusandhike sutte chaḷeva atthapadāni niddhāretabbāni, anekānusandhike sutte anusandhibhedena visuṃ visuṃ cha cha atthapadāni niddhāretabbāni.

In 'The Blessed One elucidates with syllables,' etc., if the restriction is applied as 'only the Blessed One' or 'only with syllables,' the meaning would be that 'a disciple does not elucidate, nor does one elucidate with phrases, etc.' But a disciple does elucidate, and one elucidates with phrases, etc. If it is asked, 'Where should the restriction be applied?' It should be applied as 'The Blessed One does indeed elucidate with syllables.' For in this way, the meaning elucidated by a disciple or elucidated with phrases, etc., is included. And it is established that the meaning-terms have syllables and so on as their various domains. Therefore, in a sutta with a single connection, only six meaning-terms should be determined, while in a sutta with multiple connections, six meaning-terms should be determined separately for each connection.

“Chasu [M 0.0079] byañjanapadesu katamena byañjanapadena katamaṃ kiccaṃ sādhetī”ti pucchitabbattā “iminā idaṃ kiccaṃ, iminā idaṃ kiccaṃ sādhetī”ti niyametvā dassetuṃ “tattha bhagavā akkharehi ca padehi ca ugghaṭetī”tiādimāha. Tattha tatthāti akkharādīsu byañjanapadesu. Ugghaṭetīti ugghaṭanakiccaṃ sādhetīti attho. Kiñcāpi desanāva ugghaṭanakiccaṃ sādheti, bhagavā pana desanājanakattā ugghaṭanakiccaṃ sādhetīti vuccati. Sesesupi evamattho daṭṭhabbo.

“Among the six ranges of expression, with which range of expression is which task accomplished?” Because it should be asked thus, to show by determining, “With this, this task is accomplished; with this, this task is accomplished,” it was said, “Therein, the Blessed One discloses with letters and with phrases,” and so on. Therein, “therein” refers to the ranges of expression, such as letters. “Discloses” means accomplishes the task of disclosing; this is the meaning. Although the teaching itself accomplishes the task of disclosing, the Blessed One, being the generator of the teaching, is said to accomplish the task of disclosing. The same meaning should be understood in the remaining cases as well.

“Ugghaṭanakiccasādhikā desanāyeva kiṃ vipañcanavitthāraṇakiccasādhikā desanājanakattā, udāhu visuṃ visuṃ kiccasādhikā aññā”ti pucchitabbabhāvato visuṃ visuṃ kiccasādhikā aññā [V 0.0218] desanāti niyametvā dassetuṃ “tattha ugghaṭanā ādī”tiādimāha. Atha vā “katamā ugghaṭanā, katamā vipañcanā, katamā vitthāraṇā”ti pucchitabbattā vuttaṃ “tattha ugghaṭanā ādī”tiādi. Tattha tatthāti ugghaṭanādikiccasādhikāsu desanāsu. Ugghaṭanāti ugghaṭanakiccasādhikā desanā ādidesanā hoti. Vipañcanāti vipañcanakiccasādhikā desanā majjhedesanā hoti. Vitthāraṇāti vitthāraṇakiccasādhikā desanā pariyosānadesanā hotīti attho daṭṭhabbo.

“Is the teaching that accomplishes the task of uncovering the very same as that which accomplishes the tasks of elaborating and expanding, on account of being the generator of the teaching, or are they other teachings that accomplish distinct tasks?” Because it should be asked thus, to show by determining that they are distinct teachings accomplishing distinct tasks, it is said: “Therein, uncovering, etc.” Alternatively, because it should be asked, “What is uncovering? What is elaborating? What is expanding?” it is said: “Therein, uncovering, etc.” Therein, “therein” refers to the teachings that accomplish the tasks of uncovering and so on. “Uncovering” means the teaching that accomplishes the task of uncovering—this is the initial teaching. “Elaborating” means the teaching that accomplishes the task of elaborating—this is the middle teaching. “Expanding” means the teaching that accomplishes the task of expanding—this is the final teaching. This is how the meaning should be understood.

“Ugghaṭiyanto uddisiyamāno pariyattiatthabhūto dhammavinayo katamaṃ puggalaṃ vineti, vipañciyanto niddisiyamāno pariyattiatthabhūto dhammavinayo katamaṃ puggalaṃ vineti, vitthāriyanto paṭiniddisiyamāno pariyattiatthabhūto dhammavinayo katamaṃ puggalaṃ vinetī”ti pucchitabbattā “soyaṃ dhammavinayo”tiādimāha. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana “evaṃ ‘akkharehi saṅkāsetī’tiādīnaṃ channaṃ byañjanapadānaṃ byāpāraṃ dassetvā idāni atthapadānaṃ byāpāraṃ dassetuṃ ‘soyaṃ dhammavinayo’tiādi vutta”nti (netti. aṭṭha. 9) vuttaṃ.

“Which person does the Dhamma-Vinaya, being the substance of the scriptural teaching, train when it is disclosed and pointed out? Which person does the Dhamma-Vinaya, being the substance of the scriptural teaching, train when it is analyzed and specified? Which person does the Dhamma-Vinaya, being the substance of the scriptural teaching, train when it is expanded and defined?”—because it must be asked thus, he said, “This very Dhamma-Vinaya…” and so on. In the commentary, however, it is said: “Having thus shown the function of the six terms of expression beginning with ‘he clarifies with letters,’ now to show the function of the terms of meaning, ‘This very Dhamma-Vinaya’ and so on is stated” (Netti. Aṭṭha. 9).

Tattha ugghaṭiyanto uddisiyamāno uddesapariyattiatthabhūto so ayaṃ dhammavinayo ugghaṭitaññupuggalaṃ vineti, tena ugghaṭitaññuno puggalassa vinayanena naṃ ugghaṭiyantaṃ uddisiyamānaṃ uddesapariyattiatthabhūtaṃ vinayaṃ “ādikalyāṇo”ti āhu. Vipañciyanto niddisiyamāno niddesapariyattiatthabhūto so ayaṃ dhammavinayo vipañcitaññupuggalaṃ vineti, tena [M 0.0080] vipañcitaññupuggalassa vinayanena naṃ vipañciyantaṃ niddisiyamānaṃ niddesapariyattiatthabhūtaṃ vinayaṃ “majjhekalyāṇo”ti āhu. Vitthāriyanto paṭiniddisiyamāno paṭiniddesapariyattiatthabhūto so ayaṃ dhammavinayo neyyaṃ puggalaṃ vineti vinayanaṃ janeti, tena neyyassa puggalassa vinayanena naṃ vitthāriyantaṃ paṭiniddisiyamānaṃ paṭiniddesapariyattiatthabhūtaṃ vinayaṃ “pariyosānakalyāṇo”ti āhūti yojanatthoti daṭṭhabbo.

Therein, this very Dhamma-Vinaya, being disclosed, being pointed out, being the substance of the scriptural teaching in brief, trains a person of quick understanding. By that training of a person of quick understanding, they call this Vinaya—being disclosed, being pointed out, being the substance of the scriptural teaching in brief—“good in the beginning.” This very Dhamma-Vinaya, being analyzed, being specified, being the substance of the scriptural teaching in detail, trains a person of expanded understanding. By that training of a person of expanded understanding, they call this Vinaya—being analyzed, being specified, being the substance of the scriptural teaching in detail—“good in the middle.” This very Dhamma-Vinaya, being expanded, being re-specified, being the substance of the scriptural teaching in full, trains a person who is to be led, thereby generating training. By that training of a person who is to be led, they call this Vinaya—being expanded, being re-specified, being the substance of the scriptural teaching in full—“good in the end.” Thus the meaning of the construction should be understood.

Atha vā “akkharehi saṅkāsetī”tiādinā channaṃ padānaṃ byāpāro dassito, evaṃ sati attho nibyāpāro siyā, attho ca nippariyāyato sabyāpāroyevāti codanaṃ manasi katvā āha “soyaṃ dhammavinayo”tiādi. Etena atthoyeva mukhyato veneyyattayassa vinayanakiccaṃ sādheti, atthavācako pana saddo ṭhānūpacārato veneyyattayassa vinayanakiccaṃ sādhetīti dasseti. Padaparamassa pana saccappaṭivedhassa patiṭṭhānābhāvato so idha na vutto. Sekkhaggahaṇena vā kalyāṇaputhujjanassa viya neyyaggahaṇena padaparamassa puggalassāpi gahaṇaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ[V 0.0219]. Akkharehītiādīsu karaṇatthe karaṇavacanaṃ, na hetvatthe. Akkharādīnañhi ugghaṭanādīni payojanāniyeva honti, na ugghaṭanādīnaṃ akkharādīni payojanānīti “annena vasatī”tiādīsu viya na hetuattho gahetabbo. Tattha hi annena hetunā vasati, vasanena hetunā annaṃ laddhanti vasanakiriyāya phalaṃ vasanakiriyāya hetubhāvena gahitaṃ. “Ajjhesanena vasatī”tiādīsupi eseva nayo. Tenāha “yadatthā ca kiriyā, so hetū”ti (netti. aṭṭha. 9). Tattha yadatthāti so annādiko attho yassā vasanādikiriyāyāti yadatthā, vasanādikiriyā, so annādiko attho tassā vasanādikiriyāya hetūti attho veditabbo.

Alternatively, considering the objection that if the phrase “he clarifies with letters,” etc., shows the function of the six terms, then the meaning would be functionless—while the meaning itself, being direct, is indeed functional—he stated: “This very Dhamma-Vinaya,” and so on. By this, it is shown that the meaning itself primarily accomplishes the task of training the three types of individuals to be trained, while the word that expresses the meaning accomplishes the task of training those to be trained by way of figurative application. However, the literalist is not mentioned here because there is no foundation for the realization of truth for him. Or, it should be understood that by the inclusion of the ‘neyya’ (one to be led), the person who relies on the letter is also included, just as by the inclusion of the ‘sekha’ (trainee), the virtuous ordinary person is included. In “with letters,” etc., the instrumental case is in the sense of instrument, not in the sense of cause. For revealing, etc., are only the purposes of letters, etc., and it is not that letters, etc., are the purposes of revealing, etc. Therefore, the sense of cause should not be taken, as in “lives by means of food,” etc. For there, one lives by food as the cause, and food is obtained by living as the cause; thus the result of the act of living is taken as the cause for the act of living. The same principle applies in “lives by solicitation,” etc. Therefore, he said, “That for which the action is, that is the cause” (Netti. Aṭṭha. 9). There, ‘that for which’ means: that purpose, such as food, for which the action of living, etc., exists—that is ‘that for which’ the action of living, etc., is. It should be understood that that purpose, such as food, is the cause for that action of living, etc.

10. “Tattha aparimāṇā padā”tiādinā “dhammaṃ vo bhikkhave desessāmī”ti uddiṭṭhāya pāḷiyā dvādasapadasampattisaṅkhātaṃ tividhakalyāṇataṃ dassetvā idāni chaatthapadachabyañjanapadabhedena sampattisaṅkhātaṃ atthapadabyañjanapadakalyāṇataṃ dassento “tattha chappadāni attho”tiādimāha. Atha vā “dvādasa padāni sutta”nti vuttānurūpaṃ “tattha aparimāṇā”tiādinā “dhammaṃ vo bhikkhave desessāmī”ti uddiṭṭhāya pāḷiyā dvādasapadatā [M 0.0081] dassetvā “ādikalyāṇaṃ majjhekalyāṇaṃ pariyosānakalyāṇa”nti vuttānurūpaṃ “tattha bhagavā akkharehi cā”tiādinā tassā pāḷiyā tividhakalyāṇatā dassitā, dassetvā idāni “sātthaṃ sabyañjanaṃ kevalaparipuṇṇaṃ parisuddha”nti vuttānurūpaṃ tassā pāḷiyā chaatthapadabyañjanapadasampannataṃ dassetuṃ “tattha chappadāni attho”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha tatthāti tissaṃ desanāhāravisayasaṅkhātāyaṃ pāḷiyaṃ chappadāni attho. Katamāni chappadāni? Saṅkāsanā, pakāsanā, vivaraṇā, vibhajanā, uttānīkammaṃ, paññatti imāni chappadāni. Attho yassa atthi tasmā sātthaṃ. Tatthāti tissaṃ desanāhāravisayasaṅkhātāyaṃ pāḷiyaṃ chappadāni byañjanaṃ. Katamāni chappadāni? Akkharaṃ, padaṃ, byañjanaṃ, ākāro, nirutti, niddeso imāni chappadāni. Byañjanaṃ yassa atthīti sabyañjananti yojanā kātabbā. Tenāti tassā pāḷiyā tividhakalyāṇachaatthapadasampannachabyañjanapadasampannaṭṭhena, “dhammaṃ vo, bhikkhave…pe… suddha”nti bhagavā āhāti attho.

10. By means of the passage beginning, “Therein, immeasurable are the phrases,” having shown the threefold excellence—reckoned as the accomplishment of twelve phrases—of the Pāli text indicated by “I will teach you the Dhamma, O monks,” he now, showing the excellence of the terms of meaning and the terms of expression—reckoned as the accomplishment by way of the distinction between six terms of meaning and six terms of expression—says, “Therein, six are the terms of meaning,” and so on. Alternatively, in accordance with what was said, “The sutta has twelve phrases,” having shown the twelve-phrased nature of the Pāli text indicated by “I will teach you the Dhamma, O monks,” by means of the passage beginning, “Therein, immeasurable,” and in accordance with what was said, “good in the beginning, good in the middle, good in the end,” the threefold excellence of that Pāli text was shown by means of the passage beginning, “Therein, the Blessed One with letters.” Having shown this, now, to demonstrate that that Pāli text is endowed with six terms of meaning and six terms of expression, in accordance with what was said, “with meaning, with expression, complete and pure,” it was said, “Therein, six are the terms of meaning,” and so on. Therein, “therein” refers to that Pāli text which is reckoned as the scope of the teaching method, containing six terms of meaning. What are the six terms of meaning? Clarification, declaration, exposition, analysis, making plain, and designation—these are the six terms of meaning. That which has meaning (attha) is therefore ‘with meaning’ (sāttha). Therein, in that Pāli text which is reckoned as the scope of the teaching method, there are six terms of expression. What are the six terms of expression? Letter, phrase, expression, mode, language, and exposition—these are the six terms of expression. The construction should be made that that which has expression (byañjana) is ‘with expression’ (sabyañjana). Therefore means: because that Pāli text is endowed with threefold excellence, six terms of meaning, and six terms of expression, the meaning is that the Blessed One said, “I will teach you the Dhamma, O monks… pure.”

Kevalasaddassa sakalādiatthavācakattā adhippetatthaṃ niyametvā dassetuṃ “kevalanti lokuttaraṃ na missaṃ lokiyehi dhammehī”ti vuttaṃ. Paripuṇṇanti adhippetatthe ekopi attho ūno natthi, vācakasaddesupi anatthako ekopi saddo adhiko natthīti paripuṇṇaṃ anūnaṃ anatirekaṃ. Parisuddhanti saddadosaatthadosādivirahato vā parisuddhaṃ, rāgādimalavirahato vā pariyodātānaṃ uttarimanussadhammavisesānaṃ upaṭṭhitaṭṭhānattā parisuddhaṃ pariyodātaṃ. Niggataṃ malaṃ etassa dhammassāti [V 0.0220] nimmalaṃ. Saddadosādivirahato vā rāgādivirahato vā sabbamalehi apagataṃ pari samantato odātanti pariyodātaṃ. Upaṭṭhitanti upatiṭṭhanti ettha sabbavisesāti upaṭṭhitaṃ yathā “padakkanta”nti. Padakkantaṃ padakkantaṭṭhānaṃ. Visisanti manussadhammehīti visesā, sabbe visesā sabbavisesā, sabbato vā visesāti sabbavisesā, uttarimanussadhammā. Tesaṃ sabbavisesānaṃ upaṭṭhitanti yojanā. Idanti sikkhattayasaṅgahaṃ sāsanabrahmacariyaṃ. Tathāgatassa sammāsambuddhassa padanti tathāgatapadaṃ. Padanti ca paṭipattigamanena vā desanāgamanena vā kilesaggahaṇaṃ. Ottharitvā gamanaṭṭhānaṃ itipi vuccati pavuccati, tathāgatena gocarāsevanena vā bhāvanāsevanena vā nisevitaṃ bhajitaṃ itipi vuccati, tathāgatassa mahāvajirañāṇasabbaññutaññāṇadantehi [M 0.0082] ārañjitaṃ ārañjitaṭṭhānaṃ itipi vuccati, ato tathāgatapadādibhāvena vattabbabhāvato etaṃ sāsanabrahmacariyaṃ iti paññāyati. Brahmacariyanti brahmuno sabbasattuttamassa bhagavato cariyaṃ, brahmaṃ vā sabbaseṭṭhaṃ cariyaṃ brahmacariyaṃ. Paññāyatīti yathāvuttehi pakārehi ñāyatīti attho veditabbo.

Because the word 'kevala' expresses meanings such as 'all,' to define and show the intended meaning, it is said: "'Kevala' means the supramundane, unmixed with mundane phenomena." 'Paripuṇṇa' (complete) means that in the intended meaning, not a single meaning is lacking, nor in the expressing words is there any superfluous word devoid of meaning—thus it is complete, without deficiency or excess. 'Parisuddha' (pure) means it is purified, being free from faults in words or meanings, and so on; or, it is pure and immaculate because it is the foundation for the exceedingly pure supreme human qualities, which are free from the stain of lust and so on. "Impurity is gone from this Dhamma, thus it is stainless (Niggataṃ malaṃ etassa dhammassāti nimmalaṃ)." Being free from faults in words and so on, or free from lust and so on, it is devoid of all stains; being utterly cleansed all around, it is 'pariyodāta' (immaculate). 'Upaṭṭhita' (established) means that all special qualities are established here, just as 'padakkanta' (well-trodden) means a well-trodden place. 'Visesā' (special qualities) are so called because they are distinguished from ordinary human qualities; 'sabbavisesā' means all special qualities, or special qualities in every way, that is, supreme human qualities. The connection is that it is the 'foundation' (upaṭṭhita) for all these special qualities. This refers to the holy life of the Dispensation, which comprises the threefold training. The 'pada' (path) of the Tathāgata, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, is the Tathāgata-pada. And 'pada' means the path of practice, or the path of teaching, or the eradication of defilements. It is also called 'the place of alighting and going,' or it is said to be 'frequented' or 'resorted to' by the Tathāgata through the cultivation of his range of activity or the cultivation of development. It is also called the place adorned by the Tathāgata's great diamond-wisdom, omniscient knowledge, and self-control. Therefore, because this holy life of the Dispensation is to be spoken of as being the Tathāgata's path, and so on, it is thus recognized. 'Brahmacariya' (holy life) means the conduct of the 'Brahma,' the Blessed One, who is supreme among all beings; or it is the 'brahma,' that is, the supreme, best conduct. 'Paññāyati' (is recognized) means it is known in the ways described—this is the meaning to be understood.

“Imassa sikkhattayassa saṅgahassa sāsanassa paripuṇṇabhāvaparisuddhabhāvasaṅkhātaṃ tathāgatapadabhāvaṃ!Tathāgatapadabhāvaṃ, tathāgatanisevitabhāvaṃ, tathāgataārañjitabhāvaṃ, tehi pakārehi ñāpitabhāvaṃ kathaṃ mayaṃ nikkaṅkhā jānissāmā”ti vattabbato “tenāha bhagavā”tiādi vuttaṃ, tabbhāvadīpakena bhagavatā vuttena vacanena tumhehi nikkaṅkhehi jānitabboti vuttaṃ hoti.

"How can we know, without doubt, the state of being the Tathāgata's path, which is reckoned as the complete and pure state of this holy life of the Dispensation comprising the threefold training—the state of being the Tathāgata's path, the state of being frequented by the Tathāgata, the state of being adorned by the Tathāgata, the state made known by these means?" Because this is to be said, "Therefore, the Blessed One said..." and so on, was stated. It means that you should know it without doubt by the words spoken by the Blessed One, who reveals that state.

Yadi bhagavā akkharehi ca padehi ca ugghaṭeti, byañjanehi ca ākārehi ca vipañcayati, niruttīhi ca niddesehi ca vitthāreti, evaṃ sati ācariyena racitena desanāhārena payojanaṃ na bhavati, desanāhārena na vinā bhagavato desanāyameva atthasijjhanatoti codanaṃ manasi katvā “kesaṃ ayaṃ dhammadesanā”ti pucchitvā “yogīna”nti āha. Tattha yogīnanti yujjanti catusaccakammaṭṭhānabhāvanāyanti yogino, tesaṃ yogīnaṃ. Tena mayā racitena desanāhārena saṃvaṇṇitā ayaṃ vuttappakārā bhagavato desanā ugghaṭanādikiccaṃ sādhetīti desanāhāro yogīnaṃ sātthakoyevāti daṭṭhabbo. “Desanāhārassa assādādidesanāhārabhāvo kena amhehi jānitabbo saddahitabbo”ti vattabbattā “tenāha āyasmā…pe… desanāhāro”ti vuttaṃ. Tattha tena assādādidesanāhārabhāvena āyasmā mahākaccāno “assādādīnavatā…pe… desanāhāro”ti yaṃ vacanaṃ āha, tena vacanena tumhehi desanāhārassa yogīnaṃ assādādidesanāhārabhāvo jānitabbo saddahitabboti vuttaṃ hoti.

If the Blessed One reveals through letters and words, elucidates through expressions and modes, and expands through etymologies and definitions, then in such a case, there is no purpose for a teaching material composed by a teacher. The purpose is accomplished by the Blessed One’s teaching alone—thus, considering this objection, he asked, "For whom is this Dhamma teaching?" and answered, "For the yogis." Here, 'yogis' refers to those who strive in the development of the four noble truths as meditation subjects—they are the yogis. Therefore, it should be understood that this teaching of the Blessed One, described in the aforementioned manner, when elucidated by the teaching material composed by me, accomplishes the function of revealing, etc. Thus, the teaching material is indeed beneficial for the yogis. Because it is to be asked, "How are we to know and believe that the teaching material has the nature of analyzing gratification, danger, and so on?" it was stated, "Therefore, the Venerable… said… the teaching material." Here, regarding that very nature of the teaching material as analyzing gratification, danger, and so on, the Venerable Mahākaccāna spoke the words, "'Gratification, danger...' and so on... is the teaching material." By that statement, it is meant that you should know and believe that the teaching material for the yogis has the nature of analyzing gratification, danger, and so on.

“Kiṃ [V 0.0221] pana ettāvatā desanāhāro paripuṇṇo, añño niyutto natthī”ti pucchitabbattā “niyutto desanāhāro”ti vuttaṃ. Tattha yassaṃ desanāyaṃ assādādayo yena desanāhārena niddhāritā, tassaṃ desanāyaṃ [M 0.0083] so desanāhāro niddhāretvā yojitoti attho daṭṭhabboti.

"Now, is the teaching material complete with just this much, or is there no other assigned portion?" Because this is to be asked, "the assigned teaching material" was stated. Here, the meaning to be understood is this: in whatever teaching gratification and so forth are determined by a certain teaching material, in that teaching, that teaching material is to be determined and applied.

Iti desanāhāravibhaṅge sattibalānurūpā racitā

Thus was composed this analysis of the teaching material, in accordance with my ability and strength.

Vibhāvanā niṭṭhitā.

The elucidation is completed.

Paṇḍitehi pana aṭṭhakathāṭīkānusārena gambhīrattho vitthārato vibhajitvā gahetabboti.

However, the profound meaning should be comprehensively analyzed and grasped by the learned, in accordance with the commentaries and sub-commentaries.

2. Vicayahāravibhaṅgavibhāvanā

2. Elucidation of the Analysis of the Mode of Investigation

11. Yena yena saṃvaṇṇanāvisesabhūtena desanāhāravibhaṅgena assādādayo suttatthā ācariyena vibhattā, so saṃvaṇṇanāvisesabhūto desanāhāravibhaṅgo paripuṇṇo, “katamo vicayo hāro”ti pucchitabbattā “tattha katamo vicayo hāro”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha tatthāti tesu niddiṭṭhesu soḷasasu desanāhārādīsu hāresu katamo saṃvaṇṇanāviseso vicayo hāro vicayahāravibhaṅgo nāmāti pucchati. “Yaṃ pucchitañca vissajjitañcā”tiādiniddesagāthāya idāni mayā vuccamāno “ayaṃ vicayo hāro kiṃ vicinatī”tiādiko saṃvaṇṇanāviseso vicayahāravibhaṅgo nāmāti yojanā.

11. That analysis of the mode of exposition, being the particular descriptive aspect by which the teacher has analyzed the meanings of the suttas concerning gratification and so on, is now complete. Since the question 'What is the mode of investigation?' should be asked, it is said, 'Here, what is the mode of investigation?' and so on. Here, 'here' refers to the question: Among those sixteen specified modes, beginning with the mode of exposition, what is the particular descriptive aspect, the mode of investigation, called the analysis of the mode of investigation? Now, in the explanatory verse beginning 'What is asked and answered,' the interpretation is as follows: 'This mode of investigation—what does it investigate?' and so on—this particular descriptive aspect is called the analysis of the mode of investigation.

“Ayaṃ vicayo hāro kiṃ vicinatī”ti iminā yo vicayo vicinitabbo, taṃ vicayaṃ vicinitabbaṃ pucchati, tasmā vicinitabbaṃ visayaṃ visuṃ visuṃ niyametvā dassetuṃ “padaṃ vicinati, pañhaṃ vicinatī”tiādi vuttaṃ. “Kiṃ vicayo padavicayo”tiādiṃ avatvā “kiṃ vicinati, padaṃ vicinatī”tiādivacanena vicayasaddassa kattusādhanatthaṃ dasseti. Tattha padaṃ vicinatīti navavidhassa suttantassa sabbaṃ padaṃ yāva nigamanā nāmapadādijātisaddādiitthiliṅgādiākārantādipaṭhamavibhatyantādiekavacanādivasena vicinati. Pañhaṃ vicinatīti adiṭṭhajotanādisattādhiṭṭhānādisammutivisayādiatītavisayādivasena vicinati. Vissajjanaṃ vicinatīti ekaṃsabyākaraṇavissajjanādisāvasesabyākaraṇavissajjanādi sauttarabyākaraṇa vissajjanādi lokiyabyākaraṇavissajjanādivasena vicinati. Pubbāparaṃ vicinatīti [V 0.0222] pubbena aparaṃ saṃsanditvā [M 0.0084] vicinati. Assādaṃ vicinatīti assādakataṇhādiassādetabbasukhādivasena vicinati. Ādīnavaṃ vicinatīti dukkhadukkhavipariṇāmadukkhasaṅkhāradukkhavasena vā aniṭṭhānubhavanādiādiantavantatādisaṃkilesabhāgiyādivasena vā vicinati. Nissaraṇaṃ vicinatīti maggavasena vā nibbānavasena vā maggassa vā āgamavasena, nibbānassa asaṅkhatadhātuādipariyāyavasena vā vicinati. Phalaṃ vicinatīti dhammacaraṇassa duggatigamanābhāvena vā maccutaraṇādinā vā desanāya phalaṃ, desanānusārena caraṇassa phalaṃ vicinati. Upāyaṃ vicinatīti aniccānupassanādivasena pavattananibbidāñāṇādivasena vā saddhāsativasena vā visuddhiyā upāyaṃ vicinati. Āṇattiṃ vicinatīti pāpaparivajjanāṇattivasena vā lokassa suññatāpekkhanāṇattivasena vā vicinati. Anugītiṃ vicinatīti vuttānugītivasena vā vuccamānānugītivasena vā anurūpaṃ gītiṃ vicinati. Sabbe nava suttante vicinatīti suttageyyādike nava sutte āhaccavacanavasena vā anusandhivacanavasena vā nītatthavacanavasena vā neyyatthavacanavasena vā saṃkilesabhāgiyādivasena vā vicinati.

“This method of investigation—what does it investigate?” With this, he asks about the investigation to be investigated, the object to be investigated. Therefore, to define and show the object to be investigated separately, it is said: “It investigates a word, it investigates a question,” and so on. Without stating “What is the investigation? Is it word-investigation?” and so forth, the statement “What does it investigate? It investigates a word,” and so on, indicates that the word ‘investigation’ is used in the agentive sense. Here, “it investigates a word” means it investigates every word of the ninefold division of the suttas, up to the conclusion, by way of name-words, genus-words, gender-words, words ending in ‘ā’, words ending in the first case, words in the singular number, and so on. “It investigates a question” means it investigates by way of unseen illumination, the seven bases, conventional objects, past objects, and so on. “It investigates an answer” means it investigates by way of categorical answers, qualified answers, answers involving a counter-question, worldly answers, and so on. “It investigates the before and after” means it investigates by comparing what comes before with what comes after. “It investigates gratification” means it investigates by way of craving for gratification, happiness to be enjoyed, and so on. “It investigates danger” means it investigates by way of the suffering of pain, the suffering of change, and the suffering of formations, or by way of experiencing the undesirable, having a beginning and an end, being associated with defilement, and so on. “It investigates escape” means it investigates by way of the path or by way of Nibbāna, or by way of the path’s approach, or by way of synonyms for Nibbāna, such as the unconditioned element, and so on. “It investigates the fruit” means it investigates the fruit of practicing the Dhamma—by way of not going to a bad destination or crossing over death, and so on; the fruit of the teaching; and the fruit of practicing in accordance with the teaching. “It investigates the means” means it investigates the means to purification by way of contemplation of impermanence, by way of the progression of knowledge and knowledge of disenchantment, by way of faith and mindfulness, and so on. “It investigates the injunction” means it investigates by way of the injunction to avoid evil or by way of the injunction to regard the world as empty, and so on. “It investigates the recitation” means it investigates a suitable recitation, by way of recitation following what has been said or recitation of what is being said. “It investigates all nine suttas” means it investigates the nine types of suttas—such as sutta, geyya, and so on—by way of direct statements, connecting statements, statements of definitive meaning, statements of interpretable meaning, being associated with defilement, and so on.

Kiñcāpi padavicayo paṭhamaṃ vibhatto, suttassa pana anupadaṃ vicinitabbatāya atibhāriyo, na sukaro padavicayoti taṃ aggahetvā pañhāvicayavissajjanavicaye tāva vibhajanto “yathā kiṃ bhave”tiādimāha. Tattha yathā kiṃ bhaveti yena pakārena so pañhāvicayo pavattetabbo, taṃ pakārajātaṃ kīdisaṃ bhaveyyāti attho daṭṭhabbo. Āyasmā ajito pārāyane bhagavantaṃ pañhaṃ yathā yena pakārena pucchati, tathā tena pakārena pañhāvicayo pavattetabboti attho. Tattha āyasmāti piyavacanaṃ. Ajitoti bāvarībrāhmaṇassa paricārakabhūtānaṃ soḷasannaṃ aññataro ajito. Pārāyaneti pāraṃ nibbānaṃ ayati gacchati etenāti pārāyanaṃ, ajitasuttādisoḷasasuttassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ.

Although the investigation of words was first explained, since the investigation of a sutta word by word is too burdensome and not easy, setting that aside, he first divides the investigation of questions and the investigation of answers, beginning with, “In what way should it be?” Here, “In what way should it be?” means: In what manner should this investigation of questions be conducted? The meaning to be understood is: What sort of nature should it have? The Venerable Ajita asks the Blessed One a question in the Pārāyana in a certain way; in that same way should the investigation of questions be conducted—this is the meaning. Here, ‘Venerable’ is a term of affection. ‘Ajita’ refers to Ajita, one of the sixteen attendants of the brahmin Bāvarī. ‘Pārāyana’ means: because one goes (ayati) to the far shore (pāraṃ), Nibbāna, by means of it, it is called Pārāyana. This is a designation for the sixteen suttas beginning with the Ajitasutta.

“Kenassu nivuto loko, (iccāyasmā ajito,)

Kenassu nappakāsati;

Kissābhilepanaṃ brūsi, kiṃ su tassa mahabbhaya”nti. (su. ni. 1038; cūḷani. vatthugāthā 57, ajitamāṇavapucchāniddesa 1) –

“By what is the world shrouded,

(thus asked the Venerable Ajita,)

by what does it not shine?

What do you call its defilement,

and what is its great fear?”

Gāthāya [M 0.0085] “kena dhammena loko ariyavajjo satto nivuto paṭicchādito, iti āyasmā ajito [V 0.0223] pucchati. Kena hetunā yathāvuttaloko nappakāsati, assa yathāvuttalokassa kiṃ abhilepanaṃ iti tvaṃ brūsi, tassa yathāvuttalokassa kiṃ mahabbhayanti tvaṃ brūsīti pucchatī”ti attho.

The meaning of the verse is: “By what principle is the world—the being spoken of by the noble ones—shrouded and concealed?”—thus the Venerable Ajita asks. “For what reason does the aforesaid world not shine? What do you say is the defilement of this aforesaid world? What do you say is the great fear of that aforesaid world?”—this is what he asks.

Iti iminā pabhedena cattāri imāni gāthāpādapadāni pucchitāni pucchāvasena vuttāni, pucchitatthadīpakāni vā, padhānavasena pana so “eko pañho”ti mato, yadipi catunnaṃ padānaṃ pucchanavasena pavattattā catubbidhoti vattabbo, ñātuṃ pana icchitassa ekasseva atthassa sambhavato “eko pañho”ti vuttaṃ. “Kāraṇaṃ vadehī”ti vattabbattā kāraṇamāha “ekavatthupariggahā”ti. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – “yadipi nivāraṇāpakāsanābhilepanamahabbhayasaṅkhātā cattāro atthā pucchāyaṃ gahitā, ekassa pana abhidheyyatthassa gahaṇato ‘eko pañho’ti padhānavasena gahitoti daṭṭhabbo”ti. “Ekavatthupariggahaṇaṃ kathaṃ amhehi saddahitabba”nti vattabbabhāvato “evañhi āhā”ti vuttaṃ. Evaṃ ekavatthupariggahaṇeneva bhagavā hi yasmā āha, iti tasmā ekavatthupariggahaṇaṃ tumhehi saddahitabbanti vuttaṃ hoti.

Thus, by this division, these four lines of the verse have been asked, spoken by way of a question, or as illuminators of the meaning asked. Primarily, however, it is considered ‘one question.’ Although it could be called fourfold because it proceeds by way of asking four lines, it is said to be ‘one question’ since for one who wishes to know, only one meaning arises. When it should be said, “State the reason,” he states the reason as “because it grasps one subject.” This is what is said: “Although four meanings—namely, shrouding, not shining, defilement, and great fear—are grasped in the question, it should be seen that, primarily, it is taken as ‘one question’ because it grasps a single intended meaning.” Since it should be said, “How are we to have faith in this grasping of a single subject?” it is said, “For thus he spoke.” The meaning is: because the Blessed One spoke in terms of grasping a single subject, therefore you should have faith in the grasping of a single subject.

“Kenassu nivuto loko”ti iminā lokādhiṭṭhānaṃ paṭicchādanaṃ pucchati, na nānādhammādhiṭṭhānaṃ. “Kenassu nappakāsatī”ti iminā lokasseva appakāsanaṃ pucchati, na nānāsabhāvadhammassa. “Kissābhilepanaṃ brūsī”ti iminā lokasseva abhilepanaṃ pucchati, na nānāsabhāvadhammassa. “Kiṃ su tassa mahabbhaya”nti iminā tasseva lokassa mahabbhayaṃ pucchati, na nānāsabhāvadhammassa. Tasmā “kenassu nivuto loko”tiādipañho ekādhiṭṭhānanānādhiṭṭhānesu ekādhiṭṭhāno, dhammādhiṭṭhānasattādhiṭṭhānesu sattādhiṭṭhāno, adiṭṭhajotanādīsu adiṭṭhajotanāpañhotiādinā yathāsambhavaṃ vicinitabboti adhippāyo.

“By what is the world shrouded?”—with this, he asks about the covering that has the world as its basis, not one that has various phenomena as its basis. “By what does it not shine?”—with this, he asks about the non-shining of the world itself, not of phenomena of various natures. “What do you call its defilement?”—with this, he asks about the defilement of the world itself, not of phenomena of various natures. “What is its great fear?”—with this, he asks about the great fear of that world itself, not of phenomena of various natures. Therefore, the question beginning with “By what is the world shrouded?”—among questions with a single basis and multiple bases—has a single basis; among questions with phenomena as a basis and beings as a basis, it has beings as its basis; among questions of unseen illumination and the like, it is a question of unseen illumination. The intention is that it should be investigated accordingly.

“Pañhassa yo loko ‘adhiṭṭhāno’ti gahito, so loko tividho”ti vattabbabhāvato “loko tividho”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha tayo vidhā etassa lokassāti tividho. Kilissati rāgādivasena kāmāvacarasattoti kileso, kileso ca so loko [M 0.0086] cāti kilesaloko, kāmāvacarasatto. So hi rāgādikilesabahulatāya kilesalokoti. Bhavati jhānābhiññāhi buddhīhīti bhavo, bhavo ca so loko cāti bhavaloko, rūpāvacarasatto. So hi jhānādibuddhīhi bhavatīti. Indriyena samannāgatoti indriyo, indriyo ca so loko cāti indriyaloko, arūpāvacarasatto. So hi āneñjasamādhibahulatāya visuddhindriyo hotīti lokasamaññā pariyāpannadhammavasena pavattā, tasmā ariyā na gahitāti.

Since it should be said, “The world that is taken as the ‘basis’ of the question is threefold,” the passage beginning “the world is threefold” was stated. Here, ‘threefold’ means this world has three types. A being in the sense-sphere is defiled (kilissati) by lust and so on, thus it is a defilement (kilesa); it is a defilement and it is the world (loko), thus it is the defilement-world (kilesaloko), that is, a being in the sense-sphere. For it is called the defilement-world because of its abundance of defilements such as lust. A being in the fine-material sphere comes to be (bhavati) through the growths of jhāna and direct knowledge, thus it is existence (bhavo); it is existence and it is the world, thus it is the existence-world (bhavaloko), that is, a being in the fine-material sphere. For it comes to be through the growths of jhāna and so on. A being in the immaterial sphere is endowed with a faculty (indriyena samannāgato), thus it is a faculty (indriyo); it is a faculty and it is the world, thus it is the faculty-world (indriyaloko), that is, a being in the immaterial sphere. For it has purified faculties due to an abundance of imperturbable concentration. Thus, the designation ‘world’ is applied to phenomena included in the round of existence; therefore, the noble ones are not included.

“Kenassu [V 0.0224] nivuto loko”tiādigāthāya pucchāvicayo hāro ācariyena vibhatto, amhehi ca ñāto, “vissajjanāvicayo hāro kattha vissajjanāya vibhatto”ti pucchitabbattā “tattha vissajjanā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha tatthāti tassaṃ “kenassu nivuto loko”tiādipucchāyaṃ –

In the verse beginning 'By what is the world shrouded?', the mode of investigation of the question has been explained by the teacher and is known by us. Since it should be asked, 'Where is the mode of investigation of the answer explained?', it is said, 'Therein is the answer,' and so on. Therein, 'therein' refers to that question beginning 'By what is the world shrouded?'—

“Avijjāya nivuto loko, (ajitāti bhagavā,)

Vivicchā pamādā nappakāsati;

Jappābhilepanaṃ brūmi, dukkhamassa mahabbhaya”nti. (su. ni. 1039; cūḷani. vatthugāthā 58, ajitamāṇavapucchāniddesa) –

"The world is shrouded by ignorance," (O Ajita, said the Blessed One,) "due to doubt and heedlessness it does not shine forth; I declare craving as its defilement, suffering is its great fear."

Ayaṃ gāthā vissajjanāti daṭṭhabbā. Tattha avijjāya nivuto lokoti kāḷapakkhacatuddasī, ghanavanasaṇḍa, meghapaṭalacchādana, aḍḍharattīnaṃ vasena caturaṅgasamannāgatena andhakārena rathaghaṭādi paṭicchādito viya dhammasabhāvapaṭicchādanalakkhaṇāya avijjāya sattaloko nivuto paṭicchādito. “Ajitā”ti ca ālapanaṃ katvā bhagavā āha. Vivicchāti vicikicchāya pamādahetu yathāvuttaloko nappakāsati. Jappaṃ taṇhaṃ yathāvuttalokassa “abhilepana”nti ahaṃ brūmīti bhagavā āha, dukkhaṃ jātiādivaṭṭadukkhaṃ assa yathāvuttalokassa “mahabbhaya”nti ahaṃ brūmīti bhagavā ajitaṃ āhāti attho.

This verse should be understood as the reply. Herein, the world is shrouded by ignorance—like the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, a dense forest grove, a covering of thick clouds, or midnight—concealed by fourfold darkness, just as chariots and so on are hidden. The world of beings is veiled by ignorance, which has the characteristic of obscuring the true nature of phenomena. Then, addressing Ajita, the Blessed One spoke. Vivicchā means that due to doubt and heedlessness, the world as described does not become clear. The Blessed One said: "I declare craving (jappa), that is, taṇhā, to be the 'smear' of this world." The Blessed One said to Ajita: "I declare suffering—the suffering of the round of existence beginning with birth—to be the 'great fear' of this world." This is the meaning.

“Imāya vissajjanāya kathaṃ vicineyyā”ti pucchitabbattā “imāni cattāri padānī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha imāni cattāri padānīti “kenassu nivuto loko”tiādipucchāgāthāyaṃ vuttāni gāthāpadāni. Imehi catūhi padehīti “avijjāya nivuto loko”ti vissajjanāgāthāyaṃ vuttehi gāthāpadehi vissajjitāni. Kathaṃ? Paṭhamaṃ padaṃ paṭhamena padena, dutiyaṃ padaṃ [M 0.0087] dutiyena padena, tatiyaṃ padaṃ tatiyena padena, catutthaṃ padaṃ catutthena padena vissajjitaṃ.

Because it should be asked, 'How should one analyze this explanation?', it is said, 'These four lines,' and so on. Here, 'these four lines' refer to the lines of the question verse, 'By what is the world obscured?', and so on. They are explained by the four lines stated in the answer verse, 'The world is obscured by ignorance,' and so on. How? The first line is explained by the first line, the second line by the second line, the third line by the third line, and the fourth line by the fourth line.

“Kenassu nivuto loko”ti paṭhamapañhe “avijjāya nivuto loko”ti paṭhamā vissajjanā katā, na uppaṭipāṭiyā. Vijjāya paṭipakkhā avijjā, tasmā avijjāya ajānako loko bhaveyya. Kathaṃ nivuto saddahitabboti āha “nīvaraṇehi nivuto loko”ti. Yadi evaṃ “nīvaraṇena nivuto loko”ti vissajjanā kātabbāti codanaṃ manasi [V 0.0225] katvā vuttaṃ “avijjānīvaraṇā hi sabbe sattā”ti. “Sabbasattānaṃ avijjānīvaraṇabhāvo kena vacanena saddahitabbo”ti vattabbattā “yathāha bhagavā”tiādi vuttaṃ.

"By what is the world shrouded?" In response to the first question, the first reply given was, "The world is shrouded by ignorance," not in reverse order. Ignorance is the opposite of knowledge; therefore, the world would be unknowing because of ignorance. How is it to be believed that it is shrouded? It is said: "The world is shrouded by hindrances." If so, the answer should have been, "The world is shrouded by a hindrance." Considering this objection, it is stated, "For all beings are hindered by the hindrance of ignorance." Because it should be asked, "By what statement can the fact that all beings are hindered by the hindrance of ignorance be believed?", "As the Blessed One has said," and so on was stated.

“Sabbasattānaṃ, bhikkhave, sabbapāṇānaṃ sabbabhūtānaṃ, pariyāyato ekameva nīvaraṇaṃ vadāmi, yadidaṃ avijjā. Avijjānīvaraṇā hi sabbe sattā. Sabbasova bhikkhave avijjāya nirodhā cāgā paṭinissaggā natthi sattānaṃ nīvaraṇanti vadāmī”ti yaṃ vacanaṃ yathā yena pakārena bhagavā āha, tathā tena pakārena vuttena tena vacanena tumhehi sabbasattānaṃ avijjānīvaraṇabhāvo saddahitabboti.

"Monks, for all beings, for all breathing creatures, for all living beings, I declare there is, in a certain way, only one hindrance, that is, ignorance. For all beings are hindered by the hindrance of ignorance. Monks, with the complete cessation, abandonment, and relinquishment of ignorance, there is no hindrance for beings—this I declare." By that statement, spoken by the Blessed One in just that manner, you should believe in the fact that all beings are hindered by the hindrance of ignorance.

“Avijjāya nivuto loko”ti padena “kenassu nivuto loko”ti paṭhamasseva padassa vissajjanā na siyā, “kenassu nappakāsatī”ti dutiyapadassāpi vissajjanā siyāti codanaṃ manasi katvā “tena cā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha tena “avijjāya nivuto loko”ti padena “kenassu nivuto loko”ti paṭhamassa padassa vissajjanā yuttā yuttatarā hoti, yuttatarattā “kenassu nivuto loko”ti pañhe “avijjāya nivuto loko”ti vissajjanāti mayā vattabbāyevāti adhippāyo.

Considering the objection that the line 'The world is shrouded by ignorance' might not be the answer to the first line alone, but could also be the answer to the second line, 'Why does it not shine forth?', it was said, 'And by that...' and so on. Therein, with the line 'the world is shrouded by ignorance,' the answer to the first line, 'By what is the world shrouded?' is fitting, and even more so. Because it is most fitting, the intended meaning is that the answer to the question 'By what is the world shrouded?' must indeed be stated as 'the world is shrouded by ignorance'.

“Kenassu nappakāsatī”ti imasmiṃ pañhe “vivicchā pamādā nappakāsatī”ti ayaṃ vissajjanā kātabbā, vivicchāya pavattattā, pamādā ca loko nappakāsatīti attho. Avijjānīvaraṇāya nivuto loko nappakāsatīti vissajjanā kātabbā, “kathaṃ vivicchā pamādā loko nappakāsatīti vissajjanā katā”ti vattabbattā “yo puggalo”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha yo puthujjanabhūto puggalo avijjānīvaraṇehi [M 0.0088] nivuto, so puthujjanabhūto puggalo vivicchāya vivicchati. “Yāya vivicchāya vivicchati, sā vivicchā katamā nāmā”ti pucchitabbattā “vivicchā nāma vuccati vicikicchā”ti vuttaṃ. “Tāya kasmā nappakāsatī”ti vattabbattā “so vicikicchanto”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tāya vicikicchanto so puthujjanabhūto puggalo saddahitabbesu nābhisaddahati; saddahitabbesu na abhisaddahanto akusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ pahānāya, kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ sacchikiriyāya ārabhitabbaṃ vīriyaṃ nārabhati; anārabhanto so puggalo idha loke pamādamanuyutto viharatīti, pamādena viharanto pamatto puggalo sukke dhamme na uppādiyati; anuppādayantassa tassa puggalassa te sukkā dhammā anuppādiyamānā hutvā nappakāsanti pakāsanavasena na pavattanti; tasmā “vivicchā pamādā loko nappakāsatī”ti vissajjanā kātabbāti adhippāyo.

In the question "Why does it not shine forth?" the answer should be given as "due to doubt and heedlessness, it does not shine forth," because the world does not shine forth due to the prevalence of doubt and heedlessness. The answer could be given as "the world, shrouded by the hindrance of ignorance, does not shine forth." Since it must be said, "How is the answer given that due to doubt and heedlessness, the world does not shine forth?", "that person" and so on was stated. Here, an ordinary person, shrouded by the hindrances of ignorance, is beset by doubt. When it should be asked, "What is this doubt called?", it is said, "Doubt (vivicchā) is called uncertainty (vicikicchā)." Since it must be said, "Why does it not shine forth because of that?", "being uncertain" and so on was stated. Being uncertain, that ordinary person does not place faith in what should be believed. Not placing faith in what should be believed, they do not arouse the effort that should be aroused for the abandonment of unwholesome qualities and the realization of wholesome qualities. Not arousing effort, that person lives addicted to heedlessness in this world. Living heedlessly, the heedless person does not generate bright qualities. Not generating them, those bright qualities, not being generated, do not shine forth or manifest; they do not prevail in terms of manifestation. Therefore, the answer should be given as "due to doubt and heedlessness, the world does not shine forth"—this is the intended meaning.

“Tādisassa [V 0.0226] sukkadhammānaṃ appakāsanabhāvo amhehi kena vacanena saddahitabbo”ti vattabbabhāvato “yathāha bhagavā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha –

Since it should be said, "By what statement are we to believe in the non-manifestation of bright qualities for such a person?", "as the Blessed One has said," and so on was stated. Therein—

“Dūre santo pakāsanti, himavantova pabbato;

Asantettha na dissanti, rattiṃ khittā yathā sarā;

Te guṇehi pakāsanti, kittiyā ca yasena cā”ti. –

"The good shine forth from afar, like the Himavanta mountain; the wicked are not seen here, like arrows shot at night. They shine forth through their virtues, and through fame and glory."

Yaṃ gāthāpāṭhaṃ bhagavā yathā yena appakāsanākārena āha, tathā tena appakāsanākārena vuttena tena gāthāpāṭhena tādisassa puggalassa sukkadhammānaṃ appakāsanabhāvo tumhehi saddahitabboyeva, tasmā “vivicchā pamādā loko nappakāsatī”ti vissajjanā kātabbāvāti adhippāyo.

That verse passage, just as the Blessed One spoke it in the manner of non-manifestation, by that verse passage, spoken in that manner of non-manifestation, you should indeed believe in the non-manifestation of bright qualities for such a person. Therefore, the reply should be given: "Due to doubt and heedlessness, the world does not shine forth"—this is the intended meaning.
