Gāthāttho pana – himavanto pabbato dūre ṭhito dūre ṭhitānampi sacakkhukānaṃ puggalānaṃ pakāsati iva, evaṃ santo sappurisā dūre ṭhitānampi guṇavasena pavattāya kittiyā ca guṇavasena pavattehi yasaparibhogaparivārehi ca dūre ṭhitānaṃ paṇḍitānaṃ pakāsanti, rattikāle khittā sarā usū na dissanti yathā, ettha sattaloke vivicchāpamādānaṃ vasena viharanto asanto na dissanti. Ye santo pakāsanti, te santo guṇehi pakāsantīti dassetuṃ “te guṇehi pakāsantī”ti vuttaṃ[M 0.0089]. Guṇā nāma abbhantare jātā, “kathaṃ guṇehi pakāsantī”ti vattabbattā “kittiyā ca yasena cā”ti vuttaṃ. Guṇānubhāvena pavattāya kittiyā ca guṇānubhāvena pavattena yasena ca pakāsantā puggalā guṇehi pakāsantīti vattabbāvāti.

The meaning of the verse is this: just as the Himālaya mountain, though standing far away, is manifest even to those with sight at a distance, so too do virtuous people shine forth from afar to the wise who are far away, through the fame and through the glory and retinue that arise from their virtue. Just as arrows shot at night are not seen, so too are the unvirtuous, living in this world by means of doubt and heedlessness, not seen. Those who are virtuous shine forth; to show that they shine forth through their virtue, it is said: 'They shine forth through their virtues.' Virtues, indeed, arise within; because it should be asked, 'How do they shine forth through virtue?', it is said: 'Through fame and glory.' People who shine forth through the fame arising from the power of virtue and through the glory arising from the power of virtue are said to shine forth through virtue.

Yadi vivicchāpamādānaṃ vasena nappakāsati, evaṃ sati loko nivuto hoti, tasmā paṭhamassa padassāpi vissajjanā kātabbāti codanaṃ manasi katvā “tena cā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha tenāti “vivicchā pamādā nappakāsatī”ti padena “kenassu nappakāsatī”ti dutiyassa padassa vissajjanā yuttā yuttatarāti attho. Padenāti ca padatthaṭṭhena vissajjanāti attho. Padassāti padatthassa pucchitabbassāti attho daṭṭhabbo. Esa nayo heṭṭhā, upari ca.

If it is not manifest by means of doubt and heedlessness, then the world is covered. Therefore, keeping in mind the objection that an explanation of the first phrase should also be given, 'and by that,' etc., was stated. Herein, 'by that' means that the reply to the second phrase, 'By what is it not manifest?', by the phrase 'it is not manifest due to doubt and heedlessness' is fitting, indeed, most fitting. And 'by the phrase' means the explanation is by the meaning of the phrase. 'Of the phrase' should be understood to mean 'of the meaning of the phrase that is to be questioned.' This method applies below and above.

“Kissābhilepanaṃ brūsī”ti pañhe “jappābhilepanaṃ brūmī”ti vissajjanā tassā ajitena daṭṭhabbā. “Katamā jappā nāmā”ti pucchitabbattā “jappā nāma vuccati taṇhā”ti vuttaṃ. Sā taṇhā lokaṃ abhilimpatīti kathaṃ viññāyatīti yojanā. Tena vuttaṃ “yathāha bhagavā”tiādi. Tattha yathā yena taṇhāya abhilepanabhāvena –

To the question, 'What do you call the smearing?', the reply is, 'I call longing the smearing.' That reply should be understood as given by Ajita. Because it should be asked, 'What, indeed, is this longing (jappā)?', it is said: 'Longing is called craving (taṇhā).' The connection is this: How is it to be understood that this craving smears the world? Therefore, it is said, 'As the Blessed One has said,' and so on. Herein, in the way that craving has the nature of a smearing—

“Ratto [V 0.0227] atthaṃ na jānāti, ratto dhammaṃ na passati;

Andhaṃ tamaṃ tadā hoti, yaṃ rāgo sahate nara”nti. –

"One consumed by passion does not know the goal, one consumed by passion does not see the Dhamma; then there is blinding darkness, when passion overwhelms a person."

Yaṃ gāthaṃ bhagavā āha, tathā tena abhilepanabhāvena vuttāya tāya gāthāya sā taṇhā lokaṃ abhilimpatīti viññāyatīti adhippāyo.

The intended meaning is this: by that verse which the Blessed One spoke, a verse spoken concerning this quality of smearing, it is understood that this craving smears the world.

Gāthāyaṃ pana – rajjati sattoti ratto, rāgasamaṅgīsatto. Kāraṇaṃ paṭicca asati pavattati phalanti atthaṃ, phalaṃ. Kāraṇaṃ phalaṃ dhāreti, taṃ kāraṇaṃ dhammaṃ nāma. Andhakāraṃ andhaṃ. Yanti yamhi kāle. Yanti hi bhummatthe paccattavacanaṃ. Yamhi kāle rāgo naraṃ rāgasamaṅgiṃ sahate abhibhavati, tadā kāle andhaṃ andhakāraṃ tamaṃ hotīti yojanā. Rāgo naraṃ yaṃ yasmā sahate, tasmā andhaṃ tamaṃ tadā hotīti vā, rāgo yaṃ naraṃ sahate, tassa narassa andhaṃ tamaṃ tadā hotīti vā, rāgo naraṃ yaṃ sahate abhibhūyate yaṃ sahanaṃ abhibhavanaṃ nipphādeti, taṃ sahanaṃ abhibhavanaṃ andhaṃ andhakāraṃ tamaṃ hotīti vā yojanā.

Now, in the verse: 'A being is impassioned,' thus he is 'impassioned' (ratto), a being endowed with passion. The meaning (attha) is the result (phala), which arises depending on a cause. The cause bears the result; that cause is called Dhamma. 'Blinding' (andhaṃ) means darkness. The word 'yaṃ' means 'at which time.' For 'yaṃ' is a singular expression in the locative sense. The construction is this: at the time when passion overcomes and overwhelms a person endowed with passion, at that time there is blinding darkness and gloom. Or: because passion overcomes a person, therefore at that time there is blinding darkness. Or: when passion overcomes a person, for that person there is blinding darkness at that time. Or: the overpowering of a person which passion accomplishes, that overpowering produces blinding darkness and gloom—this is the construction.

“Yadi [M 0.0090] ratto atthādikaṃ na jānāti, evaṃ sati kathaṃ jappābhilepanaṃ bhavatī”ti vattabbattā “sāyaṃ taṇhā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha ārammaṇesu āsattibahulassa āsaṅgabahulassa taṇhāsamaṅgissa puggalassa sā ayaṃ taṇhā evaṃ bahuāsaṅgavasena abhijappā pariyuṭṭhānaṭṭhāyinī hoti. Iti karitvā iminā kāraṇena tattha taṇhāya sattaloko kenaci silesena abhilitto makkhito viya jappābhilepena abhilitto nāma bhavatīti yojanā. “Jappābhilepanaṃ appakāsanassapi kāraṇaṃ bhavati, tasmā ‘kenassu nappakāsatī’ti dutiyapadatthassapi vissajjanā siyā”ti vattabbattā “tena cā”tiādi vuttaṃ.

Because it might be said, 'If a passionate person does not understand the meaning and so on, then how can there be a smearing by longing?', the words 'this craving,' etc., were stated. Herein, for a person who has much attachment to sense-objects, much clinging, and is endowed with craving, this very craving, by way of such great clinging, becomes a longing that stands as an obsession. Therefore, for this reason, the world of beings is, as it were, smeared or anointed by craving with some adhesive, and is thus said to be smeared with the smearing of longing—this is the construction. Because it might be said, 'The smearing by longing also becomes a cause for non-manifestation; therefore, it could also be the answer to the meaning of the second phrase, "By what is it not manifest?"', the words 'and by that,' etc., were stated.

“Tassa lokassa mahabbhayaṃ ki”nti imasmiṃ catutthapañhe “assa lokassa dukkhaṃ mahabbhayaṃ bhave”ti ayaṃ vissajjanā tassā ajitena daṭṭhabbā. Bhāyati loko etasmāti bhayaṃ, mahantaṃ bhayaṃ mahabbhayaṃ. “Katividhaṃ dukkha”nti pucchitabbattā “duvidhaṃ dukkha”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Dve vidhā assa dukkhassāti duvidhaṃ. “Katamaṃ duvidhaṃ dukkha”nti pucchitabbattā “kāyikañca cetasikañcā”ti vuttaṃ. “Katamaṃ kāyikaṃ, katamaṃ cetasika”nti pucchitabbattā “yaṃ kāyikaṃ, idaṃ dukkhaṃ yaṃ cetasikaṃ, idaṃ domanassa”nti vuttaṃ.

In this fourth question, 'For that world, what is the great fear?', this answer, 'For this world, suffering is the great fear,' should be understood as given by Ajita. The world fears on account of this, hence it is 'fear'; great fear is 'great fear'. Because it might be asked, 'Of how many kinds is suffering?', 'Two kinds of suffering,' etc., was stated. 'It has two kinds,' hence 'twofold.' Because it might be asked, 'What are the two kinds of suffering?', 'Bodily and mental,' etc., was stated. Because it might be asked, 'What is bodily, and what is mental?', 'That which is bodily is suffering; that which is mental is sorrow,' etc., was stated.

Rogādisatthādianiṭṭharūpaṃ sattalokassa mahabbhayaṃ bhaveyya, “kathaṃ dukkhaṃ mahabbhayaṃ bhaveti saddahetabba”nti [V 0.0228] vattabbabhāvato “sabbe sattā hī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha sabbe sattā yathāvuttassa dukkhassa ubbijjanti, dukkhena samasamaṃ aññaṃ bhayaṃ sattānaṃ natthi, dukkhato uttaritaraṃ vā pana bhayaṃ kuto atthi. Hi yasmā natthi, tasmā dukkhato aññassa bhayassa abhāvato “dukkhaṃ lokassa mahabbhaya”nti vacanaṃ saddahitabbanti adhippāyo.

Undesirable things such as sickness and weapons might be a great fear for the world of beings. Because it might be said, 'How is suffering to be believed to be the great fear?', therefore, 'All beings, indeed…' etc., was stated. Herein, all beings are agitated by the suffering as described. There is no fear for beings equal to suffering; or whence could there be a fear greater than suffering? Indeed, since there is none, therefore, because of the absence of any fear other than suffering, the statement 'Suffering is the great fear of the world' should be accepted—this is the intended meaning.

“Sabbe sattā”tiādivacanena rogādisatthādianiṭṭharūpaṃ dukkhamūlamevāti dasseti. “Kāyikacetasikavasena duvidhaṃ dukkhaṃ dukkhavedanāyeva, evaṃ sati saṅkhāradukkhavipariṇāmadukkhānaṃ mahabbhayabhāvo na āpajjeyyā”ti vattabbabhāvato “tisso dukkhatā”tiādi vuttaṃ.

The statement 'All beings,' etc., shows that undesirable things such as sickness and weapons are rooted in suffering itself. Because it might be said, 'The twofold suffering, in terms of physical and mental, is simply suffering as painful feeling; if that were the case, the state of being a great fear would not apply to the suffering of formations and the suffering of change,' therefore, 'the three kinds of suffering,' etc., was stated.

“Tisso dukkhatā sabbesaṃ sattānaṃ sabbakālesu uppajjanti, kadāci kassaci na uppajjantī”ti pucchitabbattā “tattha loko”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha tatthāti tāsu tīsu dukkhatāsu. Lokoti bhogasampanno ceva appābādho [M 0.0091] ca sattaloko. Odhaso odhiso kadāci karahaci attūpakkamamūlāya dukkhadukkhatāya muccati, kadāci parūpakkamamūlāya dukkhadukkhatāya muccati, tathā odhaso odhiso kadāci karahaci dīghāyuko loko vipariṇāmadukkhatāya muccati, “kena hetunā muccatī”ti pucchitabbattā pucchaṃ ṭhapetvā hetuṃ dassetuṃ “taṃ kissa hetū”tiādi vuttaṃ. Sattaloke appekacce appābādhā honti, te bhogasampannattā ceva appābādhattā ca dukkhadukkhatāya muccanti, visesato rūpāvacarasattā muccanti. Appekacce dīghāyukāpi honti, te dīghāyukattā vipariṇāmadukkhatāya muccanti; visesato arūpāvacarasattā muccanti arūpāvacarasattānaṃ upekkhāsamāpattibahulattā.

Because it might be asked, 'Do the three kinds of suffering arise for all beings at all times, or do they sometimes not arise for some?', therefore, 'therein the world,' etc., was stated. 'Therein' refers to those three kinds of suffering. 'The world' refers to the world of beings who are both wealthy and free from illness. Occasionally, from time to time, the world of beings is freed from the suffering-of-suffering rooted in their own actions; occasionally, they are freed from the suffering-of-suffering rooted in others’ actions. Similarly, occasionally, from time to time, the long-lived world is freed from the suffering-of-change. Because it might be asked, 'For what reason are they freed?', setting aside the question in order to show the reason, 'what is the reason for that?', etc., was stated. In the world of beings, some are free from illness. Due to being both wealthy and free from illness, they are freed from the suffering-of-suffering—especially beings in the form realm are freed. Some are also long-lived. Due to their long life, they are freed from the suffering-of-change—especially beings in the formless realm are freed, because beings in the formless realm have an abundance of attainments of equanimity.

Tesaṃ tāhi dukkhatāhi muccanaṃ anekantikaṃ hoti, tasmā tāhi anatikkantattā anekantikaṃ muccanaṃ tumhehi vuttaṃ, amhehi ca ñātaṃ, “katamaṃ ekantikamuccana”nti pucchitabbattā “saṅkhāradukkhatāya panā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha saṅkhāradukkhatāyāti dukkhavedanāpi saṅkhatattā saṅkhārapariyāpannā, tādisāya saṅkhāradukkhatāyāti attho gahetabbo. Lokoti arahā. Upādīyati vipākakkhandhacatukkakaṭattārūpasaṅkhātaṃ khandhapañcakanti upādi, upādiyeva sesaṃ upādisesaṃ, khandhapañcakaṃ, taṃ natthi etissā nibbānadhātuyāti anupādisesā. Anupādisesāya nibbānadhātuyā anupādisesanibbānadhātu hutvā muccati, itthambhūtalakkhaṇe cāyaṃ karaṇaniddeso. Nibbānadhātūti ca khandhapañcakassa nibbāyanamattaṃ adhippetaṃ, na asaṅkhatadhātu. Tasmāti saṅkhāradukkhatāya sakalalokabyāpakabhāvena sabbalokasaṅgāhakattā vuttappakārasaṅkhāradukkhatāya sabbalokassa [V 0.0229] dukkhaṃ hoti, iti katvā saṅkhāradukkhatāya sabbalokassa dukkhabhāvato “dukkhamassa mahabbhaya”nti bhagavatā vuttaṃ.

Their liberation from those sufferings is not absolute; therefore, since they have not transcended them, their liberation is not absolute, as stated by you and known by us. Because it might be asked, “What is absolute liberation?”, the words “But by the suffering of conditioned things,” etc., were stated. Here, ‘by the suffering of conditioned things’ means that even painful feeling, being conditioned, is included among conditioned phenomena; thus, the meaning should be understood as ‘by such suffering of conditioned things.’ ‘The world’ refers to the Arahant. The five aggregates—designated as the four resultant aggregates and form produced by kamma—are clung to; this is ‘clinging’ (upādi). The remainder of that very clinging is the ‘residue of clinging’ (upādisesa), that is, the five aggregates. That does not exist for this Nibbāna-element, hence it is ‘without residue of clinging’ (anupādisesā). One is liberated by means of the Nibbāna-element without residue of clinging, having become the Nibbāna-element without residue of clinging; this instrumental case indicates such a characteristic. The term ‘Nibbāna-element’ here refers merely to the stilling of the five aggregates, not to the unconditioned element. Therefore, because the suffering of conditioned things, by its nature of pervading the entire world, encompasses all the world, the suffering of conditioned things in the manner described is suffering for the entire world. Thus, because the entire world is in a state of suffering due to the suffering of conditioned things, the Blessed One said, “Suffering is its great fear.”

“Vedanāpaccayā taṇhā”ti (ma. ni. 3.126; saṃ. ni. 2.1, 3, 36; mahāva. 1; vibha. 225) vacanato “dukkhamassa mahabbhaya”nti padena “kissābhilepanaṃ brūsī”ti tatiyapadassāpi vissajjanā siyāti āsaṅkabhāvato “tena ca catutthassa padassa vissajjanā yuttā”ti vuttaṃ. “Kena yathākkamaṃ pucchāvissajjanānaṃ yuttatarabhāvo jānitabbo”ti vattabbattā “tenāha bhagavā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tena yathākkamaṃ pucchāvissajjanānaṃ yuttatarattā yuttatarajānanako bhagavā “avijjāya nivuto [M 0.0092] loko”tiādimāha, tasmā yuttatarabhāvo tumhehi jānitabboti.

According to the statement “With feeling as condition, there is craving” (Majjhima Nikāya 3.126; Saṃyutta Nikāya 2.1, 3, 36; Mahāvagga 1; Vibhaṅga 225), because of the possible doubt that the phrase “Suffering is its great fear” could also serve as a response to the third question, “What do you call its anointing?”, it is said that the response to the fourth question is therefore appropriate. Because it might be asked, “How is the more fitting nature of the questions and answers in their respective order to be known?”, it is stated, “Therefore, the Blessed One said,” etc. Because of the more fitting nature of the questions and answers in their respective order, the Blessed One, who knows what is more fitting, said, “The world is shrouded in ignorance,” etc. Therefore, you should understand this more fitting nature.

Ettha ca lokassa nīvaraṇādīni ajānantena ca titthiyavādesu samayantaresu paricayena ca tesu samayantaresu ceva nīvaraṇādīsu ca saṃsayapakkhandena ekaṃseneva sattādhiṭṭhānena pucchitabbattā, ekaṃseneva sattādhiṭṭhānena byākātabbattā ca sattādhiṭṭhānā pucchā katāti veditabbā. Sā cāyaṃ pucchā ajānantassa jānanatthāya, jātasaṃsayassa ca saṃsayavinodanatthāya vissajjetabbassa nīvaraṇādivisayassa catubbidhattā catubbidhā. Nīvaraṇādīnaṃ pana visayānaṃ loko ca ādhārabhāvena gāthāyaṃ vuttoti “eko pañho dassito”ti ayamettha pucchāvicayo, vissajjanāvicayo pana “adiṭṭhajotanā vissajjanā, vimaticchedanā vissajjanā”tiādinā pucchāvicaye vuttanayānusārena veditabbo.

Here, it should be understood that the question is made with a focus on beings, because it must be asked definitively with a focus on beings by one who does not know the hindrances and so forth of the world, who has familiarity with the doctrines of other sects, and who is inclined to doubt regarding those other doctrines and the hindrances; and because it must be answered definitively with a focus on beings. And this question is fourfold, for the purpose of making the ignorant know and for dispelling the doubt of one in whom doubt has arisen, since the subject matter to be explained—the hindrances and so forth—is fourfold. Moreover, since the world is mentioned in the verse as the basis for the subjects of the hindrances and so forth, it is said, “One question has been shown.” Here, this is the analysis of the question. The analysis of the answer, however, should be understood according to the method stated in the analysis of the question, such as: “The answer is for illuminating the unseen, the answer is for cutting off doubt.”

Ekādhāre pucchāvissajjane vicayo ācariyehi vibhatto, amhehi ca ñāto, “anekādhāre pucchāvissajjane yo vicayo vibhajanāraho, so vicayo kathaṃ amhehi viññāyati, amhākaṃ viññāpanatthāya tasmiṃ vicayaṃ vibhajathā”ti vattabbabhāvato anekādhāraṃ pucchaṃ tāva nīharitvā dassetuṃ –

The analysis of question and answer in a single instance has been set forth by the teachers, and is known by us. Because it might be said, “But in multiple instances, how is that analysis, which is fit to be set forth, to be understood by us? For the purpose of making it known to us, you should set forth that analysis,” therefore, to present it, first extracting the question related to multiple instances—

“Savanti sabbadhi sotā, (iccāyasmā ajito,)

Sotānaṃ kiṃ nivāraṇaṃ;

Sotānaṃ saṃvaraṃ brūhi, kena sotā pidhīyare”ti. (su. ni. 1040; cūḷani. vatthugāthā 59, ajitamāṇavapucchāniddesa 3) –

“Streams flow everywhere,” (thus said Venerable Ajita,) “What is the obstruction of streams? Tell me the restraint of streams; by what are streams shut off?”

Gāthamāha[V 0.0230]. Gāthāttho tāva daṭṭhabbo. Savantīti sandanti, pavattantīti attho. Sabbadhīti taṇhādīnaṃ ārammaṇabhūtesu sabbesu rūpādīsu āyatanesu. Sotāti taṇhābhijjhābyāpādādayo sotā. Iccāyasmāti iti evaṃ āyasmā ajito āha. Sotānanti taṇhābhijjhābyāpādādīnaṃ sotānaṃ. Kiṃ nivāraṇanti kiṃ katamaṃ dhammajātaṃ āvaraṇaṃ bhave, kā katamā dhammajāti rakkhā bhave. Sotānaṃ saṃvaraṃ brūhīti sotānaṃ taṇhābhijjhābyāpādādīnaṃ saṃvaraṇaṃ āvaraṇaṃ idaṃ dhammajātaṃ bhaveti sabbasattahitatthaṃ amhākaṃ tvaṃ kathehi. Kena sotā [M 0.0093] pidhīyareti kena pahāyakadhammena taṇhābhijjhābyāpādādayo sotā paṇḍitehi pidhīyareti pucchatīti pucchitāni.

He recites the verse. First, the meaning of the verse should be understood. “Flowing” (savanti) means they flow (sandanti), they proceed (pavattanti)—this is the meaning. “Everywhere” (sabbadhi) refers to all the sense bases such as forms, which are objects for craving and the like. “Streams” (sotā) are the streams of craving, covetousness, ill will, and so on. ‘Thus the Venerable one’ (iccāyasmā) means: thus the Venerable Ajita spoke. “Of the streams” (sotānaṃ) means of the streams of craving, covetousness, ill will, and the like. “What is the obstruction?” (kiṃ nivāraṇaṃ) means what kind of dhamma would be a barrier, what kind of dhamma would be a protection? “Tell me the restraint of streams” (sotānaṃ saṃvaraṃ brūhi) means, ‘Tell us, for the welfare of all beings, what dhamma is the restraint, the barrier for these streams of craving, covetousness, ill will, and the like.’ “By what are the streams shut off?” (kena sotā pidhīyare) means, ‘By what abandoning dhamma are the streams of craving, covetousness, ill will, and the like shut off by the wise?’ Thus, these are the questions asked.

“Pucchāvasena kathitāya ‘savanti…pe… pidhīyare’ti imāya gāthāya kittakāni padāni pucchitāni, kittakā pañhā”ti pucchitabbattā “imāni cattāri padāni pucchitāni, te dve pañhā”ti vuttaṃ. “Pucchāvasena pavattāya imissā gāthāya yadi cattāri padāni siyuṃ, evaṃ santesu pañhāpi catubbidhā siyuṃ, kasmā ‘dve’ti vuttā”ti vattabbattā “kasmā? Ime hi bahvādhivacanena pucchitā”ti vuttaṃ. Ime etāya gāthāya gahitā atthā bahvādhivacanena pucchitā. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – “savanti…pe… pidhīyareti bahūni vacanāni adhikicca pavattā saṃvarasaṅkhātā sati ceva pidahanahetubhūtā paññā cāti ime dve atthāva pucchitā, tasmā atthavasena dve pañhā vuttā vā”ti. “Pucchāya duvidhatthavisayatā kathaṃ vuttā”ti vattabbattā pucchāya duvidhatthavisayataṃ vivarituṃ “evaṃ samāpannassā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha evaṃ samāpannassāti imāhi duggatihetubhūtāhi ñātibyasanādisaṅkhātāhi āpadāhi vā, pāṇavadhādīhi āpadāhi vā, samaṃ saha, sabbathā vā ayaṃ sattaloko āpanno ajjhotthaṭo, evaṃ ajjhotthaṭassa vā samāpannassa. Evaṃ saṃkiliṭṭhassāti ñātibyasanādayo vā pāṇavadhādīni āgamma pavattehi dasahi kilesavatthūhi ca ayaṃ sattaloko saṃkiliṭṭho, evaṃ saṃkiliṭṭhassa ca lokassāti samāpannassa ajjhotthaṭassa lokassa vodānaṃ vuṭṭhānaṃ kiṃ katamaṃ dhammajātaṃ bhave. Iti evañhi saccaṃ ajitasutte āhāti vitthārattho, pucchāya duvidhatthavisayatā ñātabbāti adhippāyo.

Since the verse beginning with ‘savanti…pe… pidhīyare’ was spoken by way of a question, it might be asked: ‘How many phrases were questioned in this verse, and how many questions were there?’ In response, it was said: ‘These four phrases were questioned, and they are two questions.’ Because it might be said: ‘If this verse, occurring by way of a question, has four phrases, then the questions should also be fourfold. Why then was it said “two”?’, it was said: “Why? Because these were questioned with many terms.” The meanings taken from this verse were questioned with many terms. This is what was meant: concerning the many expressions in ‘savanti…pe… pidhīyare’, only two meanings were questioned: mindfulness, which is called restraint, and wisdom, which is the cause of shutting off. Therefore, in terms of meaning, two questions were stated. Since it might be asked, ‘How was the twofold subject matter of the question stated?’, to clarify the twofold subject matter of the question, it was said, beginning with ‘evaṃ samāpannassā’ (of one thus beset). Here, ‘evaṃ samāpannassā’ means this world of beings is beset and overwhelmed—either equally, together, or in every way—by these misfortunes designated as loss of relatives, which are causes for a bad destination, or by calamities like killing living beings. Thus, of one who is thus overwhelmed or beset. ‘Evaṃ saṃkiliṭṭhassā’ means this world of beings is defiled either by loss of relatives and such, or by the ten bases of defilement arising from killing living beings, etc. Thus, for such a defiled, beset, or overwhelmed world, what kind of dhamma is the cleansing, the emergence? Thus, indeed, he truly states in the Ajita Sutta—this is the detailed meaning. The intention is that the twofold subject matter of the question should be understood.

“Kiṃ nu sotā sabbassa lokassa sabbadhi savanti, udāhu, ekaccassevā”ti pucchitabbattā “savanti sabbadhi sotāti, asamāhitassa savanti abhijjhābyāpādappamādabahulassā”ti vuttaṃ. Tattha abhijjhābyāpādappamādabahulattā rūpādīsu nānārammaṇesu vikkhittacittasseva sotā savanti pavattanti, na samāhitassa abhijjhābyāpādappamādavirahitassāti [V 0.0231] adhippāyo daṭṭhabbo. “Katamā abhijjhā, katamo byāpādo, katamo pamādo”ti vattabbattā “tattha yā abhijjhā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha tatthāti tesu abhijjhābyāpādappamādesu. Yā abhijjhā, ayaṃ lobho, na abhijjhāyanamattaṃ. Lobho ca akusalamūlaṃ, na lubbhanamattaṃ. Yo byāpādo[M 0.0094], ayaṃ doso, na byāpajjanamattaṃ. Doso ca akusalamūlaṃ, na dūsanamattaṃ. Yo pamādo, ayaṃ moho, na sativippavāsamattaṃ. Moho ca akusalamūlaṃ, na mūhanamattaṃ. Evaṃ iminā vuttappakārena abhijjhādīnaṃ akusalamūlattā yassa abhijjhābyāpādappamādabahulassa asamāhitassa chasu rūpādīsu āyatanesu taṇhā savanti.

Since it should be asked, ‘Do the streams flow everywhere for the entire world, or only for some?’ it was said: ‘The streams flow everywhere—they flow for the unconcentrated, for one abundant in covetousness, ill will, and negligence.’ Here, the meaning to be understood is that because of being abundant in covetousness, ill will, and negligence, the streams flow and proceed only for one whose mind is scattered among various objects such as forms, etc., but not for one who is concentrated and free from covetousness, ill will, and negligence. Since it should be asked, ‘What is covetousness? What is ill will? What is negligence?’ it was said, beginning with ‘Here, that which is covetousness.’ Here, ‘therein’ refers to those states of covetousness, ill will, and negligence. That which is covetousness is greed (lobha), not merely the act of coveting. Greed is an unwholesome root, not just longing. That which is ill will (byāpāda) is hatred (dosa), not merely the act of wishing harm. Hatred is an unwholesome root, not just aversion. That which is negligence (pamāda) is delusion (moha), not merely lack of mindfulness. Delusion is an unwholesome root, not just confusion. Thus, in this stated manner, because covetousness and the others are unwholesome roots, craving flows in the six sense bases—forms, etc.—for one who is unconcentrated and abundant in covetousness, ill will, and negligence.

“Katividhā sā taṇhā”ti vattabbattā “rūpataṇhā…pe… dhammataṇhā”ti vuttaṃ. “Channaṃ rūpataṇhādīnaṃ chasu rūpādiāyatanesu savanaṃ kena ca vacanena amhehi saddahitabba”nti vattabbattā “yathāha bhagavā”tiādi vuttaṃ. “Savatīti ca kho, bhikkhave…pe… paṭihaññatī”ti yaṃ vacanaṃ bhagavā yathā yena pakārena āha, tathā tena pakārena vuttanayena vacanena tumhehi saddahitabbanti adhippāyo. Ettha ca cakkhādīnaṃ rūpataṇhādīnaṃ channaṃ sotānaṃ dvārabhāvena pavattattā cakkhādayo nissitūpacāravasena sayaṃ savanto viya bhagavatā vuttā. Itīti evaṃ vuttappakārena sabbā sabbasmā cakkhādidvārato ca savati pavattati. Sabbathā sabbappakārena taṇhāyanamicchābhinivesanaunnamanādippakārena savati pavattatīti attho. “Kasmā sabbasmā cakkhādidvārato ca savati pavattati, sabbappakārena taṇhāyanamicchābhinivesanaunnamanādippakārena savanabhāvo vijānitabbo”ti vattabbattā “tenāhā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha tenāti asamāhitassa abhijjhābyāpādādīnaṃ cakkhādidvārato ca taṇhāyanamicchābhinivesaunnamanākārena taṇhādivasena pavattanato pavattajānanako bhagavā “savanti sabbadhi sotā”ti āha.

Since it should be asked, ‘How many kinds of craving are there?’ it was said: ‘craving for forms… craving for mental phenomena.’ Since it should be asked, ‘By what statement should we believe that the six cravings for forms, etc., flow through the six sense bases of forms, etc.?’ it was said, beginning with ‘as the Blessed One has declared.’ The intention is that the statement ‘The eye, monks, flows… is struck,’ which the Blessed One spoke in whatever way and by whatever means, should be believed by you in that very way and by that very means, according to the method stated. Here, because the eye and so on function as doors for the six streams of craving for forms and so on, the eye and so on are spoken of by the Blessed One as if they themselves flow, by way of a figurative expression based on dependence. Thus, in this stated manner, all craving flows and proceeds from all the sense doors of the eye, etc. The meaning is that it flows and proceeds in every way, in all modes, such as craving, wrong insistence, rising up, and so forth. Since it should be asked, ‘Why does it flow and proceed from all the sense doors of the eye, etc., and how should the nature of flowing in every way, through modes of craving, wrong insistence, rising up, and so forth, be understood?’ it was said, beginning with ‘therefore he said.’ Here, ‘therefore’ means that the Blessed One, knowing the arising of craving and so on in the modes of craving, wrong insistence, and rising up from the sense doors of the eye, etc., for one who is unconcentrated and abundant in covetousness, ill will, etc., said: ‘The streams flow everywhere.’

“Sotānaṃ ‘kiṃ nivāraṇa’nti iminā kiṃ pucchati? Sotānaṃ anusayappahānaṃ pucchati kiṃ? Udāhu vītikkamappahānaṃ pucchatī”ti vattabbattā “sotānaṃ kiṃ nivāraṇanti pariyuṭṭhānavighātaṃ pucchatī”ti vuttaṃ. “Idaṃ pariyuṭṭhānavighātaṃ vodānaṃ, udāhu vuṭṭhānaṃ ki”nti vattabbattā “idaṃ vodāna”nti vuttaṃ. “Sotānaṃ saṃvaraṃ brūhi, ‘kena sotā pidhīyare’ti iminā kiṃ pucchati? Sotānaṃ pariyuṭṭhānaṃ pucchati kiṃ? Udāhu vītikkamanaṃ, samugghāṭaṃ vā pucchati ki”nti vattabbattā sotānaṃ…pe… pidhīyareti anusayasamugghāṭaṃ pucchatī”ti vuttaṃ. “Idaṃ anusayasamugghāṭaṃ vodānaṃ kiṃ, udāhu vuṭṭhānaṃ ki”nti vattabbattā “idaṃ vuṭṭhāna”nti vuttaṃ.

Since it should be asked, ‘By “What is the restraint of the streams?” (sotānaṃ kiṃ nivāraṇaṃ), what is being asked? Is it asking about the abandonment of latent tendencies (anusaya) of the streams? Or is it asking about the abandonment of transgressions (vītikkama)?’ it was said: ‘By “What is the restraint of the streams?” it is asking about the overcoming of obsessive defilements (pariyuṭṭhāna).’ Since it should be asked, ‘Is this overcoming of obsessive defilements purification (vodāna) or emergence (vuṭṭhāna)?’ it was said: ‘This is purification.’ Since it should be asked, ‘By “Speak of the restraint of the streams, by what are the streams obstructed?” (sotānaṃ saṃvaraṃ brūhi, kena sotā pidhīyare) what is being asked? Is it asking about the obsessive defilement of the streams? Or is it asking about transgression, or eradication (samugghāṭa)?’ it was said: ‘By “of the streams… are obstructed” it is asking about the eradication of latent tendencies.’ Since it should be asked, ‘Is this eradication of latent tendencies purification or emergence?’ it was said: ‘This is emergence.’

“Savanti [V 0.0232][M 0.0095] sabbadhi sotā”tiādipucchāvicayo ācariyena vutto, amhehi ca ñāto; tāya pucchāya “katamo vissajjanavicayo”ti vattabbattā “tattha vissajjanā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha pucchāyaṃ –

The analysis of the question beginning with ‘The streams flow everywhere’ was stated by the teacher and is known to us. Since it should be asked, ‘What is the analysis of the reply to that question?’ it was said, beginning with ‘Here, the reply.’ Here, regarding the question—

“Yāni sotāni lokasmiṃ, (ajitāti bhagavā,)

Sati tesaṃ nivāraṇaṃ;

Sotānaṃ saṃvaraṃ brūmi, paññāyete pidhīyare”ti. (su. ni. 1041 cūḷani. vatthugāthā 60, ajitamāṇavapucchāniddesa 4) –

“‘Whatever streams there are in the world, Ajita,’ said the Blessed One, ‘mindfulness is their restraint. I speak of the restraint for the streams; by wisdom they are obstructed.’”

Gāthā vissajjanāti daṭṭhabbā. Tassaṃ gāthāyaṃ ajita lokasmiṃ yāni sotāni savanti, tesaṃ sotānaṃ yaṃ nivāraṇaṃ, sā sati hoti; taṃ satiṃ sotānaṃ saṃvaranti ahaṃ brūmi; ete sotā paññāya pidhīyareti yojanā kātabbā. Tattha satīti vipassanāpaññāya sampayuttā sati. Paññāyāti maggapaññāya. Pidhīyareti uppajjituṃ appadānavasena pidhīyanti pacchijjanti.

The verse should be regarded as the reply. In that verse, the connection should be made thus: ‘Ajita, whatever streams flow in the world, their restraint is mindfulness; that mindfulness I declare to be the restraint of the streams; these streams are obstructed by wisdom.’ Here, ‘mindfulness’ (sati) is mindfulness associated with insight-wisdom (vipassanāpaññā). ‘By wisdom’ (paññāya) means by path-wisdom (maggapaññā). ‘Are obstructed’ (pidhīyare) means they are obstructed, cut off, in the sense of not allowing them to arise.

“Sati tesaṃ nivāraṇaṃ sotānaṃ saṃvaraṃ brūmī”ti bhagavā āha – “yāya kāyaci satiyā sotānaṃ saṃvaraṇakiccaṃ siddhaṃ kiṃ, visiṭṭhāya satiyā sotānaṃ saṃvaraṇakiccaṃ siddhaṃ kiṃ, katamāya satiyā sotānaṃ saṃvaraṇakiccaṃ siddha”nti pucchitabbattā “kāyagatāya satiyā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha kāyagatāya satiyāti rūpakāye gataṃ kesādikaṃ aniccādito vipassitvā pavattāya vipassanāñāṇasampayuttāya satiyā. Bhāvitāyāti kāyagataṃ aniccato dukkhato anattato nibbindanato virajjanato nirodhanato paṭinissajjanato anupassanāvasena bhāvitāya. Evañhi aniccato anupassanto niccasaññaṃ pajahati; dukkhato anupassanto sukhasaññaṃ pajahati; anattato anupassanto attasaññaṃ pajahati; nibbindanto nandiṃ pajahati; virajjanto rāgaṃ pajahati; nirodhento samudayaṃ pajahati; paṭinissajjanto ādānaṃ pajahatīti. Bahulīkatāyāti yathāvuttappakārena divasampi māsampi saṃvaccharampi sattasaṃvaccharampi bahulīkatāya. Cakkhunti abhijjhādipavattidvārabhāvena ṭhitaṃ cakkhuṃ, niggahitāgamaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Nāviñchatīti cakkhudvāre pavattaṃ abhijjhādisahitaṃ cittasantānaṃ, taṃsamaṅgīpuggalaṃ vā nākaḍḍhati, manāpikesu rūpesu nāviñchatīti yojanā. Amanāpikesu rūpesu na paṭihaññati[M 0.0096]. Kāyagatāya satiyā [V 0.0233] bhāvitāya bahulīkatāya sotaṃ nāviñchati. Manāpikesu saddesu…pe… amanāpikesu saddesu na paṭihaññatīti yojanā yathāsambhavato kātabbā.

The Blessed One said, ‘Mindfulness is their restraint; I speak of the restraint for the streams.’ Since it is to be asked, ‘By what mindfulness is the task of restraining the streams accomplished? By what specific mindfulness is the task of restraining the streams accomplished? By which mindfulness is the task of restraining the streams accomplished?’ it is said, ‘By mindfulness directed to the body,’ and so on. Here, ‘mindfulness directed to the body’ means mindfulness associated with insight knowledge, which arises from contemplating the physical body—from the hair of the head onwards—as impermanent, and so forth. ‘Developed’ means developed by observing the body as impermanent, as suffering, as non-self, as leading to disenchantment, to dispassion, to cessation, and to relinquishment, by way of repeated observation. For, by observing impermanence, one abandons the perception of permanence; by observing suffering, one abandons the perception of pleasure; by observing non-self, one abandons the perception of self; by disenchantment, one abandons delight; by dispassion, one abandons lust; by cessation, one abandons origination; by relinquishment, one abandons grasping. ‘Cultivated’ means cultivated in the aforementioned way—whether for a day, a month, a year, or even seven years. ‘The eye’ refers to the eye, established as the doorway for the occurrence of covetousness and so on; its approach should be seen as restrained. ‘Does not ensnare’ means that it does not drag along the stream of consciousness arising at the eye-door, accompanied by covetousness and the like, or the person possessing it; the meaning is that it does not cling to pleasing forms. It is not repelled by unpleasing forms. By mindfulness directed to the body, developed and cultivated, one is not ensnared by the ear. One does not cling to pleasing sounds… nor is one repelled by unpleasing sounds. This explanation should be applied to the other senses as is fitting.

“Kena kāraṇena nāviñchati paṭihaññatī”ti pucchati, indriyānaṃ saṃvutanivāritattā nāviñchati na paṭihaññatīti vissajjeti. “Kenārakkhena te saṃvutanivāritā”ti pucchati, satiārakkhena te saṃvutanivāritāti vissajjeti. “Satiārakkhena saṃvutanivāritabhāvo kena amhehi saddahitabbo”ti vattabbattā tenāhā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha tenāti tasmā satiārakkhena saṃvutanivāritattā saṃvutanivāritajānanako bhagavā “sati tesaṃ nivāraṇa”nti yaṃ vacanaṃ āha, tena vacanena tumhehi satiārakkhena saṃvutanivāritabhāvo saddahitabboti pubbabhāge paññā satyānugāti kiccamevettha adhikanti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

“For what reason is one not troubled and not repelled?” he asks. It is answered, “Because the senses are restrained and warded off, one is not troubled and not repelled.” “By what protection are they restrained and warded off?” he asks. It is answered, “They are restrained and warded off by the protection of mindfulness.” Since it should be stated, “By what means is the fact that they are restrained and warded off by the protection of mindfulness to be believed by us?”—therefore it was said, and so on. Here, ‘therefore’ means that because they are restrained and warded off by the protection of mindfulness, the Blessed One, who knows the state of being restrained and warded off, declared, “Mindfulness is their warding off.” By that statement, you should believe that they are restrained and warded off by the protection of mindfulness. In the previous part, it should be seen that wisdom which accords with truth is indeed the primary function here.

“Sati tesaṃ nivāraṇa”nti vissajjanassa vitthārattho ācariyena vutto, amhehi ca ñāto, “paññāyete pidhīyare”ti vissajjanassa vitthārattho “kathaṃ amhehi jānitabbo”ti vattabbattā “paññāyete pidhīyare”ti vissajjanassa vitthāratthaṃ dassento “paññāya anusayā pahīyantī”tiādimāha. Tattha paññāyāti maggapaññāya. Anusayāti anurūpaṃ kāraṇaṃ labhitvā uppajjanārahā kāmarāgānusayādayo. Pahīyanti samucchedavasena anusayesu paññāya pahīnesu pariyuṭṭhānāpi atthato pahīyanti. Kissa pahīnattā “pahīyantī”ti vuccati? Anusayassa pahīnattā pariyuṭṭhānā pahīyantīti vissajjeti.

The detailed meaning of the answer, “Mindfulness is their warding off,” was stated by the teacher and is known to us. Since it should be stated, “How are we to know the detailed meaning of the answer, ‘These are obstructed by wisdom’?”—therefore, to show the detailed meaning of the answer, “These are obstructed by wisdom,” he said, beginning with, “The underlying tendencies are abandoned by wisdom.” Herein, “by wisdom” means by the wisdom of the path. “Underlying tendencies” refers to the latent tendencies to sensual desire, and so forth, which are liable to arise when they obtain a suitable cause. “Are abandoned” means they are abandoned by way of complete eradication. When the underlying tendencies are abandoned by wisdom, the obsessions, too, are in effect abandoned. Due to the abandonment of what is it said, “are abandoned”? He answers: Due to the abandonment of the underlying tendencies, the obsessions are abandoned.

“Taṃ anusayappahānena pariyuṭṭhānappahānaṃ kiṃ viya bhavatī”ti pucchitabbattā “taṃ yathā khandhavantassā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha khandhavantassa rukkhassa kudālādinā bhūmiṃ khaṇitvā anavasesamūluddharaṇe kate tassa rukkhassa pupphaphalapallavaṅkurasantatipi kudālādinā samucchinnāva bhavati yathā, evaṃ arahattamaggañāṇena anusayesu pahīnesu anusayānaṃ pariyuṭṭhānasantati samucchinnā pidahitā paṭicchannā bhavati. Kena samucchinnā bhavati? Paññāya maggapaññāya samucchinnā bhavatīti atthayojanā daṭṭhabbā. “Paññāya paricchinnabhāvo kathaṃ saddahitabbo”ti vattabbattā “tenā”tiādi vuttaṃ. “Paññāyete pidhīyare”ti vacanato anusayānaṃ pariyuṭṭhānasantatiyā paññāya paricchinnabhāvo paṇḍitehi saddahitabboti adhippāyo.

“What is the abandoning of obsessions through the abandoning of underlying tendencies like?” Since this should be asked, it is said, “Just as in the case of a tree with a trunk,” and so on. Herein, just as when the ground around a tree with a trunk is dug with a hoe or the like, and its roots are extracted completely without remainder, the continuity of its flowers, fruits, shoots, and sprouts is also cut off by the hoe or the like; so too, when the underlying tendencies are abandoned by the knowledge of the path to Arahantship, the continuity of obsessions arising from those underlying tendencies is cut off, obstructed, and concealed. By what is it cut off? It is cut off by wisdom, the wisdom of the path—this is how the connection of the meaning should be seen. “How is the state of being delimited by wisdom to be believed?” Since this should be stated, it is said, “Therefore,” and so on. From the statement, “These are obstructed by wisdom,” the intention is that the state of the continuity of obsessions being delimited by wisdom should be believed by the wise.

Imesu [M 0.0097] pañhāvissajjanesu sotānaṃ saṃvaraṃ, pidhānañca ajānantena vā saṃsayitena vā saṃvarapidhānānaṃ pucchitabbattā dhammādhiṭṭhānā pucchāti pucchāvicayo ceva satipaññānaṃ vissajjetabbattā [V 0.0234] dhammādhiṭṭhānaṃ vissajjananti vissajjanavicayo ca veditabbo. Etesu ca “kenassu nivuto loko”tiādiko pañho nīvaraṇavicikicchāpamādajappānaṃ vasena catubbidhopi lokādhiṭṭhānavasena eko pañhoti vutto, evaṃ sati “savanti sabbadhi sotā”tiādikopi pañho saṃvarapidhānānaṃ vasena duvidhopi ekatthavasena gahetvā ekādhiṭṭhānavasena “eko pañho”ti vattabbo, sotānaṃ bahubhāvato vā “bahupañho”ti vattabbo; tathā pana avatvā sote anāmasitvā saṃvarapidhānānaṃ vasena “savanti sabbadhi sotā”tiādimhi “dve pañhā”ti vuttā. Tadanusārena “kenassu nivuto loko”tiādimhipi lokaṃ anāmasitvā nīvaraṇādīnaṃ catunnaṃ vasena “cattāro pañhā”tipi vattabbāti ayaṃ nayo dassitoti nayadassanaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ.

In these questions and answers, since the restraint and obstruction of the streams should be asked about by one who does not know or is doubtful, the question is founded on the Dhamma; thus the analysis of the question should be understood. And since the answer is to be given by way of mindfulness and wisdom, the answer is founded on the Dhamma; thus the analysis of the answer should be understood. Among these, the question beginning, “By what is the world enveloped?” is said to be one question by way of its foundation in the world, though it is fourfold by way of the hindrances, doubt, heedlessness, and chatter. This being so, the question beginning, “Streams flow everywhere,” though twofold by way of restraint and obstruction, should be taken as having a single meaning and be called “one question” by way of its single foundation. Or, because the streams are many, it could be called “many questions.” However, without referring to the streams, but by way of restraint and obstruction, regarding the passage beginning, “Streams flow everywhere,” it is said there are “two questions.” In accordance with that, regarding the passage beginning, “By what is the world enveloped?” without referring to the world, but by way of the four things—hindrances and so on—it could also be said there are “four questions.” This method is shown, and thus the demonstration of the method should be seen.

Desanākāle vuttadhammassa anusandhimaggahetvā attanā racitaniyāmeneva pucchitapañhassa ceva pañhaṃ aṭṭhapetvā, paṭiññañca akatvā vissajjanassa ca vicayahāro ācariyena vibhatto, amhehi ca ñāto, “desanākāle vuttadhammassa anusandhiṃ gahetvā pucchitapañhassa ceva taṃ pañhaṃ ṭhapetvā, paṭiññañca katvā vissajjanassa ca yo vicayo hāro vibhatto, so vicayahāro kathaṃ amhehi viññāyati, amhākaṃ viññāpanatthāya tasmiṃ vicayaṃ vibhajethā”ti vattabbabhāvato tesu vicetabbākāraṃ dassento “yāni sotānī”tiādigāthāya vicayākāradassanānantaraṃ “paññā ceva sati cā”tiādimāha.

The teacher has explained—and we have understood—the method of analysis for an answer given at the time of a discourse, where, without grasping the connection to the Dhamma that was taught, without setting aside the question asked according to one's own contrived method, and without making a declaration. Since it should be stated: “How are we to understand that method of analysis for an answer which has been explained, where, at the time of the discourse, having grasped the connection to the Dhamma that was taught, having set aside that question, and having made a declaration? For the sake of our understanding, you should explain that analysis”—therefore, showing the manner in which these things should be analyzed, after showing the method of analysis with the verse beginning, “Whatever streams…,” he then spoke the passage beginning, “Wisdom and mindfulness…”

Tattha gāthāttho tāva viññātabbo – yāya paññāya anusayappahānena sotanirujjhanaṃ vuttaṃ, yāya satiyā ca pariyuṭṭhānappahānena sotanirujjhanaṃ vuttaṃ, sāyaṃ paññā ceva sāyaṃ sati ca tāhi paññāsatīhi asesaṃ sahuppannaṃ nāmañceva rūpañca, etaṃ sabbaṃ kattha nirujjhamāne asesaṃ uparujjhatīti mārisa me mayā puṭṭho tvaṃ bhagavā mayhaṃ etaṃ nirujjhanaṃ pabrūhi, iti āyasmā ajito bhagavantaṃ pucchati.

Here, first the meaning of the verse should be understood: “That wisdom by which the cessation of the streams is spoken of through the abandoning of underlying tendencies, and that mindfulness by which the cessation of the streams is spoken of through the abandoning of obsessions—that very wisdom and that very mindfulness, and name-and-form which has arisen entirely together with them—where does all this cease without remainder? O Mārisa, being asked this by me, you, Blessed One, please declare this cessation to me.” Thus the Venerable Ajita questions the Blessed One.

Ajita tvaṃ yametaṃ pañhaṃ pucchitaṃ nirujjhanaṃ maṃ apucchi, ahaṃ te tava taṃ nirujjhanaṃ vadāmi. Yattha viññāṇanirodhe paññāsatisahitaṃ nāmañca rūpañca viññāṇassa [M 0.0098] nirodhena saha ekato asesaṃ uparujjhati, ettha viññāṇanirodhe etaṃ sabbaṃ viññāṇanirodhena ekato ekakkhaṇe apubbaṃ acarimaṃ uparujjhati, etaṃ viññāṇanirodhaṃ tassa nāmarūpassa nirodho nātivattati, taṃ taṃ nāmarūpanirodhaṃ so so viññāṇanirodho nātivattatīti.

“Ajita, this question you have asked, you have asked me about cessation. I will tell you of that cessation. Wherein, with the cessation of consciousness, name-and-form together with wisdom and mindfulness ceases entirely and simultaneously with the cessation of consciousness; there, with the cessation of consciousness, all this ceases at once, in a single moment, not before and not after. The cessation of that name-and-form does not transcend this cessation of consciousness, and that cessation of consciousness does not transcend the cessation of that name-and-form.”

“Tasmiṃ [V 0.0235] pañhe ayaṃ ajito kiṃ pucchati? Uparujjhanameva pucchati, udāhu aññaṃ pucchatī”ti vattabbato “ayaṃ pañhe anusandhiṃ pucchatī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha ayanti yo āyasmā ajito pañhaṃ apucchīti ayaṃ ajito. Pañheti “paññā ceva sati cā”tiādipañhe. Yadi anusandhiṃ pucchati, evaṃ sati “katthetaṃ uparujjhatī”ti pucchanaṃ ayuttaṃ bhaveyyāti? Na, anusandhīyati etena upanirujjhanenāti anusandhīti atthasambhavato. Tena vuttaṃ “anusandhiṃ pucchanto kiṃ…pe… nibbānadhātu”nti. Anusandhipucchanena anupādisesanibbānadhātuyāpi pucchanato “katthetaṃ uparujjhatī”ti pucchanaṃ yuttameva.

Since it should be stated, “In that question, what does this Ajita ask? Does he ask only about cessation, or does he ask about something else?”—it was said, “In this question, he asks about the connection,” and so on. Here, ‘this’ refers to the Venerable Ajita who asked the question. ‘Question’ refers to the question beginning, “Wisdom and mindfulness…” If he is asking about the connection, would the question, “Where does this cease?” then be unsuitable? No, because the meaning of ‘connection’ (anusandhi) is possible here in the sense: “it is connected by this cessation.” Therefore it is said, “In asking about the connection, what… up to… the Nibbāna-element?” Since asking about the connection is also to ask about the Nibbāna-element without remainder, the question, “Where does this cease?” is indeed suitable.

“Yā anupādisesanibbānadhātu pucchitā, taṃ katamāya paṭipadāya adhigacchatī”ti pucchitabbattā catusaccakammaṭṭhānabhāvanāsaṅkhātaṃ paṭipadaṃ visayena saha dassetuṃ “tīṇī saccānī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha saṅkhatānīti kammādipaccayehi samecca sambhūya dukkhādīni karīyantīti saṅkhatāni. Nirodhadhammānīti nirujjhanaṃ nirodho, dhammopi nirodhadhammova, tasmā nirodho dhammo sabhāvo yesaṃ dukkhādīnanti nirodhadhammānīti atthova gahetabbo. Tāni tīṇi saccāni sarūpato dassetuṃ “dukkhaṃ samudayo maggo”ti vuttaṃ. Tīṇi dukkhasamudayamaggasaccāni saṅkhatānīti vuttāni, “kiṃ nirodhasacca”nti pucchitabbattā “nirodho asaṅkhato”ti vuttaṃ. Idha “nirodhadhammo”tipi vattabbaṃ. Kammādipaccayehi asaṅkhatattā asaṅkhato. Uppādanirodhābhāvato anirodhadhammo. “Pahāyakapahātabbesu saccesu katamena pahāyakena katamo pahātabbo, katamāya bhūmiyā pahīno”ti pucchitabbattā “tattha samudayo dvīsu bhūmīsū”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha dvīsu bhūmīsūti dassanabhāvanābhūmīsu. Kāmacchandoti kāmabhavarāgo. Rūparāgoti rūpabhavarāgo. Arūparāgoti arūpabhavarāgo. Saṃyojanabhedato dasa saṃyojanāni pahīyantīti yojanā.

Since the question is to be asked, 'The Nibbāna-element without residue remaining—by which path is it attained?', in order to show the path, together with its object, which is called the development of the meditation subject of the four truths, it is said, 'Three truths,' and so on. Herein, 'conditioned' means that suffering and so on are produced by being combined through conditions such as kamma; hence they are conditioned. Regarding 'subject to cessation' (nirodhadhammāni): cessation is the act of ceasing; a state (dhamma) is also of the nature of cessation. Therefore, the meaning to be understood is that suffering and so on are 'subject to cessation' because they have cessation as their nature. To show these three truths in their own form, it is said, 'suffering, origin, path.' The three truths—suffering, origin, and path—are said to be conditioned. Since it is to be asked, 'What is the truth of cessation?', it is said, 'Cessation is unconditioned.' Here, 'a state of cessation' (nirodhadhamma) should also be said. It is unconditioned because it is not conditioned by kamma and other conditions. It is not subject to cessation (anirodhadhamma) because there is no arising or ceasing for it. Since the question is to be asked, 'Among the truths that abandon and are to be abandoned, which abandoner abandons which abandonable, and on which stage is it abandoned?', it is said, 'Herein, the origin is on two stages,' and so on. Herein, 'on two stages' refers to the stages of seeing and cultivation. 'Sensual desire' refers to craving for existence in the sensual realm. 'Craving for form' refers to craving for existence in the form realm. 'Craving for formlessness' refers to craving for existence in the formless realm. In terms of the division of fetters, ten fetters are abandoned—this is the connection.

12. Pahātabbasaṃyojanāni [M 0.0099] dassanabhūmibhāvanābhūmibhedena vibhattāni, amhehipi ñātāni, “indriyabhedato kathaṃ vibhattānī”ti vattabbabhāvato “tattha tīṇī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Atha vā “pahātabbasaṃyojanesu katamāni saṃyojanāni katamaṃ indriyaṃ attano pahāyakaṃ katvā nirujjhantī”ti pucchitabbattā “tattha tīṇī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Adhiṭṭhāya attano pahāyakaṃ katvā nirujjhanti anuppādavasena. “Anaññātaññassāmītindriyañca aññindriyañca saṃyojanānaṃ nirujjhanahetu hotu, aññātāvindriyaṃ kissa hetū”ti pucchitabbattā “yaṃ panā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha yaṃ yena aññātāvindriyena arahā “me jāti khīṇā”ti evaṃ jānāti, idaṃ jānanahetu aññātāvindriyaṃ khaye jātikkhaye arahattaphale pavattaṃ ñāṇaṃ. Yaṃ yena aññātāvindriyena arahā “itthattāya aparaṃ na bhavissāmī”ti pajānāti, idaṃ pajānanahetu [V 0.0236] aññātāvindriyaṃ. Anuppāde pana anuppajjane arahattaphale pavattaṃ ñāṇaṃ aññātāvindriyaṃ jānanahetu hotīti vuttaṃ hoti. Indriyañāṇāni pahāyakāni katvā saṃyojanāni nirujjhanti, “tāni ñāṇāni kadā nirujjhantī”ti vattabbabhāvato “tattha yañcā”tiādi vuttaṃ.

12. The fetters to be abandoned are classified according to the stages of seeing and the stages of development, and are known by us. Since it is to be said, 'How are they classified according to the faculties?', it is said, 'Herein, three,' and so on. Alternatively, since it is to be asked, 'Among the fetters to be abandoned, which fetters cease, having made which faculty their abandoner?', it is said, 'Herein, three,' and so on. Having established their own abandoner, they cease by way of non-arising. Since it is to be asked, 'Let the faculty of 'I shall know the unknown' and the faculty of final knowledge be a cause for the cessation of the fetters, but of what is the faculty of one who knows the cause?', it is said, 'But that which,' and so on. Herein, that by which the Arahant knows, 'My birth is destroyed'—this faculty of one who knows, the knowledge that occurs in the fruition of arahantship at the destruction, the destruction of birth, is the cause of knowing. That by which the Arahant understands, 'There will be no further existence for this state'—this faculty of one who knows is the cause of understanding. Furthermore, it is said that the faculty of one who knows—the knowledge that occurs in the fruition of arahantship regarding non-arising, non-production—is the cause of knowing. The fetters cease, having made the faculty-knowledges their abandoners. Since it is to be said, 'When do those knowledges cease?', it is said, 'Herein, that which,' and so on.

“Anaññātaññassāmītindriyaṃ aññindriyaṃ pāpuṇantassa nirujjhatu, aññindriyaṃ arahattaṃ pāpuṇantassa nirujjhatu, aññātāvindriyaṃ kadā nirujjhatī”ti pucchitabbattā “tattha yañca khaye”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha dveti kiccabhedena dve, sabhāvato pana ekāva.

Since the question is to be asked, 'Let the faculty of 'I shall know the unknown' cease for one attaining the faculty of final knowledge; let the faculty of final knowledge cease for one attaining arahantship. When does the faculty of one who knows cease?', it is said, 'Herein, that which is in destruction,' and so on. Herein, 'two' means two by way of difference in function, but in essence, it is only one.

“Pajānanakiccampi ekameva, kathaṃ dve siyu”nti vattabbattā “apicā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Ārammaṇapaññābhedena dve nāmāni labbhantīti vuttaṃ hoti. Sāti yā paññā pubbagāthāyaṃ sotapidhānakiccena vuttā, sā paññā pakārehi jānanasabhāvena paññā nāma. Yathādiṭṭhaṃ ārammaṇaṃ apilāpanaṭṭhena ogāhanaṭṭhena sati nāma.

Since it is to be said, 'The function of understanding is also singular; how can there be two?', it is said, 'Moreover,' and so on. It is said that two names are obtained through the difference of object and wisdom. That wisdom which was mentioned in the previous verse with the function of 'closing the ear,' that wisdom is called 'paññā' because of its nature of knowing in various ways. Mindfulness (sati) is so called because of its characteristic of not letting the object as seen float away and its characteristic of penetrating it.

13. “Paññā ceva sati cā”ti padassa attho ācariyena vibhatto, amhehi ca ñāto, “nāmarūpañcā’ti padassa attho kathaṃ amhehi ñātabbo”ti vattabbattā nāmarūpaṃ vibhajanto “tattha ye pañcupādānakkhandhā”tiādimāha. Tattha tatthāti kammavipākavaṭṭabhede bhavattaye. Tatthāti pañcupādānakkhandhasaṅkhātanāmarūpasamudāye. Pañcindriyānīti cakkhādipañcindriyāni[M 0.0100]. Viññāṇasampayuttanti sampayuttapaccayattaṃ sandhāya na vuttaṃ, pacurajanassa pana avibhajitvā gahaṇīyasabhāvamattaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Vibhāgaṃ jānantehi pana “nāmaṃ viññāṇasampayuttaṃ, rūpaṃ pana na viññāṇasampayuttaṃ, sahajāta”nti vibhajitvā gahetabbaṃ. Tassāti paññāsatisahitassa nāmarūpassa. Nirodhanti anupādisesanibbānadhātuṃ.

13. The meaning of the phrase 'wisdom and mindfulness' has been explained by the teacher and is known by us. Since it is to be said, 'How is the meaning of the phrase 'and name-and-form' to be known by us?', he, analyzing name-and-form, said, 'Herein, those five aggregates of clinging,' and so on. Herein, 'there' refers to the three realms of existence, in the division of the round of kamma and its result. 'There' refers to the collection of name-and-form designated as the five aggregates of clinging. 'The five faculties' means the five faculties beginning with the eye. 'Associated with consciousness' is not said with reference to the associated-condition, but it is said with reference to the mere nature of what is to be grasped without analysis by the multitude. However, by those who know the analysis, it should be grasped by analyzing thus: 'Name is associated with consciousness, but form is not associated with consciousness; it is co-arisen.' 'Of that' refers to name-and-form accompanied by wisdom and mindfulness. 'Cessation' means the Nibbāna-element without residue.

Bhagavantaṃ pucchanto āyasmā ajito “paññā ceva…pe… katthetaṃ uparujjhatī”ti evaṃ pārāyane āha. “Paññā cevātiādigāthāya yā anupādisesanibbānadhātu pucchitā, sā anupādisesanibbānadhātu katamena adhigamena pattabbā”ti pucchitabbattā caturiddhipādamukhena ariyamaggādhigamamukhena pattabbā, caturiddhipādabhāvanāya ca cattārindriyāni mūlabhūtāni, tasmā mūlabhūtāni tāni cattārindriyāni niddhāretvā dassento “tattha sati ca paññā cā”tiādimāha. Kusalākusaladhammagatiyo samanvesamānāya satiyā sijjhamānāya ekantena samādhi nipphādetabbo, satiggahaṇena ca pariyuṭṭhānappahānaṃ gāthāyaṃ adhippetaṃ, pariyuṭṭhānappahānena ca [V 0.0237] samādhikiccaṃ pākaṭanti āha “sati dve indriyāni satindriyañca samādhindriyañcā”ti. Paññāya anusayasamugghātaṃ catubbidhasammappadhānasaṅkhātena vīriyena sijjhati, na vinā tenāti vuttaṃ “paññā dve indriyāni paññindriyañca vīriyindriyañcā”ti.

The Venerable Ajita, questioning the Blessed One, said thus in the Pārāyana: 'Wisdom and… where does this cease?' Since the question is to be asked, 'The Nibbāna-element without residue remaining, which is asked about in the verse beginning 'Wisdom and,' by what attainment is that Nibbāna-element without residue to be reached?', it is to be reached by way of the four bases of spiritual power, by way of attaining the noble path. And since the four faculties are fundamental to the development of the four bases of spiritual power, therefore, having determined those fundamental faculties, he shows them, saying, 'Herein, mindfulness and wisdom,' and so on. Through successful mindfulness that investigates the courses of wholesome and unwholesome states, concentration is certainly to be developed. And by the term 'mindfulness,' the abandoning of obsessions is intended in the verse, and through the abandoning of obsessions, the function of concentration becomes manifest. Thus, he said: 'Mindfulness represents two faculties—the faculty of mindfulness and the faculty of concentration.' The uprooting of latent tendencies by wisdom is accomplished through energy in the form of the fourfold right striving. It is said that this is not accomplished without that. Therefore: 'Wisdom represents two faculties—the faculty of wisdom and the faculty of energy.'

Imesu yathāvuttesu catūsu indriyesu pubbabhāge vā maggakkhaṇe vā sijjhantesu taṃsampayuttā yā saddahanā okappanā siddhā, idaṃ saddahanaokappanasaṅkhātaṃ dhammajātaṃ saddhindriyaṃ siddhaṃ, “tesu mūlabhūtesu indriyesu siddhesu katamena indriyena katamo dhammo siddho”ti pucchitabbattā iminā ayaṃ siddhoti dassento “tattha yā saddhādhipateyyā”tiādimāha. Tattha tatthāti satyādīsu. Saddhādhipateyyāti paccayabhūtāya saddhāya siddho chando adhipatīti saddhādhipati, saddhādhipatinā pavattetabbā cittekaggatāti saddhādhipateyyā. Chandasamādhīti chandaṃ jeṭṭhakaṃ katvā pavattito samādhi vā chandādhipatinā sampayutto pubbabhāge pavatto samādhi vā chandasamādhi, pahānaṃ pahānahetu hotīti yojanā kātabbā. Pahānanti ca pajahati vikkhambhitakilese etena chandasamādhināti pahānanti karaṇasādhanattho gahetabbo. Paṭisaṅkhānabalenāti parikammabalena. Bhāvanābalenāti mahaggatabhāvanābalena.

Among these four faculties as mentioned, whether in the preliminary stage or at the moment of the path, when they succeed, the associated confidence and trust that is accomplished—this phenomenon, designated as confidence and trust, is the accomplished faculty of faith. Since it should be asked, 'When these root faculties are accomplished, by which faculty is which phenomenon accomplished?', to show that this is accomplished by it, it is said: 'Herein, that which has faith as its dominant factor,' and so on. Here, 'herein' refers to mindfulness and so on. 'That which has faith as its dominant factor' means that desire, accomplished through faith as its condition, is the dominant factor, hence 'faith-dominant'. The one-pointedness of mind to be brought about by that which has faith as its dominant factor is 'faith-dominance'. 'Desire-concentration' means concentration that arises with desire as the foremost factor, or concentration that arises in the preliminary stage associated with desire as the dominant factor. The connection should be made that 'abandonment is the cause of abandonment.' And 'abandonment' should be understood in the instrumental sense, meaning that one abandons the defilements suppressed by this desire-concentration. 'By the power of reflection' means by the power of preliminary work. 'By the power of development' means by the power of development of the sublime states.

“So [M 0.0101] chandasamādhi sayaṃ kevalova pahāna”nti vattabbattā “tattha ye assāsapassāsā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha tatthāti tasmiṃ samāhite citte cittuppāde. “Tasmiṃ samāhite cittuppāde assāsā”tiādinā assāsādisīsena assāsādijanakā vīriyasaṅkhārā gahitā, te ca yāva bhāvanāpāripūrī, tāva punappunaṃ saraṇato ca sarā, punappunaṃ saṅkappato ca saṅkappā. Yo pana “sarasaṅkappā, ime saṅkhārā cā”ti evaṃ vuttappakāro purimako chandasamādhi vā kilesavikkhambhanatāya ca tadaṅgappahānatāya ca pahānaṃ pahānahetupadhānaṃ vā, “ime vuttappakārā saṅkhārādayo kiṃ bhāventī”ti pucchitabbattā “ime ca saṅkhārā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha ime saṅkhārā ca tadubhayañca chandasamādhippadhānasaṅkhārasamannāgataṃ vivekanissitaṃ virāganissitaṃ nirodhanissitaṃ vossaggapariṇāmiṃ iddhipādaṃ bhāvetīti yojanā.

Because it is said that 'that concentration of will is itself simply abandonment,' therefore 'there, those in-breaths and out-breaths,' etc., are stated. There, 'there' refers to that concentrated mind, the arising of the mind. By 'in that concentrated mind, the in-breaths,' etc., under the heading of in-breaths and so on, are taken the formations of energy that generate them. And these, until the completion of development, are repeatedly recollected and thus are memories, and repeatedly intended and thus are intentions. But as for the earlier concentration of will, which is described in this way—'memories and intentions, these are formations'—it is abandonment either through the suppression of defilements or through abandonment by way of its components; or, it is the striving that is the cause of abandonment. Because it is to be asked: 'What do these formations and so on, stated in this way, develop?' Therefore, it is said, 'these formations,' etc. Here, the connection is: these formations and both of those (i.e., the concentration of will and abandonment) develop the base of spiritual power, which is endowed with the concentration of will and the striving formations, dependent on seclusion, dependent on dispassion, dependent on cessation, and culminates in relinquishment.

Chandasamādhippadhānasaṅkhārasamannāgatanti chando eva adhipati chandādhipati, chandādhipatisamādhi. Tena vuttaṃ bhagavatā – “chandaṃ ce, bhikkhave, bhikkhu adhipatiṃ karitvā labhati samādhi”nti (vibha. 432). Chandahetuko vā samādhi, chandādiko vā samādhi chandasamādhi, chandādhipatissa paccayuppanno samādhīti vuttaṃ hoti. Padhānabhūtā saṅkhārā padhānasaṅkhārā, padhānasaddena saṅkhatasaṅkhārādayo nivattāpitā, chandasamādhi ca padhānasaṅkhārā cāti chandasamādhippadhānasaṅkhārā[V 0.0238], tehi samannāgato chanda…pe… samannāgato, taṃ…pe… gataṃ. Ijjhati samijjhati nippajjatīti iddhi, koṭṭhāso, iddhi eva pādo koṭṭhāsoti iddhipādo, iddhipādacatuttho. Ijjhanti vā tāya sattā iddhā vuddhā ukkaṃsagatā hontīti iddhi, pajjati etenāti pādo, iddhiyā pādoti iddhipādo. Iddhipādoti sāmaññatthavasena vuttopi “chandasamādhippadhānasaṅkhārasamannāgata”nti vuttattā chandiddhipādova gahetabbo, taṃ iddhipādaṃ taṃ chandiddhipādaṃ bhāveti vaḍḍhetīti attho.

The phrase 'endowed with the concentration of will and the striving formations' means that will itself is the dominant factor, the dominant will, concentration with will as the dominant factor. Therefore, the Blessed One has said: 'Monks, if a monk makes will the dominant factor, he attains concentration.' Concentration caused by will, or concentration originating from will, is called concentration of will; it is said to be concentration arisen with will as the dominant condition. The formations that are striving are called striving formations. By the word 'striving,' conditioned formations and the like are excluded. The concentration of will and the striving formations are 'concentration of will and striving formations.' One who is endowed with these is 'endowed with the concentration of will and striving formations'; that which is so endowed is the base of spiritual power. 'Spiritual power' means that which succeeds, accomplishes, or is produced; it is a portion. Spiritual power itself is a foundation, a portion, thus it is called a base of spiritual power. Or, beings succeed through it, they become successful, grown, and exalted—thus it is spiritual power. One proceeds by this, thus it is a foundation. The foundation of spiritual power is a base of spiritual power. Though the term 'base of spiritual power' is used in a general sense, because it is said, 'endowed with the concentration of will and the striving formations,' only the base of spiritual power rooted in will should be taken. The meaning is: one develops and cultivates that base of spiritual power, that base of spiritual power rooted in will.

Vivekanissitaṃ virāganissitanti vipassanākkhaṇe kiccato tadaṅgavivekanissitaṃ, ajjhāsayato nissaraṇavivekanissitaṃ, maggakkhaṇe pana kiccato samucchedavivekanissitaṃ, ārammaṇato nissaraṇavivekanissitaṃ. Virāganissitanti vipassanākkhaṇe kiccato tadaṅgavirāganissitaṃ, ajjhāsayato nissaraṇavivekanissitaṃ, maggakkhaṇe pana kiccato samucchedavirāganissitaṃ[M 0.0102], ārammaṇato nissaraṇavirāganissitaṃ. Nirodhanissitanti vipassanākkhaṇe kiccato tadaṅganirodhanissitaṃ, ajjhāsayato nissaraṇanirodhanissitaṃ, maggakkhaṇe kiccato samucchedanirodhanissitaṃ, ārammaṇato nissaraṇanirodhanissitaṃ. Vossaggapariṇāminti ettha pariccāgavossaggapakkhandanavossaggavasena vossaggo duvidho. Tatthapi vipassanākkhaṇe tadaṅgavasena pariccāgavossaggo, nibbānaninnabhāvena pakkhandanavossaggo, maggakkhaṇe samucchedavasena pariccāgavossaggo, ārammaṇakaraṇena nibbānapakkhandanavossaggoti vibhajitvā gahetabbo. Yathāvuttavossaggatthaṃ pariṇamati, pariṇataṃ vā paripacati paripacanaṃ karotīti vossaggapariṇāmī, taṃ vossaggapariṇāmiṃ.

Dependent on seclusion, dependent on dispassion: at the moment of insight, functionally, it is dependent on momentary seclusion; by way of intention, it is dependent on the seclusion of escape. At the moment of the path, however, functionally, it is dependent on the seclusion of eradication; by way of object, it is dependent on the seclusion of escape. Dependent on dispassion: at the moment of insight, functionally, it is dependent on momentary dispassion; by way of intention, it is dependent on the dispassion of escape. At the moment of the path, functionally, it is dependent on the dispassion of eradication; by way of object, it is dependent on the dispassion of escape. Dependent on cessation: at the moment of insight, functionally, it is dependent on momentary cessation; by way of intention, it is dependent on the cessation of escape. At the moment of the path, functionally, it is dependent on the cessation of eradication; by way of object, it is dependent on the cessation of escape. Culminating in relinquishment: here, relinquishment is twofold, by way of abandoning and by way of plunging. In this context, at the moment of insight, it is relinquishment by way of abandoning as momentary; by virtue of inclining towards Nibbāna, it is relinquishment by way of plunging. At the moment of the path, it is relinquishment by way of abandoning as eradication; by making Nibbāna the object, it is relinquishment by way of plunging into Nibbāna. These should be understood by distinguishing them. It culminates for the sake of the relinquishment as stated, or it ripens, brings to maturity what has culminated—thus it is 'culminating in relinquishment.' That is 'culminating in relinquishment.'

Chandiddhipādabhāvanākāro ācariyena vutto, amhehi ca ñāto, “kathaṃ vīriyiddhipādabhāvanākāro amhehi vijānitabbo”ti vattabbabhāvato “tattha yā vīriyādhipateyyā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tassattho heṭṭhā vuttanayānusāreneva viññeyyo. Saṃkhittavasena pana ṭhapitaṃ pāṭhaṃ vitthārato ṭhapessāmi. Kathaṃ? –

The method of developing the base of spiritual power rooted in will has been taught by the teacher and is known to us. Since it should be said, 'How is the method of developing the base of spiritual power rooted in energy to be understood by us?', it is said, 'Here, that which has energy as its dominant factor...' Its meaning should be understood in accordance with the method stated above. However, I shall set forth in detail the passage that has been set forth concisely. How?

“Tattha yā vīriyādhipateyyā cittekaggatā, ayaṃ vīriyasamādhi. Samāhite citte kilesānaṃ vikkhambhanatāya paṭisaṅkhānabalena vā bhāvanābalena vā, idaṃ pahānaṃ. Tattha ye assāsapassāsā vitakkavicārā saññāvedayitā sarasaṅkappā, ime saṅkhārā. Iti purimako ca vīriyasamādhi, kilesavikkhambhanatāya ca pahānaṃ ime ca saṅkhārā, tadubhayaṃ vīriyasamādhippadhānasaṅkhārasamannāgataṃ [V 0.0239] iddhipādaṃ bhāveti vivekanissitaṃ virāganissitaṃ nirodhanissitaṃ vossaggapariṇāmiṃ.

Here, that one-pointedness of mind which has energy as its dominant factor—this is concentration of energy. When the mind is concentrated, this is abandonment by way of the suppression of defilements through the power of reflection or through the power of development. Here, the in-breaths and out-breaths, initial thought and sustained thought, perceptions and feelings, recollection and intention—these are formations. Thus, the aforementioned concentration of energy, the abandonment by way of the suppression of defilements, and these formations—these two together develop the base of spiritual power endowed with the concentration of energy and the striving formations, which is dependent on seclusion, dependent on dispassion, dependent on cessation, and culminates in relinquishment.

“Tattha yā cittādhipateyyā cittekaggatā, ayaṃ cittasamādhi. Samāhite citte kilesānaṃ vikkhambhanatāya paṭisaṅkhānabalena vā bhāvanābalena vā, idaṃ pahānaṃ. Tattha ye assāsapassāsā vitakkavicārā saññāvedayitā sarasaṅkappā, ime saṅkhārā. Iti purimako ca cittasamādhi, kilesavikkhambhanatāya ca pahānaṃ ime ca saṅkhārā, tadubhayaṃ cittasamādhippadhānasaṅkhārasamannāgataṃ iddhipādaṃ bhāveti vivekanissitaṃ virāganissitaṃ nirodhanissitaṃ vossaggapariṇāmiṃ.

Here, that one-pointedness of mind which has mind as its dominant factor—this is concentration of mind. When the mind is concentrated, this is abandonment by way of the suppression of defilements through the power of reflection or through the power of development. Here, the in-breaths and out-breaths, initial thought and sustained thought, perceptions and feelings, recollection and intention—these are formations. Thus, the aforementioned concentration of mind, the abandonment by way of the suppression of defilements, and these formations—these two together develop the base of spiritual power endowed with the concentration of mind and the striving formations, which is dependent on seclusion, dependent on dispassion, dependent on cessation, and culminates in relinquishment.

“Tattha [M 0.0103] yā vīmaṃsādhipateyyā cittekaggatā, ayaṃ vīmaṃsāsamādhi, samāhite citte kilesānaṃ vikkhambhanatāya paṭisaṅkhānabalena vā bhāvanābalena vā, idaṃ pahānaṃ. Tattha ye assāsapassāsā vitakkavicārā saññāvedayitā sarasaṅkappā, ime saṅkhārā. Iti purimako ca vīmaṃsāsamādhi kilesavikkhambhanatāya ca pahānaṃ ime ca saṅkhārā, tadubhayaṃ vīmaṃsāsamādhippadhānasaṅkhārasamannāgataṃ iddhipādaṃ bhāveti vivekanissitaṃ virāganissitaṃ nirodhanissitaṃ vossaggapariṇāmi”nti.

Herein, that singleness of mind which has investigation as its dominant factor—this is concentration of investigation. When the mind is concentrated, the suppression of defilements by the power of reflection or by the power of cultivation—this is abandonment. Herein, the in-breaths and out-breaths, initial thought and sustained thought, perceptions and feelings, recollection and intention—these are formations. Thus, both the aforementioned concentration of investigation, along with the abandonment by way of suppressing defilements, and these formations, develop the base of spiritual power endowed with the concentration of investigation and striving formations, which is dependent on seclusion, dependent on dispassion, dependent on cessation, and culminates in relinquishment.

Ayaṃ pana viseso – vīriyasamādhīti vīriyaṃ jeṭṭhakaṃ katvā pavattito samādhi vā vīriyādhipatinā sampayutto pubbabhāge pavatto samādhi vā vīriyasamādhi. Cittasamādhīti cittaṃ jeṭṭhakaṃ katvā pavattito samādhi vā cittādhipatinā sampayutto pubbabhāge pavatto samādhi vā cittasamādhi. Vīmaṃsāsamādhīti vīmaṃsaṃ jeṭṭhakaṃ katvā pavattito samādhi vā vīmaṃsādhipatinā sampayutto pubbabhāge pavatto samādhi vā vīmaṃsāsamādhīti.

Here, however, is the distinction: 'Concentration of energy' is either concentration that arises with energy made the chief factor, or concentration associated with energy as the dominant factor, having arisen in the earlier stage. 'Concentration of mind' is either concentration that arises with mind made the chief factor, or concentration associated with mind as the dominant factor, having arisen in the earlier stage. 'Concentration of investigation' is either concentration that arises with investigation made the chief factor, or concentration associated with investigation as the dominant factor, having arisen in the earlier stage.

Sattibalānurūpenettha saṅkhepavaṇṇanā katā, gambhīrañāṇehi pana aṭṭhakathāṭīkānurūpena vitthārato vā gambhīrato vā vibhajitvā gahetabbā.

Here, a brief explanation has been given in accordance with one's power of comprehension. But those with profound knowledge should take it by distinguishing in detail or profoundly, in accordance with the commentaries and sub-commentaries.

14. “Chandasamādhi vīriyasamādhi cittasamādhi vīmaṃsāsamādhī”ti vutto, “evaṃ sati vīmaṃsāsamādhiyeva ñāṇamūlako ñāṇapubbaṅgamo ñāṇānuparivatti bhaveyya, aññe tayo samādhayo aññāṇamūlakā aññāṇapubbaṅgamā aññāṇapavattiyo bhaveyyu”nti vattabbattā sabbe samādhayo ñāṇamūlakādayoyevāti dassetuṃ “sabbo samādhi ñāṇamūlako”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha sabbo samādhīti [V 0.0240] chandasamādhi, vīriyasamādhi, cittasamādhi, vīmaṃsāsamādhīti catubbidho samādhi. Ñāṇamūlakoti ekāvajjanavīthinānāvajjanavīthīsu pavattaṃ upacārañāṇamūlako. Ñāṇapubbaṅgamoti adhigamañāṇaṃ pubbaṅgamaṃ assāti ñāṇapubbaṅgamo. Ñāṇānuparivattīti paccavekkhaṇañāṇaṃ anuparivatti assāti ñāṇānuparivatti. Atha vā nānāvajjanūpacārañāṇaṃ vā paṭisandhiñāṇaṃ vā mūlaṃ assāti ñāṇamūlako, upacārañāṇaṃ pubbaṅgamaṃ assāti ñāṇapubbaṅgamo, appanāñāṇaṃ anuparivatti assāti ñāṇānuparivatti[M 0.0104]. Sabbaṃ vā upacārañāṇaṃ mūlaṃ assāti ñāṇamūlako. Appanāñāṇaṃ pubbaṅgamaṃ assāti ñāṇapubbaṅgamo. Abhiññāñāṇaṃ anuparivatti assāti ñāṇānuparivatti, anuparivattanaṃ vā anuparivatti, ñāṇassa anuparivatti ñāṇānuparivatti, ñāṇānuparivatti assāti ñāṇānuparivatti. Ñāṇaṃ pana pubbe vuttappakārameva.

14. It is said, 'Concentration of desire, concentration of energy, concentration of mind, and concentration of investigation.' Thus, if this were so, only concentration of investigation would be rooted in knowledge, preceded by knowledge, and followed by knowledge, while the other three concentrations would be rooted in non-knowledge, preceded by non-knowledge, and followed by non-knowledge. To show that all concentrations are indeed rooted in knowledge, preceded by knowledge, and followed by knowledge, it is said, 'All concentration is rooted in knowledge,' etc. Herein, 'all concentration' refers to the fourfold concentration: concentration of desire, concentration of energy, concentration of mind, and concentration of investigation. 'Rooted in knowledge' means rooted in the preliminary knowledge that occurs in the single-door and multiple-door cognitive processes. 'Preceded by knowledge' means having attainment-knowledge as its precursor. 'Followed by knowledge' means having reviewing knowledge as its attendant. Alternatively, 'rooted in knowledge' means having either preliminary knowledge or rebirth-linking knowledge as its root; 'preceded by knowledge' means having preliminary knowledge as its precursor; and 'followed by knowledge' means having absorption knowledge as its attendant. Or, 'rooted in knowledge' means all preliminary knowledge is its root; 'preceded by knowledge' means absorption knowledge is its precursor; and 'followed by knowledge' means direct knowledge is its attendant. Or, 'anuparivatti' means 'following'; thus, 'ñāṇānuparivatti' means 'following knowledge' or 'having knowledge as its follower.' The knowledge, however, is as previously explained.

Yathā pure tathā pacchāti yathā chandasamādhiādicatubbidhasamādhissa pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇānuparivattibhāvena pure atītāsu jātīsu asaṅkhyeyyesupi saṃvaṭṭavivaṭṭesu attano khandhapaṭibaddhassa, paresaṃ khandhapaṭibaddhassa ca suṭṭhu paṭivijjhanameva, na duppaṭivijjhanaṃ tathā tathāvuttasamādhissa anāgataṃsañāṇānuparivattibhāvena pacchā anāgatāsu jātīsu asaṅkhyeyyesupi saṃvaṭṭavivaṭṭesu attano khandhapaṭibaddhassa, paresaṃ khandhapaṭibaddhassa ca suṭṭhu paṭivijjhanameva, na duppaṭivijjhananti attho daṭṭhabbo. Yathā pacchā tathā pureti yathā yathāvuttasamādhissa cetopariyañāṇānuparivattibhāvena anāgatesu sattasuyeva divasesu parasattānaṃyeva cittassa suṭṭhu paṭivijjhanameva, na duppaṭivijjhanaṃ, tathā tathāvuttasamādhissa pure atītesu sattasuyeva divasesu parasattānaṃyeva cittassa suṭṭhu paṭivijjhanameva, na duppaṭivijjhananti attho.

As in the past, so in the future: Just as, by means of the fourfold concentration beginning with concentration of desire, when accompanied by the knowledge of the recollection of past lives, one clearly penetrates—without difficulty—one's own aggregates and the aggregates of others, bound up in countless past existences during the cycles of world contraction and expansion; so too, by means of the same concentration, when accompanied by the knowledge of the future, one clearly penetrates—without difficulty—one's own aggregates and the aggregates of others, bound up in countless future existences during the cycles of world contraction and expansion. This is the meaning to be understood. As in the future, so in the past: Just as, by means of the aforementioned concentration, when accompanied by the knowledge of the minds of others, one clearly penetrates—without difficulty—the minds of other beings within just seven days in the future; so too, by means of the aforementioned concentration, one clearly penetrates—without difficulty—the minds of other beings within just seven days in the past. This is the meaning.

Yathā divā tathā rattinti yathā cakkhumantānaṃ sattānaṃ divasabhāge sūriyālokena andhakārassa viddhaṃsitattā āpāthagataṃ cakkhuviññeyyaṃ rūpaṃ manoviññāṇenapi suviññeyyaṃ, tathā rattibhāge caturaṅgasamannāgatepi andhakāre vattamāne yathāvuttasamādhissa dibbacakkhuñāṇānuparivattibhāvena rūpāyatanassa suṭṭhu paṭivijjhanameva, na duppaṭivijjhanaṃ. Yathā rattiṃ tathā divāti yathā rattibhāge caturaṅgasamannāgatepi andhakāre yathāvuttasamādhissa dibbacakkhuñāṇānuparivattibhāvena rūpāyatanassa suṭṭhu paṭivijjhanameva, na duppaṭivijjhanaṃ, tathā divasabhāge sukhumassa rūpāyatanassa vā kenaci pākārādinā tirohitassa rūpāyatanassa vā atidūraṭṭhāne pavattassa rūpāyatanassa vā yathāvuttasamādhissa dibbacakkhuñāṇānuparivattibhāvena suṭṭhu paṭivijjhanameva, na duppaṭivijjhananti attho daṭṭhabbo.

As by day, so by night: Just as for beings with eyes, during the daytime, with the darkness dispelled by sunlight, visible forms that have come into range are easily discernible by eye-consciousness and also by mind-consciousness; so too, during the nighttime, even when darkness accompanied by the four factors is present, the sphere of forms is clearly penetrated—without difficulty—by means of the aforementioned concentration, when accompanied by the divine eye-knowledge.
