Tattha jiṇṇajarāya paṭikammaṃ kātuṃ sakkateva, maraṇassa pana paṭikammassa kātuṃ na sakkateva, imināpi kāraṇena jarāmaraṇānaṃ nānattaṃ sampaṭicchitabbamevāti attho. “Na sakkate maraṇassa paṭikammaṃ kātu”nti kasmā vuttaṃ, nanu iddhipādabhāvanāya vasībhāve sati sakkā maraṇassāpi paṭikammaṃ kātunti codanaṃ manasi katvā “aññatreva iddhimantānaṃ iddhivisayā”ti vuttaṃ.

Since it should be said, “For what reason is it fitting? For what reason should the distinction be accepted?” it is said, “For even those in the womb die.” Since beings in the womb die without having reached old age, the distinction must be accepted. Since it might be said, “Even those in the womb might have reached aging,” it is said, “but they do not become decrepit.” Even having reached aging, they die without having reached decrepit old age, because they are not decrepit. Thus, since the occurrence of death without the decrepit old age intended here is possible, it is said that it should be known that aging is one thing and death is another. Because it should be said, “It is not only for those in the womb that death occurs without reaching decrepit old age; it also occurs for others,” it is said, “And there is death for the devas.” Since it might be said, “Devas too, due to their long existence, might reach old age,” it is said, “but their bodies do not decay.” Since it might be said, “Is this all the reason for the distinction between aging and death?” to show that there is another, “it is possible…” and so on is said. Here, it is indeed possible to apply a remedy for decrepit old age, but it is not possible to apply a remedy for death. For this reason too, the meaning is that the distinction between aging and death must be accepted. Why is it said, “It is not possible to apply a remedy for death”? Having considered the objection, “Surely, when there is mastery in the development of the bases of psychic power, it is possible to apply a remedy for death too?” it is said, “except for the domain of the power of those possessing psychic power.”

Jarāmaraṇānaṃ [M 0.0122] aññamaññaṃ nānābhāvo ācariyena dassito, amhehi ca ñāto, “kathaṃ pana taṇhāya jarāmaraṇehi nānābhāvo”ti vattabbato tehi taṇhāya nānattaṃ dassetuṃ “yaṃ panāhā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Taṇhāya avijjamānāyapi jīrantāpi mīyantāpi vītarāgā yasmā dissanti, tasmā taṇhāya jarāmaraṇehi nānābhāvo sampaṭicchitabbo.

The mutual distinction between aging and death has been shown by the Teacher and is known by us. But since it should be said, “How is there a distinction between craving and aging-and-death?” to demonstrate the distinction of craving from them, “But as for what is said…” and so on is stated. Since, even when craving is non-existent, those free from lust are seen aging and dying, therefore the distinction of craving from aging-and-death must be accepted.

“Taṇhāya jīraṇabhijjanalakkhaṇaṃ atthīti tehi taṇhāya anaññatte ko nāma doso siyā”ti vattabbato dosaṃ dassetuṃ “yadi cā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Jarāmaraṇaṃ yathā yena jīraṇabhijjanalakkhaṇena pākaṭaṃ, evaṃ jīraṇabhijjanalakkhaṇena taṇhāpi pākaṭā. Yadi ca siyā; evaṃ sante yobbanaṭṭhāpi sabbe māṇavā vigatataṇhā siyuṃ, na ca vigatataṇhā, tasmā nānābhāvo sampaṭicchitabbo. Tato aññopi doso āpajjeyyāti dassetuṃ “yathā ca taṇhā dukkhassā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha jarāmaraṇānaṃ taṇhāya anaññatte sati taṇhāya bhavataṇhāya dukkhasamudayo hoti, evaṃ jarāmaraṇampi dukkhasamudayo siyā. Yasmā na jarāmaraṇaṃ dukkhasamudayo, tasmā jarāmaraṇehi taṇhāya nānattaṃ veditabbaṃ.

Since it might be said, “As craving has the characteristic of decay and breaking up, what fault would there be in its non-difference from them?” to show the fault, “And if…” and so on was said. Just as aging and death are manifest by the characteristic of decay and breaking up, so too would craving be manifest by the characteristic of decay and breaking up. And if that were so, then all young men established in youth would be without craving; but they are not without craving. Therefore, a distinct nature must be accepted. To show that another fault would be incurred, “Just as craving is the origin of suffering…” and so on was said. Here, if aging and death were non-different from craving, then just as craving, specifically craving for existence, is the origin of suffering, so too would aging and death be the origin of suffering. Since aging and death are not the origin of suffering, the distinction of craving from aging and death must be understood.

Tehi tāya anaññatte sati evampi doso āpajjeyyāti dassetuṃ “yathā ca taṇhā maggavajjhā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha tehi tāya anaññatte sati yathā taṇhā maggavajjhā hoti, evaṃ jarāmaraṇampi maggavajjhaṃ siyā. Yathā jarāmaraṇaṃ maggavajjhaṃ na hoti, evaṃ taṇhāpi maggavajjhā na siyā, tathā ca na hoti pahātabbāpahātabbabhāvato, tasmāpi jarāmaraṇehi taṇhāya nānattaṃ veditabbaṃ.

To show that a fault would also arise if they were not different from it, it is said: “And just as craving is to be abandoned by the path…” and so on. Here, if they were not different from it, then just as craving is to be abandoned by the path, so too aging and death would be to be abandoned by the path. And just as aging and death are not to be abandoned by the path, so too craving would not be to be abandoned by the path. But it is not so, because of their distinction as to what should be abandoned and what should not be abandoned. Therefore, the distinction of craving from aging and death should also be understood.

“Yadi [V 0.0257] cātiādinā vuttāya yuttiyā upapattiyā eva jarāmaraṇehi taṇhāya aññattaṃ gavesitabba”nti vattabbattā aññehipi kāraṇehi gavesitabbanti dassetuṃ “imāya yuttiyā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha imāya yuttiyāti yā yutti “yadi cā”tiādinā vuttāya imāya yuttiyā upapattiyā. Aññamaññehi kāraṇehi aññehi aññehi kāraṇabhūtehi upapattīhi jarāmaraṇehi taṇhāya aññattaṃ gavesitabbanti attho. “Aññamaññehi kāraṇehi gavesitabba”nti kasmā vuttaṃ, nanu yuttiyā, atthato ca aññattaṃ sandissatīti codanaṃ manasi katvā “yadi ca sandissatī”tiādimāha. Tattha yuttisamāruḷhaṃ atthato ca maraṇehi [M 0.0123] taṇhāya ca aññattaṃ yadi ca sandissati, byañjanatopi aññattaṃ gavesitabbamevāti attho.

Because it might be said, 'The distinction of craving from aging and death should be sought only by the reasoning and argument stated beginning with "yadi ca"', the text states 'by this reasoning,' etc., to show that it should also be sought by other reasons. Herein, 'by this reasoning' means by this reasoning, that is, by the argument which is the reasoning stated beginning with 'yadi ca'. The meaning is that the distinction of craving from aging and death should be sought by various other reasons, by other causal arguments. 'Why is it said "should be sought by various reasons"? Surely, the distinction is apparent both by reasoning and in meaning.' Considering this objection, he then said, 'and if it is apparent,' etc. Herein, the meaning is: if the distinction of craving from death, which is established by reasoning and is apparent in meaning, is indeed apparent, then the distinction should be sought by expression as well.

“Kathaṃ byañjanato aññattaṃ gavesitabba”nti vattabbattā “salloti vā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha “sallo”ti vā “dhūpāyana”nti vā dvīhi byañjanehi vuccamānānaṃ imesaṃ icchātaṇhāsaṅkhātānaṃ dhammānaṃ atthato ekattaṃ samānattaṃ yujjati, na aññattaṃ. “Sallo”ti vā “dhūpāyana”nti vā dvīhi byañjanehi avuccamānānaṃ jarāmaraṇānaṃ taṇhāya ekattaṃ na yujjati. Tamevatthaṃ vivarituṃ “na hī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha icchāya ca taṇhāya ca atthato aññattaṃ na yujjati, ekattameva yujjatīti yojanā. Icchāya ca taṇhāya ca jīraṇabhijjanasambhavato jarāmaraṇehi taṇhāya ekattaṃ siyā, “kasmā aññattaṃ yutta”nti vattabbato “taṇhāya adhippāye”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha taṇhāya adhippāye aparipūramāne navasu āghātavatthūsu kodho ca uppajjati, upanāho ca uppajjati. Jarāmaraṇesu aparipūramānesu navasu āghātavatthūsu kodho ca na uppajjati, upanāho ca na uppajjati. Iti imāya yuttiyā jarāya ca maraṇassa ca taṇhāya ca atthato aññattaṃ yujjatiyevāti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

'How should distinction by expression be sought?'—because this might be said, 'a dart' etc. was stated. Herein, for these things designated as desire and craving, when spoken of by the two expressions 'dart' or 'smoking', unity and sameness in meaning is appropriate, not distinction. For aging and death, which are not spoken of by these two expressions, unity with craving is not appropriate. To clarify that very meaning, it is said, 'for not...' etc. Herein, the connection is: distinction in meaning between desire and craving is not appropriate; only unity is appropriate. Because aging and breaking up arise from desire and craving, there might be a unity of craving with aging and death. Because it might be said, 'Why is distinction appropriate?' it is said, 'when the intention of craving...' etc. Herein, when the intention of craving is not fulfilled, anger and resentment arise regarding the nine grounds for malice. When aging and death are not fulfilled, neither anger nor resentment arises regarding the nine grounds for malice. Thus, by this reasoning, it should be seen that distinction in meaning between aging, death, and craving is indeed appropriate.

Yadi icchā taṇhāya atthato ekattaṃ yuttaṃ, evaṃ sati kasmā bhagavatā “maccunābbhāhato loko”tiādigāthāyaṃ “taṇhāsallena otiṇṇo, icchādhūpāyito sadā”ti dvidhā vuttāti codanaṃ pariharanto “yaṃ panidaṃ bhagavatā”tiādimāha. Tattha “icchā”tipi “taṇhā”tipi dvīhi nāmehi yaṃ panidaṃ abhilapitaṃ yaṃ panidaṃ abhilapanaṃ kataṃ, idaṃ abhilapanaṃ bhagavatā bāhirānaṃ icchitabbatasitabbānaṃ vatthūnaṃ rūpādiārammaṇānaṃ bhedānaṃ vasena “icchā”tipi “taṇhā”tipi dvīhi nāmehi abhilapitaṃ abhilapanavasena katanti ekattaṃ yuttameva, na nānattanti attho daṭṭhabbo.

If it is appropriate that desire (icchā) and craving (taṇhā) are one in meaning, this being so, why did the Blessed One, in the verse beginning 'The world is struck down by death,' state them twofold as 'pierced by the dart of craving' and 'always scorched by the smoke of desire'? Avoiding this objection, he said, 'But this which was spoken by the Blessed One...' etc. Herein, that which is expressed, that expression which was made with the two names, 'desire' and 'craving'—this expression was made by the Blessed One with the two names 'desire' and 'craving' according to the distinctions among external objects to be desired and thirsted for, sense objects such as form. Thus, the meaning to be understood is that their unity is indeed appropriate, not their diversity.

“Nāmavasena [V 0.0258] dvidhā vuttānaṃ icchātaṇhādīnaṃ kena ekattaṃ yuttanti saddahitabba”nti vattabbattā “sabbāhī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha nānānāmavasena pabhedā sabbā icchādikā taṇhā ajjhosānalakkhaṇena ekalakkhaṇā hi yasmā yuttā, tasmā nāmavasena bhinnānampi ekalakkhaṇena ekattaṃ yuttanti saddahitabbanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. “Kimiva yutta”nti pucchitabbattā “yathā sabbo”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha kaṭṭhaggiādivasena aneko sabbo aggi [M 0.0124] uṇhattalakkhaṇena ekalakkhaṇo yathā, evaṃ ajjhosānalakkhaṇena ekalakkhaṇāti yojanā. Sabbassa aggino upādānavasena anekāni nāmāni sarūpato dassetuṃ “apicā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tassattho pākaṭo. Ārammaṇavasena taṇhā aññehi aññehi nāmehi bhagavatā abhilapitā, upādānavasena aggi aññehi aññehi nāmehi abhilapitoti yojanā kātabbā.

Because it might be said, 'By what reason should the unity of desire, craving, etc., which are stated as twofold by name, be accepted as appropriate?' it is stated, 'all indeed,' etc. Herein, since all cravings such as desire, though differentiated by various names, are indeed unified by the single characteristic of clinging, it should therefore be understood that although they are different by name, their unity through a single characteristic is appropriate and should be accepted. Because it might be asked, 'Appropriate like what?' it is stated, 'just as all,' etc. Herein, the connection is: just as all fire, though manifold by way of wood-fire, etc., is unified by the single characteristic of heat, so too is craving unified by the single characteristic of clinging. To show in detail the many names of all fire by way of its fuel, it is further stated, 'moreover,' etc. Its meaning is clear. The connection should be made that craving is spoken of by the Blessed One with different names according to the object, just as fire is spoken of with different names according to the fuel.

“Vissajjanagāthāyaṃ āgatanāmehi eva taṇhā abhilapitā”ti pucchitabbattā anekehi nāmehi abhilapitāti dassetuṃ “icchāitipī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha icchitabbāni atthāni rūpādīni ārammaṇāni sattā icchanti etāyāti icchā. Tasanti etāyāti taṇhā. Sallati pavisati visappītaṃ sallaṃ viyāti sallā, santāpaṃ lāti ādadātīti vā sallā, santāpaṃ lāti pavattetīti vā sallā. Dhūpāyati santāpeti paridahatīti dhūpāyanā. Sarati ākaḍḍhati avaharati sīghasotā saritā viyāti saritā, sarati sallatīti vā saritā. Visaratīti visattikā. Pītivasena sinehatīti sineho. Tāsu tāsu gatīsu kilamathaṃ uppādetīti kilamatho. Sattā rūpādiārammaṇāni maññanti etāyāti maññanā. Bhavaṃ bandhatīti bandho. Āsīyate patthīyateti āsā. Āsiyati patthetīti vā āsā. Pipāsīyateti pipāsā, ārammaṇarasaṃ pipāsatīti vā pipāsā. Abhinandīyateti abhinandanā, abhinandatīti vā abhinandanā. Vitthārato aṭṭhakathāvasena (netti. aṭṭha. 20) veditabbo.

Because it might be asked, 'Is craving spoken of only by the names that appear in the verse of explanation?', to show that it is spoken of by many names, 'icchā' and so on is stated. Herein, 'icchā' (desire) is so called because beings desire desirable things, sense objects such as forms, by means of it. 'Taṇhā' (craving) is so called because beings thirst by means of it. 'Sallā' (dart) is so called because it pierces and enters, spreading like a dart; or because it takes up torment, or because it causes torment to proceed. 'Dhūpāyanā' (smoking) is so called because it smokes, torments, and burns. 'Saritā' (river) is so called because it flows, drags, and carries away like a swift-flowing river; or because it flows and pierces. 'Visattikā' (clinging) is so called because it spreads out. 'Sineho' (affection) is so called because it adheres by way of being soaked. 'Kilamatho' (weariness) is so called because it produces weariness in those various states of existence. 'Maññanā' (conceiving) is so called because beings conceive sense objects such as forms by means of it. 'Bandho' (bond) is so called because it binds to becoming. 'Āsā' (hope) is so called because it is hoped for and longed for; or because one hopes and longs for it. 'Pipāsā' (thirst) is so called because it is thirsted for; or because it thirsts for the taste of objects. 'Abhinandanā' (delight) is so called because it is delighted in; or because one delights in it. This should be understood in detail according to the commentary (Nettipakaraṇa Aṭṭhakathā 20).

“Taṇhāya icchādippakāravasena ālapitabhāvo kena saddahitabbo”ti vattabbattā “yathā ca vevacane”tiādi vuttaṃ. Vevacanahāravibhaṅge “āsā ca pīhā…pe… vevacana”nti (netti. 37) yā taṇhā yathā yena pakārena vuttā, tathā tena pakārena vuttāya taṇhāya icchādippakāravasena ālapitabhāvo saddahitabbo. “Vevacanavibhaṅge ācariyena vuttopi bhagavatā avutte kena saddahitabbo”ti vattabbattā “yathāha bhagavā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Yathā yena pakārena bhagavā “rūpe tissā”tiādikaṃ yaṃ vacanamāha, tathā tena pakārena vuttena tena vacanena saddahitabbo vāti. Evaṃ yujjatīti evaṃ vuttanayena icchātaṇhānaṃ atthato ekattā[M 0.0125], jarāya [V 0.0259] ca maraṇassa ca taṇhāya ca atthato aññattā ca “tayo pañhā”ti yaṃ vacanaṃ vuttaṃ, taṃ vacanaṃ yujjatīti attho gahetabbo.

Because it might be said, 'By what should the fact that craving is spoken of in the manner of desire and so on be accepted?' it is said, 'as in the synonyms,' etc. Just as craving is spoken of in the Analysis of the Guide to Synonyms (Netti. 37) as 'hope and longing... synonyms,' so too, the fact that craving is spoken of in the manner of desire and so on should be accepted. Because it might be said, 'In the analysis of synonyms, even if spoken by the teacher, if it is not spoken by the Blessed One, by what should it be accepted?' it is said, 'as the Blessed One said,' etc. In whatever way the Blessed One spoke the statement beginning 'craving for forms,' in that same way, by that spoken statement, it should be accepted. The meaning to be understood is that 'Thus it is fitting' means that according to the method stated—because of the unity in meaning of desire and craving, and because of the distinction in meaning between aging, death, and craving—the statement that was made, 'three questions,' is fitting.

21. “Kenassubbhāhato lokotiādigāthāya tayo pañhā vuttā”ti pañhattayabhāve yutti ācariyena vibhattā, amhehi ca ñātā. “Tato aññehi pakārehi yutti kathaṃ ñātabbā”ti vattabbabhāvato aññehi pakārehipi yuttigavesanaṃ dassento “sabbo dukkhūpacāro”tiādimāha. Tattha sabbo dukkhūpacāro kāmataṇhāsaṅkhāramūlakoti yujjati, sabbo nibbidūpacāro kāmataṇhāparikkhāramūlakoti na yujjati. Vacanatthato pana dukkhassa upacāro pavattīti dukkhūpacāro. Kāmataṇhāpaccayā pavatto saṅkhāro mūlaṃ etassāti kāmataṇhāsaṅkhāramūlako. Nibbidāya upacāro pavattīti nibbidūpacāro. Kāmataṇhāya parikkhārabhūto vatthukāmo mūlaṃ etassāti kāmataṇhāparikkhāramūlakoti. Tattha anabhiratisaṅkhātā ukkaṇṭhā nibbidā kāmataṇhāparikkhāramūlikā yujjati, ñāṇanibbidā kāmataṇhāparikkhāramūlikā na yujjati, tasmā sabbo nibbidūpacāro kāmataṇhāparikkhāramūlakoti na pana yujjatīti vuttaṃ.

21. 'By what is the world overwhelmed?'—in this verse, three questions are posed. The teacher has explained the justification for these three questions, and we too have understood them. Since it must be explained, 'How then should the reasoning be known by other methods?', the text shows how reasoning can be investigated by other methods as well, beginning with 'every approach to suffering.' Here, it is justified that 'every approach to suffering' is rooted in formations conditioned by craving for sensual pleasures, but it is not justified that 'every approach to disenchantment' is rooted in the accessories of craving for sensual pleasures. In terms of the meaning of the words, 'the approach to suffering' means the occurrence or origination of suffering. 'Rooted in formations conditioned by craving for sensual pleasures' means that formations, arising dependent on craving for sensual pleasures, are its root. 'The approach to disenchantment' means the occurrence or origination of disenchantment. 'Rooted in the accessories of craving for sensual pleasures' means that the material object of desire, being an accessory to craving for sensual pleasures, is its root. Here, disenchantment in the sense of dissatisfaction or weariness is justified as being rooted in the accessories of craving for sensual pleasures, but the disenchantment of knowledge is not justified as being rooted in the accessories of craving for sensual pleasures. Therefore, it is said that 'every approach to disenchantment' is not, however, justified as being rooted in the accessories of craving for sensual pleasures.

“Pañhattayabhāve ceva dukkhūpacāranibbidūpacāre ca yā yutti ācariyena vibhattā, sāva yutti sallakkhetabbā kiṃ, udāhu imāya yuttiyā aññāpi yutti gavesitabbā ki”nti vattabbato nayaṃ dassetuṃ “imāyā”tiādimāha. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – pañhattayabhāve ceva dukkhūpacāranibbidūpacāre ca yā yutti mayā vibhattā, imāya yuttiyā anusārena aññamaññehi kāraṇehi tesu tesu pāḷippadesesu yuttipi gavesitabbāti.

Regarding the state of having three questions, and the approach to suffering and the approach to disenchantment, the reasoning the teacher has analyzed—should only that reasoning be considered, or should other reasoning also be sought by means of this reasoning? Since this is to be said, to show the method, he said 'by this,' and so on. This is what is meant: The reasoning I have analyzed regarding the state of having three questions and the approach to suffering and the approach to disenchantment—by following this reasoning, other reasonings should also be sought in various textual passages, by different reasons.

“Idaṃ nayadassanaṃ saṃkhittaṃ, na sakkā vitthārato gavesitu”nti vattabbato taṃ nayadassanaṃ vitthārato vibhajitvā dassetuṃ “yathā hi bhagavā”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Asubhassa jigucchanīyabhāvato rāguppādo na yutto, tasmā rāgacaritassa puggalassa asubhadesanā rāgavinayāya yuttā. Mettāya dosapaṭipakkhattā dosacaritassa puggalassa mettādesanā dosavinayāya yuttā. Paṭiccasamuppādassa paññāvisayattā mohacaritassa puggalassa paṭiccasamuppādadesanā mohavinayāya yuttā. “Rāgacaritassāpi mettādidesanā yujjeyya sabbasattasādhāraṇattā”ti vattabbattā “yadi [M 0.0126] hi bhagavā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tibbakilesassa rāgacaritassa adhippetattā tādisassa puggalassa mettaṃ cetovimuttiṃ yadi deseyya, evaṃ sati mettāvasenapi rāguppajjanato desanā na yujjati. Sukhaṃ paṭipadaṃ vā yadi deseyya, evaṃ sati rāgacaritassa [V 0.0260] dukkhāpaṭipadāyujjanato desanā na yujjati. Vipassanāpubbaṅgamaṃ pahānaṃ vā yadipi deseyya, evaṃ sati rāgacaritassa asubhānupassanaṃ vajjetvā vipassanāpubbaṅgamassa pahānassa dukkarato desanā na yujjatīti yojanā.

Since it is to be said, 'This presentation of the method is concise; it cannot be investigated in detail,' in order to explain that presentation of the method in detail, the passage beginning with 'Just as the Blessed One' is commenced. Since the foul is repulsive, the arising of lust is not fitting. Therefore, for a person of lustful temperament, the teaching on the foul is appropriate for subduing lust. Because loving-kindness counteracts hatred, for a person of hateful temperament, the teaching on loving-kindness is appropriate for subduing hatred. Since dependent origination is the domain of wisdom, for a person of deluded temperament, the teaching on dependent origination is appropriate for subduing delusion. Since it is to be said, 'Even for a lustful temperament, the teaching on loving-kindness could be suitable because it is common to all beings,' the passage beginning with 'If the Blessed One' is stated. Because a person of lustful temperament with strong defilements is intended, if the Blessed One were to teach such a person the liberation of mind through loving-kindness, then the teaching would not be fitting, since lust would arise even by means of loving-kindness. If he were to teach the pleasant practice, then the teaching would not be fitting, as the painful practice is suitable for the lustful temperament. Even if he were to teach abandonment preceded by insight, then the teaching would not be fitting, as for the lustful temperament, abandonment preceded by insight is difficult without contemplating the foul. This is the application.

“Bhagavā rāgacaritassā”tiādinā niravasesavasena yutti na vibhattā, nayadassanamevāti yo nayo dassito, tena nayena aññāpi gavesitabbāti dassetuṃ “evaṃ yaṃ kiñcī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Rāgassa yaṃ kiñci anulomappahānaṃ, dosassa yaṃ kiñci anulomappahānaṃ, mohassa yaṃ kiñci anulomappahānaṃ desitaṃ, taṃ sabbaṃ anulomappahānaṃ yattakā pāḷippadesā ñāṇassa bhūmi, tattakesu vicayena hārena vicinitvā yuttihārena yojetabbanti yojanā.

By the passage beginning, 'The Blessed One, to one of lustful temperament,' the reasoning is not exhaustively analyzed; it is only a presentation of the method. To show that by the method which was shown, other reasonings should also be sought, the passage beginning, 'Thus, whatever is conducive,' is stated. Whatever is conducive to the abandoning of lust, whatever is conducive to the abandoning of hatred, and whatever is conducive to the abandoning of delusion has been taught. All that conducive abandoning, in as many textual passages as are the ground for knowledge, should be investigated by the method of investigation and connected by the method of reasoning. This is the application.

“Rāgādippahānavasena yutti gavesitabbā”ti vattabbabhāvato aññehipi mettādibrahmavihāraphalasamāpattinavānupubbasamāpattivasībhāvehi vibhajitvā yuttigavesanaṃ dassetuṃ “mettāvihārissā”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha mettāvihārissa mettāvihāralābhino sato saṃvijjamānassa puggalassa mettāya byāpādapaṭipakkhattā byāpādo cittaṃ pariyādāya ṭhassatīti desanā na yujjatīti ca, mettāvihārissa sato byāpādo pahānaṃ abbhatthaṃ gacchatīti desanā yujjati. Karuṇāvihārissa karuṇāvihāralābhino sato saṃvijjamānassa puggalassa karuṇāya vihesāya paṭipakkhattā vihesā cittaṃ pariyādāya ṭhassatīti desanā na yujjati, karuṇāvihārissa sato vihesā pahānaṃ abbhatthaṃ gacchatīti desanā yujjati. Muditāvihārissa muditāvihāralābhino sato saṃvijjamānassa puggalassa muditāya aratiyā paṭipakkhattā arati cittaṃ pariyādāya ṭhassatīti desanā na yujjati, muditāvihārissa sato arati pahānaṃ abbhatthaṃ gacchatīti desanā yujjati. Upekkhāvihārissa upekkhāvihāralābhino sato saṃvijjamānassa puggalassa upekkhāya rāgassa paṭipakkhattā rāgo cittaṃ pariyādāya ṭhassatīti desanā na yujjati, upekkhāvihārissa sato rāgo pahānaṃ abbhatthaṃ gacchatīti desanā yujjati.

Since it is to be said, “Reasoning should be sought by way of abandoning lust and other defilements,” to show the investigation of reasoning by analyzing it through other means such as the divine abidings beginning with loving-kindness, the fruition-attainments, the nine successive attainments, and states of mastery, the passage beginning “for one who abides in loving-kindness” is commenced. Here, for one who abides in loving-kindness, for a person who has gained the abiding of loving-kindness, being present and existing, it is not fitting to teach that ill-will will overwhelm the mind, since loving-kindness counteracts ill-will; rather, it is fitting to teach that for one who abides in loving-kindness, ill-will is abandoned and vanishes. For one who abides in compassion, for a person who has gained the abiding of compassion, being present and existing, it is not fitting to teach that cruelty will overwhelm the mind, since compassion counteracts cruelty; rather, it is fitting to teach that for one who abides in compassion, cruelty is abandoned and vanishes. For one who abides in sympathetic joy, for a person who has gained the abiding of sympathetic joy, being present and existing, it is not fitting to teach that discontent will overwhelm the mind, since sympathetic joy counteracts discontent; rather, it is fitting to teach that for one who abides in sympathetic joy, discontent is abandoned and vanishes. For one who abides in equanimity, for a person who has gained the abiding of equanimity, being present and existing, it is not fitting to teach that lust will overwhelm the mind, since equanimity counteracts lust; rather, it is fitting to teach that for one who abides in equanimity, lust is abandoned and vanishes.

Animittavihārissa [M 0.0127] aniccānupassanāmukhena paṭiladdhaphalasamāpattivihāralābhino sato saṃvijjamānassa puggalassa nimittānusāri tena teneva saṅkhāranimittānusāreneva niccādīsu pahīnena nimittena viññāṇaṃ pavattatīti desanā na yujjati, animittānupassanāya niccādivipallāsapaṭipakkhattā animittavihārissa sato nimittaṃ pahānaṃ abbhatthaṃ gacchatīti desanā [V 0.0261] yujjati. “Asmī”ti maññitaṃ khandhapañcakaṃ attavigataṃ “ayaṃ khandhapañcako ahaṃ asmī”ti na samanupassāmi, atha ca pana asamanupassane satipi “me kiṃ asmī”ti “kathaṃ asmī”ti vicikicchā kathaṃkathāsallaṃ cittaṃ pariyādāya ṭhassatīti desanā na yujjati, vicikicchāya pahānekaṭṭhabhāvato “ayaṃ khandhapañcako ahaṃ asmī”ti asamanupassantassa vicikicchā kathaṃkathāsallaṃ pahānaṃ abbhatthaṃ gacchatīti desanā yujjati.

For one who abides in the signless, who has gained the abiding of fruition-attainment through the door of contemplating impermanence, being present and existing, it is not fitting to teach that consciousness proceeds by following the sign, by following that very sign of formations, by means of the sign abandoned in permanence, etc.; rather, it is fitting to teach that for one who abides in the signless, because the contemplation of the signless is the opposite of the distortions concerning permanence, etc., the sign is abandoned and vanishes. It is not fitting to teach: 'The five aggregates, conceived as “I am,” are devoid of self. I do not regard this fivefold aggregate as “I am.” And yet, even while not so regarding, the doubt, the thorn of uncertainty—“What am I? How am I?”—will stand overwhelming the mind.' Because doubt has the characteristic of being abandoned, it is fitting to teach that for one who does not regard the fivefold aggregate as “I am,” the doubt, the thorn of uncertainty, is abandoned and vanishes.

“Phalasamāpattivaseneva yutti gavesitabbā ki”nti vattabbattā jhānasamāpattivasenapi yutti gavesitabbāti dassetuṃ “yathā vā pana paṭhamaṃ jhāna”ntiādi āraddhaṃ. Atha vā “phalasamāpattivihārisseva yutti gavesitabbā ki”nti vattabbattā jhānasamāpattivasenapi yutti gavesitabbāti dassetuṃ “yathā vā pana paṭhamaṃ jhāna”ntiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha yathā paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ samāpannassa phalasamāpattivihārissa yutti gavesitabbā, evaṃ jhānasamāpattivihārissapi yutti gavesitabbā. Kathaṃ? Paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ samāpannassa paṭhamajjhānasamaṅgino sato saṃvijjamānassa puggalassa nīvaraṇavikkhambhanato kāmarāgabyāpādā visesāya dutiyajjhānāya saṃvattantīti desanā na yujjati, kāmarāgabyāpādā jhānassa hānāya saṃvattantīti desanā yujjati. Vitakkasahagatā saññāmanasikārā upacāradhammena saha dutiyajjhānadhammā jhānassa hānāya saṃvattantīti desanā na yujjati, vitakkasahagatā saññāmanasikārā visesāya uparijhānatthāya saṃvattantīti desanā yujjati.

“Because it should be asked, ‘Should the reasoning be investigated only by way of fruition-attainment?’, to show that the reasoning should also be investigated by way of jhāna-attainment, the passage beginning ‘Just as, however, the first jhāna…’ is introduced. Alternatively, because it should be asked, ‘Should the reasoning be investigated only for one abiding in fruition-attainment?’, to show that the reasoning should also be investigated by way of jhāna-attainment, the passage beginning ‘Just as, however, the first jhāna…’ is introduced. Therein, just as the reasoning should be investigated for one abiding in fruition-attainment who has attained the first jhāna, so too should the reasoning be investigated for one who abides in jhāna-attainment. How? For a person who has attained the first jhāna—one who is endowed with the first jhāna, who is present and existing—the teaching that, due to the suppression of the hindrances, sensual desire and ill-will lead to distinction for the second jhāna is not fitting; rather, the teaching that sensual desire and ill-will lead to the decline of the jhāna is fitting. The teaching that perceptions and mental activities accompanied by initial thought, together with the proximate factors and the factors of the second jhāna, lead to the decline of the jhāna is not fitting; rather, the teaching that perceptions and mental activities accompanied by initial thought lead to distinction for the purpose of a higher jhāna is fitting.

Dutiyaṃ jhānaṃ samāpannassa sato saṃvijjamānassa puggalassa vitakkavicārasahagatā vā saññāmanasikārā upacāradhammena saha paṭhamajjhānadhammā visesāya uparijhānatthāya saṃvattantīti desanā na yujjati, vitakkavicārasahagatā saññāmanasikārā avitakkajhānassa hānāya saṃvattantīti desanā yujjati. Upekkhāsahagatā vā saññāmanasikārā upacāradhammena saha catutthajjhānadhammā jhānassa hānāya saṃvattantīti desanā na yujjati, upekkhāsahagatā [M 0.0128] saññāmanasikārā visesāya uparijhānatthāya saṃvattantīti desanā yujjati. Sesesupi atthānurūpaṃ yojanā kātabbā. Yathāvuttasamāpattīsu vasībhāvena paricitaṃ kallatāparicitaṃ cittaṃ nāma.

For a person who has attained the second jhāna, being present and existing, the teaching that perceptions and mental activities accompanied by initial and sustained thought, together with the proximate factors and the factors of the first jhāna, lead to distinction for the purpose of a higher jhāna is not fitting; rather, the teaching that perceptions and mental activities accompanied by initial and sustained thought lead to the decline of the jhāna without initial thought is fitting. The teaching that perceptions and mental activities accompanied by equanimity, together with the proximate factors and the factors of the fourth jhāna, lead to the decline of the jhāna is not fitting; rather, the teaching that perceptions and mental activities accompanied by equanimity lead to distinction for the purpose of a higher jhāna is fitting. In the remaining cases also, the application should be made in accordance with the meaning. A mind made familiar and ready through mastery in the aforementioned attainments is so-called.

Ettakameva yuttigavesanaṃ na kātabbaṃ, navavidhasuttantesu yathāladdhayuttigavesanampi kātabbanti dassetuṃ “evaṃ sabbe”tiādi vuttaṃ. “Sabbesaṃ hārānaṃ yathāvuttabhūmigocarānaṃ vicayahārena vicinitvā yuttihārena yojetabbabhāvo kena saddahitabbo”ti vattabbattā “tenāhā”tiādi [V 0.0262] vuttaṃ. Tattha tena yojetabbabhāvena āyasmā mahākaccāno “sabbesa”ntiādikaṃ yaṃ vacanaṃ āha, tena vacanena saddahitabboti vuttaṃ hoti.

Only this much investigation of reasoning should not be done; to show that investigation of reasoning should also be done in the ninefold suttantas according to what is obtained, the passage beginning “Thus all…” is stated. Because it should be asked, “By what should it be accepted that all the methods, whose ground and domain are as stated, having been analyzed by the method of analysis, should be connected by the method of reasoning?”, the passage beginning “Therefore, he said…” is stated. Therein, it is said that this need for connection is to be accepted on the authority of that statement beginning with 'all' which the Venerable Mahākaccāna spoke.

Iti yuttihāravibhaṅge sattibalānurūpā racitā

Thus, the exposition of the mode of reasoning has been composed in accordance with my ability.

Vibhāvanā niṭṭhitā.

The exposition is finished.

Paṇḍitehi pana aṭṭhakathāṭīkānusārena gambhīrattho vitthārato vibhajitvā gahetabboti.

However, the profound meaning should be analyzed in detail and grasped by the learned, in accordance with the commentaries and sub-commentaries.

4. Padaṭṭhānahāravibhaṅgavibhāvanā

4. Exposition of the Analysis of the Method of Proximate Cause

22. Yena yena saṃvaṇṇanāvisesabhūtena yuttihāravibhaṅgabhūtena pañhāvissajjanādīnaṃ yuttāyuttabhāvo vibhatto, so saṃvaṇṇanāvisesabhūto yuttihāravibhaṅgo paripuṇṇo, “katamo padaṭṭhānahāravibhaṅgo”ti pucchitabbattā “tattha katamo padaṭṭhāno hāro”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha tatthāti tesu niddiṭṭhesu soḷasasu desanāhārādīsu hāresu katamo saṃvaṇṇanāviseso padaṭṭhāno hāro padaṭṭhānahāravibhaṅgoti pucchati. “Dhammaṃ desesi jino”tiādiniddesassa idāni mayā vuccamāno “ayaṃ padaṭṭhāno hāro”tiādiko vitthārasaṃvaṇṇanāviseso padaṭṭhānahāravibhaṅgoti viññeyyo. Tena vuttaṃ – “tattha katamo padaṭṭhāno hārotiādi padaṭṭhānahāravibhaṅgo”ti (netti. aṭṭha. 22). “Ayaṃ idāni vuccamāno vitthārabhūto padaṭṭhāno hāro piṭakattaye desitesu dhammesu [M 0.0129] kiṃ nāma dhammaṃ desayati saṃvaṇṇetī”ti pucchaṃ ṭhapetvā “idaṃ āsannakāraṇaṃ imassa āsannaphalassa padaṭṭhāna”nti niyametvā vibhajituṃ “ayaṃ padaṭṭhāno”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tassattho – sabbesu viññeyyadhammesu yāthāvato asampaṭivedho lakkhaṇaṃ etissā avijjāyāti sabbadhammayāthāvaasampaṭivedhalakkhaṇā, avijjā, tassā avijjāya asubhe “subha”ntiādivipallāsā padaṭṭhānaṃ āsannakāraṇaṃ. Vipallāse sati avijjā vattati uparūpari jāyati na hāyati, tasmā vipallāsā avijjāya padaṭṭhānaṃ āsannakāraṇaṃ bhavanti. Avijjāya vaṭṭamūlakattā taṃ ādiṃ katvā padaṭṭhānaṃ vibhattanti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

22. That special exposition, the analysis of the method of reasoning, by which the appropriateness and inappropriateness of questions and answers and so forth was analyzed, is now complete. Because one should ask, 'What is the analysis of the method of proximate cause?', the passage beginning 'Among these, what is the method of proximate cause?' and so on is introduced. Therein, 'among these' means: among those sixteen indicated methods, such as the method of exposition, the question is asked: 'What specific exposition is the method of proximate cause, the analysis of the method of proximate cause?' Regarding the indication beginning 'The Conqueror taught the Dhamma,' the detailed specific exposition, such as 'this is the method of proximate cause,' which is now being stated by me, should be understood as the analysis of the method of proximate cause. Hence it is said: 'Among these, what is the method of proximate cause? Thus is the analysis of the method of proximate cause.' Having set aside the question, 'What Dhamma does this detailed method of proximate cause, now being stated, teach and expound among the Dhammas taught in the three Piṭakas?', to define and analyze, 'This proximate cause is the proximate cause of this proximate result,' the passage beginning, 'This is the proximate cause,' and so on is stated. Its meaning is this: Ignorance is characterized by the non-penetration of the reality of all phenomena. For this ignorance, the perversions of perceiving the unattractive as 'attractive' and so forth are the proximate cause. When there are perversions, ignorance persists, arises again and again, and does not diminish. Therefore, perversions become the proximate cause for ignorance. Since ignorance is the root of the cycle of existence, it should be understood that the proximate cause is analyzed beginning with it.

Taṇhāyapi vaṭṭamūlakattā tadanantaraṃ taṇhāya padaṭṭhānaṃ vibhajituṃ “ajjhosānalakkhaṇā”tiādi [V 0.0263] vuttaṃ. Tattha piyarūpaṃ sātarūpanti piyasabhāvaṃ sātasabhāvaṃ cakkhādidhammajātaṃ. Piyanīyasātanīye cakkhādike sati taṇhā vattati uparūpari jāyati, tasmā piyarūpaṃ sātarūpaṃ taṇhāya padaṭṭhānaṃ āsannakāraṇaṃ bhavati.

Because craving is also a root of the cycle of existence, immediately after that, to analyze the proximate cause of craving, the passage beginning 'characterized by clinging' is stated. Here, 'pleasing form' and 'delightful form' refer to the class of phenomena beginning with the eye, which have a pleasing and delightful nature. When there are things that are pleasing and delightful, such as the eye and so forth, craving persists and arises again and again. Therefore, pleasing form and delightful form become the proximate cause for craving.

Adinnādāne sati lobho vattati, tasmā adinnādānaṃ lobhassa padaṭṭhānaṃ bhavati. Adinnādānañhi ekavāraṃ uppannampi anādīnavadassanato lobhassa āsannakāraṇaṃ bhavatveva.

When there is taking what is not given, greed persists; therefore, taking what is not given becomes the proximate cause for greed. For taking what is not given, even having arisen just once, because of not seeing the danger in it, certainly becomes a proximate cause for greed.

Kesādīsu asubhesu pavattāyapi subhasaññāya nīlādivaṇṇadīghādisaṇṭhānahasanādibyañjanaggahaṇalakkhaṇattā cakkhundriyādīnaṃ asaṃvaro subhasaññāya padaṭṭhānaṃ bhavati.

For the perception of beauty, even when it occurs in relation to impure things such as hair, the non-restraint of the eye faculty and so forth becomes the proximate cause, because it is characterized by the grasping of signs such as blue color, long shape, smiling, and so forth.

Dukkhadukkhādīsu pavattāyapi sukhasaññāya sāsavaphassūpagamanalakkhaṇattā rūpādīsu assādo sukhasaññāya padaṭṭhānaṃ.

For the perception of pleasure, even when it occurs in relation to suffering due to pain and so forth, the enjoyment in forms and so forth is the proximate cause, because it is characterized by approaching contact accompanied by taints.

Rūpakkhandhādīsu aniccesu pavattāyapi niccasaññāya saṅkhatalakkhaṇānaṃ dhammānaṃ asamanupassanalakkhaṇattā rūpakkhandhādīsu niccaggahaṇaṃ viññāṇaṃ niccasaññāya padaṭṭhānaṃ.

For the perception of permanence, even when it occurs in relation to the impermanent aggregates beginning with form, the consciousness that grasps permanence in the aggregates beginning with form is the proximate cause, because it is characterized by not properly observing the characteristics of conditioned phenomena.

Aniccadukkhānattasaṅkhātesu khandhādīsu pavattāyapi attasaññāya aniccasaññādukkhasaññānaṃ asamanupassanalakkhaṇattā ahaṃmamādivasena pavatto nāmakāyo attasaññāya padaṭṭhānaṃ.

For the perception of self, even when it occurs in relation to the aggregates and so forth, which are designated as impermanent, suffering, and non-self, the mental body that proceeds by way of 'I' and 'mine' is the proximate cause, because it is characterized by not properly observing the perceptions of impermanence and suffering.

Evaṃ [M 0.0130] avijjādīnaṃ akusalapakkhānaṃ dhammānaṃ padaṭṭhānaṃ dassetvā idāni tappaṭipakkhānaṃ vijjādīnaṃ dhammānaṃ padaṭṭhānaṃ dassetuṃ “sabbadhammasampaṭivedhalakkhaṇā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Sabbesu ñeyyadhammesu pavattāya vijjāya sabbadhammasampaṭivedhalakkhaṇattā sabbaṃ neyyaṃ vijjāya padaṭṭhānaṃ.

Having thus shown the proximate cause for unwholesome states such as ignorance and so forth, now, to show the proximate cause for their opposing states such as true knowledge and so forth, the phrase 'characterized by the complete penetration of all phenomena' and so forth was stated. Because true knowledge, which occurs in relation to all knowable phenomena, has the characteristic of completely penetrating all phenomena, all that is knowable is the proximate cause for true knowledge.

Samathassa cittavikkhepasaṅkhātauddhaccapaṭisaṃharaṇasaṅkhātavikkhambhanalakkhaṇattā paṭibhāganimittabhūtā asubhā samathassa padaṭṭhānaṃ. Asubhāya hi taṇhāpaṭipakkhattā, taṇhāya ca abhāve samatho tiṭṭhatīti.

For serenity, the repulsive object that has become a counterpart sign is the proximate cause, because it is characterized by suppression, which is the withdrawal of restlessness designated as mental distraction. For the repulsive is indeed opposed to craving, and in the absence of craving, serenity is established.

Adinnādānā veramaṇivasena pavattassa alobhassa icchāvacarapaṭisaṃharaṇalakkhaṇattā adinnādānā veramaṇī alobhassa padaṭṭhānaṃ.

For non-greed, which persists by way of abstaining from taking what is not given, abstaining from taking what is not given is the proximate cause, because it is characterized by the withdrawal from the sphere of desire.

Pāṇātipātā [V 0.0264] veramaṇivasena pavattassa adosassa abyāpajjalakkhaṇattā pāṇātipātā veramaṇī adosassa padaṭṭhānaṃ.

For non-hatred, which persists by way of abstaining from killing living beings, abstaining from killing living beings is the proximate cause, because it is characterized by non-affliction.

Sammāpaṭipattivasena pavattassa amohassa vatthuavippaṭipattilakkhaṇattā sammāpaṭipatti amohassa padaṭṭhānaṃ.

For non-delusion, which persists by way of right practice, right practice is the proximate cause, because it is characterized by non-deviation from the object.

Nibbidāvasena pavattāya asubhasaññāya vinīlakavipubbakagahaṇalakkhaṇattā nibbidā asubhasaññāya padaṭṭhānaṃ. Nibbidāñāṇena hi anabhirati pavattati, anabhiratiyā ca asubhasaññā ṭhitāti.

For the perception of the repulsive, which persists by way of disenchantment, disenchantment is the proximate cause, because it is characterized by grasping the livid and festering corpse. For indeed, through the knowledge of disenchantment, dispassion persists, and through dispassion, the perception of the repulsive is established.

Dukkhavedanāvasena pavattāya dukkhasaññāya sāsavaphassaparijānanalakkhaṇattā vedanā dukkhasaññāya padaṭṭhānaṃ.

For the perception of suffering, which persists by way of painful feeling, feeling is the proximate cause, because it is characterized by fully understanding tainted contact.

Uppādavayavasena pavattāya aniccasaññāya saṅkhatalakkhaṇānaṃ dhammānaṃ samanupassanalakkhaṇattā uppādavayā aniccasaññāya padaṭṭhānaṃ. Uppādavayañhi samanupassitvā aniccasaññā pavattā.

For the perception of impermanence, which persists by way of arising and passing away, arising and passing away are the proximate cause, because it is characterized by properly observing the characteristics of conditioned phenomena. For indeed, having properly observed arising and passing away, the perception of impermanence persists.

Dhammamattasaññāvasena pavattāya anattasaññāya sabbadhammaabhinivesalakkhaṇattā dhammasaññā anattasaññāya padaṭṭhānaṃ.

For the perception of non-self, which persists by way of the perception of mere phenomena, the perception of phenomena is the proximate cause, because it is characterized by non-adherence to all phenomena.

Kāmarāgassa rūpādipañcakāmaguṇārammaṇattā pañca kāmaguṇā kāmarāgassa padaṭṭhānaṃ.

The five strands of sensual pleasure are the proximate cause for sensual desire, because sensual desire has the five strands of sensual pleasure beginning with forms as its object.

Rūpasaṅkhāte kāye ārabbha pavattassa rūparāgassa cakkhādipañcindriyānaṃ anusārena pavattanato pañcindriyāni rūpāni rūparāgassa padaṭṭhānaṃ.

For desire for form, which persists in dependence on the body designated as form, the five physical sense faculties are the proximate cause, because it persists in accordance with the five faculties beginning with the eye.

Bhavanikantivasena pavattassa bhavarāgassa chaḷāyatanaṃ padaṭṭhānaṃ. Nibbattabhavānupassitāti “edisaṃ aniṭṭhaṃ rūpaṃ mā nibbattatu, edisaṃ iṭṭhaṃ rūpaṃ nibbattatu edisī [M 0.0131] dukkhā vedanā mā nibbattatu, edisī sukhā vedanā nibbattatū”ti evamādinā pakārena pavattā rūpābhinandanā, sā pañcannaṃ upādānakkhandhānaṃ padaṭṭhānaṃ.

For craving for existence, which persists by way of delight in existence, the six sense bases are the proximate cause. Having observed future existence, the delight in form that persists in such ways as 'May such undesirable form not arise, may such desirable form arise, may such painful feeling not arise, may such pleasant feeling arise,' is the proximate cause for the five aggregates subject to clinging.

Kammassakataññāṇassa [V 0.0265] pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇānugatattā pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇadassanaṃ kammassakataññāṇassa padaṭṭhānaṃ.

The vision of the knowledge of recollection of past lives is the proximate cause for the knowledge of ownership of kamma, because the knowledge of ownership of kamma is accompanied by the knowledge of recollection of past lives.

Okappanaṃ lakkhaṇaṃ yassā saddhāyāti okappanalakkhaṇā saddhā. Adhimutti paccupaṭṭhānaṃ yassā saddhāyāti adhimuttipaccupaṭṭhānā ca saddhā. Anāvilaṃ lakkhaṇaṃ yassa pasādassāti anāvilalakkhaṇoti pasādo. Sampasīdanaṃ paccupaṭṭhānaṃ yassa pasādassāti sampasīdanapaccupaṭṭhāno ca pasādo. So pana pasādo saddhāya eva avatthāvisesoti veditabbo. Aveccapasādo abhipatthiyanalakkhaṇāya saddhāya padaṭṭhānaṃ, okappanalakkhaṇā saddhā anāvilalakkhaṇassa pasādassa padaṭṭhānaṃ, catubbidhaṃ sammappadhānaṃ vīriyaṃ ārambhalakkhaṇassa vīriyassa padaṭṭhānaṃ, kāyādisatipaṭṭhānaṃ apilāpanalakkhaṇāya satiyā padaṭṭhānaṃ, jhānasahitassa samādhissa ekaggalakkhaṇattā vitakkādijhānāni samādhissa padaṭṭhānaṃ, paññāya kiccapajānanaārammaṇapajānanalakkhaṇattā saccāni paññāya padaṭṭhānaṃ.

That faith of which settling down is the characteristic is faith characterized by settling down. That faith of which resolution is the manifestation is faith having resolution as its manifestation. That clarity of which being unclouded is the characteristic is clarity characterized by being unclouded. That clarity of which causing serenity is the manifestation is clarity having causing serenity as its manifestation. That clarity, moreover, should be understood as merely a particular state of faith. Unwavering clarity is the proximate cause for faith characterized by the mark of aspiration. Faith characterized by settling down is the proximate cause for clarity characterized by being unclouded. The fourfold right effort is the proximate cause for energy characterized by initiating. The foundations of mindfulness beginning with the body are the proximate cause for mindfulness characterized by non-wavering. The jhāna factors beginning with initial application are the proximate cause for concentration, because concentration, when accompanied by jhāna, has the characteristic of one-pointedness. The truths are the proximate cause for wisdom, because wisdom is characterized by knowing the task and knowing the object.

“Yesaṃ avijjādīnaṃ padaṭṭhānāni ācariyena vibhattāni, te avijjādayo katamesaṃ dhammānaṃ padaṭṭhānānī”ti pucchitabbattā te avijjādayopi imesaṃ dhammānaṃ padaṭṭhānāti dassetuṃ “aparo nayo”tiādi vuttaṃ. Avijjā assādamanasikāralakkhaṇassa ayonisomanasikārassa padaṭṭhānaṃ. Avijjāya hi ādīnavacchādanato ayonisomanasikāro jātoti. Saccasammohanalakkhaṇā avijjā puññāpuññāneñjābhisaṅkhārānaṃ padaṭṭhānaṃ, punabbhavavirohanalakkhaṇā tebhūmakacetanā saṅkhārā vipākaviññāṇassa padaṭṭhānaṃ, opapaccayikasaṅkhātena upapattibhavabhāvena nibbattilakkhaṇaṃ paṭisandhiviññāṇaṃ nāmarūpassa padaṭṭhānaṃ, nāmakāyarūpakāyasaṅghātalakkhaṇaṃ nāmarūpaṃ chaḷāyatanassa padaṭṭhānaṃ sahajātādipaccayabhāvato, cakkhādīnaṃ channaṃ indriyānaṃ pavattānaṃ lakkhaṇaṃ chaḷāyatanaṃ chabbidhassa phassassa yathākkamaṃ padaṭṭhānaṃ nissayādipaccayabhāvato, cakkhupasādarūpārammaṇaṃ cakkhuviññāṇādisannipātalakkhaṇo chabbidho phasso, taṃ vedanāya tena chabbidhena phassena sahajātāya chabbidhāya vedanāya yathākkamaṃ padaṭṭhānaṃ sahajātādipaccayabhāvato, iṭṭhānubhavanaaniṭṭhānubhavanaiṭṭhāniṭṭhānubhavanalakkhaṇā tividhā vedanā, taṃ taṇhāya tāya tividhāya vedanāya vasena pavattāya [M 0.0132] taṇhāya padaṭṭhānaṃ upanissayādipaccayabhāvato, saparasantānesu ajjhosānalakkhaṇā taṇhā, taṃ upādānassa tāya taṇhāya vasena pavattassa catubbidhassa upādānassa padaṭṭhānaṃ upanissayādipaccayabhāvato. “So vedanāyā”ti ca “sā taṇhāyā”ti ca “sā upādānassā”ti ca pāṭhena bhavitabbaṃ, liṅgavipallāsaniddeso vā siyā.

“Since the proximate causes of ignorance and so on have been analyzed by the teacher, the question should be asked: ‘For which phenomena are ignorance and so on the proximate causes?’” To show that ignorance and so on are indeed the proximate causes for these phenomena, the phrase “another method” and so on is stated. Ignorance is the proximate cause for unwise attention, which has the characteristic of attending to enjoyment. For unwise attention arises from ignorance, because it conceals danger. Ignorance, characterized by delusion about the truths, is the proximate cause for the meritorious, demeritorious, and imperturbable volitional formations. The volitional formations, which are volitions pertaining to the three realms and are characterized by producing rebirth, are the proximate cause for resultant consciousness. Rebirth-linking consciousness, characterized by arising as the state of rebirth-becoming designated as apparitional, is the proximate cause for name-and-form. Name-and-form, characterized by the aggregation of the mental and physical bodies, is the proximate cause for the six sense bases, due to being a co-nascent condition and so on. The six sense bases, characterized by the functioning of the six faculties such as the eye, are the proximate cause for the six kinds of contact in due order, due to being a dependence condition and so on. The sixfold contact, characterized by the convergence of eye-sensitivity, a visual object, eye-consciousness, and so on, is the proximate cause for the sixfold feeling that arises simultaneously with it in due order, due to being a co-nascent condition and so on. The threefold feeling, characterized by experiencing the pleasant, the unpleasant, and the neither-pleasant-nor-unpleasant, is the proximate cause for craving, which arises dependent on that threefold feeling, due to being a decisive support condition and so on. Craving, characterized by attachment in one’s own and others’ continuities, is the proximate cause for the fourfold clinging, which arises dependent on that craving, due to being a decisive support condition and so on. The text should read: “So [phasso] vedanāya” (“That [contact] is for feeling”), “Sā [vedanā] taṇhāya” (“That [feeling] is for craving”), and “Sā [taṇhā] upādānassā…” (“That [craving] is for clinging...”). Alternatively, it could be an indication of gender disagreement.

Yaṃ [V 0.0266] upādānaṃ opapaccayikaṃ upapattikkhandhanibbattakaṃ, taṃ upādānaṃ duvidhassa bhavassa padaṭṭhānaṃ. Yo kammabhavo nāmakāyarūpakāyasambhavanalakkhaṇo, so kammabhavo jātiyā padaṭṭhānaṃ. Yā upapattibhūtā jāti khandhapātubhāvalakkhaṇā, taṃ sā jāti jarāya padaṭṭhānaṃ. Yā jiṇṇajarā upadhikkhandhaparipākalakkhaṇā, taṃ sā jiṇṇajarā maraṇassa padaṭṭhānaṃ. Yampi yassa sammutimaraṇaṃ jīvitindriyupacchedalakkhaṇaṃ, tampi tassa sammutimaraṇaṃ sokassa padaṭṭhānaṃ. Piyassa maraṇaṃ cintentassa yebhuyyena sokuppajjanato yo soko ñātiādipiyesu ussukkakārako, taṃ so soko paridevassa padaṭṭhānaṃ. Yo paridevo lālappakārako, taṃ so paridevo kāyikadukkhassa padaṭṭhānaṃ. Yaṃ kāyikaṃ dukkhaṃ kāyasampīḷanalakkhaṇaṃ, taṃ kāyikaṃ dukkhaṃ domanassassa padaṭṭhānaṃ. Yaṃ domanassaṃ cittasampīḷanalakkhaṇaṃ, taṃ domanassaṃ upāyāsassa padaṭṭhānaṃ. Yo upāyāso odahanakārako avadahanakārako, taṃ so upāyāso bhavassa upāyāsassa nissayasantānabhavassa padaṭṭhānaṃ.

That clinging which is related to rebirth and productive of the aggregates of rebirth—that clinging is the proximate cause for the two kinds of becoming. The kamma-becoming, characterized by the production of the mental and physical bodies—that kamma-becoming is the proximate cause for birth. That birth which is rebirth, characterized by the manifestation of the aggregates—that birth is the proximate cause for aging. That aging which is decay, characterized by the ripening of the aggregates of substratum—that aging is the proximate cause for death. And whatever conventional death there is, characterized by the cutting off of the life faculty—that conventional death is the proximate cause for sorrow. Since sorrow mostly arises in one who contemplates the death of a dear one, that sorrow, which is the cause of agitation regarding beloved relatives and others—that sorrow is the proximate cause for lamentation. That lamentation, which is characterized by wailing—that lamentation is the proximate cause for bodily suffering. That bodily suffering, characterized by the oppression of the body—that bodily suffering is the proximate cause for mental distress. That mental distress, characterized by the oppression of the mind—that mental distress is the proximate cause for despair. That despair, which causes burning and tormenting—that despair is the proximate cause for the becoming of the continuity of existence that is the support for despair.

Bhavassāti vuttabhavaṃ dassetuṃ “imānī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha bhavaṅgāni kileso bhavassa aṅgaṃ kāraṇaṃ kammavaṭṭavipākavaṭṭāni bhavasaṅkhātāni aṅgāni avayavāni. Yadā paccuppannādikāle samaggāni nibbattāni bhavanti, tadā so kilesavaṭṭakammavaṭṭavipākavaṭṭasaṅkhāto dhammasamūho “bhavassā”ti ettha bhavoti daṭṭhabbo. Taṃ bhavasaṅkhātaṃ kilesavaṭṭakammavaṭṭavipākavaṭṭattayaṃ saṃsārassa padaṭṭhānaṃ purimaṃ purimaṃ jātinipphannakilesādivaṭṭena saṃsārassa abbocchinnuppajjanato, yo ariyamaggo niyyānikalakkhaṇo, taṃ so ariyamaggo nirodhassa nibbānassa padaṭṭhānaṃ sampāpakahetubhāvato.

To show the meaning of ‘becoming’ as stated, the phrase ‘these’ and so on was uttered. Herein, defilement is a factor and cause of becoming, and the round of kamma and the round of result are factors or parts reckoned as becoming. When these factors arise harmoniously at the time of the present, etc., then that aggregate of phenomena, consisting of the round of defilements, the round of kamma, and the round of result, is to be seen here as “becoming.” That triad considered becoming—the round of defilements, the round of kamma, and the round of result—is the basis of saṃsāra, because saṃsāra arises uninterruptedly through each previous round of defilements, etc., produced from birth; the noble path, characterized as leading out, is the basis for cessation, Nibbāna, since it is the cause of attainment.

Bahussuto sabbasissādīnaṃ patiṭṭhānattā titthaṃ viyāti titthaṃ, jānātīti ñū, titthaṃ ñūti titthaññū, titthaññuno bhāvo titthaññutā, sammāpayirupāsanā, sā pītaññutāya padaṭṭhānaṃ. Bahussutassa hi sammāpayirupāsanāya [M 0.0133] dhammūpasañhitaṃ pāmojjaṃ jāyati, pāmojjena ca kammaṭṭhānabrūhanā jāyatīti sappāyadhammassavanena pītiṃ jānātīti pītaññū, pītaññuno bhāvo pītaññutā, kammaṭṭhānassa brūhanā, sā pattaññutāya padaṭṭhānaṃ. Kammaṭṭhānabrūhanāya hi bhāvanāpattajānanatā jāyatīti pattaññutā. Bhāvanāpattajānanatā attaññutāya padaṭṭhānaṃ. Bhāvanāpattajānanatāya hi pañcahi padhāniyaṅgehi samannāgatassa attano jānanatā jāyatīti attaññutā pubbekatapuññatāya padaṭṭhānaṃ.

A learned person is called ‘tittha’ because he is a foundation for all disciples and others, like a ford. He knows, thus he is ‘ñū.’ ‘Titthaññū’ means one who knows the ford. The state of being a ‘titthaññū’ is ‘titthaññutā,’ which is proper attendance. That is the basis for ‘pītaññutā’ (knowledge of joy). For one who is learned, proper attendance gives rise to joy connected with the Dhamma. Through joy, the development of the meditation subject arises. Thus, by hearing the beneficial Dhamma, one knows joy—hence, ‘pītaññū.’ The state of being a ‘pītaññū’ is ‘pītaññutā,’ which is the development of the meditation subject. That is the basis for ‘pattaññutā’ (knowledge of attainment). Through the development of the meditation subject, the knowledge of attainment in development arises—hence, ‘pattaññutā.’ Knowledge of attainment in development is the basis for ‘attaññutā’ (self-knowledge). Through knowledge of attainment in development, the knowledge of oneself as endowed with the five striving factors arises—hence, ‘attaññutā’ is the basis for past merit.

Padhāniyaṅgesu samannāgatattajānanatāya hi pubbe puññakaraṇaṃ jātaṃ, pubbekatapuññatā patirūpadesavāsassa padaṭṭhānaṃ. Pubbe hi katena puññena patirūpadesavāso laddho, patirūpadesavāso sappurisūpanissayassa [V 0.0267] padaṭṭhānaṃ. Patirūpadesavāsena hi sappurisūpanissayo laddho, sappurisūpanissayo attasammāpaṇidhānassa padaṭṭhānaṃ. Sappurisūpanissayena hi attasammāpaṇidhānaṃ jātaṃ, attasammāpaṇidhānaṃ sīlānaṃ padaṭṭhānaṃ. Attasammāpaṇidhānena hi sīlāni sampatiṭṭhitāni, sīlāni avippaṭisārassa padaṭṭhānaṃ. Attani hi sampatiṭṭhitaṃ sīlaṃ paccavekkhantassa vippaṭisāro natthevāti, avippaṭisārena pāmojjaṃ jāyati, tasmā avippaṭisāro pāmojjassa padaṭṭhānaṃ. Pāmojjena pīti jāyati, tasmā pāmojjaṃ pītiyā padaṭṭhānaṃ. Pītiyā passaddhi jāyati, tasmā pīti passaddhiyā padaṭṭhānaṃ. Passaddhiyā sukhaṃ jāyati, tasmā passaddhi sukhassa padaṭṭhānaṃ. Sukhena samādhi jāyati, tasmā sukhaṃ samādhissa padaṭṭhānaṃ. Samādhinā yathābhūtañāṇadassanaṃ jāyati, tasmā samādhi yathābhūtañāṇassa padaṭṭhānaṃ. Yathābhūtañāṇadassanena nibbidāñāṇaṃ jāyati, tasmā yathābhūtañāṇadassanaṃ nibbidāya padaṭṭhānaṃ. Nibbidāya virāgo jāyati, tasmā nibbidā virāgassa padaṭṭhānaṃ. Virāgena vimutti jāyati, tasmā virāgo vimuttiyā padaṭṭhānaṃ. Vimuttiyā vimuttiñāṇadassanaṃ jāyati, tasmā vimutti vimuttiñāṇadassanassa padaṭṭhānaṃ. Evaṃ yathāvuttanayena yo koci dhammo upanissayo hoti, yo koci dhammo paccayo hoti, sabbo so dhammo attano paccayuppannassa dhammassa padaṭṭhānanti daṭṭhabbo.

For by the knowledge of being endowed with the factors of striving, the making of merit in the past has occurred. The making of merit in the past is the basis for dwelling in a suitable place. For through merit made in the past, dwelling in a suitable place is obtained. Dwelling in a suitable place is the basis for reliance on good people. Through dwelling in a suitable place, reliance on good people is obtained. Reliance on good people is the basis for proper self-direction. Through reliance on good people, proper self-direction arises. Proper self-direction is the basis for virtue. Through proper self-direction, virtue is well-established. Virtue is the basis for freedom from remorse. For one reflecting on virtue well-established within oneself, there is no remorse. From freedom from remorse, joy arises; therefore, freedom from remorse is the basis for joy. From joy, rapture arises; therefore, joy is the basis for rapture. From rapture, tranquility arises; therefore, rapture is the basis for tranquility. From tranquility, happiness arises; therefore, tranquility is the basis for happiness. From happiness, concentration arises; therefore, happiness is the basis for concentration. From concentration, knowledge and vision of things as they are arises; therefore, concentration is the basis for knowledge of things as they are. From knowledge and vision of things as they are, knowledge of disenchantment arises; therefore, knowledge and vision of things as they are is the basis for disenchantment. From disenchantment, dispassion arises; therefore, disenchantment is the basis for dispassion. From dispassion, liberation arises; therefore, dispassion is the basis for liberation. From liberation, knowledge and vision of liberation arise; therefore, liberation is the basis for knowledge and vision of liberation. Thus, in the aforesaid manner, whatever phenomenon is a supporting condition, whatever phenomenon is a condition—all such phenomena should be seen as the basis for the phenomena that arise dependent on them.

“Upanissayadhammassa, paccayadhammassa vā paccayuppannadhammassa padaṭṭhānabhāvo kena saddahitabbo”ti vattabbattā “tenāhā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha tenāti yassa kassaci upanissayadhammassa, paccayadhammassa ca paccayuppannadhammassa padaṭṭhānabhāvena [M 0.0134] āyasmā mahākaccāno “dhammaṃ deseti jino”tiādikaṃ yaṃ vacanaṃ āha, tena vacanena tesaṃ upanissayadhammapaccayadhammānaṃ padaṭṭhānabhāvo saddahitabboti. “Yathāvutto padaṭṭhāno hāro paripuṇṇo kiṃ, udāhu añño niddhāretvā yojetabbo atthi ki”nti vattabbattā “niyutto padaṭṭhāno hāro”ti vuttaṃ. Idha pāḷiyaṃ avibhattampi yathālābhavasena padaṭṭhāno hāro nīharitvā yutto yujjitabbo, vibhajitabbanti vuttaṃ hoti.

Since it should be asked, ‘By what should the state of being a basis for a decisive support condition phenomenon, a condition phenomenon, or a conditionally arisen phenomenon be believed?’, the phrase ‘Therefore he said,’ and so on, was uttered. Here, ‘by that’ means: by whatever statement the Venerable Mahākaccāna spoke, such as ‘the Victor teaches the Dhamma,’ regarding the state of being a basis for any decisive support condition phenomenon, condition phenomenon, and conditionally arisen phenomenon—by that statement, their state of being a basis should be believed. Since it should be asked, ‘Is the method of bases as stated complete, or is there another to be determined and applied?’, the phrase ‘the method of bases is applied’ was uttered. Here, even if not distinguished in the Pāli text, the method of bases should be extracted according to what is available and applied; it is said that it should be analyzed.

Iti padaṭṭhānahāravibhaṅge sattibalānurūpā racitā

Thus, in the analysis of the method of bases, this was composed in accordance with one’s power and strength.

Vibhāvanā niṭṭhitā.

The elucidation is finished.

Paṇḍitehi pana aṭṭhakathāṭīkānusārena gambhīrattho vitthārato vibhajitvā gahetabboti.

However, the profound meaning should be analyzed in detail and grasped by the learned, in accordance with the commentaries and sub-commentaries.

5. Lakkhaṇahāravibhaṅgavibhāvanā

5. The Elucidation of the Analysis of the Method of Characteristics

23. Yena [V 0.0268] yena saṃvaṇṇanāvisesabhūtena padaṭṭhānavibhaṅgena avijjādīnaṃ padaṭṭhānāni vibhattāni, so saṃvaṇṇanāvisesabhūto padaṭṭhānahāravibhaṅgo paripuṇṇo, “katamo lakkhaṇahāravibhaṅgo”ti pucchitabbattā “tattha katamo lakkhaṇo hāro”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha tattha-saddassa attho vuttova. Katamo saṃvaṇṇanāviseso lakkhaṇo hāro lakkhaṇahāravibhaṅgoti pucchati. “Vuttamhi ekadhamme”tiādiniddesassa idāni mayā vuccamāno “ye dhammā”tiādiko vitthārasaṃvaṇṇanāviseso lakkhaṇo hāro lakkhaṇahāravibhaṅgo nāmāti viññeyyoti. Tena vuttaṃ –“tattha katamo lakkhaṇo hārotiādi lakkhaṇahāravibhaṅgo nāmā”ti (netti. aṭṭha. 23). Ayaṃ idāni vuccamāno vitthārabhūto lakkhaṇo hāro piṭakattaye desitesu dhammesu kiṃ nāma lakkhitabbaṃ dhammaṃ lakkhīyatīti pucchitvā pucchite lakkhaṇahāravicaye dhamme saṅkhepena dassetuṃ “ye dhammā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha ye dhammāti ye samūhā dhammā. Ekalakkhaṇāti samānalakkhaṇā. Tesaṃ dhammānanti samānalakkhaṇānaṃ tesaṃ samūhadhammānaṃ, niddhāraṇe cetaṃ. Ekasmiṃ dhammeti samānalakkhaṇe [M 0.0135] ekasmiṃ dhamme, pāḷiyaṃ bhagavatā vutte sati vuttadhammato avasiṭṭhasamānalakkhaṇā dhammā samānalakkhaṇena vuttā bhavantīti attho.

23. By whatever specific descriptive analysis of proximate causes the proximate causes of ignorance, etc., have been distinguished, that specific descriptive analysis of the method of proximate causes is complete. Because it should be asked, ‘What is the analysis of the method of characteristics?’, the phrase ‘Herein, what is the method of characteristics?’ and so on was uttered. Herein, the meaning of the word ‘herein’ has already been stated. It asks, ‘What specific description is the method of characteristics, the analysis of the method of characteristics?’ It should be understood that for the exposition beginning with ‘When one phenomenon has been stated,’ the detailed specific descriptive method of characteristics, the analysis of the method of characteristics, beginning with ‘those phenomena,’ which is now being explained by me, is its name. Therefore, it is said: ‘Herein, what is the method of characteristics?’ and so on, is called the analysis of the method of characteristics (Netti. Aṭṭha. 23). This detailed method of characteristics now being explained—having asked, concerning the phenomena taught in the three Piṭakas, ‘What phenomenon to be characterized does it characterize?’—to show concisely the phenomenon in the investigation of the method of characteristics that was asked about, the phrase ‘those phenomena’ and so on was uttered. Herein, ‘those phenomena’ means those groups of phenomena. ‘Having one characteristic’ means having a common characteristic. ‘Of those phenomena’ means of those groups of phenomena having a common characteristic; and this is in the sense of specification. ‘In one phenomenon’ means in one phenomenon having a common characteristic. When something has been said by the Blessed One in the Pāli, the meaning is that the remaining phenomena with a common characteristic are said by means of that common characteristic of the stated phenomenon.

Lakkhaṇahāravisaye dhamme vitthārato imasmiṃ dhamme vutte ime samānalakkhaṇā dhammāpi vuttā bhavantīti niyametvā dassetuṃ “yathā kiṃ bhave”tiādimāha. Tassattho – yathā yena pakārena vuttā bhavanti, so pakāro kiṃ bhaveti pucchati. Yathā yena pakārena vuttā bhavanti, so pakāro samānalakkhaṇāti bhāvo bhaveti attho. Kinti bhagavā āha? “Cakkhuṃ bhikkhave”tiādiṃ bhagavā āha. “Cakkhuṃ, bhikkhave, anavaṭṭhita”ntiādimhi vutte “sotaṃ, bhikkhave, anavaṭṭhita”ntiādivacanampi vuttameva bhavati.

In the sphere of the mode of characteristics, to determine and show that when this dhamma is stated in detail, these dhammas having the same characteristic are also stated, he says, 'How would this be?' and so on. The meaning of that is: He asks, 'In what way are they stated? What would that way be?' The meaning is: The way in which they are stated is the state of having the same characteristic. What did the Blessed One say? The Blessed One said, 'The eye, monks,' and so on. When it is said, 'The eye, monks, is unstable,' and so on, the statement, 'The ear, monks, is unstable,' and so on, is also stated.

“Anavaṭṭhitādilakkhaṇena samānalakkhaṇattā vā ajjhattikāyatanabhāvena samānalakkhaṇattā vāti āyatanavaseneva ekalakkhaṇaṃ vattabba”nti vattabbattā khandhavasenapi ekalakkhaṇaṃ dassetuṃ “yathā cāhā”tiādi vuttaṃ. “Atīte, rādha, rūpe anapekkho hoti, anāgataṃ rūpaṃ mā abhinandi[V 0.0269], paccuppannassa rūpassa nibbidāya virāgāya nirodhāya cāgāya paṭinissaggāya paṭipajjā”ti vutte “atītāya, rādha, vedanāya anapekkho hoti, anāgataṃ vedanaṃ mā abhinandi, paccuppannāya vedanāya nibbidāya virāgāya nirodhāya cāgāya paṭinissaggāya paṭipajjā”tiādi vuttaṃ bhave.

Because it is to be stated that 'either due to having the same characteristic of being unstable, etc., or due to having the same characteristic of being an internal sense base, the single characteristic should be stated only by way of the sense bases,' in order to show the single characteristic also by way of the aggregates, 'and as he said,' and so on, is stated. When it is said, 'Radha, be unconcerned with past form, do not delight in future form, and practice for the disenchantment, dispassion, cessation, relinquishment, and letting go of present form,' then it would be said regarding feeling, 'Radha, be unconcerned with past feeling, do not delight in future feeling, and practice for the disenchantment, dispassion, cessation, relinquishment, and letting go of present feeling,' and so on.

“Anapekkhanīyalakkhaṇena samānalakkhaṇattā vā khandhalakkhaṇena samānalakkhaṇattā vāti khandhāyatanavaseneva ekalakkhaṇadhammā vattabbā”ti vattabbattā satipaṭṭhānavasenāpi vattabbāti dassetuṃ “yathāhā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha yathā yena ekalakkhaṇattena ca bhagavā āha, tathā ca tena ekalakkhaṇattena ca avuttāpi dhammā vuttā bhavantīti attho. Ye vipassakā puggalā pañcasu khandhesu niccaṃ susamāraddhā niccaṃ kāyagatāsatiṃ bhāventi, te vipassakā akiccaṃ subhasukhādikaṃ, kasivāṇijjādikammaṃ vā na sevanti, kicce asubhāsukhādike, kāyādike vā sātaccakārino hontīti bhagavā āhāti yojanā.

Because it is to be stated that 'either due to having the same characteristic of being unworthy of regard, or due to having the same characteristic of being an aggregate, these dhammas with a single characteristic should be stated only by way of the aggregates and sense bases,' in order to show that they should also be stated by way of the establishments of mindfulness, 'as he said,' and so on, is stated. Here, the meaning is: just as the Blessed One spoke by means of a single characteristic, so too, by means of that same single characteristic, even unstated dhammas are stated. Those insight meditators who are constantly well-established in the five aggregates and constantly develop mindfulness immersed in the body—those insight meditators do not cultivate what is not to be done, such as the attractive, pleasant, and so on, or activities like farming and trade. Instead, they are persevering in what is to be done, such as the unattractive, suffering, or mindfulness of the body, etc. This is how the Blessed One spoke; this is the connection.

Itisaddassa cettha ekassa lopo. Iti evaṃ “yesañcā”tiādigāthāya kesādike kāye gatāya pavattāya satiyā bhagavatā sarūpena [M 0.0136] vuttāya vijjamānāya tadavasesā vedanāgatā sati ca cittagatā sati ca dhammagatā sati ca satipaṭṭhānabhāvena ekalakkhaṇattena vuttā bhavantīti saṅkhepato niccaṃ susamāraddhā niccaṃ vedanāgatā sati ca…pe… niccaṃ cittagatā sati ca…pe… niccaṃ dhammagatā satīti vattabbāti.

Here, there is an elision of one 'iti' word. Thus, in this way, in the verse beginning with 'yesañcā,' when mindfulness, existing as taught by the Blessed One in its own form, is directed toward the body, such as hair, etc., the remaining mindfulness directed toward feelings, mindfulness directed toward the mind, and mindfulness directed toward phenomena are spoken of as having a single characteristic due to their nature as the establishments of mindfulness. Briefly, it should be said: 'Mindfulness directed toward feelings is constantly well-established... etc.... Mindfulness directed toward the mind is constantly well-established... etc.... Mindfulness directed toward phenomena is constantly well-established.'

“Satipaṭṭhānavaseneva ekalakkhaṇā dhammā vattabbā”ti vattabbattā “tathā yaṃ kiñcī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha yaṃ kiñci rūpāyatanaṃ cakkhuviññāṇena diṭṭhaṃ, yaṃ kiñci saddāyatanaṃ sotaviññāṇena sutaṃ, yaṃ kiñci gandharasaphoṭṭhabbāyatanaṃ ghānaviññāṇādittayena viññāṇena mutaṃ, iti evaṃ diṭṭhādittaye bhagavatā sarūpena vutte sati tadavasesaṃ yaṃ kiñci viññātaṃ dhammārammaṇapariyāpannaṃ rūpaṃ bhagavatā ālambitabbabhāvena ekalakkhaṇattā vuttaṃ bhavatīti attho. Atha vā yaṃ kiñci rūpāyatanaṃ diṭṭhaṃ bhagavatā vuttaṃ, tasmiṃ vutte sati tadavasesaṃ sutādikampi vuttaṃ hotīti ādiattho visuṃ visuṃ yojetabbo. Tena vuttaṃ – “diṭṭhaṃ vā sutaṃ vā mutaṃ vā”ti.

Because it is to be stated that 'phenomena with a single characteristic should be stated only by way of the establishments of mindfulness,' 'similarly, whatever,' and so on, is stated. Herein, whatever form base is seen by eye-consciousness, whatever sound base is heard by ear-consciousness, whatever odor, taste, and tangible bases are sensed by the three consciousnesses beginning with nose-consciousness—thus, when the Blessed One has spoken in this way regarding the triad beginning with the seen, in its own form, the meaning is that the remainder, whatever is cognized as form included in the mental object, is spoken of by the Blessed One as having a single characteristic due to its nature as an object to be taken up. Alternatively, when whatever form base is seen is spoken of by the Blessed One, the meaning of 'and so on'—that the remaining heard, etc., are also stated—should be applied separately to each case. Therefore, it is said: 'seen or heard or sensed.'

“Kāyagatāya satiyā vuttāya tadavasesā vedanāgatāsatiādayoyeva vattabbā”ti pucchitabbattā sattatiṃsabodhipakkhiyadhammāpi vuttā bhavantīti dassetuṃ “yathā cāha bhagavā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha yathā yena niyyānikalakkhaṇena ekalakkhaṇattena ca bhagavā āha, tathā tena ekalakkhaṇattena ca bhagavā āha, tathā tena ekalakkhaṇattena ca vuttā bhavantīti [V 0.0270] attho. “Tasmā abhijjhādomanassena abhibhūtattā iha mama sāsane, bhikkhu, tvaṃ ātāpī sampajāno satimā hutvā loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ tadaṅgappahānena vā vikkhambhanappahānena vā vineyya vinayitvā kāye kesādirūpakāye kāyānupassī kesādirūpakāyānupassī hutvā viharāhī”ti bhagavatā vutte sati “tasmātiha, tvaṃ bhikkhu, vedanāsu vedanānupassī viharāhi ātāpī sampajāno satimā vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ, tasmātiha, tvaṃ bhikkhu, citte cittānupassī viharāhi…pe… domanassaṃ, tasmātiha, tvaṃ bhikkhu, dhammesu dhammānupassī viharāhi…pe… domanassa”nti vuttaṃ bhavatīti saṅkhepattho veditabbo. Vitthārattho pana aṭṭhakathāyaṃ (netti. aṭṭha. 23) bahudhā vuttoti amhehi na vitthārito.

Because it is to be asked, 'When mindfulness directed to the body is stated, why should the remaining mindfulness directed to feelings, etc., also be stated?', to show that the thirty-seven aids to enlightenment are also stated, 'and as the Blessed One said,' and so on, is stated. Herein, the meaning is that just as the Blessed One spoke with the characteristic of leading out and by having a single characteristic, so too are they stated by that same single characteristic. 'Therefore, because you are overcome by covetousness and grief, here in my dispensation, monk, you should be ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, and having subdued covetousness and grief in the world either by abandonment by substitution or by abandonment by suppression, dwell contemplating the body in the body—the body consisting of hair, etc.' When the Blessed One said this, 'Therefore, monk, dwell contemplating feelings in feelings—ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having subdued covetousness and grief in the world. Therefore, monk, dwell contemplating mind in mind…subduing grief. Therefore, monk, dwell contemplating phenomena in phenomena…subduing grief' is also stated. This is what is meant in brief. The detailed meaning, however, is explained in many ways in the commentary (Netti. Aṭṭha. 23), therefore it has not been elaborated by us.

“Ekasmiṃ [M 0.0137] satipaṭṭhāne vutte kasmā cattāro satipaṭṭhānā vuttā bhaveyyu”nti vattabbattā “ātāpīti vīriyindriya”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha “ātāpī”ti iminā padena kāyavedanācittadhammesu pavattaṃ vīriyindriyaṃ vuttaṃ. “Sampajāno”ti padena kāyavedanācittadhammesu pavattaṃ paññindriyaṃ vuttaṃ. “Satimā”ti padena kāyavedanācittadhammesu pavattaṃ satindriyaṃ vuttaṃ. “Vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassa”nti padena kāyavedanācittadhammesu pavattaṃ samādhindriyaṃ vuttaṃ, na kāyeyeva pavattaṃ. Evaṃ pakārena kāye kāyānupassino yogāvacarassa cattāro satipaṭṭhānā bhāvanāpāripūriṃ gacchantīti ce vadeyya, evaṃ sati catunnaṃ vīriyapaññāsatisamādhīnaṃ indriyānaṃ catunnaṃ satipaṭṭhānānaṃ sādhakabhāvena ekalakkhaṇattā samānalakkhaṇattā pāripūriṃ gacchantīti yojanā. Tena vuttaṃ aṭṭhakathāyaṃ – “catusatipaṭṭhānasādhane imesaṃ indriyānaṃ sabhāvabhedābhāvato samānalakkhaṇattā”ti (netti. aṭṭha. 23).

Because it is to be stated, 'When one establishment of mindfulness is stated, why would the four establishments of mindfulness be stated?', 'ardent—that is, the faculty of energy,' and so on, is stated. Herein, by the word 'ardent,' the faculty of energy operating in body, feelings, mind, and phenomena is spoken of. By the word 'clearly comprehending,' the faculty of wisdom operating in body, feelings, mind, and phenomena is spoken of. By the word 'mindful,' the faculty of mindfulness operating in body, feelings, mind, and phenomena is spoken of. By the phrase 'having subdued covetousness and grief in the world,' the faculty of concentration operating in body, feelings, mind, and phenomena is spoken of, not merely operating in the body. In this way, if one were to say that for a meditator contemplating the body in the body, the four establishments of mindfulness reach fulfillment in development, then, in that case, the connection is that because these four faculties—energy, wisdom, mindfulness, and concentration—serve as the means to accomplish the four establishments of mindfulness, having a single characteristic and a shared characteristic, they reach fulfillment. Therefore, it is said in the commentary: 'Due to the absence of a difference in intrinsic nature and their shared characteristic, these faculties accomplish the four establishments of mindfulness' (Netti. Aṭṭha. 23).

24. “Evaṃ vuttepi cattāro satipaṭṭhānāyeva vattabbā bhaveyyuṃ, kathaṃ sattatiṃsabodhipakkhiyadhammā vattabbā”ti vattabbattā “catūsu satipaṭṭhānesū”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha catūsu satipaṭṭhānesu yena yogāvacarena bhāviyamānesu tassa yogāvacarassa cattāro sammappadhānā bhāvanāpāripūriṃ gacchanti. Evaṃ sesesupi yojanā kātabbā. Catunnaṃ saccānaṃ bujjhanaṃ bodhaṃ, ariyamaggañāṇaṃ, bodhaṃ gacchantīti bodhaṅgamā. Bodhassa ariyamaggañāṇassa pakkhe bhavāti bodhipakkhiyā.

24. Because it could be said, 'Even when this is stated, only the four establishments of mindfulness should be mentioned; how can the thirty-seven requisites of enlightenment be mentioned?', the passage beginning with 'in the four establishments of mindfulness' was stated. Therein, when the four establishments of mindfulness are being developed by a meditator, for that meditator the four right strivings go to fulfillment in development. In this way, the application should be made to the remaining ones as well. The understanding of the four truths is enlightenment, the knowledge of the noble path. They go towards enlightenment, thus they are 'factors of enlightenment.' They are on the side of enlightenment, the knowledge of the noble path, thus they are 'requisites of enlightenment.'

“Kusalāyeva dhammā ekalakkhaṇabhāvena nīharitā kiṃ, udāhu akusalāpi dhammā”ti pucchitabbattā “evaṃ akusalāpī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha kusalā dhammā ekalakkhaṇattena niddhāritā [V 0.0271] yathā, evaṃ akusalāpi dhammā ekalakkhaṇattena niddhāritabbāyevāti attho. “Kathaṃ niddhāretabbā”ti pucchitabbattā pahānekaṭṭhabhāvena niddhāretabbāti dassento “ekalakkhaṇattā pahānaṃ abbhatthaṃ gacchantī”ti āha. Tattha ekalakkhaṇattāti pahānekaṭṭhabhāvena samānalakkhaṇattā. “Katamaṃ pahānaṃ abbhatthaṃ gacchantī”ti pucchitabbattā “catūsu satipaṭṭhānesū”tiādi vuttaṃ.

Because the question could be asked, 'Are only wholesome states extracted as having a single characteristic, or unwholesome states as well?', the passage beginning with 'so too unwholesome states' was stated. The meaning is: just as wholesome states are determined as having a single characteristic, so too unwholesome states must be determined as having a single characteristic.
