Because the question could be asked, 'How are they to be determined?', showing that they are to be determined by having the single function of abandonment, he said, 'due to having a single characteristic, they go to abandonment.' Therein, 'due to having a single characteristic' means due to having a common characteristic in that they have the single function of abandonment. Because the question could be asked, 'To what abandonment do they go?', the passage beginning with 'in the four establishments of mindfulness' was stated.

Tattha [M 0.0138] catūsu…pe… pariññaṃ gacchantīti kāyāgatāsatipaṭṭhāne yogāvacarena bhāviyamāne sati tena yogāvacarena asubhe kesādike rūpakāye “subha”nti vipallāso pahīyati, assa yogāvacarassa kabaḷīkārāhāro pariññaṃ gacchati, “āhārasamudayā rūpasamudayo”ti (saṃ. ni. 3.56) vuttattā rūpakāye chandarāgaṃ pajahantassa tassa samudaye kabaḷīkārāhārepi chandarāgo pahīyatīti attho. Vedanāgatāsatipaṭṭhāne bhāviyamāne sati dukkhe “sukha”nti vipallāso pahīyati, assa yogāvacarassa phassāhāro pariññaṃ gacchati, “phassapaccayā vedanā”ti (ma. ni. 3.126; saṃ. ni. 2.1, 39; mahāva. 1; udā. 1; vibha. 225) vuttattā vedanāya chandarāgaṃ pajahantassa tassa paccaye phassāhāre chandarāgo pahīyati. Cittagatāsatipaṭṭhāne bhāviyamāne anicce “nicca”nti vipallāso pahīyati, assa yogāvacarassa viññāṇāhāro pariññaṃ gacchati. Dhammagatāsatipaṭṭhāne bhāviyamāne anattani “attā”ti vipallāso pahīyati, assa yogāvacarassa manosañcetanāhāro pariññaṃ gacchatīti visuṃ visuṃ yojetvā ekekasmiṃ pahātabbe vutte tadavasesā pahātabbā vuttā bhavanti pahātabbabhāvena ekalakkhaṇattāti attho gahetabbo.

Therein, 'in the four... etc. ...they go to full understanding' means: when the establishment of mindfulness directed to the body is being developed by a meditator, the perversion of 'beautiful' regarding the foul physical body, beginning with the hair of the head, is abandoned by that meditator. For this meditator, the nutriment of physical food goes to full understanding. Because it is said, 'from the arising of nutriment, there is the arising of form,' the meaning is that for one who abandons sensual desire for the physical body, sensual desire is also abandoned for its origin, the nutriment of physical food. When the establishment of mindfulness directed to feelings is being developed, the perversion of 'pleasant' in what is suffering is abandoned; for this meditator, the nutriment of contact goes to full understanding. Because it is said, 'with contact as condition, feeling arises,' for one who abandons sensual desire for feeling, sensual desire is also abandoned for its condition, the nutriment of contact. When the establishment of mindfulness directed to the mind is being developed, the perversion of 'permanent' in what is impermanent is abandoned; for this meditator, the nutriment of consciousness goes to full understanding. When the establishment of mindfulness directed to phenomena is being developed, the perversion of 'self' in what is not-self is abandoned; for this meditator, the nutriment of mental volition goes to full understanding. The meaning should be understood that, having applied this separately to each, when one thing to be abandoned is mentioned, the remaining things to be abandoned are also stated, because they have a single characteristic in that they are to be abandoned.

“Āhārā cassa pariññaṃ gacchantī”ti vacane āhāresu pavattā kāmarāgadosamohā byantīkatā hontīti attho gahito. Kabaḷīkārāhārañhi ārabbha pavatte kāmarāge vijjamāne kabaḷīkārāhārassa vijānanā nattheva, tasmiṃ kāmarāge pana pahīne parijānanā bhavatīti. Sesāhārajānanampi eseva nayo. Yassa yogāvacarassa satipaṭṭhānā bhāvitā, vipallāsā pahīnā, āhāraparijānanā uppannā, so yogāvacaro upādānehi anupādāno bhavati. Subhasaññite hi kāye kāmupādānaṃ visesena bhavatīti subhasaññito kāyo kāmupādānassa vatthu, kāyagatāya satiyā anusaritabbo asubhasaññito kesādi kāmupādānassa vatthu na hotveva. Sukhavedanāya assādavasena diṭṭhupādānaṃ bhavatīti sukhasaññitā vedanā diṭṭhupādānassa vatthu, vedanāgatāya pana satiyā anupassitabbā vedanā diṭṭhupādānassa vatthu na hotveva. “Cittaṃ nicca”nti diṭṭhigahaṇavasena tassa tassa attano sīlavatavasena parisuddhīti parāmasanaṃ hotīti cittaṃ sīlabbatupādānassa [M 0.0139] vatthu, cittagatāya pana satiyā anupassitabbaṃ cittaṃ sīlabbatupādānassa [V 0.0272] vatthu na hotveva. Dhamme nāmarūpaparicchedena yathābhūtaṃ apassantassa dhammesu attābhiniveso hotīti dhammā attavādupādānassa vatthu, dhammagatāya pana satiyā anupassitabbā dhammā attavādupādānassa vatthu na honti eva. Tasmā catūsu satipaṭṭhānesu bhāviyamānesu upādānehi anupādāno bhavatīti vuttanti adhippāyo gahetabbo.

In the statement 'and the nutriments go to full understanding for him,' the meaning is taken that sensual craving, ill will, and delusion that occur in relation to the nutriments are brought to an end. For when sensual craving, which arises in relation to physical food, is present, there is no understanding of physical food; but when that sensual craving is abandoned, there is full understanding. This is the same method for understanding the remaining nutriments. That meditator for whom the establishments of mindfulness have been developed, the perversions abandoned, and the full understanding of the nutriments has arisen, that meditator becomes one who does not cling to the objects of clinging. For in a body perceived as beautiful, sensual clinging especially arises; thus, a body perceived as beautiful is the basis for sensual clinging. But the body perceived as foul, beginning with the hair of the head, which is to be recollected with mindfulness directed to the body, is not a basis for sensual clinging at all. Through gratification in pleasant feeling, clinging to views arises; thus, a feeling perceived as pleasant is the basis for clinging to views. But a feeling that is to be contemplated with mindfulness directed to feelings is not a basis for clinging to views at all. Through grasping the view 'the mind is permanent,' there is the misapprehension that one is purified by this or that rule and observance of one's own; thus, the mind is the basis for clinging to rules and observances. But a mind that is to be contemplated with mindfulness directed to the mind is not a basis for clinging to rules and observances at all. For one who does not see phenomena as they really are by way of the delimitation of mind-and-matter, there is adherence to self in phenomena; thus, phenomena are the basis for clinging to the doctrine of self. But phenomena that are to be contemplated with mindfulness directed to phenomena are not a basis for clinging to the doctrine of self at all. Therefore, the intention should be understood that it was said, 'when the four establishments of mindfulness are being developed, one becomes one who does not cling to the objects of clinging.'

“Yena yogāvacarena satipaṭṭhānā bhāvitā, so yogāvacaro upādānehiyeva anupādāno bhavatī”ti pucchitabbattā yogādīhipi visaṃyutto bhavatīti dassetuṃ “yogehi ca visaṃyutto”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha yogehi cāti kāmayogabhavayogadiṭṭhiyogaavijjāyogehi ca. Visaṃyuttoti tadaṅgappahānavikkhambhanappahānasamucchedappahānavasena vigato, vimutto ca bhavatīti attho. Subhasaññito hi rūpakāyo kāmarāgassa vatthu hoti, kāyagatāya pana satiyā anupassitabbo kāyo kāmarāgassa vatthu na hotveva. “Sukho”ti vā “sukhahetū”ti vā gahaṇīyo bhavo bhavarāgassa vatthu hoti, vedanāgatāya pana satiyā anupassitabbo bhavo bhavarāgassa vatthu na hoti. “Attā”ti abhinivisitabbaṃ cittaṃ diṭṭhiyogassa vatthu hoti, cittagatāya pana satiyā anupassitabbaṃ cittaṃ diṭṭhiyogassa vatthu na hoti. Vinibbhogassa dukkarattā, dhammānaṃ dhammamattatāya ca duppaṭivijjhattā avinibbhujitabbā, dhammamattatāya appaṭivijjhitabbā dhammā avijjāyogassa vatthu honti, dhammagatāya pana satiyā anupassitabbā dhammā avijjāyogassa vatthu na honti. Tasmā catusatipaṭṭhānānupassako “yogehi ca visaṃyutto”ti vutto. Ayaṃ nayo āsavehi ca anāsavo bhavati, oghehi ca nitthiṇṇo bhavatīti etthāpi yojetabbo.

Because the question could be asked, 'The meditator by whom the establishments of mindfulness have been developed, does that meditator become one who does not cling only to the objects of clinging?', to show that one becomes disjoined from the yokes and so on as well, the passage beginning with 'and disjoined from the yokes' was stated. Therein, 'and from the yokes' means from the yoke of sensuality, the yoke of existence, the yoke of views, and the yoke of ignorance. 'Disjoined' means departed, liberated by way of abandonment by substitution of opposites, abandonment by suppression, and abandonment by cutting off. For a physical body perceived as beautiful is a basis for sensual craving; but a body that is to be contemplated with mindfulness directed to the body is not a basis for sensual craving at all. Existence that is to be grasped as 'pleasant' or 'a cause of pleasure' is a basis for craving for existence; but existence that is to be contemplated with mindfulness directed to feelings is not a basis for craving for existence. A mind that is to be adhered to as 'self' is a basis for the yoke of views; but a mind that is to be contemplated with mindfulness directed to the mind is not a basis for the yoke of views. Because analysis is difficult, and because phenomena are difficult to penetrate as mere phenomena, phenomena that are not analyzed and not penetrated as mere phenomena are a basis for the yoke of ignorance. But phenomena that are to be contemplated with mindfulness directed to phenomena are not a basis for the yoke of ignorance. Therefore, one who contemplates the four establishments of mindfulness is said to be 'and disjoined from the yokes.' This method should also be applied to 'and becomes taintless from the taints, and becomes one who has crossed over the floods.'

Ganthehi ca vippayutto bhavatīti ettha pana subhasaññito rūpakāyo abhijjhākāyaganthassa vatthu, kāyagatāya pana satiyā anupassitabbo rūpakāyo abhijjhākāyaganthassa vatthu na hoti. Dukkhadukkhavipariṇāmadukkhasaṅkhāradukkhabhūtā vedanā byāpādakāyaganthassa vatthu honti, tena vuttaṃ – “dukkhāya vedanāya paṭighānusayo anusetī”ti (ma. ni. 1.465). Vedanāgatāya [M 0.0140] pana satiyā anupassitabbā vedanā byāpādakāyaganthassa vatthu na hoti. “Cittaṃ nicca”nti abhinivesavasena sassatassa “attano sīlena suddhi, vatena suddhī”ti parāmasanaṃ hoti, tasmā “nicca”nti gahitaṃ cittaṃ sīlabbataparāmāsakāyaganthassa vatthu, cittagatāya pana satiyā anupassitabbaṃ cittaṃ sīlabbataparāmāsassa vatthu na hoti. Dhammānaṃ sappaccayanāmarūpasabhāvassa adassanato bhavadiṭṭhivibhavadiṭṭhi hoti, tasmā “idaṃ sacca”nti abhinivisitabbā dhammā idaṃsaccābhinivesakāyaganthassa vatthu, dhammagatāya pana satiyā anupassitabbā [V 0.0273] dhammā idaṃsaccābhinivesakāyaganthassa vatthu na honti, tasmā catusatipaṭṭhānānupassako “ganthehi ca vippayutto”ti vutto.

"And he becomes disjoined from the knots." Herein, the physical body perceived as beautiful is the basis for the bodily knot of covetousness, but the physical body, when contemplated with mindfulness directed to the body, is not a basis for the bodily knot of covetousness. Feelings that are pain as pain, pain in change, and pain in conditioned formations are the basis for the bodily knot of ill will. Thus it is said: “The underlying tendency to aversion lies latent in regard to painful feeling” (MN 44). But feeling, when contemplated with mindfulness directed to feeling, is not a basis for the bodily knot of ill will. Through adherence to the view “the mind is permanent,” there is the grasping of eternalism, such as “purity is through one's own virtue, purity is through one's own observance.” Therefore, the mind grasped as “permanent” is the basis for the bodily knot of adherence to rules and observances. But the mind, when contemplated with mindfulness directed to the mind, is not a basis for adherence to rules and observances. From not seeing the nature of phenomena as conditioned name-and-form, there arises the view of being and the view of non-being. Therefore, phenomena adhered to as “this is the truth” are the basis for the bodily knot of dogmatic adherence that “this alone is the truth.” But phenomena, when contemplated with mindfulness directed to phenomena, are not a basis for the bodily knot of dogmatic adherence that “this alone is the truth.” Therefore, one who contemplates the four foundations of mindfulness is said to be “disjoined from the knots.”

Subhasaññito ca kāyo rāgasallassa vatthu, kāyagatāya pana satiyā anupassitabbo kāyo rāgasallassa vatthu na hoti. Sukhasaññitāya vedanāya doso hoti, tasmā vedanā dosasallassa vatthu, vedanāgatāya pana satiyā anupassitabbā vedanā dosasallassa vatthu na hoti. “Cittaṃ attā”ti gahetvā “attā seyyo”tiādivasena pavattassa mānasallassa cittaṃ vatthu, cittagatāya pana satiyā anupassitabbaṃ cittaṃ mānasallassa vatthu na hoti. Dhammānaṃ sappaccayanāmarūpasabhāvassa ajānanato dhammā mohasallassa vatthu, dhammagatāya pana satiyā anupassitabbā dhammā mohasallassa vatthu na honti, tasmā catusatipaṭṭhānānupassako “sallehi ca visallo bhavatī”ti vutto.

The body perceived as beautiful is the basis for the dart of lust, but the body, when contemplated with mindfulness directed to the body, is not a basis for the dart of lust. From feeling perceived as pleasant, aversion arises; therefore, feeling is the basis for the dart of aversion. But feeling, when contemplated with mindfulness directed to feeling, is not a basis for the dart of aversion. The mind, grasped as 'self', is the basis for the dart of conceit that proceeds by way of such thoughts as 'I am better.' But the mind, when contemplated with mindfulness directed to the mind, is not a basis for the dart of conceit. Due to not knowing the nature of phenomena as conditioned name-and-form, phenomena are the basis for the dart of delusion. But phenomena, when contemplated with mindfulness directed to phenomena, are not a basis for the dart of delusion. Therefore, one who contemplates the four foundations of mindfulness is said to be 'dartless'.

“Āhārā cassa pariññaṃ gacchantī”ti ācariyena vuttaṃ, “kiṃ pana āhārāva assa yogāvacarassa pariññaṃ gacchanti, udāhu aññepī”ti pucchitabbattā viññāṇaṭṭhitiyo ca assa yogāvacarassa pariññaṃ gacchantīti dassetuṃ “viññāṇaṭṭhitiyo cassa pariññaṃ gacchantī”ti vuttaṃ. Yena yogāvacarena cattāro satipaṭṭhānā bhāvitā, tassa yogāvacarassa kāyavedanācittadhammāva pariññaṃ gaccheyyuṃ, na viññāṇaṭṭhitiyoti ce vadeyya kāyānupassanādīhi ca kāyavedanācittadhammesu pariññātesu saññāyapi pariññātabbabhāvato. Sā hi vedanācittasaṅkhātena dhammesu pariññātesu avinābhāvato pariññātāvāti.

“For him, the nutriments come to be fully understood,” was said by the teacher. Since the question should be asked, “But do only the nutriments come to be fully understood by this meditator, or do others as well?”—to show that for this meditator the stations of consciousness also come to be fully understood, it was said, “For him, the stations of consciousness also come to be fully understood.” If one were to say that for a meditator who has developed the four foundations of mindfulness, only body, feelings, mind, and phenomena would come to be fully understood, not the stations of consciousness—this is not so, because when body, feelings, mind, and phenomena are fully understood through contemplation of the body and so on, perception also must be fully understood. For it, being inseparable from the phenomena designated as feeling and mind, is indeed fully understood when they are fully understood.

Yena [M 0.0141] cattāro satipaṭṭhānā bhāvitā, so yogāvacaro upādānehi anupādāno ca, yogehi visaṃyutto ca, khandhehi vippayutto ca, āsavehi anāsavo ca, oghehi nitthiṇṇo ca, sallehi visallo ca bhavatīti vutto, “kiṃ pana tathāvidhova hoti, udāhu aññathāpī”ti pucchitabbattā agatimpi na gacchatīti dassento “agatigamanehi ca na agatiṃ gacchatī”ti āha. Subhādisaññite rūpakāye apekkhamāno puggalo chandāgatiṃ gacchatīti subhādisaññito rūpakāyo visesato chandāgatiyā vatthu hoti, kāyānupassanāsatipaṭṭhānena pana anupassitabbo assāsapassāsādiko kāyo chandāgatiyā vatthu na hoti, tasmā kāyānupassanāsatipaṭṭhānabhāvanaṃ bhāvento puggalo chandāgatiṃ na gacchati. Sukhavedanassādavasena vedayamāno tadabhāvena byāpādaṃ āgacchatīti sukhavedanā dosāgatiyā vatthu hoti, vedanānupassanāsatipaṭṭhānena pana anupassitabbā vedanā dosāgatiyā vatthu na hoti[V 0.0274], tasmā vedanāsatipaṭṭhānabhāvanaṃ bhāvento puggalo dosāgatiṃ na gacchati. Santatighanavasena “niccaṃ, dhuva”nti gahitaṃ cittaṃ mohassa vatthu hoti, cittānupassanāsatipaṭṭhānena pana anupassitabbaṃ cittaṃ mohassa vatthu na hoti, tasmā cittānupassanāsatipaṭṭhānabhāvanaṃ bhāvento puggalo dosāgatiṃ na gacchati. Vibhajitvā dhammasabhāvaṃ ajānantassa bhayaṃ jāyatīti vibhajitvā ajāniyasabhāvā dhammā bhayassa vatthu honti, dhammānupassanāsatipaṭṭhānena pana anupassitabbā vibhajitvā jānitabbā dhammā rāgassa vatthu na honti, tasmā dhammānupassanāsatipaṭṭhānabhāvanaṃ bhāvento puggalo bhayāgatiṃ na gacchati. Evaṃ pahātabbabhāvena ekalakkhaṇe akusalepi dhamme nīharitvā idāni nigametuṃ “evaṃ akusalāpi dhammā ekalakkhaṇattā pahānaṃ abbhatthaṃ gacchantī”ti puna vuttaṃ.

A meditator by whom the four foundations of mindfulness have been developed is said to become one who does not cling to what is clung to, is disjoined from the yokes, is separated from the aggregates, is without taints, has crossed over the floods, and is dartless. Because the question should be asked, 'But is he only of such a kind, or is he otherwise as well?', showing that he does not go to a wrong course, it was said, 'And he does not go to a wrong course by the goings to wrong courses.' A person who longs for a physical body perceived as beautiful goes to the wrong course of desire; thus, the physical body perceived as beautiful is specifically a basis for the wrong course of desire. However, the body to be contemplated through mindfulness of the body—such as the in-breath and out-breath—is not a basis for the wrong course of desire. Therefore, a person developing the cultivation of mindfulness of the body does not go to the wrong course of desire. One who experiences feeling by way of savoring pleasant feeling comes to ill will through its absence; thus, pleasant feeling is a basis for the wrong course of aversion. However, feeling to be contemplated through mindfulness of feeling is not a basis for the wrong course of aversion. Therefore, a person developing the cultivation of mindfulness of feeling does not go to the wrong course of aversion. A mind grasped as 'permanent, stable' due to the density of continuity is a basis for delusion. However, the mind to be contemplated through mindfulness of the mind is not a basis for delusion. Therefore, a person developing the cultivation of mindfulness of the mind does not go to the wrong course of aversion. For one who does not know the inherent nature of phenomena by analysis, fear arises; thus, phenomena whose nature is not known by analysis are a basis for fear. However, phenomena to be contemplated through mindfulness of phenomena—to be known by analysis—are not a basis for desire. Therefore, a person developing the cultivation of mindfulness of phenomena does not go to the wrong course of fear. Thus, having brought out even unwholesome states that have a single characteristic in that they are to be abandoned, now to conclude, it is said again: 'In this way, even unwholesome states, due to having a single characteristic, go to destruction by abandonment.'

Bhāvetabbesu dhammesu ekadesesu vutte tadavasesāpi bhāvetabbā dhammā ekalakkhaṇattā nīharitvā vattabbā, pahātabbesupi dhammesu ekadese vutte tadavasesāpi dhammā pahātabbā ekalakkhaṇattā nīharitvā vattabbāti ācariyena vuttā, amhehi ca ñātā, “aññathāpi yadi vattabbā siyuṃ, tepi vadathā”ti vattabbabhāvato aññenapi pariyāyena lakkhaṇahārassa udāharaṇāni dassetuṃ “yattha vā panā”tiādi vuttaṃ[M 0.0142]. Tattha yattha yassaṃ rūpekadesadesanāyaṃ rūpindriyaṃ ruppanalakkhaṇaṃ cakkhundriyādijīvitindriyapariyosānaṃ aṭṭhavidhaṃ indriyaṃ rūpekadesaṃ bhagavatā desitaṃ. Tattheva tassaṃ rūpekadesadesanāyaṃ rūpadhātu ruppanalakkhaṇā cakkhudhātādiphoṭṭhabbadhātupariyosānā dasavidhā rūpadhātu ruppanalakkhaṇena ekalakkhaṇattā desitā. Sabbo rūpakkhandho ca desito. Rūpāyatanaṃ ruppanalakkhaṇaṃ cakkhāyatanādiphoṭṭhabbāyatanapariyosānaṃ dasavidhaṃ āyatanaṃ ruppanalakkhaṇena ekalakkhaṇattā bhagavatā desitaṃ.

It was stated by the teacher and understood by us that: 'When a portion of the phenomena to be developed is stated, the remaining phenomena to be developed should be brought out and stated, due to having a single characteristic. And when a portion of the phenomena to be abandoned is stated, the remaining phenomena to be abandoned should be brought out and stated, due to having a single characteristic.' Because it should be said, 'If they should be stated in another way, state them also,' the passage beginning 'Wherever...' was stated in order to show examples of the application of characteristics in another way. Therein, wherever in a teaching on a portion of form, the eightfold faculty which is a portion of form—the form-faculty characterized by being afflicted, beginning with the eye-faculty and ending with the life-faculty—is taught by the Blessed One. In that very teaching on a portion of form, the tenfold form-element, characterized by being afflicted, beginning with the eye-element and ending with the tangible-element, is taught as having the single characteristic of being afflicted. And the entire form aggregate is taught. The tenfold sense base of form, characterized by being afflicted, beginning with the eye sense base and ending with the tangible sense base, is taught by the Blessed One as having the single characteristic of being afflicted.

Yattha vā pana yassaṃ vedanekadesadesanāyaṃ sukhā vedanā bhagavatā desitā, tattha tassaṃ vedanekadesadesanāyaṃ sukhindriyañca desitaṃ, somanassindriyañca desitaṃ, dukkhasamudayo ariyasaccañca desitaṃ sukhavedanābhāvena ekalakkhaṇattā. Yattha vā pana yassaṃ vedanekadesadesanāyaṃ dukkhā vedanā bhagavatā desitā, tattha tassaṃ vedanekadesadesanāyaṃ dukkhindriyañca desitaṃ domanassindriyañca desitaṃ, dukkhaṃ ariyasaccañca desitaṃ dukkhavedanābhāvena ekalakkhaṇattā. Yattha vā pana yassaṃ vedanekadesadesanāyaṃ adukkhamasukhā vedanā bhagavatā desitā, tattha tassaṃ vedanekadesadesanāyaṃ upekkhindriyañca desitaṃ, sabbo paṭiccasamuppādo ca desitoti yojanā kātabbā.

Wherever, in whatever partial exposition of feeling, pleasant feeling was taught by the Blessed One, there in that partial exposition of feeling the faculty of pleasure was also taught, the faculty of joy was also taught, and the noble truth of the origin of suffering was taught—because of the single characteristic of having the nature of pleasant feeling. Wherever, in whatever partial exposition of feeling, painful feeling was taught by the Blessed One, there in that partial exposition of feeling the faculty of pain was also taught, the faculty of displeasure was also taught, and the noble truth of suffering was taught—because of the single characteristic of having the nature of painful feeling. Wherever, in whatever partial exposition of feeling, neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling was taught by the Blessed One, there in that partial exposition of feeling the faculty of equanimity was also taught, and all of dependent origination was taught—thus the connection should be made.

Yassaṃ [V 0.0275] desanāyaṃ adukkhamasukhā vedanā desitā, tassaṃ desanāyaṃ upekkhindriyaṃ desitaṃ hotu samānalakkhaṇattā, “kena paṭiccasamuppādo desito bhaveyyā”ti vattabbabhāvato “kena kāraṇenā”ti pucchitvā kāraṇaṃ dassetuṃ “adukkhamasukhāyā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha adukkhamasukhāya vedanāya hi yasmā avijjā anuseti, tasmā avijjā desitā hoti. Avijjāya ca desitāya avijjāmūlako sabbopi paṭiccasamuppādo “avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā…pe… dukkhakkhandhassa samudayo hotī”ti desitova hotīti adhippāyo daṭṭhabbo.

In that teaching where neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling is taught, in that teaching the faculty of equanimity is taught because of having the same characteristic. Because it will be asked, “By what should dependent origination be taught?”—having asked, “By what reason?”—to show the reason, it is said, “By neither-painful-nor-pleasant,” and so on. Here, because ignorance underlies neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, therefore ignorance is taught. And with the teaching of ignorance, the entire dependent origination rooted in ignorance is taught: “With ignorance as condition, formations arise…up to…the arising of this whole mass of suffering.” This meaning should be understood.

“Avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā…pe… samudayo hotī”ti anulomavasena pavatto yo paṭiccasamuppādo desitoti ācariyena vutto, “yadi tathā pavatto so ca paṭiccasamuppādo desito, evaṃ sati sabbo ca paṭiccasamuppādo desito”ti na vattabboti codanaṃ manasi katvā “so cā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha yo ca anulomavasena pavatto, so ca sarāgasadosasamohasaṃkilesapakkhena hātabbo. Yo ca [M 0.0143] paṭilomavasena “avijjāya tveva asesavirāganirodhā saṅkhāranirodho”tiādiko pavatto, so ca vītarāgavītadosavītamohaariyadhammehi hātabbo. Yo ca anulomapaṭilomavasena pavatto, so ca tadubhayehi hātabbo. Tasmā “sabbo ca paṭiccasamuppādo desito”ti vattabbovāti adhippāyo gahetabbo.

“With ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise… and so on… the origination comes to be.” Thus the teacher spoke of dependent origination as it proceeds in the forward order. Considering the objection that 'If dependent origination is taught as proceeding in this way, then it should not be said that the entire dependent origination is taught,' the statement 'and that…' and so on was made. Therein, that which proceeds in the forward order is to be understood as being on the side of passion, aversion, delusion, and defilements. And that which proceeds in the reverse order, such as 'with the remainderless fading away and cessation of that very ignorance, there is the cessation of volitional formations,' is to be understood by means of the noble dhammas free from passion, free from aversion, and free from delusion. That which proceeds in both forward and reverse order is to be understood by means of both of these. Therefore, the meaning should be taken that it can be said, 'The entire dependent origination is taught.'

“Ye dhammā ekalakkhaṇā, tesaṃ dhammānaṃ ekasmiṃ dhamme vutte avasiṭṭhā dhammā vuttā bhavantītiādinā (netti. 23) ācariyena yā lakkhaṇahārayojanā vuttā, sāva kātabbā, na aññathā kātabbā”ti pucchitabbabhāvato aññathāpi lakkhaṇahārayojanā kātabbāyevāti dassetuṃ “evaṃ ye dhammā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha ye pathavīādayo rūpadhammā, ye phassādayo arūpadhammā sandhāraṇādikiccato saṅghaṭṭanādikiccato ekalakkhaṇā, tesaṃ rūpārūpadhammānaṃ ekasmiṃ dhamme vutte avasiṭṭhā rūpārūpadhammā vuttā bhavanti. Ye pathavīādayo rūpadhammā, ye phassādayo arūpadhammā kakkhaḷādilakkhaṇato phusanādilakkhaṇato ekalakkhaṇā, tesaṃ rūpārūpadhammānaṃ ekasmiṃ dhamme vutte avasiṭṭhā rūpārūpadhammā vuttā bhavanti. Ye dhammā ruppanasāmaññato namanasāmaññato aniccādisāmaññato vā khandhāyatanādisāmaññato vā ekalakkhaṇā, tesaṃ saṅkhatadhammānaṃ ekasmiṃ saṅkhatadhamme vutte avasiṭṭhā dhammā vuttā bhavanti. Ye saṅkhatadhammā bhaṅguppādato saṅkhato cutūpapātato samānanirodhuppādasaṅkhatato vā cutūpapātato ekalakkhaṇā, tesaṃ saṅkhatadhammānaṃ ekasmiṃ saṅkhatadhamme vutte avasiṭṭhā saṅkhatadhammā vuttā bhavantīti atthayojanā kātabbā.

The teacher stated, “Those phenomena which have a single characteristic, when one such phenomenon is stated, the remaining phenomena are thereby stated” (Netti 23), and that this application of the characteristic mode should be followed and not done otherwise. However, because it might be asked whether it should only be done in that way or also differently, to show that the application of the characteristic mode can indeed be done differently, it was said, “Thus, those phenomena…” Herein, the material phenomena such as the earth element, etc., and the immaterial phenomena such as contact, etc., are considered to have a single characteristic due to their shared functions, such as the function of supporting or the function of striking. When one such phenomenon is stated, the remaining material and immaterial phenomena are thereby stated. Similarly, the material phenomena such as the earth element, etc., and the immaterial phenomena such as contact, etc., are considered to have a single characteristic due to their defining marks, such as hardness or touching. When one such phenomenon is stated, the remaining material and immaterial phenomena are thereby stated. Those phenomena that share a commonality in being afflicted (ruppana), in bending (namana), or in being impermanent, etc., or a commonality as aggregates, sense bases, etc., are considered to have a single characteristic. When one such conditioned phenomenon is stated, the remaining conditioned phenomena are thereby stated. Those conditioned phenomena that are of a single characteristic due to their breaking and arising, or due to the passing away and rearising of the conditioned, or due to the conditioned’s similar cessation and arising or passing away and rearising, when one such conditioned phenomenon is stated, the remaining conditioned phenomena are thereby stated. This is how the meaning should be applied.

Kiccato ca lakkhaṇato cātiādīsu ca-saddena sahacaraṇasamānahetutādayo saṅgahitāti daṭṭhabbā[V 0.0276]. Sahacaraṇādīsu ca yaṃ vattabbaṃ, taṃ “nānattakāyanānattasaññino (dī. ni. 3.341, 357, 359; a. ni. 9.24), nānattasaññānaṃ amanasikārā”tiādīsu sahacāritāya saññāsahagatā dhammā niddhāritātiādinā vuttameva.

In the phrase 'By function and by characteristic, etc.,' it should be understood that co-occurrence, common cause, and so forth are included by the particle 'ca'. And what is to be said regarding co-occurrence, etc., has already been stated in passages such as 'those with diverse bodies and diverse perceptions' (Dī. Ni. 3.341, 357, 359; A. Ni. 9.24), and 'by not attending to diverse perceptions,' etc., where phenomena accompanied by perception are determined through their co-occurrence, and so forth.

“Ekasmiṃ dhamme sarūpato vutte ekalakkhaṇādito avasiṭṭhadhammānampi vuttabhāvo kena amhehi jānitabbo saddahitabbo”ti vattabbabhāvato “tenā”tiādi [M 0.0144] vuttaṃ. Tattha tena avasiṭṭhadhammānampi vuttabhāvena “vuttamhi ekadhamme”tiādikaṃ yaṃ vacanaṃ āyasmā mahākaccāno āha, tena vacanena tumhehi avasiṭṭhānampi vuttabhāvo jānitabbo saddahitabboti vuttaṃ hoti.

Because it should be asked, 'When one phenomenon is stated in terms of its own nature or by a single characteristic, etc., how are we to know and believe that the remaining phenomena are also stated?' the statement 'Therefore…' and so on was made. Herein, by that very fact that the remaining phenomena are also stated, through the statement, 'When one phenomenon has been stated…' and so on—whatever words the Venerable Mahākaccāna spoke—by those words, you should know and believe that the remaining phenomena are also stated. This is what is said.

“Ettāvatā ca lakkhaṇahāro paripuṇṇo, añño niyutto natthī”ti vattabbattā “niyutto lakkhaṇo hāro”ti vuttaṃ. Tattha yassaṃ pāḷiyaṃ ekasmiṃ dhamme vutte avasiṭṭhadhammāpi yena lakkhaṇahārena niddhāritā, tassaṃ pāḷiyaṃ so lakkhaṇo hāro niyutto niddhāretvā yojitoti attho daṭṭhabboti.

Because it can be said, 'With this much, the characteristic mode is complete, and there is no other prescribed mode,' therefore it is said, 'the prescribed characteristic mode.' Here, in whatever Pāli passage one phenomenon is stated, and the remaining phenomena are determined by a certain characteristic mode, in that passage, that characteristic mode should be understood as prescribed, determined, and applied. This is the meaning.

Iti lakkhaṇahāravibhaṅge sattibalānurūpā racitā

Thus, in the Analysis of the Characteristic Mode, this has been composed in accordance with my ability and strength.

Vibhāvanā niṭṭhitā.

The Elucidation is completed.

Paṇḍitehi pana aṭṭhakathāṭīkānusārena gambhīrattho vitthārato vibhajitvā gahetabboti.

However, the profound meaning should be extensively analyzed and grasped by the wise in accordance with the commentaries and sub-commentaries.

6. Catubyūhahāravibhaṅgavibhāvanā

6. Elucidation of the Analysis of the Fourfold Mode

25. Yena yena saṃvaṇṇanāvisesabhūtena lakkhaṇahāravibhaṅgena suttatthehi samānatthā vibhattā, so saṃvaṇṇanāvisesabhūto lakkhaṇahāravibhaṅgo paripuṇṇo, “katamo catubyūhahāravibhaṅgo”ti pucchitabbattā “tattha katamo catubyūho hāro”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha tatthāti tesu niddiṭṭhesu soḷasasu desanāhārādīsu. Katamoti katamo saṃvaṇṇanāviseso catubyūho hāro catubyūhahāravibhaṅgo nāmāti viññeyyo. Tena vuttaṃ – “tattha katamo catubyūho hāroti catubyūhahāravibhaṅgo”ti (netti. aṭṭha. 25). “Iminā catubyūhahārena katamassa [V 0.0277] neruttādayo gavesitabbā”ti pucchitabbattā “byañjanenā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha byañjanenāti catubyūhahārassa suttassa visesato byañjanavicayabhāvato “byañjanā”ti vohāritena iminā catubyūhahārena suttassa neruttañca, suttassa adhippāyo ca, suttassa nidānañca, suttassa pubbāparasandhi ca saṃvaṇṇentehi gavesitabboti attho.

25. Since the analysis of the characteristic mode—which is a specific mode of exposition by which meanings similar to those of the suttas are distinguished—is complete, and because it should be asked, 'What is the analysis of the fourfold mode?', therefore 'Here, what is the fourfold mode?' and so forth, was said. Here, 'there' refers to those sixteen modes of exposition, etc., that have been indicated. 'What' should be understood as: what specific mode of exposition is known as the fourfold mode, the analysis of the fourfold mode? Therefore it is said: 'Here, what is the fourfold mode? It is the analysis of the fourfold mode' (Netti. Aṭṭha. 25). Because it should be asked, 'By this fourfold mode, which aspects such as etymology are to be sought?', 'by the wording,' and so forth, was said. Here, 'by the wording' means that by this fourfold mode—which is called 'wording' because its nature is specifically the examination of the wording of a sutta—the etymology of the sutta, the intention of the sutta, the occasion of the sutta, and the connection between the preceding and following parts of the sutta should be sought by those who are explaining it. This is the meaning.

“Catubyūhahārena [M 0.0145] gavesitabbesu neruttādīsu katamaṃ suttassa gavesitabbaṃ nerutta”nti pucchitabbattā “tattha katamaṃ nerutta”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Tassattho – tattha tesu iminā catubyūhahārena gavesitabbesu neruttādīsu katamaṃ suttassa neruttaṃ nibbacanaṃ nāmāti ce puccheyya? Suttassa yā nirutti niddhāretvā vuttā sabhāvapaññatti gavesitabbā, idaṃ sabhāvaniruttibhūtaṃ nibbacanaṃ neruttaṃ nāmāti. “Yā nirutti neruttaṃ nāmāti vuttā, kā pana sā niruttī”ti pucchitabbattā “padasaṃhitā”ti vuttaṃ. Padesu saṃhitā yuttā padasaṃhitā. Yathā yathā suttattho vattabbo, tathā tathā yā sabhāvanirutti pavattā, sā pavattā sabhāvaniruttiyeva nirutti nāmāti yojanā. “Kā pana sā sabhāvaniruttī”ti pucchitabbattā ca “yaṃ dhammānaṃ nāmaso ñāṇa”nti vuttaṃ. Yaṃ yāya kāraṇabhūtāya nāmapaññattiyā dhammānaṃ neyyānaṃ nāmaso pathavīnāmādinā vā phassanāmādinā vā khandhanāmādinā vā vividhena nāmena atthadhammādīsu kusalassa puggalassa ñāṇaṃ pavattati, sā kāraṇabhūtā nāmapaññatti sabhāvanirutti nāmāti attho. Yanti ca liṅgavipallāso, yāyāti attho. “Liṅgapakatidhammānaṃ nāmaso pavattamānaṃ ñāṇaṃ vivaritvā kathehī”ti vattabbattā “yadā hī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana “yadā hi bhikkhūtiādinā ‘dhammānaṃ nāmaso ñāṇa’nti padassa atthaṃ vivaratī”ti (netti. aṭṭha. 25) vuttaṃ. Tassattho aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vibhajitvā vuttovāti na vicārito.

Because it should be asked, 'Among etymology and so forth, which are to be investigated by the fourfold array, what is the etymology of the sutta to be investigated?', the passage beginning 'Therein, what is etymology?' was stated. Its meaning is this: If one were to ask, 'Therein, among those things such as etymology to be investigated by this fourfold array, what is the etymology of the sutta, its derivation by name?', the answer is: The natural designation, which is the linguistic expression of the sutta stated after having been determined, is to be investigated; this derivation, which has become the natural linguistic expression, is called etymology. Because it should be asked, 'That linguistic expression which is called etymology, what is that linguistic expression?', the phrase 'the connection of words' was stated. 'Padasaṃhitā' is that which is connected and joined in words. The construction is: In whatever way the meaning of the sutta is to be expressed, in that way the natural linguistic expression has occurred; that very natural linguistic expression which has occurred is called 'linguistic expression'. And because it should be asked, 'And what is that natural linguistic expression?', the phrase 'the knowledge of phenomena by name' was stated. The meaning is: That causal name-designation by which knowledge proceeds for a person skilled in the meaning of phenomena, etc., concerning the phenomena to be known, by various names such as the name 'earth,' the name 'contact,' or the name 'aggregate'—that causal name-designation is called the natural linguistic expression. The word 'yaṃ' is a change of gender; the meaning is 'yāya'. Because it should be said, 'Explain the knowledge that proceeds by name concerning phenomena of gender and nature,' the passage beginning 'For when' was stated. In the commentary, however, it is said: 'By the passage beginning "For when, monks," he explains the meaning of the phrase "the knowledge of phenomena by name"' (Netti-aṭṭha. 25). Its meaning has been stated after being analyzed in the commentary, so it is not examined here.

26. Neruttaṃ ācariyena vibhattaṃ, amhehi ca ñātaṃ “katamo sutte gavesitabbo bhagavato adhippāyo”ti pucchitabbattā “tattha katamo adhippāyo”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tassattho pākaṭo. Apica “dhammo have rakkhatī”tiādīsu yena puggalena attanā rakkhitena dhammena rakkhitabbabhāvo icchito, so dhammaṃ rakkhissatīti bhagavato adhippāyo. Yo puggalo duggatito muccitukāmo, so dhammaṃ rakkhissatīti bhagavato adhippāyo.

26. Etymology has been analyzed by the teacher and understood by us. Because it should be asked, 'What intention of the Blessed One is to be sought in the sutta?', the passage beginning 'Therein, what is the intention?' was stated. Its meaning is clear. Furthermore, in passages such as 'The Dhamma, indeed, protects,' the Blessed One's intention is this: that person will protect the Dhamma who desires to be protected by the Dhamma that he himself has protected. The Blessed One's intention is that the person who desires to be freed from a woeful state will protect the Dhamma.

Coro yathā sandhimukhe gahitotiādīsu yo coro ghātanato muccitukāmo, so corakammaṃ na karissatīti bhagavato adhippāyo. Yo puggalo apāyādidukkhato muccitukāmo, so pāpakammaṃ na karissatīti bhagavato adhippāyo.

In passages such as 'Just as a thief is caught at the opening of a housebreaking,' the Blessed One's intention is that the thief who wishes to be freed from execution will not commit the act of theft. The Blessed One's intention is that the person who wishes to be freed from the suffering of the planes of misery and so forth will not commit evil deeds.

Sukhakāmānītiādīsu [V 0.0278][M 0.0146] ye puggalā sukhaṃ icchanti, te parahiṃsanato vivajjissantīti bhagavato adhippāyo.

In passages such as 'desiring happiness,' the Blessed One's intention is that those individuals who desire happiness will abstain from harming others.

Middhī yadā hoti mahagghaso cātiādīsu ye puggalā punappunaṃ pavattamānajātijarāmaraṇato muccitukāmā, te bhojane mattaññuno bhavissanti, santuṭṭhā bhavissanti, suddhājīvā bhavissanti, pātimokkhasaṃvarasīlasampannā bhavissanti, atandino bhavissanti, vipassakā bhavissanti, sagāravā sappatissā bhavissantīti bhagavato adhippāyo.

In passages such as 'When one is drowsy and has a great appetite,' the Blessed One's intention is that those individuals who wish to be freed from repeatedly occurring birth, aging, and death will be moderate in eating, content, pure in livelihood, accomplished in the virtue of the Pātimokkha restraint, diligent, insightful, and respectful and deferential.

Appamādo amatapadantiādīsu ye puggalā maccuno bhāyanti, nibbānamicchanti, te puggalā dānasīlabhāvanākammesu appamattā bhavissantīti bhagavato adhippāyo.

In passages such as 'Heedfulness is the path to the Deathless,' the Blessed One's intention is that those individuals who fear death and desire Nibbāna will be heedful in the deeds of giving, virtue, and mental development.

27. Sutte gavesitabbo adhippāyo ācariyena vibhatto, amhehi ca viññāto, “katamaṃ suttassa gavesitabbaṃ nidāna”nti pucchitabbattā “tattha katamaṃ nidāna”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha nidānanti phalaṃ nīharitvā detīti nidānaṃ. Kiṃ taṃ? Kāraṇaṃ. Dhaniyoti dhanavaḍḍhanakāraṇe niyuttoti dhaniyo. Gopālakoti gāvo issarabhāvena pāleti rakkhatīti gopālako. Upadhīhīti puttagoṇādīhi (su. ni. aṭṭha. 1.33). Narassāti puttimantassa vā gopālakassa vā narassāti ca padaṭṭhānavasena vā yebhuyyavasena vā gāthāyaṃ āgatavasena vā vuttaṃ, nāriyāpi upadhīhi nandanā atthevāti daṭṭhabbā.

27. The intention to be sought in the sutta has been analyzed by the teacher and understood by us. Because it should be asked, 'What origin of the sutta is to be sought?', the passage beginning 'Therein, what is the origin?' was stated. Therein, 'origin' (nidāna) means that which brings forth and gives a result; thus, it is an origin. What is that? A cause. 'Dhaniyo' means one engaged in the cause of increasing wealth; hence, Dhaniyo. 'Gopālako' means one who, as their master, tends and protects cattle; hence, Gopālako. 'Upadhīhi' refers to sons, cattle, and so forth (Snp-a 1.33). 'Narassa' refers to a man, either one with sons or a cowherd; this is stated based on the word's position, on general usage, or on its occurrence in the verse. It should be understood that for a woman, too, there is delight in attachments.

Iminā vatthunāti upadhisaṅkhātena imināva puttagavādinā vatthunā. Vasati pavattati nandanā ettha puttagoṇādiketi vatthu. Nandanaṃ nīharitvā deti puttagoṇādikanti nidānanti atthaṃ gahetvā dhaniyo “upadhīhi narassa nandanā”ti āha. Bhagavā pana “vasati pavattati socanā ettha puttagoṇādikehi vatthu, socanaṃ nīharitvā deti puttagoṇādikanti nidāna”nti atthaṃ gahetvā “upadhīhi narassa socanā”ti āha. Pariggahīyateti pariggahaṃ. Kiṃ taṃ? Puttagoṇādikaṃ, taṃ pariggahaṃ “upadhī”ti āha, na kilesūpadhikāyakhandhūpadhinti.

'By this basis' means by this very basis of sons, cattle, and so forth, which is designated as 'upadhi'. 'Vatthu' (basis) is so called because delight dwells (vasati) and proceeds (pavattati) in it, that is, in sons, cattle, and so forth. Taking the meaning that 'sons, cattle, and so forth bring forth and give delight, hence they are the origin (nidāna),' Dhaniya said, 'For a man, delight is from attachments (upadhi).' The Blessed One, however, taking the meaning that 'vatthu (basis) is so called because sorrow dwells and proceeds in it, that is, in sons, cattle, and so forth, and sons, cattle, and so forth bring forth and give sorrow, hence they are the origin (nidāna),' said, 'For a man, sorrow is from attachments (upadhi).' 'Pariggaha' (possession) is so called because it is possessed. What is that? Sons, cattle, and so forth. That possession he calls 'upadhi,' not the upadhi of defilements or the upadhi of the bodily aggregates.

Upadhīsūti khandhasaṅkhātesu kāyesu. Kāyaṃ “upadhī”ti āha, na puttagavādikaṃ, na pariggahaṃ.

'In the attachments' (upadhīsu) means in the bodies designated as the aggregates. He calls the body 'upadhi,' not sons, cattle, and so forth, nor possessions.

Bāhiresu [M 0.0147] vatthūsūti maṇikuṇḍalaputtadārādīsu vatthūsu.

'In external objects' means in objects such as jewels, earrings, sons, wives, and so forth.

Kāmasukhanti [V 0.0279] kāmanīyesu assādasukhavasena pavattā taṇhā. Bāhiravatthukāya taṇhāyāti kāmanīyesu bāhiravatthūsu assādasukhavasena pavattāya taṇhāya.

'Sensual pleasure' (kāmasukha) is the craving that proceeds by way of the pleasure of gratification in desirable things. 'By craving related to external objects' means by the craving that proceeds by way of the pleasure of gratification in desirable external objects.

Ajjhattikavatthukāyāti rūpakāyasaṅkhāte ajjhattikavatthumhi abhinandanavasena pavattāya.

'By that which is related to an internal basis' means by that (craving) which proceeds by way of delight in the internal basis designated as the material body.

Puna ajjhattikavatthukāyāti pañcakkhandhasaṅkhāte ajjhattikavatthumhi sinehavasena pavattāya.

Again, 'by that which is related to an internal basis' means by that (craving) which proceeds by way of affection for the internal basis designated as the five aggregates.

Gavesitabbaṃ nidānaṃ vibhattaṃ, amhehi ca ñātaṃ, “katamo gavesitabbo pubbāparasandhī”ti pucchitabbattā tattha katamo pubbāparasandhī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha tatthāti tesu neruttādhippāyanidānapubbāparasandhīsu. Yathāti yena andhakārādinā sabhāvena “kāmandhā…pe… mātara”nti yaṃ kāmataṇhaṃ bhagavā āha, ayaṃ kāmataṇhā tathā tena andhakārādinā sabhāvena “kāmandhā…pe… mātara”nti gāthā vuttāti yojanā.

The origin to be investigated has been analyzed, and it has been understood by us. Because it should be asked, 'What is the connection between the preceding and the following that is to be investigated?', the passage beginning 'Therein, what is the connection between the preceding and the following?' was stated. Therein, 'therein' refers to these: etymology, intention, origin, and the connection between preceding and following. The construction is: Just as (yathā), by that nature of causing blindness and so forth, the Blessed One spoke of that sensual craving in the verse 'Blinded by sensual desire... up to... mother,' so too (tathā), because of that same nature of causing blindness and so forth, this sensual craving is why the verse 'Blinded by sensual desire... up to... mother' was spoken.

Gāthāttho pana – kāmetīti kāmo, kāmataṇhā, kāmena atthassa ajānanatāya dhammassa, apassanatāya ca andhāti kāmandhā. Kāmataṇhāsaṅkhātena jālena atthadhammānaṃ ajānanāpassanena sañchannā paliguṇṭhitāti jālasañchannā. Taṇhāsaṅkhātena chadanena tesaṃyeva atthadhammānaṃ ajānanāpassanena chāditā pihitāti taṇhāchadanachāditā. Atthadhammesu pamattasaṅkhātena pamādena bandhanena baddhā bandhitabbā puggalā jarāmaraṇaṃ anventi, kumināmukhe pavattā macchā maraṇaṃ anventi iva ca, khīrapako vaccho mātaraṃ anveti iva ca, tathā jarāmaraṇaṃ anventīti gahetabbo.

The meaning of the verse is as follows: 'Kāmeti' (desires) means kāma (sensual pleasure), which is sensual craving. Due to not knowing the meaning and the Dhamma through sensual desire, and due to not seeing, one is blind—hence 'kāmandhā' (blinded by sensual desire). Covered and enveloped by the net designated as sensual craving, through not knowing or seeing the meaning and the Dhamma—thus 'jālasañchannā' (covered by a net). Shrouded and concealed by the covering designated as craving, through not knowing or seeing those very meanings and the Dhamma—thus 'taṇhāchadanachāditā' (covered by the covering of craving). Individuals who are bound, and are to be bound, by the fetter of heedlessness, which is designated as negligence regarding meaning and Dhamma, follow aging and death. Just as fish that have entered the mouth of a fish-trap follow death, and just as a suckling calf follows its mother, so too do they follow aging and death—this is to be understood.

“Kāmandhā…pe… mātara’nti yāya desanāya, gāthāya vā kāmataṇhā vuttā, sā desanā, gāthā vā katamena desanābhūtena aparena yujjatī”ti pucchitabbattā tathā pucchitvā imāya desanāya, gāthāya vā yujjatīti dassetuṃ “sā katamenā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha sāti “kāmandhā…pe… anventī”ti desanā, gāthā vā. Pubbāparenāti tato desanāto pubbena desanāvacanena, gāthāvacanena vā aparena desanāvacanena, gāthāvacanena vā. Yujjati yujjanaṃ eti sametīti pucchati.

Because it should be asked, 'That teaching or verse, “blinded by sensual desire… up to mother,” by which sensual craving is spoken of, with what other teaching, which serves as a basis for exposition, does it connect?'—having asked thus, to show that it connects with this teaching or verse, 'With what...' and so on was stated. Herein, 'that' refers to the teaching or verse 'blinded by sensual desire… up to 'they follow'.' 'By the preceding and the following' (Pubbāparena) means by a teaching statement or verse statement that precedes, or by a teaching statement or verse statement that follows that teaching. 'Connects' (Yujjati) means it comes together, it fits, it aligns—thus he asks.

Yathāti [M 0.0148] yena andhakaraṇādinā. “Ratto…pe… nara”nti yaṃ gāthāvacanaṃ bhagavā āha, tena gāthāvacanena tathā andhakaraṇādinā yujjatīti yojanā. Gāthāttho pana – ratto rañjanto puggalo atthaṃ attahitapayojanaṃ parahitapayojanaṃ na jānāti. Ratto rañjanto dhammaṃ yathāvuttassa atthassa [V 0.0280] hetuṃ paññācakkhunā na passati. Rāgo yaṃ naraṃ yadā sahate, tadā tassa narassa andhaṃ andhakāraṃ tamaṃ aññāṇaṃ hotīti gahetabbo.

‘Just as’ means by what causes blindness and so on. The verse statement 'one who is impassioned... up to a person' which the Blessed One spoke—by that verse statement, it connects in that same way, by what causes blindness and so on. Such is the connection. The meaning of the verse, however, is: An impassioned person, delighting in passion, does not know the goal, the purpose of one's own welfare and the welfare of others. An impassioned person, delighting in passion, does not see with the eye of wisdom the Dhamma, the cause of the goal as stated. When passion overcomes a person, then for that person there is blindness, darkness, gloom, and ignorance—this is to be understood.

Itīti evaṃ. Andhatāya andhakaraṇatāya sañchannatāya sañchannakaraṇatāya. Sāyeva taṇhāti “kāmandhā…pe… mātara”nti gāthāvacanena yā kāmataṇhā vuttā, sāyeva kāmataṇhā. Abhilapitāti “ratto…pe… nara”nti aparena gāthāvacanena bhagavatā vohāritā voharaṇena ñāpitā, abhilapitassa atthassa samānatā pubbadesanā aparadesanāya yujjatīti vuttaṃ hoti.

'Thus' (iti) means 'in this way' (evaṃ). Due to blindness, due to causing blindness; due to being obscured, due to causing obscuration. 'That very craving' means that very sensual craving which was spoken of by the verse statement 'blinded by sensual desire... up to mother'. 'Declared' (abhilapitā) means that it was expressed by the Blessed One with another verse statement, 'one who is impassioned... up to a person,' and made known by expression. It is said that the earlier teaching connects with the later teaching due to the sameness of the declared meaning.

“Dvīsu gāthāsu katamehi padehi sāyeva taṇhā abhilapitā”ti pucchitabbattā imehi abhilapitāti niyametvā dassetuṃ “yañcāhā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha paṭhamagāthāyaṃ “kāmandhā…pe… chāditā”ti yañca padaṃ āha, dutiyagāthāyañca “ratto…pe… na passatī”ti yañca padaṃ āha. Pariyuṭṭhānehi pariyuṭṭhānadīpakehi imehi “kāmandhā…pe… passatī”ti padehi sāyeva paṭhamagāthāya vuttā kāmataṇhā ca bhagavatā abhilapitā.

Because it should be asked, 'In the two verses, with which words is that same craving declared?'—to show by specifying 'declared' with these words, 'what was said' and so on was stated. Here, in the first verse, the words 'blinded by sensual desire… up to covered' were spoken, and in the second verse, the words 'one who is impassioned… up to does not see' were spoken. With these words, 'blinded by sensual desire… up to does not see,' which indicate obsession, that very sensual craving spoken of in the first verse was also declared by the Blessed One.

“Yaṃ andhakāraṃ vuttaṃ, katamaṃ taṃ? Yā taṇhā ponobhavikā vuttā, katamā sā”ti pucchitabbattā “yaṃ andhakāra”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha andhakāraṃ yaṃ aññāṇaṃ vuttaṃ, ayaṃ dukkhasamudayo bhave. Yā ca taṇhā ponobhavikā vuttā, ayañca dukkhasamudayo bhaveti yojanā.

Because it should be asked, 'What is that darkness that was spoken of? What is that craving leading to renewed existence that was spoken of?'—'the darkness' and so on was stated. Here, the darkness that was spoken of, which is ignorance, this is the origin of suffering in existence. And the craving leading to renewed existence that was spoken of, this also is the origin of suffering in existence—this is the interpretation.

“Kāmā”ti yañca padaṃ bhagavā āha, tena padena ime kilesakāmā vuttā. “Jālasañchannā”ti yañca padaṃ bhagavā āha, tena padena tesaṃyeva kilesakāmānaṃ payogena samudācārena pariyuṭṭhānaṃ bhagavā dasseti. Tasmāti yasmā yasmiṃ santāne taṇhā uppannā, taṃ santānaṃ saṃsārato nissarituṃ adatvā rūpārammaṇādīhi palobhayamānā hutvā cittaṃ kilesehi pariyādāya tiṭṭhati, tasmā taṇhāya cittaṃ pariyādāya santāne tiṭṭhamānattā. Kilesavasenāti vītikkamakilesavasena. Pariyuṭṭhānavasenāti [M 0.0149] vītikkamanaṃ appatvā uppajjamānavasena. Yeti vuttappakārataṇhāsahitapuggalasadisā. Teti te taṇhābandhanabaddhā ca edisakā ca puggalā. Jarāmaraṇaṃ anventi jarāmaraṇaṃ atikkamituṃ na sakkuṇanti. Ayanti jarāmaraṇānuppavatti “jarāmaraṇamanventī”ti iminā vacanena bhagavatā dassitāti yojanā.

By the word 'sensual pleasures' (kāmā) which the Blessed One spoke, these defilements of sensuality were spoken of. By the word 'covered by a net' (jālasañchannā) which the Blessed One spoke, the Blessed One shows the obsession through the application and manifestation of those very defilements of sensuality. 'Therefore' (tasmā) means: because when craving arises in a mental continuum, it does not allow that continuum to escape from saṃsāra, but rather, having become enticing with objects such as forms, it remains overwhelming the mind with defilements; for this reason, craving remains in the continuum, overwhelming the mind. 'By the power of defilements' (kilesavasena) means by the power of defilements involving transgression. 'By the power of obsession' (pariyuṭṭhānavasena) means by the power of arising without reaching transgression. 'Those' (ye) refers to individuals similar to those associated with craving of the described kind. 'They' (te) refers to those individuals who are bound by the fetter of craving and are of such a kind. 'They follow aging and death' (jarāmaraṇaṃ anventi) means they cannot overcome aging and death. 'This' (ayaṃ) refers to the sequence of aging and death—this is shown by the Blessed One’s statement 'they follow aging and death'—such is the connection.

“Kāmandhā”tiādigāthāya ceva “ratto”tiādigāthāya ca pubbāparasandhi ācariyena vibhatto[V 0.0281], amhehi ca ñāto, “kathaṃ ‘yassa papañcā ṭhitī cā’tiādigāthāsu pubbāparasandhi amhehi viññātabbo”ti vattabbattā yassa papañcā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tassā gāthāya – yassa munino papañcā taṇhāmānadiṭṭhī ca natthi, taṇhāmānadiṭṭhīhi abhisaṅkhatā saṅkhārā ca natthi, ṭhitī anusayā taṇhā ca natthi, sandānasadisaṃ taṇhāpariyuṭṭhānaṃ natthi, palighasadiso moho ca natthi, so muni papañcādikaṃ sabbaṃ vītivatto atikkantoti vuccati. Nittaṇhaṃ nimānaṃ nidiṭṭhiṃ nisandānaṃ nipalighaṃ loke carantaṃ taṃ muniṃ sadevako taṇhāsahito loko na vijānātīti attho.

The connection between the preceding and following in the verse beginning with 'blinded by sensual desire' and the verse beginning with 'one who is impassioned' has been explained by the teacher and is known by us. Because it should be stated, 'How should the connection between the preceding and following in the verses beginning with 'whose proliferation and persistence' be understood by us?'—'whose proliferation' and so on was stated. In that verse: For that sage, there is no proliferation, which is craving, conceit, and views; and there are no formations conditioned by craving, conceit, and views; there is no persistence, which is craving as an underlying tendency; there is no obsession of craving, which is like a tether; and there is no delusion, which is like a bar. That sage is said to have gone beyond, to have transcended all proliferation and the like. The meaning is: the world with its deities, which is accompanied by craving, does not know that sage who wanders in the world free from craving, free from conceit, free from views, free from tethers, and free from bars.

Gāthāyaṃ papañcādayo bhagavatā vuttā, “katame te”ti pucchitabbattā “papañcā nāmā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Attano ādhārapuggalaṃ saṃsāre ciraṃ papañcantāpentī taṇhāmānadiṭṭhiyo ca, tāhi taṇhāmānadiṭṭhīhi sahajātavasena vā upatthambhanavasena vā abhisaṅkhatā saṅkhārā ca papañcā nāma. Santāne appahīnaṭṭhena anusayā taṇhā sattānaṃ tiṭṭhanahetuttā ṭhitī nāma. Pavattamānāya taṇhāya yaṃ pariyuṭṭhānañca chattiṃsataṇhāya jāliniyā yāni vicaritāni ca vuttāni, idaṃ sabbaṃ attano ādhāraṃ puggalaṃ bandhanaṭṭhena sandānasadisattā sandānaṃ nāma. Moho attano ādhārassa puggalassa nibbānanagarappavesanassa paṭisedhakattā palighasadisattā paligho nāma. “Yassa papañcādayo natthi, so kiṃ vītivatto”ti pucchitabbattā “ye cā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Ye vuttappakārā papañcā saṅkhārā, yā ca vuttappakārā ṭhiti, yaṃ vuttappakāraṃ sandānañca, yaṃ vuttappakāraṃ palighañca natthīti vuttā, sabbaṃ etaṃ papañcādikaṃ yo muni samatikkanto, ayaṃ muni “nittaṇho”ti vuccatīti daṭṭhabbo.

In the verse, proliferation and the like were spoken of by the Blessed One. Because it should be asked, 'What are these?'—'proliferation' and so on was stated. The cravings, conceits, and views that cause proliferation and torment for the supporting individual in saṃsāra for a long time, and the formations conditioned by them, either by way of co-arising or by way of support—these are called 'proliferation' (papañca). Craving as an underlying tendency, due to its unabandoned nature in the mental continuum, is called 'persistence' (ṭhiti) because it is the cause for beings to persist. The obsession of active craving and the various roamings of the thirty-sixfold web of craving that were described—all this, due to its nature of binding the supporting individual, is similar to a tether, hence called 'tether' (sandāna). Delusion (moha), due to its nature of obstructing the supporting individual from entering the city of Nibbāna, is similar to a bar, hence called 'bar' (paligha). Because it should be asked, 'He for whom proliferation and the like do not exist—what has he transcended?'—'and which' and so on was stated. The sage who has transcended all this proliferation and the like—that is, the proliferations and formations, the persistence, the tether, and the bar of the kind described, which were said to be non-existent—this sage, it should be understood, is called 'one free from craving'.

28. “Yassa papañcātiādigāthāyaṃ ye papañcādayo vuttā, tesu taṇhāmānadiṭṭhihetukā saṅkhārā kadā katividhaṃ phalaṃ denti, taṃsaṅkhārasampayuttā [M 0.0150] taṇhā kadā katividhaṃ phalaṃ detī”ti pucchitabbattā “tattha pariyuṭṭhānasaṅkhārā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha tatthāti tesu papañcasaṅkhārādīsu. Pariyuṭṭhānasaṅkhārāti vītikkamavasena pavattā pariyuṭṭhānā akusalasaṅkhārā cetanā. Diṭṭhadhammavedanīyādīti diṭṭhe passitabbe dhamme attabhāve vedanīyaṃ phalaṃ detīti diṭṭhadhammavedanīyā, diṭṭhe dhamme phalaṃ vedetīti vā diṭṭhadhammavedanīyā. Kā sā? Apadussanīyādīsu atidussanādivasena pavattā paṭhamajavanacetanā. Upapajje phalaṃ vedetīti upapajjavedanīyā, sattamajavanacetanā. Aparāpariyāye attabhāve phalaṃ vedetīti aparāpariyāyavedanīyā, majjhe pavattā pañca javanacetanā. Tiphaladānavasena tividhā saṅkhārā. Evaṃ imāya tividhāya saṅkhāracetanāya sampayuttā tividhā taṇhā tividhaṃ phalaṃ diṭṭhe vā dhamme attabhāve[V 0.0282], upapajje vā anantarabhave, apare vā pariyāye bhave deti nibbattetīti evaṃ phalanibbattakasaṅkhāraṃ vā taṃsampayuttaṃ taṇhaṃ vā bhagavā āha.

28. Because one should ask: 'In the verse beginning "Yassa papañcā…," where proliferations and so on are mentioned, when and how many kinds of results do the formations rooted in craving, conceit, and views produce? And when and how many kinds of results does the craving associated with those formations produce?'—for this reason, the passage beginning 'Therein, the obsessive formations…' was stated. Here, 'therein' refers to those proliferations, formations, and so on. 'Obsessive formations' are unwholesome formations, that is, volitions (cetanā) that occur by way of transgression. 'To be experienced in this very life' (diṭṭhadhammavedanīya) means it gives a result to be experienced in the present existence, or it causes a result to be experienced in the present existence. What is that? It is the first impulsion-volition that arises as extreme corruption, etc., in cases of non-corruption, etc. 'To be experienced upon rebirth' (upapajjavedanīya) is the seventh impulsion-volition, which gives its result in the next existence. 'To be experienced in some subsequent existence' (aparāpariyāyavedanīya) are the five intermediate impulsion-volitions, which give their result in a future existence. Thus, the formations are threefold in that they give three kinds of results. In this way, the threefold craving associated with these threefold formational volitions produces a threefold result—either in this very life, or in the immediately following existence, or in some subsequent existence. Thus the Blessed One spoke of the formations that produce results or the craving associated with them.

“Yāya desanāya, gāthāya vā phalanibbattakaṃ saṅkhāraṃ āha, sā desanā, gāthā vā katamena desanābhūtena vā aparena yujjatī”ti pucchitabbattā “yaṃ lobhapakataṃ kammaṃ karotī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Yā “yassa…pe… loko”ti desanā ca yā “yaṃ lobhapakataṃ kammaṃ…pe… apare vā pariyāye”ti desanā ca vuttā, bhagavato idaṃ desanādvayaṃ aññamaññaṃ pubbāparena pubbaṃ aparena aparaṃ pubbena yujjati yujjanaṃ eti sameti, yathā gaṅgodakaṃ yamunodakena, yamunodakampi gaṅgodakena saṃsandati sameti. “Yassa…pe… loko”ti desanā “yaṃ lobhapakataṃ…pe… pariyāye”ti desanāya saṃsandati sameti, “yaṃ lobhapakataṃ…pe… pariyāye”ti desanāpi “yassa…pe… loko”ti desanāya saṃsandati sametīti attho gahetabbo. “Kathaṃ yujjatī”ti pucchitabbattā “tattha pariyuṭṭhāna”ntiādi vuttaṃ, diṭṭhadhammavedanīyādiphalattayanibbattakaṭṭhena yujjatīti vuttaṃ hoti.

Because one should ask: 'The teaching or verse by which he spoke of the formation that produces a result—with what other kind of teaching does that teaching or verse connect?'—for this reason, the passage beginning 'Whatever kamma is performed out of greed…' was stated. The teaching 'For whom… the world' and the teaching 'Whatever kamma is performed out of greed… or in some subsequent existence' have both been stated. These two teachings of the Blessed One connect with each other, the former with the latter and the latter with the former; they come together and meet, just as the water of the Ganges flows together and meets with the water of the Yamunā, and the water of the Yamunā flows together and meets with the water of the Ganges. The meaning should be understood thus: the teaching 'For whom… the world' flows together and meets with the teaching 'Whatever kamma is performed out of greed… or in some subsequent existence,' and the teaching 'Whatever kamma is performed out of greed… or in some subsequent existence' also flows together and meets with the teaching 'For whom… the world.' Because one should ask, 'How does it connect?' the passage beginning 'Therein, the obsession…' was stated. This means that it is said to connect in the sense of producing the triad of results: to be experienced in this very life, and so on.

Yaṃ yaṃ suttaṃ bhagavatā desitaṃ pubbāparena yujjati, taṃ taṃ suttampi nīharitvā pubbāparasaṃsandanaṃ dassetuṃ “yathāhā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Saṃsandanākāro vuttanayānusārena gahetabbo. Tatthāti tesu pariyuṭṭhānasaṅkhārataṇhāvicaritesu. Pariyuṭṭhānanti rūpārammaṇādīni ayonisomanasikārena ārabbha sattasantāne pavattaṃ taṇhācaritaṃ. Paṭisaṅkhānabalenāti [M 0.0151] asubhāniccādidassanabalena tadaṅgappahānavasena pahātabbaṃ. Saṅkhārāti dassanapahātabbā saṅkhārā. Dassanabalenāti dassanasaṅkhātapaṭhamamaggañāṇabalena pahātabbā. Chattiṃsa taṇhāvicaritānīti dassanena pahātabbataṇhāvicaritehi avasesāni chattiṃsa taṇhāvicaritāni. Niggatā taṇhā yassa so nittaṇho, nittaṇhassa bhāvo nittaṇhatā, kā sā? Saupādisesā nibbānadhātu.

To show the connection between the earlier and later parts by extracting whatever sutta taught by the Blessed One connects in its earlier and later parts, the passage beginning 'As he said…' was stated. The mode of connection should be understood according to the method stated. 'Therein' refers to these: obsession, formations, and courses of craving. 'Obsession' is the course of craving that arises in a being's continuity, taking as its object forms, etc., through unwise attention. 'By the power of reflection' means: it is to be abandoned by the power of seeing the foul, impermanence, etc., by way of abandonment by suppression of the specific factor. 'Formations' are the formations to be abandoned by seeing. 'By the power of seeing' means: they are to be abandoned by the power of the knowledge of the first path, which is called 'seeing.' 'The thirty-six courses of craving' are the thirty-six courses of craving that remain after those to be abandoned by seeing. 'He for whom craving has departed is one without craving (nittaṇho).' The state of one without craving is 'freedom from craving' (nittaṇhatā). What is that? It is the Nibbāna-element with residue remaining.

Papañcasaṅkhārābhinandanattayaṃ yadipi atthato ekaṃ samānaṃ, desanāya pana padakkharādīhi viseso atthīti dassetuṃ “apicā”tiādi vuttaṃ.

To show that although the triad of proliferation, formations, and delighting are one and the same in meaning, there is a difference in the teaching in terms of words, syllables, and so on, the passage beginning 'Furthermore…' was stated.

“Yoyaṃ pubbāparasandhi ācariyena vibhatto, soyaṃ katividho”ti pucchitabbattā “so cāyaṃ pubbāparo sandhī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana vuttaṃ – “na kevalaṃ suttantarasaṃsandanameva pubbāparasandhi, atha kho aññopi atthīti dassetuṃ ‘so cāya’ntiādi vutta”nti (netti. aṭṭha. 28). Tattha atthasandhīti kiriyākārakādivasena atthassa atthena sandhi. Padasandhīti nāmapadādikassa [V 0.0283] nāmapadādikantarena sandhi. Desanāsandhīti vuttappakārassa desanantarassa vuttappakārena desanantarena sandhi. Niddesasandhīti niddesantarassa niddesantarena sandhi.

Because one should ask: 'This connection between the earlier and later parts that has been analyzed by the teacher—of how many kinds is it?'—for this reason, the passage beginning 'And this connection between the earlier and later parts…' was stated. But in the commentary it is said: 'To show that the connection between the earlier and later parts is not merely the connection between different suttas, but that there is also another kind, the passage beginning "And this…" was stated' (Netti-aṭṭha 28). Therein, 'connection of meaning' is the connection of a meaning with a meaning by way of action, agent, and so on. 'Connection of terms' is the connection of a nominal term, etc., with another nominal term, etc. 'Connection of teachings' is the connection of one teaching of a stated type with another teaching of a stated type. 'Connection of exposition' is the connection of one exposition with another exposition.

Sandhi ca nāma atthādayo muñcitvā añño sabhāvadhammo nāma natthi, atthādīnañca chaatthapadādīsu avarodhanato “atthasandhi chappadānī”tiādi vuttaṃ.

A 'connection' is not some other phenomenon with its own intrinsic nature apart from meaning and so on. And because meaning and so on are included within the six items beginning with the term 'meaning,' the passage beginning 'The connection of meaning has six terms…' was stated.

Atthasandhibyañjanasandhayo ācariyena vibhattā, amhehi ca ñātā, “katamā desanāsandhī”ti pucchitabbattā “desanāsandhi na ca pathavi”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha na ca pathaviṃ nissāya jhāyati jhāyī jhāyati cāti ettha jhāyī jhānasamaṅgī puggalo pathaviṃ nissāya ālambitvā na ca jhāyati, sabbasaṅkhāranissaṭaṃ pana nibbānaṃ nissāya ālambitvā phalasamāpattiṃ jhāyati samāpajjati evāti attho daṭṭhabbo. Na ca āpantiādīsupi esa nayo yojetabbo. Phalasamāpattisamaṅgī puggalo hi pathavīādayo muñcitvā nibbānameva ārabbha phalasamāpattiṃ samāpajjatīti. Ettha ca pathavīādīhi mahābhūtehi kāmabhavarūpabhavā gahitā rūpapaṭibaddhavuttitāya. Ākāsānañcāyatanādīhipi arūpabhavo gahito, bhavattayaṃ vajjetvā ca [M 0.0152] jhāyatīti adhippāyo. Yadi pathavīādayo nissāya na jhāyī jhāyati ca, evaṃ sati idhalokasaṅkhātaṃ sattasantānaṃ vā paralokasaṅkhātaṃ sattasantānaṃ vā anindriyasantānaṃ vā nissāya jhāyī jhāyatīti āsaṅkanīyattā taṃ pariharanto “na ca imaṃ loka”ntiādimāha. Tattha imaṃ lokanti idhalokasaṅkhāto diṭṭho attabhāvo sattasantāno vutto, tasmiṃ nissāya na jhāyati jhāyī jhāyati ca. Paralokanti idhalokato añño bhavantarasaṅkhāto sattasantāno vutto, tasmiṃ nissāya na ca jhāyati jhāyī jhāyati ca.

The connections of meaning and phrasing have been analyzed by the teacher and understood by us. Because one should ask, 'What is the connection of teaching?' the passage beginning 'The connection of teaching: not depending on earth…' was stated. Here, in the phrase 'a meditator does not meditate depending on earth, and yet he meditates,' the meaning should be understood thus: the meditator, a person endowed with jhāna, does not meditate by depending on the earth element and taking it as an object; rather, having departed from all formations, he meditates and enters into the attainment of fruition, depending on Nibbāna and taking it as his object. This same method should be applied in the cases of 'nor water,' and so on. For a person endowed with the attainment of fruition, having relinquished the earth element and so on, enters the attainment of fruition taking Nibbāna alone as his object. Here, by the great elements—earth, etc.—the sense-sphere existence and the form-sphere existence are included, as their occurrence is bound up with form. By the base of the infinity of space, etc., the formless existence is included. The intention is that one meditates having avoided the three kinds of existence. If a meditator does not meditate depending on the earth element, etc., and yet he meditates, one might suspect that the meditator meditates depending on the continuity of beings called 'this world,' or the continuity of beings called 'the next world,' or a continuity without faculties. To ward this off, he says, 'nor this world,' and so on. Here, 'this world' refers to the visible individual existence, the continuity of beings. The meditator does not meditate depending on that, and yet he meditates. 'The next world' refers to the continuity of beings in another existence apart from this world. The meditator does not meditate depending on that, and yet he meditates.

Yamidaṃ ubhayantiādīsu idaṃ ubhayaṃ idhalokaparalokadvayaṃ antarena vajjetvā yaṃ rūpāyatanaṃ diṭṭhaṃ, taṃ rūpāyatanampi. Yaṃ saddāyatanaṃ sutaṃ, taṃ saddāyatanampi. Yaṃ gandhāyatanarasāyatanaphoṭṭhabbāyatanaṃ mutaṃ, taṃ gandhāyatanarasāyatanaphoṭṭhabbāyatanampi. Yaṃ āpodhātu ākāsadhātu lakkhaṇarūpaṃ ojāsaṅkhātaṃ dhammāyatanekadesarūpaṃ viññātaṃ, taṃ āpodhātādikaṃ dhammāyatanekadesarūpampi. Yaṃ vatthu pariyesitaṃ vā apariyesitaṃ vā santike pattaṃ, taṃ vatthumpi. Yaṃ vatthu pattaṃ vā appattaṃ vā pariyesitaṃ pariyesanārahaṃ sundaraṃ, taṃ vatthumpi. Yaṃ vatthu vitakkitaṃ vitakkanavasena ālambitabbaṃ, taṃ vatthumpi. Yaṃ vatthu vicāritaṃ anumajjanavasena ālambitabbaṃ, taṃ vatthumpi. Yaṃ vatthu manasā citteneva anucintitaṃ anucintanavasena ālambitabbaṃ, taṃ vatthumpi nissāya na jhāyati jhāyī jhāyati cāti yojanā kātabbā.

In the passage beginning 'Whatever is this duality…': having excluded this duality—the pair of this world and the next—the connection should be made thus: A meditator does not meditate depending on whatever form base is seen, nor on whatever sound base is heard, nor on whatever odor, taste, and tangible bases are sensed; nor on whatever water element, space element, characteristic form, the form called nutriment, or portion of form included in the mental-phenomena base is cognized; nor on whatever object, sought or unsought, has come near; nor on whatever object, attained or unattained, is sought, worthy of being sought, beautiful; nor on whatever object is thought of, to be taken as an object by way of thinking; nor on whatever object is examined, to be taken as an object by way of examination; nor on whatever object is reflected upon by the mind, by consciousness itself, to be taken as an object by way of reflection—and yet he meditates.

Ettha [V 0.0284] diṭṭhādikaṃ bahiddhārūpameva gahetabbaṃ anindriyabaddharūpassa adhippetattā. Tenāha aṭṭhakathācariyo – “tadubhayavinimutto anindriyabaddho rūpasantāno”ti (netti. aṭṭha. 28). “Yadi jhāyī puggalo yathāvutte pathavīādayo nissāya na jhāyati jhāyī jhāyati ca, evaṃ sati ayaṃ jhāyī puggalo idaṃ nāma nissāya jhāyatīti loke kenaci ñāyati kiṃ, udāhu na ñāyatī”ti pucchitabbattā na ñāyatīti dassetuṃ “ayaṃ sadevake loke”tiādimāha. Tattha phalasamāpattijhānena jhāyanto ayaṃ khīṇāsavapuggalo sadevake loke…pe… sadevamanussāya pajāya yattha katthacipi anissitena cittena jhāyatīti sadevake loke…pe… sadevamanussāya [M 0.0153] pajāya kenaci na ñāyatīti attho gahetabbo. Tena vuttaṃ –

Here, what is seen and so on should be taken only as external form, since what is intended is form not bound up with the sense faculties. Therefore the Commentator said: “A continuum of form liberated from both and not bound up with the sense faculties” (Netti-aṭṭha. 28). Because it should be asked: “If a meditator does not meditate depending on the earth element and so on as stated, and yet the meditator does meditate, in that case is it known by anyone in the world that ‘this meditator meditates depending on this,’ or is it not known?”—to show that it is not known, he said: “this one in this world with its gods….” Here, this one whose taints are destroyed, meditating with the jhāna of the attainment of fruition, meditates with a mind that is not dependent on anything anywhere in this world with its gods… (pe)… with its generation of gods and humans; thus it is not known by anyone in this world with its gods… (pe)… with its generation of gods and humans. This is the meaning to be taken. Therefore it is said:

“Namo te purisājañña, namo te purisuttama;

Yassa te nābhijānāma, kiṃ tvaṃ nissāya jhāyasī”ti. (saṃ. ni. 3.79; netti. 104);

“Homage to you, O thoroughbred of men, homage to you, O supreme man; we do not know what you rely on to meditate.”

“Kenaci aviññāyabhāvo kena suttena vibhāvetabbo”ti pucchitabbattā iminā godhikasuttena (saṃ. ni. 1.159) vibhāvetabboti dassetuṃ “yathā māro pāpimā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana “idāni khīṇāsavacittassa katthacipi anissitabhāvaṃ godhikasuttena (saṃ. ni. 1.159) vakkalisuttena (saṃ. ni. 3.87) ca vibhāvetuṃ ‘yathā māro’tiādi vutta”nti (netti. aṭṭha. 28) vuttaṃ. Tattha dānādipuññakārake, puññe vā māreti nivāretīti māro, attahitaparahite māretīti vā māro. Pāpacittuppādavantatāya pāpimā. Pubbattabhāve godhassa ghātakattā “godhiko”ti laddhanāmassa parinibbāyantassa kulaputtassa parinibbānato uddhaṃ paṭisandhādi viññāṇaṃ samanvesanto na jānāti na passati. “Paracittajānanako māro kasmā na jānātī”ti vattabbattā “so hī”tiādi vuttaṃ. So godhiko hi yasmā papañcātīto, tasmā taṇhāpahānena diṭṭhinissayopi assa godhikassa yasmā natthi, tasmā ca na jānātīti.

Because it should be asked: “By which sutta should the state of not being known by anyone be explained?”—to show that it should be explained by this Godhika Sutta (SN 4.23), it is said: “as Māra the Evil One…,” etc. But in the Commentary it is said: “Now, to explain by means of the Godhika Sutta (SN 4.23) and the Vakkali Sutta (SN 22.87) the non-dependence on anything of the mind of one whose taints are destroyed, it is said: ‘as Māra…,’ etc.” (Netti-aṭṭha. 28). Here, Māra is so called because he kills (māreti) or obstructs merit in one who performs meritorious deeds such as giving, or he kills what is for one’s own welfare and the welfare of others. He is the Evil One (pāpimā) because he possesses the arising of evil thoughts. Because in a former existence he was a killer of iguanas (godha), the clansman who obtained the name “Godhika” was attaining final Nibbāna. After his final Nibbāna, Māra, searching for his relinking consciousness, etc., does not know, does not see. Because it should be said: “Since Māra knows the minds of others, why does he not know?”—it is said: “For he…,” etc. For since that Godhika has transcended proliferation, and since, through the abandoning of craving, he has no dependence on views, therefore Māra does not know.

“Godhikasutteneva vibhāvetabbo”ti pucchitabbattā “yathā cā”tiādi vuttaṃ. “Godhikasuttavakkalisuttehi anupādisesāya nibbānadhātuyā anissitabhāvo vibhāvito, evaṃ sati saupādisesanibbānadhātuyā anissitabhāvo kena viññāyatīti attho bhaveyyā”ti vattabbattā tadāpi na viññāyatiyevāti dassetuṃ “sadevakena lokenā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha saupādisesāya nibbānadhātuyā phalasamāpattijhānena jhāyamānā ime khīṇāsavā katthaci anissitacittā [V 0.0285] jhāyantīti sadevakena lokena na ñāyanti samārakena…pe… sadevamanussāya na ñāyantīti yojanā kātabbā. Anissitacittā na ñāyantīti ettha hi na-kāro ca “jhāyamānā”ti pade na sambandhitabbo “na jhāyamānā”ti atthassa sambhavato. “Na ñāyantī”ti pana sambandhitabbo [M 0.0154] heṭṭhā aṭṭhakathāyaṃ eva “loke kenacipi na ñāyatī”ti vuttattā. Ayaṃ desanāsandhīti godhikasuttavakkalisuttānaṃ aññamaññaṃ atthavasena saṃsandanā niddhāritā viya “na ca pathaviṃ nissāyā”tiādidesanāya ca “na ca imaṃ loka”ntiādidesanāya ca yāya desanāya atthavasena saṃsandanā niddhāritā, tāya desanāya yattha katthaci yaṃ kiñci nissāya jhāyī na jhāyati, nibbānaṃ nissāya jhāyī jhāyatīti atthavasena niddhāritā, ayaṃ saṃsandanā desanāsandhi nāmāti attho gahetabbo.

Because it should be asked: “Should it be explained only by the Godhika Sutta?”—it is said: “and as…,” etc. Because it should be said: “By the Godhika Sutta and the Vakkali Sutta the non-dependence of the Nibbāna-element without residue remaining is explained. This being so, by what is the non-dependence of the Nibbāna-element with residue remaining known? This would be the meaning.”—to show that even then it is not known, it is said: “by the world with its gods…,” etc. Here, the construction should be made thus: these whose taints are destroyed, meditating with the jhāna of the attainment of fruition in regard to the Nibbāna-element with residue remaining, meditate with a mind that is not dependent on anything, so they are not known by the world with its gods, with its Māra… (pe)… with its generation of gods and humans. Here, in the phrase ‘they are not known as having a non-dependent mind’ (anissitacittā na ñāyanti), the negative particle ‘na’ should not be connected with the word ‘meditating’ (jhāyamānā), since the meaning would be ‘not meditating.’ Rather, it should be connected with ‘are not known’ (na ñāyanti), because it was said below in the Commentary: ‘it is not known by anyone in the world.’ This is the connection of teaching: just as the mutual connection of the Godhika Sutta and the Vakkali Sutta is determined by way of meaning, so too, by the teaching ‘not depending on earth…,’ etc., and by the teaching ‘not this world…,’ etc., by which teaching the connection is determined by way of meaning, by that teaching it is determined by way of meaning that a meditator does not meditate depending on anything anywhere, but a meditator meditates depending on Nibbāna. This connection is called the connection of teaching; this is the meaning to be taken.

Desanāsandhi ācariyena vibhattā, amhehi ca ñātā, “katamā niddesasandhī”ti pucchitabbattā “tattha katamā niddesasandhīti nissitacittā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha tatthāti tesu catūsu atthasandhibyañjanasandhidesanāsandhiniddesasandhīsu yā sandhi “niddesasandhī”ti uddiṭṭhā, sā niddesato katamāti pucchatīti attho. Nissitacittāti taṇhādiṭṭhisahajātavasena vā upanissayavasena vā nissitaṃ cittaṃ yesaṃ puthujjanānanti nissitacittā, puthujjanā puggalā niddisitabbā imāya desanāya puggalādhiṭṭhānattā.
