Yadi desanā dhammādhiṭṭhānā, evaṃ sati nissitaṃ cittaṃ ettha suttappadesesu desitanti nissitacittā nissitacittajānanatthāya desitā suttappadesā. Anissitaṃ cittaṃ yesaṃ ariyapuggalānanti anissitacittā, ariyapuggalā niddisitabbā imāya desanāya puggalādhiṭṭhānattā. Dhammādhiṭṭhānāya pana anissitaṃ cittaṃ yattha suttappadesesu desitanti anissitacittā, anissitacittajānanatthāya desitā suttappadesā.

The connection of teaching has been analyzed by the Teacher and is known by us. Because it should be asked: “What is the connection of exposition?”—it is said: “Therein, what is the connection of exposition? The dependent mind…,” etc. Here, the meaning of the question is: among these four connections—the connection of meaning, of phrasing, of teaching, and of exposition—the connection that was designated as ‘the connection of exposition,’ what is it by way of exposition? ‘Dependent mind’ (nissitacittā): worldlings are those who have a dependent mind, a mind that depends by way of co-nascent craving and views or by way of decisive support. These worldlings are to be indicated, since this teaching is founded on persons. If the teaching is founded on phenomena, in that case ‘dependent mind’ refers to the passages of the suttas where the dependent mind is taught; they are taught for the purpose of knowing the dependent mind. ‘Non-dependent mind’ (anissitacittā): noble persons are those who have a non-dependent mind. These noble persons are to be indicated, since this teaching is founded on persons. But when it is founded on phenomena, ‘non-dependent mind’ refers to the passages of the suttas where the non-dependent mind is taught; they are taught for the purpose of knowing the non-dependent mind.

“Nissitacittā kena niddesena niddisitabbā, anissitacittā kena niddesena niddisitabbā”ti pucchitabbattā “nissitacittā akusalapakkhena niddisitabbā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Akusalapakkhena niddesena niddisitabbā. Kusalapakkhenātiādīsupi esa nayo yojetabbo. Akusalapakkhasāmaññakusalapakkhasāmaññehi dassetvā akusalavisesakusalavisesehi dassetuṃ “nissitacittā saṃkilesenā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Ayaṃ niddesasandhīti akusalapakkhādikassa purimaniddesassa saṃkilesādikena pacchimena niddesena nissitacittavasena ayaṃ saṃsandanā ca niddesasandhi nāma. Kusalapakkhādikassa purimassa niddesassa vodānādikena pacchimena niddesena anissitacittavasena ayaṃ saṃsandanā ca niddesasandhi nāmāti vibhajitvā veditabbā.

Because it should be asked: “By what exposition should the dependent mind be expounded? By what exposition should the non-dependent mind be expounded?”—it is said: “The dependent mind should be expounded by the unwholesome side…,” etc. It should be expounded by the exposition of the unwholesome side. This method should be applied also in the cases of the wholesome side, etc. Having shown them by the general unwholesome side and the general wholesome side, to show them by the specific unwholesome and the specific wholesome, it is said: “The dependent mind is by way of defilement…,” etc. This is the connection of exposition: this connection of the former exposition, of the unwholesome side, etc., with the latter exposition, of defilement, etc., by way of the dependent mind, is called the connection of exposition. This connection of the former exposition, of the wholesome side, etc., with the latter exposition, of cleansing, etc., by way of the non-dependent mind, is also called the connection of exposition. This should be understood by making this division.

“Catubyūhahārassa [V 0.0286][M 0.0155] neruttamadhippāyanidānapubbāparasandhippabhedena ceva atthabyañjanasandhiniddesasandhidesanāsandhippabhedena ca vibhajitabbabhāvo kena amhehi jānitabbo saddahitabbo”ti vattabbabhāvato “tenāhā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha tena tathā vibhajitabbabhāvena āyasmā mahākaccāno “neruttamadhippāyo”tiādikaṃ (netti. 4 hārasaṅkhepa) yaṃ vacanaṃ āha, tena vacanena tumhehi catubyūhahārassa tathā vibhajitabbabhāvo jānitabbo saddahitabboti vuttaṃ hoti.

Because it should be said: “By what means should we know and have faith that the Fourfold Array mode is to be analyzed by the divisions of linguistic analysis, intention, source, and the connection of prior and posterior, and by the divisions of the connection of meaning, the connection of phrasing, the connection of exposition, and the connection of teaching?”—it is said: “Therefore he said…,” etc. Therein, it is meant that by the statement beginning “linguistic analysis, intention…” (Netti. p. 4), which the Venerable Mahākaccāna spoke, you should know and have faith that the Fourfold Array mode is to be analyzed in that way, because it is to be analyzed in that way.

“Ettāvatā ca catubyūhahāro paripuṇṇo, añño niyutto natthī”ti vattabbattā “niyutto catubyūho hāro”ti vuttaṃ. Tattha yassaṃ yassaṃ pāḷiyaṃ yo yo catubbidho, so so catubyūhahāro ca yathālābhavasena yojito, tassaṃ tassaṃ pāḷiyaṃ so so catubbidho catubyūhahāro tathā niddhāretvā yutto yojitoti attho daṭṭhabbo.

Because it should be said: “To this extent the Fourfold Array mode is complete; there is no other that is appointed,” it is said: “The Fourfold Array mode is appointed.” Here, the meaning should be seen thus: in whatever Pāḷi text there is something that is fourfold, that is the Fourfold Array mode, and it is applied according to how it is found. In whatever Pāḷi text that fourfold thing is, that Fourfold Array mode, having been determined thus, is applied, is yoked.

Iti catubyūhahāravibhaṅge sattibalānurūpā racitā

Thus in the Analysis of the Fourfold Array mode, this was composed in accordance with my ability and strength.

Vibhāvanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation is finished.

Paṇḍitehi pana aṭṭhakathāṭīkānusārena gambhīrattho vitthārato vibhajitvā gahetabboti.

But the profound meaning should be analyzed in detail and grasped by the wise in accordance with the commentaries and subcommentaries.

7. Āvaṭṭahāravibhaṅgavibhāvanā

7. Elucidation of the Analysis of the Reversion Method

29. Yena yena saṃvaṇṇanāvisesabhūtena catubyūhahāravibhaṅgena neruttādayo vibhattā, so…pe… catubyūhahāravibhaṅgo paripuṇṇo, “katamo āvaṭṭo hāravibhaṅgo”ti pucchitabbattā tattha katamo āvaṭṭo hāro”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha tatthāti tesu niddiṭṭhesu soḷasasu desanāhārādīsu katamo saṃvaṇṇanāviseso āvaṭṭo hāro āvaṭṭahāravibhaṅgo nāmāti pucchati. “Ekamhi padaṭṭhāne”ntiādiniddesassa idāni mayā vuccamāno “ārambhathā”tiādiko vitthārasaṃvaṇṇanāviseso āvaṭṭahāravibhaṅgo nāmāti gahito. “Tattha desanāyaṃ [M 0.0156] ekasmiṃ padaṭṭhāne [V 0.0287] desanāruḷhe sesakaṃ padaṭṭhānaṃ pariyesati, pariyesitvā kathaṃ paṭipakkhe āvaṭṭetī”ti vattabbattā –

29. By whatever particular descriptive quality the analysis of the fourfold method has analyzed etymology and so on, that ...pe... analysis of the fourfold method is complete. Since it should be asked, 'What is the analysis of the reversion method?' it is therefore said, 'What is the reversion method?' and so on. Herein, among those sixteen specified methods beginning with the teaching method, it is asked: 'What particular descriptive quality is the reversion method, called the analysis of the reversion method?' The detailed particular descriptive quality beginning with 'Strive...', which I will now state, is taken as the analysis of the reversion method for the exposition beginning 'In one foundation...'. Because it is to be stated: 'Here, in the teaching, when one foundation is established in the teaching, one seeks the remaining foundation. Having sought it, how does one turn it back against its opposite?'—

“Ārambhatha nikkamatha, yuñjatha buddhasāsane;

Dhunātha maccuno senaṃ, naḷāgāraṃva kuñjaro”ti. –

“Strive, go forth, apply yourselves in the Buddha’s dispensation; shake off the army of Death, as an elephant does a reed hut.”

Gāthā vuttā. Idha gāthāyaṃ ekasmiṃ padaṭṭhāne desanāruḷhe sesakaṃ padaṭṭhānaṃ pariyesatīti vuttaṃ hoti. Gāthāttho pana aṭṭhakathāyaṃ (netti. aṭṭha. 29) vutto.

The verse has been stated. Here, in this verse, it is said that when one foundation is established in the teaching, one seeks the remaining foundation. The meaning of the verse, however, is explained in the commentary (Netti. Aṭṭha. 29).

“Ārambhathā’tiādigāthāyaṃ katarasmiṃ padaṭṭhāne desanāruḷhe katamaṃ sesakaṃ padaṭṭhānaṃ pariyesatī”ti vattabbattā “ārambhatha nikkamathāti vīriyassa padaṭṭhāna”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha “vīriyassa padaṭṭhāna”nti sāmaññavasena vuttampi ārambhadhātusaṅkhātaṃ vīriyaṃ nikkamadhātusaṅkhātassa vīriyassa padaṭṭhānaṃ, nikkamadhātusaṅkhātaṃ vīriyaṃ parakkamadhātusaṅkhātassa vīriyassa padaṭṭhānaṃ, parakkamadhātusaṅkhātaṃ vīriyaṃ samathabhāvanāsahitassa vīriyassa padaṭṭhānantiādinā pariyesitabbanti gahetabbaṃ. “Yuñjathā”ti iminā vuttaṃ samathabhāvanāsahitaṃ vīriyaṃ “buddhasāsane”ti iminā vuttassa mahaggatasamādhissa padaṭṭhānaṃ, desanāruḷhaṃ sukhādikaṃ sesakampi padaṭṭhānaṃ pariyesitabbaṃ. “Dhunātha maccuno sena”nti padena gahitaṃ vipassanāsahitaṃ vīriyaṃ kilesadhunane samatthāya paññāya padaṭṭhānaṃ, desanāruḷhaṃ samādhiādikaṃ sesakampi padaṭṭhānaṃ pariyesitabbaṃ.

Since it should be stated, 'In the verse beginning with “Strive,” on which foundation is the teaching established, and what remaining foundation does one seek?' it is said: '“Strive, go forth” is the foundation of energy,' and so on. Here, although 'the foundation of energy' is stated in a general sense, it should be understood that the energy reckoned as the element of initiative is the foundation for the energy reckoned as the element of exertion; the energy reckoned as the element of exertion is the foundation for the energy reckoned as the element of striving; and the energy reckoned as the element of striving is the foundation for the energy accompanied by the development of serenity, and so on, which are to be sought. The energy accompanied by the development of serenity, stated by 'Apply yourselves,' is the foundation for the exalted concentration stated by 'in the Buddha’s dispensation'; the remaining foundation, such as the pleasant, on which the teaching is established, should also be sought. The energy accompanied by insight, taken by the phrase 'Shake off the army of Death,' is the foundation for the wisdom capable of shaking off the defilements; the remaining foundation, such as concentration, on which the teaching is established, should also be sought.

“Yadi ‘ārambhathā’tiādikaṃ vuttaṃ vīriyaṃ sāmaññabhūtānaṃ vīriyasamādhipaññānaṃyeva padaṭṭhānaṃ siyā, evaṃ sati kathaṃ vaṭṭamūlaṃ chinditvā vivaṭṭaṃ pāpessantī”ti vattabbattā puna “ārambhatha nikkamathāti vīriyindriyassa padaṭṭhāna”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Ādhipaccakiccatāya yuttassāpi vīriyādhikassa padaṭṭhānattā ārabhantā yogāvacarapuggalā vaṭṭamūlaṃ chinditvā vivaṭṭaṃ pāpentīti vuttaṃ hoti. “Ārambhathā”tiādikā pana yasmā vīriyārambhavatthuādidesanā hoti, tasmā ārambhavatthuādīniyeva saṃvaṇṇitāni padaṭṭhānanti codanaṃ manasi katvā āha “imāni padaṭṭhānāni desanā”ti. “Ārambhathā”tiādikā yathāvuttapadaṭṭhānāni desanā hoti, na vīriyārambhavatthuādīni, tasmā padaṭṭhānaṃyeva saṃvaṇṇitanti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Since it could be said: 'If the energy spoken of beginning with “Strive” were the foundation only for the general energy, concentration, and wisdom, in that case how would they cut off the root of the round and attain the unrounding?' it was again said: '“Strive, go forth” is the foundation for the faculty of energy,' and so on. It is said that because it is a foundation even for one with a predominance of energy, owing to its function of sovereignty, striving practitioners of yoga cut off the root of the round and attain the unrounding. However, since the passage beginning 'Strive' is a teaching on the grounds for arousing energy, etc., having considered the objection that it is these grounds for arousing energy, etc., that are being described as the foundation, he said: 'These foundations are the teaching.' It should be understood that the passage beginning 'Strive' is a teaching on the foundations as stated, not on the grounds for arousing energy, etc.; therefore, it is the foundation itself that is described.

Evaṃ [M 0.0157] “ārambhathā”tiādidesanāya padaṭṭhānavasena attho vibhatto, amhehi ca ñāto, “kathaṃ tassāyeva desanāya paṭipakkhavasena attho vibhajitabbo”ti vattabbattā “ayuñjantānaṃ vā”tiādi [V 0.0288] vuttaṃ. Tattha yoge bhāvanāyaṃ ayuñjantānaṃ sattānaṃ aparipakkañāṇānaṃ yoge yogahetu vāsanābhāgiyavasena āyatiṃ jānanatthāya “ārambhathā”tiādidesanā āraddhā. Yuñjantānaṃ paripakkañāṇānaṃ sattānaṃ ārambhe ārambhahetu diṭṭheva dhamme parijānanatthāya “ārambhathā”tiādidesanā āraddhā.

Thus, for the teaching beginning with 'Strive,' the meaning has been analyzed by way of the foundation and is known by us. Since it should be stated, 'How is the meaning of that same teaching to be analyzed by way of its opposite?' the phrase 'Or for those not applying themselves...' and so on was stated. Herein, for beings not applying themselves to the practice and development, whose knowledge is immature, the teaching beginning with 'Strive' was undertaken for the sake of their knowing the future, by way of it being a condition for latent tendencies related to the practice. For beings applying themselves, whose knowledge is mature, the teaching beginning with 'Strive' was undertaken for the sake of their full understanding in this very life, based on the cause of their striving.

Tattha tesu yuñjantāyuñjantesu paripakkāparipakkañāṇesu ye aparipakkañāṇā sattā na yuñjanti, te aparipakkañāṇā sattā pamādamūlakā hutvā yoge bhāvanāyaṃ yena pamādena na yuñjanti, so pamādo taṇhāmūlako pamādo, avijjāmūlako pamādoti dubbidho hoti. Tattha tasmiṃ dubbidhe pamāde aññāṇena nivuto avijjāmūlako satto yena pamādena ñeyyaṭṭhānaṃ “ime uppādavayadhammā pañcakkhandhā ñeyyaṭṭhānaṃ nāmā”ti nappajānāti, ayaṃ aññāṇahetuko pamādo avijjāmūlako pamādā nāma. Yo pamādo taṇhāmūlako, so pamādo tividho anuppannānaṃ bhogānaṃ uppādāya pariyesanto taṇhiko satto yaṃ pamādaṃ āpajjati, ayaṃ pamādo ca, uppannānaṃ bhogānaṃ ṭhitatthāya rakkhanto taṇhiko satto ārakkhanimittaṃ yaṃ pamādaṃ āpajjati, ayaṃ pamādo ca, ṭhitaṃ bhogaṃ paribhuñjanto taṇhiko satto paribhoganimittaṃ yaṃ pamādaṃ āpajjati, ayaṃ pamādo cāti tividho hoti. Iti loke ayaṃ pamādo catubbidho avijjāpadaṭṭhāno ekavidho pamādo, taṇhāpadaṭṭhāno tividho pamādoti catubbidho hoti. Tattha tāsu avijjātaṇhāsu nāmakāyo phassādināmasamūho avijjāya padaṭṭhānaṃ, rūpakāyo pathavīādirūpasamūho taṇhāya padaṭṭhānaṃ hoti. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – ārambhadhātunikkamadhātusaṅkhātassa vīriyassa paṭipakkho catubbidho pamādo niddhāretabbo, niddhāretvā ekavidhassa pamādassa avijjā padaṭṭhānaṃ, tividhassa pamādassa taṇhā padaṭṭhānaṃ. Avijjāya nāmakāyo padaṭṭhānaṃ, taṇhāya rūpakāyo padaṭṭhānanti paṭipakkhe āvaṭṭetvā padaṭṭhānaṃ pariyesitabbanti.

Here, among those applying and not applying themselves, with mature and immature knowledge: those beings with immature knowledge who do not apply themselves, being rooted in negligence, do not apply themselves to the practice and development because of that negligence. That negligence is twofold: negligence rooted in craving and negligence rooted in ignorance. Therein, in that twofold negligence, a being shrouded by non-knowledge, rooted in ignorance, is one who through negligence does not understand the object of knowledge, that 'these five aggregates, subject to arising and passing away, are called the object of knowledge.' This negligence caused by non-knowledge is called negligence rooted in ignorance. The negligence rooted in craving is threefold: the negligence that a being driven by craving falls into while seeking to generate unarisen possessions; the negligence that a being driven by craving falls into on account of guarding in order to maintain arisen possessions; and the negligence that a being driven by craving falls into on account of enjoying possessions that are maintained. Thus this negligence in the world is fourfold: one kind of negligence that has ignorance as its foundation, and three kinds of negligence that have craving as their foundation. Therein, with regard to ignorance and craving, the mentality-body—the collection of mental phenomena such as contact—is the foundation for ignorance; the materiality-body—the collection of material phenomena such as the earth element—is the foundation for craving. This is what is meant: the fourfold negligence, the opposite of the energy reckoned as the element of initiative and the element of exertion, should be determined. Having determined it, ignorance is the foundation for the one kind of negligence, and craving is the foundation for the three kinds. The mentality-body is the foundation for ignorance, and the materiality-body is the foundation for craving. Thus, having turned back to the opposite, the foundation should be sought.

“Kasmā [M 0.0158] nāmakāyo avijjāya padaṭṭhānaṃ bhavati, rūpakāyo taṇhāya padaṭṭhānaṃ bhavatī”ti pucchitabbattā “taṃ kissa hetū”ti pucchitvā “rūpīsu bhavesu ajjhosānaṃ, arūpīsu sammoho”ti vuttaṃ. Rūpīsu bhavesu rūpadhammesu ahaṃmamādivasena ajjhosānaṃ taṇhābhiniveso sattesu patiṭṭhito yasmā hoti, tasmā rūpakāyo taṇhāya padaṭṭhānaṃ bhavati. Anamatagge hi saṃsāre itthipurisā aññamaññarūpābhirāmā bhavanti. Arūpīsu phassādīsu sukhumabhāvato sammoho sattesu patiṭṭhito yasmā hoti, tasmā nāmakāyo avijjāya padaṭṭhānaṃ bhavatīti yojanā kātabbā. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – rūpakāyanāmakāyesu ārammaṇakaraṇavasena taṇhāya [V 0.0289] ca avijjāya ca uppajjanato rūpakāyo taṇhāya padaṭṭhānaṃ, nāmakāyo avijjāya padaṭṭhānanti nīharitabbāvāti.

Since it should be asked, 'Why does the mentality-body become the foundation for ignorance, and the materiality-body become the foundation for craving?' one asks, 'For what reason?' and it is said: 'Cleaving to form existences, delusion regarding formless phenomena.' Because cleaving, the adherence of craving, is established in beings by way of such notions as 'I' and 'mine' in regard to material phenomena in form existences, the materiality-body becomes the foundation for craving. For in beginningless saṃsāra, men and women delight in each other’s forms. And because delusion is established in beings due to the subtle nature of formless phenomena such as contact, the mentality-body becomes the foundation for ignorance. This construction should be made. This is what is meant: because craving and ignorance arise by way of making the materiality-body and mentality-body their objects, it should be deduced that the materiality-body is the foundation for craving and the mentality-body is the foundation for ignorance.

“Katamo rūpakāyo, katamo nāmakāyo”ti pucchitabbattā “tattha rūpakāyo rūpakkhandho, nāmakāyo cattāro arūpino khandhā”ti vuttaṃ. Tattha tesu rūpakāyanāmakāyesu rūpakāyo rūpasamūho nāma rūpakkhandho hoti, nāmakāyo nāmasamūho nāma cattāro arūpino khandhāti. Ime pañcakkhandhā avijjātaṇhānaṃ ārammaṇattā saupādānā bhaveyyuṃ, “katamena upādānena saupādānā bhavantī”ti pucchitabbattā tatheva pucchitvā vissajjetuṃ “ime pañcakkhandhā katamena upādānena saupādānā? Taṇhāya ca avijjāya cā”ti vuttaṃ. Tattha upādānabhūtāya taṇhāya ca upādānabhūtāya avijjāya ca ime pañcakkhandhā saupādānā nāma bhavantīti yojanā kātabbā.

Since it should be asked, 'What is the materiality-body, what is the mentality-body?' it is said: 'Here, the materiality-body is the form aggregate; the mentality-body is the four formless aggregates.' Here, of these two, the materiality-body, the collection of material phenomena, is the form aggregate; the mentality-body, the collection of mental phenomena, is the four formless aggregates. These five aggregates, being objects for ignorance and craving, would be subject to clinging. Since it should be asked, 'By what clinging are they subject to clinging?' one asks just so and, in order to answer, it is said: 'By what clinging are these five aggregates subject to clinging? By craving and by ignorance.' Here, the construction should be made that these five aggregates are called 'subject to clinging' because of craving that is clinging and ignorance that is clinging.

“Kittakāni upādānāni taṇhā nāma bhavanti, kittakāni upādānāni avijjā nāma bhavantī”ti pucchitabbattā “tattha taṇhā dve”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tatthāti tāsu taṇhāavijjāsu. Kāmupādānañca sīlabbatupādānañca dve upādānāni taṇhā nāma bhavanti. Taṇhāvasena hi “mama sīlaṃ, mama vata”nti parāmasanaṃ bhavati. Diṭṭhupādānañca attavādupādānañca dve upādānāni avijjā nāma bhavanti. Avijjāvasena hi sassatadiṭṭhi ceva ahaṃmamādidiṭṭhi ca bhavanti. “Imehi catūhi upādānehi saupādānakkhandhā catūsu saccesu kittakaṃ saccaṃ nāmā”ti pucchitabbattā “imehī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Ye lokiyakkhandhā saupādānā khandhā bhavanti, upādānena hi [M 0.0159] upādānānipi bhavanti, idaṃ saupādānakkhandhapañcakaṃ dukkhaṃ dukkhasaccaṃ nāma. Yāni cattāri upādānāni dukkhakāraṇāni bhavanti, ayaṃ upādānacatukko samudayo samudayasaccaṃ nāma bhavati. Pañcakkhandhāti saupādānā pañcakkhandhā dukkhavatthubhāvato dukkhaṃ. Tesanti saupādānānaṃ pañcakkhandhānaṃ. Dhammaṃ desetīti “ārambhathā”tiādikaṃ dhammaṃ veneyyānurūpaṃ bhagavā deseti. Sāmaññena pubbe vuttampi atthavasena visesaṃ dassetuṃ puna “dukkhassa pariññāya, samudayassa pahānāyā”ti vuttaṃ.

Because it should be asked, 'How many kinds of clinging are called craving, and how many kinds of clinging are called ignorance?' it is said, 'Therein, craving is twofold,' and so on. Herein means among that craving and ignorance. Clinging to sensual pleasures and clinging to rules and observances—these two clingings are called craving. For it is by way of craving that the grasping, 'my virtue, my observance,' occurs. Clinging to views and clinging to the doctrine of self—these two clingings are called ignorance. For it is by way of ignorance that both the eternalist view and the view of 'I' and 'mine' arise. Because it should be asked, 'Among the four truths, what truth are the aggregates subject to clinging, which are conditioned by these four clingings, called?' it is said, 'By these,' and so on. Those worldly aggregates are aggregates subject to clinging. For by clinging, they become objects of clinging. This pentad of aggregates subject to clinging is suffering, called the truth of suffering. The four clingings that are the cause of suffering—this tetrad of clingings is the origin, called the truth of the origin. The five aggregates means: the five aggregates subject to clinging are suffering because they are the basis for suffering. Of these means: of the five aggregates subject to clinging. He teaches the Dhamma means: the Blessed One teaches the Dhamma, such as 'Strive,' etc., in accordance with the disposition of those to be trained. Although stated generally before, to show the specific meaning, it is said again, 'for the full understanding of suffering, for the abandoning of the origin.'

30. Ārambhapaṭipakkhabhūtapamādavasena purimasaccadvayaṃ ācariyena niddhāritaṃ, amhehi ca ñātaṃ, “itarasaccadvayaṃ kathaṃ niddhāritabba”nti vattabbattā taṃ dvayampi pamādamukheneva niddhāritabbanti dassetuṃ “tattha yo tividho”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha tatthāti tesu taṇhāmūlakaavijjāmūlakesu pamādesu. Tassāti tividhassa taṇhāmūlakassa pamādassa. Sampaṭivedhenāti assādādīnaṃ parijānanena. Rakkhaṇāti attacittassa rakkhaṇasaṅkhātā. Paṭisaṃharaṇāti “tassā”ti [V 0.0290] iminā vuttassa pamādassa paṭipakkhabhūtena appamādānanuyogena saṃharaṇā yā khepanā atthi, ayaṃ pamādassa paṭipakkhabhūtena appamādānuyogena pavattā khepanasaṅkhātā bhāvanā samatho nāmāti pamādassa paṭipakkhamukhena puna āvaṭṭetvā samatho niddhāritoti.

30. The first pair of truths has been determined by the teacher by way of negligence, which is the counterpart to striving, and it is known by us. Because it should be said, 'How is the other pair of truths to be determined?' to show that this pair, too, is to be determined through the avenue of negligence, it is said, 'Therein, that which is threefold,' and so on. Herein means: in those instances of negligence rooted in craving and rooted in ignorance. Of that means: of the threefold negligence rooted in craving. By penetration means: by fully understanding gratification, etc. Guarding means: that which is designated as the guarding of one’s own mind. Removal means: the removal, the destruction, that occurs through the application of diligence, which is the counterpart to the negligence mentioned by 'of that.' This development, designated as destruction, which proceeds through the application of diligence that is the counterpart to negligence, is called serenity. Thus serenity is determined by turning back again through the avenue of the counterpart to negligence.

“So samatho kathaṃ kena upāyena bhavatī”ti pucchitabbattā tathā pucchitvā upāyaṃ dassetuṃ “so katha”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha kathanti kena upāyena. “Kāmentīti kāmā, kāmīyantīti vā kāmā”ti vuttānaṃ dvinnaṃ kāmānaṃ paṭicca uppajjamānaṃ assādañca, “appassādā kāmā bahudukkhā”tiādi (ma. ni. 1.235) vacanato appassādanīyānaṃ kāmānaṃ paṭicca uppajjamānaṃ ādīnavañca. Kāmānanti ca kammatthe sāmivacanaṃ. Tena vuttaṃ –“kāme paṭiccā”ti (netti. aṭṭha. 30). “Kāmānametaṃ nissaraṇaṃ, yadidaṃ nekkhamma”nti (itivu. 72) vacanato nissaraṇanti idha paṭhamajjhānaṃ adhippetaṃ. Vokāranti ettha va-kāro āgamo, o-kāraṃ lāmakabhāvaṃ. Ānisaṃsanti catupārisuddhisīlādikaṃ. Yadā jānāti, tadā tena upāyena samatho bhavatīti attho.

Because it should be asked, 'How, by what means, does that serenity come to be?' to show the means after being asked thus, it is said, 'How is it?' and so on. Herein, 'how' means by what means. And the gratification that arises in dependence on the two kinds of sensual pleasures (kāma) spoken of as 'they desire, thus they are sensual pleasures' or 'they are desired, thus they are sensual pleasures'; and the danger that arises in dependence on sensual pleasures which provide little gratification, in accordance with the statement, 'Sensual pleasures provide little gratification and much suffering,' etc. And kāmānaṃ is the genitive case in the sense of the object. Therefore it is said: 'in dependence on sensual pleasures.' In accordance with the statement, 'This is the escape from sensual pleasures, that is, renunciation,' here 'escape' is intended to mean the first jhāna. In vokāraṃ, the 'va' is an augment; 'okāra' means inferiority. Benefit (ānisaṃsaṃ) means the fourfold purification virtue, etc. The meaning is: when one knows, then by that means serenity comes to be.

Samatho [M 0.0160] ācariyena vibhatto, amhehi ca ñāto, “katamā vipassanā”ti pucchitabbattā vipassanaṃ vibhajituṃ “tattha yā vīmaṃsā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Atha vā kāmānaṃ assādādayo yadā jānāti, tadā samatho bhavatīti vutto, “tasmiṃ samathe bhavamāne sati katamā bhavatī”ti pucchitabbattā “tattha yā vīmaṃsā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha tatthāti tasmiṃ samathe bhavamāne sati assādādīnaṃ yā aniccādivīmaṃsā upaparikkhā paññā bhavati, ayaṃ vīmaṃsā upaparikkhā paññā visesena passanato vipassanā nāma. Atha vā tividhassa taṇhāmūlakassa pamādassa sampaṭivedhena rakkhaṇā paṭisaṃharaṇā, ayaṃ samathoti ācariyena vutto, “katamā vipassanā”ti pucchitabbattā “tattha yā vīmaṃsā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha tatthāti tasmiṃ yathāvutte samathe sati yathāvuttassa pamādassa aniccādivasena yā vīmaṃsā upaparikkhā paññā uppannā, ayaṃ vīmaṃsā upaparikkhā paññā visesena passanato vipassanā nāma. Vīmaṃsāva dubbalā, upaparikkhā balavatīti viseso.

Serenity has been analyzed by the teacher and is known by us. Because it should be asked, 'What is insight?' to analyze insight, it is said, 'Therein, that which is investigation,' and so on. Alternatively, it was said that when one knows the gratification, etc., of sensual pleasures, then serenity comes to be. Because it should be asked, 'When that serenity is present, what comes to be?' it is said, 'Therein, that which is investigation,' and so on. Herein (tattha) means: when that serenity is present, there is the investigating and examining wisdom regarding the impermanence, etc., of gratification and so on. This investigating and examining wisdom is named insight because it sees with special clarity. Or again, it was stated by the teacher that serenity is the penetration, guarding, and removal of the threefold negligence rooted in craving. Because it should be asked, 'What is insight?' it is said, 'Therein, that which is investigation,' and so on. Herein (tattha) means: when the aforesaid serenity is present, there arises an investigating and examining wisdom regarding the aforesaid negligence by way of impermanence, etc. This investigating and examining wisdom is named insight because it sees with special clarity. Investigation is weak, while examination is strong—this is the distinction.

Samatho ceva vipassanā ca dve dhammā ācariyena niddhāritā, “ime niddhāritā dve dhammā kiṃ gacchantī”ti vattabbattā “ime dve”tiādi vuttaṃ. Samatho samathabhāvanāpāripūriṃ gacchati, vipassanā vipassanābhāvanāpāripūriṃ gacchati. “Imesu dvīsu dhammesu bhāviyamānesu katame yogāvacarena pahīyantī”ti vattabbattā “imesū”tiādi vuttaṃ. Samathe dhamme bhāviyamāne taṇhā [V 0.0291] yogāvacarena pahīyati, vipassanāya bhāviyamānāya avijjā yogāvacarena pahīyatīti ime dve pahātabbā dhammā pahīyanti taṇhā ceva avijjā ca. “Imesu dvīsu dhammesu pahīyamānesu katame dhammā nirujjhantī”ti pucchitabbattā upādānādayopi nirujjhantīti sakalavaṭṭadukkhanirodhaṃ dassento “imesu dvīsu dhammesu pahīnesū”tiādimāha. Tattha taṇhāya samathabhāvanāya pahīyamānāya, avijjāya vipassanābhāvanāya pahīyamānāya imesu dvīsu dhammesu dvīhi bhāvanāhi pahīnesu kāmupādānādīni cattāri upādānāni vikkhambhanasamucchedavasena nirujjhanti, na bhaṅgakkhaṇavasena.

Serenity and insight, these two states, have been determined by the teacher. Because it should be said, 'Where do these two determined states lead?' it is said, 'These two,' and so on. Serenity goes to the fulfillment of the development of serenity; insight goes to the fulfillment of the development of insight. Because it should be said, 'When these two states are being developed, what is abandoned by the yogi?' it is said, 'In these,' and so on. When the state of serenity is being developed, craving is abandoned by the yogi; when insight is being developed, ignorance is abandoned by the yogi. Thus these two states to be abandoned are abandoned: craving and ignorance. Because it should be asked, 'When these two states are being abandoned, what states cease?' showing the cessation of all the suffering of the round by explaining that clinging, etc., also cease, he said, 'When these two states are abandoned,' and so on. Herein, when craving is being abandoned by the development of serenity and ignorance is being abandoned by the development of insight, when these two states have been abandoned by the two developments, the four clingings beginning with clinging to sensual pleasures cease by way of suppression and eradication, not by way of momentary dissolution.

Etthāha – “taṇhānirodhā upādānanirodho”ti vuttattā “taṇhāya pahīyamānāya upādānāni nirujjhantī”ti vacanaṃ yuttaṃ hotu, kathaṃ avijjāya pahīyamānāya upādānāni nirujjhantīti? “Taṇhānirodhā upādānanirodho”ti [M 0.0161] pāṭhe avijjāsahitataṇhānirodhā upādānanirodhoti atthasambhavato. Yathā hi taṇhāsahitāva avijjā saṅkhārānaṃ paccayo, evaṃ avijjāsahitāva taṇhā upādānānaṃ paccayo hotīti avijjāsahitataṇhānirodhā upādānanirodhoti attho sambhavatīti gahetabbo. Vikkhambhanasamucchedavasena upādānanirodhā tatheva bhavanirodhoti esa nayo sesesupi. Evametassa kevalassa dukkhakkhandhassa nirodhoti etthāpi taṇhāsahitaavijjānirodhā saṅkhāranirodhotiādiko gahitoti daṭṭhabbo. Itīti evaṃ visabhāgasabhāgadhammānaṃ āvaṭṭanavasena niddhāritāni ca purimakāni dve saccāni ca, samatho ca vipassanā ca ime dve dhammā maggo ca maggasaccañca, vaṭṭanirodho vaṭṭanirodhasaccañca nibbānanti cattāri saccāni niddhāritāni.

Here he says: Since it is said, 'With the cessation of craving, there is the cessation of clinging,' let the statement, 'When craving is being abandoned, the clingings cease,' be correct. But how is it that when ignorance is being abandoned, the clingings cease? Because in the text, 'With the cessation of craving, there is the cessation of clinging,' the meaning, 'with the cessation of craving accompanied by ignorance, there is the cessation of clinging,' is possible. For just as it is ignorance accompanied by craving that is a condition for formations, so it is craving accompanied by ignorance that is a condition for the clingings. Thus, it should be understood that the meaning, 'with the cessation of craving accompanied by ignorance, there is the cessation of clinging,' is possible. By way of suppression and eradication, with the cessation of clinging, there is in the same way the cessation of becoming. This method applies to the remaining cases as well. Thus, 'this is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering.' Here too, it should be understood that what is taken is 'with the cessation of ignorance accompanied by craving, there is the cessation of formations,' and so on. Thus (iti): in this way, by way of turning back to dissimilar and similar states, the former two truths have been determined; and serenity and insight—these two states—are the path and the truth of the path; and the cessation of the round is the truth of the cessation of the round, which is Nibbāna. In this way, the four truths have been determined.

“Vīriyapaṭipakkhabhūtassa pamādādidhammassa vasena vā sabhāgabhūtassa pamādādidhammassa vasena vā āvaṭṭetvā catunnaṃ saccānaṃ niddhāritabbabhāvo amhehi kena saddahitabbo”ti vattabbattā “tenāhā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tena tathā niddhāritabbabhāvena bhagavā “ārambhatha nikkamathā”tiādigāthāvacanaṃ āha, tena “ārambhatha nikkamathā”tiādigāthāvacanena tathā catunnaṃ saccānaṃ niddhāritabbabhāvo tumhehi saddahitabboti vuttaṃ hoti.

Because it should be said, 'By what are we to be convinced of the fact that the four truths must be determined by turning back, either by way of a state such as negligence which is the counterpart to energy, or by way of a state such as negligence which is of a similar nature?' it is said, 'Therefore he said,' and so on. Because of that fact that they must be determined in such a way, the Blessed One spoke the verse beginning, 'Strive, go forth.' This means it is said: 'By that verse beginning, "Strive, go forth," you should be convinced of the fact that the four truths must be determined in such a way.'

“Ārambhatha nikkamathā’tiādinā vodānapakkhaṃyeva nikkhipitvā tasseva vodānapakkhassa visabhāgadhammasabhāgadhammavaseneva āvaṭṭetvā catusaccaniddhāraṇaṃ kātabba”nti pucchitabbattā saṃkilesapakkhampi nikkhipitvā tasseva saṃkilesassa visabhāgadhammasabhāgadhammavasenapi āvaṭṭetvā catusaccaniddhāraṇaṃ dassento “yathāpi mūle”tiādigāthāvacanamāha. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana –

Since one might ask, 'Should the determination of the four truths be made by setting aside only the aspect of purification, such as in “Strive, go forth,” and revolving it by way of dissimilar and similar phenomena of that very aspect of purification?'—in order to show that the determination of the four truths is also made by setting aside the aspect of defilement and revolving it by way of dissimilar and similar phenomena of that very defilement, the verse beginning 'Just as, though its root…' was spoken. In the commentary, however:

“Evaṃ [V 0.0292] vodānapakkhaṃ nikkhipitvā tassa visabhāgadhammavasena, sabhāgadhammavasena ca āvaṭṭanaṃ dassetvā idāni saṃkilesapakkhaṃ nikkhipitvā tassa visabhāgadhammavasena, sabhāgadhammavasena ca āvaṭṭanaṃ dassetuṃ ‘yathāpi mūle’ti gāthamāhā”ti (netti. aṭṭha. 30) –

“Thus, having set aside the aspect of purification and shown its revolution by way of dissimilar phenomena and similar phenomena, now, in order to show the revolution of the aspect of defilement by way of its dissimilar phenomena and similar phenomena after setting it aside, he spoke the verse beginning, ‘Just as, though its root….’” (Netti. Aṭṭha. 30).

Vuttaṃ. Gāthātthopi aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vutto. Tathāpi yatipotānaṃ atthāya aṭṭhakathānusāreneva kathayissāma.

So it is said. The meaning of the verse has also been stated in the commentary. Nevertheless, for the benefit of young monks, we will explain it in accordance with the commentary.

Samūho [M 0.0162] rukkho mūlati patiṭṭhāti etena avayavena bhūmibhāge ṭhitenāti mūlaṃ, kiṃ taṃ? Bhūmibhāge ṭhito mūlasaṅkhāto rukkhāvayavo, tasmiṃ mūle. Natthi upaddavo pharasuchedādiantarāyo assa mūlassāti anupaddavo. Daḷheti upaddavābhāvena sabhāvato thire sati. Chindīyatīti chinno, ko so? Bhūmiyaṃ patiṭṭhitamūlasahito rukkhāvayavo, na chinditvā gahito rukkhāvayavo. Ruhati vaḍḍhatīti rukkho. So ca bhūmiyaṃ patiṭṭhitamūlasahito rukkhāvayavo rukkhoti vutto yathā “samuddo diṭṭho”ti. Punareva rūhatīti puna aṅkuruppādanaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Taṇhānusayeti attabhāvasaṅkhātassa rukkhassa mūle. Anūhateti arahattamaggañāṇena anupacchinne sati idaṃ attabhāvasaṅkhātaṃ dukkhaṃ dukkhahetu punappunaṃ abbocchinnaṃ nibbattati na nirujjhatiyevāti gāthāttho.

A tree as a collection is rooted (mūlati), established (patiṭṭhāti), by this part standing in the ground; thus it is a 'root' (mūlaṃ). What is that? The part of the tree standing in the ground, designated as the root. 'In that root' (tasmiṃ mūle). There is no harm (upaddavo), no danger such as being cut by an axe, for this root; thus it is 'unharmed' (anupaddavo). 'Firm' (daḷhe) means: when it is inherently stable due to the absence of harm. 'Cut down' (chinno): what is that? The part of the tree together with its root established in the ground, not a part of the tree that has been cut and taken away. It grows (ruhati), it increases (vaḍḍhati); thus it is a 'tree' (rukkho). And that part of the tree together with its root established in the ground is called a 'tree,' just as when it is said, 'the ocean has been seen.' 'Grows again' (punareva rūhati) is said with reference to the production of new shoots. 'The latent tendency of craving' (taṇhānusaye) refers to the root of the tree designated as individual existence. 'Not uprooted' (anūhate) means: when it has not been cut off by the knowledge of the path to arahantship, this suffering designated as individual existence, this cause of suffering, is generated again and again without interruption; it does not cease at all. This is the meaning of the verse.

“Idha gāthāyaṃ yo taṇhānusayo anūhatabhāvena dukkhassa nibbattanassa mūlanti vutto, ayaṃ taṇhānusayo katamassā taṇhāya anusayo”ti pucchati, “taṇhāya kāmataṇhādivasena bahuvidhattā bhavataṇhāya anusayo”ti vissajjeti bhavassādataṇhābhāvato. Yo anusayo etassa bhavataṇhāsaṅkhātassa dhammassa paccayo hoti, ayaṃ anusayo avijjānusayo hoti. “Anusayo bahuvidho, kasmā avijjānusayoti saddahitabbo”ti vattabbattā “avijjāpaccayā hi bhavataṇhā”ti vuttaṃ. Avijjāya bhavataṇhāya paccayattā avijjānusayo saddahitabbo. Avijjāya hi bhavesu ādīnavassa adassanavasena bhavassādataṇhā bhavatīti. Ime dve kilesātiādimhi heṭṭhā vuttanayānusārena cattāri saccāni niddhāretvā visabhāgasabhāgadhammāvaṭṭanaṃ viññātabbaṃ, samathavipassanā pana maggasampayuttāva gahetabbā.

He asks: 'Here in this verse, the latent tendency of craving is said to be the root of the generation of suffering because it is not uprooted. Of which craving is this latent tendency of craving a latent tendency?' He answers: 'Because craving is manifold—such as sensual craving, etc.—it is the latent tendency of the craving for existence,' for it is the craving for the gratification of existence. Whatever latent tendency is a condition for this phenomenon designated as craving for existence, that latent tendency is the latent tendency of ignorance. Since one might say, 'Latent tendencies are manifold; why should it be believed to be the latent tendency of ignorance?' it is stated: 'For craving for existence is conditioned by ignorance.' Because ignorance is a condition for craving for existence, the latent tendency of ignorance should be accepted. For through ignorance, by not seeing the danger in states of existence, the craving for the gratification of existence arises. Beginning with 'These two defilements,' the four truths should be determined according to the method stated above, and the revolution of dissimilar and similar phenomena should be understood. But serenity and insight should be taken only as conjoined with the path.

“Sabbapāpassā”tiādikassa anusandhyattho aṭṭhakathāyaṃ (netti. aṭṭha. 30) vutto. Sabbapāpassāti kammapathabhāvappattāpattassa niravasesassa akusalassa. Akaraṇanti saparasantānesu anuppādanaṃ[V 0.0293]. Kusalassāti kammapathabhāvappattāpattassa tebhūmakakusalassa ceva lokuttarakusalassa ca. Upasampadāti santāne uppādanavasena sampadā. Sassa attano cittanti sacittaṃ, sacittassa pariyodāpanaṃ vodānaṃ arahattaphaluppattiyāti sacittapariyodāpanaṃ[M 0.0163]. Arahattamagguppādo pana “kusalassa upasampadā”ti padena gahito. Etaṃ akaraṇādittayadīpanaṃ buddhānaṃ sammāsambuddhānaṃ sāsanaṃ ovādoti gāthāttho.

The connected meaning of the passage beginning 'Of all evil…' is stated in the commentary (Netti. Aṭṭha. 30). 'Of all evil' means: of all unwholesome kamma without exception, whether or not it has reached the state of a course of action. 'The non-doing' means the non-production in one's own and others' mental continuities. 'Of the wholesome' means: of wholesome kamma of the three planes and supramundane wholesome kamma, whether or not it has reached the state of a course of action. 'Accomplishment' means accomplishment by way of production in one's own mental continuity. 'One's own mind' (sacittaṃ) is the mind of oneself; the 'purification of one's own mind' (sacittapariyodāpanaṃ) is the cleansing for the purpose of the arising of the fruit of arahantship. The arising of the path to arahantship, however, is included in the phrase 'the accomplishment of the wholesome.' This elucidation of the triad beginning with non-doing is the teaching, the instruction, of the Buddhas, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened Ones. This is the meaning of the verse.

Gāthāyaṃ yassa pāpassa akaraṇaṃ vuttaṃ, taṃ pāpaṃ duccaritakammapathavasena vibhajituṃ “sabbapāpaṃ nāmā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Dosasamuṭṭhānanti yebhuyyavasena vuttaṃ, lobhasamuṭṭhānampi bhavati. Lobhasamuṭṭhānantipi yebhuyyavasena vuttaṃ, dosasamuṭṭhānampi bhavati. Mohasamuṭṭhānampi tatheva vuttaṃ. Lobhasamuṭṭhānadosasamuṭṭhānampi sambhavatīti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Sabbapāpo duccaritakammapathappabhedena vibhatto, “ettakeneva vibhajitabbo, udāhu aññena vibhajitabbo”ti pucchitabbattā aññena akusalamūlaagatigamanabhedenapi vibhajituṃ “yā abhijjhā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana “evaṃ duccaritaakusalakammapathakammavibhāgena ‘sabbapāpa’nti ettha vuttapāpaṃ vibhajitvā idānissa akusalamūlavasena agatigamanavibhāgampi dassetuṃ ‘akusalamūla’ntiādi vutta”nti (netti. aṭṭha. 30) anusandhyattho vutto. Mohavasena sabhāvaṃ ajānantassa bhayasambhavato yaṃ bhayā ca mohā ca agatiṃ gacchati, idaṃ mohasamuṭṭhānanti vuttaṃ.

In order to classify the evil whose non-doing is mentioned in the verse by way of the courses of action of misconduct, the passage beginning 'All evil, namely…' is stated. 'Originating from hatred' is said generally, but it can also originate from greed. 'Originating from greed' is also said generally, but it can also originate from hatred. 'Originating from delusion' is stated in the same way. It should be understood that it can also originate from greed and hatred. All evil has been classified by the divisions of the courses of action of misconduct. Since one might ask, 'Should it be classified only to this extent, or should it be classified in another way?'—in order to classify it also by the divisions of unwholesome roots and going on wrong courses, the passage beginning 'Whatever covetousness…' is stated. In the commentary, however, the connected meaning is stated: 'Having thus classified the evil mentioned here as “all evil” by the classification of misconduct and unwholesome courses of action, now, to show its classification also by way of unwholesome roots and wrong courses, the passage beginning “unwholesome roots…” is stated' (Netti. Aṭṭha. 30). Because fear is possible for one who does not know the intrinsic nature due to delusion, when one goes on a wrong course out of fear and delusion, this is said to be 'originating from delusion.'

Sabbapāpo ācariyena vibhatto, amhehi ca ñāto, “katamaṃ sabbapāpassa akaraṇa”nti pucchitabbattā tattha lobho asubhāyā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana –

All evil has been classified by the teacher and is known by us. Since the question should be asked, 'What is the non-doing of all evil?' the passage beginning 'Therein, greed by means of the unattractive…' is stated. In the commentary, however—

“Ettāvatā ‘sabbapāpassa akaraṇa’nti ettha pāpaṃ dassetvā idāni tassa akaraṇaṃ dassento ‘lobho…pe… paññāyā’ti tīhi kusalamūlehi tiṇṇaṃ akusalamūlānaṃ pahānavasena sabbapāpassa akaraṇaṃ anuppādanamāhā”ti (netti. aṭṭha. 30) –

“To this extent, having shown the evil in the phrase ‘the non-doing of all evil,’ now, in order to show the non-doing of it, he states the non-doing and non-arising of all evil as the abandonment of the three unwholesome roots by means of the three wholesome roots, with the words ‘greed… and so on… by wisdom.’” (Netti. Aṭṭha. 30)

Vuttaṃ. Subhādhimuttavasena pavatto lobho asubhāya asubhabhāvanāya tathāpavattena alobhena tadaṅgavikkhambhanappahānena pahīyati, sattesu kujjhanadussanavasena pavatto doso mettāya mettābhāvanāya tathāpavattena adosena ca tadaṅgavikkhambhanappahānena pahīyati, sattesu ceva saṅkhāresu ca muyhanavasena pavatto moho paññāya [M 0.0164] vicāraṇapaññāya ca bhāvanāmaggapaññāya ca tadaṅgavikkhambhanasamucchedappahānena pahīyati.

It has been said: Greed that occurs through being intent on the beautiful is abandoned by means of the unattractive perception, by the development of the unattractive, and by non-greed that occurs in such a way, through abandonment by substitution and by suppression. Hatred that occurs through anger and ill will towards beings is abandoned by loving-kindness, by the development of loving-kindness, and by non-hatred that occurs in such a way, through abandonment by substitution and by suppression. Delusion that occurs through confusion about beings and formations is abandoned by wisdom, by the wisdom of investigation, and by the wisdom of the path of development, through abandonment by substitution, by suppression, and by cutting off.

“Yadi [V 0.0294] tīhi kusalamūleheva akusalamūlāni pahīyanti, evaṃ sati upekkhākaruṇāmuditā niratthakā bhaveyyu”nti vattabbattā “tathā lobho upekkhāyā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Upekkhāyāti “sabbe sattā kammassakā”tiādinā bhāvitāya upekkhāya. Muditā aratiṃ vūpasametvā aratiyā mūlabhūtaṃ mohampi pajahatīti manasi katvā “moho muditāya pahānaṃ abbhatthaṃ gacchatī”ti vuttaṃ. “Akusalamūlānaṃ kusalamūlādīhi pahātabbattaṃ kena amhehi saddahitabba”nti vattabbattā “tenāhā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tena tathā pahātabbattena bhagavā “sabbapāpassa akaraṇa”nti vacanaṃ āha, tena “sabbapāpassa akaraṇa”nti vacanena tathā pahātabbattaṃ tumhehi saddahitabbanti vuttaṃ hoti.

Since one might say, 'If the unwholesome roots are abandoned by the three wholesome roots alone, then equanimity, compassion, and altruistic joy would be useless,' the passage beginning 'Similarly, greed by equanimity…' is stated. 'By equanimity' means: by the equanimity developed by means of the reflection 'All beings are owners of their kamma,' etc. Having kept in mind that altruistic joy, by pacifying discontent, also abandons delusion, which is the root of discontent, it is said: 'Delusion goes to abandonment, to disappearance, by altruistic joy.' Since one might say, 'By what should we have faith that the unwholesome roots are to be abandoned by the wholesome roots and so on?' the passage beginning 'Therefore he said…' is stated. For that reason—because they are to be abandoned in such a way—the Blessed One spoke the words 'the non-doing of all evil.' This means that by those words, 'the non-doing of all evil,' you should have faith that they are to be abandoned in that way.

31. “Ettāvatā ca sabbapāpo vibhatto, tassa akaraṇañca vibhattaṃ siyā, evaṃ sati aṭṭhamicchattānaṃ akaraṇaṃ anivāritaṃ siyā”ti vattabbattā “sabbapāpaṃ nāma aṭṭha micchattānī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Micchāsatīti aniccādīsu “nicca”nti anussaraṇacintanādivasena pavattaakusalappavatti.

31. Since one might say: 'To this extent, all evil would have been classified, and its non-doing would have been classified. This being so, the non-doing of the eight kinds of wrongness would be unaddressed,' the passage beginning 'All evil, namely, the eight kinds of wrongness…' is stated. 'Wrong mindfulness' is the unwholesome occurrence that proceeds by way of recollecting, thinking, etc., of the impermanent and so on as 'permanent.'

Sabbapāpassa akaraṇaṃ bahudhā ācariyena vibhattaṃ, amhehi ca viññātaṃ, “kathaṃ kusalassa sampadā vibhajitabbā viññātabbā”ti vattabbattā kusalassa sampadaṃ vibhajitvā dassento “aṭṭhasu micchattesu pahīnesū”tiādimāha. Aṭṭha sammattānīti sammādiṭṭhi sammāsaṅkappo sammāvācā sammākammanto sammāājīvo sammāvāyāmo sammāsati sammāsamādhīti aṭṭhasammattāni visabhāgaparivattanadhammavasena sampajjanti. Atītassāti atītena sammāsambuddhena desitassa. Vipassino hi bhagavato ayaṃ pātimokkhuddesagāthā. Citte pariyodāpiteti cittapaṭibaddhā pañcakkhandhāpi pariyodāpitā bhavanti. “Cittapariyodāpitena pañcannaṃ khandhānaṃ pariyodāpitabhāvo kathaṃ amhehi saddahitabbo”ti vattabbattā “evañhī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Evaṃ vuttappakārena bhagavā yaṃ “cetovisuddhatthaṃ bhikkhave tathāgate brahmacariyaṃ vussatī”ti vacanaṃ āha, tena “ceto…pe… vussatī”ti vacanena tumhehi saddahitabboti vuttaṃ hoti. “Pariyodāpanā katividhā bhavantī”ti vattabbattā “duvidhā hī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Samathavipassanāya [M 0.0165] nīvaraṇappahānañca ariyamaggabhāvanāya anusayasamugghāto cāti pariyodāpanassa duvidhattā pañcakkhandhā pariyodāpitā bhavantīti attho. Pahīnanīvaraṇānusayā hi puggalā pasādanīyavaṇṇā honti.

The non-doing of all evil has been analyzed in many ways by the teacher and understood by us. Since it should be said, 'How is the accomplishment of the wholesome to be analyzed and understood?', analyzing and showing the accomplishment of the wholesome, he states, 'When the eight wrongnesses are abandoned,' and so on. The eight rightnesses are: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration. These eight rightnesses are accomplished by way of the principle of transformation of dissimilar states. 'Of the past' means taught by the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One of the past. For this verse of the Pātimokkha exhortation belongs to the Blessed One Vipassī. When the mind has been purified, the five aggregates connected with the mind are also purified. Since it should be said, 'How are we to have faith that the five aggregates are purified through the purification of the mind?', 'For thus...' and so on is stated. In the way thus stated, the Blessed One spoke the words, 'Bhikkhus, it is for the sake of the purification of mind that the holy life is lived under the Tathāgata.' By this statement, 'For the purification of mind... is lived,' it is meant that you should have faith. Since it should be said, 'How many kinds of purification are there?', 'For there are two kinds...' and so on is stated. The abandoning of the hindrances by means of serenity and insight, and the uprooting of the underlying tendencies by means of the development of the noble path—since purification is twofold in this way, the meaning is that the five aggregates are purified. For persons who have abandoned the hindrances and underlying tendencies are of inspiring appearance.

“Pariyodāpanassa kittikā bhūmiyo”ti pucchitabbattā “dve pariyodāpanabhūmiyo”tiādi vuttaṃ. “‘Sabbapāpassa akaraṇa’ntiādigāthāya desitesu dhammesu katamaṃ dukkhasaccaṃ, katamaṃ samudayasaccaṃ[V 0.0295], katamaṃ maggasaccaṃ, katamaṃ nirodhasacca”nti pucchitabbattā “tattha yaṃ paṭivedhenā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tatthāti gāthāya desitesu dhammesu yaṃ khandhapañcakaṃ paṭivedhena pariññābhisamayena pariyodāpeti, idaṃ khandhapañcakaṃ dukkhaṃ dukkhasaccaṃ bhave. Yato taṇhāsaṃkilesato khandhapañcakaṃ pariyodāpeti, ayaṃ taṇhāsaṃkileso samudayo samudayasaccaṃ. Yena ariyamaggaṅgena pariyodāpeti, ayaṃ ariyamaggo maggasaccaṃ. Yaṃ asaṅkhatadhātuṃ adhigatena puggalena pariyodāpitaṃ, ayaṃ asaṅkhatadhātudhammo nirodho nirodhasaccaṃ bhave. Imāni cattāri saccāni gāthāya desitadhammānaṃ sabhāgavisabhāgadhammāvaṭṭanavasena niddhāritāni. “Tenāhā”tiādikassa attho heṭṭhā vuttanayena veditabbo.

Since it should be asked, 'How many grounds of purification are there?', 'There are two grounds of purification...' and so on is stated. Since it should be asked, 'Among the dhammas taught in the verse beginning "The non-doing of all evil," which is the truth of suffering, which is the truth of the origin, which is the truth of the path, and which is the truth of cessation?', 'Therein, that which by penetration...' and so on is stated. 'Therein' means: among the dhammas taught in the verse, that pentad of aggregates which one purifies by penetration, by the comprehension of full understanding—this pentad of aggregates would be suffering, the truth of suffering. That from which one purifies the pentad of aggregates, namely, craving and defilement—this craving and defilement is the origin, the truth of the origin. That by which one purifies, namely, the noble path-factor—this noble path is the path, the truth of the path. That which is purified by the person who has attained the unconditioned element—this dhamma, the unconditioned element, would be cessation, the truth of cessation. These four truths are determined from the dhammas taught in the verse by way of the application of similar and dissimilar dhammas. The meaning of 'Therefore he said...' and so on should be understood according to the method stated below.

“Sabbapāpassa akaraṇa”ntiādigāthāya desitānaṃ dhammānaṃ sabhāgavisabhāgadhammāvaṭṭanavasena cattāri saccāni ācariyena niddhāritāni, amhehi ca viññātāni.

By way of the application of similar and dissimilar dhammas to the dhammas taught in the verse beginning 'The non-doing of all evil,' the four truths have been determined by the teacher and understood by us.

“‘Dhammo have rakkhati dhammacāriṃ, chattaṃ mahantaṃ yatha vassakāle;

Esānisaṃso dhamme suciṇṇe, na duggatiṃ gacchati dhammacārī’ti –

'The Dhamma surely protects the Dhamma-farer, like a great umbrella in the rainy season. This is the benefit in the Dhamma well-practiced: the Dhamma-farer does not go to a bad destination.'

Gāthāya desitānaṃ dhammānaṃ visabhāgasabhāgadhammānaṃ āvaṭṭanavasena kathaṃ cattāri saccāni niddhāritānī”ti vattabbattā “dhammo have”tiādimāha. Tāya gāthāya desite dhamme vibhajitvā dassento “dhammo nāmā”tiādimāha. Tattha dhammo nāmāti puññadhammo nāma. Indriyasaṃvaroti manacchaṭṭhindriyasaṃvarasīlādiko sabbo saṃvaro. Tena vuttaṃ –“indriyasaṃvarasīsena [M 0.0166] cettha sabbampi sīlaṃ gahitanti daṭṭhabba”nti (netti. aṭṭha. 31). Cattāro apāyā dukkaṭakammakārīnaṃ gatibhūtattā duggati. Sabbā upapattiyo pana dukkhadukkhasaṅkhāradukkhavipariṇāmadukkhasamaṅgīnaṃ gatibhūtattā duggati nāma.

Since it should be said, 'How are the four truths determined by way of the application of dissimilar and similar dhammas to the dhammas taught in the verse?', he states, 'The Dhamma surely...' and so on. Analyzing and showing the Dhamma taught in that verse, he states, 'Dhamma means...' and so on. Therein, 'Dhamma means' refers to meritorious Dhamma. 'Restraint of the senses' means all restraint, such as the virtue of restraint of the six senses with the mind as the sixth. Hence it is said: 'Herein, all virtue should be seen as included under the heading of restraint of the senses' (Netti. Aṭṭha. 31). The four planes of deprivation are a 'bad destination' because they are the destination for those who do evil deeds. But all forms of rebirth are called a 'bad destination' because they are the destination for those endowed with the suffering of pain, the suffering due to formations, and the suffering due to change.

“Tasmiṃ duvidhe dhamme indriyasaṃvaradhammo kattha ṭhito, kathaṃ suciṇṇo, kuto rakkhatī”ti pucchitabbattā “tattha yā saṃvarasīle”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tatthāti tasmiṃ duvidhe dhamme. Saṃvarasīle ṭhitā yā akhaṇḍakāritā hoti, ayaṃ akhaṇḍavasena kātabbo saṃvarasīle ṭhito suṭṭhu āciṇṇapariciṇṇo puññadhammo catūhi apāyehi attano ādhāraṃ attānaṃ rakkhantaṃ puggalaṃ ekantikabhāvena rakkhati, anekantikabhāvena pana rakkhitamatto puññadhammopi rakkhatīti attho gahetabbo. Apāyehīti ca padhānavasena vuttaṃ, rogādiantarāyatopi rakkhati. Rogādiantarāyo vā ayato apagatattā apāyantogadhoti daṭṭhabbo.

Since it should be asked, 'In that twofold Dhamma, where does the Dhamma of sense-restraint stand, how is it well-practiced, and from what does it protect?', 'Therein, in the virtue of restraint...' and so on is stated. 'Therein' means in that twofold Dhamma. That unbroken practice which is established in the virtue of restraint—this meritorious Dhamma, which should be practiced as unbroken, established in the virtue of restraint, well-practiced and cultivated, definitely protects from the four planes of deprivation the person who protects himself, his own support. But in a non-definite sense, even the meritorious Dhamma that merely protects also protects—this is the meaning to be understood. And 'from the planes of deprivation' is said in a primary sense; it also protects from dangers such as disease. Or, dangers such as disease should be seen as included within 'planes of deprivation' because they arise from a lack of restraint.

“Tathā [V 0.0296] rakkhatīti kena amhehi saddahitabbo”ti vattabbattā “evaṃ bhagavā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Evaṃ vuttappakārena lakkhaṇapakāradassanaṃ bhagavā “dvemā, bhikkhave, sīlavato gatiyo devā ca manussā cā”ti yaṃ vacanaṃ āha, tena “dvemā…pe… manussā cā”ti vacanena tumhehi saddahitabboti vuttaṃ hoti. “Saṃvarasīle ṭhitassa akhaṇḍakātabbassa suciṇṇassa puññadhammassa apāyehi rakkhaṇe ekantikabhāvo kena suttena dīpetabbo”ti vattabbattā “evañca nāḷandāya”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha evañcāti iminā idāni vuccamānena pakārenapi vuttappakāro attho veditabbo. Nāḷandāyanti nāḷandanāmake nigame nisinno asibandhakanāmassa putto gāmaṇi gāmajeṭṭhako bhagavantaṃ etaṃ vuccamānaṃ “brāhmaṇā, bhante”tiādivacanaṃ avoca.

Since it should be said, 'How are we to have faith that it protects in such a way?', 'Thus the Blessed One...' and so on is stated. The Blessed One, seeing the characteristic manner in the way thus stated, spoke the words, 'Bhikkhus, there are these two destinations for one who is virtuous: devas and humans.' By this statement, 'These two... and humans,' it is meant that you should have faith. Since it should be said, 'By what sutta is the definiteness of protection from the planes of deprivation to be shown for the meritorious Dhamma that is well-practiced, to be practiced as unbroken, and established in the virtue of restraint?', 'And thus at Nāḷandā...' and so on is stated. Therein, 'and thus' means that the meaning stated should be understood also by this manner now being spoken of. 'At Nāḷandā' means: while seated in the market town named Nāḷandā, the headman Asibandhakaputta, the village chief, said this to the Blessed One: 'Venerable sir, the brahmins...' and so on.

Brāhmaṇāti bāhirakā brāhmaṇā. Bhanteti bhagavantaṃ gāmaṇi ālapati. Pacchābhūmakāti pacchimadisāya nisinnakā. Uyyāpentīti manussalokato uddhaṃ devalokaṃ yāpenti pāpenti.

'Brahmins' means externalist brahmins. 'Venerable sir': the headman addresses the Blessed One. 'Of the western land' means those dwelling in the western region. 'They send up' means they cause them to go, to reach, from the human world up to the deva world.

Idhassāti idhaloke assa bhaveyya. Puriso pāṇātipātī…pe… micchādiṭṭhiko assa bhaveyyāti yojanā. Sesaṃ pāḷito ceva vuttānusārena ca ñeyyaṃ.

'Here there might be' means 'here in this world there might be.' The construction is: 'A person might be one who destroys life... one who holds wrong view.' The rest should be understood from the Pāli text and in accordance with what has been said.

32. “Visabhāgadhammasabhāgadhammāvaṭṭanavasena [M 0.0167] catunnaṃ saccānaṃ niddhāritabhāvo kena amhehi saddahitabbo”ti vattabbattā “tenāha mahākaccāno ekamhi padaṭṭhāne”ti vuttaṃ.

32. Since it should be said, 'How are we to have faith in the determination of the four truths by way of the application of dissimilar and similar dhammas?', it is stated, 'Therefore Mahākaccāna said: "On one foundation..."'

“Ettāvatā ca āvaṭṭo hāro paripuṇṇo, añño niyutto natthī”ti vattabbattā “niyutto āvaṭṭo hāro”ti vuttaṃ. Yassaṃ yassaṃ pāḷiyaṃ yo yo āvaṭṭo hāro yathālābhavasena yojito, tassaṃ tassaṃ pāḷiyaṃ so so āvaṭṭo hāro tathā niddhāretvā yutto yojitoti attho daṭṭhabbo.

Since it can be said, 'To this extent the Revolving Guideline is complete, there is no other one applied,' it is called the 'Applied Revolving Guideline.' The meaning should be seen thus: in whatever Pāli passage a particular Revolving Guideline is applied in whatever way is available, in that Pāli passage that particular Revolving Guideline, having been determined in that way, is suitable and is applied.

Iti āvaṭṭahāravibhaṅge sattibalānurūpā racitā

Thus, in the Analysis of the Revolving Guideline, this was composed in accordance with my ability and strength.

Vibhāvanā niṭṭhitā.

The Elucidation is concluded.

Paṇḍitehi pana aṭṭhakathāṭīkānusāreneva gambhīrattho vitthārato vibhajitvā gahetabboti.

But by the wise, the profound meaning should be grasped by analyzing it in detail only in accordance with the commentaries and subcommentaries.

8. Vibhattihāravibhaṅgavibhāvanā

8. Elucidation of the Analysis of the Classification Garland

33. Yena [V 0.0297] yena saṃvaṇṇanāvisesabhūtena āvaṭṭahāravibhaṅgena āvaṭṭetabbā padaṭṭhānādayo vibhattā, so saṃvaṇṇanāvisesabhūto āvaṭṭahāravibhaṅgo paripuṇṇo, “tattha katamo vibhattihāravibhaṅgo”ti pucchitabbattā “tattha katamo vibhattihāro”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha tatthāti tesu niddiṭṭhesu soḷasasu desanāhārādīsu katamo saṃvaṇṇanāviseso vibhattihāro vibhattihāravibhaṅgo nāmāti pucchati. “Dhammañca padaṭṭhānaṃ bhūmiñcā”tiādiniddesassa idāni mayā vuccamāno “dve suttānī”tiādiko vitthārabhūto saṃvaṇṇanāviseso vibhattihāro vibhattihāravibhaṅgo nāmāti attho gahetabbo.

33. Since the bases and so on to be revolved have been classified by means of the analysis of the revolving garland, which is a particular kind of explanation, that analysis of the revolving garland is now complete. As it is to be asked, “Therein, what is the analysis of the classification garland?,” it is said, “Therein, what is the classification garland?” and so on. Here, “therein” refers to those sixteen indicated teaching garlands and so on. He asks: “Which particular explanation is called the classification garland, the analysis of the classification garland?” The meaning should be understood thus: the detailed particular explanation beginning “Two suttas,” which I am now stating in reference to the exposition beginning “The Dhamma, the basis, and the ground,” is what is called the classification garland, the analysis of the classification garland.

“Yesu suttesu vuttā dhammapadaṭṭhānabhūmiyo iminā vibhattihārena vibhattā, tāni suttāni kittakānī”ti pucchitabbattā tāni suttāni paṭhamaṃ dassetuṃ “dve suttāni vāsanābhāgiyañca nibbedhabhāgiyañcā”ti vuttaṃ. Tattha vāsanābhāgiyanti puññabhāvanā vāsanā nāma, vāsanāya bhāgo koṭṭhāso vāsanābhāgo, vāsanābhāge vācakabhāvena niyuttaṃ [M 0.0168] suttanti vāsanābhāgiyaṃ, katamaṃ taṃ? Yasmiṃ sutte tīṇi puññakiriyavatthūni bhagavatā desitāni, taṃ suttaṃ vāsanābhāgiyaṃ. Nibbedhabhāgiyanti lobhakkhandhādīnaṃ nibbijjhanaṃ padālanaṃ nibbedho, nibbedhassa bhāgo koṭṭhāso nibbedhabhāgo, nibbedhabhāge vācakabhāvena niyuttaṃ suttanti nibbedhabhāgiyaṃ, katamaṃ taṃ? Yasmiṃ sutte sekkhāsekkhadhammā bhagavatā desitā, taṃ suttaṃ nibbedhabhāgiyaṃ.

Since it should be asked, “How many are the suttas in which the grounds that are the bases for the teachings are spoken of and classified by this classification garland?,” in order to first point out those suttas, it is said: “Two suttas: that pertaining to the portion of latent tendencies and that pertaining to the portion of penetration.” Herein, “pertaining to the portion of latent tendencies”: the cultivation of merit is called a “latent tendency.” A share or portion of a latent tendency is the “latent-tendency-portion.” A sutta employed to designate the latent-tendency-portion is a “sutta pertaining to the portion of latent tendencies.” Which is that? The sutta in which the Blessed One taught the three grounds for meritorious activity is the sutta pertaining to the portion of latent tendencies. “Pertaining to the portion of penetration”: disenchantment with and the breaking up of the aggregates of greed and so on is “penetration.” A share or portion of penetration is the “penetration-portion.” A sutta employed to designate the penetration-portion is a “sutta pertaining to the portion of penetration.” Which is that? The sutta in which the Blessed One taught the qualities of trainees and those beyond training is the sutta pertaining to the portion of penetration.

“Tesaṃ suttānaṃ paṭiggāhakā puggalā yāhi paṭipadāhi sampajjanti, tā paṭipadā kittikā”ti pucchitabbattā “dve paṭipadā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Dānasīlabhāvanāmayapuññabhāge bhavā paṭipadāti puññabhāgiyā. Phalabhāge bhavā paṭipadāti phalabhāgiyā. “Yesu sīlesu ṭhitā paṭiggāhakā paṭipajjanti, tāni sīlāni kittakānī”ti pucchitabbattā “dve sīlānī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Saṃvarati etena saṃvarenāti saṃvaro, so saṃvaro pātimokkhasaṃvaro, satisaṃvaro, ñāṇasaṃvaro, khantisaṃvaro, vīriyasaṃvaroti pañcavidho. Sabbopi pāpasaṃvaraṇato saṃvaro, lokiyalokuttarasampattiṭṭhānattā sīlaṃ nāma. Pajahati etena pahātabbeti pahānaṃ, pajahanaṃ vā pahānaṃ, tañca pahānaṃ tadaṅgappahānaṃ, vikkhambhanappahānaṃ, samucchedappahānaṃ, paṭipassaddhippahānaṃ, nissaraṇappahānanti pañcavidhaṃ. Tattha nissaraṇappahānaṃ vajjetvā catubbidhaṃ pahānaṃ vuttanayena sīlaṃ nāma.

Since it should be asked: “By how many courses of practice do the persons who are recipients of those suttas succeed?,” it is said: “Two courses of practice,” etc. The course of practice that occurs in the portion of merit consisting of giving, virtue, and cultivation is “pertaining to the portion of merit.” The course of practice that occurs in the portion of fruit is “pertaining to the portion of fruit.” Since it should be asked: “Established in which virtues do the recipients practice, and how many are those virtues?,” it is said: “Two virtues,” etc. One restrains with it, thus it is “restraint” (saṃvaro); that restraint is fivefold: restraint by the Pātimokkha, restraint by mindfulness, restraint by knowledge, restraint by patience, and restraint by energy. All of it is “restraint” because it restrains from evil; it is called “virtue” (sīlaṃ) because it is the basis for worldly and supramundane attainment. One abandons what should be abandoned with it, thus it is “abandoning” (pahānaṃ), or the act of abandoning is “abandoning”; and that abandoning is fivefold: abandoning by substitution of opposites, abandoning by suppression, abandoning by cutting off, abandoning by tranquillization, and abandoning by escape. Therein, excluding abandoning by escape, the fourfold abandoning is called “virtue” in the way stated.

“Tesu [V 0.0298] suttādīsu bhagavā katamaṃ suttaṃ katamāya paṭipadāya desayati, katarasmiṃ sīle ṭhito puggalo katamena sīlena brahmacārī bhavatī”ti pucchitabbattā tathā vibhajitvā dassetuṃ “tattha bhagavā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha tesu vāsanābhāgiyādīsu suttesu vāsanābhāgiyaṃ suttaṃ tattha tāsu puññabhāgiyādipaṭipadāsu puññabhāgiyāya paṭipadāya bhagavā yassa puggalassa desayati, so vāsanābhāgiyasuttapaṭiggāhako puggalo tattha saṃvarasīlādīsu saṃvarasīle ṭhito hutvā tena saṃvarasīlasaṅkhātena brahmacariyena seṭṭhacariyena brahmacārī seṭṭhācārapūrako bhavati. Tattha tesu vāsanābhāgiyādīsu suttesu nibbedhabhāgiyaṃ suttaṃ tattha tāsu puññabhāgiyādipaṭipadāsu phalabhāgiyāya paṭipadāya yassa puggalassa bhagavā desayati, so nibbedhabhāgiyasuttapaṭiggāhako puggalo tattha saṃvarasīlādīsu pahānasīle samucchedappassaddhippahānavasena [M 0.0169] ṭhito hutvā tena pahānasīlasaṅkhātena visesabhūtena maggasaṅkhātena brahmacariyena brahmacārī bhavatīti yojanā kātabbā.

Since it should be asked: “Among those suttas and so on, which sutta does the Blessed One teach by which course of practice? And established in which virtue does a person become a practitioner of the holy life by means of which virtue?,” in order to show this by classifying it, it is said: “Therein the Blessed One…,” etc. Therein, among suttas such as that pertaining to the portion of latent tendencies, the Blessed One teaches the sutta pertaining to the portion of latent tendencies to a person by means of the course of practice pertaining to the portion of merit. That person, the recipient of the sutta pertaining to the portion of latent tendencies, being established in the virtue of restraint, becomes a practitioner of the holy life, a fulfiller of the noble conduct, by means of that holy life designated as the virtue of restraint, as the noble conduct. Therein, among suttas such as that pertaining to the portion of latent tendencies, the Blessed One teaches the sutta pertaining to the portion of penetration to a person by means of the course of practice pertaining to the portion of fruit. That person, the recipient of the sutta pertaining to the portion of penetration, being established in the virtue of abandoning by way of abandoning by cutting off and by tranquillization, becomes a practitioner of the holy life by means of that holy life which is the virtue of abandoning, which is distinguished and designated as the path. The connection should be made thus.

“Vāsanābhāgiyasuttādīsu katamaṃ vāsanābhāgiyaṃ sutta”nti pucchitabbattā “tattha katama”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha tatthāti tesu vāsanābhāgiyasuttādīsu. Dānakathāti sappurisadānadānaphalaasappurisadānadānaphalakathā. Sīlakathāti pañcasīlādisīlaphalakathā. Saggakathāti saggasampattisukhakathā ceva sagge nibbattāpakapuññakathā ca. Ādīnavoti ādīnavadassako suttanto. Ānisaṃsoti ānisaṃsadassako suttanto. Vāsanābhāgiyaṃ suttaṃ nāmāti yojanā.

Since it should be asked: “Among the suttas such as that pertaining to the portion of latent tendencies, which is the sutta pertaining to the portion of latent tendencies?,” it is said: “Therein, which…,” etc. Here, the word “therein” refers to those suttas such as that pertaining to the portion of latent tendencies. “Talk on giving” is talk on the giving of true persons and its fruit, and on the giving of untrue persons and its fruit. “Talk on virtue” is talk on the five precepts and other virtues, and their fruit. “Talk on heaven” is talk on the happiness of heavenly attainment and on the merit that brings about rebirth in heaven. “Drawback” means a sutta that shows the drawback. “Benefit” means a sutta that shows the benefit. The connection is: “…is called the sutta pertaining to the portion of latent tendencies.”

“Tattha katama”ntiādīsu anusandhyattho vuttanayova. Yā desanā catusaccappakāsanā, sā desanā nibbedhabhāgiyaṃ suttaṃ nāmāti yojanā. Evañca sati vāsanābhāgiyasuttassapi nibbedhabhāgiyasuttabhāvo āpajjeyya catusaccappakāsanatoti codanaṃ manasi katvā “vāsanābhāgiye sutte”tiādi vuttaṃ. Vāsanābhāgiye sutte pajānanā vuṭṭhānagāminivipassanā ariyamaggapadaṭṭhānabhūtā paññā natthi, maggo ariyamaggo natthi, phalaṃ ariyaphalaṃ natthi. Nibbedhabhāgiye sutte pana pajānanādayo atthi, vāsanābhāgiye sutte natthi. “Pajānanā”tiādinā catusaccappakāsanā dānakathādikā nibbedhabhāgiye sutte antogadhā, itaraṃyeva vāsanābhāgiyasuttanti nāmāti dasseti. Yesu suttesu vuttā dhammapadaṭṭhānabhūmiyo vibhattā, tāni suttāni dveyeva na honti, kasmā “dveyeva suttāni niddhāritānī”ti ce vadeyyuṃ? Asaṅkarato sutte vuttānaṃ dhammapadaṭṭhānabhūmīnaṃ vibhajitabbānaṃ suviññeyyattā. “Yadi evaṃ saṃkilesabhāgiyaasekkhabhāgiyasuttānipi niddhāritāni asaṅkarattā”ti ce vadeyyuṃ? No niddhāritāni, vāsanābhāgiyasutte niddhārite saṃkilesabhāgiyasuttampi niddhāritaṃ, saṃkilesadhammato nissaṭṭhadhammānaṃyeva vāsanābhāgiyadhammattā nibbedhabhāgiyasutte ca niddhārite asekkhabhāgiyasuttampi niddhāritaṃ anaññattā.

In “Therein, which…,” etc., the meaning of the connection is as stated before. The connection is: “A teaching that proclaims the Four Noble Truths is called a sutta pertaining to the portion of penetration.” Having considered the objection that, this being so, even a sutta pertaining to the portion of latent tendencies would become a sutta pertaining to the portion of penetration because it proclaims the Four Noble Truths, it is said: “In the sutta pertaining to the portion of latent tendencies…,” etc. In the sutta pertaining to the portion of latent tendencies there is no understanding, no insight leading to emergence, no wisdom that is the basis for the noble path, no noble path, and no noble fruit. But in the sutta pertaining to the portion of penetration, these things exist, whereas in the sutta pertaining to the portion of latent tendencies, they do not. By “understanding,” etc., he shows that the proclamation of the Four Truths, such as the talk on giving, is included in the sutta pertaining to the portion of penetration, while the other is just called the sutta pertaining to the portion of latent tendencies. If they should say: “The grounds for the teachings spoken of and classified in the suttas are not just two, so why are only two suttas specified?,” the answer is: because of their non-confusion, the things to be classified that are mentioned in the suttas are easily understood. If they should say: “If so, then suttas pertaining to the portion of defilement and pertaining to the portion of the adept should also be specified, because of their non-confusion,” the answer is: they are not specified. When the sutta pertaining to the portion of latent tendencies is specified, the sutta pertaining to the portion of defilement is also specified, since the quality of pertaining to the portion of latent tendencies belongs only to phenomena that have escaped from the phenomena of defilement. And when the sutta pertaining to the portion of penetration is specified, the sutta pertaining to the portion of the adept is also specified, since they are not different.

“Yesu [V 0.0299] suttesu vuttā dhammapadaṭṭhānabhūmiyo vibhattihārena vibhattā, tāni suttāni katamena phalena yojayitabbānī”ti pucchitabbattā “imāni cattāri suttānī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha imāni cattāri suttānīti [M 0.0170] yathāniddhāritāni vāsanābhāgiyanibbedhabhāgiyasuttāni ceva taṃniddhāraṇena niddhāritāni saṃkilesabhāgiyaasekkhabhāgiyasuttāni cāti cattāri suttāni imesaṃyeva catunnaṃ suttānaṃ desanāya nayena nītena phalena sabbato sabbabhāgena saṃvarasīlappahānasīlena brahmacariyena yojayitabbāni. Yojentena ca sabbato sabbabhāgena ca padādivicayena hārena saṃvarasīlādikaṃ phalaṃ vicinitvā yuttihārena yuttaṃ phalaṃ gavesitvā “idaṃ phalaṃ imassa puggalassa phalaṃ, idaṃ phalaṃ imassa suttassa phala”nti suttāni visuṃ visuṃ phalena yojayitabbānīti attho gahetabbo.

Since it should be asked, 'With what fruit should those suttas be connected, in which the grounds that are the bases for the teachings are spoken of and classified by the mode of distribution?,' it is said, 'These four suttas…,' etc. Herein, 'these four suttas' means the four suttas, namely: the suttas pertaining to the portion of latent tendencies and pertaining to the portion of penetration, which were specified, and the suttas pertaining to the portion of defilement and pertaining to the portion of the adept, which were specified by that same specification. These four suttas should be connected in every way and in all their parts with the fruit which is brought about by the method of the teaching of these very four suttas, that is, with the holy life consisting of the virtue of restraint and the virtue of abandoning. And the one who connects them should, in every way and in all their parts, investigate the fruit, such as the virtue of restraint, by the mode of investigating words, etc., and having sought the appropriate fruit by the mode of reasoning, should connect the suttas separately with their fruit, understanding, 'This is the fruit for this person; this is the fruit of this sutta.' This is the meaning to be understood.

“Kittakena phalena brahmacariyena yojetabbānī”ti pucchitabbattā “yāvatikā ñāṇassa bhūmī”ti vuttaṃ. Bhagavatā desitena vāsanābhāgiyasuttena siddhā yāvatikā puññabhāgiyā paṭipadādayo vibhajanañāṇassa bhūmi ārammaṇā bhavitumarahanti, tāvatikāhi bhūmīhi vāsanābhāgiyasuttaṃ yojayitabbaṃ. Nibbedhabhāgiyasuttena siddhā yāvatikā phalabhāgiyā paṭipadādayo vibhajanañāṇassa bhūmi ārammaṇā bhavitumarahanti, tāvatikāhi bhūmīhi nibbedhabhāgiyasuttaṃ yojetabbaṃ. Itaradvayampi suttaṃ yathāsambhavaṃ yojetabbaṃ. Etena ñāṇassa bhūmīnaṃ suttatthānaṃ bahuvidhattaṃ dasseti.

Because it should be asked, 'With how much of the fruit that is the holy life should they be connected?' it was said, 'As many as are the grounds of knowledge.' However many grounds there are that are established by the Sutta Pertaining to the Portion of Latent Tendencies taught by the Blessed One—being the courses of practice partaking of merit and so forth that are fit to become the ground and object for the knowledge of analysis—with that many grounds should the Sutta Pertaining to the Portion of Latent Tendencies be connected. However many grounds there are that are established by the Sutta Pertaining to the Portion of Penetration—being the courses of practice partaking of fruition and so forth that are fit to become the ground and object for the knowledge of analysis—with that many grounds should the Sutta Pertaining to the Portion of Penetration be connected. The other two suttas should also be connected as is appropriate. By this is shown the manifold nature of the grounds of knowledge and of the meanings of the suttas.

34. Vāsanābhāgiyasuttādīsu vuttā dhammā vāsanābhāgiyanibbedhabhāgiyabhāvehi ācariyena vibhattā, amhehi ca ñātā, “kathaṃ saṃkilesabhāgiyaasekkhābhāgiyabhāvehi asādhāraṇāsādhāraṇabhāvehi vibhajitabbā”ti pucchitabbattā “tattha katame dhammā sādhāraṇā”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Aṭṭhakathāya pana –

34. The states mentioned in the Sutta Pertaining to the Portion of Latent Tendencies and others were analyzed by the teacher in terms of being portions pertaining to latent tendencies and portions pertaining to penetration, and they have been understood by us. Because it should be asked, 'How should they be analyzed in terms of being portions pertaining to defilement and portions pertaining to one beyond training, and in terms of being uncommon and common?' the passage beginning, 'Therein, what states are common?' was introduced. But in the commentary—

“Evaṃ vāsanābhāgiyanibbedhabhāgiyabhāvehi dhamme ekadesena vibhajitvā idāni tesaṃ kilesabhāgiyaasekkhabhāgiyabhāvehi sādhāraṇāsādhāraṇabhāvehi vibhajituṃ ‘tattha katame dhammā sādhāraṇā’tiādi āraddha”nti (netti. aṭṭha. 34) –

'Having thus partially analyzed the states in terms of being portions pertaining to latent tendencies and portions pertaining to penetration, now, in order to analyze them in terms of being portions pertaining to defilement and portions pertaining to one beyond training, and in terms of their common and uncommon aspects, the passage beginning, “Therein, what states are common?” was introduced' (Netti. Aṭṭha. 34).

Vuttaṃ. Tattha tatthāti ye dhammā sutte vuttā vibhattihārena vibhajitabbā, tesu dhammesu katame dhammā sādhāraṇāti pucchati, dve dhammā sādhāraṇāti [M 0.0171] vissajjeti. Te dve dhamme sarūpato dassetuṃ “nāmasādhāraṇā, vatthusādhāraṇā cā”ti vuttaṃ. Tattha nāmasādhāraṇāti nāmena nāmapaññattiyā [V 0.0300] sādhāraṇā samānā, “kusalā”ti nāmena ekavīsati cittuppādā samānā, “akusalā”tyādināmena dvādasa cittuppādā samānā, kusalādināmapaññattivacanena vacanīyā atthā kusalādināmasādhāraṇāti vuttā. Tena ṭīkāyaṃ –

It is said. Herein, 'therein' refers to those states stated in the sutta that are to be analyzed by the mode of distribution. Among those states, he asks, 'Which states are common?'
