He answers, 'Two states are common.' To show those two states in their own nature, it is said, 'Common by name and common by basis.' Herein, 'common by name' means common by way of name, by way of nominal designation. The twenty-one arisings of consciousness are the same under the name 'wholesome'; the twelve arisings of consciousness are the same under the name 'unwholesome,' and so on. The meanings expressible by the utterance of a nominal designation such as 'wholesome' are said to be common by name. Therefore, in the subcommentary—

“Nāmaṃ nāmapaññatti, taṃmukheneva saddato tadatthāvagamo. Saddena ca sāmaññarūpeneva tathārūpassa atthassa gahaṇaṃ, na visesarūpena. Tasmā saddavacanīyā atthā sādhāraṇarūpanāmāyattagahaṇīyatāya nāmasādhāraṇā vuttā”ti –

'A name is a nominal designation, and it is by means of it that the meaning is understood from the sound. And by the sound, the meaning of such a form is grasped only in its general aspect, not in its specific aspect. Therefore, meanings expressible by sound are said to be common by name because they are to be apprehended as dependent on a name that has a common form.'

Vuttaṃ. Vatthusādhāraṇāti patiṭṭhānabhūtena vatthunā sādhāraṇā. Yasmiṃ patiṭṭhānabhūte santāne vā cittuppādādimhi vā ye dhammā pavattanti, te dhammā tena santānena vā vatthunā tena cittuppādādinā vā sādhāraṇā samānāti attho. Ekasantāne patitattā phusanādisabhāvato bhinnāpi vatthusādhāraṇā samānavatthukāyeva bhavantīti vibhattihārena vibhajitvāti vuttaṃ hoti.

'Common by basis' means common by the basis that serves as a foundation. The meaning is: whatever states occur in a certain continuum or in an arising of consciousness, etc., that serves as a foundation, those states are common with that continuum or that basis, that arising of consciousness, etc.; they are the same. Because they fall within a single continuum, even though they are distinct by nature—such as contact, etc.—they are common by basis, having the very same basis. Thus it is said, 'having analyzed by the mode of distribution.'

“Kiṃ nāmasādhāraṇavatthusādhāraṇāyeva vibhajitabbā, aññaṃ vibhajitabbaṃ natthī”ti pucchitabbattā “yaṃ vā panā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Nāmasādhāraṇavatthusādhāraṇehi aññaṃ yaṃ vā pana kiccasādhāraṇapaccayasādhāraṇapaṭipakkhādisādhāraṇampi dhammajātaṃ evaṃjātiyaṃ sādhāraṇajātiyaṃ, tampi sabbaṃ vicayahārena vicinitvā yuttihārena gavesitvā yuttaṃ sādhāraṇaṃ vibhattihārena vibhajitabbanti adhippāyo. “Tesu nāmasādhāraṇādīsu katame nāmasādhāraṇā, katame vatthusādhāraṇā”ti pucchitabbattā “micchattaniyatānaṃ sattāna”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Mātughātakādīnaṃ channaṃ micchattaniyatakammakarānaṃ sattānañca duggatiahetukasugatiahetukaduhetukatihetukānaṃ catunnaṃ puthujjanānaṃ aniyatakammakarānaṃ sattānañca santāne pavattā dassanapahātabbā kilesā dassanapahātabbanāmasādhāraṇā samānā bhavanti sakkāyadiṭṭhivicikicchāsīlabbataparāmasanavasena bhinnasabhāvānampi dassanapahātabbanāmanātivattanato. Vuttappakārānaṃ niyatāniyatasattānaṃ [M 0.0172] dassanapahātabbānaṃ kilesānaṃ patiṭṭhānavatthubhāvato vatthusādhāraṇā ca samānavatthukāti attho. Puthujjanassa duggatiahetukādicatubbidhasattassa, sotāpannassa ca santāne pavattā kāmarāgabyāpādā kilesā kāmarāgabyāpādanāmasādhāraṇā samānā bhavanti sakadāgāmimaggappahātabbaanāgāmimaggappahātabbavasena bhinnasabhāvānampi kāmarāgabyāpādanāmanātivattanato. Vuttappakārassa puthujjanassa, sotāpannassa ca kāmarāgabyāpādānaṃ patiṭṭhānavatthubhāvato vatthusādhāraṇā samānavatthukāti attho ca gahetabbo. Puthujjanassa, anāgāmissa ca santāne pavattā uddhaṃbhāgiyā saṃyojanā uddhambhāgiyanāmasādhāraṇā samānā bhavanti rūparāgādivasena bhinnasabhāvānampi [V 0.0301] uddhaṃbhāgiyanāmanātivattanato. Puthujjanassa, anāgāmissa ca uddhaṃbhāgiyānaṃ patiṭṭhānavatthubhāvato vatthusādhāraṇā samānavatthukāti attho ca gahetabbo. Tena vuttaṃ ṭīkāyaṃ – “dassanapahātabbānañhi yathā micchattaniyatasattā pavattiṭṭhānaṃ, evaṃ aniyatāpī”ti vuttaṃ. Saṅkhepato pana saṃkilesapakkhe pahānekaṭṭhā kilesā nāmasādhāraṇā honti, sahajekaṭṭhā kilesā vatthusādhāraṇāti daṭṭhabbā.

Because it should be asked, 'Are they to be analyzed only as common by name and common by basis? Is there nothing else to be analyzed?' the passage beginning, 'Or whatever...' was stated. The intention is that whatever other collection of states there may be apart from those common by name and common by basis—such as those common by function, common by condition, common by opposition, etc., of a similar kind, of a common kind—all that too should be investigated with the mode of inquiry, sought with the mode of reasoning, and what is suitable and common should be analyzed with the mode of distribution. Because it should be asked, 'Among these—those common by name, etc.—which are common by name and which are common by basis?' the passage beginning, 'Of beings fixed in wrongness...' was stated. The defilements to be abandoned by seeing that occur in the continuum of the six kinds of beings who perform deeds with fixed wrong result, such as matricide, and of the four kinds of worldlings who perform deeds with unfixed result—those with rootless rebirth-linking in a woeful destination, those with rootless rebirth-linking in a happy destination, those with two roots, and those with three roots—are common by the name 'to be abandoned by seeing' because, although they are of different natures—namely, identity view, doubt, and grasping at precepts and practices—they do not transcend the name 'to be abandoned by seeing.' And the meaning is that they are common by basis, having the same basis, because they are the foundational basis for the defilements to be abandoned by seeing of the aforesaid kinds of beings with fixed and unfixed destinies. The defilements of sensual lust and ill will that occur in the continuum of a worldling—one of the four kinds of beings, such as those with rootless rebirth-linking in a woeful destination—and of a stream-enterer are common by the name 'sensual lust and ill will' because, although they are of different natures in that they are to be abandoned by the path of the once-returner and the path of the non-returner, they do not transcend the name 'sensual lust and ill will.' And the meaning that they are common by basis, having the same basis, because they are the foundational basis for the sensual lust and ill will of the aforesaid worldling and stream-enterer, should be understood. The higher fetters that occur in the continuum of a worldling and of a non-returner are common by the name 'higher fetters' because, although they are of different natures—such as lust for form, etc.—they do not transcend the name 'higher fetters.' And the meaning that they are common by basis, having the same basis, because they are the foundational basis for the higher fetters of a worldling and a non-returner, should be understood. Therefore it is said in the subcommentary: 'For just as beings fixed in wrongness are the ground of occurrence for the defilements to be abandoned by seeing, so too are those who are unfixed.' In brief, however, on the side of defilement, defilements that are in the same group for abandonment are common by name; defilements that are in the same group of co-nascence are to be seen as common by basis.

Saṃkilesapakkhe sādhāraṇā ācariyena vibhattā, amhehi ca ñātā, “kathaṃ vodānapakkhe sādhāraṇā vibhattā”ti pucchitabbattā “yaṃ kiñci ariyasāvako”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha yaṃ kiñcīti sāmaññavasena vuttā paṭhamajjhānasamāpattiādikā lokiyā samāpattiyeva gahitā. Ariyasāvakoti ariyassa bhagavato sāvako ariyasāvakoti vattabbo, jhānalābhī ca phalaṭṭho ca puggalo, na maggaṭṭho. Maggaṭṭho hi lokiyaṃ yaṃ kiñci samāpattiṃ na samāpajjati. Sabbā sā lokiyasamāpatti rūpāvacarā arūpāvacarā dibbavihāro brahmavihāro paṭhamajjhānasamāpattīti evamādīhi pariyāyehi sādhāraṇā taṃsamaṅgīhi vītarāgāvītarāgehi sādhāraṇā lokiyasamāpattināmanātivattanato ca vītarāgāvītarāgehi samāpajjitabbato ca. “Ariyasāvako ca lokiyaṃ samāpattiṃ samāpajjanto odhiso odhiso samāpajjati, evaṃ sati kathaṃ vītarāgehi sādhāraṇāti saddahitabbā”ti vattabbattā “sādhāraṇā hi dhammā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana – “kathaṃ te odhiso gahitā, atha [M 0.0173] odhiso gahetabbā, kathaṃ sādhāraṇāti anuyogaṃ manasi katvā taṃ visodhento āha – ‘sādhāraṇā hi dhammā evaṃ aññamañña’ntiādī”ti vuttaṃ.

The common states on the side of defilement were analyzed by the teacher and have been understood by us. Because it should be asked, 'How are the common states on the side of purification analyzed?' the passage beginning 'Whatever noble disciple...' was stated. Herein, by 'whatever,' stated in a general sense, are taken only the worldly attainments, such as the attainment of the first jhāna. 'Noble disciple' should be spoken of as a disciple of the noble Blessed One; it refers to a person who is an obtainer of jhāna and established in the fruit, not one established in the path. For one established in the path does not attain any worldly attainment whatsoever. All those worldly attainments—of the form realm, the formless realm, the divine abidings, the brahmā abidings, the attainment of the first jhāna, and so on—are common by these various expressions. They are common to those with lust and those without lust because they do not transcend the name 'worldly attainment' and because they can be attained by both those with lust and those without lust. Because it must be said, 'But when a noble disciple attains a worldly attainment, he attains it with limitation; this being so, how should it be believed that it is common with those without lust?' the passage beginning 'For common are the states...' was stated. But in the commentary it is said: 'Having considered the question, “How are they taken with limitation? Or, if they are to be taken with limitation, how are they common?” he said, clarifying it: “For common are the states thus mutually...” etc.'

Tattha evaṃ vītarāgāvītarāgehi odhiso odhiso samāpajjitabbā dhammā paraṃ paraṃ pacchā pacchā pavattiyamānaṃ dhammajātaṃ sakaṃ sakaṃ pubbe pubbe jātaṃ “lokiyasamāpattī”ti nāmaṃ niyatavisayaṃ aññamaññaṃ hutvā hi yasmā nātivattanti, tasmā sādhāraṇāti saddahitabbā gahetabbāti attho. “Paraṃ paraṃ samāpajjanto kathaṃ nātivattatī”ti vattabbattā nātivattanaṃ pākaṭaṃ kātuṃ “yopī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Yo ariyasāvako vā avītarāgo vā. Imehi lokiyasamāpattidhammehi samannāgato, so ariyasāvako vā avītarāgo vā paraṃ paraṃ samāpajjantopi taṃ dhammaṃ lokiyaṃ samāpattidhammaṃ nātivattati, aññaṃ upagantvā nātikkamatīti attho. Yehi lokiyasamāpattidhammehi samannāgato, ime lokiyasamāpatti dhammā sādhāraṇāvāti daṭṭhabbā.

Herein, the meaning is this: because the collection of states that are to be attained with limitation by those with and without lust—a collection which arises successively, later after later—does not, being mutually related, transcend the name and fixed domain 'worldly attainment' of its own respective state that arose earlier and earlier, they should therefore be believed and understood as common. Because it must be said, 'How does one who is attaining them successively not transcend them?' the passage beginning 'Whoever also...' was stated in order to make the non-transcending clear. Whoever, whether a noble disciple or one not without lust, is endowed with these states of worldly attainment, that person, even while attaining them successively, does not transcend that state, that state of worldly attainment. The meaning is that one does not go beyond it by resorting to another. These states of worldly attainment with which one is endowed should be seen as common.

“Vāsanābhāgiyādisuttesu vuttā ye dhammā iminā vibhattihārena vibhattā, yesu dhammesu katame dhammā asādhāraṇā”ti pucchitabbattā “tattha katame dhammā asādhāraṇā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha [V 0.0302] tesu vibhajitabbesu dhammesu katame dhammā asādhāraṇāti pucchati, pucchitvā yāva desanaṃ upādāya asādhāraṇā dhammā gavesitabbā, “sekkhāsekkhā”ti vā gavesitabbā, “bhabbābhabbā”ti vā gavesitabbā. Atha vā yāva “sekkhāsekkhā bhabbābhabbā”ti desanā vuttā, tāva desanaṃ upādāya asādhāraṇā gavesitabbā. Kathaṃ gavesitabbā? Ariyesu sekkhāsekkhadhammavasena “sekkhā”ti nāmaṃ asekkhena asādhāraṇaṃ, “asekkhā”ti nāmaṃ sekkhena asādhāraṇanti vā, anariyesu “bhabbā”ti nāmaṃ abhabbena asādhāraṇaṃ, “abhabbā”ti nāmaṃ bhabbena asādhāraṇanti vā gavesitabbā. Kāmarāgabyāpādā saṃyojanā appahīnattā anusayabhāvena uppajjanārahattā aṭṭhamakassa sotāpattimaggaṭṭhassa ca sotāpannassa phalaṭṭhassa ca sādhāraṇā bhavanti, dhammatā dhammasabhāvo asādhāraṇo. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – “aṭṭhamakassa sotāpattimaggaṭṭhatā sotāpannassa asādhāraṇā, sotāpannassa [M 0.0174] sotāpannaphalaṭṭhatā ca aṭṭhamakassa sotāpattimaggaṭṭhassa asādhāraṇā. Aṭṭhamakassa vā pahīyamānakilesatā sotāpannassa asādhāraṇā, sotāpannassa pahīnakilesatā ca aṭṭhamakassa asādhāraṇā”ti.

Since it should be asked: 'Among the phenomena taught in the suttas such as the Vāsanābhāgiya, which have been analyzed by this method of analysis, what phenomena are unshared?' the passage beginning 'Therein, what phenomena are unshared?' was stated. Here, among those phenomena to be analyzed, one asks, 'What phenomena are unshared?' Having asked, the unshared phenomena should be sought by reference to the teaching. They should be sought as 'trainees and those beyond training,' or as 'the capable and the incapable.' Alternatively, the unshared phenomena should be sought by reference to the teaching insofar as it speaks of 'trainees and those beyond training, the capable and the incapable.' How should they be sought? Among the noble ones, in terms of the phenomena of trainees and those beyond training, the designation 'trainee' is unshared with one beyond training, and the designation 'one beyond training' is unshared with a trainee. Among the non-noble ones, the designation 'capable' is unshared with the incapable, and the designation 'incapable' is unshared with the capable. Thus they should be sought. The fetters of sensual lust and ill will, because they are unabandoned and are fit to arise as underlying tendencies, are common to the eighth person, who is established in the path of stream-entry, and to the stream-enterer, who is established in fruition. Their intrinsic nature, the specific nature of the phenomena, is unshared. This is what is meant: 'The state of being the eighth person established in the path of stream-entry is unshared with the stream-enterer, and the state of the stream-enterer established in the fruition of stream-entry is unshared with the eighth person established in the path of stream-entry. Alternatively, the state of abandoning defilements on the part of the eighth person is unshared with the stream-enterer, and the state of having abandoned defilements on the part of the stream-enterer is unshared with the eighth person.'

Uddhambhāgiyā saṃyojanā appahīnattā anusayabhāvena uppajjanārahattā aṭṭhamakassa maggaṭṭhabhāvena aṭṭhamakasadisassa anāgāmimaggaṭṭhassa ca anāgāmissa phalaṭṭhassa ca sādhāraṇā, dhammatā dhammasabhāvo asādhāraṇā. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – “aṭṭhamakassa anāgāmimaggaṭṭhatā anāgāmissa phalaṭṭhassa asādhāraṇā, anāgāmissa anāgāmiphalaṭṭhatā ca aṭṭhamakassa asādhāraṇā. Aṭṭhamakassa vā pahīyamānakilesatā anāgāmissa asādhāraṇā, anāgāmissa phalaṭṭhassa pahīnakilesatā ca aṭṭhamakassa asādhāraṇā”ti. “Maggaṭṭhatā phalaṭṭhatāya asādhāraṇā, phalaṭṭhatā ca maggaṭṭhatāya asādhāraṇā”tipi vattuṃ vaṭṭati. Sabbesaṃ sattannaṃ sekkhānaṃ puggalānaṃ nāmaṃ “sekkhā”ti nāmaṃ sādhāraṇaṃ. Dhammatā asādhāraṇāti catunnaṃ maggaṭṭhānaṃ taṃtaṃmaggaṭṭhatā aññamaññaṃ maggaṭṭhānaṃ asādhāraṇā. Heṭṭhimaphalattayaṭṭhānañca asādhāraṇā, heṭṭhimaphalattayaṭṭhānaṃ taṃtaṃphalaṭṭhatā ca aññamaññaṃ phalaṭṭhānaṃ asādhāraṇā, catunnaṃ maggaṭṭhānañca asādhāraṇāti attho. “Sekkhānaṃ taṃtaṃmaggaṭṭhatā taṃtaṃphalaṭṭhatāya asādhāraṇā, taṃtaṃphalaṭṭhatā ca taṃtaṃmaggaṭṭhatāya asādhāraṇā”ti vattumpi vaṭṭati. Sabbesaṃ paṭipannakānanti phalatthāya paṭipajjantīti paṭipannakā, tesaṃ maggasamaṅgīnaṃ catunnaṃ puggalānaṃ nāmaṃ “paṭipannakā”ti nāmaṃ sādhāraṇaṃ, dhammatā taṃtaṃmaggaṭṭhatā asādhāraṇā. Sabbesaṃ sekkhānaṃ sattannaṃ puggalānaṃ sekkhānaṃ sīlaṃ sādhāraṇaṃ, dhammatā taṃtaṃmaggaṭṭhaphalaṭṭhatā asādhāraṇāti. Vāsanābhāgiyasaṃkilesabhāgiyasuttesu vuttā dassanenapahātabbādayo ceva nibbedhabhāgiyaasekkhabhāgiyasuttesu vuttā sekkhādayo ca dhammā sādhāraṇāsādhāraṇabhedena vibhattihārena vibhajitabbāti adhippāyo veditabbo.

The higher fetters, because they are unabandoned and are fit to arise as underlying tendencies, are common to the one established in the path of non-returning—who is similar to the eighth person in being established in a path—and to the non-returner established in fruition; but their intrinsic nature, the specific nature of the phenomena, is unshared. This is what is meant: 'The state of being established in the path of non-returning on the part of the path-person is unshared with the one established in the fruition of non-returning, and the state of being established in the fruition of non-returning on the part of the non-returner is unshared with the path-person. Alternatively, the state of abandoning defilements on the part of the path-person is unshared with the non-returner, and the state of having abandoned defilements on the part of the one established in the fruition of non-returning is unshared with the path-person.' It is also right to say: 'The state of being established in the path is unshared with the state of being established in fruition, and the state of being established in fruition is unshared with the state of being established in the path.' For all seven persons who are trainees, the designation 'trainee' is common, but their intrinsic nature is unshared. That is, for the four established in the paths, their respective states of being established in a path are unshared with one another and are also unshared with the three established in the lower fruitions. For those established in the three lower fruitions, their respective states of being established in a fruition are unshared with one another and are also unshared with the four established in the paths. This is the meaning. It is also right to say: 'For the trainees, their respective states of being established in a path are unshared with their respective states of being established in fruition, and their respective states of being established in fruition are unshared with their respective states of being established in a path.' For all practitioners—that is, those practicing for the sake of fruition—for these four persons endowed with the path, the designation 'practitioner' is common, but their intrinsic nature, their respective states of being established in a path, is unshared. For all seven persons who are trainees, their virtue is common, but their intrinsic nature—their respective states of being established in a path or fruition—is unshared. The phenomena to be abandoned by seeing, etc., taught in the suttas on what partakes of habitual tendencies and what partakes of defilement, and the phenomena of trainees, etc., taught in the suttas on what partakes of penetration and what partakes of the state beyond training, should be analyzed by the method of analysis with the distinction of shared and unshared—this is the intention to be understood.

“Aṭṭhamakassā”tiādinā [V 0.0303] ariyesu puggalesu asādhāraṇā ācariyena vibhattā, amhehi ca ñātā, “kathaṃ anariyesu asādhāraṇā vibhattā”ti pucchitabbattā ariyesu vuttanayānusārena anariyesupi vibhajitvā gavesitabbāti dassetuṃ “evaṃ visesānupassinā”tiādi vuttaṃ[M 0.0175]. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana – “evaṃ ‘aṭṭhamakassā’tiādinā ariyapuggalesu asādhāraṇadhammaṃ dassetvā itaresu nayadassanatthaṃ ‘evaṃ visesānupassinā’tiādi vutta”nti vuttaṃ. Evaṃ ariyesu vuttanayānusārena bhabbābhabbesu anariyesu visesānupassinā asādhāraṇato visesaṃ asādhāraṇaṃ anupassinā gavesakena paṇḍitena bhabbābhabbesupi hīnukkaṭṭhamajjhimaṃ upādāya gavesitabbaṃ. Kathaṃ? Mātughātādivasena pavattānaṃ paṭighasampayuttadiṭṭhisampayuttasattamajavanacittuppādānaṃ micchattaniyatānaṃ taṃsamaṅgīnaṃ vā tathāpavattā paṭhamajavanacittupādādayo aniyatā dhammā paṭighasampayuttādibhāvena sādhāraṇā, micchattaniyatā dhammā ekacittuppādattā asādhāraṇā. Yathā hi cittaṃ “cittasaṃsaṭṭha”nti na vattabbaṃ, evaṃ micchattaniyatāpi “micchattaniyatasādhāraṇā”ti na vattabbā. Micchattaniyatesupi niyatamicchādiṭṭhikānaṃ diṭṭhisampayuttasattamajavanacittuppādasamaṅgīnaṃ aniyatā diṭṭhisampayuttapaṭhamajavanacittuppādādayo dhammā diṭṭhisampayuttādibhāvena sādhāraṇā, niyatamicchādiṭṭhi ekacittuppādasamaṅgībhāvato asādhāraṇā. Tenāha aṭṭhakathācariyo –

By the words 'Of the eighth person,' etc., the unshared phenomena among noble persons have been analyzed by the teacher and are known by us. Since it should be asked, 'How are the unshared phenomena among non-noble persons analyzed?' it is said, 'Thus, by one who discerns distinctions,' etc., to show that they should also be sought among the non-noble ones by analyzing them in accordance with the method stated for the noble ones. In the commentary, however, it is said: 'Thus, having shown the unshared phenomena among noble persons with the words "Of the eighth person," etc., the words "Thus, by one who discerns distinctions," etc., are stated to show the method for the others.' Thus, in accordance with the method stated for the noble ones, a wise seeker who discerns distinctions and discerns the unshared as a distinction should also seek among the capable and incapable non-noble ones with reference to the inferior, superior, and middling. How? For one endowed with the seventh javana consciousness-moments associated with aversion and wrong view that have occurred by way of matricide, etc., and are fixed in wrongness, the indeterminate phenomena such as the first javana consciousness-moment that have occurred in such a way are common in being associated with aversion, etc., but the phenomena fixed in wrongness are unshared because they belong to a single consciousness-moment. For just as it should not be said that 'consciousness is associated with consciousness,' so too it should not be said that 'what is fixed in wrongness is common to what is fixed in wrongness.' Even among those fixed in wrongness, for those with fixed wrong view who are endowed with the seventh javana consciousness-moment associated with wrong view, the indeterminate phenomena such as the first javana consciousness-moment associated with wrong view are common in being associated with wrong view, etc., but the fixed wrong view is unshared because it is endowed with a single consciousness-moment. Therefore the author of the commentary says:

“Micchattaniyatānaṃ aniyatā dhammā sādhāraṇa, micchattaniyatā dhammā asādhāraṇā. Micchattaniyatesupi niyatamicchādiṭṭhikānaṃ aniyatā dhammā sādhāraṇā, niyatamicchādiṭṭhi asādhāraṇāti iminā nayena visesānupassinā veditabbā”ti (netti. aṭṭha. 34).

'For those fixed in wrongness, indeterminate phenomena are common, but phenomena fixed in wrongness are unshared. Even among those fixed in wrongness, for those with fixed wrong view, indeterminate phenomena are common, but the fixed wrong view is unshared. This should be understood in this way by one who discerns distinctions.'

Tattha “iminā nayenā”ti iminā micchattaniyatānaṃ uppajjituṃ bhabbā aniyatā dhammā sādhāraṇā, uppajjituṃ abhabbā aniyatā dhammā asādhāraṇāti gahitā. Tena vuttaṃ “bhabbābhabbā”ti. Tathā hīnassa hīno hīnabhāvena sādhāraṇo, majjhimukkaṭṭhā asādhāraṇā. Majjhimassa majjhimo sādhāraṇo, hīnukkaṭṭhā asādhāraṇā. Ukkaṭṭhassa ukkaṭṭho ukkaṭṭhabhāvena sādhāraṇo, hīnamajjhimā asādhāraṇātipi gavesitabbā. Tenāha – “hīnukkaṭṭhamajjhimaṃ upādāya gavesitabba”nti.

Therein, by 'in this way' is meant this: for those fixed in wrongness, the indeterminate phenomena that are capable of arising are common, while the indeterminate phenomena that are incapable of arising are unshared. For this reason it was said, 'the capable and the incapable.' Similarly, it should also be sought thus: for an inferior person, another inferior person is common in being inferior, while middling and superior persons are unshared. For a middling person, another middling person is common, while inferior and superior persons are unshared. For a superior person, another superior person is common in being superior, while inferior and middling persons are unshared. Therefore it is said: 'It should be sought with reference to the inferior, superior, and middling.'

“Tattha katame dhammā sādhāraṇā”tiādinā nānāvidhena vibhattihāranayena dhammā vibhajitvā dassitā, amhehi ca ñātā, “kathaṃ bhūmipadaṭṭhānāni vibhattihāranayena vibhajitvā dassitānī”ti pucchitabbabhāvato dhammavibhajanānantaraṃ [M 0.0176] bhūmipadaṭṭhānāni vibhajitvā dassento “dassanabhūmī”tiādimāha. Tattha dassanabhūmīti dassanaṃ bhavati ettha paṭhamamaggeti dassanabhūmi, sotāpattimaggo[V 0.0304]. Niyāmāvakkantiyāti niyamanaṃ niyāmo, ko so? Sampattaniyāmo, avakkanaṃ avakkanti, sotāpattiphalaṃ, niyāmassa avakkanti niyāmāvakkanti, tāya. Dassanabhūmināmako sotāpattimaggo niyāmāvakkantināmakassa sotāpattiphalassa pattiyā padaṭṭhānaṃ. Paṭhamamaggasamaṅgī puggalo hi niyāmaṃ okkamanto nāma, phalasamaṅgī pana niyāmaṃ okkanto nāma hoti, tasmā niyāmāvakkantisaddena paṭhamaphaluppatti gahitā. Bhāvanābhūmīti uparimaggattayaṃ. Uttarikānanti tassa tassa maggassa uparipavattānaṃ taṃtaṃphalānaṃ pattiyā padaṭṭhānanti paccekaṃ yojetabbaṃ.

By the words 'Therein, what phenomena are common?' etc., phenomena have been analyzed and shown by the method of analysis in its various modes, and they are known by us. Since it should be asked, 'How are the grounds and foundations analyzed and shown by the method of analysis?' after the analysis of phenomena, analyzing and showing the grounds and foundations, he says, 'The ground of vision,' etc. Therein, 'the ground of vision' is so called because vision occurs in it, that is, in the first path; the ground of vision is the path of stream-entry. By 'entry into the fixed course': the fixing is the fixed course. What is that? The fixed course of rightness. The entering is the entry, the fruit of stream-entry. The entry into the fixed course is niyāmāvakkanti. The path of stream-entry, called 'the ground of vision,' is the foundation for the attainment of the fruit of stream-entry, called 'the entry into the fixed course.' For a person endowed with the first path is called one who is entering the fixed course, while one endowed with the fruit is called one who has entered the fixed course. Therefore, by the word 'entry into the fixed course,' the arising of the first fruit is to be understood. 'The ground of development' is the three higher paths. 'Of the subsequent ones' should be connected with each individually thus: it is the foundation for the attainment of the respective fruits that arise subsequent to each respective path.

Dukkhā paṭipadā dandhābhiññā mandapaññassa uppajjanato samathaṃ āvahantī hutvā samathassa padaṭṭhānaṃ hoti, sukhāpaṭipadā khippābhiññā ñāṇādhikassa uppajjanato vipassanāvahantī hutvā vipassanāya padaṭṭhānaṃ, avasesā dve paṭipadāpi nātipaññassa uppajjanato samathassa padaṭṭhānanti gahetabbā. Tena aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttaṃ – “itarā pana tissopi paṭipadā samathaṃ āvahantī”tiādi (netti. aṭṭha. 34). Dānamayaṃ puññakiriyavatthu sayameva ekantena dhammassavanassa padaṭṭhānaṃ na hoti, vandanayācanapañhāpucchanādayopi padaṭṭhānaṃ honti, tasmā tehi kāraṇehi sādhāraṇaṃ hutvā paratoghosassa padaṭṭhānaṃ hoti, paratoghoso ca dhammassavanapañhāvissajjanādivasena pavatto. Dātabbavatthupariccajanavandanayācanakālesu hi yebhuyyena dhammaṃ desenti, pañhāpucchanādikālesu ca vissajjenti, paṭipucchasākacchādīni vā karonti. Sīlamayaṃ puññakiriyavatthu pāmojjapītipassaddhisukhasamādhīhi padaṭṭhānabhāvena sādhāraṇaṃ hutvā cintāmayiyā paññāya padaṭṭhānaṃ hoti. Sīlavantassa hi sīlaṃ paccavekkhantassa pāmojjādayo honti, samāhito ca dhammacintane samattho hoti.

The painful practice with slow direct knowledge, arising for one of dull wisdom, brings serenity and thus becomes a proximate cause for serenity. The pleasant practice with quick direct knowledge, arising for one of superior wisdom, brings insight and thus becomes a proximate cause for insight. The remaining two practices, arising for one of not much wisdom, are also to be taken as a proximate cause for serenity. Therefore it is said in the commentary: “The other three practices also bring serenity,” and so on. The meritorious action of giving is not by itself exclusively the proximate cause for hearing the Dhamma; paying homage, requesting, asking questions, and so on are also proximate causes. Therefore, being a common factor on account of these causes, it becomes the proximate cause for a voice from another. And a voice from another proceeds by way of hearing the Dhamma, answering questions, and so on. For at the times of giving gifts, relinquishing possessions, paying homage, and requesting, they generally teach the Dhamma; and at the times of asking questions and the like, they answer, or they engage in counter-questions, discussion, and so on. The meritorious action of virtue, being a common factor through its nature as a proximate cause by way of gladness, rapture, tranquility, happiness, and concentration, becomes the proximate cause for wisdom born of reflection. For when a virtuous person reflects on their virtue, gladness and so on arise, and one who is concentrated is capable of reflecting on the Dhamma.

Bhāvanāmayaṃ puññakiriyavatthūti purimā purimā samathabhāvanā ceva vipassanābhāvanā ca puññakiriyavatthudānasīlādīhi kāraṇehi sādhāraṇaṃ hutvā bhāvanāmayiyā paññāya pacchimāya pacchimāya samathabhāvanāya ceva vipassanābhāvanāya ca padaṭṭhānaṃ. Tena vuttaṃ aṭṭhakathāyaṃ – “sādhāraṇanti na bījaṃ viya aṅkurassa, dassanabhūmiādayo viya niyāmāvakkantiādīnaṃ āveṇikaṃ[M 0.0177], atha kho sādhāraṇaṃ tadaññakāraṇehipī”ti. “Dānamayasīlamayabhāvanāmayapuññakiriyavatthūnaṃ paratoghosacintāmayibhāvanāmayipaññānaṃ padaṭṭhānabhāvo ācariyena vibhatto, evaṃ sati tesaṃ dānamayādīnaṃ yathākkamaṃ pariyattibāhusaccakammaṭṭhānānuyogamaggasammādiṭṭhīnaṃ padaṭṭhānabhāvo na bhaveyyā”ti vattabbattā tathāpavattaṃ padaṭṭhānabhāvampi dassetuṃ “dānamayaṃ puññakiriyavatthu parato ca ghosassa sutamayiyā ca paññāyā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana –

The meritorious action consisting of development is this: earlier and earlier serenity development and insight development, being a common factor on account of causes such as the meritorious actions of giving and virtue, become the proximate cause for wisdom born of development, and for later and later serenity development and insight development. Therefore it is said in the commentary: “ ‘Common’ does not mean exclusive like a seed for a sprout, or like the stages of vision and so on for entering the fixed course, but rather common with other causes as well.” The teacher has analyzed the role as proximate cause of the meritorious actions of giving, virtue, and development for the wisdoms born of a voice from another, of reflection, and of development. Since it could be said that, this being so, those meritorious actions of giving and so on would not, respectively, be the proximate cause for learning the scriptures, great learning, application to a meditation subject, and the right view of the path, in order to show that they do have such a role as proximate cause, it is said: “The meritorious action of giving is a proximate cause for a voice from another and for wisdom born of listening,” and so on. But in the commentary—

“Idāni [V 0.0305] yasmā dānaṃ, sīlaṃ, lokiyabhāvanā ca na kevalaṃ yathāvuttaparatoghosādīnaṃyeva, atha kho yathākkamaṃ pariyattibāhusaccakammaṭṭhānānuyogamaggasammādiṭṭhīnampi paccayā honti, tasmā tampi nayaṃ dassetuṃ puna ‘dānamaya’ntiādinā desanaṃ vaḍḍhesī”ti (netti. aṭṭha. 34) –

“Now, since giving, virtue, and worldly development are conditions not only for a voice from another and so on as stated, but also, respectively, for learning the scriptures, great learning, application to a meditation subject, and right view of the path, therefore, to show this method as well, the teaching is again expanded with ‘consisting of giving,’ and so on.” (Netti. Aṭṭha. 34)

Vuttaṃ. Tattha dānamayapuññakiriyavatthuno paratoghosassa sādhāraṇapadaṭṭhānabhāvo heṭṭhā vuttanayena ñātabbo. Dānaṃ pana datvā desanaṃ sutvā sutānusārena vitthāretvā cintentassa pavattamānāya sutamayiyā paññāya vandanayācanādīhi sādhāraṇaṃ hutvā padaṭṭhānaṃ hoti. Sīlamayapuññakiriyavatthunopi cintāmayiyā paññāya sādhāraṇapadaṭṭhānabhāvo vuttoyeva. Parisuddhasīlaṃ pana nissāya “jhānaṃ nibbattessāmi, maggaphalaṃ nibbattessāmī”tiādinā paccavekkhantassa pavattamānassa yonisomanasikārassa pāmojjādīhi sādhāraṇaṃ hutvā padaṭṭhānaṃ hoti. Bhāvanāmayapuññakiriyavatthuno bhāvanāmayiyā paññāya sādhāraṇapadaṭṭhānabhāvopi vuttoyeva. Samathabhāvanāsaṅkhātaṃ pana jhānaṃ pādakaṃ katvā vā paripākaṃ vipassanābhāvaṃyeva vā nissāya pavattamānāya sammādiṭṭhiyā parisuddhasīlādīhi sādhāraṇaṃ hutvā padaṭṭhānaṃ hoti.

It has been said. Therein, the nature of the meritorious action of giving as a common proximate cause for a voice from another should be understood by the method stated below. However, for one who, having given a gift, listens to the teaching, expands upon it in accordance with what was heard, and reflects, the meritorious action of giving becomes a proximate cause for the arising wisdom born of listening, being a common factor with paying homage, requesting, and so on. The nature of the meritorious action of virtue as a common proximate cause for wisdom born of reflection has also been stated. However, for one who relies on perfectly pure virtue and reflects, ‘I will produce jhāna, I will produce the path and fruit,’ and so on, the meritorious action of virtue becomes a proximate cause for the arising wise attention, being a common factor with gladness and so on. The nature of the meritorious action of development as a common proximate cause for wisdom born of development has also been stated. However, for the right view that arises either by making jhāna—designated as serenity development—its basis, or by relying on the matured state of insight itself, the meritorious action of development becomes a proximate cause, being a common factor with perfectly pure virtue and so on.

Dānamayapuññakiriyavatthuādīnaṃ paratoghosādīnaṃ padaṭṭhānabhāvo punappunaṃ ācariyena vibhatto, amhehi ca ñāto, “patirūpadesavāsādayopi imesaṃ dhammānaṃ padaṭṭhānānīti yathā vibhajitabbā, amhehi ca viññātabbā, tathā vibhajitvā dassethā”ti vattabbattā tepi vibhajitvā dassetuṃ “patirūpadesavāso”tiādimāha. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana “tathā [M 0.0178] patirūpadesavāsādayo kāyavivekacittavivekādīnaṃ kāraṇaṃ hontīti imaṃ nayaṃ dassetuṃ ‘patirūpadesavāso’tiādimāhā”ti (netti. aṭṭha. 34) vuttaṃ. Patirūpadesaṃ nissāya vasantassa kāyavivekacittavivekavaḍḍhanato, samādhivaḍḍhanato ca patirūpadesavāso kāyacittavivekassa ca upacārasamādhiappanāsamādhissa ca sīlādīhi sādhāraṇaṃ hutvā padaṭṭhānaṃ. Sappurisūpanissayoti sappurisasantāne pavatto payirupāsato ālambitabbo pasādo, tato vā upanissayaṃ labhitvā payirupāsantānaṃ santāne pavatto pubbapasādo yathāvidho sappurisūpanissayo payirupāsantassa saddhāsampannassa ratanattaye tiṇṇaṃ aveccappasādānaṃ ratanattayaguṇādīhi sādhāraṇaṃ hutvā padaṭṭhānaṃ, samathassa labhananimittadāyakaṃ sappurisaṃ payirupāsitvā tena dinnanaye ṭhatvā pavattetabbassa samathassa sappurisūpanissayo sīlapāmojjapītādīhi [V 0.0306] sādhāraṇaṃ hutvā padaṭṭhānaṃ. Attasammāpaṇihitassa pāpajigucchādīnaṃ sambhavato attasammāpaṇidhānaṃ jātivayādipaccavekkhaṇena sādhāraṇaṃ hutvā hiriyā ca padaṭṭhānaṃ, attasammāpaṇihitassa nibbidādīnaṃ sambhavato sīlādīhi sādhāraṇaṃ hutvā vipassanāya ca padaṭṭhānaṃ.

The role as proximate cause of the meritorious actions of giving and so on for a voice from another and so on has been repeatedly analyzed by the teacher and is known by us. Since it should be asked: “How dwelling in a suitable region and so on are also proximate causes for these phenomena should be analyzed and understood by us; therefore, having analyzed them, please explain them,” to show them by analysis, he said, “dwelling in a suitable region,” and so on. In the commentary, however, it is said: “To show this method—that dwelling in a suitable region and so on are causes for physical seclusion, mental seclusion, and so on—he said, ‘dwelling in a suitable region,’ and so on” (Netti. Aṭṭha. 34). For one who dwells in reliance on a suitable region, because physical and mental seclusion and concentration increase, dwelling in a suitable region becomes a proximate cause for physical and mental seclusion and for access and absorption concentration, being a common factor with virtue and so on. Reliance on good persons is the confidence present in the mental continuum of a good person, which is to be taken as an object by one who associates with them; or it is the prior confidence that arises in the mental continuum of one who associates after obtaining reliance from them. Such reliance on good persons becomes a proximate cause for the three kinds of confirmed confidence in the Triple Gem for a faithful person who associates with them, being a common factor with the qualities of the Triple Gem and so on. Reliance on good persons becomes a proximate cause for the serenity to be developed by one who, having associated with a good person who gives a sign for obtaining serenity, abides in the method taught by him, being a common factor with virtue, gladness, rapture, and so on. Because for one who is rightly self-directed, disgust with evil and so on arises, right self-direction becomes a proximate cause for moral shame, being a common factor with reflection on birth, age, and so on. Because for one who is rightly self-directed, disenchantment and so on arises, right self-direction becomes a proximate cause for insight, being a common factor with virtue and so on.

Tadaṅgādivasena akusalapariccāgo nibbidāñāṇādīhi sādhāraṇaṃ hutvā kusalavīmaṃsāya paṭisaṅkhānupassanāya paññāya ca ariyamaggasamādhindriyassa ca padaṭṭhānaṃ. Dhammasvākkhātatā svākkhātadhammassavanānusārena pavattakusalamūlakā lokiyalokuttarasampatti kusalamūlaropanā nāma, tāya ca tathāvidhakusalamūlakāya phalasamāpattiyā ca padaṭṭhānaṃ. Saṅghasuppaṭipannatā saṅghasuṭṭhutāya saṅghassa upaṭṭhākānaṃ suṭṭhubhāvāya sappatissavāya vacanasampaṭicchanabhāvāya padaṭṭhānaṃ. Satthusampadā satthari ceva dhammādīsu ca guṇaajānanatāya appasannānañca pasādāya pasannānañca appamattakapasādānañca bhiyyobhāvāya vaḍḍhanāya padaṭṭhānaṃ. Appaṭihatapātimokkhatā saṅghamajjhe vā parisamajjhe vā dummaṅkūnaṃ dummukhānaṃ dussīlānaṃ puggalānaṃ niggahāya, pesalānaṃ pātimokkhasaṃvarādisīlasampannānaṃ puggalānaṃ phāsuvihārāya ca padaṭṭhānaṃ hoti. Honto pana yathānurūpehi aññehi kāraṇehi sādhāraṇaṃ hutvā hotīti veditabbo.

The abandonment of unwholesome states by way of substitution of opposites and so on, being a common factor with knowledge of disenchantment and so on, becomes a proximate cause for wholesome inquiry, for the wisdom of reflective contemplation, and for the faculty of concentration of the noble path. The well-proclaimed nature of the Dhamma: the worldly and supramundane success rooted in wholesome qualities that proceeds in accordance with hearing the well-proclaimed Dhamma is called ‘the planting of wholesome roots.’ And it is a proximate cause for such wholesome roots and for the attainment of fruition. The good practice of the Sangha is a proximate cause for the excellence of the Sangha, for the good state of the Sangha's supporters, for their deference, and for their acceptance of speech. The accomplishment of the Teacher is a proximate cause for inspiring confidence in the unconfident who do not know his qualities and those of the Dhamma and so on, and for the increase and growth of the confidence of the confident, even if their confidence is slight. The unhindered nature of the Pātimokkha becomes a proximate cause for the censure of unruly, foul-mouthed, and immoral persons in the midst of the Sangha or an assembly, and for the comfortable abiding of amiable persons endowed with the Pātimokkha restraint and other virtues. However, it should be understood that in being so, it is a common factor with other suitable causes.

“Vāsanābhāgiyasuttādīsu [M 0.0179] vuttadhammabhūmipadaṭṭhānānaṃ vibhattihārena vibhajitabbabhāvo amhehi kena jānitabbo saddahitabbo”ti pucchitabbattā “tenāhā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tassattho vuttanayānusārena veditabbo.

Because it should be asked: “By what means are we to know and have faith that the grounds and proximate causes of the phenomena stated in the Vāsanābhāgiyasutta and other texts are to be analyzed by the guideline of analysis?” it was said, “Therefore he said,” and so on. Its meaning should be understood in accordance with the method that has been stated.

“Ettāvatā ca vibhattihāro paripuṇṇo, añño niyutto natthī”ti vattabbattā “niyutto vibhattihāro”ti vuttaṃ. Yattha yattha sutte ye ye dhammādayo vuttā, tattha tattha sutte vuttesu tesu tesu dhammādīsu yathālābhavasena yo yo vibhattihāro yojito, so so vibhattihāro niddhāretvā yutto yojitoti attho daṭṭhabbo.

Because it can be said, “To this extent the guideline of analysis is complete; there is no other to be assigned,” it is called ‘the assigned guideline of analysis.’ The meaning should be seen thus: in whatever sutta whatever phenomena and so on are stated, in that very sutta, regarding those very phenomena and so on stated therein, whatever guideline of analysis is applied according to what is available, that very guideline of analysis is determined to be suitable and is applied.

Iti vibhattihāravibhaṅge sattibalānurūpā racitā

Thus, the analysis of the Guideline of Analysis has been composed in accordance with my strength and ability.

Vibhāvanā niṭṭhitā.

The elucidation is finished.

Paṇḍitehi pana aṭṭhakathāṭīkānusāreneva gambhīrattho vitthārato vibhajitvā gahetabboti.

However, the profound meaning should be extensively analyzed and grasped by the wise only in accordance with the commentaries and subcommentaries.

9. Parivattanahāravibhaṅgavibhāvanā

9. Elucidation of the Analysis of the Transformation Mode of Exposition

35. Yena [V 0.0307] yena saṃvaṇṇāvisesabhūtena vibhattihāravibhaṅgena sutte vuttā dhammādayo vibhattā, so saṃvaṇṇāvisesabhūto vibhaṅgo paripuṇṇo, “katamo parivattanahāravibhaṅgo”ti pucchitabbattā “tattha katamo parivattano hāro”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha tatthāti tesu niddiṭṭhesu soḷasasu desanāhārādīsu katamo saṃvaṇṇanāviseso parivattano hāro parivattanahāravibhaṅgo nāmāti pucchati. “Kusalākusale dhamme”tiādiniddesassa idāni mayā vuccamāno “sammādiṭṭhissa purisapuggalassā”tiādiko vitthārasaṃvaṇṇanāviseso parivattano hāro parivattanahāravibhaṅgo nāmāti attho gahetabbo.

35. The analysis of the mode of exposition, which is a particular kind of explanation, by which the states, etc., mentioned in the Sutta are distinguished—that analysis, being a particular kind of explanation, is complete. Because it is to be asked, ‘What is the analysis of the transformation mode of exposition?’, it is said, ‘Here, what is the transformation mode of exposition?’ and so on. Here, in those sixteen modes of exposition, etc., that have been indicated, it is asked: ‘Which particular explanation is called the transformation mode of exposition, the analysis of the transformation mode of exposition?’ The meaning to be understood is that the particular detailed explanation of the instruction beginning with ‘wholesome and unwholesome states’—an explanation now being stated by me and beginning with ‘for a person with right view’—is called the transformation mode of exposition, the analysis of the transformation mode of exposition.

“Saṃvaṇṇiyamāne sutte niddiṭṭhassa katamassa bhāvitabbassa kusalassa katamo paṭipakkho, kathaṃ parivattetabbo”ti pucchitabbattā imassa bhāvitabbassa kusalassa ayaṃ paṭipakkho, evaṃ pahātabbabhāvavasena parivattetabboti [M 0.0180] dassento “sammādiṭṭhissa purisapuggalassā”tiādimāha. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana –

Because it is to be asked, ‘In the Sutta being explained, what is the opposite of which wholesome state that is to be developed, and how is it to be transformed?’, showing that ‘this is the opposite of this wholesome state to be developed, and it is to be transformed by way of its nature as something to be abandoned,’ he said, ‘For a person with right view…’ In the commentary, however—

“Tattha yasmā saṃvaṇṇiyamāne sutte yathāniddiṭṭhānaṃ kusalākusaladhammānaṃ paṭipakkhabhūte akusalakusaladhamme pahātabbabhāvādivasena niddhāraṇaṃ paṭipakkhato parivattanaṃ, tasmā ‘sammādiṭṭhissa purisapuggalassa micchādiṭṭhi nijjiṇṇā bhavatī’tiādi āraddha”nti (netti. aṭṭha. 35) –

Here, because in the Sutta being explained, the determination of the unwholesome and wholesome states that are the opposites of the wholesome and unwholesome states as indicated, by way of their nature as things to be abandoned, etc., is a transformation from the opposite, therefore the passage beginning 'For a person with right view, wrong view is worn out' is commenced." (Netti. Aṭṭha. 35) –

Vuttaṃ. Pahāyakassa hi dhammassa pahātabbabhāvavasena niddhāraṇaṃ, pahātabbassa ca dhammassa pahāyakabhāvavasena niddhāraṇaṃ paṭipakkhato parivattanaṃ nāma hoti. Tattha sammādiṭṭhissāti sammā sundarā pasatthā diṭṭhi yassa puggalassāti sammādiṭṭhi. Puggalapadaṭṭhānā hi ayaṃ desanā. Tena vuttaṃ “purisapuggalassā”ti. Sā pana sammādiṭṭhi kammakammaphalādisaddahanavasena vā aniccādivipassanāvasena vā maggasammādassanavasena vā pavattā niravasesāva gahitā. “Yāya bhāvitāya sammādiṭṭhiyā pahātabbā micchādiṭṭhi nijjiṇṇā bhavati, yadi kevalā micchādiṭṭhiyeva nijjiṇṇā bhavati, evaṃ sati tadavasesā akusalā dhammā ajiṇṇā

It is said. Indeed, the determination of a state that abandons in terms of the nature of what is to be abandoned, and the determination of a state to be abandoned in terms of the nature of what abandons, is called transformation from the opposite. Here, 'of one with right view' means: right, beautiful, and praiseworthy is the view of the person who possesses it; hence, right view. Indeed, this teaching has the individual as its basis. Therefore it is said, 'of a person.' That right view, however, whether it arises through conviction in kamma and its results, etc., or through insight into impermanence, etc., or through the right vision of the path, is grasped completely, without remainder. 'By which developed right view, the wrong view to be abandoned is worn out; if only wrong view itself is worn out, then the remaining unwholesome states would not be worn out...'

Bhaveyyu”nti [V 0.0308] vattabbattā “ye cassa micchādiṭṭhipaccayā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Micchādiṭṭhipaccayā aneke pāpakā akusalāyeva dhammā ca uppajjeyyuṃ uppajjanārahā bhaveyyuṃ, te ca akusalā dhammā assa sammādiṭṭhisampannassa purisapuggalassa nijjiṇṇā pahātabbārahā anuppajjanasabhāvā honti. Tenāha bhagavā – “upādānanirodhā bhavanirodho”ti (udā. 2; mahāva. 1).

Because it must be said, '...would be,' therefore 'and those which for him are conditioned by wrong view' and so on is stated. Due to the condition of wrong view, many evil, unwholesome states would arise or would be liable to arise; but for that person endowed with right view, those unwholesome states are worn out, liable to abandonment, and of a nature not to arise. Therefore, the Blessed One said: 'With the cessation of clinging, there is cessation of existence' (Ud. 2; Mahāva. 1).

“Yadi sammādiṭṭhissa purisapuggalassa micchādiṭṭhi, tappaccayā akusaladhammāyeva nijjiṇṇā bhavanti, evaṃ sati sammādiṭṭhipaccayā kusalā dhammā na sambhaveyyu”nti vattabbattā “sammādiṭṭhipaccayā cā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Assa sammādiṭṭhisampannassa purisapuggalassa uppajjanārahā sammādiṭṭhipaccayā aneke kusalā samathavipassanā vā bodhipakkhiyā vā dhammā sambhavanti, uppannā ca te dhammā assa sammādiṭṭhisampannassa purisapuggalassa santāne punappunaṃ pavattanavasena bhāvanāpāripūriṃ gacchanti.

Because it must be said, 'If for a person with right view, only wrong view and unwholesome states conditioned by it were worn out, then wholesome states conditioned by right view would not arise,' therefore 'and due to the condition of right view...' and so on was stated. For that person endowed with right view, many wholesome states—such as serenity and insight, or the factors of enlightenment—are capable of arising due to the condition of right view. And those arisen states, through repeated occurrence in the mental continuum of that person endowed with right view, go to the fullness of development.

Sammādiṭṭhiyā [M 0.0181] paṭipakkhānaṃ micchādiṭṭhiyā, tappaccayānaṃ akusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ parivattanabhāvo ācariyena vibhatto, amhehi ca ñāto, “sammāsaṅkappassa dhammassa paṭipakkho dhammo kathaṃ parivattetabbo”ti vattabbattā “sammāsaṅkappassa purisapuggalassā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Yojanattha ādayo vuttanayānusārena veditabbā. Sammā sundarā pasatthā vācā yassa puggalassāti sammāvāco, tassa sammāvācassa. “Purisapuggalassā”tiādīnaṃ atthopi vuttanayena veditabbo. Ayaṃ pana visesatthosammā aviparītato vimuttiñāṇadassanaṃ yassa puggalassāti sammāvimuttiñāṇadassano, tassa sammāvimuttiñāṇadassanassa paccavekkhaṇañāṇadassanasampannassa purisapuggalassa “avimuttāva samānā vimuttā maya”nti micchābhinivesavasena pavattaṃ micchāvimuttiñāṇadassanaṃ nijjiṇṇaṃ vigataṃ bhavati. “Ye cassā”tiādīnaṃ anusandhyādiko vuttanayānusārena veditabbo.

The state of transformation of wrong view, which is the opposite of right view, and of the unwholesome states conditioned by it, has been explained by the teacher and is known to us. Because it must be said, 'How is the state that is the opposite of the state of right intention to be transformed?', therefore 'of the person with right intention' and so on has been stated. The meaning of the connection, etc., should be understood according to the method explained. Right, beautiful, or praiseworthy speech is that of which person, thus one with right speech; of that one with right speech. The meaning of 'of a person,' etc., should also be understood according to the method explained. Here, however, is a special meaning: Right, undistorted knowledge and vision of liberation is that of which person, thus one with right knowledge and vision of liberation; for that person with right knowledge and vision of liberation, endowed with the knowledge and vision of review, the wrong knowledge and vision of liberation, which arises through adherence to the false conceit that 'Though we are not liberated, we are liberated,' is worn out and has ceased. The connection, sequence, and so on, of the phrase beginning 'And for whom...' should be understood according to the method explained.

36. “Sammādiṭṭhissātiādinā sammādiṭṭhiādīnaṃ kusalānaṃ paṭipakkhā micchādiṭṭhādikāyeva akusalā pahātabbabhāvena parivattetabbā”ti pucchitabbattā pāṇātipātāveramaṇiādīnaṃ kusalānaṃ paṭipakkhā pāṇātipātādikāpi akusalā pahātabbabhāvena parivattetabbāti dassetuṃ “yassa vā pāṇātipātā paṭiviratassā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana “evaṃ sammādiṭṭhiādimukhena micchādiṭṭhiādiṃ dassetvā puna pāṇātipātaadinnādānakāmesumicchācārādito veramaṇiyādīhi pāṇātipātādīnaṃ parivattanaṃ dassetuṃ ‘yassā’tiādi āraddha”nti (netti. aṭṭha. 36) vuttaṃ. Tadaṅgādivasenapahīno hoti. Kālavādissāti vaditabbakāle vaditabbaṃ vadati sīlenāti kālavādī, tassa.

36. Because it must be asked, 'By 'one with right view,' etc., are only wrong view and other unwholesome states, which are the opposites of right view and other wholesome states, to be transformed by way of their nature as things to be abandoned?', therefore, to show that unwholesome states such as killing living beings, which are the opposites of wholesome states such as abstaining from killing living beings, are also to be transformed by way of their nature as things to be abandoned, 'For one who abstains from killing living beings,' etc., is stated. In the commentary, however, it is said: 'Having thus shown wrong view, etc., through the perspective of right view, etc., then to demonstrate the transformation of killing, taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, etc., by means of abstaining from killing, taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, etc., the passage beginning 'for one who' is commenced.' (Netti. Aṭṭha. 36) It is abandoned by way of substitution, etc. 'A timely speaker' means one whose nature is to speak what should be spoken at the appropriate time; of him.

“Yathāvuttappakāreneva [V 0.0309] parivattetabbā”ti pucchitabbattā aññena pakārenapi parivattetabbāti dassetuṃ “ye ca kho kecī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana “ye ca kho kecītiādinā sammādiṭṭhiādimukheneva micchādiṭṭhiādīhi eva parivattanaṃ pakārantarena dassetī”ti (netti. aṭṭha. 36) vuttaṃ. Tattha keci micchādiṭṭhikamicchāsaṅkappādikāyeva puggalā paresaṃ ariyānaṃ ariyaṃ aṭṭhaṅgikaṃ maggaṃ garahanti. Sandiṭṭhikā sandiṭṭhe niyuttā, sahadhammikā saha dhammena kāraṇena ye vattanti sahadhammikā. Gārayhā garahitabbākāre yuttā[M 0.0182]. Vādā ca anuvādā ca vādānuvādā, te bhavanto sammādiṭṭhiñca dhammaṃ garahanti. Tena garahaṇena. Pujjā pūjitabbā ca na bhavanti, pāsaṃsā pasaṃsitabbā ca na bhavanti. Evantiādīsu sammāsaṅkappaṃ vā sammāvācādikaṃ vā visuṃ visuṃ sammāsaṅkappañca te bhavanto dhammaṃ garahanti. Tena hi ye micchāsaṅkappikā, te bhavanto na pujjā ca pāsaṃsā ca…pe… sammāvimuttiñca te bhavanto dhammaṃ garahanti. Tena hi ye micchādiṭṭhivācikā, te bhavanto na pujjā ca pāsaṃsā ca. Sammāvimuttiñāṇadassanañca te bhavanto dhammaṃ garahanti. Tena hi ye micchāvimuttikā, te bhavanto na pujjā ca pāsaṃsā ca. Sammāvimuttiñāṇadassanañca te bhavanto dhammaṃ garahanti. Tena hi ye micchāvimuttiñāṇadassanikā, te bhavanto na pujjā ca pāsaṃsā cāti yojanā kātabbā. “Micchāvimuttiñāṇadassanā”tipi pāṭho atthi.

Because it must be asked, 'Should it be transformed only in the way it has been stated?', to show that it should be transformed in another way as well, 'And whoever...' etc. is stated. However, in the commentary, it is said, 'By 'And whoever...' etc., it shows the transformation from right view etc. by means of wrong view etc. in a different manner.' (Netti. Aṭṭha. 36). Therein, some individuals, being only those with wrong view, wrong intention, etc., criticize the Noble Eightfold Path of others, the noble ones. 'Sandiṭṭhikā' means those engaged in what is seen. 'Sahadhammikā' means those who conduct themselves with the Dhamma, with reason. 'Gārayhā' means those fit for the manner of being criticized. 'Vādā ca anuvādā ca' means assertions and subsequent assertions. Those venerable ones criticize right view and the Dhamma. By that criticism, they are neither worthy of reverence nor worthy of praise. In these cases, etc., those venerable ones criticize right intention, or right speech, etc., separately. They criticize right intention and the Dhamma. Therefore, those who have wrong intention are neither worthy of reverence nor worthy of praise... They criticize right liberation and the Dhamma. Therefore, those who are speakers of wrong view are neither worthy of reverence nor worthy of praise. They criticize right knowledge and vision of liberation and the Dhamma. Therefore, those who have wrong liberation are neither worthy of reverence nor worthy of praise. They criticize right knowledge and vision of liberation and the Dhamma. Therefore, those who have wrong knowledge and vision of liberation are neither worthy of reverence nor worthy of praise. The connection should be made thus. There is also a reading 'micchāvimuttiñāṇadassanā'.

“Ariyamaggasammādiṭṭhādīnaṃ garahavaseneva micchādiṭṭhādayo ca parivattetabbā, nāvasesānaṃ pasaṃsāvasenā”ti vattabbattā kāmādīnaṃ pasaṃsāvasenapi kāmānaṃ paṭipakkhā veramaṇiyādayopi parivattetabbāti dassetuṃ “ye ca kho keci evamāhaṃsū”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha bhuñjitabbā kāmā, paribhuñjitabbā kāmā, āsevitabbā kāmā, nisevitabbā kāmāti ettha kāmīyanteti kāmāti kammasādhanavasena vatthukāmā gahitā, nātipaṇītā kāmā bhuñjitabbā, atipaṇītā kāmā pari samantato bhuñjitabbā. Atipaṇītatarā kāmā ā bhuso sevitabbā, niyatā sevitabbā. Bhāvayitabbā kāmā, bahulīkātabbā kāmāti ettha pana kāmentīti kāmāti kattusādhanavasena kilesakāmā gahitā, punappunaṃ uppādanavasena bhāvayitabbā vaḍḍhāpetabbā pavattetabbā kilesakāmā, bahūnaṃ punappunaṃ uppādanavasena kātabbā vaḍḍhāpetabbā kilesakāmāti ye ca kāmavasikā puthujjanā keci evamāhaṃsu tesaṃ kāmavasikānaṃ puthujjanānaṃ kesañci tādisehi kāmehi veramaṇī kusalacetanā paṭipakkhavasena adhammo asevitabbo nāma āpajjeyyāti adhippāyo gahetabbo.

Because it is to be said, 'Wrong views and so forth are to be transformed only by way of criticizing the noble path's right view and so forth, not by way of praising the remaining things,' in order to show that even abstinences, which are the opponents of sensual pleasures, etc., should be transformed by way of praising sensual pleasures, etc., it is said: 'But whoever said thus…' Herein, regarding the phrases 'sensual pleasures to be enjoyed, sensual pleasures to be indulged in, sensual pleasures to be frequented, sensual pleasures to be devoted to,' the term 'sensual pleasures' (kāmā) is understood as objective sensual pleasures, derived in the objective sense (kammasādhana) because they are desired (kāmīyanti). Sensual pleasures that are not very refined are to be enjoyed; those that are very refined are to be fully enjoyed. Those that are even more refined are to be greatly frequented and regularly devoted to. However, regarding 'sensual pleasures to be cultivated, sensual pleasures to be made much of,' the term 'sensual pleasures' (kāmā) is understood as defilement-sensual pleasures, derived in the agentive sense (kattusādhana) because they desire (kāmenti). Defilement-sensual pleasures are to be cultivated, increased, and maintained by way of repeated arising; and defilement-sensual pleasures are to be made much of and increased by way of causing them to arise repeatedly for many. And for whichever ordinary persons under the sway of sensual pleasures said thus, for some of those ordinary persons under the sway of sensual pleasures, abstinence from such sensual pleasures, being wholesome volition, would, by way of opposition, amount to what is called 'an unrighteousness not to be practiced'—this meaning should be understood.

Antadvayavasena [V 0.0310] parivattanaṃ dassetuṃ “ye vā pana kecī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Attakilamathānuyogo dhammoti niyyānikoti ye vā pana pañcātapādipaṭipannakā tatthiyā evamāhaṃsu, tesaṃ pañcātapādipaṭipannakānaṃ niyyāniko dhammo majjhimāpaṭipadāsaṅkhāto vipassanāsahito ariyamaggo [M 0.0183] adhammo aniyyāniko abhāvetabbo nāma āpajjeyyāti. Sukhadukkhavasenapi parivattanaṃ dassetuṃ “ye ca kho”tiādi vuttaṃ. “Pāpaṃ nijjarāpessāmā”ti attahiṃsanādivasena paṭipannakānaṃ pavatto sarīratāpano dukkho dhammo niyyānikoti.

To show the transformation by means of the two extremes, it is said: “Or whoever else…” “The practice of self-mortification is the Dhamma, the path to liberation”—so the sectarians who follow the fivefold austerity said thus. For those practitioners of the fivefold austerity, the Dhamma leading to liberation, which is the Noble Path accompanied by insight (vipassanā) and designated as the Middle Way, would amount to what is called “non-Dhamma, not leading to liberation, something not to be developed.” To show the transformation based on pleasure and pain, it is said: “And whoever indeed…” “We will wear away evil”—thus, for those who practice by way of self-harm and so forth, the painful Dhamma, which is the tormenting of the body that has arisen, is leading to liberation.

Ye ca tathāpaṭipannakā keci evamāhaṃsu, tesaṃ tathāpaṭipannakānaṃ anavajjapaccayaparibhogavasena pavatto sarīradukkhūpasamo sukho dhammo adhammo appavattetabbo āpajjeyyāti.

And for whichever persons who practice thus said thus, for those who practice thus, the pleasant Dhamma—the calming of bodily suffering that proceeds from the blameless use of requisites—would amount to what is called 'non-Dhamma, not to be maintained.'

Antadvayādivasena parivattanaṃ ācariyena vibhattaṃ, amhehi ca ñātaṃ, “kathaṃ asubhasaññādivasena parivattetabbo”ti pucchitabbattā evaṃ asubhasaññādivasena subhasaññādikā parivattetabbāti dassetuṃ “yathā vā panā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana “idāni asubhasaññādimukhena subhasaññādiparivattanaṃ dassetuṃ ‘yathā vā panā’tiādi vutta”nti (netti. aṭṭha. 36) vuttaṃ. Sabbasaṅkhāresūti tebhūmakasaṅkhāresu. Āraddhavipassakassa hi tebhūmakā dhammā kilesāsucipaggharaṇakattā asubhato upaṭṭhahanti.

The transformation by way of the two extremes and so forth has been explained by the teacher, and it is known by us. Because it should be asked, “How should it be transformed by way of the perception of foulness and so forth?,” to show that the perception of beauty and so forth should thus be transformed by way of the perception of foulness and so forth, it is said: “Or alternatively…” In the commentary, however, it is said: “Now, to show the transformation of the perception of beauty and so forth through the perception of foulness and so forth, ‘Or alternatively,’ etc., is stated” (Netti. Aṭṭha. 36). “In all conditioned things” means in the conditioned things of the three planes of existence. For one who has undertaken insight meditation, the phenomena of the three planes of existence appear as foul because they ooze the impurity of the defilements.

“Yadi sarūpatoyeva imesaṃ ime paṭipakkhāti aparivattetabbā siyuṃ, evaṃ sati niravasesā ca paṭipakkhā na sakkā parivattetuṃ, kathaṃ sakkā parivattetu”nti vattabbattā parivattanalakkhaṇaṃ dassento “yaṃ yaṃ vā panā”tiādimāha. Tattha kusalaṃ vā akusalaṃ vā yaṃ yaṃ dhammaṃ parivattetukāmo ācariyo cittena rocayati diṭṭhiyā upagacchati, kusalassa vā akusalassa vā tassa tassa rucikassa upagatassa dhammassa yo paṭipakkho, so paṭipakkhadhammo asaddhammo assa dhammassa aniṭṭhato paccanīkato ajjhāpanno pariññāto. Iṭṭhaṃ vā aniṭṭhaṃ vā yaṃ yaṃ dhammaṃ parivattetukāmo ācariyo cittena rocayati diṭṭhiyā upagacchati, iṭṭhassa vā aniṭṭhassa vā tassa tassa rucikassa dhammassa yo paṭipakkho, so paṭipakkhadhammo assa dhammassa aniṭṭhato paccanīkadhammato ajjhāpanno pariññāto bhavatīti parivattetukāmena icchitabbadhammānurūpapaṭipakkhavasena parivattanaṃ kātabbanti parivattane paṭipakkhalakkhaṇaṃ vuttaṃ. Tena aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttaṃ – “paṭipakkhassa lakkhaṇaṃ vibhāvetī”ti.

“If these were their opposing states merely by their own nature, then they would be untransformable. In that case, all remaining opposing states could not be transformed. How then could they be transformed?” Because it should be said thus, showing the characteristic of transformation, he said: “Whatever, indeed…” Herein, whether wholesome or unwholesome, whatever state the teacher wishes to transform, he approves of with his mind and adopts with his view. The opposing state of that particular liked and adopted wholesome or unwholesome state—that opposing state is known as a false state, undesirable, contrary, and comprised within opposition to that state. Whether desirable or undesirable, whatever state the teacher wishes to transform, he approves of with his mind and adopts with his view. The opposing state of that particular liked desirable or undesirable state—that opposing state is known as undesirable, as a contrary state, and comprised within opposition to that state. Thus, transformation should be done by way of an opposing state corresponding to the desired state one wishes to transform. In transformation, the characteristic of the opposing state has been stated. Therefore, it is said in the commentary: “He elucidates the characteristic of the opposing state.”

“Evaṃ [V 0.0311][M 0.0184] vuttappakāraṃ parivattanaṃ amhehi kathaṃ saddahitabba”nti vattabbatā “tenāhā”tiādi vuttaṃ.

Because it should be said, “How are we to believe a transformation described in this way?,” it is said: “Therefore, he said,” and so forth.

“Ettāvatā parivatto hāro paripuṇṇo, añño niyutto natthī”ti vattabbattā “niyutto parivattano hāro”ti vuttaṃ. Yasmiṃ sutte kusalākusale niddiṭṭhe paṭipakkhavasena nīharitvā yathāsambhavaṃ yo yo parivattano hāro niyutto, tasmiṃ sutte niddiṭṭhe paṭipakkhavasena nīharitvā so so parivattano hāro niyutto niddhāretvā yutto yojitoti attho gahetabboti.

“Thus far the mode of transformation is complete; there is no other appointed.” Because it should be said thus, it is said: “The appointed mode of transformation.” In whichever discourse the wholesome and unwholesome are indicated, by extracting them through their opposites, whatever mode of transformation is appointed according to possibility, in that discourse, by indicating them through their opposites, that mode of transformation is appointed, determined, connected, and applied—this meaning should be understood.

Iti parivattanahāravibhaṅge sattibalānurūpā racitā

Thus, in the Analysis of the Mode of Transformation, it was composed in accordance with ability and strength.

Vibhāvanā niṭṭhitā.

The Exposition is finished.

Paṇḍitehi pana aṭṭhakathāṭīkānusārena gambhīrattho vitthārato vibhajitvā gahetabboti.

However, the profound meaning should be analyzed in detail and grasped by the learned, according to the commentaries and sub-commentaries.

10. Vevacanahāravibhaṅgavibhāvanā

10. An Exposition on the Analysis of the Method of Synonyms

37. Yena yena saṃvaṇṇanāvisesabhūtena pavattanahāravibhaṅgena parivattetabbā suttatthā vibhattā, so saṃvaṇṇanāvisesabhūto parivattanahāravibhaṅgo paripuṇṇo, “katamo vevacanahāravibhaṅgo”ti pucchitabbattā “tattha katamo vevacano hāro”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha tatthāti tesu niddiṭṭhesu soḷasasu desanāhārādīsu katamo saṃvaṇṇanāviseso vevacano hāro vevacanahāravibhaṅgo nāmāti pucchati. “Vevacanāni bahūnī”tiādiniddesassa idāni mayā vuccamāno “ekaṃ bhagavā dhamma”ntiādiko vitthārasaṃvaṇṇanāviseso vevacano hāro vevacanahāravibhaṅgo nāmāti attho gahetabbo. “Yāni vevacanāni niddhāritāni, katamāni tāni vevacanānī”ti pucchitabbattā “yathā eka”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Ekaṃ viññātabbaṃ dhammaṃ sabhāvadhammaṃ paññāpetabbaṃ vā dhammaṃ aññamaññehi yathā yehi pakārehi ceva vevacanehi ca bhagavā niddisati, tathāpakārāni vevacanāni viññātabbānīti attho. “Tāni vevacanāni kinti [M 0.0185] bhagavā āhā”ti vattabbattā “yathāha bhagavā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Yathā yaṃyaṃpakārāni vevacanāni –

37. That special mode of exposition, the Analysis of the Method of Transformation, by which the meanings of the suttas to be transformed have been analyzed, is now complete. Because it should be asked, 'What is the analysis of the method of synonyms?,' it is said, 'Therein, what is the method of synonyms?' and so on. Therein—that is, among those sixteen specified methods of teaching and so on—he asks: 'What special mode of exposition is the method of synonyms, what is called the analysis of the method of synonyms?' The meaning should be taken thus: in reference to the statement beginning 'Synonyms are many,' this detailed special mode of exposition that is now being stated by me, beginning 'The Blessed One... one Dhamma,' is the method of synonyms, what is called the analysis of the method of synonyms. Because it should be asked, 'Which are those synonyms that have been determined?,' it is said, 'For example, one,' and so on. The meaning is: in whatever ways and by whatever various synonyms the Blessed One indicates one thing—a Dhamma to be understood, a Dhamma that is a specific nature, or a Dhamma to be made known—in such ways are the synonyms to be understood. Because it should be said, 'How did the Blessed One state those synonyms?,' it is said, 'As the Blessed One said,' and so on. Just as whatever kinds of synonyms—

“Āsā [V 0.0312] ca pihā ca abhinandanā ca, anekadhātūsu sarā patiṭṭhitā;

Aññāṇamūlappabhavā pajappitā, sabbā mayā byantikatā samūlikā”ti. –

“Hope and yearning and delight—attachments established in the diverse elements; sprung from the root of ignorance, they are proliferated. All these I have terminated, together with their root.”

Bhagavā āha, taṃtaṃpakārāni vevacanāni viññātabbānīti attho.

The Blessed One has spoken. The meaning is that those various kinds of synonyms are to be understood.

Ekasseva dhammassa anekehi pariyāyabhūtehi vevacanehi niddisane phalaṃ aṭṭhakathāyaṃ (netti. aṭṭha. 37) bahudhā vuttaṃ, tasmā amhehi na dassitaṃ. “Katamā āsā, katamā pihādī”ti pucchitabbattā “āsā nāma vuccatī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Yā bhavissassa atthassa āsīsanā avassaṃ āgamissatīti yā āsā assa āsīsantassa puggalassa uppajjati, tassa āsīsanā “āsā nāmā”ti vuccati. Vattamānassa yā patthanā assa patthayantassa uppajjati, seyyataraṃ vā aññaṃ disvā “ediso ahaṃ bhaveyya”nti yā pihā assa pihayantassa uppajjati, sā patthanā “pihā nāmā”ti vuccati. Anāgatatthaṃ ārabbha pavattā taṇhā “āsā”ti vuccati, anāgatapaccuppannatthaṃ ārabbha pavattā taṇhā “pihā”ti vuccati, tathāpi taṇhābhāvena ekattā eko dhammova atthassa icchitassa nipphatti atthanipphatti, paṭipāleti etāya taṇhāyāti paṭipālanā, atthanipphattiyā paṭipālanāti atthanipphattipaṭipālanā. Yā taṇhā assa pālayantassa puggalassa uppajjati, sā taṇhā “abhinandanā”ti vuccati.

The benefit of indicating a single thing by many synonymous expressions has been stated in many ways in the commentary (Netti-aṭṭha. 37); therefore, it is not shown by us. Because it should be asked, 'What is hope, what is yearning, etc.?', it is said, 'Hope is the name...' and so on. The aspiration for a future matter—the hope that arises in a person who hopes, thinking, 'It will surely come to be'—that aspiration is called 'hope.' The wish that arises in one who wishes for something present, or, upon seeing something better or different, the yearning that arises in one who yearns, 'May I be like this!'—that wish is called 'yearning.' Craving that proceeds in relation to a future object is called 'hope'; craving that proceeds in relation to a future or present object is called 'yearning.' Nevertheless, because they are one in being craving, they are a single thing. The accomplishment of a desired object is the 'accomplishment of the object.' One maintains it with this craving, thus this is 'maintenance.' The maintenance of the accomplishment of the object. The craving that arises in a person who is maintaining it is called 'delight'.

“Yā atthanipphatti taṇhāya paṭipāletabbā, katamā sā atthanipphattī”ti pucchitabbattā taṃ atthanipphattiṃ sattato vā saṅkhārato vā vibhajitvā dassento “piyaṃ vā ñātiṃ, piyaṃ vā dhamma”ntiādimāha. Tattha “ñāti”nti iminā mittabandhavādayopi gahitā. Dhammaṃ pana piyarūpārammaṇādikaṃ chabbidhampi yāya taṇhāya taṇhiko abhinandati, sā taṇhā “abhinandanā nāmā”ti vuccati. Paṭikkūlaṃ ñātiṃ vā dhammaṃ vā vipallāsavasena appaṭikkūlaṃ ñātiṃ vā dhammaṃ vā sabhāvavasena appaṭikkūlato yāya taṇhāya taṇhiko abhinandati[M 0.0186], sā taṇhā vā “abhinandanā nāmā”ti vuccatīti yojetvā attho gahetabbo.

Because it should be asked, 'That accomplishment of an object which is to be maintained by craving—what is that accomplishment of an object?', showing that accomplishment of an object by analyzing it in terms of beings or formations, he said, 'a dear relative, or a dear thing,' and so on. Therein, by 'relative' are included friends, kin, and so on. But as to 'thing,' the craving with which a person given to craving delights in any of the six kinds of pleasing objects, such as forms, etc., that craving is called 'delight.' The meaning should be understood by connecting it thus: the craving with which a person given to craving delights in a repulsive relative or thing due to distortion, or in an unrepulsive relative or thing due to its own nature because it is unrepulsive—that craving, too, is called 'delight'.

“Yāsu anekāsu dhātūsu vuttappakārā taṇhā ‘sarā’ti bhagavatā vuttā, katamā tā dhātuyo”ti pucchitabbattā tā dhātuyo sarūpato dassetuṃ “cakkhudhātū”tiādi vuttaṃ.

Because it should be asked, 'In which diverse elements has the aforesaid kind of craving been called 'attachments' by the Blessed One? What are those elements?', in order to show those elements by their own nature, it is said, 'the eye element,' and so on.

“Tāsu dhātūsu katamāya dhātuyā katamā sarā patiṭṭhitā pavattā”ti pucchitabbattā imāya dhātuyā ayaṃ sarā patiṭṭhitā pavattāti niyametvā dassetuṃ “sarāti keci rūpādhimuttā”tiādi [V 0.0313] vuttaṃ. Tattha kecīti sarāsaṅkhātāya rūpataṇhāya taṇhikā puggalā. Rūpādhimuttāti rūpadhātusaṅkhāte ārammaṇe adhimuttā ajjhositā. Iminā padena rūpataṇhāsaṅkhātā sarā rūpadhātuyā patiṭṭhitā pavattāti gahitā, “keci saddādhimuttā”tiādīhipi saddataṇhāsaṅkhātādayo sarā saddadhātuyādīsu patiṭṭhitā pavattā sarāva gahitā. Keci dhammādhimuttāti ettha dhammaggahaṇena cakkhudhātusotadhātughānadhātujivhādhātukāyadhātusattaviññāṇadhātudhammadhātuyo gahitā, tasmā aṭṭhārasa dhātuyo patiṭṭhānabhāvena gahitāpi chabbidhāva gahitāti daṭṭhabbā. “Rūpādhimuttādīsu kittakāni padāni taṇhāpakkhe taṇhāya vevacanā”ti pucchitabbattā etādisāni ettakāni padāni taṇhāpakkhe taṇhāvevacanānīti niyametvā dassetuṃ “tattha yāni cha gehasitānī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tatthāti tesu chasu rūpādīsu. Cha gehasitāni domanassānīti chasu rūpādīsu pavattaṃ taṇhāpemaṃ nissāya pavattāni cha domanassāni. Esa nayo sesesupi. “Cha upekkhā gehasitāpi bhagavatā vuttā, kasmā na gahitā”ti vattabbattā “yā cha upekkhā gehasitā, ayaṃ diṭṭhipakkho”ti vuttaṃ, diṭṭhipakkhattā na gahitāti attho.

Because it should be asked, 'Among those elements, in which element is which attachment established and operative?', in order to show definitively that 'in this element this attachment is established and operative,' it is said, 'As to attachments, some are intent on forms,' and so on. Therein, 'some' means persons given to craving, to the craving for forms which is called 'attachment.' 'Intent on forms' means they are intent on and cling to the object called the form element. By this term it is understood that the attachment called craving for forms is established and operative in the form element. Similarly, by 'some are intent on sounds,' etc., the attachments called craving for sounds, etc., are understood as established and operative in the sound element, etc. When it says, 'Some are intent on mental phenomena,' here by the term 'mental phenomena,' the eye element, ear element, nose element, tongue element, body element, the seven consciousness elements, and the mental-phenomena element are included. Therefore, it should be seen that although the eighteen elements are taken as the basis, they are taken as just sixfold. Because it should be asked, 'Among those intent on forms, etc., how many terms are on the side of craving, being synonyms for craving?', in order to show definitively that such and such a number of terms are on the side of craving, being synonyms for craving, it is said, 'Therein, the six sorrows based on the household life,' and so on. Therein, this means in regard to those six, forms, etc. The six sorrows based on the household life are the six sorrows that arise in dependence on the craving and affection that occur in regard to the six things, forms, etc. The same method applies to the rest. Because it should be said, 'The six kinds of equanimity based on the household life have also been spoken of by the Blessed One; why are they not included?', it is said, 'Those six kinds of equanimity based on the household life belong to the side of views.' The meaning is that they are not included because they belong to the side of views.

38. “Kathaṃ vuttappakārā taṇhā eva gahitā”ti vattabbattā “sāyeva patthanākārenā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Sā vuttappakārā eva taṇhā patthanākārena pavattanato āsādipariyāyena vuttā, rūpādiārammaṇadhammesu nandanato “dhammanandī”ti pariyāyena vuttā, rūpādiārammaṇadhammesu gilitvā pariniṭṭhapeti viya ajjhosāya tiṭṭhanato “dhammajjhosāna”nti pariyāyena vuttā, tasmā taṇhāya vevacanāni honti.

38. Because it should be said, 'How is it that only craving of the aforesaid kind is taken?', it is said, 'It is that same craving in the mode of wishing,' and so on. That same aforesaid craving, because it operates in the mode of wishing, is spoken of by the synonymous expression 'hope,' etc.; because it delights in things that are objects, such as forms, etc., it is spoken of by the synonymous expression 'delight in things'; because it abides clinging to things that are objects, such as forms, etc., as if having swallowed and consumed them, it is spoken of by the synonymous expression 'clinging to things.' Therefore, they are synonyms for craving.

Taṇhāya [M 0.0187] vevacanāni ācariyena niddiṭṭhāni, amhehi ca ñātāni, “katamāni cittassa vevacanānī”ti pucchitabbattā “cittaṃ mano”tiādi vuttaṃ. “Ārammaṇaṃ cintetīti cittaṃ. Manati jānātīti mano. Vijānātīti viññāṇa”ntiādinā attho pakaraṇesu (dha. sa. aṭṭha. 5) vuttova, tasmā amhehi na vitthārito. Vevacanāniyeva imāni imassa vevacanānīti ettakāniyeva kathayissāma. “Paññindriyaṃ paññābala”ntiādīni paññāvevacanāni.

The synonyms for craving have been pointed out by the Teacher and are known by us. Because it should be asked, 'What are the synonyms for mind?', it is said, 'Mind, mentality,' and so on. The meaning of such phrases as 'It thinks of an object, thus it is mind (citta); it minds, it knows, thus it is mentality (mano); it cognizes, thus it is consciousness (viññāṇa)' has already been stated in the treatises (Dhs.A. 5); therefore it is not elaborated upon by us. We will state only this much: that these are just synonyms, that these are its synonyms. 'The faculty of wisdom, the power of wisdom,' and so on are synonyms for wisdom.

“Arahaṃ sammāsambuddho”tiādīni buddhassa vevacanāni. “Tāni kattha desitānī”ti pucchitabbattā “yathā ca buddhānussatiyaṃ vutta”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Buddhānussatidesanāyaṃ yathā ca yaṃyaṃpakāraṃ [V 0.0314] vevacanaṃ bhagavatā “itipi so bhagavā arahaṃ…pe… bhagavato”ti vuttaṃ, etaṃpakāraṃ vevacanaṃ buddhānussatiyā vevacanaṃ buddhassa vevacananti daṭṭhabbaṃ. “Yathā ca dhammānussatiyaṃ vutta”ntiādīsupi evameva yojanā kātabbā.

'Arahant, Perfectly Self-Enlightened One,' and so on are synonyms for the Buddha. Because it should be asked, 'Where are these taught?', it is said, 'And as it is stated in the Recollection of the Buddha,' and so on. It should be seen that in the teaching on the Recollection of the Buddha, whatever kind of synonym was spoken by the Blessed One, thus: 'For this reason, the Blessed One is an Arahant ... the Blessed One,' that kind of synonym is a synonym from the Recollection of the Buddha, a synonym for the Buddha. Similarly, the connection should be made in the same way for 'And as it is stated in the Recollection of the Dhamma,' and so on.

“Tenāhā”tiādyānusandhyādiattho ceva “niyutto vevacano hāro”tiānusandhyādiattho ca vuttanayānusārena veditabbo.

The meaning of the connection beginning 'Therefore he said,' and the meaning of the connection beginning 'The method of synonyms is concluded,' should be understood according to the method already stated.

Iti vevacanahāravibhaṅge sattibalānurūpā racitā

Thus, in the Analysis of the Method of Synonyms, this Exposition has been composed in accordance with my own power and strength.

Vibhāvanā niṭṭhitā.

The Exposition is concluded.

Paṇḍitehi pana aṭṭhakathāṭīkānusārena gambhīrattho vitthārato vibhajitvā gahetabboti.

However, the profound meaning should be comprehensively analyzed and grasped by the learned, according to the commentaries and subcommentaries.

11. Paññattihāravibhaṅgavibhāvanā

11. Exposition of the Analysis of the Method of Designations

39. Yena yena saṃvaṇṇanāvisesabhūtena vibhaṅgena vevacanāni vibhattāni, so saṃvaṇṇanāvisesabhūto vibhaṅgo paripuṇṇo, “katamo paññattihāravibhaṅgo”ti pucchitabbattā “tattha katamo paññattihāro”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha tatthāti tesu niddiṭṭhesu soḷasasu desanāhārādīsu katamo saṃvaṇṇanāviseso paññattihāro paññattihāravibhaṅgo nāmāti pucchati. “Ekaṃ bhagavā dhammaṃ paññattīhi vividhāhi desetī”tiādiniddesassa idāni mayā vuccamāno “yā pakatikathāya desanā”tiādiko vitthārasaṃvaṇṇanāviseso paññattihāro paññattihāravibhaṅgo nāmāti gahetabbo.

39. By whatever analysis, which is a special mode of exposition, the synonyms are analyzed, that analysis, which is a special mode of exposition, is complete. Because it should be asked, 'What is the analysis of the method of designations?', it is said, 'There, what is the method of designations?' and so on.
