Samāpattīti saññāsamāpatyādivisesaṃ anapekkhitvā yā sāmaññasamāpattitā vuttā, sā sāmaññasamāpattitā samāpattiyā ekattatā nāma. “Tattha katamā samāpattī”ti pucchitvā “saññāsamāpatti asaññāsamāpatti…pe… nirodhasamāpattī”ti saññāsamāpatyādivisesaṃ apekkhitvā yā visesasamāpattitā vuttā, sā ayaṃ visesasamāpattitā samāpattiyā vemattatā nāma.

Attainment: The generality of attainment that is stated without regard to the specifics of the attainment with perception and so forth, that generality of attainment is called the unity of attainment. When asked, “Therein, what is attainment?” and answered, “The attainment with perception, the attainment without perception… up to… the attainment of cessation”—the specificity of attainment that is stated with regard to the specifics of the attainment with perception and so forth, that specificity of attainment is called the diversity of attainment.

Jhāyīti [V 0.0331] sekkhajhāyīādivisesaṃ anapekkhitvā yā jhāyīsāmaññatā vuttā, sā jhāyīsāmaññatā jhāyino ekattatā nāma. “Tattha katamo jhāyī”ti pucchitvā “atthi sekkho jhāyī, atthi asekkho jhāyī…pe… paññuttaro jhāyī”ti sekkhajhāyīasekkhajhāyīādivisesamapekkhitvā yā jhāyīvisesatā vuttā, sā ayaṃ jhāyīvisesatā jhāyino vemattatā nāma.

A meditator: The generality of a meditator that is stated without regard to the specifics of a trainee meditator and so forth, that generality of a meditator is called the unity of a meditator. When asked, “Therein, who is a meditator?” and answered, “There is a trainee meditator, there is an adept meditator… up to… a meditator who is supreme in wisdom”—the specificity of a meditator that is stated with regard to the specifics of a trainee meditator, an adept meditator, and so forth, that specificity of a meditator is called the diversity of a meditator.

Samādhīti saraṇasamādhyādivisesamanapekkhitvā yā samādhisāmaññatā vuttā, sā ayaṃ samādhisāmaññatā samādhino ekattatā nāma. “Tattha katamo samādhī”ti pucchitvā “saraṇo samādhi, araṇo samādhi…pe… micchāsamādhi, sammāsamādhī”ti saraṇasamādhyādivisesamapekkhitvā yā samādhivisesatā vuttā, sā ayaṃ samādhivisesatā samādhino vemattatā nāma.

Concentration: The generality of concentration that is stated without regard to the specifics of defiled concentration and so forth, that generality of concentration is called the unity of concentration. When asked, “Therein, what is concentration?” and answered, “Defiled concentration, undefiled concentration… wrong concentration, right concentration”—the specificity of concentration that is stated with regard to the specifics of defiled concentration and so forth, that specificity of concentration is called the diversity of concentration.

Paṭipadāti āgāḷhapaṭipadādivisesamanapekkhitvā yā paṭipadāsāmaññatā vuttā, ayaṃ paṭipadāsāmaññatā paṭipadāya ekattatā nāma. “Tattha katamā paṭipadā”ti pucchitvā “āgāḷhapaṭipadā, nijjhāmapaṭipadā…pe… sukhā paṭipadā khippābhiññā”ti āgāḷhapaṭipadādivisesamapekkhitvā yā paṭipadāvisesatā vuttā, sā ayaṃ paṭipadāvisesatā paṭipadāya vemattatā nāma.

Practice: The generality of practice that is stated without regard to the specifics of rigorous practice and so forth, this generality of practice is called the unity of practice. When asked, “Therein, what is practice?” and answered, “Rigorous practice, gentle practice… pleasant practice with quick direct knowledge”—the specificity of practice that is stated with regard to the specifics of rigorous practice and so forth, that specificity of practice is called the diversity of practice.

Kāyoti nāmakāyādivisesamanapekkhitvā yā kāyasāmaññatā vuttā, sā ayaṃ kāyasāmaññatā kāyassa ekattatā nāma. “Tattha katamo kāyo”ti pucchitvā “nāmakāyo rūpakāyo…pe… ayaṃ nāmakāyo”ti nāmakāyādivisesamapekkhitvā yā kāyavisesatā [M 0.0206] vuttā, sā ayaṃ kāyavisesatā kāyassa vemattatā nāmāti yojanā kātabbā. Padatthādiko viseso aṭṭhakathāyaṃ (netti. aṭṭha. 47) vitthārato vutto.

The body: The generality of body that is stated without regard to the specifics of the name-body and so forth, that generality of body is called the unity of body. When asked, “Therein, what is the body?” and answered, “The name-body, the form-body… up to… this is the name-body”—the specificity of body that is stated with regard to the specifics of the name-body and so forth, that specificity of body is called the diversity of body. The explanation should be applied accordingly. The detailed distinctions regarding terms and meanings are extensively discussed in the commentary (Netti. Aṭṭha. 47).

Vuttappakārassa dukkhasamudayādikassa dhammassa ekattatādilakkhaṇaṃ nigamanavasena dassetuṃ “evaṃ yo dhammo”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha evanti iminā mayā vuttena “dukkhanti ekattatā. Tattha katamaṃ dukkhaṃ? Jāti dukkhā, jarā dukkhā”tiādivacanena. Yo dhammoti yo koci jātijarābyādhyādivisesadhammo. Yassa dhammassāti tato jātiādivisesadhammato aññassa jarādivisesadhammassa. Samānabhāvoti jātiādivisesadhammena jarādivisesadhammassa dukkhabhāvena samānabhāvo. Tassa dhammassāti jarādivisesadhammassa. Ekattatāyāti dukkhasamudayatādisamānatāya [V 0.0332] dukkhasamudayādibhāvānaṃ ekībhāvena. Ekībhavatīti jātiādivisesabhedena anekopi “dukkhasamudayo”tiādinā ekasaddābhidheyyatāya ekībhavati. Yena yena vā pana vilakkhaṇo, tena tena vemattaṃ gacchati. Yassa jātiādidhammassa yena yena abhinibbattanaparipācanādisabhāvena yo jātiādidhammo jarādidhammena vilakkhaṇo visadiso hoti, tassa jātiādidhammassa tena tena abhinibbattanaparipācanādisabhāvena so jātiādidhammo jarādidhammena vemattataṃ visadisattaṃ gacchati, dukkhasamudayādibhāvena samānopi jātiādidhammo jarādidhammassa visiṭṭhataṃ gacchatīti attho daṭṭhabbo.

To show, by way of conclusion, the characteristic of unity and so forth of the teaching beginning with the origin of suffering and so forth, as previously explained, the phrase 'evaṃ yo dhammo' and so forth was stated. Here, 'evaṃ' refers to what was said by me: 'Suffering is unity. And what is suffering? Birth is suffering, aging is suffering,' and so on. 'Yo dhammo' means any particular phenomenon such as birth, aging, sickness, etc. 'Yassa dhammassa' refers to another particular phenomenon, such as aging, etc., in relation to that particular phenomenon of birth, etc. 'Samānabhāvo' means the common nature, as suffering, between the particular phenomenon of birth, etc., and the particular phenomenon of aging, etc. 'Tassa dhammassa' refers to the particular phenomenon of aging, etc. 'Ekattatāya' means by the unity of the states of the origin of suffering, etc., due to the shared nature of being the origin of suffering, etc. 'Ekībhavati' means that although there are many distinctions such as birth, etc., they become unified by being expressed through a single term like 'origin of suffering,' etc. Alternatively, by whatever it is dissimilar, by that it becomes distinct. By whatever nature, such as arising, maturing, etc., a phenomenon of birth, etc., is dissimilar to a phenomenon of aging, etc., by that very nature of arising, maturing, etc., that phenomenon of birth, etc., becomes distinct from the phenomenon of aging, etc. The meaning should be understood that even though the phenomenon of birth, etc., is similar in being the origin of suffering, etc., it becomes distinguished from the phenomenon of aging, etc.

Dukkhasamudayādidhammassa ekattavemattatā ācariyena vibhattā, amhehi ca ñātā, “tāya ekattavemattatāya kattha pucchite sati adhiṭṭhānaṃ vīmaṃsitabba”nti pucchitabbattā suttādike pucchite sati vīmaṃsitabbanti dassetuṃ “evaṃ sutte vā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha evaṃ iminā vuttappakārena sutte vā pucchite, veyyākaraṇe vā pucchite, gāthāyaṃ vā pucchitāyaṃ sati adhiṭṭhānaṃ vīmaṃsitabbaṃ. “Kiṃ vīmaṃsitabba”nti puccheyya “ekattatāya pucchati kiṃ, udāhu vemattatāya pucchati ki”nti vīmaṃsitabbanti yojanā. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana – “idāni tāva ekattavemattatāvisaye niyojetvā dassetuṃ ‘sutte vā veyyākaraṇe vā’tiādi vutta”nti (netti. aṭṭha. 48) vuttaṃ. “Kathaṃ pucchitaṃ, kathaṃ vissajjitabba”nti vattabbattā “yadi ekattatāyā”tiādi [M 0.0207] vuttaṃ. “Tenāhā”tiādyānusandhyādiko ca “niyutto adhiṭṭhāno hāro”ti imassa anusandhyādiko ca vuttanayānusārena veditabbo.

The unity and diversity of the phenomena of the origin of suffering, etc., have been distinguished by the teacher and are known to us. Since it is to be asked, 'Where should the determination be investigated when questioned about that unity and diversity?', to show that it should be investigated when a sutta or similar text is questioned, 'thus in the sutta,' etc., was stated. Here, in this way, when the sutta is questioned, or the exposition is questioned, or a verse is questioned, the determination should be investigated. If one were to ask, 'What should be investigated?', the construction is: 'Should one investigate whether the question pertains to unity or to diversity?' In the commentary, however, it is said: 'Now, in order to direct attention to the sphere of unity and diversity, it is stated, 'in the sutta or in the exposition,' etc.' (Netti. Aṭṭha. 48). Since it should be said, 'How is it questioned, how should it be answered?', therefore, 'if it is about unity,' etc., is stated. The connection, etc., of 'therefore he said,' etc., and the connection, etc., of 'the fixed determination is the guiding principle,' should be understood according to the method stated.

Iti adhiṭṭhānahāravibhaṅge sattibalānurūpā racitā

Thus, in the analysis of the determination-method, composed in accordance with one's ability and strength.

Vibhāvanā niṭṭhitā.

The elucidation is finished.

Paṇḍitehi pana aṭṭhakathāṭīkānusārena gambhīrattho vitthārato vibhajitvā gahetabboti.

However, the profound meaning should be extensively analyzed and grasped by the wise, in accordance with the commentaries and sub-commentaries.

15. Parikkhārahāravibhaṅgavibhāvanā

15. Elucidation of the Analysis of the Requisite-Method

49. Yena [V 0.0333] yena saṃvaṇṇanāvisesabhūtena vibhaṅgena dukkhasaccādīnaṃ ekattatādayo vibhattā, so saṃvaṇṇanāvisesabhūto paripuṇṇo, “katamo parikkhārahāravibhaṅgo nāmā”ti pucchitabbattā “tattha katamo parikkhāro hāro”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha tatthāti tesu niddiṭṭhesu soḷasasu desanāhārādīsu katamo saṃvaṇṇanāviseso parikkhāro hāro parikkhārahāravibhaṅgo nāmāti pucchati. “Ye dhammā yaṃ dhammaṃ janayantī”tiādiniddesassa idāni mayā vuccamāno “yo dhammo yaṃ dhammaṃ janayati, tassa so parikkhāro”tiādiko parikkhārabhūtassa hetuno ceva paccayassa ca vitthārasaṃvaṇṇanāviseso parikkhāravibhaṅgo nāma.

49. By whatever analysis that is a distinctive explanation the unity, etc., of the truths of suffering, etc., are distinguished, that distinctive explanation is complete. Since it is to be asked, 'What is called the analysis of the requisite-method?', 'Herein, what is the requisite-method?' etc., was stated. Here, 'therein' means: among those sixteen designated items beginning with the exposition-methods, etc., what distinctive analysis, what requisite-method, is called the analysis of the requisite-method? he asks. In relation to the specification beginning, 'Those phenomena which generate a phenomenon,' the detailed and distinctive explanation of the cause and condition that constitutes the requisite—which is now being stated by me, beginning with, 'That phenomenon which generates another phenomenon, that is its requisite,' etc.—is called the analysis of requisites.

“Katamo saṃvaṇṇetabbo parikkhāro”ti pucchitabbattā “yo dhammo”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha yo hetupaccayappakāro dhammo yaṃ phalabhūtaṃ dhammaṃ janayati janeti, tassa phaladhammassa so hetupaccayappakāro dhammo parikkhāro nāma. “Kiṃlakkhaṇo parikkhāro”ti pucchitabbattā tathā pucchitvā lakkhaṇavisesaṃ dassetuṃ “kiṃlakkhaṇo”tiādi vuttaṃ. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana – “tattha ‘yo dhammo yaṃ dhammaṃ janayati, tassa so parikkhāro’ti saṅkhepato parikkhāralakkhaṇaṃ vatvā taṃ vibhāgena dassetuṃ ‘kiṃlakkhaṇo’tiādi vutta”nti (netti. aṭṭha. 49) vuttaṃ. “Kittakā dhammā janayantī”ti pucchitabbattā “dve dhammā janayanti hetu ca paccayo cā”ti vuttaṃ. “Hetupi kāraṇaṃ, paccayopi kāraṇaṃ[M 0.0208], tasmā kāraṇāyeva kena lakkhaṇena dvidhā vuttā”ti vattabbattā “tattha kiṃlakkhaṇo”tiādi vuttaṃ. Janitabbaphalato aññehi phalehi asādhāraṇalakkhaṇo hetu, sabbaphalehi sādhāraṇalakkhaṇo paccayo, iminā visesalakkhaṇena dvidhā vattabbāti attho. “Sādhāraṇāsādhāraṇaviseso kīdiso bhave”ti pucchitabbattā “yathā kiṃ bhave”ti pucchitvā “yathā aṅkurassā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Yathā yo sādhāraṇāsādhāraṇaviseso atthi, tathā so sādhāraṇāsādhāraṇaviseso kiṃ viya bhaveti attho. Aṅkurassa nibbattiyā bījaṃ asādhāraṇaṃ yathā, tathā hetu phalassa nibbattiyā asādhāraṇo bhave. Pathavī ca āpo ca aṅkurassa nibbattiyā sādhāraṇā bhavanti yathā, tathā paccayo phalassa nibbattiyā sādhāraṇo bhave. Sabbaphalassa paccayattā aṅkurassa bījaṃ asādhāraṇaṃ janakaṃ hetu. “Kathaṃ pathavī, āpo ca sādhāraṇā janakāti saddahitabbā”ti pucchitabbattā “aṅkurassa hī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Samaṃ samānaṃ phalaṃ bhavāpetīti sabhāvo, ko so? Bījaṃ hetuyeva. “Kiṃ hetupaccayānaṃ viseso bījaṅkuropamāyeva dassetabbo, udāhu aññūpamāyapi dassetabbo”ti vattabbattā aññāya upamāyapi [V 0.0334] visesaṃ dassetuṃ “yathā vā panā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Imāya upamāyapi hetupaccayānaṃ viseso vijānitabboti adhippāyo.

Since it is to be asked, 'What requisite should be explained?', 'whatever phenomenon,' etc., was stated. Herein, whatever phenomenon of the nature of a cause and condition generates or brings forth a resultant phenomenon, that phenomenon of the nature of a cause and condition is called a requisite for that resultant phenomenon. Since it is to be asked, 'What is the characteristic of a requisite?', having asked thus to show the distinguishing characteristic, 'what is the characteristic?' etc., was stated. In the commentary, however, it is said: 'Here, having stated the characteristic of a requisite in brief as 'that phenomenon which generates a phenomenon, that is its requisite,' to show that in detail, 'what is the characteristic?' etc., was stated' (Netti. Aṭṭha. 49). Since it is to be asked, 'How many phenomena generate?', 'two phenomena generate: cause and condition,' was stated. Since it should be said, 'A cause is a reason, and a condition is a reason; therefore, since they are only reasons, by what characteristic were they spoken of as twofold?', 'there, what is the characteristic?' etc., was stated. A cause has a characteristic that is uncommon to other results than the result to be generated; a condition has a characteristic that is common to all results. By this distinguishing characteristic, they should be spoken of as twofold—this is the meaning. Since it is to be asked, 'What might the common and uncommon distinction be like?', having asked, 'like what might it be?', 'like a sprout,' etc., was stated. The meaning is: just as there is a common and uncommon distinction, what is that common and uncommon distinction like? As a seed is uncommon to the arising of a sprout, so a cause is uncommon to the arising of a result. And as earth and water are common to the arising of a sprout, so a condition is common to the arising of a result. Because it is a condition for all results, a condition is common. The seed of a sprout, however, is an uncommon generative cause. Since it is to be asked, 'How should it be accepted that earth and water are common generative causes?', 'for a sprout,' etc., was stated. 'Own-nature' (sabhāvo) is so-called because it brings about a similar result. What is that? It is the seed, the cause itself. Since it should be said, 'Should the distinction between cause and condition be shown only by the simile of a seed and sprout, or should it also be shown by another simile?', to show the distinction by another simile as well, 'or as,' etc., was stated. By this simile too, the distinction between cause and condition should be understood—this is the intention.

Bījaṅkurādīsu bāhiresu parikkhārabhūtānaṃ hetupaccayānaṃ viseso ācariyena vibhatto, amhehi ca ñāto, “kathaṃ ajjhattikesu vibhatto”ti pucchitabbattā “ayañhi saṃsāro”tiādi vuttaṃ. Atha vā “bāhiresu parikkhārabhūto hetupaccayo yutto hotu, kathaṃ ajjhattikesu yutto”ti vattabbattā “ayañhi saṃsāro”tiādi vuttaṃ. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana – “evaṃ bāhiraṃ hetupaccayavibhāgaṃ dassetvā idāni ajjhattikaṃ dassetuṃ ‘ayañhi saṃsāro’tiādi vutta”nti (netti. aṭṭha. 49) vuttaṃ. Hetupaccayehi saha saṃsāro bhavatīti sahetupaccayo. Ayaṃ saṃsāro hi yasmā sahetupaccayo hutvā nibbatto, tasmā ajjhattikepi parikkhārabhūto hetupaccayo yuttoyevāti daṭṭhabboti adhippāyo.

The distinction of root-cause and condition as requisites in external things like seeds and sprouts has been analyzed by the teacher and is known to us. Since it is to be asked, 'How is it analyzed in internal things?', 'For this is the cycle of existence,' etc., was stated. Alternatively, since it should be said, 'Let the root-cause and condition as requisites be applicable in external things; but how is it applicable in internal things?', 'For this is the cycle of existence,' etc., was stated. In the commentary, however, it is said: 'Having thus shown the classification of root-cause and condition in external things, now to show it in internal things, it is stated, "For this is the cycle of existence"' (Netti. Aṭṭha. 49). The cycle of existence arises together with root-causes and conditions; hence, it is 'with root-causes and conditions.' Since this cycle of existence arises, being endowed with root-causes and conditions, the root-cause and condition as requisites are indeed applicable even in internal things—this is the meaning to be understood.

So [M 0.0209] imassa saṃsārassa sahetupaccayattaṃ yadi bhagavatā vuttaṃ, evaṃ sati amhehi saddahitabbaṃ, “kathaṃ saddahitabba”nti vattabbattā “evañhī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Evanti iminā avijjādinā hetupaccayena sabbo paṭiccasamuppādo saṃsāroti nibbattoti bhagavatā saṃsārassa sahetupaccayattaṃ vuttaṃ, tasmā saddahitabbaṃ. Avijjādayo saṅkhārādīnaṃ paccayo hotu, “katamo avijjāya hetū”ti pucchitabbattā “iti avijjā avijjāya hetū”ti vuttaṃ. “Katamo avijjāya paccayo”ti pucchitabbattā “ayoniso manasikāro paccayo”ti vuttaṃ. “Katamā avijjā katamāya avijjāya hetū”ti pucchitabbattā “purimikā avijjā pacchimikāya avijjāya hetū”ti vuttaṃ. “Katamā purimikā avijjā katamā pacchimikā avijjā”ti pucchitabbattā “tatthā”tiādi vuttaṃ. “Avijjāpariyuṭṭhānassa hetubhūto purimo avijjānusayo samanantarova kiṃ, udāhu paramparahetupi hotī”ti pucchitabbattā “bījaṅkuro viyā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Bījaṅkuroti bījānaṃ aṅkuroti bījaṅkuro, bījānaṃ samanantarahetutāya aṅkuro nibbattati viya. Yattha rukkhādike yaṃ phalaṃ nibbattati, tasmiṃ rukkhādike nibbattassa assa phalassa idaṃ bījaṃ pana paramparahetutāya hetubhūtaṃ bhavati.

If the Blessed One has stated that this cycle of existence has root-causes and conditions, then we should believe it. Since it should be said, 'How should one believe?', it is said, 'Thus indeed.' Thus, because the Blessed One has stated that the entire dependent origination, which is the cycle of existence, arises with this root-cause and condition such as ignorance, it should therefore be believed. Let ignorance and the like be the condition for formations and the like, but since it should be asked, 'What is the root-cause of ignorance?', it is said, 'Thus, ignorance is the root-cause of ignorance.' Since it should be asked, 'What is the condition for ignorance?', it is said, 'Unwise attention is the condition.' Since it should be asked, 'Which ignorance is the root-cause of which ignorance?', it is said, 'Former ignorance is the root-cause of later ignorance.' Since it should be asked, 'What is former ignorance and what is later ignorance?', it is said, 'Therein...' Since it should be asked, 'Is the prior underlying tendency of ignorance, which is the root-cause for the obsession of ignorance, immediately proximate, or is it also a successive root-cause?', it is said, 'Like a seed and sprout...' 'Seed-sprout' means a sprout of seeds; just as a sprout arises due to the immediate causality of seeds, so too, wherever a fruit arises in a tree or the like, the seed of that fruit, which arises in that tree or the like, becomes the root-cause through successive causality.

“Bījaṃ pana ekaṃyeva hoti, kathaṃ dvidhā vattabba”nti vattabbattā “duvidho hī”tiādi vuttaṃ, samanantarakālaparamparakālabhedena hetupi duvidho hotiyevāti attho. Bījabhūto hetu duvidho yathā, evaṃ avijjāya hetubhūto avijjānusayopi samanantarahetu ca paramparahetu cāti kālabhedena duvidho bhavati, samanantaro avijjānusayo samanantarassa avijjāpariyuṭṭhānassa samanantarahetu [V 0.0335] hoti. Purimataro avijjānusayo pacchimatarassa avijjāpariyuṭṭhānassa paramparahetu hoti. Iti bījabhūto asādhāraṇo hetu, pathavīāpādiko sādhāraṇo paccayoti viseso pākaṭo yathā, evaṃ avijjānusayo asādhāraṇo hetu, ayonisomanasikāro sādhāraṇo paccayoti viseso daṭṭhabbo.

Since it might be asked, 'The seed is indeed one; how can it be said to be twofold?', it is said, 'for it is twofold,' and so on. The meaning is that the root-cause is indeed twofold by the distinction between immediate and successive time. Just as the seed-like root-cause is twofold, so too the underlying tendency of ignorance, which is a root-cause for ignorance, becomes twofold by the distinction of time: as an immediate root-cause and a successive root-cause. The immediate underlying tendency of ignorance is the immediate root-cause for the immediate obsession of ignorance, while the earlier underlying tendency of ignorance is the successive root-cause for the later obsession of ignorance. Thus, just as the distinction is clear that the seed-like root-cause is the particular root-cause, and the earth and water element is the general condition, similarly, the distinction should be understood that the underlying tendency of ignorance is the particular root-cause, while unwise attention is the general condition.

“Ettakeneva hetupaccayānaṃ viseso vattabbo”ti vattabbattā “yathā vā pana thālakañcā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana – “yathā vā panātiādināpi [M 0.0210] hetupaccayavibhāgameva dassetī”ti vuttaṃ. Tattha padīpassa paccayabhūtaṃ thālakañca vaṭṭi ca telañca padīpassa sabhāvahetu samānahetu na hotīti yojanā. “Padīpassa paccayabhūtampi thālakādikaṃ sabhāvahetu na hotīti kasmā saddahitabba”nti vattabbattā “na hi sakkā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Padīpassa paccayabhūtaṃ anaggikaṃ aggirahitaṃ thālakañca vaṭṭiñca telañca dīpetuṃ jāletuṃ hi yasmā na sakkā, tasmā purimo padīpo pacchimassa padīpassa sabhāvahetu hoti viya, evaṃ thālakādikaṃ sabhāvahetu na hoti. Iti evaṃpakāro sabhāvo samāno padīpo hetu hoti yathā, parabhāvo asamāno thālakādiko paccayo hoti yathā ca, tathā ajjhattiko sabhāvo hetu hoti, bāhiro asamāno paccayo hoti. Janako avijjānusayo avijjāpariyuṭṭhānassa hetu hoti, pariggāhako upatthambhako paccayo hoti. Aññehi phalehi asādhāraṇo hetu hoti, sabbehi phalehi sādhāraṇo paccayo hotīti yojetvā padīpopamāyapi hetupaccayānaṃ pākaṭo viseso daṭṭhabboti adhippāyo.

Since it should be said, 'The distinction between root-cause and condition should be stated only to this extent,' it is said, 'or just as in the case of a lamp-holder,' and so on. In the commentary, it is said: 'By the phrase 'or just as...' and so on, he shows the very classification of root-cause and condition.' Therein, the connection is that the lamp-holder, the wick, and the oil, being conditions for the lamp, are not the intrinsic root-cause or a root-cause of the same nature as the lamp. Since it should be asked, 'Why should one believe that the lamp-holder and so on, though being conditions for the lamp, are not its intrinsic root-cause?', it is said, 'for it is not possible,' and so on. Because it is not possible to illuminate or ignite the lamp-holder, wick, and oil, which are conditions for the lamp but are without fire, therefore, just as the previous lamp is the intrinsic root-cause for the subsequent lamp, so the lamp-holder and so on are not the intrinsic root-cause. Thus, just as the lamp, being of the same nature, is the root-cause, and the lamp-holder and so on, being of a different nature, are the condition, so too what is internal and of the same nature is the root-cause, while what is external and of a dissimilar nature is the condition. The generating underlying tendency of ignorance is the root-cause for the obsession of ignorance, while that which grasps and supports is the condition. Having connected it thus: the root-cause is particular to its own result, while the condition is general to all results, the clear distinction between root-cause and condition should also be seen in the lamp simile—this is the intention.

Hetupaccayappabhedaṃ kāraṇaṃ parikkhāroti ācariyena vuttaṃ, tassa kāraṇassa kāraṇabhāvo ca phalāpekkho hoti, tasmā “yo kāraṇabhāvo yenākārena hoti, katamo so kāraṇabhāvo, katamo so ākāro”ti pucchitabbattā ca “yaṃ phalaṃ yena visesena hoti, katamaṃ taṃ phalaṃ, katamo so viseso”ti pucchitabbattā ca “kāraṇaphalānaṃ yo sambandho hoti, katamo so sambandho”ti pucchitabbattā ca taṃ sabbaṃ vibhāvetuṃ “avupacchedattho”tiādi vuttaṃ. Ayamanusandhyattho ca aṭṭhakathāyaṃ “idāni yasmā kāraṇaṃ ‘parikkhāro’ti vuttaṃ, kāraṇabhāvo ca phalāpekkhāya, tasmā kāraṇassa yo kāraṇabhāvo yathā ca so hoti, yañca phalaṃ, yo ca tassa viseso, yo ca kāraṇaphalānaṃ sambandho, taṃ sabbaṃ vibhāvetuṃ ‘avupacchedattho’tiādi vutta”nti (netti. aṭṭha. 49) iminā vuttoti daṭṭhabbo.

The teacher has stated that the cause, differentiated as root-cause and condition, is a 'requisite.' And the state of being a cause is dependent on the expectation of a result. Therefore, since it should be asked what the state of being a cause is and in what manner it occurs, what the result is and what its particular distinction is, and what the connection between cause and result is, to clarify all that, the phrase 'having the meaning of non-interruption,' and so on, was stated. This contextual meaning is also stated in the commentary: 'Now, because a cause is said to be 'requisite,' and the state of being a cause depends on the expectation of a result, therefore, to clarify the state of being a cause, and how it occurs, and what the result is, and what its distinction is, and what the connection between cause and result is, 'having the meaning of non-interruption,' etc., was said' (Netti.A. 49); this should be understood as stated by this passage.

Tattha avupacchinnassa hetupaccayasaṅkhātassa kāraṇassa yo anupacchedattho atthi, so anupacchedattho [V 0.0336] santatiattho hoti phalena sambandhattā[M 0.0211], yañca kāraṇaṃ attano phalassa janakaṃ upatthambhakaṃ hutvā nirujjhati, so anupacchinno eva nāma hotīti. Yañca phalaṃ aññassa kāraṇaṃ hutvā nirujjhati, tasmiṃ anupacchinne tassa ca santatiattho hoti. Yaṃ pana phalaṃ aññassa phalassa kāraṇaṃ ahutvā nirujjhati, taṃ upacchinnaṃ hoti, yathā taṃ arahato cuticittanti. Kāraṇato nibbattassa phalassa yo nibbattiattho atthi, so nibbattiattho phalattho hoti. Paṭisandhikkhandhānaṃ yo paṭisandhiattho paṭisandahanattho atthi, so paṭisandhiattho punabbhavattho punabbhavanattho hoti. Kilesānaṃ yo palibodhattho santāne uppajjanattho atthi, so palibodhattho pariyuṭṭhānattho hoti. Kilesānaṃ maggena yo asamugghātattho atthi, so asamugghātattho anusayattho hoti. Avijjāya catunnaṃ saccānaṃ yo asampaṭivedhattho atthi, so asampaṭivedhattho avijjattho hoti. Arahattamaggena yo apariññātattho atthi, so apariññātattho viññāṇassa paṭisandhiviññāṇassa bījattho hoti.

Herein, for the uninterrupted cause designated as 'cause-condition', its meaning of non-interruption is the meaning of continuity because it is connected with its result. And that cause, which ceases after having generated and supported its result, is indeed called 'uninterrupted.' And for that result which ceases after having been a cause for another, when it is uninterrupted, there is also the meaning of continuity. But that result which ceases without having been a cause for another result is called 'interrupted,' such as the death-consciousness of an Arahant. For a result produced from a cause, the meaning of arising is the meaning of the result. For the aggregates of rebirth-linking, the meaning of relinking, which is the meaning of connecting rebirth, is the meaning of renewed existence, the meaning of becoming again. For the defilements, the meaning of hindrance, which is the meaning of arising in the continuity, is the meaning of obsession. For the defilements, the meaning of not being uprooted by the path is the meaning of latent tendency. For ignorance, the meaning of not penetrating the four truths is the meaning of ignorance. The meaning of 'not fully understood' that is overcome by the path of Arahantship is the meaning of being a seed for consciousness, for rebirth-linking consciousness.

Ettāvatā kāraṇabhāvo ca kāraṇākāro ca phalañca phalaviseso ca ācariyena vibhatto, amhehi ca ñāto, “katamo paramparahetupaccayattho, katamo ca sambandhattho”ti pucchitabbattā “yattha avupacchedo”tiādi vuttaṃ. Yattha yassaṃ rūpārūpapavattiyaṃ avupacchinnassa hetupaccayappabhedassa kāraṇassa yo avupacchedo atthi, so avupacchedo tattha tissaṃ rūpārūpapavattiyaṃ santati hoti. Yattha yassaṃ rūpārūpapavattiyaṃ yā santati atthi, sā santatitattha rūpārūpapavattiyaṃ nibbatti hotītiādinā yojetvā paramparahetuādiko viññātabbo.

Thus far, the state of being a cause, the mode of a cause, the result, and the specific result have been distinguished by the teacher and understood by us. Since it should be asked, 'What is the meaning of successive cause-condition, and what is the meaning of connection?', it is said, 'Where there is non-interruption,' and so on. Where, in whatever material or immaterial process, there is non-interruption of the cause differentiated as cause-condition, that non-interruption is continuity in that material or immaterial process. Where, in whatever material or immaterial process, there is continuity, that continuity is origination in that material or immaterial process. By connecting in this way, successive cause and so on should be understood.

Sīlakkhandhoti parisuddhasīlakkhandho. Samādhikkhandhassāti mahaggatakkhandhassa, samādhipaṭṭhāno hi mahaggatadhammo. Paññākkhandhoti maggaphalapaññāpadhānakkhandho. So hi vimuttiñāṇadassanasaṅkhātassa paccavekkhaṇañāṇakkhandhassa paccayo hoti. Titthaññutādīnaṃ attho padaṭṭhānahāravibhaṅgavaṇṇanāyaṃ vuttova.

The aggregate of virtue means the aggregate of pure virtue. The aggregate of concentration means the aggregate of exalted states, for exalted states are based on concentration. The aggregate of wisdom means the aggregate whose principal is path-wisdom and fruition-wisdom. For it is the condition for the aggregate of reviewing knowledge, called knowledge and vision of liberation. The meaning of 'knower of the fords' and so on has already been explained in the commentary on the Analysis of the Method of Proximate Causes.

Sabhāvo hetūti ācariyena vutto, “kīdiso so sabhāvo hetū”ti pucchitabbattā “yathā vā pana cakkhuñca paṭiccā”tiādi vuttaṃ[M 0.0212]. Cakkhuviññāṇaṃ cakkhuñca cakkhundriyañca paṭicca nissayaṃ katvā rūpe paṭicca ārammaṇaṃ katvā uppajjati. Tattha cakkhādīsu cakkhundriyaṃ ādhipateyyapaccayatāya indriyapaccayatāya cakkhuviññāṇassa paccayo, rūpārammaṇaṃ purejātārammaṇapaccayatāya [V 0.0337] paccayo, āloko sannissayatāya upanissayatāya paccayo hoti. So paccayo honto phalena cakkhuviññāṇena asamānattā sabhāvo hetu na hoti, paccayo ca hoti manasikāro. Kiriyamanodhātu pana phalena cakkhuviññāṇena viññāṇabhāvena samānattā sabhāvo hetu hoti yathā, evaṃ saṅkhārā nāmakkhandhabhāvena samānattā viññāṇassa paccayā hontā sabhāvo hetu honti. Viññāṇaṃ nāmarūpena ekasantativasena samānattā nāmarūpassa paccayo hontaṃ sabhāvo hetu hoti. Iminā nayena “nāmarūpaṃ saḷāyatanassā”tiādīsupi attho veditabbo. Evaṃ vuttappakāro hetu, paccayo janako, upatthambhako ca yo koci upanissayo balavapaccayo hoti, sabbo so hetupaccayo janakaupatthambhako janitabbupatthambhiyassa phalassa parikkharaṇato abhisaṅkharaṇato nippariyāyato parikkhāro nāma.

“A cause by its own nature” was stated by the teacher. Because it should be asked, “Of what kind is that cause by its own nature?” it is said, “Just as, for example, dependent on the eye,” and so on. Eye-consciousness arises dependent on the eye and the eye-faculty as its support, and dependent on forms as its object. Therein, among the eye, etc., the eye-faculty is a condition for eye-consciousness by way of dominance condition and faculty condition. The form-object is a condition by way of prenascent object condition. Light is a condition by way of dependence condition and decisive support condition. That condition, being a condition, is not a cause by its own nature because it is dissimilar to the result, eye-consciousness; and attention is a condition. The functional mind-element, however, being similar to the result, eye-consciousness, by its nature as consciousness, is a cause by its own nature. Similarly, formations, being similar by their nature as mental aggregates, are conditions for consciousness and are causes by their own nature. Consciousness, being similar to name-and-form by way of a single continuity, is a condition for name-and-form and is a cause by its own nature. By this method, the meaning should also be understood in such cases as “name-and-form is a condition for the six sense bases.” Thus, the kind of cause stated—a generative and supportive condition, whatever strong condition there is, such as a decisive support—all that cause-condition, being generative and supportive, is called a “furnishing” because it furnishes, prepares, and is the direct means for the result to be generated and supported.

“Vuttappakāro hetupaccayo parikkhāro nāmāti kena amhehi saddahitabbo”ti vattabbattā “tenāhā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tena kāraṇabhūtena sabbassa hetupaccayassa parikkhārabhāvena āyasmā mahākaccāno “ye dhammā yaṃ dhammaṃ janayantī”ti yaṃ vacanaṃ āha, tena vacanena saddahitabbo, “ye dhammā yaṃ dhammaṃ janayantī”ti vacanaṃ nissāya tumhehi sallakkhetabboti adhippāyo.

Because it should be said, “By what should we believe that the cause-condition of the kind stated is called a ‘furnishing’?” it is said, “Therefore he said,” and so on. Because of that reason—that every cause-condition has the nature of a furnishing—the Venerable Mahākaccāna spoke the words, “Whatever phenomena generate whatever phenomenon.” It should be believed on account of that statement. The intention is: “You should discern this based on the statement, ‘Whatever phenomena generate whatever phenomenon.’”

“Ettakova parikkhāro hāro yuñjitabbo”ti vattabbattā “niyutto parikkhāro hāro”ti vuttaṃ, yo yo parikkhāro hāro yuñjitabbo, so so parikkhāro hāro nīharitvā yutto yuñjitabboti.

Because it should be said, “Only this much of the furnishing method should be applied,” it is stated, “The furnishing method is determined.” Whatever furnishing method is to be applied, that furnishing method should be extracted and properly applied.

Iti parikkhārahāravibhaṅge sattibalānurūpā racitā

Thus is composed the analysis of the furnishing method, in accordance with my strength and ability.

Vibhāvanā niṭṭhitā.

The Elucidation is finished.

Paṇḍitehi pana aṭṭhakathāṭīkānusārena gambhīrattho vitthārato vibhajitvā gahetabboti.

But the profound meaning should be grasped by the wise, after analyzing it in detail in accordance with the commentaries and subcommentaries.

16. Samāropanahāravibhaṅgavibhāvanā

16. Elucidation of the Analysis of the Application Method

50. Yena [V 0.0338][M 0.0213] yena saṃvaṇṇanāvisesabhūtena parikkhārahāravibhaṅgena suttatthānaṃ hetupaccayo vibhatto, so…pe… vibhaṅgo paripuṇṇo, “katamo samāropanahāravibhaṅgo”ti pucchitabbattā “tattha katamo samāropano hāro”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha tesu niddiṭṭhesu soḷasasu desanāhārādīsu katamo saṃvaṇṇanāviseso samāropano hāro samāropanahāravibhaṅgo nāmāti pucchati. “Ye dhammā yaṃmūlā”tiādiniddesassa idāni mayā vuccamāno “ekasmiṃ padaṭṭhāne yattakāni padaṭṭhānāni otarantī”tiādiko vitthārasaṃvaṇṇanāviseso samāropanahāravibhaṅgo nāma.

50. That analysis of the furnishing method, the particular mode of exegesis by which the cause-condition of the sutta meanings was analyzed, that… analysis is complete. Because it should be asked, “What is the analysis of the application method?” it is said, “Therein, what is the application method?” and so on. He asks: Therein, among the sixteen specified methods of teaching, etc., what particular mode of exegesis is the application method, called the analysis of the application method? The detailed particular mode of exegesis that is now being stated by me for the exposition beginning, “Those phenomena that are rooted in what…”—such as, “Into one proximate cause, how many proximate causes descend?”—is called the analysis of the application method.

“Kittake padaṭṭhāne sutte vutte kittakāni padaṭṭhānāni samāropayitabbānī”ti pucchitabbattā “ekasmiṃ padaṭṭhāne”tiādi vuttaṃ. Ekasmiṃ padaṭṭhāne sutte vutte sati avuttāni yattakāni padaṭṭhānāni otaranti samosaranti, sabbāni tāni avuttāni padaṭṭhānāni sutte vuttāni viya niddhāraṇavasena ānetvā desanāya āropayitabbāni. “Kāni viya samāropayitabbānī”ti vattabbattā “yathā āvaṭṭe”tiādi vuttaṃ. Āvaṭṭe hāre ekasmiṃ padaṭṭhāne sutte vutte sati sutte avuttāni bahukāni padaṭṭhānāni otaranti, tāni bahukāni padaṭṭhānāni pariyesitabbāni yathā, evaṃ samāropane hārepi bahukāni padaṭṭhānāni desanāya samāropayitabbānīti attho.

Because it should be asked, “When a certain number of proximate causes are stated in a sutta, how many proximate causes should be applied?” it is said, “In one proximate cause,” and so on. When one proximate cause is stated in a sutta, however many unstated proximate causes descend into it and converge, all those unstated proximate causes should be brought in by way of determination as if they were stated in the sutta, and applied to the teaching. Because it should be said, “Like what should they be applied?” it is said, “Just as in the revolving method,” and so on. The meaning is: just as in the revolving method, when one proximate cause is stated in the sutta, many unstated proximate causes descend into it, and those many proximate causes should be sought out, so too in the application method, many proximate causes should be applied to the teaching.

“Kevalaṃ pana padaṭṭhānavaseneva samāropanā kātabbā kiṃ, udāhu aññavasenāpi samāropanā kātabbā ki”nti vattabbattā aññavasenāpi samāropanā kātabbā; tasmā samāropanā catubbidhā kātabbāti dassento “tattha samāropanā catubbidhā”tiādimāha. Tattha tatthāti tāsu samāropayitabbasamāropanāsu padaṭṭhānaṃ padaṭṭhānasamāropanā, vevacanaṃ vevacanasamāropanā, bhāvanā bhāvanāsamāropanā, pahānaṃ pahānasamāropanā, iti iminā pabhedena samāropanā catubbidhā kātabbā.

Because it should be said, “Should the application be made solely by way of the proximate cause, or should the application also be made by way of other things?”—the application should also be made by way of other things. Therefore, to show that the application should be made in four ways, he said, “Therein, the application is fourfold,” and so on. Therein, that is, among those applications to be applied, there is the application of the proximate cause, the application of synonyms, the application of development, and the application of abandonment. Thus, by this division, the application should be made in four ways.

“Tāsu catubbidhāsu samāropanāsu katamā padaṭṭhānasamāropanā”ti pucchitabbattā tathā pucchitvā padaṭṭhānasamāropanaṃ dassetuṃ “tattha [M 0.0214] katamā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Sutte vuttena padaṭṭhānena sutte avuttānaṃ padaṭṭhānānaṃ samāropanā katamāti pucchati.

Because it should be asked, “Among those four kinds of application, what is the application of the proximate cause?”—having asked thus, to show the application of the proximate cause, it is said, “Therein, what is…” and so on. He asks: What is the application of proximate causes not stated in the sutta by means of a proximate cause that is stated in the sutta?

Sabbapāpassa [V 0.0339] akusalassa yaṃ akaraṇaṃ akaraṇahetu sāsanaṃ atthi, etaṃ sāsanaṃ buddhānaṃ sāsanaṃ ovādo hoti, atha vā akaraṇaṃ akaraṇatthāya yaṃ sāsanaṃ atthi, etaṃ buddhānaṃ sāsanaṃ ovādo hoti, na yassa kassaci sāsananti attho. Akaraṇanti hi sampadānatthe pavattaṃ paccattavacanaṃ yathā “kissa atthāya kimattha”nti. Kusalassa sampadā sampadāya yaṃ sāsanaṃ atthi, etaṃ buddhānaṃ sāsanaṃ. Sacittapariyodāpanaṃ sacittapariyodāpanatthaṃ yaṃ sāsanaṃ atthi, etaṃ buddhānaṃ sāsanaṃ hoti.

The teaching that is the non-doing of all evil, of what is unwholesome, the cause for non-doing—this teaching is the teaching of the Buddhas, their admonition. Or, the teaching that exists for the purpose of non-doing—this is the teaching of the Buddhas, their admonition. The meaning is that it is not the teaching of just anyone. For “non-doing” is a nominative singular used in the dative sense, as in “For what purpose? For what reason?” The teaching that exists for the accomplishment of the wholesome, for its accomplishment, is the teaching of the Buddhas. The teaching that exists for the purification of one's own mind, for the purpose of purifying one's own mind, is the teaching of the Buddhas.

Iti evaṃpakārena vuttassa tassa sāsanassa kiṃ padaṭṭhānanti visesassa visesapadaṭṭhānaṃ puna pucchati. Idaṃ sucaritattayaṃ sāsanassa ovādassa padaṭṭhānaṃ sucaritattayena hetunā sāsanattāti daṭṭhabbaṃ yathā “annena vasatī”tiādi. “Sucaritattaye padaṭṭhāne vutte katamaṃ padaṭṭhānaṃ samāropayitabba”nti pucchitabbattā “tattha yaṃ kāyikañcā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Idaṃ khandhattayaṃ sāsanassa padaṭṭhānaṃ samāropayitabbaṃ, “khandhattaye padaṭṭhāne samāropayite katamaṃ samāropayitabba”nti pucchitabbattā “tattha sīlakkhandho cā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Idaṃ samathavipassanādvayaṃ sāsanassa padaṭṭhānaṃ samāropayitabbaṃ. “Samathavipassanādvaye padaṭṭhāne samāropayite katamaṃ padaṭṭhānaṃ samāropayitabba”nti pucchitabbattā “tattha samathassa phala”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Idaṃ phaladvayaṃ sāsanassa padaṭṭhānaṃ samāropayitabbaṃ.

Thus, of the teaching stated in this way, he again asks for the specific proximate cause of this specific thing: “What is its proximate cause?” This triad of good conduct is the proximate cause of the teaching, the admonition. It should be seen that because of the triad of good conduct as the cause, it is a teaching, just as in “one lives by food,” and so on. Because it should be asked, “When the triad of good conduct is stated as the proximate cause, what proximate cause should be applied?” it is said, “Therein, whatever is bodily…” and so on. This triad of aggregates should be applied as the proximate cause of the teaching. Because it should be asked, “When the triad of aggregates has been applied as the proximate cause, what should be applied?” it is said, “Therein, the aggregate of virtue…” and so on. This pair of serenity and insight should be applied as the proximate cause of the teaching. Because it should be asked, “When the pair of serenity and insight has been applied as the proximate cause, what proximate cause should be applied?” it is said, “Therein, the fruit of serenity…” and so on. This pair of fruits should be applied as the proximate cause of the teaching.

Sāsanassa padaṭṭhānāni samāropayitabbānīti ācariyena niddhāretvā vibhattāni, amhehi ca ñātāni, “idāni katamassa katamaṃ padaṭṭhānaṃ samāropayitabba”nti pucchitabbattā “vanaṃ vanathassā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Idaṃ kāmaguṇapañcakaṃ vanaṃ taṇhābhūtassa vanathassa padaṭṭhānaṃ taṇhāvatthubhāvato, “itthī”ti vā “puriso”ti vā nimittaggāhasaṅkhātaṃ idaṃ vanaṃ “aho cakkhu, aho sotaṃ, aho ghānaṃ, aho jivhā, aho kāyo”ti tesaṃ tesaṃ aṅgapaccaṅgānaṃ anubyañjanaggāhasaṅkhātassa vanathassa padaṭṭhānaṃ samāropayitabbaṃ. Apariññātaṃ dvādasāyatanasaṅkhātaṃ idaṃ vanaṃ saṃyojanasaṅkhātassa vanathassa padaṭṭhānaṃ samāropayitabbaṃ, āyatanaṃ paṭicca saṃyojanuppajjanato [M 0.0215] anusayasaṅkhātaṃ idaṃ vanaṃ pariyuṭṭhānasaṅkhātassa vanathassa padaṭṭhānaṃ samāropayitabbaṃ. “Pañcakāmaguṇādīnaṃ vanabhāvo ca taṇhādīnaṃ vanathabhāvo ca kena amhehi saddahitabbo”ti vattabbattā “tenāha bhagavā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tena pañcakāmaguṇādīnaṃ vanabhāvena ca taṇhādīnaṃ vanathabhāvena ca bhagavā “chetvā vanañca vanathañcā”ti yaṃ vacanaṃ āha, tena bhagavato vacanena vacanānusārena saddahitabboti. Ayanti ayaṃ “ekasmiṃ padaṭṭhāne”tiādisaṃvaṇṇanā. Padaṭṭhānenāti ekekena padaṭṭhānena. Samāropanāti tadaññapadaṭṭhānānaṃ samāropanā[V 0.0340]. Samāropenti samāropayitabbāni etāya saṃvaṇṇanāyāti samāropanāti viggahoti. (1)

The proximate causes of the teaching should be applied—thus, having been determined and classified by the teacher, they are known to us. And because it is to be asked, 'Now, for which, which proximate cause should be applied?' it was said, 'The forest is for the thicket,' and so on. This fivefold realm of sensual pleasures is the forest, the proximate cause for the thicket that is craving, because it is the basis for craving. This forest, designated as the grasping of signs, whether 'a woman' or 'a man,' should be applied as the proximate cause for the thicket designated as the grasping of the features of various limbs, such as 'Ah, the eye! Ah, the ear! Ah, the nose! Ah, the tongue! Ah, the body!' This forest, designated as the uncomprehended twelve sense-spheres, should be applied as the proximate cause for the thicket designated as fetters, because fetters arise dependent on the sense-spheres. This forest, designated as latent tendencies, should be applied as the proximate cause for the thicket designated as obsessions. Because it is to be said, 'How should we believe that the fivefold realm of sensual pleasures, etc., is the forest, and that craving, etc., is the thicket?' therefore, 'Thus said the Blessed One,' and so on, was stated. Because the fivefold realm of sensual pleasures, etc., is the forest, and craving, etc., is the thicket, the Blessed One said the statement 'Having cut down the forest and the thicket'; by that statement of the Blessed One, in accordance with that statement, it should be believed. This is the explanation beginning with 'in one proximate cause.' 'By the proximate cause' means by each individual proximate cause. 'Application' means the application of other proximate causes. 'Samāropanā' is the analysis (vigraha) of 'samāropenti' (they apply) and 'samāropayitabbāni' (what should be applied) by this explanation. (1)

51. Padaṭṭhānena samāropanā ācariyena niddiṭṭhā, amhehi ca ñātā, “katamā vevacanena samāropanā”ti pucchitabbattā “tattha katamā vevacanenā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tatthāti tāsu catūsu padaṭṭhānasamāropanādīsu samāropanāsu vevacanena ekekena rotadaññavevacanānaṃ samāropanā katamāti pucchati. “Rāgavirāgā”ti ca “cetovimuttī”ti ca “sekkhaphala”nti ca idaṃ vacanattayaṃ anāgāmiphalatthattā anāgāmiphalassa vevacanaṃ. “Avijjāvirāgā”ti ca “paññāvimuttī”ti ca “asekkhaphala”nti ca idaṃ vacanattayaṃ arahattaphalatthattā arahattaphalassa vevacanaṃ. Iminā nayena sesesu yojanā kātabbā. (2)

51. The application by way of proximate cause has been specified by the teacher and is known to us. Because it is to be asked, 'What is the application by way of synonymous terms?' therefore it is said, 'Herein, what is it by way of synonymous terms?' and so on. 'Herein' means among those four applications, namely, application by way of proximate cause, etc., the question is asked: 'What is the application of other synonymous terms by means of each single synonymous term?' 'Dispassion for lust,' 'liberation of mind,' and 'fruit of the trainee'—these three expressions, because they have the meaning of the fruit of non-returning, are synonymous terms for the fruit of non-returning. 'Dispassion for ignorance,' 'liberation by wisdom,' and 'fruit of the non-trainee'—these three expressions, because they have the meaning of the fruit of arahantship, are synonymous terms for the fruit of arahantship. In this way, the remaining connections should be made. (2)

Vevacanena samāropanā ācariyena niddiṭṭhā, amhehi ca ñātā, “katamā bhāvanāya samāropanā”ti pucchitabbattā “tattha katamā bhāvanāyā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tatthāti tāsu catūsu padaṭṭhānasamāropanādīsu katamāya desitāya bhāvanāya katamesānaṃ adesitānaṃ bhāvanāropanā katamāti pucchati. Yathā yena pakārena yaṃ bhāvanaṃ bhagavā “tasmātiha, tvaṃ bhikkhu, kāye kāyānupassī viharati, ātāpī sampajāno satimā vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassa”nti (saṃ. ni. 5.369, 371, 395, 415) āha, tathā tena pakārena tāya bhāvanāya tadaññabhāvanāpi samāropayitabbāti attho.

The application by way of synonymous terms has been specified by the teacher and is known to us. Because it is to be asked, 'What is the application by way of development?' therefore it is said, 'Herein, what is it by way of development?' and so on. 'Herein' means among those four applications, namely, application by way of proximate cause, etc., the question is asked: 'By which taught development is the application of which untaught developments made?' The meaning is that in whatever way the Blessed One taught a development, such as, 'Therefore, monk, dwell contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world,' in that same way, other developments should also be applied by that development.

“Tasmātihā”tiādipāṭhe [M 0.0216] “kiṃ bhāvanaṃ bhagavā āhā”ti pucchitabbattā “ātāpī”tiādi vuttaṃ. “Ātāpī”ti vacanena vīriyindriyaṃ bhagavā āha. “Sampajāno”ti vacanena paññindriyaṃ bhagavā āha. “Satimā”ti vacanena satindriyaṃ āha. “Vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassa”nti vacanena samādhindriyaṃ āha. “Evaṃ vutte katamā bhāvanā samāropayitabbā”ti pucchitabbattā “evaṃ kāye kāyānupassino viharato cattāro satipaṭṭhānā bhāvanāpāripūriṃ gacchantī”ti vuttaṃ. Evaṃ vuttāya vīriyindriyādibhāvanāya cattāro satipaṭṭhānā samāropayitabbāti attho. Kena kāraṇena bhāvanāpāripūriṃ gacchantīti pucchati. Catunnaṃ indriyānaṃ indriyabhāvena, bhāvetabbabhāvena vā ekalakkhaṇattā bhāvanāpāripūriṃ gacchantīti vissajjeti. “Tesu samāropitesu katame samāropayitabbā”ti pucchitabbattā “catūsū”tiādi vuttaṃ. Catūsu satipaṭṭhānesu bhāviyamānesu samāropayitabbesu cattāro sammappadhānā bhāvanāpāripūriṃ gacchantīti samāropayitabbāti attho. Sesesupi evameva samāropayitabbā.

In the passage beginning with 'Therefore,' since it is to be asked, 'What development did the Blessed One teach?' 'ardent,' and so on, was stated. By the word 'ardent,' the Blessed One taught the faculty of energy. By the word 'clearly comprehending,' the Blessed One taught the faculty of wisdom. By the word 'mindful,' he taught the faculty of mindfulness. By the phrase 'having subdued covetousness and displeasure in the world,' he taught the faculty of concentration. Since it is to be asked, 'When this is said, what development should be applied?' it is said, 'For one who dwells thus contemplating the body in the body, the four foundations of mindfulness reach fulfillment in development.' The meaning is that the four foundations of mindfulness should be applied by the development of the faculty of energy, and so on, as stated. He asks, 'For what reason do they reach fulfillment in development?' He answers, 'Because of the four faculties' nature as faculties, or because of their single characteristic as that which is to be developed, they reach fulfillment in development.' Since it is to be asked, 'When these are applied, what should be applied?' 'in the four,' and so on, was stated. The meaning is that when the four foundations of mindfulness are being developed and applied, the four right efforts reach fulfillment in development; thus they should be applied. The rest should also be applied in the same way.

Bhāvanāya [V 0.0341] samāropanā ācariyena vibhattā, amhehi ca ñātā, “katamā pahānena samāropanā”ti pucchitabbattā “tattha katamā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tatthāti tāsu catūsu padaṭṭhānasamāropanādīsu katamena desitena pahānena katamesaṃ adesitānaṃ pahānānaṃ katamā samāropanāti pucchati. “Kāye kāyānupassī viharanto asubhe ‘subha’nti vipallāsaṃ pajahatī”ti desitena “subha”nti vipallāsappahānena kabaḷīkārāhārapariññāya paribandhakilesakāmupādānappahānādayopi samāropayitabbā.

The application by way of development has been classified by the teacher and is known to us. Since it is to be asked, 'What is the application by way of abandoning?' 'Here, what,' and so on, was stated. 'Here' means among those four applications of the foundations, and so on, the question is asked: 'By which taught abandoning is there the application of which untaught abandonings?' By the abandoning taught as, 'Dwelling contemplating the body in the body, one abandons the distortion of perceiving the unattractive as attractive,' and by this abandoning of the 'attractive' distortion, the abandoning of the binding defilements, sensual clinging, and so on, should also be applied through the full understanding of edible food.

“Vedanāsu vedanānupassī viharanto dukkhe ‘sukha’nti vipallāsaṃ pajahatī”ti desitena “sukha”nti vipallāsappahānena phassāhārapariññāya paribandhakilesabhavupādānappahānādayopi samāropayitabbā.

By the abandoning taught as, 'Dwelling contemplating feelings in feelings, one abandons the distortion of perceiving pleasure in suffering,' and by this abandoning of the 'pleasure' distortion, the abandoning of the binding defilements, clinging to becoming, and so on, should also be applied through the full understanding of contact as nutriment.

“Citte cittānupassī viharanto anicce ‘nicca’nti vipallāsaṃ pajahatī”ti desitena “nicca”nti vipallāsappahānena viññāṇāhārapariññāya paribandhakilesadiṭṭhupādānappahānādayopi samāropayitabbā.

By the abandoning taught as, 'Dwelling contemplating mind in mind, one abandons the distortion of perceiving the impermanent as permanent,' and by this abandoning of the 'permanent' distortion, the abandoning of the binding defilements, clinging to views, and so on, should also be applied through the full understanding of consciousness as nutriment.

“Dhammesu [M 0.0217] dhammānupassī viharanto anattani ‘attā’ti vipallāsaṃ pajahatī”ti desitena “attā”ti vipallāsappahānena manosañcetanāhārapariññāya? Manosañcetanāhārapariññāya paribandhakilesaattavādupādānappahānādayopi samāropayitabbāti adhippāyo. (4)

By the abandoning taught as, 'Dwelling contemplating phenomena in phenomena, one abandons the distortion of perceiving 'self' in what is not-self,' and by this abandoning of the 'self' distortion, the abandoning of the binding defilements, clinging to a self-doctrine, and so on, should also be applied through the full understanding of mental volition as nutriment—this is the intention. (4)

Pahānahāro pana lakkhaṇahāravibhaṅgavaṇṇanāyaṃ vuttoyevāti idha na vadāma.

However, the method of abandoning has already been stated in the explanation of the analysis of the characteristic method; therefore, we do not speak of it here.

“Sutte desitena ekekena padaṭṭhānādikena adesitānaṃ padaṭṭhānādīnaṃ samāropanabhāvo kena amhehi vijānitabbo saddahitabbo”ti vattabbattā “tenāha āyasmā”tiādimāha. Tena tathā samāropanabhāvena āyasmā mahākaccāno –

Because it is to be said, 'By what means should we understand and believe the fact that the unstated foundations, etc., are applied by each stated foundation, etc., taught in the Sutta?' 'thus said the Venerable One,' and so on, was stated. By that very fact of application, the Venerable Mahākaccāyana—

“Ye dhammā yaṃmūlā, ye cekatthā pakāsitā muninā;

Te samāropayitabbā, esa samāropano hāro”ti –

“Those phenomena that have a certain root, and those that have a single meaning, revealed by the Sage; these should be applied—this is the method of application.”

Yaṃ vacanaṃ āha, tena vacanena vacanānusārena tathā samāropanabhāvo tumhehi vijānitabbo saddahitabboti vuttaṃ hoti.

By the statement he made, in accordance with that statement, the fact of such application should be understood and believed by you—thus it is said.

“Kiṃ [V 0.0342] pana ettāvatā samāropano hāro paripuṇṇo, añño niyutto natthī”ti vattabbattā “niyutto samāropano hāro”ti vuttaṃ. Sutte desitena nayena padaṭṭhānādikena adesitāni padaṭṭhānāni samāropayitabbāni bhavanti, tena tena padaṭṭhānādikena adesitānaṃ padaṭṭhānādīnaṃ samāropano hāro niyutto niddhāretvā yuñjitabboti attho daṭṭhabbo.

Because it is to be said, 'Is the method of application complete to this extent, or is there no other prescribed method?' 'there is a prescribed method of application,' was stated. Unstated foundations, etc., are to be applied by the method of the stated foundations, etc., in the Sutta. The meaning should be understood as follows: the method of application for unstated foundations, etc., by means of this or that stated foundation, etc., is a prescribed one, to be determined and then applied.

Iti samāropanahāravibhaṅge sattibalānurūpā racitā

Thus, in the Analysis of the Method of Application, it was composed in accordance with ability and strength.

Vibhāvanā niṭṭhitā.

The Elucidation is completed.

Paṇḍitehi pana aṭṭhakathāṭīkānusārena gambhīrattho vitthārato vibhajitvā gahetabbo.

However, the profound meaning should be analyzed and grasped in detail by the learned, according to the commentaries and sub-commentaries.

Ime yathāvuttā soḷasa saṃvaṇṇanāvisesā saṃvaṇṇetabbatthesu aññāṇasaṃsayānaṃ haraṇato apanayanato hārā nāmāti.

These sixteen distinctions of explanation, as mentioned, are called 'methods' (hārā) because they remove and dispel ignorance and doubt concerning the matters to be explained.

Niṭṭhitā hāravibhaṅgavāravibhāvanā.

The Elucidation of the Section on the Analysis of the Methods is completed.

1. Desanāhārasampātavibhāvanā

1. The Elucidation of the Concurrence of the Teaching-Methods

52. Yena [M 0.0218] yena saṃvaṇṇanāvisesabhūtena desanāhāravibhaṅgādihāravibhaṅgena assādādayo nānāsuttatthā vibhattā, so saṃvaṇṇanāvisesabhūto desanāhāravibhaṅgādihāravibhaṅgo paripuṇṇo.

52. By whatever special mode of exposition—namely, the analysis of the teaching-method and other analyses of methods—the diverse meanings of the suttas, such as gratification and so forth, have been distinguished, that special mode of exposition, which is the analysis of the teaching-method and other analyses of methods, is complete.

“Soḷasa hārā paṭhamaṃ, disālocanato disā viloketvā;

Saṅkhipiya aṅkusena hi, nayehi tīhi niddise sutta”nti. (netti. 4 nayasaṅkhepa) –

“Sixteen methods first, having surveyed the directions and looked around; having summarized with the hook, by the three guidelines one should expound the sutta.”

Gāthā niddesavāre ācariyena vuttā, tassā gāthāya niddeso hāravibhaṅgavārassa ādimhi na vibhatto, “kuhiñci vibhatto, hārasampāte vā vibhatto kiṃ, udāhu nayasamuṭṭhānahāre vā vibhatto [V 0.0343] ki”nti pucchitabbattā “hārasampāte vibhatto”ti tumhehi daṭṭhabboti viññāpanatthaṃ “soḷasa hārā paṭhama”ntiādi vuttaṃ.

The verse was stated by the teacher in the Niddesa chapter. The exposition of that verse was not analyzed at the beginning of the Hāravibhaṅga chapter. Because it should be asked, 'Was it analyzed somewhere? Was it analyzed in the Hārasampāta, or was it analyzed in the Nayasamuṭṭhāna-hāra?'—to make it known that 'it should be understood by you that it was analyzed in the Hārasampāta,' 'Sixteen methods first,' etc., was said.

Atha vā suparikammakatabhūmisadisesu saṃvaṇṇetabbesu nānāsuttappadesesu nānāvaṇṇasugandhapupphasadise soḷasa hāre saṃvaṇṇanābhāvena yojetvā soḷasa hārā ācariyena vibhattā, tathā susikkhitasippācariyasuvicāritajambunadābharaṇasadisesu saṃvaṇṇetabbesu nānāsuttappadesesu nānāvidharaṃsijālavividhamaṇiratanasadise soḷasa hāre saṃvaṇṇanābhāvena yojetvāva soḷasa hārā vibhattā, mahāpathaviṃ parivattetvā pappaṭakojassa khādāpanaṃ atidukkaraṃ viya, nānāvidhesu saṃvaṇṇetabbesu suttappadesesu paramatthojāya soḷasahi hārehi atidukkarakhādāpanasadisaṃ viññāpanaṃ karontena ca yojanikamadhugaṇḍaṃ pīḷetvā sumadhurasassa pāyāpanaṃ atidukkaraṃ viya nānāvidhesu saṃvaṇṇetabbesu suttappadesesu paramatthamadhurasassa soḷasahi hārehi atidukkaraṃ pāyāpanasadisaṃ viññāpanaṃ karontena ca ācariyena anekesu saṃvaṇṇetabbasuttappadesesu soḷasa hāre saṃvaṇṇanābhāvena yojetvā soḷasa hārā vibhattā, amhehi ca ñātā, “nānāvidhasuttappadesesu te saṃvaṇṇanābhāvena yojetvā soḷasa hārā vibhattā kiṃ[M 0.0219], udāhu ekasmimpi saṃvaṇṇetabbasuttappadese saṃvaṇṇanābhāvena yojetvā soḷasa hārā vibhattā ki”nti vattabbattā ekasmimpi saṃvaṇṇetabbasuttappadese saṃvaṇṇanābhāvena yojetvā soḷasa hārā vibhattāyevāti tathā vibhajanto “soḷasa hārā paṭhama”ntiādikaṃ hārasampātavāraṃ āha.

Alternatively, the sixteen aspects, like flowers of various colors and fragrances, were distinguished by the teacher, having been connected in the manner of exposition in the sutta passages to be expounded, which resemble well-prepared grounds; similarly, the sixteen aspects, like various kinds of gems and jewels shining with diverse rays, were distinguished, having been connected in the manner of exposition in the sutta passages to be expounded, which resemble golden ornaments carefully considered by well-trained master artisans. And just as causing one to eat the essence of a wafer made by transforming the great earth is exceedingly difficult, so too, the teacher, by making known the essence of the ultimate meaning through the sixteen aspects in various sutta passages to be expounded, performs something like an exceedingly difficult causing to eat. And just as causing one to drink the very sweet juice by squeezing a lump of honeycomb a league in size is exceedingly difficult, so too, the teacher, by making known the supremely sweet essence of the ultimate meaning through the sixteen aspects in various sutta passages to be expounded, performs something like an exceedingly difficult causing to drink. And the sixteen aspects were distinguished by the teacher, having connected them in the manner of exposition in numerous sutta passages to be expounded, and this is known by us. Because it should be said: 'Were those sixteen aspects distinguished, having been connected in the manner of exposition, in various sutta passages, or were the sixteen aspects distinguished, having been connected in the manner of exposition, in just one sutta passage to be expounded?'—he, thus distinguishing, spoke the Hārasampāta chapter beginning with 'Sixteen aspects first,' implying that the sixteen aspects have indeed been distinguished, having been connected in the manner of exposition, in just one sutta passage to be expounded.

Nanu hārasampātavāraṃ kathetukāmena ācariyena “tattha katamo desanāhārasampāto”tiādivacanaṃ vattabbaṃ, atha kasmā “soḷasa hārā paṭhama”ntiādi vattabbanti ce? Niddese vuttaṃ “soḷasa hārā paṭhama”ntiādikaṃ gāthaṃ hāravibhaṅgavāro nappayojeti vippakiṇṇavisayattā ca nayavicārassa ca antaritattā. Hārasampātavāro pana taṃ gāthaṃ payojeti avikiṇṇavisayattā. Tasmā taṃ gāthaṃ paccāmasitvā hārasampātavāre tassā gāthāya niddeso daṭṭhabboti viññāpanatthaṃ “soḷasa hārā paṭhama”ntiādi vattabbaṃyevāti. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana –

If it is said: 'Surely the teacher, intending to explain the Hārasampāta chapter, should say, "Here, what is the Desanāhārasampāta?" etc.; why then is "Sixteen aspects first," etc., said?' The Hāravibhaṅga chapter does not employ the verse beginning 'Sixteen aspects first,' which was stated in the Niddesa, because its subject matter is scattered and because it is separated from the investigation of methods. However, the Hārasampāta chapter does employ that verse because its subject matter is not scattered. Therefore, to make it known that the exposition of that verse should be understood in the Hārasampāta chapter, having reverted to that verse, 'Sixteen aspects first,' etc., must indeed be said. But in the commentary—

Evaṃ suparikammakatāya bhūmiyā nānāvaṇṇāni muttapupphāni pakiranto viya, susikkhitasippācariyavicāritesu surattasuvaṇṇālaṅkāresu nānāvidharaṃsijālasamujjalāni vividhāni maṇiratanāni bandhanto viya, mahāpathaviṃ parivattetvā pappaṭakojaṃ khādāpento viya[V 0.0344], yojanikamadhugaṇḍaṃ pīḷetvā sumadhurasaṃ pāyento viya ca āyasmā mahākaccāno nānāsuttappadese udāharanto soḷasa hāre vibhajitvā idāni te ekasmiṃyeva sutte yojetvā dassento hārasampātavāraṃ ārabhi. Ārabhanto ca yāyaṃ niddesavāre –

Just as one might scatter various colored loose flowers on a well-prepared ground; just as one might string together various kinds of gems and jewels, glittering with diverse arrays of rays, on well-wrought golden ornaments carefully considered by well-trained master artisans; just as one might cause another to eat the essence of a wafer, having transformed the great earth into one; and just as one might cause another to drink the very sweet juice by squeezing a lump of honeycomb a league in size—so too, the Venerable Mahākaccāna, citing various passages from the suttas, having divided the sixteen aspects, now began the Hārasampāta chapter, showing them connected in a single sutta. And in beginning, that which in the Niddesa chapter—

“Soḷasa hārā paṭhamaṃ, disālocanato disā viloketvā;

Saṅkhipiya aṅkusena hi, nayehi tīhi niddise sutta”nti. –

"Sixteen aspects first, having surveyed the directions by looking around; having summarized indeed with the hook, by the three methods one should expound the sutta."

Gāthā vuttā. Yasmā taṃ hāravibhaṅgavāro nappayojeti vippakiṇṇavisayattā, nayavicārassa ca antaritattā. Anekehi suttappadesehi hārānaṃ vibhāgadassanameva hi hāravibhaṅgavāro. Hārasampātavāro pana taṃ payojeti ekasmiṃyeva suttappadese [M 0.0220] soḷasa hāre yojetvāva tadanantaraṃ nayasamuṭṭhānassa kathitattā. Tasmā “soḷasa hārā paṭhama”nti gāthaṃ paccāmasitvā “tassā niddeso kuhiṃ daṭṭhabbo? Hārasampāteti āhā”ti –

The verse was stated. The Hāravibhaṅga chapter does not employ it, because its subject matter is scattered and because it is separated from the investigation of methods. Indeed, the Hāravibhaṅga chapter is merely the showing of the division of aspects by means of many sutta passages. However, the Hārasampāta chapter does employ it, because the sixteen aspects are connected in a single sutta passage, and immediately thereafter the Nayasamuṭṭhāna is explained. Therefore, having reverted to the verse 'Sixteen aspects first,' it is said, 'Where should its exposition be seen? In the Hārasampāta.'

Vuttaṃ. Gāthāttho niddesavibhāvanāyaṃ vuttova. “Soḷasa…pe… sutta”nti yā gāthā niddese ācariyena vuttā, tassā gāthāya niddeso kuhiṃ daṭṭhabbo, hāravibhaṅgassa ādimhi ācariyena na vibhatto, hārasampāte vā paccāmasitvā vibhattoti daṭṭhabbo kiṃ, udāhu nayasamuṭṭhāne vā paccāmasitvā vibhattoti daṭṭhabbo kinti pucchati. Hārasampāte paccāmasitvā vibhattoti daṭṭhabboti vissajjanā.

It is stated. The meaning of the verse has already been stated in the Niddesavibhāvanā. He asks: 'Where should the exposition of that verse, which was stated by the teacher in the Niddesa—"Sixteen... up to the sutta"—be understood? Was it not analyzed by the teacher at the beginning of the Hāravibhaṅga, or should it be understood as analyzed after reverting to it in the Hārasampāta, or should it be understood as analyzed after reverting to it in the Nayasamuṭṭhāna?' The answer is: 'It should be understood as analyzed after reverting to it in the Hārasampāta.'

Hārasampāte tassā gāthāya niddeso daṭṭhabboti ācariyena vutto, so hārasampāto desanāhārasampātabhedena soḷasavidho, “tattha katamo hārasampāto desanāhārasampāto”ti pucchitabbattā imasmiṃ sutte saṃvaṇṇetabbe saṃvaṇṇanābhāvena mayā vibhajiyamāno hārasampātabhūto saṃvaṇṇanāviseso desanāhārasampāto nāmāti tathā vibhajituṃ “tattha katamo desanāhārasampāto”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tatthāti tasmiṃ soḷasavidhe desanāhārasampātādike hārasampāte. Katamo hārasampātabhūto saṃvaṇṇanāviseso desanāhārasampāto nāmāti pucchati.

The teacher stated that the exposition of that verse should be understood in the Hārasampāta. That Hārasampāta is sixteenfold, by way of the division beginning with the Desanāhārasampāta. Because it should be asked, 'Among those, what is the Desanāhārasampāta?'—in order to distinguish thus, 'Among those, what is the Desanāhārasampāta?' etc., was said, meaning that the special exposition which is a Hārasampāta, being distinguished by me in the manner of exposition in this sutta to be expounded, is called the Desanāhārasampāta. 'Tattha' (therein) means in that sixteenfold Hārasampāta, beginning with the Desanāhārasampāta. He asks: 'What special exposition, which is a Hārasampāta, is called the Desanāhārasampāta?'

“Arakkhitena cittena, micchādiṭṭhihatena ca;

Thinamiddhābhibhūtena, vasaṃ mārassa gacchatī”ti. –

"With an unguarded mind, and struck down by wrong view, overcome by sloth and torpor, one goes under Māra's control."

Sutte “arakkhitena cittenāti kiṃdesayatī”ti pucchitvā “pamādaṃ desayatī”tiādisaṃvaṇṇanāviseso [V 0.0345] desanāhārasampāto nāmāti vuttaṃ hoti. Gāthāttho aṭṭhakathāyaṃ (netti. aṭṭha. 52) vibhatto. Yojanattho pana arakkhitena cittena arakkhitacittasamaṅgī puggalo mārassa maccuno vasaṃ gacchati. Micchādiṭṭhihatena vipallāsena vipallāsasamaṅgī puggalo mārassa vasaṃ gacchati. Thinamiddhābhibhūtena sasaṅkhārikacittena kusītacittena taṃcittasamaṅgī puggalo mārassa kilesādimārassa vasaṃ gacchatīti.

In the sutta, having asked, 'What does "with an unguarded mind" indicate?' it is said that the special exposition beginning with 'it indicates heedlessness' is called the Desanāhārasampāta. The meaning of the verse is analyzed in the commentary (Netti. Aṭṭha. 52). As for the applied meaning: By an unguarded mind, a person endowed with an unguarded mind goes under the control of Māra, Death. By being struck down by wrong view, that is, by perversion, a person endowed with perversion goes under the control of Māra. By being overcome by sloth and torpor, that is, with a prompted and sluggish mind, a person endowed with such a mind goes under the control of Māra, the Māra of defilements, and so on.

“Arakkhitena [M 0.0221] cittenā’ti padena desitaṃ taṃ pamādadhammajātaṃ kassa pada”nti vattabbattā “taṃ maccuno pada”nti vuttaṃ. “Arakkhitena cittenā”ti iminā suttappadesena desito attho ācariyena vibhatto, amhehi ca ñāto, “micchādiṭṭhihatena cāti suttappadesena desito attho kathaṃ vibhatto”ti vattabbattā “micchādiṭṭhihatena cā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Yena vipallāsena yadā anicce “nicca”nti passati, tadā pavatto so vipallāso “micchādiṭṭhihataṃ nāmā”ti vuccati. “So pana vipallāso kiṃlakkhaṇo”ti pucchitabbattā tathā pucchitvā “viparītaggāhalakkhaṇo vipallāso”ti vuttaṃ.

Because it should be said, 'Whose domain is that state born of heedlessness, indicated by the phrase "By an unguarded mind"?' it is said, 'It is Death's domain.' The meaning indicated by this sutta passage 'by an unguarded mind' has been analyzed by the teacher and is known by us. Because it should be said, 'How is the meaning indicated by the sutta passage "and by one struck down by wrong view" analyzed?' therefore 'and by one struck down by wrong view,' etc., was said. When, by means of a certain perversion, one perceives 'permanent' in the impermanent, that perversion which has arisen at that time is called 'struck down by wrong view.' Because it should be asked, 'But what is the characteristic of that perversion?' having asked thus, it is said, 'The perversion has the characteristic of apprehending the opposite.'

Viparītaggāhalakkhaṇoti asubhādīnaṃyeva subhādiviparītaggāhalakkhaṇo vipallāso “vipallāsayatī”ti kāritatthasambhavato. Kiṃ vipallāso viparītaggāhalakkhaṇo? So vipallāso saññaṃ vipallāsayati, cittampi vipallāsayati, diṭṭhimpi vipallāsayati. Iti tayo dhamme vipallāsayatīti vipallāsetabbānaṃ tividhattā vipallāsāpi tividhā honti. Tesu saññāvipallāso muduko dubbalo subhādivasena upaṭṭhitākāraggahaṇamattattā, cittavipallāso saññāvipallāsato balavā subhādivasena upaṭṭhahantānaṃ rūpakkhandhādīnaṃ subhādivasena sanniṭṭhānaṃ katvā gahaṇato. Diṭṭhivipallāso saññāvipallāsacittavipallāsehi balavataro, yaṃ yaṃ ārammaṇaṃ subhādiākārena upaṭṭhāti. Taṃ taṃ ārammaṇaṃ sassatādivasena abhinivisitvā gahaṇato. Tasmā saññāvipallāso paṭhamaṃ vutto, tadanantaraṃ cittavipallāso, tadanantaraṃ diṭṭhivipallāso vutto. Vitthārato pana ekekassa subhasukhaattaniccaggahaṇavasena catubbidhattā dvādasavidhā honti.

The characteristic of perversion is the grasping of the opposite, such as the beautiful in the unbeautiful, etc., because of the possibility of the causative meaning 'it perverts'. What is the perversion characterized by distorted grasping? That perversion perverts perception, perverts the mind, and perverts views. Thus, because it perverts these three things, and because what is to be perverted is threefold, perversions are also threefold. Among these, perceptual perversion is soft and weak, being merely the grasping of the appearance that presents itself as beautiful, etc. Mental perversion is stronger than perceptual perversion, because it grasps by making a determination of the beautiful, etc., regarding the aggregates of form, etc., that present themselves as beautiful, etc. View perversion is stronger than perceptual perversion and mental perversion, because it grasps by clinging to whatever object presents itself with the aspect of beauty, etc., and grasping it as eternal, etc. Therefore, perceptual perversion is mentioned first, then mental perversion, and then view perversion. However, in detail, each of them is fourfold by way of grasping the beautiful, the pleasant, the self, and the permanent, thus they are twelvefold.

Vipallāsā ācariyena vibhattā, amhehi ca ñātā, “katame vipallāsapavattiṭṭhānavisayā”ti pucchitabbattā imāni attabhāvavatthūni vipallāsapavattiṭṭhānavisayānīti dassetuṃ “so kuhiṃ vipallāsayati catūsu attabhāvavatthūsū”ti vuttaṃ. Catūsu rūpakāyavedanācittadhammasaṅkhātesu attabhāvavatthūsu so sabbo vipallāso saññācittadiṭṭhiyo vipallāsayati. “Kathaṃ samanupassantassa vipallāsayatī”ti pucchitabbattā “rūpaṃ attato samanupassatī”tiādi [V 0.0346] vuttaṃ. Yo puggalo rūpaṃ vā attato samanupassati, rūpavantaṃ attānaṃ vā attato samanupassati[M 0.0222], attani rūpaṃ vā attato samanupassati. Rūpasmiṃ attānaṃ vā attato samanupassati, evaṃ tassa samanupassantassa puggalassa vipallāso rūpakāye saññācittadiṭṭhiyo vipallāsayati. Eseva nayo vedanādīsupi.

The perversions have been analyzed by the teacher and are known to us. Because the question 'What are the locations and objects of the occurrence of perversions?' must be asked, to show that these bases of individuality are the locations and objects of the occurrence of perversions, it is said, 'Where does it pervert? In the four bases of individuality.' In the four bases of individuality—namely, the body of form, feeling, mind, and mental phenomena—all that perversion perverts perceptions, mind, and views. Because the question 'How does it pervert for one who perceives?' must be asked, it is said, 'One perceives form as self,' etc. A person who perceives form as self, or self as possessing form, or form in self, or self in form—thus, for such a perceiving person, perversion perverts perceptions, mind, and views in the body of form. The same principle applies to feelings, etc.

“Tesu rūpakāyādīsu katamaṃ katamassa vipallāsassa vatthū”ti pucchitabbattā evaṃ pavattamānassa vipallāsassa idaṃ imassa vatthūti vibhajituṃ “tattha rūpa”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Tatthāti tesu rūpādīsu catūsu paṭhamaṃ vipallāsavatthu rūpaṃ “asubhe subha”nti evaṃ pavattamānassa vipallāsassa vatthu hotīti vibhajitvā gahetabbaṃ. Esa nayo sesesupi. Evaṃ “asubhe subha”ntiādippakārena vipallāsā catubbidhā bhavanti.

Because the question 'Among these, which of the body of form, etc., is the basis for which perversion?' must be asked, to distinguish that this is the basis for this perversion that thus occurs, it is said, 'There, form,' etc. 'There' means among these four, form, etc. The first basis of perversion, form, should be understood by distinguishing it as the basis for the perversion occurring as 'the beautiful in the unbeautiful'. This method applies to the rest as well. Thus, perversions are fourfold in the manner of 'the beautiful in the unbeautiful,' etc.

Idaṃ imassa vatthūti ācariyena vibhajitvā dassitā, amhehi ca ñātā, “tesaṃ vipallāsānaṃ katame mūlakāraṇadhammā”ti pucchitabbattā “dve dhammā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Cittassa saṃkilesā, taṇhā ca avijjā ca – ime dve dhammā vipallāsānaṃ mūlakāraṇabhūtā bhavanti.

This is the basis for this, as analyzed and shown by the teacher, and known to us. Because the question 'What are the root-cause phenomena of these perversions?' must be asked, it is said, 'Two phenomena,' etc. The defilements of the mind, craving and ignorance—these two phenomena become the root causes of perversions.

“Ime dve dhammā ekato vipallāsānaṃ mūlakāraṇaṃ kiṃ honti, udāhu visuṃ visu”nti vattabbattā visuṃ visuṃ vibhajituṃ “taṇhānivuta”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Avijjārahitā taṇhā nāma natthi, tasmā “taṇhāavijjānivuta”nti vattabbanti? Na, taṇhāya sātisayapaccayattā. Sātisayāya hi taṇhāya asubhepi “subha”nti, dukkhepi “sukha”nti samanupassanti. “Taṇhā ca avijjā cā”ti vuttattā “avijjānivuta”nti vattabbaṃ, kasmā “diṭṭhinivuta”nti vuttanti? Avijjāya diṭṭhi bhavatīti diṭṭhisīsena avijjaṃ gahetvā “diṭṭhinivuta”nti vuttaṃ, avijjānivutanti attho gahetabbo. “Avijjānivuta”nti vutte pana diṭṭhirahitā avijjāpi gahitā siyā, diṭṭhisahitāya hi avijjāya aniccepi “nicca”nti, anattaniyepi “attā”ti samanupassanti.

Because it must be stated whether these two phenomena are the root cause of perversions together or separately, to distinguish them separately, it is said, 'covered by craving,' etc. There is no craving devoid of ignorance, so should it be said 'covered by craving and ignorance'? No, because craving is a preponderant condition. Indeed, due to preponderant craving, they perceive even the unbeautiful as 'beautiful' and even suffering as 'pleasure'. Since 'craving and ignorance' has been stated, it should be said 'covered by ignorance'; why then is it said 'covered by views'? Because views arise from ignorance, taking ignorance under the heading of views, it is said 'covered by views'; the meaning should be understood as 'covered by ignorance'. However, if 'covered by ignorance' were said, ignorance devoid of views might also be included. For it is with ignorance accompanied by views that they perceive even the impermanent as 'permanent' and even the non-self as 'self'.

“Kathaṃ taṇhāmūlako vipallāso pavatto, kathaṃ diṭṭhisahitāvijjāmūlako vipallāso pavatto”ti vattabbattā “tattha yo diṭṭhivipallāso”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tatthāti tesu taṇhāmūlakadiṭṭhisahitāvijjāmūlakesu. Diṭṭhivipallāsoti diṭṭhisahitāvijjāmūlakavipallāso. Atītaṃ rūpaṃ attato samanupassatīti adabbabhūtopi dabbabhūto viya vutto. Taṇhāvipallāsoti diṭṭhisahitataṇhāmūlako vipallāso anāgataṃ [M 0.0223] rūpaṃ diṭṭhibhinandanavasena abhinandatīti. Evaṃ atītasamanupassanaanāgatābhinandanabhedena [V 0.0347] pavattiviseso daṭṭhabbo. “Cittassa saṃkileso taṇhāavijjāyeva dve dhammā na honti, atha kho dasa kilesāpi, kasmā dveyeva vuttā”ti vattabbattā “dve dhammā cittassa upakkilesā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Taṇhā ca avijjā ca – ime dveyeva dhammā paramasāvajjassa vipallāsassa mūlakāraṇattā. Tāhi taṇhāavijjāhi visujjhantaṃ cittaṃ sabbehi kilesehi visujjhati, tasmā ca visesato cittassa upakkilesā hontīti dve dhammā vuttā. Na hi tāsu taṇhāavijjāsu arahattamaggena pahīnāsu koci saṃkileso appahīno nāma natthīti.

Because it must be stated 'How does the perversion rooted in craving arise, and how does the perversion rooted in ignorance accompanied by views arise?', it is said, 'Here, the perversion of view,' etc. 'Here' means among those rooted in craving and those rooted in ignorance accompanied by views. Perversion of view means the perversion rooted in ignorance accompanied by views. 'One perceives past form as self' means that even what is not substantial is spoken of as if it were substantial. Perversion of craving means the perversion rooted in craving accompanied by views, delighting in future form by way of the enjoyment of views. Thus, the distinction in occurrence should be seen by the division of perceiving the past and delighting in the future. Because it must be stated 'The defilements of the mind are not just craving and ignorance—there are not merely two phenomena, but indeed ten defilements. Why then are only two mentioned?', it is said, 'Two phenomena are the corruptions of the mind,' etc. Craving and ignorance—these two phenomena are the root causes of the most blameworthy perversion.
