It should be applied to the side of purification as a common feature of purification. ‘Among these nineteen pairs taught, which have become directions, which wholesome state is the direction for which individual?’ Having mentally considered them as directional states, one should discern: ‘This first wholesome state is the first direction for an individual with a craving temperament on the side of purification; this second wholesome state is the second direction for an individual with a speculative temperament on the side of purification.’ Having distinguished them separately, one should extract the truths of the path and cessation as appropriate. The nature of the phenomena to be analyzed, which is shown by a particular mode of exposition, that particular mode of exposition is the origination of the Nandiyāvaṭṭa method. The examination of this, which is shown by that particular mode of exposition, that particular mode of exposition is the origination of the method of examining the directions. And having examined thus, the guiding of individuals to the particular state that has become a specific direction, by which that particular mode of exposition guides, that particular mode of exposition is the origination of the method of the goad.

“Kathaṃ tipukkhalanayasamuṭṭhānaṃ bhavatī”ti ce puccheyya, “tīṇi akusalamūlāni – lobho akusalamūlaṃ, doso akusalamūlaṃ, moho akusalamūlaṃ. Tīṇi duccaritāni – kāyaduccaritaṃ[V 0.0395], vacīduccaritaṃ, manoduccaritaṃ. Tayo akusalavitakkā – kāmavitakko, byāpādavitakko, vihiṃsāvitakko. Tisso akusalasaññā – kāmasaññā, byāpādasaññā, vihiṃsāsaññā. Tisso viparītasaññā – niccasaññā, sukhasaññā, attasaññā. Tisso vedanā – sukhā vedanā, dukkhā vedanā, adukkhamasukhā vedanā. Tisso dukkhatā – dukkhadukkhatā, saṅkhāradukkhatā, vipariṇāmadukkhatā. Tayo aggī – rāgaggi, dosaggi, mohaggi. Tayo sallā – rāgasallo, dosasallo, mohasallo. Tisso jaṭā – rāgajaṭā, dosajaṭā, mohajaṭā. Tisso akusalūpaparikkhā – akusalaṃ kāyakammaṃ[M 0.0276], akusalaṃ vacīkammaṃ, akusalaṃ manokammaṃ. Tisso vipattiyo – sīlavipatti, diṭṭhivipatti, ācāravipattī”ti (netti. 88) tikavasena desito ayaṃ disābhūto akusaladhammasamūho tiṇṇaṃ ugghaṭitaññuvipañcitaññuneyyapuggalānaṃ saṃkileso hotīti saṃkilesapakkhe saṃkilesasāmaññabhāvena yojetvā “imesu dvādasasu tikatikavasena desitesu disābhūtesu akusaladhammesu katamo katamo akusalo dhammo katamassa katamassa puggalassa disā”ti manasāva disādhammabhāvena oloketvā “ayaṃ ayaṃ paṭhamo paṭhamo akusaladhammo ugghaṭitaññupuggalassa saṃkilesapakkhe paṭhamā disā nāma. Ayaṃ ayaṃ dutiyo dutiyo akusaladhammo vipañcitaññupuggalassa saṃkilesapakkhe dutiyā disā nāma. Ayaṃ ayaṃ tatiyo tatiyo akusaladhammo neyyassa puggalassa saṃkilesapakkhe tatiyā disā nāmā”ti visuṃ visuṃ yojetvā samudayasaccadukkhasaccāni yathārahaṃ nīharitvā vibhajitabbadhammasabhāvo ca yena saṃvaṇṇanāvisesena dassito. So saṃvaṇṇanāviseso ca tipukkhalanayasamuṭṭhānaṃ bhavati. Tassa olokanā ca yena saṃvaṇṇanāvisesena dassitā, so saṃvaṇṇanāviseso ca disālocananayasamuṭṭhānaṃ bhavati tathā oloketvā disāvisesabhūtassa dhammavisesassa puggalānaṃ nayanañca yena saṃvaṇṇanāvisesena nayati, so saṃvaṇṇanāviseso aṅkusanayasamuṭṭhānaṃ bhavati.

“If asked, ‘How does the origination of the method of the three individuals occur?’ it should be said: ‘The three unwholesome roots: greed is an unwholesome root, hatred is an unwholesome root, delusion is an unwholesome root. The three kinds of misconduct: bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, mental misconduct. The three unwholesome thoughts: thoughts of sensuality, thoughts of ill will, thoughts of harm. The three unwholesome perceptions: perception of sensuality, perception of ill will, perception of harm. The three distorted perceptions: the perception of permanence, the perception of pleasure, the perception of self. The three feelings: pleasant feeling, painful feeling, neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. The three kinds of suffering: suffering as pain, suffering due to formations, suffering due to change. The three fires: the fire of lust, the fire of hatred, the fire of delusion. The three darts: the dart of lust, the dart of hatred, the dart of delusion. The three tangles: the tangle of lust, the tangle of hatred, the tangle of delusion. The three unwholesome investigations: of unwholesome bodily action, of unwholesome verbal action, of unwholesome mental action. The three kinds of failure: failure in virtue, failure in view, failure in conduct.’ (Netti. 88) This mass of unwholesome states, taught in triads, which has become a direction, is the defilement for the three types of individuals—those of quick understanding, those of expanded understanding, and those to be guided. It should be applied to the side of defilement as a common feature of defilement. ‘Among these twelve triads taught, which have become directions, which unwholesome state is the direction for which individual?’ Having mentally considered them as directional states, one should discern: ‘This first unwholesome state is the first direction for an individual of quick understanding on the side of defilement. This second unwholesome state is the second direction for an individual of expanded understanding on the side of defilement. This third unwholesome state is the third direction for an individual to be guided on the side of defilement.’ Having distinguished them separately, one should extract the truths of origin and suffering as appropriate. And the nature of the phenomena to be analyzed, which is shown by a particular mode of exposition, that particular mode of exposition is the origination of the method of the three individuals. The examination of this, which is shown by that particular mode of exposition, that particular mode of exposition is the origination of the method of examining the directions. And having examined thus, the guiding of individuals to the particular state that has become a specific direction, by which that particular mode of exposition guides, that particular mode of exposition is the origination of the method of the goad.

“Tīṇi kusalamūlāni – alobho kusalamūlaṃ, adoso kusalamūlaṃ, amoho kusalamūlaṃ. Tīṇi sucaritāni – kāyasucaritaṃ, vacīsucaritaṃ, manosucaritaṃ. Tayo kusalavitakkā – nekkhammavitakko, abyāpādavitakko, avihiṃsāvitakko. Tayo samādhī – savitakko savicāro samādhi, avitakko vicāramatto samādhi, avitakko avicāro samādhi. Tisso kusalasaññā – nekkhammasaññā, abyāpādasaññā, avihiṃsāsaññā. Tisso aviparītasaññā – aniccasaññā, dukkhasaññā, anattasaññā. Tisso kusalūpaparikkhā – kusalaṃ kāyakammaṃ, kusalaṃ vacīkammaṃ, kusalaṃ manokammaṃ. Tīṇi soceyyāni – kāyasoceyyaṃ, vacīsoceyyaṃ, manosoceyyaṃ. Tisso sampattiyo – sīlasampatti, samādhisampatti, paññāsampatti[V 0.0396]. Tisso sikkhā – adhisīlasikkhā, adhicittasikkhā[M 0.0277], adhipaññāsikkhā. Tayo khandhā – sīlakkhandho, samādhikkhandho, paññākkhandho. Tīṇi vimokkhamukhāni – suññataṃ, animittaṃ, appaṇihita”nti (netti. 88) tikatikavasena desitaṃ idaṃ disābhūtaṃ kusalasamūhadhammajātaṃ tiṇṇaṃ ugghaṭitaññuvipañcitaññuneyyapuggalānaṃ vodānaṃ hotīti vodānapakkhe vodānasāmaññabhāvena yojetvā “imesu dvīsu dvādasasu tikatikavasena desitesu disābhūtesu kusaladhammesu katamo katamo kusaladhammo katamassa katamassa puggalassa disā”ti manasāva disādhammabhāvena oloketvā “ayaṃ ayaṃ paṭhamo paṭhamo kusaladhammo ugghaṭitaññupuggalassa vodānapakkhe paṭhamā disā nāma. Ayaṃ ayaṃ dutiyo dutiyo kusalo dhammo vipañcitaññupuggalassa vodānapakkhe dutiyā disā nāma. Ayaṃ ayaṃ tatiyo tatiyo kusaladhammo neyyapuggalassa vodānapakkhe tatiyā disā nāmā”ti visuṃ visuṃ disābhāvena yojetvā maggasaccanirodhasaccāni yathārahaṃ nīharitvā vibhajitabbadhammasabhāvo ca yena saṃvaṇṇanāvisesena dassito. So saṃvaṇṇanāviseso ca tipukkhalanayasamuṭṭhānaṃ bhavati. Tassa olokanā ca yena saṃvaṇṇanāvisesena dassitā, so saṃvaṇṇanāviseso ca disālocananayasamuṭṭhānaṃ bhavati. Tathā oloketvā disāvisesabhūtassa dhammassa puggalānaṃ nayanañca yena saṃvaṇṇanāvisesena nayati, so saṃvaṇṇanāviseso ca aṅkusanayasamuṭṭhānaṃ bhavati.

“Three wholesome roots: non-greed is a wholesome root, non-hatred is a wholesome root, non-delusion is a wholesome root. Three kinds of good conduct: good bodily conduct, good verbal conduct, good mental conduct. Three wholesome thoughts: the thought of renunciation, the thought of non-ill will, the thought of non-cruelty. Three kinds of concentration: concentration with initial and sustained thought, concentration without initial thought but with sustained thought only, concentration without initial and sustained thought. Three wholesome perceptions: the perception of renunciation, the perception of non-ill will, the perception of non-cruelty. Three non-distorted perceptions: the perception of impermanence, the perception of suffering, the perception of non-self. Three wholesome investigations: wholesome bodily action, wholesome verbal action, wholesome mental action. Three kinds of purity: bodily purity, verbal purity, mental purity. Three accomplishments: accomplishment in virtue, accomplishment in concentration, accomplishment in wisdom. Three trainings: the training in the higher virtue, the training in the higher mind, the training in the higher wisdom. Three aggregates: the aggregate of virtue, the aggregate of concentration, the aggregate of wisdom. Three gateways to liberation: emptiness, the signless, the undirected.” This collection of wholesome states, taught by way of triads, is directional and serves for the purification of three types of individuals: the one of quick-wittedness, the one who understands after elaboration, and the one who is trainable. Therefore, having connected it to the aspect of purification by way of the common characteristic of purification, and having mentally regarded it by way of its directional nature, asking: “Among these twelve directional wholesome states taught by way of triads, which wholesome state is the direction for which individual?” one should connect them separately by way of direction thus: “This first wholesome state is the first direction for the individual of quick-wittedness in the aspect of purification. This second wholesome state is the second direction for the individual who understands after elaboration in the aspect of purification. This third wholesome state is the third direction for the trainable individual in the aspect of purification.” Having thus connected them separately by way of direction, the truths of the path and cessation are to be extracted as appropriate, and the intrinsic nature of the states to be analyzed is shown by a special mode of exposition. That special mode of exposition arises from the method of the three individuals. The observation of that is shown by a special mode of exposition, and that special mode of exposition arises from the method of observing the directions. Having observed thus, the guiding of individuals to the state that is a special direction is accomplished by a special mode of exposition, and that special mode of exposition arises from the method of the hook.

“Kathaṃ sīhavikkīḷitanayasamuṭṭhāna”nti ce puccheyya, “cattāro āhārā, cattāro vipallāsā, cattāri upādānāni, cattāro yogā, cattāro ganthā, cattāro āsavā, cattāro oghā, cattāro sallā, catasso viññāṇaṭṭhitiyo, cattāri agatigamanānī”ti (netti. 87) catukkacatukkavasena desito ayaṃ disābhūto catukko catukko akusaladhammo “dukkhāya paṭipadāya dandhābhiññāya niyyakassa mudindriyassa taṇhācaritassa ca dukkhāya paṭipadāya khippābhiññāya niyyakassa tikkhindriyassa taṇhācaritassa ca sukhāya paṭipadāya dandhābhiññāya niyyakassa mudindriyassa diṭṭhicaritassa ca sukhāya paṭipadāya khippābhiññāya niyyakassa tikkhindriyassa diṭṭhicaritassa cā”ti catunnaṃ puggalānaṃ saṃkilesoti saṃkilesapakkhe saṃkilesasāmaññabhāvena yojetvā “imesu catukkacatukkavasena desitesu dasasu [M 0.0278] catukkesu dhammesu katamo katamo akusaladhammo katamassa katamassa puggalassa disā”ti manasāva saṃkilesapakkhe disādhammabhāvena oloketvā “ayaṃ ayaṃ paṭhamo paṭhamo akusaladhammo dukkhāya paṭipadāya dandhābhiññāya niyyakassa mudindriyassa taṇhācaritassa puggalassa paṭhamā disā nāma. Ayaṃ ayaṃ dutiyo dutiyo akusaladhammo dukkhāya paṭipadāya khippābhiññāya niyyakassa tikkhindriyassa taṇhācaritassa puggalassa dutiyā disā nāma. Ayaṃ [V 0.0397] ayaṃ tatiyo tatiyo akusaladhammo sukhāya paṭipadāya dandhābhiññāya niyyakassa mudindriyassa diṭṭhicaritassa puggalassa tatiyā disā nāma. Ayaṃ ayaṃ catuttho catuttho akusaladhammo sukhāya paṭipadāya khippābhiññāya niyyakassa tikkhindriyassa diṭṭhicaritassa puggalassa catutthā disā nāmā”ti visuṃ visuṃ disābhāvena yojetvā, samudayasaccadukkhasaccāni yathārahaṃ nīharitvā, vibhajitabbadhammasabhāvo ca yena saṃvaṇṇanāvisesena dassito. So saṃvaṇṇanāviseso ca sīhavikkīḷitanayasamuṭṭhānaṃ bhavati. Tassa olokanā ca yena saṃvaṇṇanāvisesena dassitā, so saṃvaṇṇanāviseso ca disālocananayasamuṭṭhānaṃ bhavati. Tathā oloketvā disāvisesabhūtassa dhammassa puggalānaṃ nayanañca yena saṃvaṇṇanāvisesena nayati, so saṃvaṇṇanāviseso ca aṅkusanayasamuṭṭhānaṃ bhavati.

If it is asked, “How does the method of the lion’s sport arise?”: “The four nutriments, the four perversions, the four kinds of clinging, the four yokes, the four bonds, the four taints, the four floods, the four darts, the four stations of consciousness, and the four ways of going astray.” This directional unwholesome state, taught by way of tetrads, is the defilement for four types of individuals: (1) the one progressing by the painful practice with slow direct knowledge, who is to be led out, of dull faculties and of craving-temperament; (2) the one progressing by the painful practice with quick direct knowledge, who is to be led out, of sharp faculties and of craving-temperament; (3) the one progressing by the pleasant practice with slow direct knowledge, who is to be led out, of dull faculties and of speculative-temperament; and (4) the one progressing by the pleasant practice with quick direct knowledge, who is to be led out, of sharp faculties and of speculative-temperament. Thus, in the aspect of defilement, one should connect it by way of the common characteristic of defilement. Having mentally regarded it by way of its directional nature in the aspect of defilement, asking: “Among these ten tetrads of states taught by way of tetrads, which unwholesome state is the direction for which individual?” one should connect them separately by way of direction thus: “This first unwholesome state is the first direction for the individual progressing by the painful practice with slow direct knowledge, who is to be led out, of dull faculties and of craving-temperament. This second unwholesome state is the second direction for the individual progressing by the painful practice with quick direct knowledge, who is to be led out, of sharp faculties and of craving-temperament. This third unwholesome state is the third direction for the individual progressing by the pleasant practice with slow direct knowledge, who is to be led out, of dull faculties and of speculative-temperament. This fourth unwholesome state is the fourth direction for the individual progressing by the pleasant practice with quick direct knowledge, who is to be led out, of sharp faculties and of speculative-temperament.” Having thus connected them separately by way of direction, the truths of origin and suffering are to be extracted as appropriate, and the intrinsic nature of the states to be analyzed is shown by a special mode of exposition. That special mode of exposition arises from the method of the lion’s sport. The observation of that is shown by a special mode of exposition, and that special mode of exposition arises from the method of observing the directions. Having observed thus, the guiding of individuals to the state that is a special direction is accomplished by a special mode of exposition, and that special mode of exposition arises from the method of the hook.

“Catasso paṭipadā, cattāro satipaṭṭhānā, cattāri jhānāni, cattāro vihārā, cattāro sammappadhānā, cattāro acchariyā abbhutā dhammā, cattāri adhiṭṭhānāni, catasso samādhibhāvanā, cattāro sukhabhāgiyā dhammā, catasso appamāṇā”ti (netti. 86) catukkacatukkavasena desitaṃ idaṃ disābhūtaṃ kusalasamūhadhammajātaṃ “dukkhāya paṭipadāya dandhābhiññāya niyyakassa mudindriyassa taṇhācaritassa ca dukkhāya paṭipadāya khippābhiññāya niyyakassa tikkhindriyassa taṇhācaritassa ca sukhāya paṭipadāya dandhābhiññāya niyyakassa mudindriyassa diṭṭhicaritassa sa sukhāya paṭipadāya khippābhiññāya niyyakassa tikkhindriyassa diṭṭhicaritassa cā”ti catunnaṃ puggalānaṃ vodānaṃ hotīti vodānapakkhe vodānasāmaññabhāvena yojetvā “imesu catukkacatukkavasena desitesu dasasu catukkesu kusaladhammesu katamo [M 0.0279] katamo kusaladhammo katamassa katamassa puggalassa disā”ti manasāva disādhammabhāvena oloketvā, “ayaṃ ayaṃ paṭhamo paṭhamo kusaladhammo dukkhāya paṭipadāya dandhābhiññāya niyyakassa mudindriyassa taṇhācaritassa puggalassa paṭhamā disā nāma. Ayaṃ ayaṃ dutiyo dutiyo kusaladhammo dukkhāya paṭipadāya khippābhiññāya niyyakassa tikkhindriyassa taṇhācaritassa puggalassa dutiyā disā nāma. Ayaṃ ayaṃ tatiyo tatiyo kusaladhammo sukhāya paṭipadāya dandhābhiññāya niyyakassa mudindriyassa diṭṭhicaritassa puggalassa tatiyā disā nāma. Ayaṃ ayaṃ catuttho catuttho kusaladhammo sukhāya paṭipadāya khippābhiññāya niyyakassa tikkhindriyassa diṭṭhicaritassa puggalassa catutthā disā nāmā”ti visuṃ visuṃ disābhāvena yojetvā, maggasaccanirodhasaccāni yathārahaṃ nīharitvā, vibhajitabbadhammasabhāvo ca yena saṃvaṇṇanāvisesena dassito. So saṃvaṇṇanāviseso ca sīhavikkīḷitanayasamuṭṭhānaṃ bhavati. Tassa olokanā ca yena saṃvaṇṇanāvisesena dassitā. So saṃvaṇṇanāviseso ca disālocananayasamuṭṭhānaṃ [V 0.0398] bhavati. Tathā oloketvā disāvisesassa dhammassa puggalānaṃ nayanañca yena saṃvaṇṇanāvisesena nayati, so saṃvaṇṇanāviseso ca aṅkusanayasamuṭṭhānaṃ bhavatīti nayakkamena saṅkhepato nayasamuṭṭhānaṃ bhavatīti viññātabbanti.

“The four modes of practice, the four establishments of mindfulness, the four jhānas, the four abodes, the four right strivings, the four wonderful and marvelous phenomena, the four resolutions, the four developments of concentration, the four qualities partaking of happiness, and the four immeasurables.” This directional collection of wholesome states, taught by way of tetrads, serves for the purification of four types of individuals: (1) the one progressing by the painful practice with slow direct knowledge, who is to be led out, of dull faculties and of craving-temperament; (2) the one progressing by the painful practice with quick direct knowledge, who is to be led out, of sharp faculties and of craving-temperament; (3) the one progressing by the pleasant practice with slow direct knowledge, who is to be led out, of dull faculties and of speculative-temperament; and (4) the one progressing by the pleasant practice with quick direct knowledge, who is to be led out, of sharp faculties and of speculative-temperament. Thus, in the aspect of purification, one should connect it by way of the common characteristic of purification. Having mentally regarded it by way of its directional nature, asking: “Among these ten wholesome states taught by way of tetrads, which wholesome state is the direction for which individual?” one should connect them separately by way of direction thus: “This first wholesome state is the first direction for the individual progressing by the painful practice with slow direct knowledge, who is to be led out, of dull faculties and of craving-temperament. This second wholesome state is the second direction for the individual progressing by the painful practice with quick direct knowledge, who is to be led out, of sharp faculties and of craving-temperament. This third wholesome state is the third direction for the individual progressing by the pleasant practice with slow direct knowledge, who is to be led out, of dull faculties and of speculative-temperament. This fourth wholesome state is the fourth direction for the individual progressing by the pleasant practice with quick direct knowledge, who is to be led out, of sharp faculties and of speculative-temperament.” Having thus connected them separately by way of direction, the truths of the path and cessation are to be extracted as appropriate, and the intrinsic nature of the states to be analyzed is shown by a special mode of exposition. That special mode of exposition arises from the method of the lion’s sport. The observation of that is shown by a special mode of exposition, and that special mode of exposition arises from the method of observing the directions. Having observed thus, the guiding of individuals to the state that is a special direction is accomplished by a special mode of exposition, and that special mode of exposition arises from the method of the hook. Thus it should be understood that, in brief, the arising of the methods occurs in sequence.

Iti nayasamuṭṭhāne sattibalānurūpā racitā

Thus this explanation on the Arising of the Methods has been composed in accordance with my ability and power.

Vibhāvanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation is concluded.

Paṇḍitehi pana aṭṭhakathāṭīkānusārena gambhīrattho vitthārato vibhajitvā gahetabboti.

However, the profound meaning should be analyzed in detail and grasped by the learned in accordance with the commentaries and subcommentaries.

Sāsanapaṭṭhānavibhāvanā

The Elucidation of the Foundation of the Dispensation

89. “Tattha katamaṃ nayasamuṭṭhāna”ntiādinā ācariyena sabbathā nayasamuṭṭhānaṃ ṭhapitaṃ, amhehi ca ñātaṃ, “soḷasahārapañcanayaaṭṭhārasamūlapadesu aṭṭhārasa mūlapadā kathaṃ vibhattā, kuhiṃ amhehi daṭṭhabbā”ti vattabbabhāvato [M 0.0280] “tattha aṭṭhārasa mūlapadā kuhiṃ daṭṭhabbā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tatthāti tesu soḷasahārapañcanayaaṭṭhārasamūlapadesu aṭṭhārasa mūlapadā kena padena ācariyena vibhattā, kuhiṃ amhehi vitthārato daṭṭhabbāti pucchati. Aṭṭhārasa mūlapadā sāsanapaṭṭhāne mayā vibhattā, tumhehi ca vitthārato sāsanapaṭṭhāne daṭṭhabbāti vissajjeti. Vibhattāyeva hi aṭṭhārasa mūlapadā daṭṭhabbā bhavanti. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ (netti. aṭṭha. 89) pana –

89. “Therein, what is the Arising of the Methods?”—with this the teacher has established the Arising of the Methods in every way, and we know it. Because it should be asked, “How are the eighteen root-terms divided among the sixteen modes of conveyance, five guidelines, and eighteen root-terms? Where should we see them?”, therefore it is stated, “Therein, where should the eighteen root-terms be seen?” and so on. “Therein” means among those sixteen modes of conveyance, five guidelines, and eighteen root-terms. It is asked: “By which term have the eighteen root-terms been divided by the teacher? Where should we see them in detail?” The reply is: “The eighteen root-terms have been divided by me in the Foundation of the Dispensation, and you should see them in detail in the Foundation of the Dispensation.” For indeed, the eighteen root-terms should be seen as already divided. But in the commentary (Netti-aṭṭha. 89):

“Evaṃ sabbathā nayasamuṭṭhānaṃ vibhajitvā idāni sāsanapaṭṭhānaṃ vibhajanto yasmā saṅgahavārādīsu mūlapadeheva paṭṭhānaṃ saṅgahetvā sarūpato na dassitaṃ, tasmā yathā mūlapadehi paṭṭhānaṃ niddhāretabbaṃ, evaṃ paṭṭhānatopi mūlapadāni niddhāretabbānīti dassanatthaṃ ‘aṭṭhārasa mūlapadā kuhiṃ daṭṭhabbā? Sāsanapaṭṭhāne’ti āhā”ti –

“Having thus analyzed the Arising of the Methods in every way, now, when analyzing the Foundation of the Dispensation, because in the sections on inclusion and so on the foundation was established only with the root-terms and not shown in its own form, therefore, in order to show that just as the foundation should be determined from the root-terms, so too the root-terms should be determined from the foundation, he said: ‘Where are the eighteen root-terms to be seen? In the Foundation of the Dispensation.’”

Vuttaṃ. Sāsanapaṭṭhāne aṭṭhārasa mūlapadā daṭṭhabbāti ācariyena vuttā, “katamaṃ taṃ sāsanapaṭṭhāna”nti pucchitabbattā “tattha katamaṃ sāsanapaṭṭhāna”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Tatthāti tesu aṭṭhārasamūlapadasāsanapaṭṭhānesu katamaṃ taṃ sāsanapaṭṭhānanti idāni mayā niddhāriyamānaṃ bhagavatā desitaṃ [V 0.0399] saṃkilesabhāgiyādisuttaṃ sāsanapaṭṭhānaṃ nāmāti vissajjeti. Sāsananti pariyattisāsanaṃ. Paṭṭhānanti tassa pariyattisāsanassa saṃkilesabhāgiyatādīhi pakārehi ṭhānaṃ pavattanaṃ paṭṭhānaṃ, taṃdīpanasuttaṃ pana idha paṭṭhānaṃ nāma. Tena vuttaṃ – “saṃkilesabhāgiyaṃ sutta”ntiādi. Atha vā sāsananti adhisīlaadhicittaadhipaññāsikkhattayaṃ sāsanaṃ nāma, taṃ sikkhattayaṃ patiṭṭhahati etena saṃkilesādināti paṭṭhānaṃ, sikkhattayassa sāsanassa paṭṭhānanti sāsanapaṭṭhānaṃ. Tadādhārabhūtaṃ suttampi ṭhānyūpacārato sāsanapaṭṭhānaṃ nāma. Taṃ sāsanapaṭṭhānasuttaṃ sarūpato dassetuṃ –

It has been said. It was stated by the teacher that the eighteen root-terms are to be seen in the Foundation of the Dispensation. Because it should be asked, “What is that Foundation of the Dispensation?”, the words beginning, “Therein, what is the Foundation of the Dispensation?” are stated. “Therein” means among those eighteen root-terms and the Foundation of the Dispensation. The reply to “What is that Foundation of the Dispensation?” is: what is now being determined by me, the discourse taught by the Blessed One beginning with “pertaining to defilement,” is called the Foundation of the Dispensation. “Dispensation” means the scriptural dispensation. “Foundation” means the basis, the proceeding of that scriptural dispensation by way of such aspects as “pertaining to defilement.” But here the discourse that illuminates this is called “foundation.” Therefore it is said: “The discourse pertaining to defilement,” and so on. Alternatively, “dispensation” is the name for the threefold training in higher virtue, higher mind, and higher wisdom. That threefold training is established by this—defilement and so on—hence this is the “foundation.” The foundation of the dispensation is the Foundation of the Dispensation. The discourse that serves as its basis is also called “Foundation of the Dispensation” by a figure of speech. To show that Sutta on the Foundation of the Dispensation in its own form:

“Saṃkilesabhāgiyaṃ suttaṃ, vāsanābhāgiyaṃ suttaṃ, nibbedhabhāgiyaṃ suttaṃ, asekkhabhāgiyaṃ suttaṃ, saṃkilesabhāgiyañca vāsanābhāgiyañca suttaṃ, saṃkilesabhāgiyañca nibbedhabhāgiyañca suttaṃ, saṃkilesabhāgiyañca asekkhabhāgiyañca suttaṃ, saṃkilesabhāgiyañca nibbedhabhāgiyañca asekkhabhāgiyañca suttaṃ, saṃkilesabhāgiyañca vāsanābhāgiyañca nibbedhabhāgiyañca suttaṃ, vāsanābhāgiyañca [M 0.0281] nibbedhabhāgiyañca suttaṃ, taṇhāsaṃkilesabhāgiyaṃ suttaṃ, diṭṭhisaṃkilesabhāgiyaṃ suttaṃ, duccaritasaṃkilesabhāgiyaṃ suttaṃ, taṇhāvodānabhāgiyaṃ suttaṃ, diṭṭhivodānabhāgiyaṃ suttaṃ, duccaritavodānabhāgiyaṃ sutta”nti –

“A discourse pertaining to defilement, a discourse pertaining to latent tendencies, a discourse pertaining to penetration, a discourse pertaining to the non-trainee, a discourse pertaining to defilement and latent tendencies, a discourse pertaining to defilement and penetration, a discourse pertaining to defilement and the non-trainee, a discourse pertaining to defilement, penetration, and the non-trainee, a discourse pertaining to defilement, latent tendencies, and penetration, a discourse pertaining to latent tendencies and penetration, a discourse pertaining to defilement by craving, a discourse pertaining to defilement by views, a discourse pertaining to defilement by misconduct, a discourse pertaining to purification from craving, a discourse pertaining to purification from views, a discourse pertaining to purification from misconduct.”

Vuttaṃ. “Tesu suttesu ye saṃkilesādayo bhagavatā vuttā, tesu saṃkilesādīsu saṃkileso kittako”ti pucchitabbattā “tattha saṃkileso tividho taṇhāsaṃkileso diṭṭhisaṃkileso duccaritasaṃkileso”ti vuttaṃ. Tatthāti tesu suttantesu saṃkilesādīsu dhammesu. “Tividhe tasmiṃ saṃkilese taṇhāsaṃkileso katamena kusalena visujjhatī”ti pucchitabbattā “tattha taṇhāsaṃkileso samathena visujjhatī”ti vuttaṃ. Tatthāti tasmiṃ tividhe taṇhāsaṃkilesādike. “So samatho khandhesu katamo khandho”ti pucchitabbattā “so samatho samādhikkhandho”ti vuttaṃ. “Diṭṭhisaṃkileso kena visujjhatī”ti pucchitabbattā “diṭṭhisaṃkileso vipassanāya visujjhatī”ti vuttaṃ. “Sā vipassanā katamo khandho”ti vattabbattā “sā vipassanā paññākkhandho”ti vuttaṃ. “Duccaritasaṃkileso kena visujjhatī”ti vattabbattā “duccaritasaṃkileso sucaritena visujjhatī”ti vuttaṃ. “Taṃ sucaritaṃ katamo khandho”ti vattabbattā “taṃ sucaritaṃ sīlakkhandho”ti vuttaṃ. “Tasmiṃ sīle ṭhitassa puggalassa kiṃ bhavatī”ti vattabbattā “tassa sīle patiṭṭhitassā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Sīle sucaritasaṅkhāte sīlakkhandhe patiṭṭhitassa tassa sīlavantassa puggalassa bhavesu kāmabhavarūpārūpabhavesu āsatti bhavapatthanā yadi uppajjati, evaṃsāyanti evaṃ assa ayanti padacchedo. Evaṃ sati assa sīle [V 0.0400] patiṭṭhitassa ayaṃ āsatti bhavapatthanā samathavipassanābhāvanāmayapuññakiriyavatthu ca bhavati, ca-saddena dānamayasīlamayapuññakiriyavatthu ca bhavatīti attho saṅgahito. Tatrāti tesu kāmabhavarūpārūpabhavesu upapattiyā saṃvattatīti.

It has been said. Because it should be asked, “Among those discourses, of the defilements and so on spoken of by the Blessed One, what constitutes defilement?”, it is said: “Therein, defilement is threefold: defilement of craving, defilement of views, and defilement of misconduct.” “Therein” means among the things such as defilement in those discourses. Because it should be asked, “In that threefold defilement, by what wholesome quality is the defilement of craving purified?”, it is said: “Therein, the defilement of craving is purified by serenity.” “Therein” means in that threefold defilement beginning with craving. Because it should be asked, “Among the aggregates, which aggregate is that serenity?”, it is said: “That serenity is the aggregate of concentration.” Because it should be asked, “By what is the defilement of views purified?”, it is said: “The defilement of views is purified by insight.” Because it should be stated, “Which aggregate is that insight?”, it is said: “That insight is the aggregate of wisdom.” Because it should be stated, “By what is the defilement of misconduct purified?”, it is said: “The defilement of misconduct is purified by good conduct.” Because it should be stated, “Which aggregate is that good conduct?”, it is said: “That good conduct is the aggregate of virtue.” Because it should be stated, “What happens for a person established in that virtue?”, the words beginning “For one established in that virtue…” are stated. For that virtuous person established in virtue—the aggregate of virtue called good conduct—if attachment, a wish for existence, arises in regard to existences—sensual existence, form existence, or formless existence—the word-division of “evaṃsāyanti” is “evaṃ assa ayaṃ.” This being so, for one established in virtue, this attachment and wish for existence becomes a basis for meritorious action consisting of the development of serenity and insight; and by the word “and,” the meaning is included that it also becomes a basis for meritorious action consisting of giving and virtue. “Therein” means it conduces to rebirth in those existences: the sensual existence, the form existence, and the formless existence.

“Saṃkilesādayo yehi suttehi dassitā, tāni suttāni kittakānī”ti vattabbattā “imāni cattāri suttānī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Asādhāraṇāni saṃkilesabhāgiyasuttavāsanābhāgiyasuttanibbedhabhāgiyasuttaasekkhabhāgiyasuttāni cattāri suttāni bhavanti, sādhāraṇāni [M 0.0282] saṃkilesabhāgiyavāsanābhāgiyasutta, saṃkilesabhāgiyanibbedhabhāgiyasutta, saṃkilesabhāgiyaasekkhabhāgiyasutta, vāsanābhāgiyanibbedhabhāgiyasuttāni katāni missitāni cattāri bhavanti. Iti aṭṭha suttāni bhavanti. Tāniyeva vuttappakārāni aṭṭha suttāni bhavanti. Sādhāraṇāni vāsanābhāgiyaasekkhabhāgiyasuttanibbedhabhāgiyaasekkhabhāgiyasutta- saṃkilesabhāgiyavāsanābhāgiyanibbedhabhāgiyasuttasaṃkilesa- bhāgiyavāsanābhāgiyaasekkhabhāgiyasutta- saṃkilesabhāgiyanibbedhabhāgiyaasekkhabhāgiyasutta- vāsanābhāgiyanibbedhabhāgiyaasekkhabhāgiyasutta- saṃkilesabhāgiyavāsanābhāgiyanibbedhabhāgiyaasekkhabhāgiyasutta- nevasaṃkilesabhāgiyanavāsanā- bhāgiyananibbedhabhāgiyanaasekkhabhāgiyasuttāni katāni missitāni aṭṭha suttāni bhavantīti soḷasa suttāni bhavanti. Tesu soḷasasuttesu cattāri ekakāni suttāni ca cattāri dukāni suttāni ca dve tikāni ca pāḷiyaṃ āgatāni, dve dukāni suttāni ca dve tikāni ca dve catukkāni suttāni ca aṭṭhakathāyaṃ (netti. aṭṭha. 89) āgatāni.

Because it should be stated, “How many are the discourses by which defilement and so on are shown?”, the words beginning “These four discourses…” are stated. There are four unshared discourses: the discourse pertaining to defilement, the discourse pertaining to latent tendencies, the discourse pertaining to penetration, and the discourse pertaining to the non-trainee. There are four shared, mixed discourses: the one pertaining to defilement and latent tendencies, the one pertaining to defilement and penetration, the one pertaining to defilement and the non-trainee, and the one pertaining to latent tendencies and penetration. Thus there are eight discourses. These are the eight discourses of the kind described. The eight shared, mixed discourses are: the one pertaining to latent tendencies and the non-trainee, the one pertaining to penetration and the non-trainee, the one pertaining to defilement, latent tendencies, and penetration, the one pertaining to defilement, latent tendencies, and the non-trainee, the one pertaining to defilement, penetration, and the non-trainee, the one pertaining to latent tendencies, penetration, and the non-trainee, the one pertaining to defilement, latent tendencies, penetration, and the non-trainee, and the one pertaining to neither defilement, nor latent tendencies, nor penetration, nor the non-trainee. Thus there are sixteen discourses. Among these sixteen discourses, four single discourses, four dual discourses, and two triple discourses are found in the Pāḷi; two dual discourses, two triple discourses, and two quadruple discourses are found in the commentary.

“Yadi paṭṭhānanayena vuttappakārāni soḷasa suttāniyeva vibhattāni, evaṃ sati suttageyyādinavavidhaṃ sakalaṃ pariyattisāsanaṃ paṭṭhānanayena avibhattaṃ bhaveyyā”ti vattabbattā “imehi soḷasahi suttehī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Paṭṭhānanayena vibhattehi soḷasahi imehi suttehi navavidhaṃ sakalaṃ pariyattisuttaṃ paṭṭhānanayena vibhattaṃyeva hutvā bhinnaṃ bhavati. Saṃkilesabhāgiyādipabhedāya gāthāya gāthā anuminitabbā, saṃkilesabhāgiyādipabhedena veyyākaraṇena veyyākaraṇaṃ anuminitabbaṃ. Saṃkilesabhāgiyādipabhedena suttena suttaṃ anuminitabbaṃ bhavatiyevāti.

Because it would have to be said, “If only the sixteen discourses of the kind described were analyzed by the guideline of the Paṭṭhāna, then the entire ninefold scriptural dispensation—prose, verse, etc.—would remain unanalyzed by the guideline of the Paṭṭhāna,” the words beginning “By these sixteen discourses…” were stated. By these sixteen discourses, analyzed by the guideline of the Paṭṭhāna, the entire ninefold scriptural teaching becomes analyzed by the guideline of the Paṭṭhāna and is thus differentiated. A verse should be inferred from a verse with the division “pertaining to defilement,” etc. An exposition should be inferred from an exposition with the division “pertaining to defilement,” etc. A discourse should indeed be inferred from a discourse with the division “pertaining to defilement,” etc.

90. “Tesu soḷasasu saṃkilesabhāgiyādīsu suttesu katamaṃ saṃkilesabhāgiyaṃ sutta”nti pucchitabbattā “tattha katamaṃ saṃkilesabhāgiyaṃ sutta”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Tatthāti tesu soḷasasu saṃkilesabhāgiyādīsu suttesu katamaṃ suttaṃ saṃkilesabhāgiyaṃ suttaṃ nāmāti pucchati.

90. Because it should be asked, ‘Among those sixteen discourses beginning with those pertaining to defilement, which is the discourse pertaining to defilement?’ the text states, ‘Among them, which is the discourse pertaining to defilement?’ and so on. Here, ‘among them’ refers to those sixteen discourses beginning with those pertaining to defilement, and the question is asked: ‘Which discourse is called the discourse pertaining to defilement?’

“Kāmandhā [V 0.0401][M 0.0283] jālasañchannā, taṇhāchadanachāditā;

Pamattabandhanābaddhā, macchāva kumināmukhe;

Jarāmaraṇamanventi, vaccho khīrapakova mātara”nti. –

“Blinded by sensual lust, covered by a net, shrouded by the veil of craving; bound by the bond of heedlessness, like fish in the mouth of a fish-trap, they proceed to aging and death, as a suckling calf follows its mother.”

Idaṃ suttaṃ saṃkilesabhāge vācakañāpakabhāvena pavattanato saṃkilesabhāgiyaṃ suttaṃ nāma. Ye sattā kāmandhā kāmena andhā jālasañchannā taṇhāchadanena chāditā, pamattabandhanāya baddhā bandhitabbā, te satte jarāmaraṇaṃ anveti, yathā taṃ kumināmukhe ye macchā gahitā, te macche jarāmaraṇaṃ anveti iva, evaṃ te satte jarāmaraṇaṃ anveti. Khīrapako vaccho mātaraṃ anveti iva, evaṃ te satte jarāmaraṇaṃ anvetīti yojanā kātabbā. Atha vā khīrapako vaccho mātaraṃ anveti iva, kumināmukhe gahitā macchā jarāmaraṇaṃ anventi iva ca, evaṃ ye sattā kāmandhā pamattabandhanāya bandhitabbā, te sattā jarāmaraṇaṃ anventīti yojanā.

This discourse is called a discourse pertaining to defilement because it proceeds by way of expressing and indicating the portion of defilement. Aging and death follows those beings who are blinded by sensual desire, covered by a net, shrouded by the veil of craving, bound and liable to be bound by the bond of heedlessness, just as aging and death follows the fish that have been caught in the mouth of a fish-trap. The connection should be made thus: as a suckling calf follows its mother, so aging and death follows these beings. Or else, the connection is: as a suckling calf follows its mother, and as fish caught in the mouth of a fish-trap proceed to aging and death, so too those beings who are blinded by sensual desire and liable to be bound by the bond of heedlessness proceed to aging and death.

“Idaṃ suttaṃyevā”ti vattabbattā –

Because this very discourse is to be stated—

“Cattārimāni, bhikkhave, agatigamanāni. Katamāni cattāri? Chandāgatiṃ gacchati, dosāgatiṃ gacchati, mohāgatiṃ gacchati, bhayāgatiṃ gacchati, imāni kho, bhikkhave, cattāri agatigamanāni. Idamavoca bhagavā, idaṃ vatvāna sugato, athāparaṃ etadavoca satthā –

“Bhikkhus, there are these four wrong courses. What four? One goes on a wrong course because of desire, one goes on a wrong course because of hatred, one goes on a wrong course because of delusion, and one goes on a wrong course because of fear. These, bhikkhus, are the four wrong courses. The Blessed One said this. Having said this, the Well-Farer, the Teacher, further said this:”

“Chandā dosā bhayā mohā, yo dhammaṃ ativattati;

Nihīyati tassa yaso, kāḷapakkheva candimā”ti. –

“Whoever transgresses the Dhamma out of desire, hatred, fear, or delusion—his fame diminishes like the moon in the dark fortnight.”

Idaṃ saṃkilesabhāgiyaṃ suttanti –

This is the discourse pertaining to defilement—

Vuttaṃ. Chandā chandahetunā dosā dosahetunā bhayā bhayahetunā mohā mohahetunā yo rājādiko yo vinayadharādiko vā dhammaṃ sappurisadhammaṃ ativattati atikkamitvā vattati, tassa rājādino vā tassa vinayadharādino vā yaso kitti ca parivāro ca bhogo ca nihīyati. Candimā kāḷapakkhe pabhāya nihīyati iva, evaṃ nihīyatīti yojanā.

It has been said. Whoever—whether a king or the like, or an expert in the Vinaya or the like—transgresses the Dhamma, the law of good people, for the reason of desire, for the reason of hatred, for the reason of fear, or for the reason of delusion, his fame, renown, retinue, and wealth decline. The connection is as follows: just as the moon wanes in its radiance during the dark fortnight, so do they decline.

“Ettakaṃyevā”ti [V 0.0402][M 0.0284] vattabbattā “manopubbaṅgamā dhammā…pe… cakkaṃva vahato padanti idaṃ saṃkilesabhāgiyaṃ sutta”nti vuttaṃ. Attho pākaṭo. Aṭṭhakathāyampi vibhatto.

Because only this much is to be stated, it is said: '“Mind precedes all phenomena … as the wheel follows the foot of the beast of burden”—this is the sutta pertaining to defilement.' The meaning is evident. It is also analyzed in the commentary.

“Middhī yadā hoti mahagghaso ca, niddāyitā samparivattasāyī;

Mahāvarāhova nivāpapuṭṭho, punappunaṃ gabbhamupeti mando”ti. –

“When one is torpid and a glutton, drowsy and rolling about as he lies, like a great hog fattened on swill, the fool enters the womb again and again.”

Idaṃ suttampi saṃkilesabhāge visaye vācakañāpakabhāvena pavattanato saṃkilesabhāgiyaṃ suttaṃ nāma. Nivāpapuṭṭho mahāvarāho gāmasūkaro niddāyitā supanasīlo samparivattasāyī hoti iva, evaṃ yo mando satto yadā mahagghaso hoti, so mando satto middhī thinamiddhābhibhūto hutvā niddāyitā muduphassasayane muduhatthehi parāmasito samparivattasāyī punappunaṃ gabbhaṃ upetīti yojanā.

This sutta, too, is called a sutta pertaining to defilement because it proceeds by way of expressing and indicating the subject of the portion of defilement. The connection is as follows: Just as a great boar fattened on fodder—a village pig—is drowsy, of sleepy habit, and lies rolling about, so too, when a foolish being is a glutton, that foolish being, overcome by sloth and torpor, becomes drowsy and—fond of a soft bed and of being caressed by soft hands—lies rolling about and enters the womb again and again.

“Ayasāva malaṃ samuṭṭhitaṃ, tatuṭṭhāya tameva khādati;

Evaṃ atidhonacārinaṃ, sāni kammāni nayanti duggati”nti. –

“Just as rust arisen from iron, having arisen from it, eats that very iron, so his own deeds lead one who overindulges to a bad destination.”

Idaṃ suttampi saṃkilesabhāgiyaṃ suttaṃ nāma. Ayasā ayato samuṭṭhitaṃ jātamalaṃ tatuṭṭhāya tato ayato uṭṭhahitvā tameva ayaṃ khādati iva, evaṃ atidhonacārinaṃ atikkamitvā dhonacāripuggalaṃ sāni sayaṃ katāni akusalakammāni duggatiṃ nayantīti yojanā.

This sutta, too, is called a sutta pertaining to defilement. The connection is as follows: Just as rust arisen from iron, having sprung from that iron, eats that very iron, so one's own unwholesome deeds, done by oneself, lead to a bad destination the one who overindulges, that is, one who transgresses the conduct of a person of pure ways.

“Coro yathā sandhimukhe gahīto, sakammunā haññati bajjhate ca;

Evaṃ ayaṃ pecca pajā parattha, sakammunā haññati bajjhate cā”ti. –

“Just as a thief caught at a house-breaking is slain and bound for his own deed, so after death people are slain and bound in the next world for their own deeds.”

Idaṃ suttampi saṃkilesabhāgiyaṃ suttaṃ nāma. Sandhimukhe rājapurisādīhi gahito coro sakammunā attanā katena corakammena haññati ca bajjhate ca yathā, evaṃ ayaṃ pāpakārinī pajā parattha paraloke pecca sakammunā sayaṃ katena akusalakammunā satthādīhi haññati ca addubandhanādīhi bajjhate cāti yojanā.

This sutta, too, is called a sutta pertaining to defilement. The connection is as follows: Just as a thief caught at a house-breaking by the king's men and others is slain and bound for his own act of thievery, so this evil-doing populace, having passed away, is slain with weapons and the like and bound with chains and the like in the next world for their own unwholesome deeds.

“Sukhakāmāni [M 0.0285] bhūtāni, yo daṇḍena vihiṃsati;

Attano sukhamesāno, pecca so na labhate sukha”nti. –

“Whoever, seeking his own happiness, harms with a rod beings who desire happiness, does not find happiness after death.”

Idaṃ [V 0.0403] suttampi saṃkilesabhāgiyaṃ suttaṃ nāma. Attano sukhaṃ esāno esamāno yo satto aññāni sukhakāmāni bhūtāni daṇḍena vihiṃsati, so hiṃsako satto paraloke pecca sukhaṃ na labhatīti yojanā.

This sutta, too, is called a sutta pertaining to defilement. The connection is as follows: Whatever being, seeking his own happiness, harms with a rod other beings who desire happiness, that harmful being does not find happiness after death in the next world.

“Gunnaṃ ce taramānānaṃ, jimhaṃ gacchati puṅgavo;

Sabbā tā jimhaṃ gacchanti, nette jimhaṃ gate sati.

“If, when cattle are crossing over, the lead bull goes crookedly, they all go crookedly, since their leader has gone crookedly.

“Evameva manussesu, yo hoti seṭṭhasammato;

So ce adhammaṃ carati, pageva itarā pajā;

Sabbaṃ raṭṭhaṃ dukkhaṃ seti, rājā ce hoti adhammiko”ti. –

“So too among humans, if the one considered best lives unrighteously, how much more so the other people? The whole country dwells in suffering if the king is unrighteous.”

Idaṃ suttampi saṃkilesabhāgiyaṃ suttaṃ nāma. Nadiṃ taramānānaṃ gunnaṃ puṅgavo jimhaṃ ce gacchati, evaṃ nette jimhaṃ gate sati sabbā tā gāviyo jimhaṃ gacchanti yathā, evameva manussesu yo rājā seṭṭhasammato, so rājā adhammaṃ carati, evaṃ raññe adhammaṃ carante sati itarā pajā pageva paṭhamameva adhammaṃ carati. Rājā adhammiko ce hoti, evaṃ raññe adhammike sati sabbaṃ raṭṭhaṃ dukkhaṃ setīti yojanā.

This sutta, too, is called a sutta pertaining to defilement. The connection is as follows: Just as, when the lead bull of cattle crossing a river goes crookedly, all the cows go crookedly since their leader has gone crookedly, so too among humans, if the king who is considered the best practices unrighteously, then the other people practice unrighteously all the more. If the king is unrighteous, the whole country dwells in suffering when the king is unrighteous.

“Sukiccharūpā vatime manussā, karonti pāpaṃ upadhīsu rattā;

Gacchanti te bahujanasannivāsaṃ, nirayaṃ avīciṃ kaṭukaṃ bhayānaka”nti. –

“How truly wretched are these humans who, attached to acquisitions, commit evil. They go to the Avīci hell, a bitter, frightful place, the abode of many.”

Idaṃ suttampi saṃkilesabhāgiyaṃ suttaṃ nāma. Ye manussā upadhīsu kāmaguṇūpadhīsu rattā rāgābhibhūtā hutvā pāpaṃ akusalakammaṃ karonti, ime pāpakammakarā manussā sukiccharūpā vata suṭṭhu kicchāpannarūpā vata bhavanti, te pāpakammakarā manussā kaṭukaṃ bhayānakaṃ bahujanasannivāsaṃ nirayaṃ avīciṃ gacchantīti yojanā.

This sutta, too, is called a sutta pertaining to defilement. The connection is as follows: Those humans who, attached to the substrates of existence—the cords of sensual pleasure—and overcome by lust, commit evil, unwholesome deeds, these evil-doing humans are indeed in a wretched state, having fallen into misery. Those evil-doing humans go to the bitter, frightful Avīci hell, the abode of many.

“Phalaṃ ve kadaliṃ hanti, phalaṃ veḷuṃ phalaṃ naḷaṃ;

Sakkāro kāpurisaṃ hanti, gabbho assatariṃ yathā”ti. –

“Fruit certainly destroys the plantain, fruit the bamboo, and fruit the reed; honor destroys a bad person, as a fetus destroys the she-mule that conceived it.”

Idaṃ [M 0.0286] suttampi saṃkilesabhāgiyaṃ suttaṃ nāma. Phalaṃ kadaliyā phalaṃ kadaliṃ ve ekantena hanti yathā, phalaṃ veḷuṃ ve ekantena hanti yathā, phalaṃ naḷaṃ ve ekantena hanti yathā, gabbho assatariṃ [V 0.0404] mātaraṃ ve ekantena hanti yathā, evaṃ sakkāro kāpurisaṃ ve ekantena hantīti yojanā.

This sutta, too, is called a sutta pertaining to defilement. The connection is as follows: Just as its fruit certainly destroys the plantain, as its fruit certainly destroys the bamboo, as its fruit certainly destroys the reed, and as the embryo certainly destroys the she-mule, its mother, so honor certainly destroys a bad person.

“Kodhamakkhagaru bhikkhu, lābhasakkāragāravo;

Sukhette pūtibījaṃva, saddhamme na virūhatī”ti. –

“A bhikkhu who esteems anger and contempt, who is reverential toward gains and honor, does not grow in the good Dhamma, like a rotten seed in a fertile field.”

Idaṃ suttampi saṃkilesabhāgiyaṃ suttaṃ nāma. Sukhette sundare khettepi khittaṃ pūtibījaṃ na ruhati iva, evaṃ yo bhikkhu lābhasakkāragāravo kodhaṃ kujjhanalakkhaṇaṃ kodhaṃ, makkhaṃ paraguṇasīlamakkhanalakkhaṇaṃ makkhañca garuṃ katvā carati, so caranto bhikkhu saddhammasmiṃ na ruhatīti yojanā.

This sutta, too, is called a sutta pertaining to defilement. The connection is as follows: Just as a rotten seed sown even in a good, beautiful field does not sprout, so too a bhikkhu who esteems gains and honor and who lives holding in high regard anger, which has the characteristic of wrath, and contempt, which has the characteristic of disparaging the virtue of others, does not grow in the good Dhamma.

91. “Idhāhaṃ, bhikkhave, ekaccaṃ puggalaṃ paduṭṭhacittaṃ evaṃ cetasā ceto paricca pajānāmi…pe… iti me suta”nti idaṃ suttampi saṃkilesabhāgiyaṃ suttaṃ nāma. Bhikkhave idha sāsane, loke vā ahaṃ ekaccaṃ puggalaṃ paduṭṭhacittaṃ mama cetasā tassa ceto cittaṃ paricca paricchinditvā buddhacakkhunā evaṃ pajānāmi. “Kathaṃ pajānāmī”ti ce puccheyya, yañca paṭipadaṃ paṭipanno, yañca maggaṃ samāruḷho ayaṃ puggalo yathā yāya duppaṭipadāya yena dummaggena iriyati pavattati, tāya duppaṭipadāya tena dummaggena imamhi imasmiṃ samaye duppaṭipajjanakāle ayaṃ duppaṭipannaṃ paṭipanno dummaggasamāruḷho puggalo ce kālaṃ kareyya, evaṃ sati ābhataṃ vatthu nikkhittaṃ yathā, evaṃ niraye nikkhitto. Taṃ kissa hetu? Bhikkhave assa puggalassa cittaṃ paduṭṭhaṃ padositaṃ hi yasmā hoti, tasmā nikkhitto. Evaṃ idha sāsane, loke vā cetopadosahetu ca pana ekacce sattā puggalā kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā apāyaṃ duggatiṃ vinipātaṃ upapajjantīti pajānāmīti. Etamatthaṃ bhagavā avoca. Tattha tasmiṃ sutte etaṃ “paduṭṭhacittaṃ ñatvāna…pe… nirayaṃ so upapajjatī”ti gāthāvacanaṃ iti evaṃ vuccati.

91. “Here, monks, I understand with my mind the mind of a certain person with a corrupt mind… as I have heard.” This sutta, too, is called a sutta pertaining to defilement. Monks, in this Dispensation, or in the world, having encompassed with my mind the mind of a certain person with a corrupt mind, I understand it thus with the Buddha-eye. If one should ask, “How do you understand?”—this person has entered upon such a practice and embarked on such a path that he comports himself and proceeds along that wrong practice and wrong path. If this person, who has undertaken wrong practice and embarked on a wrong path, were to pass away at this very time, he would be deposited in hell just as something brought is set down. For what reason? Because, monks, that person’s mind is corrupt and defiled. Thus, in this Dispensation, or in the world, I understand that on account of corruption of mind, with the breakup of the body, after death, some beings are reborn in a plane of misery, a bad destination, a state of ruin. The Blessed One stated this matter. In that sutta, this verse is spoken: “Having known a corrupt mind… he is reborn in hell.”

Satthā idha sāsane, loke vā paduṭṭhacittaṃ ekaccaṃ puggalaṃ ñatvāna bhikkhūnaṃ santike etamatthaṃ byākāsi. Imamhi imasmiṃ samaye ayaṃ puggalo ce kālaṃ kayirātha, evaṃ sati paduṭṭhacittasamaṅgī hi nirayasmiṃ upapajjeyya, puggalassa cittaṃ padūsitaṃ hi yasmā hoti, tasmā upapajjeyya, cetopadosahetu [M 0.0287] sattā duggatiṃ gacchanti ābhataṃ vatthuṃ nikkhipeyya yathā, evamevaṃ [V 0.0405] tathāvidho duppañño so padosacitto puggalo kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā nirayaṃ upapajjatīti ayampi attho bhagavatā vutto, iti me mayā sutanti yojanā.

The Teacher, here in this Dispensation or in the world, having known a certain individual with a corrupt mind, explained this matter to the monks: “If this individual were to pass away at this time, being possessed of a corrupt mind, he would be reborn in hell. Because that individual’s mind is corrupt, he would be reborn there. On account of corruption of mind, beings go to a bad destination. Just as one would set down something that has been brought, so too such an unwise person, that individual with a corrupt mind, with the breakup of the body, after death, is reborn in hell.” This meaning, too, was spoken by the Blessed One. The syntactical connection is: “Thus have I heard.”

“Sace bhāyatha dukkhassa, sace vo dukkhamappiyaṃ;

Mākattha pāpakaṃ kammaṃ, āvi vā yadi vā raho.

“If you fear suffering, if suffering is displeasing to you, do not do any evil deed, either openly or in secret.

“Sace ca pāpakaṃ kammaṃ, karissatha karotha vā;

Na vo dukkhā pamutyatthi, upeccapi palāyata”nti. –

“And if you should do an evil deed, or are doing one, there is no escape from suffering for you, even if you take flight and run away.”

Idaṃ suttampi saṃkilesabhāgiyaṃ suttaṃ nāma. Sappurisā tumhe dukkhassa jātidukkhajarādukkhabyādhidukkhamaraṇadukkhaapāyadukkha- atītavaṭṭamūlakadukkhaanāgatavaṭṭamūlakadukkhapaccuppannāhāramūlakadukkhāti aṭṭhavidhassa dukkhassa sace bhāyatha, vo tumhehi dukkhaṃ tathā aṭṭhavidhaṃ dukkhaṃ sace appiyaṃ, evaṃ sati āvi vā yadi raho vā pāpakaṃ kammaṃ mākattha mā akattha. Sappurisā tumhe āvi vā yadi raho vā pāpakaṃ kammaṃ sace karissatha vā sace karotha vā, evaṃ sati upeccapi sañciccāpi palāyataṃ palāyantānaṃ vo tumhākaṃ dukkhā aṭṭhavidhā dukkhato pamutti muccanaṃ natthevāti yojanā.

This discourse is also called a discourse connected with defilement. Good persons, if you fear the eight kinds of suffering—the suffering of birth, the suffering of aging, the suffering of sickness, the suffering of death, the suffering of the plane of misery, suffering rooted in the past round, suffering rooted in the future round, and suffering rooted in present nutriment—and if such eightfold suffering is displeasing to you, then do not do an evil deed, do not commit it, either openly or in secret. Good persons, if you should do or are doing an evil deed, either openly or in secret, then even for you who are deliberately fleeing, there is no release, no liberation from the eight kinds of suffering. This is the syntactical connection.

“Adhammena dhanaṃ laddhā, musāvādena cūbhayaṃ;

Mameti bālā maññanti, taṃ kathaṃ nu bhavissati.

“Having acquired both kinds of wealth unrighteously and through false speech, fools think, ‘This is mine.’ How indeed will that turn out for them?

“Antarāyā su bhavissanti, sambhatassa vinassati;

Matā saggaṃ na gacchanti, nanu ettāvatā hatā”ti. –

“Obstacles will surely arise for them, their amassed wealth will perish; having died, they do not go to heaven—are they not by that much destroyed?”

Idaṃ suttampi saṃkilesabhāgiyaṃ suttaṃ nāma. Ye bālā adhammena ca musāvādena ca dhanaṃ saviññāṇāviññāṇaṃ sabbaṃ labhitabbaṃ dhanaṃ laddhā ubhayaṃ dhanaṃ “mama dhana”nti maññanti, tesaṃ bālānaṃ taṃ ubhayaṃ dhanaṃ kathaṃ kena nu pakārena bhavissati, adhammena sambhatattā ciraṭṭhitikaṃ na hoti. Antarāyā rājantarāyādayo antarāyā tesaṃ bālānaṃ bhavissanti. Yena adhammavohārādikena yaṃ dhanaṃ sambhataṃ, assa adhammavohārādikassa taṃ sambhataṃ dhanaṃ vinassati. Matā marantā te bālā saggaṃ sugatiṃ na gacchanti. Sugati hi sobhanehi bhogehi aggoti “saggo”ti [V 0.0406] adhippetā[M 0.0288]. Ettāvatā ettakena diṭṭhadhammikasamparāyikānaṃ attahitānaṃ hāyanena te bālā hatā vinaṭṭhā bhavanti nanūti yojanā.

This discourse is also called a discourse connected with defilement. Those fools who, having acquired all obtainable wealth, both animate and inanimate, unrighteously and through false speech, think of both kinds of wealth, ‘This is my wealth’—how, in what way, will those two kinds of wealth be for those fools? Because it was amassed unrighteously, it is not long-lasting. Obstacles will arise for those fools, such as obstacles from kings. The wealth that was amassed by unrighteous dealings and so on perishes. Having died, those fools do not go to heaven, to a good destination. For ‘heaven’ (sagga) is intended here as the highest (agga) state with beautiful enjoyments. Are they not destroyed and ruined to this extent, through the decline of their own welfare both in the present life and in the lives to come? This is the syntactical connection.

“Kathaṃ khaṇati attānaṃ, kathaṃ mittehi jīrati;

Kathaṃ vivaṭṭate dhammā, kathaṃ saggaṃ na gacchati”.

“How does one dig up oneself? How does one become estranged from friends? How does one turn away from the Dhamma? How does one not go to heaven?”

“Lobhā khaṇati attānaṃ, luddho mittehi jīrati;

Lobhā vivaṭṭate dhammā, lobhā saggaṃ na gacchatī”ti. –

“Through greed one digs up oneself; the greedy one becomes estranged from friends. Through greed one turns away from the Dhamma; through greed one does not go to heaven.”

Idaṃ suttampi saṃkilesabhāgiyaṃ suttaṃ nāma. Yojanattho pākaṭo.

This discourse is also called a discourse connected with defilement. The syntactical meaning is clear.

“Caranti bālā dummedhā, amitteneva attanā;

Karontā pāpakaṃ kammaṃ, yaṃ hoti kaṭukapphalaṃ.

“Fools of little wisdom fare on as their own enemies, doing evil kamma that has a bitter fruit.

“Na taṃ kammaṃ kataṃ sādhu, yaṃ katvā anutappati;

Yassa assumukho rodaṃ, vipākaṃ paṭisevatī”ti. –

“That kamma is not well done which, when one has done it, one regrets, and whose result one reaps weeping, with a tearful face.”

Idaṃ suttampi saṃkilesabhāgiyaṃ suttaṃ nāma. Dummedhā nippaññā bālā amittena pāpakaṃ kammaṃ kataṃ iva, evaṃ attanā kaṭukapphalaṃ yaṃ kammaṃ kataṃ hoti, taṃ pāpakaṃ kataṃ kammaṃ karontā caranti. Yaṃ kammaṃ katvā karonto pacchā anutappati, taṃ kataṃ kammaṃ na sādhu. Yassa kammassa vipākaṃ rodaṃ rudanto assumukho paṭisevati, taṃ kataṃ kammaṃ na sādhūti yojanā.

This discourse is also called a discourse connected with defilement. Witless, unwise fools fare on, doing an evil deed that has a bitter fruit, as if an evil deed were done by an enemy. That kamma is not well done which, having done it, one later regrets. That kamma is not well done whose result one experiences weeping, with a tearful face. This is the syntactical connection.

“Dukkaraṃ duttitikkhañca…pe… avītarāgo”ti idaṃ suttampi saṃkilesabhāgiyaṃ suttaṃ nāma. Suttattho aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vitthārato vutto.

“‘Hard to do and hard to endure… one not devoid of lust.’ This discourse is also called a discourse connected with defilement. The meaning of the sutta has been explained in detail in the commentary.

“Appameyyaṃ paminanto, kodha vidvā vikappaye;

Appameyyaṃ pamāyinaṃ, nivutaṃ taṃ maññe akissava”nti. –

“What wise person here, measuring the immeasurable, would form judgments? I consider one who measures the immeasurable to be hindered, not a true sage.”

Idaṃ suttampi saṃkilesabhāgiyaṃ suttaṃ nāma. Idha sāsane appameyyaṃ appameyyaguṇaṃ khīṇāsavaṃ puggalaṃ “ayaṃ khīṇāsavo puggalo ettakasīlo ettakasamādhi ettakapañño”ti paminanto ko puthujjano [V 0.0407] vikappaye. Appameyyaṃ khīṇāsavapuggalaṃ pamāyinaṃ pamāyantaṃ taṃ puthujjanaṃ ayaṃ nivutaṃ avakujjapaññaṃ akissavaṃ apaññanti maññe maññāmīti yojanā.

This discourse is also called a discourse connected with defilement. Here in this Dispensation, what worldling, measuring an immeasurable person, a taint-destroyer of immeasurable qualities, would form judgments, thinking: ‘This taint-destroyer has such virtue, such concentration, such wisdom’? I consider that worldling who measures an immeasurable taint-destroyer to be hindered, of overturned wisdom, unskilled, and unwise. This is the syntactical connection.

“Purisassa [M 0.0289] hi jātassa, kuṭhārī jāyate mukhe;

Yāya chindati attānaṃ, bālo dubbhāsitaṃ bhaṇaṃ.

“For when a person is born, an axe is born in his mouth, with which the fool, uttering ill-spoken words, cuts himself down.

“Na hi satthaṃ sunisitaṃ, visaṃ halāhalaṃ iva;

Evaṃ viraddhaṃ pāteti, vācā dubbhāsitā yathā”ti. –

“For a well-sharpened sword or halāhala poison does not cause one who has gone wrong to fall in the way that ill-spoken speech does.”

Idaṃ suttampi saṃkilesabhāgiyaṃ suttaṃ nāma. Dubbhāsitaṃ ariyūpavādasaṅkhātaṃ pharusavācaṃ bhaṇaṃ bhaṇanto bālo duṭṭho puriso yāya kuṭhārīsadisiyā dubbhāsitavācāya attānaṃ chindati, sā kuṭhārīsadisī dubbhāsitavācā jātassa purisassa mukhe jāyate jāyati, sā dubbhāsitavācā mukhe jāyati iva, evaṃ sunisitaṃ satthaṃ mukhe na jāyati, yathā halāhalaṃ visaṃ mukhe na jāyati, dubbhāsitā vācā apāyesu viraddhaṃ puggalaṃ pāteti yathā, evaṃ sunisitaṃ satthaṃ apāyesu na pāteti, halāhalaṃ visaṃ apāyesu na pātetīti yojanā.

This discourse is also called a discourse connected with defilement. A foolish, corrupt person, uttering harsh speech reckoned as abuse of the noble ones, cuts himself with that axe-like ill-spoken speech. That axe-like ill-spoken speech is born in the mouth of a person when he is born. Just as that ill-spoken speech is born in the mouth, a well-sharpened sword is not born in the mouth, and halāhala poison is not born in the mouth. Just as ill-spoken speech causes a person who has gone wrong to fall into the planes of misery, a well-sharpened sword does not cause one to fall into the planes of misery, nor does halāhala poison. This is the syntactical connection.

92.

92.

“Yo nindiyaṃ pasaṃsati, taṃ vā nindati yo pasaṃsiyo;

Vicināti mukhena so kaliṃ, kalinā tena sukhaṃ na vindati.

“One who praises the blameworthy or blames the praiseworthy gathers demerit with his mouth; through that demerit he finds no happiness.

“Appamatto ayaṃ kali, yo akkhesu dhanaparājayo;

Sabbassāpi sahāpi attanā, ayameva mahantataro kali;

Yo sugatesu manaṃ padosaye.

“A small matter is the demerit from loss of wealth at dice, even of all one’s property together with oneself. This is a much greater demerit: that one should corrupt one’s mind against the Well-Gone Ones.

“Sataṃ sahassānaṃ nirabbudānaṃ, chattiṃsatī pañca ca abbudāni;

Yamariyagarahī nirayaṃ upeti, vācaṃ manañca paṇidhāya pāpaka”nti. –

“For one hundred thousand nirabbudas and for thirty-six and five abbudas, the one who reviles noble ones goes to hell, having directed evil speech and mind.”

Idaṃ suttampi saṃkilesabhāgiyaṃ suttaṃ nāma. Yo puggalo nindiyaṃ duccaraṃ dussīlaṃ puggalaṃ pasaṃsati, so pasaṃsako puggalo mukhena kaliṃ vicināti upacināti, tena kalinā sukhaṃ na vindati. Yo sucārī sīlavā puggalo pasaṃsiyo hoti, taṃ vā sucāriṃ vā sīlavantaṃ puggalaṃ [V 0.0408] yo puggalo [M 0.0290] nindati, so nindanto puggalo mukhena kaliṃ vicināti upacināti, tena kalinā sukhaṃ na vindati.

This discourse is also called a discourse connected with defilement. Whoever praises a blameworthy, badly-conducted, immoral person, that praising individual gathers and accumulates misfortune with their mouth—through that misfortune, they find no happiness. Whoever blames a well-conducted, moral person worthy of praise, that blaming individual gathers and accumulates misfortune with their mouth—through that misfortune, they find no happiness.

Attanā sahāpi sabbassa dhanassa vasenapi akkhesu yo dhanaparājayo bhavati, ayaṃ kali ayaṃ dhanaparājayo appamatto hoti. Yo puggalo sugatesu manaṃ padosaye, tassa puggalassa yo kali bhavati, ayameva kali mahantataro hoti.

Even if one loses all one's wealth, and even oneself, through gambling, this misfortune, this loss of wealth, is insignificant. But whoever should harbor ill will toward the Sugatas, for that person the misfortune is far greater.

Kasmā? Vācañca manañca paṇidhāya ariyagarahī puggalo yaṃ kālaṃ pāpakaṃ nirayaṃ upeti, so kālo “sataṃ sahassānaṃ nirabbudānañca chattiṃsa nirabbudāni ca pañca abbudāni ca yasmiṃ kāle gaṇīyantī”ti tena kālena samo hoti, tasmā mahantataro hotīti yojanā.

Why? Because a person who, having directed speech and mind, reviles the noble ones, goes to a terrible hell. The duration is equal to the time counted as one hundred thousand nirabbudas, thirty-six nirabbudas, and five abbudas. Therefore, it is far greater. This is the explanation.

“Yo lobhaguṇe anuyutto…pe…

Gacchasi kho papataṃ ciraratta”nti. –

“One who is attached to the quality of greed… …You will surely fall into the abyss for a long time.”

Idaṃ suttampi saṃkilesabhāgiyaṃ suttaṃ nāma. Yo puggalo lobhaguṇe anuyutto anu punappunaṃ yutto hoti, so puggalo aññe puggale vacasā paribhāsati, assaddho kadariyo avadaññū buddhānaṃ ovādaññū na hoti, maccharī pesuṇiyaṃ pesuṇiyasmiṃ anuyutto hoti.

This discourse is also called a discourse pertaining to defilement. Whoever is engaged and repeatedly occupied with the quality of greed, that person verbally abuses others, is faithless, stingy, ungrateful, does not understand the advice of the Buddhas, is miserly, and is devoted to slander.

Mukhadugga mukhavisama vibhūta vigatabhūta anariya bhūnahu buddhivināsaka pāpaka dukkaṭakāri purisanta purisalāmaka kali alakkhi avajātaputta tvaṃ nerayiko asi. Idha idāni bahubhāṇī mā hohi.

Foul-mouthed, crooked-tongued, insignificant, inauthentic, ignoble, a destroyer of beings, a destroyer of wisdom, an evil-doer, a doer of wrong deeds—you are the lowest of men, a wretched man, a person of strife, unlucky, a degenerate son. You are one bound for hell. Do not be a loudmouth here and now.

Ahitāya rajaṃ attani mā ākirasi mā pakkhipasi. Kibbisakāri tvaṃ sante khīṇāsave puggale garahasi, bahūni duccaritāni kammāni carasi, caritvā tvaṃ cirarattaṃ racanavirahitaṃ papataṃ narakaṃ nirayaṃ gacchasi kho ekaṃsenāti yojanā.

Do not scatter dust upon yourself for your own harm; do not cast it. You, a wrongdoer, blame the peaceful ones, those whose taints are destroyed. You commit many evil deeds, and having done so, you will for a long time certainly fall into the abyss, the woeful state, the netherworld, devoid of refuge. This is the explanation.

Nānāvidhaṃ saṃkilesabhāgiyaṃ suttaṃ ācariyena niddhāritaṃ, amhehi ca ñātaṃ, “katamaṃ vāsanābhāgiyaṃ sutta”nti pucchitabbattā “tattha katamaṃ vāsanābhāgiyaṃ sutta”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Tatthāti tesu soḷasasu saṃkilesabhāgiyādīsu suttesu katamaṃ suttaṃ vāsanābhāgiyaṃ suttaṃ nāmāti [V 0.0409] pucchati. “Manopubbaṅgamā dhammā…pe… chāyāva anapāyinī”ti idaṃ vāsanābhāge puññabhāge visaye vācakañāpakabhāvena pavattanato vāsanābhāgiyaṃ suttaṃ nāma. Attho pākaṭo.

Various discourses pertaining to defilement have been determined by the teacher, and have been learned by us. Because it should be asked, “Which is the discourse pertaining to dispositional tendencies?” it was said, “Therein, which is the discourse pertaining to dispositional tendencies?” and so on. Therein means: among those sixteen discourses pertaining to defilement and so on, he asks which discourse is called the discourse pertaining to dispositional tendencies. The phrase, “Mind precedes all phenomena… …like a shadow that never leaves,” is called the discourse pertaining to dispositional tendencies because it proceeds by way of expressing and making known in the sphere of dispositional tendencies, the sphere of merit, or the object. The meaning is clear.

93. “Mahānāmo [M 0.0291] sakko bhagavantaṃ etadavoca…pe… apāpikā kālaṅkiriyā”ti idaṃ suttampi vāsanābhāge puññabhāge visaye vācakañāpakabhāvena pavattanato vāsanābhāgiyaṃ suttaṃ nāma. Attho pākaṭo.

93. “Mahānāma the Sakyan said this to the Blessed One… …a death that is not evil.” This discourse, too, is called a discourse pertaining to dispositional tendencies because it proceeds by way of expressing and making known in the sphere of dispositional tendencies, the sphere of merit, or the object. The meaning is clear.

“Sukhakāmāni bhūtāni, yo daṇḍena na hiṃsati;

Attano sukhamesāno, pecca so labhate sukha”nti. –

“Beings desire happiness. Whoever, seeking his own happiness, does not harm them with a rod, obtains happiness after death.”

Idaṃ suttampi vāsanābhāgiyaṃ suttaṃ nāma. Attho pākaṭo.

This discourse is also called the discourse pertaining to dispositional tendencies. The meaning is clear.

“Gunnaṃ ce taramānānaṃ…pe… rājā ce hoti dhammiko”ti idaṃ suttampi vāsanābhāgiyaṃ suttaṃ nāma. Attho pākaṭo.

“If, of cattle crossing… …if the king is righteous,” this discourse too is called a discourse pertaining to dispositional tendencies. The meaning is clear.

94. “Bhagavā sāvatthiyaṃ viharati…pe… evaṃ pajānātī”ti idaṃ suttampi vāsanā…pe… suttaṃ nāma. Attho pākaṭo.

94. “The Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī… …thus he understands.” This discourse too is called a discourse pertaining to dispositional tendencies. The meaning is clear.

“Kasmā bhagavā janapadacārikaṃ caratī”ti puccheyya, sattahi kāraṇehi buddhā bhagavanto janapadacārikaṃ caranti. Katamehi sattahi? Desantaragatānaṃ veneyyānaṃ vinayanatthaṃ, tatra ṭhitānaṃ ussukkasamuppādanatthaṃ, sāvakānaṃ ekasmiṃ ṭhāne nibaddhavāsanivāraṇatthaṃ, attano ca tattha nibaddhavāse anāsaṅgadassanatthaṃ, sambuddhavasitaṭṭhānatāya desānaṃ cetiyabhāvasampādanatthaṃ, bahūnaṃ sattānaṃ dassanūpasaṅkamanādīhi puññoghappasavanatthaṃ, avuṭṭhiādiupaddavūpasamanatthañcāti imehi sattahi kāraṇehi buddhā bhagavanto janapadacārikaṃ carantīti janapadacaraṇakāraṇaṃ veditabbaṃ.

“Why does the Blessed One wander on tour in the country?” one might ask. For seven reasons the Blessed Buddhas wander on tour in the country. What seven? For the sake of disciplining those to be trained who have gone to other regions; for the sake of inspiring diligence in those who dwell there; for the sake of preventing disciples from constantly dwelling in a single place; for the sake of showing non-attachment to a constant dwelling there for oneself; for the sake of establishing places as shrines due to the Fully Awakened One having resided there; for the sake of causing a flood of merit to flow for many beings through seeing, approaching, and so on; and for the sake of pacifying calamities such as drought. For these seven reasons the Blessed Buddhas wander on tour in the country. Thus, the reason for wandering in the country should be understood.

“Ekapupphaṃ cajitvāna, sahassaṃ kappakoṭiyo;

Deve ceva manusse ca, sesena parinibbuto”ti. –

“Having offered a single flower, for a thousand koṭis of aeons, among both gods and humans, with the remainder he attained final Nibbāna.”

Idaṃ suttampi vāsanābhāgiyaṃ suttaṃ nāma. Sahassaṃ kappakoṭiyoti sahassaṃ attabhāvato koṭiyo.

This discourse is also called the discourse pertaining to dispositional tendencies. ‘A thousand koṭis of aeons’ means a thousand koṭis of existences.

“Assatthe [V 0.0410] haritobhāse, saṃvirūḷhamhi pādape;

Ekaṃ buddhagataṃ saññaṃ, alabhiṃhaṃ patissato.

“At the green-shining Assattha tree, the well-grown tree, being mindful, I attained a single perception directed towards the Buddha.”

“Ajja tiṃsaṃ tato kappā, nābhijānāmi duggatiṃ;

Tisso vijjā sacchikatā, tassā saññāya vāsanā”ti. –

“For thirty aeons from then until today, I recall no unhappy destination; the three knowledges have been realized by me, by the dispositional tendency of that perception.”

Idaṃ suttampi vāsanābhāgiyaṃ suttaṃ nāma. Haritobhāseti haritaobhāse. Alabhiṃhanti ahaṃ alabhiṃ.

This discourse is also called the discourse pertaining to dispositional tendencies. ‘Haritobhāse’ means ‘green-shining.’ ‘Alabhiṃhaṃ’ means ‘I obtained.’

“Piṇḍāya [M 0.0292] kosalaṃ puraṃ…pe… vipāko hoti acintiyo”ti idaṃ suttampi vāsanābhāgiyaṃ suttaṃ nāma. Aggapuggalo anukampako taṇhānighātako muni sambuddho purebhattaṃ piṇḍāya piṇḍaṃ paṭiggaṇhituṃ kosalaṃ puraṃ pāvisi.

“For alms in the city of Kosala… …the result is inconceivable.” This discourse is also called the discourse pertaining to dispositional tendencies. The foremost person, the compassionate one, the destroyer of craving, the sage, the Fully Awakened One, entered the city of Kosala before the meal to receive almsfood.

Yassa purisassa hatthe sabbapupphehi alaṅkato vaṭaṃsako pupphavaṭaṃsakova atthi, so ayaṃ puriso rājamaggena kosalapuraṃ pavisantaṃ bhikkhusaṅghapurakkhataṃ devamānusapūjitaṃ sambuddhaṃ addasa, disvā haṭṭho cittaṃ pasādesi; pasādetvā sambuddhaṃ upasaṅkami.

A certain man had in his hand a floral wreath adorned with all kinds of flowers. This man saw the Fully Enlightened One, preceded by the community of monks and honored by gods and humans, entering the city of Kosala by the royal road. Having seen him, he was joyful and his mind was gladdened. With a gladdened mind, he approached the Fully Enlightened One.

Upasaṅkamitvā so ayaṃ pasanno hutvā surabhiṃ vaṇṇavantaṃ manoramaṃ taṃ vaṭaṃsakaṃ sambuddhassa sehi pāṇībhi upanāmesi.

Having approached, he, filled with faith, offered that fragrant, beautiful, and delightful wreath to the Fully Awakened One with his own hands.

Tato buddhassa lapanantarā lapanassa vadanassa antarā aggisikhā vaṇṇā sahassaraṃsi okkā pabhā nikkhami, abbhā vijju nikkhamati iva, evaṃ ānanā sahassaraṃsi nikkhamitvā ādiccabandhuno sīse tikkhattuṃ padakkhiṇaṃ karitvāna parivaṭṭetvā muddhani antaradhāyatha.

Then, from between the Buddha's speech, from between his utterance and words, a radiance of a thousand rays, a splendor the color of a flame-tip, emerged, like lightning flashing from a cloud. Thus emerging from his face with a thousand rays, it circled the head of the Kinsman of the Sun three times, circumambulating, and then vanished into the crown of his head.

Ānando acchariyaṃ abbhutaṃ lomahaṃsanaṃ idaṃ pāṭihāriyaṃ disvā cīvaraṃ ekaṃsaṃ karitvā etaṃ abravi – “mahāmuni, sitakammassa hetu ko? Taṃ hetuṃ byākarohi, dhammāloko bhavissatī”ti.

Ānanda, seeing this astonishing, amazing, and hair-raising miracle, arranged his robe over one shoulder and said this: “Great Sage, what is the cause of this bright deed? Explain that cause, so there will be a light of the Dhamma.”

Yassa bhagavato sabbadhammesu ñāṇaṃ sadā pavattati, kaṅkhāvitaraṇo muni so bhagavā kaṅkhiṃ vematikaṃ [V 0.0411] ānandaṃ theraṃ etaṃ abravi. Ānanda, yo sopuriso mayi cittaṃ pasādayi, so puriso caturāsītikappāni duggatiṃ na gamissati, devesu devasobhaggaṃ dibbaṃ rajjaṃ pasāsitvā manujesu raṭṭhe sakalaraṭṭhe manujindo rājā bhavissati. So puriso carimaṃ pabbajitvā, dhammataṃ sacchikatvā ca dhutarāgo vaṭaṃsako nāma paccekabuddho bhavissati.

The Blessed One, whose knowledge of all phenomena is ever-present, the sage who overcomes doubt, said this to the elder Ānanda, who was doubtful and hesitant: “Ānanda, that man who gladdened his mind towards me will not go to an unhappy destination for eighty-four aeons. Having enjoyed divine splendor among the gods and ruled a divine kingdom, he will become a king among humans, a lord of men in the entire country. In his final existence, that man, having gone forth and realized the true nature of things, will become a Paccekabuddha named Vaṭaṃsaka, one who has shaken off passion.”

Tathāgate vā sammāsambuddhe vā paccekasambuddhe vā tassa tathāgatassa sāvake vā citte pasannamhi dakkhiṇā appakā nāma natthi.

When the mind is gladdened toward a Tathāgata, or a Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, or a Paccekabuddha, or a disciple of that Tathāgata, there is no such thing as a small offering.

Buddhā evaṃ ettakāti acintiyā bhavanti. Buddhadhammā buddhaguṇā evaṃ ettakāti acintiyā bhavanti, acintiye pasannānaṃ vipāko puññavipāko evaṃ ettakoti acintiyo hotīti etaṃ abravīti yojanā.

The Buddhas are thus inconceivable as to their extent. The teachings of the Buddha, the qualities of a Buddha, are thus inconceivable as to their extent. For those with confidence in the inconceivable, the result, the meritorious result, is thus of an inconceivable extent. This was said; this is the connection.

96. “Idhāhaṃ[M 0.0293], bhikkhave, ekaccaṃ puggalaṃ…pe… ayampi attho vutto bhagavatā iti me suta”nti idaṃ suttampi vāsanābhāgiyaṃ suttaṃ nāma. Bhikkhave, idha imasmiṃ sāsane ahaṃ ekaccaṃ puggalaṃ evaṃ mama cetasā ekaccassa puggalassa ceto cittaṃ paricca buddhacakkhunā evaṃ pajānāmi, yathā yena pakārena ayaṃ puggalo yañca dānādipaṭipadaṃ paṭipanno, yañca dassanādimaggaṃ samāruḷho hutvā taṃ paṭipadaṃ, maggañca iriyati pavatteti, imamhi imasmiñca samaye ayaṃ puggalo ce kālaṃ kareyya, evaṃ sati ābhataṃ vatthuṃ nikkhipati yathā, evaṃ tāya paṭipadāya tena maggena sagge attanikkhitto bhave. Taṃ kissa hetu? Bhikkhave, assa puggalassa cittaṃ hi yasmā pasannaṃ pasāditaṃ, tasmā nikkhitto bhave. Idha sāsane, loke vā ekacce sattā puggalā kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā sugatiṃ saggaṃ lokaṃ cetopasādahetu kho pana upapajjantīti evaṃ ahaṃ pajānāmīti bhagavā etamatthaṃ avoca. Tattha tasmiṃ atthe saṅgahavasena pavattaṃ etaṃ “pasannacittaṃ ñatvāna…pe… saggaṃ so upapajjatī”ti gāthāvacanaṃ vuccati. Ayampi attho bhagavatā vutto, iti me mayā sutanti yojanā.

96. “Here, bhikkhus, I understand a certain person… this meaning was spoken by the Blessed One, thus I have heard.” This discourse, too, is called a discourse connected with past dispositions. Bhikkhus, here in this teaching, with my own mind I encompass the mind of a certain person and understand with the Buddha-eye thus: “In whatever way this person has entered upon the practice of giving and so on, and has embarked upon the path of vision and so on, and conducts himself along that practice and path, if this person were to pass away at this time, just as something brought is set down, so he would be established in heaven by that practice and that path.” For what reason? Because, bhikkhus, that person’s mind is serene and bright. Here in this teaching, or in the world, certain beings, with the breakup of the body, after death, are reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world, on account of confidence of mind—thus I understand. The Blessed One spoke this meaning. In that context, this verse, spoken by way of summary, is uttered: “Having known a serene mind… he is reborn in heaven.” This meaning, too, was spoken by the Blessed One; thus I have heard—this is the connection.

“Suvaṇṇacchadanaṃ nāvaṃ…pe… etādisaṃ katapuññā labhi”nti idaṃ suttampi vāsanābhāgiyaṃ suttaṃ nāma. Nāri devadhītā suvaṇṇacchadanaṃ suvaṇṇālaṅkārehi chāditaṃ nāvaṃ āruyha tiṭṭhasi, pokkharaṇiṃ devapokkharaṇiṃ ogāhasi, padumaṃ pāṇinā chindasi.

“A boat with a golden canopy… those who have made merit obtain such.” This discourse, too, is called a discourse connected with past dispositions. O woman, O devatā, you stand having boarded a boat with a golden canopy, a boat covered with golden ornaments. You enter a divine lotus pond; with your hand you pluck a lotus.

Devate [V 0.0412] kena kammena te tava tādiso vaṇṇo tādiso ānubhāvo tādisī juti bhavati, devate te tava ye keci bhogā manasā icchitā bhavanti, te bhogā ca kena kammena uppajjanti. Devate me pucchitā tvaṃ saṃsa saṃsāhi idaṃ sabbaṃ kissa kammassa ca phalanti sakko pucchati.

Sakka asks: “O devatā, by what kamma is it that you have such a complexion, such power, such radiance? O devatā, whatever enjoyments you desire in your mind, by what kamma do those enjoyments arise? O devatā, questioned by me, please explain this: of what kamma is all this the fruit?”

Devarājena pucchitā sā devadhītā attamanā hutvā pañhaṃ puṭṭhā sakkassa byākāsi. Devarājā addhānaṃ dīghamaggaṃ paṭipannā ahaṃ yasassino kassapassa bhagavato manoramaṃ thūpaṃ addassaṃ, disvā tattha thūpe cittaṃ pasādesiṃ. Pasannāhaṃ sehi pāṇīhi padumapupphehi pūjesiṃ. Tasseva kammassa idaṃ sabbaṃ phalaṃ vipāko bhave. Katapuññāhaṃ etādisaṃ phalaṃ alabhinti sakkassa byākāsi. Iti me sutanti mahāmoggallāno vadatīti yojanā.

Questioned by the king of the devas, that devatā, being pleased, answered the question put to her by Sakka: “O king of devas, while traveling a long road, I saw the delightful stūpa of the glorious Blessed One Kassapa. Having seen it, I made my mind confident toward that stūpa. With a confident mind, I worshipped it with lotus flowers in my own hands. This is all the fruit and result of that very kamma. Having made merit, I obtained such a result.” Thus she answered Sakka. “Thus have I heard”—this is the connection, as spoken by Mahāmoggallāna.

“Yathāniddhāritasuttāniyeva [M 0.0294] vāsanābhāgiyasuttāni paripuṇṇānī”ti vattabbattā “dānakathā sīlakathā saggakathā puññakathā puññavipākakathāti idaṃ vāsanābhāgiya”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha yāya desanāya dānañca dānaphalañca dassitaṃ, sā desanā dānakathā nāma. Yāya desanāya sīlañca sīlaphalañca dassitaṃ, sā desanā sīlakathā nāma. Yāya desanāya saggā ca saggesu nibbattāpakañca kammaṃ dassitaṃ, sā saggakathā nāma. Yāya desanāya dānasīlabhāvanādivasena dasavidhaṃ puññakammaṃ dassitaṃ, sā puññakathā nāma. Yāya desanāya tādisassa puññakammassa vividho ayaṃ vipāko imassa puññassa vipākoti niyametvā dassito, sā puññavipākakathā nāma.

Since it should be said: “The fully complete discourses are precisely the discourses connected with past dispositions as defined,” it is therefore said: “The talk on giving, the talk on virtuous behavior, the talk on heaven, the talk on merit, the talk on the result of merit—this is what is connected with past dispositions.” Herein, the teaching by which giving and the fruit of giving are shown is called the talk on giving.
