The teaching by which virtuous behavior and the fruit of virtuous behavior are shown is called the talk on virtuous behavior. The teaching by which the heavens and the kamma that leads to rebirth in the heavens are shown is called the talk on heaven. The teaching by which the tenfold meritorious kamma is shown by way of giving, virtuous behavior, mental development, and so on, is called the talk on merit. The teaching by which the diverse result of such meritorious kamma is shown by defining it—“This is the result of this merit”—is called the talk on the result of merit.

Dasabaladharānaṃ sammāsambuddhānaṃ uddissakatesu sarīradhātuṃ abbhantare ṭhapetvā paṃsūhi katesu thūpesu ye narā pasannā, te narā tattha thūpe kāraṃ puññaṃ katvā saggesu uppajjitvā pamodantīti yojanā. Idaṃ suttaṃ vā…pe… suttaṃ.

When bodily relics of the Perfectly Self-Enlightened Ones, the possessors of the ten powers, have been placed inside stūpas made of earth and dedicated to them, those people who are confident, having performed a meritorious act of veneration at that stūpa, are reborn in the heavens and rejoice. This is the connection. This discourse… the discourse.

97. Devaputtasarīravaṇṇā devaputtasarīrasadisavaṇṇā subhagasaṇṭhiti sobhaggayuttasaṇṭhānā sabbe janā udakena paṃsuṃ temetvā thūpaṃ vaḍḍhetha, so ayaṃ thūpo kassa puggalassa thūpoti pucchati.

97. “With complexions like those of devaputtas, with beautiful builds, endowed with fortunate forms, all you people should moisten the earth with water and enlarge the stūpa.” He asks: “This stūpa, whose stūpa is it?”

Sugatte sundaragatte devate tasmiṃ thūpe pasannā ime devamanujā kāraṃ puññaṃ karontā hutvā jarāmaraṇato [V 0.0413] pamuccare. So ayaṃ thūpo mahesino dasabaladhammadhārino sugatassa thūpoti veditabboti āhāti yojanā. Idaṃ suttaṃ vā…pe… suttaṃ.

He says: “O devatā of beautiful form, of lovely body, these devas and humans, being confident toward that stūpa and performing a meritorious act of veneration, are freed from aging and death. This stūpa should be known as the stūpa of the Great Sage, the possessor of the ten powers, the bearer of the Dhamma, the Well-Farer.” This is the connection. This discourse… the discourse.

Yāhaṃ yā ahaṃ mahesino thūpaṃ cattāri uppalāni ca mālañca abhiropayiṃ, tena mayā kataṃ taṃ puññaṃ uḷāraṃ vata āsi ahosi. Tato kappato ajja kappā tiṃsaṃ dharanti satthuno thūpaṃ pūjetvā tattakāni duggatiṃ na jānāmi, vinipātaṃ na gacchāmīti yojanā. Idaṃ suttaṃ vā…pe… suttaṃ.

“I offered four water lilies and a garland at the stūpa of the Great Sage. That merit made by me was truly magnificent! It has been thirty aeons since that aeon. Having worshipped the Teacher’s stūpa, for all that time I have not known a bad destination; I do not go to the plane of misery.” This is the connection. This discourse… the discourse.

Ahaṃ bāttiṃsalakkhaṇadharassa bāttiṃsalakkhaṇadharena sampannassa vijitavijayassa lokanāthassa thūpaṃ apūjesiṃ, pūjetvā satasahassaṃ kappe āyukappe pamudito āsiṃ. Mayā yaṃ puññaṃ pasutaṃ, tena puññena vinipātaṃ anāgantuna anāgantvā devasobhaggaṃ sampattiṃ ca devarajjāni ca tāni akāriṃ[M 0.0295]. Atha vā devasobhaggañca mayā kāritaṃ, rajjāni ca mayā kāritāni.

“I worshipped the stūpa of the Protector of the World, the victorious conqueror, the bearer of the thirty-two marks, endowed with them. Having worshipped it, I rejoiced for a hundred thousand world-cycles. By the merit I generated, not having gone to the plane of misery, I brought about divine beauty, fortune, and the kingdoms of the devas. Or rather, divine beauty was brought about by me, and kingdoms were brought about by me.”

Adantadamakassa sāsane yaṃ cakkhu paññācakkhu paṇihitaṃ, tathā cittaṃ yaṃ vimuttacittaṃ paṇihitaṃ, taṃ sabbaṃ paññācakkhu vimuttacittaṃ me mayā laddhaṃ, ahaṃ vidhutalatāsaṅkhātataṇhā hutvā vimuttacittā phalavimuttacittasampannā amhīti avocāti yojanā. Idaṃ suttaṃ vā…pe… suttaṃ.

“In the teaching of the Tamer of the untamed, the eye that is the wisdom-eye was directed, and so the mind that is the liberated mind was directed. All that—the wisdom-eye and the liberated mind—has been obtained by me. Having shaken off craving, which is reckoned as a creeper, I am one with a liberated mind, endowed with the mind of fruition-liberation.” Thus she spoke. This is the connection. This discourse… the discourse.

98. Vimuttacitte phalavimuttacittasampanne akhile pañcacetokhīlarahite anāsave araṇavihārimhi araṇavihārasīle asaṅgamānase alaggamānase paccekabuddhasmiṃ sāmākapatthodanamattameva dakkhiṇaṃ adāsiṃ.

98. To a Paccekabuddha—one with a liberated mind, endowed with the mind of fruition-liberation, flawless, devoid of the five mental barrennesses, taintless, dwelling in a conflict-free abiding, of conflict-free conduct, with an unattached mind, with an unadhering mind—I gave a gift consisting only of a measure of millet gruel.

Tasmiṃ paccekabuddhe uttamaṃ dhammaṃ paccekabodhidhammaṃ okappayiṃ “so uttamo dhammo atthī”ti saddahiṃ. Evaṃ ariyavihārena vihārīhi paccekabuddhehi me mama saṅgamo kato siyā bhave, kudāsupi ca ahaṃ apekkhavā mā bhaveyyanti mānasaṃ tasmiñca dhamme paṇidhesiṃ “iminā paccekabuddhena laddhadhammaṃ ahampi sacchikareyya”nti cittaṃ paṇidahiṃ.

I placed faith in the supreme Dhamma of that Paccekabuddha, the Dhamma of an individual Buddha’s enlightenment, believing: “That supreme Dhamma exists.” I made an aspiration: “Thus may I have an encounter with Paccekabuddhas who dwell in the noble abiding, and may I never be one with longing.” And I directed my mind toward that Dhamma, aspiring: “May I too realize the Dhamma obtained by this Paccekabuddha.”

Tasseva paccekabuddhe katasseva kammassa vipākato ahaṃ dīghāyukesu amamesu “mama pariggaho”ti pariggahābhāvena apariggahesu visesagāmīsu ahīnagāmīsu kurūsu uttarakurūsu pāṇīsu sattesu sahassakkhattuṃ upapajjatha upapajjiṃ.

As the result of that very kamma done towards that Paccekabuddha, I was reborn a thousand times among the beings in Uttarakuru—long-lived, without possessiveness, that is, free from the notion “this is my possession,” who have attained distinction, who have not declined.

Tasseva [V 0.0414] kammassa vipākato vicitramālābharaṇānulepīsu yasassīsu parivāravantesu tidaso devo ahaṃ visiṭṭhakāyūpagato hutvā sahassakkhattuṃ upapajjatha.

As the result of that very kamma, I was reborn a thousand times as a deva among the Thirty-three, having attained a distinguished body, adorned with diverse garlands, ornaments, and ointments, renowned, and possessing a retinue.

Tasseva kammassa vipākato ahaṃ vimuttacitto akhīlo anāsavo hutvā hitāhitāsīhi kusalākusalavītivattehi antimadehadhāribhi imehi paccekabuddhehi, buddhasāvakehi vā me mama samāgamo āsi.

As the result of that very kamma, I, having become one with a liberated mind, flawless, and taintless, had an encounter with these Paccekabuddhas or disciples of the Buddha, who have gone beyond the beneficial and the unbeneficial, who have transcended the skillful and the unskillful, and who are bearers of their final bodies.

“Sīlavato yaṃ icchitaṃ, taṃ samijjhate”ti imaṃ vacanaṃ tathāgato jino paccakkhaṃ katvā avaca kho, yathā yathā yena yena pakārena me manasā vicintitaṃ, tathā tathā tena tena pakārena samiddhaṃ bhavati. Ayaṃ bhavo antimo bhavoti yojanā. Idaṃ suttaṃ vā…pe… suttaṃ.

“‘Whatever a virtuous person wishes, that succeeds for him.’ The Tathāgata, the Victor, having realized this for himself, indeed spoke this utterance: ‘In whatever way it was conceived by my mind, in that very way it succeeded. This existence is the final existence.’ This is the connection. This discourse… the discourse.

Ekatiṃsamhi [M 0.0296] kappamhi jino anejo anantadassī “sikhī”ti itināmako uppajji. Tassāpi bhagavato rājā bhātā sikhiddhe ca sikhī itināmake buddhe ca tassa bhagavato dhamme ca abhippasanno lokavināyakamhi parinibbute sati devātidevassa naruttamassa mahesino vipulaṃ mahantaṃ samantato gāvutikaṃ thūpaṃ akāsiṃ.

Thirty-one aeons ago, the Victor arose, the Imperturbable, the Infinite Seer named Sikhī. I was a king’s brother, confident in the Buddha named Sikhī, in Sikhiddha, and in the Dhamma of that Blessed One. When the Leader of the World attained Parinibbāna, I constructed a vast and great stūpa, a gāvuta all around, for the deva of devas, the supreme among men, the Great Sage.

Tasmiṃ thūpe baliṃ pūjābaliṃ abhihārī manusso jātisumanaṃ paggayha pahaṭṭho pūjesi. Assa manussassa ekaṃ pupphaṃ vātena paharitaṃ hutvā patitaṃ. Ahaṃ taṃ patitaṃ ekaṃ pupphaṃ gahetvā tasseva pupphasāmikassa adāsiṃ.

At that stūpa, a man bringing offerings and sacrificial gifts, being delighted, raised a jasmine flower and worshipped. A flower belonging to this man was struck by the wind and fell. Taking that one fallen flower, I gave it back to the owner of that very flower.

So manusso pupphasāmiko abhippasannacitto hutvā maṃ “tvameva etaṃ ekaṃ pupphaṃ pūjā”ti adāsi. Dadāsīti ettha da-kāro āgamo. Ahaṃ taṃ ekaṃ pupphaṃ gahetvā buddhaṃ buddhaguṇaṃ punappunaṃ anussaranto yasmiṃ kappe abhiropayiṃ, tato kappato ajja kappā tiṃsaṃ ahesuṃ. Tesu kappesu duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, vinipātañca na gacchāmi, idaṃ phalaṃ thūpapūjāya phalanti avocāti yojanā. Idaṃ suttaṃ vā…pe… suttaṃ.

That man, the owner of the flowers, with a confident mind, gave it to me, saying: 'You yourself should offer this one flower.' Here, in 'dadāsi,' the 'da' is an augment. Taking that one flower and repeatedly recollecting the Buddha and the qualities of the Buddha, I made the offering in that aeon. From that aeon until today, thirty aeons have passed. In those aeons I have known no bad destination, nor have I gone to the plane of misery. 'This is the fruit of worshiping a stūpa,' he spoke thus. This is the connection. This sutta... the sutta.

Brahmadattassa brahmadattanāmakassa rājino kapilaṃ nāma nagaraṃ suvibhattaṃ bhāgato suṭṭhu vibhattaṃ, mahāpathaṃ mahāpathasampannaṃ ākiṇṇaṃ, nānājātikehi manussehi paripuṇṇaṃ, iddhaṃ phītañca āsi.

The city named Kapila, belonging to King Brahmadatta, was well-divided into sections, endowed with great roads, crowded, filled with people of various kinds, and it was prosperous and flourishing.

Pañcālānaṃ [V 0.0415] tattha puruttame ahaṃ kummāsaṃ vikkiṇiṃ, so ahaṃ yasassinaṃ upariṭṭhaṃ upasamīpe ṭhitaṃ ariṭṭhaṃ nāma sambuddhaṃ paccekabuddhaṃ addasiṃ, disvā haṭṭho cittaṃ pasādetvā naruttamaṃ ariṭṭhaṃ me gehasmiṃ yaṃ dhuvabhattaṃ vijjatha vijji, tena dhuvabhattena nimantesiṃ.

There in the chief city of the Pañcālas, I was selling curd-cakes. I saw the glorious Paccekabuddha named Ariṭṭha standing nearby. Having seen him, I was joyful and my mind became confident, and I invited that supreme man, Ariṭṭha, with whatever regular meal was available in my house.

Yato ca yasmiṃ kāle ca kattiko yassaṃ pannarasīpuṇṇo, sā puṇṇamāsī pannarasī upaṭṭhitā, tato ca tasmiṃ kāle ca ahaṃ navaṃ dussayugaṃ gayha ariṭṭhassa ariṭṭhanāmakassa paccekabuddhassa upanāmesiṃ.

And when the time came, when the fifteenth full moon day of the month Kattika had arrived, then at that time, taking a new pair of cloths, I presented them to the Paccekabuddha named Ariṭṭha.

Naruttamo anukampako kāruṇiko taṇhānighātako muni paccekabuddho pasannacittaṃ maṃ ñatvāna paṭiggaṇhi.

That supreme man, the compassionate and merciful sage, the Paccekabuddha, the destroyer of craving, knowing that my mind was confident, accepted it.

Ahaṃ [M 0.0297] kalyāṇaṃ buddhavaṇṇitaṃ kammaṃ karitvāna deve ca manusse ca sandhāvitvā tato cuto bārāṇasiyaṃ nagare aḍḍhe kulasmiṃ seṭṭhissa ekaputtako uppajjiṃ, pāṇehi ca piyataro āsiṃ.

Having performed a good deed praised by the Buddha, I transmigrated among devas and humans. Passing away from there, I was reborn in the city of Bārāṇasī in the wealthy family of a guild-master as their only son, and I was dearer to them than their own lives.

Tato ca tasmiṃ kāle viññutaṃ patto hutvā devaputtena codito ahaṃ pāsādā oruhitvāna sambuddhaṃ bhagavantaṃ gotamaṃ upasaṅkamiṃ.

Then, at that time, having reached the age of discretion and being urged on by a devaputta, I descended from the palace and approached the Blessed One, the Enlightened One, Gotama.

So sambuddho bhagavā gotamo anukampāya me dhammaṃ adesesi. Dukkhaṃ dukkhasaccañca dukkhasamuppādaṃ samudayasaccañca dukkhassa atikkamaṃ nirodhasaccañca ariyaṃ aṭṭhaṅgikaṃ dukkhūpasamagāminaṃ maggaṃ maggasaccañca iti cattāri saccāni desitāni, taduppādakaṃ dhammaṃ muni bhagavā gotamo adesayi.

Out of compassion, that Enlightened One, the Blessed One Gotama, taught me the Dhamma. He taught the four truths: suffering, the truth of suffering; the origin of suffering, the truth of origin; the overcoming of suffering, the truth of cessation; and the noble eightfold path leading to the appeasement of suffering, the truth of the path. The sage, the Blessed One Gotama, taught the Dhamma that gives rise to this.

Ahaṃ tassa bhagavato gotamassa vacanaṃ sutvā sāsane rato hutvā vihariṃ, ahaṃ rattindivaṃ atandito hutvā samathaṃ paṭivijjhiṃ.

Having heard the word of the Blessed One Gotama, I dwelt delighting in his Dispensation. Day and night, being unwearied, I penetrated serenity.

Ajjhattañca ye āsavā, bahiddhā ca ye āsavā maggena samucchinnā āsuṃ, sabbe te āsavā me mama vijjiṃsu, puna na ca uppajjare.

The taints that are internal and the taints that are external have been cut off by the path. I have understood all those taints of mine, and they will not arise again.

Dukkhaṃ “pariyantakataṃ yassa dukkhassā”ti pariyantakataṃ āsi, ayaṃ samussayo jātimaraṇasaṃsāro [V 0.0416] carimo antimo āsi, idāni imassa attabhāvassa anantaraṃ punabbhavo mama natthīti avocāti yojanā. Yaṃ nānāvidhaṃ vāsanābhāgiyaṃ suttaṃ udāharaṇavasena niddhāritaṃ, idaṃ nānāvidhaṃ suttaṃ vāsanābhāge puññakoṭṭhāse visaye vācakañāpakabhāvena pavattanato vāsanābhāgiyaṃ suttaṃ nāma.

Suffering was made to have an end—as in 'for whom suffering has been made to have an end'—it was made to have an end. This heap, this saṃsāra of birth and death, was the last, the final one. 'Now, after this present existence, there is no further becoming for me'—he spoke thus. This is the connection. The various suttas pertaining to the portion of dispositions, which were set forth by way of example, are called 'Suttas Pertaining to the Portion of Dispositions' because these various suttas proceed in the domain of the portion of dispositions, in the section on merit, functioning to express and indicate.

Nānāvidhaṃ vāsanābhāgiyaṃ suttaṃ ācariyena niddhāritaṃ, amhehi ca ñātaṃ, “katamaṃ nibbedhabhāgiyaṃ sutta”nti pucchitabbattā “tattha katamaṃ nibbedhabhāgiyaṃ sutta”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha tesu soḷasasu saṃkilesabhāgiyādīsu suttesu katamaṃ suttaṃ nibbedhabhāgiyaṃ suttaṃ nāmāti pucchati.

The various suttas pertaining to the portion of dispositions have been set forth by the teacher and understood by us. Since the question 'Which is the sutta pertaining to the portion of penetration?' is to be asked, the passage beginning 'Now, which is the sutta pertaining to the portion of penetration?' was stated. Therein, among those sixteen suttas beginning with those pertaining to the portion of defilement, he asks which sutta is called the 'sutta pertaining to the portion of penetration.'

Uddhaṃ brahmaloke adho kāmāvacare bhave sabbadhi sabbesu bhavesu vippamutto arahā “ayaṃ nāma dhammo ahaṃ asmī”ti anānupassī, evaṃ vimutto arahā atiṇṇapubbaṃ oghaṃ apunabbhavāya udatāri uttiṇṇoti yojanā. Idaṃ suttaṃ nibbedhabhāge sekkhadhamme visaye vācakañāpakabhāvena pavattanato nibbedhabhāgiyaṃ suttaṃ nāma.

The arahant is liberated everywhere in all kinds of becoming—above, in the Brahma-world, and below, in the sphere of sensual existence. He does not contemplate, 'I am this so-called Dhamma.' The arahant, thus liberated, has crossed over, has gone beyond the flood not crossed before, for the sake of no further becoming. This is the connection. This sutta is called a 'sutta pertaining to the portion of penetration' because it proceeds in the domain of the learner's qualities, in the section on penetration, functioning to express and indicate.

“Ettakamevā”ti [M 0.0298] vattabbattā “sīlavato”tiādi vuttaṃ. Ānanda, sīlavato puggalassa “kinti me mama avippaṭisāro jāyeyya pavatteyyā”ti cetanā na karaṇīyā na kātabbā. Ānanda, sīlavato avippaṭisāro yaṃ jāyeyya pavatteyya, esā avippaṭisārassa jāyanā pavattanā dhammatā bhavati. Ānanda, avippaṭisārinā puggalena “kinti me mama pāmojjaṃ jāyeyya pavatteyyā”ti cetanā na karaṇīyā, ānanda, avippaṭisārino puggalassa pāmojjaṃ yaṃ jāyeyya pavatteyya, esā pāmojjassa jāyanā pavattanā dhammatā. Sesesupi imassa yojanānayānusārena yojanānayo gahetabbo. Idaṃ suttampi nibbedhabhāgiyaṃ suttaṃ nāma.

Because it should be said, 'It is just this much,' the passage beginning 'For a virtuous person' was stated. 'Ānanda, a virtuous person need not form the intention: “Oh, that non-remorse might arise in me!” It is natural, Ānanda, that non-remorse arises in a virtuous person. Ānanda, a person free from remorse need not form the intention: “Oh, that joy might arise in me!” It is natural, Ānanda, that joy arises in a person free from remorse.' The method of connection for the remaining items should be understood in accordance with this method. This sutta, too, is called a 'sutta pertaining to the portion of penetration.'

Ātāpino kilesānaṃ ātāpena sammappadhānena samannāgatassa jhāyato jhāyantassa brāhmaṇassa bāhitapāpassa khīṇāsavassa dhammā anulomapaccayākārapaṭivedhasādhakā bodhipakkhiyadhammā yadā yasmiṃ kāle have ekantena pātubhavanti uppajjanti. Atha vā dhammā catuariyasaccadhammā pātubhavanti pakāsayanti abhisamayavasena pākaṭā honti. Atha vā pātubhavanakāle assa ātāpino jhāyato brāhmaṇassa khīṇāsavassa sabbā kaṅkhā vapayanti apagacchanti nirujjhanti. Kasmā? Sahetudhammaṃ avijjādikena hetunā saha pavattaṃ saṅkhārādikaṃ sukhena asammissaṃ dukkhakkhandhadhammaṃ yato yasmā pajānāti aññāsi paṭivijjhati[V 0.0417], tato tasmā vapayanti apagacchanti nirujjhantīti yojanā. Idaṃ suttaṃ nibbedhabhāgiyaṃ suttaṃ nāma.

When for the ardent, meditating brahmin—one endowed with right striving, the ardour that burns up the defilements, who has dispelled evil and destroyed the taints—the dhammas, that is, the requisites of enlightenment that bring about penetration in conformity with the causal structure, become manifest, then... Or: the dhammas, that is, the Four Noble Truths, become manifest, are revealed, and become clear through comprehension. Or: at the time of their manifestation, all doubts of that ardent, meditating brahmin whose taints are destroyed are dispelled, they depart and cease. Why? Because he fully understands, has known, and penetrates the Dhamma together with its cause—that is, the mass of suffering consisting of formations, etc., which proceeds along with its cause, ignorance, etc., and is unmixed with pleasure—therefore they are dispelled, they depart and cease. This is the connection. This sutta is called a 'sutta pertaining to the portion of penetration.'

Dutiyagāthāyaṃ pana paccayānaṃ khayaṃ khayasaṅkhātaṃ nibbānaṃ yato yasmā avedi aññāsi paṭivijjhi, tato tasmā sabbāpi kaṅkhā vapayantīti yojanā. Idaṃ suttaṃ nibbedhabhāgiyaṃ suttaṃ.

But in the second verse, because he has understood, known, and penetrated the destruction of conditions—that is, Nibbāna, which is designated as destruction—therefore all his doubts are dispelled. This is the connection. This sutta is a sutta pertaining to the portion of penetration.

Tissa, tvaṃ kiṃ nu kujjhasi? Mā kujjhi, tissa, te tava akkodho akujjhanaṃ varaṃ uttamaṃ, hi saccaṃ, tissa, tayā kodhamānamakkhavinayatthaṃ brahmacariyaṃ vussati nūti bhagavā avocāti yojanā.

'Tissa, why now are you angry? Do not be angry, Tissa. For you non-anger is better. Indeed, Tissa, is not the holy life lived by you for the purpose of removing anger, conceit, and contempt?' the Blessed One said. This is the connection.

Āraññaṃ āraññakaṃ paṃsukūlikaṃ aññātuñchena aññātaanabhilakkhitagharapaṭipāṭiyā ṭhatvā uñchena piṇḍapātacaraṇavīriyena laddhena missakabhojanena yāpentaṃ nandaṃ kadā kāle ahaṃ passeyyanti avocāti yojanā. Idaṃ suttaṃ nibbedhabhāgiyaṃ suttaṃ.

'When will I see Nanda, dwelling in the forest, a forest-dweller, a wearer of rag-robes, who maintains himself on mixed food obtained by the effort of going for alms by gleaning from unknown and unmarked houses?' he spoke thus. This is the connection. This sutta is a sutta pertaining to the portion of penetration.

Gotama[M 0.0299], kiṃsu katamaṃ chetvā vadhitvā vadhanto kodhapariḷāhena aparidayhamāno hutvā sukhaṃ seti sayati, kiṃsu katamaṃ chetvā vadhitvā vadhanto kodhavināsena vinaṭṭhadomanasso hutvā na socati, gotama, tvaṃ kissa ekadhammassa vadhaṃ vadhanaṃ rocesīti brāhmaṇo pucchati.

The brahmin asks: 'Gotama, having slain what does one sleep happily, not being tormented by the fever of anger? Having slain what does one not sorrow, with dejection vanished by the destruction of anger? Gotama, the slaying of what one thing do you approve of?'

Brāhmaṇa, kodhaṃ kujjhanaṃ chetvā vadhitvā vadhanto kodhapariḷāhena aparidayhamāno hutvā sukhaṃ seti sayati, kodhaṃ kujjhanaṃ chetvā vadhitvā vadhanto kodhavināsena vinaṭṭhadomanasso hutvā na socati, visamūlassa visasadisassa dukkhassa mūlabhūtassa madhuraggassa madhurasaṅkhātassa sukhapariyosānassa kodhassa kujjhanassa vadhaṃ vadhanaṃ ariyā buddhādayo puggalā pasaṃsanti. Hi saccaṃ taṃ kodhaṃ kujjhanaṃ chetvā vadhitvā vadhanto kodhavināsena vinaṭṭhadomanasso hutvā seti sayatīti yojanā. Madhuraggassāti ca madhuraṃ cetasikasukhaṃ assādaaggaṃ pariyosānaṃ assa kodhassāti madhuraggoti samāso veditabbo. Kujjhantassa hi akkositvā paribhāsitvā paharitvā pariyosāne cetasikasukhassādo uppajjatīti. Idaṃ suttaṃ nibbedhabhāgiyaṃ suttaṃ.

'Brahmin, having slain anger one sleeps happily. Having slain anger one does not sorrow. The noble ones praise the slaying of anger, which has a poisoned root and a honeyed tip. For indeed, having slain that anger, one sleeps happily.' This is the connection. And 'honeyed tip' should be understood as a compound: anger has a sweet mental pleasure as its foremost taste and culmination. For when one is angry, after reviling, abusing, and striking, a taste of mental pleasure arises at the end. This sutta is a sutta pertaining to the portion of penetration.

Gotama, hananto dhīro uppatitaṃ kiṃsu katamaṃ hane haneyya. Vinodento dhīro jātaṃ kiṃsu [V 0.0418] katamaṃ vinodaye vinodayeyya. Pajahanto dhīro kiṃ ca katamaṃ pajahe pajaheyya. Dhīrassa kissa dhammassa abhisamayo sukhoti devatā pucchati.

The devatā asks: ‘Gotama, slaying what arisen thing should a wise person slay? Dispelling what born thing should one dispel? And what should one abandon? For a wise person, the realization of what dhamma is happiness?’” }, {

Devaputta, hananto dhīro uppatitaṃ kodhaṃ kujjhanaṃ hane haneyya. Vinodento dhīro jātaṃ rāgaṃ vinodaye vinodayeyya. Pajahanto dhīro avijjaṃ pajahe pajaheyya. Saccadhammassa abhisamayo sukhoti bhagavā avocāti yojanā. Idaṃ suttaṃ nibbedhabhāgiyaṃ suttaṃ.

The Blessed One said: ‘Devaputta, a wise person should slay arisen anger. A wise person should dispel born lust. A wise person should abandon ignorance. The realization of the true Dhamma is happiness.’ This is the connection. This sutta is one pertaining to penetration.

101. Bhagavā sattiyā omaṭṭho uparito yāva heṭṭhā viddho puriso sattippahānāya vīriyaṃ ārabhati viya, agginā matthake ḍayhamāno ādittasiro puriso agginibbāpanatthāya vīriyaṃ ārabhati iva, evaṃ kāmarāgena ḍayhamāno bhikkhu kāmarāgappahānāya kāmarāgavikkhambhanāya appamatto vāyamamāno sato satisampanno hutvā paribbaje vihareyyāti devatā kathesi.

101. The devatā said: ‘Just as a man struck by a spear, pierced from above down to below, arouses energy to remove the spear, or as a man with his head ablaze arouses energy to extinguish the fire, so too a bhikkhu burning with sensual passion should strive diligently, mindful and clearly comprehending, for the abandoning and suppression of sensual passion; he should wander and dwell.’

Bhagavā [M 0.0300] pana “samucchedappahānāya vīriyaṃ ārabhīyatī”ti dassetuṃ “sattiyā viya omaṭṭho”tiādimāha. Devaputta, sattiyā omaṭṭho puriso sattippahānāya vīriyaṃ ārabhati viya, agginā matthake ḍayhamāno ādittasiro puriso agginibbāpanatthāya vīriyaṃ ārabhati iva, evaṃ sakkāyadiṭṭhiyā abhibhūto bhikkhu sakkāyadiṭṭhiyā pahānāya maggena samucchedappahānāya appamatto vāyamamāno sato satisampanno hutvā paribbaje vihareyyāti bhagavā avocāti yojanā. Idaṃ suttaṃ nibbedhabhāgiyaṃ suttaṃ nāma.

The Blessed One, however, in order to show that ‘energy is to be aroused for abandonment by eradication,’ spoke the verse beginning ‘As if struck by a spear.’ He said: ‘Devaputta, just as a man struck by a spear arouses energy to remove the spear, or as a man with his head ablaze arouses energy to extinguish the fire, so too a bhikkhu overcome by identity view, for the abandonment of identity view by means of the path, for its abandonment by eradication, should strive diligently, mindful and clearly comprehending; he should wander and dwell.’ This is the connection. This sutta is called one pertaining to penetration.

Sabbe nicayā bhogā khayantā khayapariyosānā bhavanti, sabbe samussayā dhammā patanantā patanapariyosānā bhavanti, sabbesaṃ sattānaṃ maraṇamāgamma sabbesaṃ sattānaṃ jīvitaṃ addhuvaṃ bhavati, iti etaṃ vuttappakāraṃ bhayaṃ bhayahetuṃ maraṇaṃ sammutimaraṇaṃ apekkhamāno paṇḍito sukhāvahāni diṭṭhadhammikasamparāyikasukhāvahāni puññāni dānasīlabhāvanāmayapuññāni kayirāthāti devatā avoca.

The devatā said: ‘All accumulations of wealth end in destruction; all things built up end in falling. Life for all beings culminates in death; life is impermanent. Considering this declared fear, this cause of fear, this death—conventional death—a wise person should perform meritorious deeds that bring happiness in this life and the next: meritorious deeds consisting of giving, virtuous behavior, and mental development.’

Devaputta, sabbe nicayā bhogā khayantā khayapariyosānā, sabbe samussayā dhammā patanantā patanapariyosānā, sabbesaṃ sattānaṃ maraṇamāgamma sabbesaṃ sattānaṃ jīvitaṃ addhuvaṃ, iti etaṃ vuttappakāraṃ bhayaṃ bhayahetuṃ maraṇaṃ apekkhamāno santipekkho sabbasaṅkhārupasamaṃ nibbānaṃ apekkhamāno [V 0.0419] paṇḍito lokāmisaṃ kāmaguṇaṃ pajahe pajaheyyāti bhagavā avocāti yojanā. Idaṃ suttaṃ nibbedhabhāgiyaṃ suttaṃ nāma.

The Blessed One said: ‘Devaputta, all accumulations of wealth end in destruction; all things built up end in falling. Life for all beings culminates in death; life is impermanent. Considering this declared fear, this cause of fear, this death, a wise person, seeking peace, seeking Nibbāna, the stilling of all formations, should abandon the world’s bait, the strands of sensual pleasure.’ This is the connection. This sutta is called one pertaining to penetration.

Māvidha yesaṃ munīnaṃ cittaṃ jhānarataṃ jhāne rataṃ hoti, te munayo sukhaṃ sayanti na socanti. Paññavā maggapaññavā susamāhito āraddhavīriyo pahitatto nibbānaṃ pesitacitto puggalo duttaraṃ oghaṃ saṃsāroghaṃ tarati.

Let there be no agitation here for those sages whose minds delight in jhāna. Those sages sleep happily and do not grieve. The wise person, endowed with the wisdom of the path, well-concentrated, with aroused energy and resolute mind, with a mind directed to Nibbāna, crosses the hard-to-cross flood, the flood of saṃsāra.

Kāmasaññāya virato vigatacitto yo khīṇāsavo sabbasaṃyojanātīto arahattamaggena sabbe saṃyojane atīto nandibhavaparikkhīṇo ahosi, so khīṇāsavo gambhīre saṃsāraṇṇave na sīdatīti yojanā. Nandisaṅkhātā taṇhā ca kāmabhavarūpabhavaarūpabhavā ca nandibhavā, nandibhavā parikkhīṇā yassa khīṇāsavassāti nandibhavaparikkhīṇoti samāso veditabbo. Idaṃ suttaṃ nibbedhabhāgiyaṃ suttaṃ nāma.

This is the connection: One who is detached from sensual perception, with mind aloof, a destroyer of taints who has gone beyond all fetters—having transcended all fetters by the path of arahantship—has become one for whom delight in existence is exhausted. That destroyer of taints does not sink in the deep ocean of saṃsāra. ‘Delight in existence’ refers to craving and the existences of the sensual realm, the form realm, and the formless realm. The compound ‘one for whom delight in existence is exhausted’ is to be understood thus: he is that destroyer of taints for whom delight in existence is exhausted. This sutta is called one pertaining to penetration.

Arahataṃ [M 0.0301] arahantānaṃ buddhapaccekabuddhasāvakānaṃ dhammaṃ sucaritādibhedañca sattatiṃsabodhipakkhiyabhedañca dhammaṃ yo paṇḍito saddahāno saddahanto hutvā nibbānappattiyā appamatto vicakkhaṇo hutvā sussūsaṃ sussūsanto bhave, so paṇḍito paññaṃ lokiyalokuttarapaññaṃ labhate labhati.

A wise person who, placing faith in the Dhamma of the Arahants—the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and their disciples—and in the Dhamma distinguished as good conduct and so on, and as the thirty-seven aids to enlightenment; who, for the sake of attaining Nibbāna, is diligent and discerning; and who wishes to listen and lends an ear—that wise person gains and obtains wisdom, both worldly and supramundane.

Yo vīriyavā puggalo patirūpadesakārī desakālādīni ahāpetvā lokiyalokuttaradhammapatirūpaṃ adhigamūpāyaṃ karoti, dhuravā cetasikavīriyena anikkhittadhuro uṭṭhātā kāyikavīriyavasena uṭṭhānasampanno hoti, so vīriyavā puggalo dhanaṃ lokiyalokuttaradhanaṃ vindate adhigacchati. Saccena vacīsaccena ca paramatthasaccena ca buddhādiko saccadhamme ṭhito sappuriso kittiṃ pappoti. Dadaṃ dadanto yaṃ kiñci icchitaṃ patthitaṃ catusaṅgahavatthuṃ dadanto saṅgahanto sappuriso mittāni ekantamittāni ganthati sampādeti, evaṃ catūhi saccadhammadhiticāgehi samannāgato so sappuriso asmā lokā paraṃ lokaṃ pecca gantvā ekantena sokakāraṇassa abhāvato na socatīti yojanā.

An energetic person who acts suitably, not neglecting such things as a suitable place and time, makes this the means for attaining what is fitting, both worldly and supramundane Dhamma. One is steadfast with mental energy, not shirking the burden; one is an exerter, accomplished in exertion by way of bodily energy. That energetic person finds and obtains wealth, both worldly and supramundane. By truth—both truth of speech and ultimate truth—a good person like the Buddha and others, established in the true Dhamma, obtains fame. Giving, constantly giving whatever is desired and wished for, giving and showing sympathy through the four bases of beneficence, a good person makes friends, steadfast friends. Thus, endowed with these four qualities—truth, Dhamma, fortitude, and relinquishment—that good person, having passed on from this world to the next, surely does not grieve, owing to the absence of any cause for sorrow. This is the connection.

Gotama, sabbaganthappahīno tīhi bhavehi vippamutto sato satisampanno tvaṃ, samaṇo, aññaṃ devamanussādikaṃ yaṃ anusāsasi yaṃ anusāsanaṃ karosi, taṃ anusāsanaṃ sabbaganthappahīnassa [V 0.0420] tīhi bhavehi vippamuttassa samaṇassa te tava na sādhūti sakkanāmako mārapakkhiko yakkho gāthāya ajjhabhāsi.

The yakkha named Sakka, a partisan of Māra, addressed him in verse: ‘Gotama, you have abandoned all ties, you are released from the three kinds of existence, mindful and aware. O recluse, you instruct others—devas, humans, and the like. Whatever instruction you give, that instruction is not good for you, a recluse who has abandoned all ties and is released from the three kinds of existence.’

“Sakka sakkanāmaka yakkha anukampitena purisena saddhiṃ yena kenaci vaṇṇena kāraṇena saṃvāso ekasmiṃ ṭhāne sahavāso jāyati, taṃ anukampitabbaṃ sahavāsagataṃ purisaṃ sappañño manasā anukampituṃ na arahati anukampituṃyeva arahati. Yā anukampā karuṇā, yā anuddayā mettā, muditā ca uppannā, tāya anukampāya karuṇāya, tāya anuddayāya mettāya muditāya ca samussāhitena pasannena manasā yo sappañño sappuriso aññaṃ devamanussādikaṃ yaṃ anusāsati yaṃ anusāsanaṃ karoti, so sappañño sappuriso tena anusāsanena saṃyutto kāmacchandādīnaṃ saṃyojanānaṃ vasena ananulomasaṃyogena saṃyutto na hotīti bhagavā avocāti yojanā.

The Blessed One said: ‘Sakka, yakkha, for whatever reason, association and living together in one place arises with a person who is to be shown compassion. Is it not fitting that a wise person should mentally feel compassion for that person who is to be shown compassion and with whom one lives? It is indeed fitting. Whatever compassion, sympathy, and gladness have arisen, spurred on by that compassion, sympathy, and gladness, with a confident mind, a wise and good person instructs another—a deva, human, or the like. Being connected with that instruction, that wise and good person is not yoked by an unsuitable connection through the fetters of sensual desire and so on.’ This is the connection.

102. Samaṇa[M 0.0302], rāgo ca doso ca ime dve dhammā kutonidānā, kiṃnidānā, kiṃpaccayā bhavanti, arati ca rati ca lomahaṃso ca ime tayo kutojā kuto bhavanti? Kumārakā dhaṅkaṃ kākaṃ gahetvā pāde dīghasuttakena bandhitvā suttakoṭiṃ aṅguliyaṃ veṭhetvā osajanti iva, evaṃ manovitakkā kuto samuṭṭhāya cittaṃ osajantīti sūcilomayakkho bhagavantaṃ pucchi.

102. The yakkha Sūciloma asked the Blessed One: ‘Recluse, from what source, what origin, what condition do these two things arise: lust and hatred? From where are these three born: discontent, delight, and horror? Just as boys, having caught a crow, tie its foot with a long string and let it go, from where do mental thoughts arise to assail the mind?’

Rāgo ca doso ca ime dve dhammā itonidānā ito attabhāvato nidānā jāyanti; arati ca rati ca lomahaṃso ca ime tayo itojā ito attato bhavanti; kumārakā dhaṅkaṃ kākaṃ gahetvā pāde dīghasuttakena bandhitvā suttakoṭiṃ aṅguliyaṃ veṭhetvā osajanti iva, evaṃ manovitakkā ito attabhāvato samuṭṭhāya cittaṃ osajanti.

‘Lust and hatred, these two things, have this as their source; they are born having this individual existence as their source. Discontent, delight, and horror, these three, are born from this; they arise from this self. Just as boys let go of a crow they have tied by the foot with a long string, so mental thoughts, arising from this individual existence, assail the mind.’

Nigrodhassa khandhajā pārohā sākhāsu jāyanti iva, vane rukkhaṃ nissāya jātā māluvā latā taṃ rukkhaṃ ajjhottharitvā vitatā otatavitatā tiṭṭhati iva, evaṃ, yakkha, tvaṃ suṇohi snehajā taṇhāsnehato jātā attasambhūtā attani sambhūtā puna anekappakārā manovitakkā pāpamanovitakkā ceva taṃsampayuttakilesā ca kāmesu vatthukāmesu visattā laggā saṃsibbitā ṭhitā.

‘Just as the trunk-born offshoots of a banyan tree grow from its branches, and as the māluvā creeper, born in the forest depending on a tree, stands having spread all over it, so too, yakkha, listen: those thoughts born of affection, born from the affection that is craving, self-arisen, produced in oneself—those manifold evil mental thoughts and their associated defilements—are attached to, cling to, and are enmeshed in sensual pleasures, the objects of sensuality.’

Ye paṇḍitā “yaṃ nidānaṃ assa attabhāvassā”ti yatonidānaṃ naṃ kilesagahanaṃ samudayasaccaṃ [V 0.0421] pajānanti, te paṇḍitā attabhāvasaṅkhātassa dukkhasaccassa nidānabhūtaṃ naṃ kilesagahanaṃ samudayasaccaṃ maggasaccena vinodenti. Apunabbhavāya apunabhavasaṅkhātāya nirodhasaccatthāya atiṇṇapubbaṃ anamatagge saṃsāre supinenāpi atiṇṇapubbaṃ duttaraṃ imaṃ oghaṃ catubbidhaṃ saṃkilesoghaṃ tarantīti bhagavā avocāti yojanā.

The Blessed One said: ‘Those wise ones who understand that thicket of defilements, the truth of the origin, as the source from which this individual existence arises—those wise ones dispel by the truth of the path that thicket of defilements, the truth of the origin, which is the source of the truth of suffering designated as individual existence. For the sake of non-becoming-again, for the purpose of the truth of cessation called non-becoming-again, they cross this hard-to-cross fourfold flood of defilements, never crossed before in beginningless saṃsāra, not even in a dream.’ This is the connection.

“Bhagavā, samaṇadhammassa karaṇaṃ nāma dukkaraṃ, bhagavā, samaṇadhammassa karaṇaṃ nāma sudukkaraṃ suṭṭhutaraṃ dukkara”nti eko kulaputto pabbajitvā samaṇadhammaṃ katvā ariyabhūmiṃ appatvā kālaṃ katvā devaloke nibbatto, so devaputto bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamitvā āha. Kāmada, sīlasamāhitā ṭhitattā ṭhitasabhāvā satta sekkhā puggalā dukkaraṃ vāpi samaṇadhammaṃ karonti. Anagāriyupetassa anagāriyaṃ niggehabhāvaṃ upagatassa pabbajitassa [M 0.0303] tuṭṭhi catupaccayasantoso sukhāvahā hotī”ti bhagavā avoca.

A certain clansman who had gone forth and practiced the ascetic's life, but passed away without reaching the noble stage and was reborn in the deva world, approached the Blessed One and said: "Blessed One, practicing the ascetic's life is difficult; Blessed One, practicing the ascetic's life is very difficult, exceedingly difficult." The Blessed One said: "Kāmada, established in virtue and concentration, firm in their state, the seven trainees practice the ascetic's life, difficult though it is. For one who has entered the homeless life, for one gone forth who has attained the state of being without a home, contentment with the four requisites brings happiness."

“Bhagavā, yadidaṃ yā esā tuṭṭhi sukhāvahā, esā tuṭṭhi dullabhā”ti so devaputto āha. “Kāmada, yesaṃ sekkhānaṃ mano divā ca ratto ca bhāvanāya rato cittavūpasame rato, te sekkhā dullabhaṃ vāpi tussanaṃ labhantī”ti bhagavā avoca.

"Blessed One, this contentment that brings happiness, this contentment is difficult to obtain," said that devaputta. The Blessed One said: "Kāmada, those trainees whose minds delight day and night in mental development, who delight in the calming of the mind—those trainees obtain that contentment, difficult though it is to obtain."

“Bhagavā, yadidaṃ yaṃ idaṃ cittaṃ bhāvanāya rataṃ, taṃ cittaṃ dussamādaha”nti so devaputto āha. “Kāmada, ye ariyā indriyūpasame rattindivaṃ ratā, te ariyā dussamādahaṃ vāpi cittaṃ samādahanti, kāmada, te ariyā maccuno jālaṃ kilesajālaṃ chetvā maggaṃ gacchantī”ti bhagavā avoca.

"Blessed One, this mind that delights in mental development, that mind is difficult to concentrate," said that devaputta. The Blessed One said: "Kāmada, those noble ones who delight day and night in the calming of the faculties, those noble ones concentrate the mind, even though it is difficult to concentrate. Kāmada, having cut through the net of Death, the net of defilements, those noble ones proceed along the path."

“Bhagavā, yo maggo pubbabhāgapaṭipadāvasena visamo, so maggo duggamo”ti so devaputto āha. “Kāmada, ariyā duggame visame vāpi maggaṃ gacchanti, anariyā visame magge avaṃsirā papatanti, ariyānaṃ so maggo samova bhave, na asamo. Hi saccaṃ visame visattakāye ariyā samā bhavantī”ti bhagavā avocāti yojanā.

"Blessed One, that path which is uneven by way of the preliminary practice, that path is difficult to traverse," said that devaputta. The Blessed One said: "Kāmada, the noble ones traverse a path that is difficult and uneven, but the ignoble fall headlong on an uneven path. For the noble ones that path becomes even, not uneven. For truly, though in an uneven body subject to attachment, the noble ones are even-minded." This is the connection.

103. Yaṃ jetavanaṃ isisaṅghanisevitaṃ dhammarājena āvutthaṃ, idaṃ taṃ jetavanaṃ mama pītisañjananaṃ pītiyā sañjananaṃ karaṃ hi karaṃ eva.

103. The Jetavana, frequented by the community of seers, inhabited by the King of Dhamma—this is that Jetavana, the generator of my joy, which creates delight, indeed, it creates it.

Kammaṃ maggacetanākammañca vijjā maggapaññā ca dhammo samādhi ceva samādhipakkhiko ca [V 0.0422] dhammo sīlaṃ, sīle ṭhitassa jīvitaṃ uttamaṃ, etena aṭṭhaṅgikena maggena sattā sujjhanti, gottena vā dhanena vā sattā na sujjhanti.

Kamma is the kamma of path-volition; knowledge is the wisdom of the path; Dhamma is concentration and the things pertaining to concentration; and virtue. For one established in virtue, life is supreme. It is by this Eightfold Path that beings are purified, not by clan or by wealth.

Tasmā maggeneva sattānaṃ visujjhanato attano atthaṃ sampassaṃ passanto paṇḍito poso yoniso upāyena dhammaṃ bodhipakkhiyadhammaṃ vicine vicineyya, evaṃ vicinane sati tattha ariyamagge vicinanto puggalo sujjhati.

Therefore, since beings are purified only by the path, a wise person, seeing his own good, should wisely and methodically investigate the Dhamma, the requisites of enlightenment. When one investigates in this way, by investigating the noble path a person is purified.

Sāriputto sīlena ca upasamena ca pāraṅgato iva, evaṃ yopi bhikkhu sīlena ca upasamena ca pāraṅgato, so bhikkhu etāva paramo sāriputtasadisova siyāti anāthapiṇḍikanāmo devaputto bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamitvā āhāti yojanā. Idaṃ suttaṃ nibbedhabhāgiyaṃ suttaṃ nāma.

“Sāriputta has, as it were, gone to the far shore through virtue and peace. So too, any bhikkhu who has gone to the far shore through virtue and peace would be supreme to that extent, just like Sāriputta.” Thus spoke the devaputta named Anāthapiṇḍika, having approached the Blessed One. This is called the Sutta Pertaining to Penetration.

Atītaṃ [M 0.0304] atītakkhandhapañcakaṃ taṇhādiṭṭhīhi nānvāgameyya, anāgataṃ anāgatakkhandhapañcakaṃ taṇhādiṭṭhīhi nappaṭikaṅkhe na pattheyya. Yaṃ yasmā atītaṃ pahīnaṃ niruddhaṃ atthaṅgataṃ, tasmā atītassa pahīnattā niruddhattā atthaṅgatattā nānvāgameyya. Yaṃ yasmā anāgataṃ appattaṃ, tasmā na paṭikaṅkhe.

One should not run back after the past—that is, the past five aggregates—with craving and views; one should not long for the future—that is, the future five aggregates—with craving and views. Since the past is abandoned, ceased, and has passed away, one should not run back after it. Since the future has not been attained, one should not long for it.

Paccuppannaṃ khandhapañcakaṃ vayadhammaṃ yattha yattha santāne vā, yattha yattha araññādīsu vā uppannaṃ, tattha tattha santāne vā, tattha tattha araññādīsu vā naṃ paccuppannadhammaṃ yāhi aniccānupassanādīhi vipassati, tāhi aniccānupassanādīhi nibbānaṃ rāgādīhi asaṃhīraṃ asaṃkuppaṃ bhavati, taṃ nibbānaṃ vipassako puggalo vidvā nibbānārammaṇaṃ phalasamāpattiṃ appento hutvā anubrūhaye vaḍḍheyya.

As to the present phenomenon—the five aggregates, which are subject to vanishing—wherever it has arisen, whether in one's own continuity or in the wilderness and so on, one should see it with insight, with contemplation of impermanence and so on. Through these contemplations of impermanence and so on, Nibbāna becomes unassailable and unshakable by lust and so on. Having known that Nibbāna, the insight meditator, entering upon the fruition attainment which has Nibbāna as its object, should cultivate and develop it.

Ātappaṃ saṃkilesānaṃ ātapantaṃ vīriyaṃ ajjeva kiccaṃ kātabbaṃ, suve jīvitaṃ vā maraṇaṃ vā ko jaññā jāneyya, “suve vā dānādipuññaṃ jānissāmī”ti cittaṃ anuppādetvā “ajjeva karissāmī”ti evaṃ vīriyaṃ kātabbaṃ. Hi saccaṃ maraṇakāraṇabhāvatāya ahivicchikavisasatthādianekāya senāya vasena mahāsenena tena maccunā saddhiṃ mittasanthavākārena vā lañjadānena vā saṅgaraṃ natthīti.

Ardor—the energy that burns up the defilements—is a task to be done today. Who knows whether tomorrow will bring life or death? One should not give rise to the thought, ‘Tomorrow I will make merit by giving, etc.,’ but should make the effort thinking, ‘I will do it today.’ For truly, there is no making an agreement with that great army, with Death, either by way of making friends or by giving a bribe, with its vast host of snakes, scorpions, poison, weapons, and so on, which are the causes of death.

Evaṃ [V 0.0423] manasi katvā vihāriṃ viharantaṃ ātāpiṃ ahorattaṃ atanditaṃ analasaṃ uṭṭhāhakaṃ sappurisaṃ “bhaddekaratto”ti santo muni ve ekantena ācikkhate ācikkhatiyevāti yojanā.

The peaceful sage unequivocally declares such a one to be ‘one who has a single auspicious night’: that good person who dwells thus ardently, tireless day and night, energetic and not lazy.

“Cattārimāni bhikkhave”tyādisuttaṃ pāḷito ca aṭṭhakathāto ca pākaṭaṃ.

The sutta beginning, “Bhikkhus, there are these four…” is evident from both the Pāli text and the commentary.

104. Nānāvidhaṃ nibbedhabhāgiyaṃ suttaṃ ācariyena niddhāritaṃ, amhehi ca ñātaṃ, “katamaṃ asekkhabhāgiyaṃ sutta”nti pucchitabbattā “tattha katamaṃ asekkhabhāgiyaṃ sutta”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Tatthāti tesu soḷasasu saṃkilesabhāgiyādīsu suttesu katamaṃ suttaṃ asekkhabhāgiyaṃ suttaṃ nāmāti pucchati.

104. Various suttas pertaining to penetration have been set forth by the teacher and understood by us. Since the question should be asked, “Which is the sutta pertaining to the one beyond training?” the text says, “Therein, which is the sutta pertaining to the one beyond training?” and so on. ‘Therein’ means: among those sixteen suttas beginning with the one pertaining to defilement, which sutta is called the sutta pertaining to the one beyond training? That is the question.

Yassa uttamapurisassa cittaṃ selūpamaṃ ṭhitaṃ lokadhammavātehi nānukampati, rajanīyesu lābhādīsu virattaṃ bhave, so uttamapuriso kopaneyye [M 0.0305] alābhādike na kuppati, tassa uttamapurisassa cittaṃ evaṃ aniccatādinā bhāvitaṃ, naṃ bhāvitacittaṃ uttamapurisaṃ vītikkantalokadhammahetukaṃ dukkhaṃ kuto essatīti yojanā. Idaṃ suttaṃ asekkhabhāge visaye vācakañāpakabhāvena pavattanato asekkhabhāgiyaṃ suttaṃ nāma. Esa nayo ito paresupi veditabbo.

The mind of that superior person stands firm like a rock, unshaken by the winds of worldly conditions. It is dispassionate towards enticing things such as gain, and that superior person is not angered by provoking things such as loss. For that superior person whose mind has been so developed by contemplating impermanence and so on, from where can suffering come, since he has transcended the causes of worldly conditions? This sutta is called one ‘pertaining to the one beyond training’ because it proceeds by way of expressing and making known the domain of the one beyond training. This same method should be understood in the cases that follow.

“Asekkhabhāgiyaṃ suttaṃ idamevā”ti vattabbabhāvato “āyasmato cā”tiādi vuttaṃ.

Because it should be stated, “This itself is the sutta pertaining to the one beyond training,” the text says, “And of the venerable one…” and so on.

Yo brāhmaṇo bāhitapāpadhammattā bāhitapāpadhammo bhave, so brāhmaṇo niggatahuṃhuṃkattā nihuṃhuṅko bhave, niggatakilesakasāvattā nikkasāvo bhave, sīlasaṃvarena saṃyatacittatāya yatatto bhave, yo brāhmaṇo catumaggañāṇavedehi antaṃ nibbānaṃ gatattā vedantagū bhave, dhammena vusitabrahmacariyattā vusitabrahmacariyo bhave. Yassa brāhmaṇassa kuhiñci loke ussadā rāgussado dosussado mohussado mānussado diṭṭhussado natthi, so brāhmaṇo brahmavādaṃ “ahaṃ brāhmaṇomhī”ti vācaṃ vadeyyāti bhagavā avocāti yojanā.

A brahmin is one who has banished evil because he has banished evil states. He is free from condescension because he has no ‘hum-hum’ sound of arrogance. He is stainless because his stains of defilement are gone. He is self-controlled because his mind is restrained by virtuous conduct. He has reached the end of knowledge because he has gone to the end, Nibbāna, by the knowledge of the four paths. He has lived the holy life because he has lived the holy life in accordance with the Dhamma. The brahmin for whom there are no protuberances anywhere in the world—no protuberance of lust, of hatred, of delusion, of conceit, or of views—that brahmin may rightly utter the brahmin's claim, ‘I am a brahmin.’ Thus spoke the Blessed One.

Ye buddhā pāpake akusale dhamme bāhitvā sadā caranti satā satisampannā khīṇasaṃyojanā, te buddhā lokasmiṃ brāhmaṇāti ve ekantena kathīyantīti avocāti yojanā.

Those awakened ones who, having banished evil, unwholesome states, ever move about mindful and fully aware, their fetters destroyed—they are indeed called ‘brahmins’ in the world. Thus he spoke.

Yattha nibbāne āpo ca pathavī ca tejo ca vāyo ca na gādhati na patiṭṭhahati, tattha [V 0.0424] nibbāne sukkā gahā ceva tārakā ca na jotanti, tattha nibbāne ādicco nappakāsati, tattha nibbāne candimā na bhāti, tattha nibbāne tamo na vijjati.

There, in Nibbāna, water, earth, fire, and air find no footing, gain no support. There the planets and stars do not gleam; the sun does not radiate light; the moon does not shine. There darkness is not found.

Yo brāhmaṇo attanā sayaṃ muni monena yadā taṃ nibbānaṃ avedi vindati paṭilabhati paṭivijjhati, atha paṭivijjhanakkhaṇe so brāhmaṇo rūpā rūpadhammato ca arūpā arūpadhammato ca sukhadukkhā sukhadukkhato ca pamuccatīti avocāti yojanā.

When a brahmin, a sage, has by his own sagacity directly known Nibbāna, then at that moment of penetration he is freed from form and the formless, from pleasure and pain. Thus he spoke.

Yakkha, yo brāhmaṇo sakesu sakaattabhāvesu dhammesu upādānakkhandhesu saccesu, dhammesu ca pāragū hoti, atha pāragamanakkhaṇe so brāhmaṇo etaṃ ajakalāpakaṃ tayā vuttaṃ etaṃ pisācaṃ kilesapisācañca[M 0.0306], tayā kataṃ akkulañca akkulaṃ, pakkulakaraṇaṃ ativattatīti avocāti yojanā.

Yakkha, the brahmin who has gone to the far shore in regard to his own states—that is, his own individual existences, the aggregates subject to clinging, the truths, and the dhammas—at the moment of going to the far shore, that brahmin overcomes this ‘goat-flock’ spoken of by you, this ‘demon,’ that is, the demon of defilements, and this ‘tangle’ and ‘confusion’ created by you. Thus he spoke.

Yo bhikkhu āyantiṃ āgacchantiṃ purāṇadutiyikaṃ bhariyaṃ vā, aññaṃ āgacchantiṃ itthiṃ vā cittena na abhinandati, pakkamantiṃ purāṇadutiyikaṃ bhariyaṃ vā, aññaṃ pakkamantiṃ itthiṃ vā cittena na socati, saṅgā pañcavidhatopi saṅgato muttaṃ saṅgāmajiṃ taṃ bhikkhuṃ “brāhmaṇa”nti ahaṃ vadāmīti avocāti yojanā.

The bhikkhu who does not delight in his former wife or another woman when she is approaching, and does not grieve for his former wife or another woman when she is departing—that bhikkhu, freed from the five kinds of attachment, victorious in the battle, I call a brahmin. Thus he spoke.

Ettha nadiyaṃ bahujano nhāyati, so bahujano nhāyako udakena udakanhānena sucī na hoti. Yamhi puggale saccaṃ, saccato sesadhammo ca atthi, so puggalo sucī ca hoti, so puggalo brāhmaṇo ca hotīti avocāti yojanā; suciasucibhāvo ṭīkāyaṃ vitthārato vuttova.

Here in the river, many people bathe; those many people who bathe are not purified by bathing with water. In whatever person there is truth, and from truth the other dhammas, that person is pure and is a brahmin. The state of being pure and impure has already been explained in detail in the sub-commentary.

Ātāpino jhāyato yassa brāhmaṇassa dhammā saccadhammā yadā have ekantena pātubhavanti, tadā dhammānaṃ pātubhavanakkhaṇe so brāhmaṇo mārasenaṃ vidhūpayaṃ vidhūpayanto tiṭṭhati. “Kimivā”ti vattabbattā “sūriyova obhāsayamantalikkha”nti vuttaṃ. Sūriyo antalikkhaṃ obhāsayanto tiṭṭhati iva, evaṃ tiṭṭhatīti yojanā.

For the ardent, meditating brahmin, when the true dhammas have completely manifested, then, at the moment of the manifestation of the dhammas, that brahmin stands dispelling Māra’s army. Because one should ask, ‘Like what?’, it is said: ‘Like the sun illuminating the sky.’ Just as the sun stands illuminating the sky, so he stands—this is the construction.

Yo paṃsukūliko bhikkhu sabbāni cattāri yogāni upātivatto sakiñcane loke akiñcano iriyati catubbidhairiyāpathaṃ vatteti. Apahānadhammaṃ kenaci maggena appahānasabhāvaṃ appattakāyena appattaṃ tevijjapattaṃ, iriyamānaṃ santindriyaṃ taṃ paṃsukūlikaṃ bhikkhuṃ tumhe passatha.

The monk who wears rag-robes, having overcome all four yokes, wanders without possessions in a world with possessions, practicing the four postures. Do you see that rag-robed monk, moving about with tranquil faculties, whose nature is not to be lost by any path, who with a body that has not yet attained has not reached the attainment of the threefold knowledge?

Ājāniyaṃ [V 0.0425] purisaājānīyaṃ jātibalanisedhaṃ “ahaṃ jātibrāhmaṇo”ti jātimattakena pavattamānabalanisedhakaṃ taṃ paṃsukūlikaṃ bhikkhuṃ sambahulā uḷārā devatā brahmaṃ vimānaṃ upasaṅkamitvā idha sāsane, brahmavimāne vā pasannacittā hutvā namassanti. Nidhāti ca ettha na-kāro āgamo.

That rag-robed monk—a thoroughbred, a thoroughbred among men, who has restrained the power of birth, who restrains the power that proceeds merely from the thought, 'I am a brahmin by birth'—many exalted deities, having approached a Brahmā-mansion, pay homage to him with confident minds, either here in this Dispensation or in a Brahmā-mansion. And here, in the word `nidhāti`, the letter `na` is an insertion.

Purisājañña te tava amhākaṃ namo atthu, purisuttama te tava amhākaṃ namo atthu, yassa te tava nissayaṃ mayaṃ nābhijānāma, so tvaṃ kiṃ puggalaṃ nissāya jhāyasīti avocunti yojanā.

‘O thoroughbred of men, homage to you! O supreme among men, homage to you! We do not know your support; relying on what person do you meditate?’—thus they spoke. This is the construction.

Ye [M 0.0307] bhikkhū kālena kālaṃ dhammassavanavasena cirarattaṃ sametikā bhavanti, ime bhikkhū sahāyā honti vata. Nesaṃ sahāyānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ dhamme buddhappavedite dhamme saddhammo sameti.

Those monks who gather from time to time over a long period for the purpose of hearing the Dhamma—these monks are truly companions. For those companion monks, the good Dhamma is in accord with the Dhamma declared by the Buddha.

Kappinena ariyappavedite dhamme suvinītā te sahāyakā bhikkhū savāhiniṃ māraṃ jetvā antimaṃ dehaṃ attabhāvaṃ dhārentīti avocāti yojanā.

Well-trained by Kappina in the Dhamma proclaimed by the noble ones, those companion monks, having conquered Māra with his army, bear their final body, their final existence—so it was said. This is the construction.

Sithilaṃ vīriyaṃ ārabbha sabbadukkhappamocanaṃ idaṃ nibbānaṃ yogāvacarena na adhigantabbaṃ, appena appakena thāmasā idaṃ nibbānaṃ na adhigantabbaṃ.

Having aroused slack effort, this Nibbāna, the release from all suffering, is not to be attained by the meditator. Nor is this Nibbāna to be attained with little, insignificant strength.

Ayañca yogāvacaro bhikkhu daharo, yo puriso savāhiniṃ māraṃ jetvā antimaṃ dehaṃ attabhāvaṃ dhāreti, so ayaṃ puriso so uttamapurisovāti avocāti yojanā. “Puriso”ti vattabbe chandānurakkhaṇavasena “poriso”ti vuttaṃ.

And this meditator monk is young. The person who, having conquered Māra with his army, bears his final body, his final existence—that very person is the supreme person—so it was said. This is the construction. When 'puriso' should be said, 'poriso' is said for the sake of preserving the meter.

Mogharāja, dubbaṇṇako lūkhacīvaro sadā sato satisampanno khīṇāsavo ca visaṃyutto ca katakicco ca anāsavo ca tevijjo ca iddhippatto ca cetopariyāyakovido ca so bhikkhu savāhiniṃ māraṃ jetvā antimaṃ dehaṃ dhāretīti avocāti yojanā.

Mogharāja—of poor appearance, wearing rough robes, ever mindful and accomplished in mindfulness, one whose taints are destroyed, detached, who has done what had to be done, taintless, possessing the threefold knowledge, who has attained psychic power, and is skilled in encompassing the minds of others—that monk, having conquered Māra with his army, bears his final body—so it was said. This is the construction.

105. “Tathāgato”tiādīsu yojanā pākaṭā. Idaṃ suttaṃ asekkhabhāge visaye vācakañāpakabhāvena pavattanato asekkhabhāgiyaṃ suttaṃ nāma.

105. In such terms as 'Tathāgata,' the construction is clear. Because this sutta proceeds by way of indicating and making known matters in the domain of the one beyond training, it is called 'a sutta pertaining to the one beyond training.'

106. Nānāvidhaṃ [V 0.0426] asekkhabhāgiyaṃ suttaṃ ācariyena niddhāritaṃ, amhehi ca ñātaṃ, “katamaṃ saṃkilesabhāgiyañca vāsanābhāgiyañca sutta”nti vattabbattā “tattha katamaṃ saṃkilesabhāgiyañca vāsanābhāgiyañca sutta”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Tatthāti tesu soḷasasu saṃkilesabhāgiyādīsu suttesu katamaṃ suttaṃ saṃkilesabhāgiyañca vāsanābhāgiyañca suttaṃ nāmāti pucchati.

106. Various suttas pertaining to the one beyond training have been determined by the teacher and are known by us. Because one should ask, 'Which sutta pertains to defilement and to latent tendencies?,' it is therefore said: 'Therein, which sutta pertains to defilement and to latent tendencies?' and so on. 'Therein' means: among those sixteen suttas pertaining to defilement and so on. He asks: 'Which sutta is called a sutta pertaining to defilement and to latent tendencies?'

Channaṃ āpattiṃ āpajjitvā channaṃ chādentaṃ bhikkhuṃ dukkaṭādivasso ativassati, vivaṭaṃ āpattiṃ āpajjitvā vivaṭaṃ desentaṃ ācikkhantaṃ bhikkhuṃ dukkaṭādivasso nātivassati, tasmā channassa ativassanato ca vivaṭassa nātivassanato ca channaṃ chāditabbaṃ āpattiṃ vivaretha desetha ārocetha[M 0.0308], evaṃ vivaraṇe sati taṃ vivarantaṃ bhikkhuṃ dukkaṭādivasso nātivassatīti yojanā.

A downpour of wrong-doing offenses and so on rains down upon a monk who, having committed a concealed offense, conceals it. A downpour of wrong-doing offenses and so on does not rain down upon a monk who, having committed an open offense, declares and announces it openly. Therefore, because the concealer is rained upon and the revealer is not, you should uncover, declare, and announce a concealed offense. When it is thus uncovered, a downpour of wrong-doing offenses and so on does not rain down upon the monk who uncovers it—this is the construction.

“Imasmiṃ sutte kittakena saṃkileso dassito, kittakena vāsanā dassitā”ti pucchitabbattā “channamativassatī”ti saṃkileso, ‘vivaṭaṃ nātivassatī’ti vāsanā, ‘tasmā channaṃ vivaretha, evaṃ taṃ nātivassatī’ti ayaṃ saṃkileso ca vāsanā cā”ti vuttaṃ. “Channamativassatī”ti ettakena saṃkileso dassito. “Vivaṭaṃ nātivassatī”ti ettakena vāsanā dassitā. “Tasmā channaṃ vivaretha, evaṃ taṃ nātivassatī”ti ettakena ayaṃ saṃkileso ca dassito, ayaṃ vāsanā ca dassitā. Idaṃ “channaṃ…pe... vassatī”ti suttaṃ saṃkilesabhāge visaye ca vāsanābhāge visaye ca vācakañāpakabhāvena pavattanato saṃkilesabhāgiyañca vāsanābhāgiyañca suttaṃ nāma.

Because one should ask, 'In this sutta, by what portion is defilement shown, and by what portion is latent tendency shown?,' it is said: '"It rains down upon the concealed one"—this is defilement. "It does not rain down upon the revealed one"—this is latent tendency. "Therefore, uncover the concealed; thus it will not rain down upon you"—this is both defilement and latent tendency.' By 'It rains down upon the concealed one,' defilement is shown. By 'It does not rain down upon the revealed one,' latent tendency is shown. By 'Therefore, uncover the concealed; thus it will not rain down upon you,' both defilement and latent tendency are shown. This sutta, 'The concealed one... rains down,' because it proceeds by way of indicating and making known matters in the domain of defilement and in the domain of latent tendency, is called a sutta pertaining to both defilement and latent tendency.

“Saṃkilesabhāgiyañca vāsanābhāgiyañca suttaṃ ettakamevā”ti vattabbattā “cattārome mahārājā”tiādi vuttaṃ. “Tesu catūsu puggalesu katame puggalā saṃkilesabhāgiyā, katame puggalā vāsanābhāgiyā”ti pucchitabbattā “tattha yo ca puggalo”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tatthāti tesu catūsu tamotamaparāyaṇādīsu puggalesu. Tassattho pākaṭo. Idaṃ “cattārome”tiādikaṃ suttaṃ saṃkilesabhāgiyesu dvīsu puggalesu ca vāsanābhāgiyesu dvīsu puggalesu ca vācakañāpakabhāvena pavattanato saṃkilesabhāgiyañca vāsanābhāgiyañca suttaṃ nāma.

Because one might ask, 'Is that the only sutta pertaining to both defilement and latent tendency?,' the text continues, saying: 'These four, great king...' and so on. Because one should ask, 'Among those four persons, which persons pertain to defilement and which pertain to latent tendency?,' it is said: 'Therein, the person who...' and so on. 'Therein' refers to those four persons, such as the one heading from darkness to darkness. Its meaning is clear. This sutta beginning 'These four,' because it proceeds by way of indicating and making known two persons who pertain to defilement and two persons who pertain to latent tendency, is called a sutta pertaining to both defilement and latent tendency.

Nānāvidhaṃ saṃkilesabhāgiyañca vāsanābhāgiyañca suttaṃ ācariyena niddhāritaṃ, amhehi ca ñātaṃ, “katamaṃ saṃkilesabhāgiyañca nibbedhabhāgiyañca suttaṃ nāmā”ti pucchitabbattā tattha katamaṃ [V 0.0427] saṃkilesabhāgiyañca nibbedhabhāgiyañca sutta”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Tassattho vuttanayena veditabbo.

Various suttas pertaining to defilement and to latent tendency have been determined by the teacher and are known by us. Because one should ask, 'Which sutta is called one pertaining to defilement and to penetration?,' it is therefore said: 'Therein, which sutta pertains to defilement and to penetration?' and so on. Its meaning should be understood according to the method already explained.

Ayasaṃ yaṃ bandhanañca dārujaṃ yaṃ bandhanañca pabbajaṃ yaṃ bandhanañca loke atthi, taṃ ayasādibandhanaṃ “daḷhaṃ bandhana”nti dhīrā buddhādayo paṇḍitapurisā na āhu. Maṇikuṇḍalesu ca puttesu ca dāresu ca yā sārattarattā balavarāgarattā apekkhā loke vijjati, taṃ sārattarattaapekkhāsaṅkhātaṃ rāgabandhanaṃ “daḷhaṃ bandhana”nti dhīrā paṇḍitapurisā āhu. Iminā suttappadesena ayaṃ sārattarattaapekkhāsaṅkhāto akusaladhammo saṃkileso dassito.

The wise—the Buddhas and other sagacious persons—do not say that the bond of iron, the bond of wood, and the bond of fiber that exist in the world are a strong bond. But whatever longing for jeweled earrings, for children, and for wives exists in the world, a longing that is intensely impassioned and colored by powerful lust—that bond of lust, known as intensely impassioned longing, the wise, sagacious persons call a strong bond. By this portion of the sutta, this unwholesome state, this defilement known as intensely impassioned longing, is shown.

“Kena [M 0.0309] nibbedho dassito”ti vattabbattā “eta”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Dhīrā paṇḍitapurisā etaṃ rāgabandhanaṃ “daḷhaṃ bandhana”nti āhu. Etaṃ rāgabandhanaṃ ohārinaṃ heṭṭhā apāyaṃ avaharaṇaṃ hoti, sithilaṃ bandhanaṭṭhāne chaviādīni akopetattā sithilaṃ hoti, duppamuñcaṃ lobhavasena ekavārampi uppannassa rāgabandhanassa dummocayattā duppamuñcaṃ hoti, paṇḍitapurisā etampi vuttappakāraṃ rāgabandhanampi maggena chetvāna anapekkhino hutvā kāmasukhaṃ pahāya paribbajanti. Iti iminā suttappadesena ayaṃ maggo nibbedho dassito. Idaṃ “ayasa”ntiādikaṃ suttaṃ rāgādisaṃkilesabhāge visaye ca vāsanābhāge visaye ca vācakañāpakabhāvena pavattanato saṃkilesabhāgiyañca vāsanābhāgiyañca suttaṃ nāma.

Because it should be said, 'By what is penetration shown?,' it is said, 'This…' and so on. The wise, sagacious persons call this bond of lust a 'strong bond.' This bond of lust is down-dragging, as it drags one down to the lower worlds. It is slack, as it does not injure the skin and so on at the place of binding. It is hard to escape, as this bond of lust, once arisen through greed, is difficult to be freed from. Sagacious persons, having cut even this bond of lust of the kind described with the path, become free from longing, and having abandoned sensual pleasure, they go forth. Thus, by this portion of the sutta, this path—penetration—is shown. This sutta beginning 'Of iron…,' because it proceeds by way of indicating and making known matters in the domain of the part of defilements such as lust and in the domain of the part of latent tendencies, is called a sutta pertaining to both defilement and latent tendency.

107. Bhikkhave, yañca ceteti yañca cetanaṃ nibbatteti, yañca pakappeti yañca pakappanaṃ karoti, yañca anuseti yañca anusayanaṃ bhavati, etaṃ cetanaṃ etaṃ pakappanaṃ etaṃ anusayanaṃ viññāṇassa ṭhitiyā ārammaṇaṃ paccayo hoti. Ārammaṇe paccaye sati tassa abhisaṅkhāra viññāṇassa patiṭṭhā hoti. Tasmiṃ abhisaṅkhāraviññāṇe patiṭṭhite viruḷhe sati āyatiṃ punabbhavābhinibbatti viññāṇādinibbatti hoti. Āyatiṃ punabbhavābhinibbattiyā sati āyatiṃ jātijarāmaraṇaṃ sambhavati. Āyatiṃ soka…pe… samudayo hoti.

107. “Bhikkhus, whatever one intends and whatever intention one generates, whatever one plans and whatever one conceives, and for whatever one has an underlying tendency and whatever becomes a latent tendency—this intention, this planning, this latent tendency becomes a support and a condition for the station of consciousness. When there is a support and a condition, there is a footing for consciousness conditioned by volitional formations. When that consciousness conditioned by volitional formations is established and has grown, in the future there is the production of renewed existence, the production of consciousness and so on. With the production of renewed existence in the future, birth, aging, and death come to be. In the future, sorrow… and the origin of this whole mass of suffering comes to be.”

Bhikkhave, ce no ceteti, ce no pakappeti, atha tathāpi ce anuseti anusayanaṃ bhavati, evaṃ sati etaṃ anusayanaṃ viññāṇassa abhisaṅkhāraviññāṇassa ārammaṇaṃ paccayo hoti…pe… samudayo hoti. Iti iminā suttappadesena ayaṃ vuttappakāro cetayanādiko akusaladhammo saṃkileso dassito.

“Bhikkhus, if one does not intend, and if one does not plan, yet still a latent tendency persists, in that case that latent tendency becomes a support and a condition for consciousness, for consciousness conditioned by volitional formations… the origin comes to be. Thus, by this passage of the discourse, this unwholesome state of defilement, beginning with intention, has been shown.”

“Kena [V 0.0428] nibbedho dassito”ti vattabbattā “yato cā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Bhikkhave, yato ca ariyamaggiko neva ceteti, no ca pakappeti, no ca anuseti, etaṃ acetayanaṃ etaṃ akappanaṃ etaṃ ananusayanaṃ viññāṇassa abhisaṅkhāraviññāṇassa ārammaṇaṃ paccayo na hoti…pe… āyatiṃ jātijarāmaraṇaṃ nirujjhati, āyatiṃ soka…pe… yāsā nirujjhanti…pe… nirodho hoti. Iti iminā suttappadesena ayaṃ ariyamaggo nibbedho dassito. Idaṃ “yañca bhikkhave”tiādikaṃ suttaṃ [M 0.0310] saṃkilesabhāge visaye ca nibbedhabhāge visaye ca vācakañāpakabhāvena pavattanato saṃkilesabhāgiyañca nibbedhabhāgiyañca suttaṃ nāma.

Because it should be asked, 'By what is penetration shown?' the phrase 'When...' and so on is stated. “Bhikkhus, when one on the noble path neither intends, nor plans, nor has an underlying tendency, this non-intending, this non-planning, this absence of an underlying tendency does not become a support and a condition for consciousness, for consciousness conditioned by volitional formations… future birth, aging, and death cease, future sorrow… despair ceases… cessation occurs.” Thus, by this passage of the discourse, this noble path is shown as penetration. This discourse, beginning with 'And what, bhikkhus,' because it proceeds by way of indicating and making known matters in the domain of defilement and in the domain of penetration, is called a discourse pertaining to both defilement and penetration.

108. Nānāvidhaṃ saṃkilesabhāgiyañca nibbedhabhāgiyañca suttaṃ ācariyena niddhāritaṃ, amhehi ca ñātaṃ, “katamaṃ saṃkilesabhāgiyañca asekkhabhāgiyañca sutta”nti pucchitabbattā “tattha katamaṃ saṃkilesabhāgiyañca asekkhabhāgiyañca sutta”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Tassattho vuttanayena veditabbo.

108. Various kinds of discourses pertaining to defilement and those pertaining to penetration have been determined by the teacher and are known to us. Because it is to be asked, “Which discourse pertains to defilement and which pertains to the non-trainee?,” it was said, “Here, which discourse pertains to defilement and which pertains to the non-trainee?,” and so on. Its meaning should be understood in the way explained.

Bhikkhave, assutavā puthujjano samuddo jalasāgarasamuddo “samuddo samuddo”ti bhāsati. Kenaṭṭhena bhāsati? Duppūraṇaṭṭhena ca saṃsaraṇaṭṭhena ca duratikkamanaṭṭhena ca samuddoti bhāsati. Evaṃ sati, bhikkhave, eso jalasāgarasamuddo ariyassa bhagavato vinaye vuttappakāraṭṭhena samuddo na hoti. Bhikkhave, eso jalasāgarasamuddo mahā udakarāsi mahā udakaṇṇavo hoti. Bhikkhave, cakkhu purisassa samuddo hoti, tassa cakkhussa rūpamayo rūpāyatanamayo vego. Kenaṭṭhena? Pathavito yāva akaniṭṭhabrahmalokā nīlādirūpārammaṇaṃ samosarantampi duppūraṇaṭṭhena ca anamatagge saṃsāre saṃsaraṇaṭṭhena ca duratikkamanaṭṭhena ca cakkhumeva samuddo hoti. Nīlādirūpāyatanassa appameyyassa appameyyena ūmimayena vegena saṃsaraṇaṭṭhena nīlādirūpameva vego hoti. Iti iminā suttappadesena ayaṃ cakkhu samuddo rūpamayo vego ca saṃkileso saṃkilesahetu dassito.

“Bhikkhus, the uninstructed ordinary person speaks of the ocean, the water-ocean, as 'the ocean, the ocean.' By what meaning does he speak? He speaks of it as the ocean because it is hard to fill, because of its wandering nature, and because it is difficult to cross over. But in this way, bhikkhus, this water-ocean is not an ocean in the sense meant in the Blessed One's Discipline. Bhikkhus, this water-ocean is just a great mass of water, a great expanse of water. Bhikkhus, the eye of a person is an ocean. The surge of that eye is made of form, made of the form-base. By what meaning? Because even when form-objects such as blue, from the earth up to the Akaniṭṭha Brahma world, converge, it is hard to fill; because of wandering on in beginningless saṃsāra; and because it is difficult to cross over, the eye itself is the ocean. Form itself, such as blue and so on, is the surge, because of the wandering on of the immeasurable form-base with its immeasurable, wave-like current. Thus, by this passage of the discourse, this has been shown: the eye is the ocean, and the surge made of form is defilement and the cause of defilement.”

“Kena asekkho dassito”ti vattabbattā “yo ta”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Yasmiṃ arahattaphale ṭhito yo arahā rūpamayaṃ taṃ vegaṃ sahati manāpe rūpe rāgaṃ, amanāpe rūpe dosaṃ, asamapekkhane mohaṃ anuppādento hutvā upekkhakabhāvena sahati, ayaṃ arahā, bhikkhave, saūmiṃ sāvaṭṭaṃ sagahaṃ sarakkhasaṃ cakkhusamuddaṃ atarīti vuccati, tiṇṇo pāraṅgato thale tiṭṭhati brāhmaṇoti vuccati. Iti iminā suttappadesena ayaṃ arahattaphalabhūto asekkho dassito.

Because it must be said, 'By what is the non-trainee shown?,' 'He who...' and so on was stated. The arahant, standing in the fruit of arahantship, endures that surge of form; not generating passion for pleasant forms, aversion for unpleasant forms, or delusion in the absence of equanimity, he endures with equanimity. This arahant, bhikkhus, is said to have crossed the eye-ocean with its waves, whirlpools, sea-monsters, and ogres; having crossed over, gone to the far shore, he stands on dry land and is called a brahmin. Thus, by this passage of the discourse, this non-trainee, who is the fruit of arahantship, is shown.

“Sotaṃ [V 0.0429][M 0.0311] bhikkhave”tiādīsupi iminā nayena yathāsambhavaṃ attho veditabbo. Idaṃ “samuddo”tiādikaṃ suttaṃ saṃkilesabhāge visaye ca asekkhabhāge visaye ca vācakañāpakabhāvena pavattanato saṃkilesabhāgiyañca asekkhabhāgiyañca suttaṃ nāma.

In 'The ear, bhikkhus...' and so on, the meaning should be understood appropriately in this same way. This discourse, beginning with 'The ocean...,' because it proceeds by way of indicating and making known matters in the domain of defilement and in the domain of the non-trainee, is called a discourse pertaining to both defilement and the non-trainee.

“Ettakamevā”ti vattabbattā “chayime”tiādi vuttaṃ. Bhikkhave, lokasmiṃ sattānaṃ anayāya anatthāya pāṇīnaṃ byābādhāya ime mayā vuccamānā baḷisā cha bhavanti. Katame cha? Bhikkhave, cakkhuviññeyyā cakkhuviññāṇena viññeyyā iṭṭhā kantā kāmanīyā manāpā manavaḍḍhakā piyarūpā piyasabhāvā kāmūpasaṃhitā kilesakāmasahitā rajanīyā rūpā nīlādirūpārammaṇā santi, taṃ vuttappakāraṃ rūpaṃ bhikkhu ce abhinandati sappītikataṇhāya abhimukho nandati, ce abhivadati “aho sukhaṃ aho sukha”nti vadāpentiyā taṇhāyanavasena abhivadati, ce ajjhosāya tiṭṭhati gilitvā viya pariniṭṭhapetvā tiṭṭhati, evaṃ sati, bhikkhave, ayaṃ bhikkhu “gilitabaḷiso…pe… pāpimato”ti vuccati. Ettha ca nīlādibhedena anekavidhattā “rūpā iṭṭhā…pe… rajanīyā”ti bahuvacananiddeso katopi rūpāyatanarūpārammaṇabhāvena ca cakkhuviññeyyabhāvena ca ekavidhataṃ anativattanato “ta”nti ekavacananiddeso katoti veditabbo. “Santi, bhikkhave, sotaviññeyyā”tiādīsupi iminā nayena yathāsambhavaṃ attho veditabbo. Iti iminā suttappadesena ayaṃ cakkhuviññeyyādiko chabbidho baḷiso saṃkileso kilesahetu dassito.

Because it should be said, 'It is only this much,' it is said, 'These six...' and so on. “Bhikkhus, in the world, for the detriment, for the harm of beings, for the affliction of living creatures, there are these six hooks spoken of by me. What six? Bhikkhus, there are forms cognizable by the eye, perceivable by eye-consciousness, that are desirable, lovely, charming, pleasing, gladdening the mind, dear, of a dear nature, connected with sensual desire, accompanied by defilements, arousing passion—form-objects such as blue and so on. If a bhikkhu delights in such a form, that is, he rejoices in it with craving accompanied by joy; if he welcomes it, that is, he welcomes it through the influence of craving which makes one say, 'Ah, what bliss!'; if he stands clinging to it, that is, he stands having consumed it as if having swallowed it; then, bhikkhus, this bhikkhu is called 'one who has swallowed the hook... of the Evil One.' And here, although the plural designation, 'forms, desirable... arousing passion,' is made because of the variety due to the distinctions of blue and so on, it should be understood that the singular designation 'that' is made because it does not go beyond the single nature of being the form-base, a form-object, and cognizable by the eye. In 'Bhikkhus, there are sounds cognizable by the ear...' and so on, the meaning should also be understood appropriately in this way. Thus, by this passage of the discourse, this sixfold hook, beginning with what is cognizable by the eye, is shown as defilement and the cause of defilements.”

“Kena asekkho dassito”ti vattabbattā “santi cā”tiādi vuttaṃ.

Because it should be said, 'By what is the non-trainee shown?' it is said, 'And there are...' and so on.

Abhedi bhindi, paribhedi parisamantato bhindi. Iti iminā suttappadesena ayaṃ arahattaphalabhūto asekkho dassito. Idaṃ “chayime”tiādikaṃ suttaṃ vuttanayena saṃkilesabhāgiyañca asekkhabhāgiyañca suttaṃ nāma.

He shattered, he broke, he broke apart, he broke apart completely. Thus, by this passage of the discourse, this non-trainee, who is the fruit of arahantship, is shown. This discourse, beginning 'These six,' and so on, is called a discourse that, in the manner stated, pertains both to defilement and to the non-trainee.

109. Nānāvidhaṃ saṃkilesabhāgiyañca asekkhabhāgiyañca suttaṃ ācariyena niddhāritaṃ, amhehi ca ñātaṃ, “katamaṃ saṃkilesabhāgiyañca nibbedhabhāgiyañca asekkhabhāgiyañca sutta”nti pucchitabbattā “tattha katamaṃ saṃkilesabhāgiyañca nibbedhabhāgiyañca asekkhabhāgiyañca sutta”ntiādi vuttaṃ.

109. Various kinds of discourses pertaining to defilement and those pertaining to the non-trainee have been determined by the teacher and are known to us. Because the question to be asked is, 'Which discourse pertains to defilement, which to penetration, and which to the non-trainee?', it was therefore said, 'Herein, which discourse pertains to defilement, which to penetration, and which to the non-trainee?' and so on.

Ayaṃ [M 0.0312] loko sattaloko santāpajāto ñātibyasanādivasena jātasokasantāpo ceva rāgādivasena [V 0.0430] jātapariḷāhasantāpo ca phassapareto anekehi dukkhasamphassehi abhibhūto rodaṃ rodanto vadati. Kinti vadati? Attanā phuṭṭhaṃ dukkhaṃ abhāvitakāyatāya adhivāsetuṃ asakkonto hutvā “aho dukkhaṃ, īdisaṃ dukkhaṃ mayhaṃ sattunopi mā hotū”tiādinā rodanto vilapanto vadati, “kasmā evaṃ vadatī”ti vattabbattā “attato yena yena hi maññantī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Ete sattā yena yena kāmajjhosādinā pakārena attato dukkhassa paṭikāraṃ maññanti, tato pakārato aññathā aññena pakārena taṃ dukkhaṃ tikicchitabbaṃ hi yasmā hoti.

This world, the world of beings, is born of affliction. It is afflicted with sorrow born from the loss of relatives and the like, and scorched by the burning anguish born from lust and so on. Overcome by contact, overwhelmed by many painful contacts, it weeps and wails. How does it speak? Unable to endure the suffering it has encountered due to an undeveloped body, it weeps and laments, saying, 'Alas, suffering! May such suffering not befall even my enemies!' and so on. Because it should be asked, 'Why does it speak thus?', it was said, 'For in whatever way they conceive...' and so on. These beings, in whatever way, by means of attachment to sensual pleasures and the like, conceive a remedy for suffering from the self; but that suffering must indeed be treated otherwise, by another means, than that means.

Aññathābhāvīti yasmā rodaṃ rodanto vadati, yena yena vā paravihiṃsādipakārena attano vaḍḍhiṃ maññanti āsīsanti, tato pakārato aññathā avaḍḍhi eva hoti. Taṃ āsīsitabbaṃ aññathābhāvi avaḍḍhitabhāvi eva hi yasmā hoti, tasmā maññitabbassa āsīsitabbassa aññathā bhavanasīlattā rodaṃ rodanto vadati, ayaṃ sattaloko rodanto ca hutvā vadati. “Ki”nti pucchitabbattā “bhavasatto”tiādi vuttaṃ. Bhavasatto kāmabhavādīsu satto visatto loko bhavameva kāmabhavādibhavameva abhinandati. Yaṃ bhavaṃ abhinandati, taṃ jarāmaraṇādianekabyasanānubandhattā bhayānakaṭṭhena bhayaṃ hoti. Yassa yato jarāmaraṇādito bhāyati, taṃ jarāmaraṇādidukkhassa adhiṭṭhānabhāvato dukkhaṃ dukkhādhiṭṭhānaṃ hoti. Iti iminā suttappadesena ayaṃ santāpādiko saṃkileso saṃkilesahetu dassito.

It becomes otherwise, and for that reason it weeps and wails. Or, by whatever means, such as harming others, they imagine and wish for their own growth, from that very means there is, on the contrary, only decline. For what is wished for is indeed 'otherwise-becoming,' that is, it becomes only decline. Therefore, because what is imagined and wished for has the nature of becoming otherwise, this world of beings weeps and wails. Because the question 'What?' should be asked, the words 'attached to existence' and so on were stated. The world, attached and clinging to sensual existence and the like, delights only in existence itself. But that very existence, being followed by aging, death, and many calamities, is fearful in the sense of being dreadful. That which one fears—aging, death, and so on—is suffering and a basis for suffering, because it is the basis for the suffering of aging, death, and so on. Thus, by this passage of the discourse, this defilement beginning with affliction and its cause is shown.

Saṃkileso dassito, “kena nibbedho dassito”ti vattabbattā “bhavavippahānāya kho”tiādi vuttaṃ. Bhavavippahānāya kho pana kāmabhavādikassa bhavassa pajahanatthāya eva idaṃ mayā adhigataṃ maggabrahmacariyaṃ vussati. Iti iminā suttappadesena ayaṃ brahmacariyabhūto maggo nibbedho dassito.

The defilement has been shown. Since it must be asked, 'By what is penetration shown?', the words 'For the abandonment of existence…' and so on were stated. Indeed, it is for the abandonment of existence—that is, for the purpose of abandoning existence such as sensual existence—that this holy life, the path attained by me, is lived. Thus, by this passage of the discourse, this path, which is the holy life, is shown as penetration.

“Bhavavippahānāyā”tiādinā ekantena niyyānikamaggo nibbedho ācariyena dassito, amhehi ca ñāto, “katamo aniyyānikamaggo”ti pucchitabbattā “ye hi keci samaṇā vā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Hi-saddo vācāsiliṭṭhattho. Ye keci samaṇā vā ye keci brāhmaṇā vā bhavena [M 0.0313] rūpabhavena bhavassa kāmabhavassa vippamokkhaṃ āhaṃsu, bhavena arūpabhavena bhavassa kāmabhavassa ceva rūpabhavassa ca vippamokkhaṃ āhaṃsu, sabbe te samaṇā vā sabbe te brāhmaṇā vā bhavasmā vuttappakārabhavato avippamuttā bhavantīti ahaṃ vadāmi.

By the words 'For the abandonment of existence…' and so on, the path of penetration, which is exclusively liberative, has been shown by the Teacher and understood by us. Because the question 'What is the path that is not liberative?' must be asked, the words 'Whatever ascetics or brahmins…' and so on were stated. The particle 'hi' is for the elegance of speech.
