Whatever ascetics or brahmins have declared liberation from sensual existence by means of form existence, or have declared liberation from both sensual existence and form existence by means of formless existence—all those ascetics and all those brahmins, I say, are not liberated from existence, from existence of the kind stated.

“Rūpabhavādinā [V 0.0431] ye ca kāmabhavādibhavassa vippamokkhaṃ āhaṃsū”ti vattabbattā vibhavena bhavassa nissaraṇaṃ āhaṃsūti dassetuṃ “ye vā panā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Ye vā pana keci samaṇā vā ye vā pana keci brāhmaṇā vā vibhavena ucchedadiṭṭhiyā bhavassa saṃsārabhavassa nissaraṇaṃ āhaṃsu, sabbe te samaṇā vā sabbe te brāhmaṇā vā bhavasmā saṃsārabhavato anissaṭāva hontīti ahaṃ vadāmi. “Kasmā anissaṭā”ti vattabbattā anissaṭakāraṇaṃ dassetuṃ “upadhiṃ hī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Idaṃ dukkhaṃ saṃsāradukkhaṃ upadhiṃ khandhūpadhikilesūpadhiabhisaṅkhārūpadhayo paṭicca hi yasmā sambhoti, tasmā anissaṭā honti. Iti iminā suttappadesena ayaṃ micchādiṭṭhisaṅkhāto saṃkileso dassito.

Because it should be said, 'And those who declared liberation from existence such as sensual existence by means of existence such as form existence,' in order to show that they declared an escape from existence by means of non-existence, the words 'Or whatever others…' and so on were stated. Or whatever ascetics or brahmins have declared an escape from existence—from saṃsāric existence—by means of non-existence, that is, the annihilationist view, all those ascetics and all those brahmins, I say, have not escaped from existence, from saṃsāric existence. Because it must be asked, 'Why have they not escaped?', in order to show the reason for their non-escape, the words 'For on account of the substrates…' and so on were stated. For this suffering, the suffering of saṃsāra, arises in dependence on the substrates—the substrates of the aggregates, the substrates of the defilements, and the substrates of volitional formations. Therefore they have not escaped. Thus, by this passage of the discourse, this defilement, reckoned as wrong view, is shown.

Ye hi “kecī”tiādinā saṃkileso dassito, “kena nibbedho dassito”ti vattabbattā “sabbupādānakkhayā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Sabbupādānakkhayā ariyamaggato dukkhassa saṃsāradukkhassa sambhavo natthi. Iti iminā suttappadesena ayaṃ ariyamaggo nibbedho dassito.

By the words 'Whatever…' and so on, defilement has been shown. Since it must be asked, 'By what is penetration shown?', the words 'through the destruction of all clinging…' and so on were stated. From the noble path, through the destruction of all clinging, there is no arising of suffering, the suffering of saṃsāra. Thus, by this passage of the discourse, this noble path is shown as penetration.

“Vuttappakārā aññasuttappadesenapi dassito”ti dassetuṃ “lokamima”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Puthū visuṃ visuṃ avijjāya paretaṃ abhibhūtaṃ bhūtarataṃ bhūtesu itthipurisesu aññamaññarataṃ bhūtaṃ khandhapañcakaṃ bhavehi aparimuttaṃ imaṃ lokaṃ mama citta tvaṃ passa. Ye keci bhavā ittarakhaṇā vā bhavā, dīghāyukā vā bhavā, sātavanto vā bhavā, asātavanto vā bhavā pañcakkhandhā sabbadhi “uddhaṃ adho tiriya”nti imesu sabbesu sabbatthatāya sabbatthabhāvena ahesuṃ, sabbe te vuttappakārā bhavā niccadhuvarahitattā aniccā sampīḷitattā dukkhā vipariṇāmabhāvato vipariṇāmadhammā ahesuṃ. Iti iminā suttappadesena ayaṃ avijjādiko saṃkileso dassito.

In order to show that this matter of the kind stated has also been shown by another passage of a discourse, the words 'See this world…' and so on were stated. O my mind, see this world, which is overcome and overwhelmed by ignorance in many different ways, delighting in what has come to be, mutually delighting in beings—in women and men—and which has become the five aggregates, not freed from existences. Whatever existences there were—whether short-lived or long-lived, pleasant or unpleasant—the five aggregates were everywhere, in all these 'above, below, and across,' in every way and in every respect. All those existences of the kind stated were impermanent, being devoid of permanence and stability; suffering, being oppressed; and subject to change, having the nature of changing. Thus, by this passage of the discourse, this defilement beginning with ignorance is shown.

“Lokamima”ntiādinā saṃkileso dassito, “kena nibbedho dassito”ti vattabbattā “evameta”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Evaṃ vuttappakārena etaṃ khandhapañcakaṃ [M 0.0314] yathābhūtaṃ sammappaññāya sassa attano maggapaññāya, vipassanāpaññāya vā passato passantassa puggalassa bhavataṇhā pahīyati, sammappaññāya yathābhūtaṃ khandhapañcakaṃ passanto vibhavaṃ ucchedadiṭṭhiṃ nābhinandati na pattheti. Tassa puggalassa sabbaso taṇhānaṃ khayā asesavirāganirodho asesavirāgasaṅkhātena maggena nirodho nirujjhanaṃ nibbānaṃ nibbuti hoti. Iti iminā suttappadesena ayaṃ maggo nibbedho dassito.

By the words 'See this world…' and so on, defilement has been shown. Since it must be asked, 'By what is penetration shown?', the words 'Thus this is…' and so on were stated. When a person sees these five aggregates as they really are in the way stated—with right wisdom, with one's own path-wisdom, or with insight-wisdom—for such a one who sees, craving for existence is abandoned. Seeing the five aggregates as they really are with right wisdom, one does not delight in or yearn for non-existence, the annihilationist view. For that person, through the utter destruction of cravings, there is remainderless fading away and cessation; by means of the path reckoned as remainderless fading away, there is cessation, the ceasing, Nibbāna, extinguishment. Thus, by this passage of the discourse, this path is shown as penetration.

“Evameta”ntiādinā [V 0.0432] nibbedho dassito, “kena asekkho dassito”ti vattabbattā “tassa nibbutassā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Taṇhādiṭṭhinibbutassa tassa bhikkhuno anupādā kilesābhisaṅkhārānaṃ anuppādanato aggahaṇato punabbhavo na hoti, evaṃbhūtena ariyapuggalena pubbe attānaṃ abhibhūto pañcavidho māro vijito ahosi, anena ariyapuggalena pañcahi mārehi saṅgāmo vijito, saṅgāme, iṭṭhāniṭṭhādīsu vā tādī tādilakkhaṇappatto ariyapuggalo sabbabhavāni upaccagā atikkantova jāto. Iti iminā suttappadesena ayaṃ asekkho dassito. Idaṃ vuttappakāraṃ “ayaṃ loko”tiādikaṃ suttaṃ saṃkilesabhāge visaye ca nibbedhabhāge visaye ca asekkhabhāge visaye ca vācakañāpakabhāvena ekadesavasena pavattanato saṃkilesabhāgiyañca nibbedhabhāgiyañca asekkhabhāgiyañca suttaṃ nāma.

By the words 'Thus this is…' and so on, penetration has been shown. Since it must be asked, 'By what is the one beyond training shown?' the words 'For that extinguished one…' and so on were stated. For that bhikkhu who is extinguished in regard to craving and views, since he does not grasp, there is no production of defilements and volitional formations, and thus there is no further becoming. By such a noble person the fivefold Māra that formerly overwhelmed him has been conquered. This noble person has won the battle with the five Māras. In battle, or in regard to agreeable and disagreeable things, such a noble person, one who is 'such,' having attained the characteristic of being 'such,' has passed beyond all existences, has become one who has transcended them. Thus, by this passage of the sutta, the one beyond training is shown. This sutta of the kind described, beginning with 'This world…,' because it proceeds in part as an exponent and indicator in the domain of the part on defilement, the part on penetration, and the part on the one beyond training, is called a sutta pertaining to defilement, pertaining to penetration, and pertaining to the one beyond training.

“Ettakamevā”ti vattabbattā “cattārome”tiādi vuttaṃ. Andhaputhujjano saṃsārasotassa anukūlabhāvena gacchanato anusotagāmī nāma, kalyāṇaputhujjano saṃsārasotassa nibbidānupassanādīhi paṭikkūlavasena pavattanato paṭisotagāmī nāma, sekkho acalappasādādisamannāgamena ṭhitasabhāvattā ṭhitatto nāma, asekkho saṃsārapāraṅgatavasena tiṭṭhanato “thale tiṭṭhatī”ti vuccati.

Because it should be said, 'Is it only this much?' the words 'These four…' and so on were stated. The blind worldling, because he goes favorably with the stream of saṃsāra, is called 'one who goes with the stream.' The virtuous worldling, because he proceeds against the stream of saṃsāra by means of disenchantment, insight, and so on, is called 'one who goes against the stream.' The trainee, because he has a steadfast nature due to being endowed with unshakable confidence and so on, is called 'one who is established.' The one beyond training, because he stands having gone to the far shore of saṃsāra, is said to 'stand on high ground.'

“Tesu catūsu puggalesu katamo puggalo saṃkilesabhāgiyādī”ti vattabbabhāvato “tattha yoya”ntiādi vuttaṃ.

Since it should be stated, 'Among these four persons, which person pertains to the part on defilement, etc.?' the words 'Therein, whichever…' and so on were stated.

110. Nānāvidhaṃ saṃkilesabhāgiyañca nibbedhabhāgiyañca asekkhabhāgiyañca suttaṃ ācariyena niddhāritaṃ, amhehi ca ñātaṃ, “katamaṃ saṃkilesabhāgiyañca vāsanābhāgiyañca nibbedhabhāgiyañca sutta”nti pucchitabbattā “tattha katama”ntiādi vuttaṃ.

110. Various suttas—pertaining to defilement, pertaining to penetration, and pertaining to the one beyond training—have been determined by the Teacher and understood by us. Because it must be asked, 'Which sutta pertains to defilement, to latent tendencies, and to penetration?' the words 'Therein, which…' and so on were stated.

Abhijātiyo [M 0.0315] puggalā cha saṃvijjanti lokasmiṃ, kaṇhe nīce kule nibbatto kaṇhābhijātiko, kaṇhadhammasamannāgatattā vā kaṇho kaṇhābhijātiko hutvā kaṇhaṃ kāḷakaṃ dasavidhaṃ dussīlyadhammaṃ abhijāyati pasavati, eso puggalo atthi. Vuttappakārena kaṇho kaṇhābhijātiko hutvā sukkaṃ dasavidhaṃ kusaladhammaṃ abhijāyati, eso puggalo atthi. Kaṇho kaṇhābhijātiko hutvā akaṇhaṃ asukkaṃ akaṇhaasukkavipākaṃ accantadiṭṭhaṃ nibbānaṃ ārādheti, eso puggalo atthi. Vuttavipariyāyena tayo puggalā jānitabbā.

There exist in the world six types of birth of persons. One born into a dark, low family is of dark birth. Or, being endowed with dark qualities, one is dark. Being of dark birth, one generates and produces the tenfold dark, black, immoral states; such a person exists. In the stated manner, one of dark birth generates the tenfold bright, wholesome states; such a person exists. One of dark birth attains Nibbāna, which is neither dark nor bright, has a result that is neither dark nor bright, and is the ultimate state; such a person exists. The three persons who are the opposite of those stated should be understood.

“Tesu [V 0.0433] katame puggalā saṃkilesabhāgiyā”tiādinā vattabbattā “tattha yo cā”tiādi vuttaṃ.

Since it should be stated, 'Among them, which persons pertain to the part on defilement?' and so on, the words 'Therein, the one who…' and so on were stated.

“Ettakamevā”ti vattabbattā “cattārimānī”tiādi vuttaṃ.

Because it should be said, 'Is it only this much?' the words 'These four…' and so on were stated.

111. Nānāvidhaṃ saṃkilesabhāgiyañca vāsanābhāgiyañca nibbedhabhāgiyañca suttaṃ ācariyena niddhāritaṃ, amhehi ca ñātaṃ, “katamaṃ vāsanābhāgiyañca nibbedhabhāgiyañca sutta”nti pucchitabbattā “tattha katamaṃ vāsanābhāgiyañca nibbedhabhāgiyañcā”tiādi vuttaṃ.

111. Various suttas—pertaining to defilement, to latent tendencies, and to penetration—have been determined by the Teacher and understood by us. Because it must be asked, 'Which sutta pertains to latent tendencies and to penetration?' the words 'Therein, which pertains to latent tendencies and to penetration…' and so on were stated.

Mānusattaṃ manussabhāvaṃ laddhāna kiccaṃ, akiccañca dve bhavanti, dve kiccāniyeva kattabbāni. Tenāha aṭṭhakathācariyo (netti. aṭṭha. 111) “kattabba”nti dasseti. “Katamaṃ kattabbaṃ kicca”nti vattabbattā kattabbakiccaṃ dassetuṃ “sukiccaṃ cevā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Puññāni ca kattabbattā sukiccaṃ eva, saṃyojanavippahānaṃ vā kattabbattā sukiccaṃ nāmāti yojanā.

Having attained the human state, there are two things: what should be done and what should not be done; two duties are to be performed. Therefore the Commentator (Netti-aṭṭha. 111) states, 'should be done.' Because it must be said, 'What is the duty that should be done?' the words 'what is well done, etc.' were stated to show the duty that should be done. Meritorious deeds, because they should be done, are 'what is well done'; or the abandonment of the fetters, because it should be done, is called 'what is well done.' This is the construction.

“Tattha sutte katamena katamo dassito”ti vattabbattā “sukiccaṃceva puññānīti vāsanā, saṃyojanavippahānaṃ vāti nibbedho”ti vutto.

Because it must be said, 'Therein, in the sutta, which is shown by which?' it is stated: '“What is well done is meritorious deeds”—this is accumulation; “or the abandonment of the fetters”—this is penetration.'

“Ettakamevā”ti vattabbattā “puññāni karitvānā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Puññāni karitvāna katapuññā puggalā saggā saggato saggaṃyeva vajanti. Saṃyojanappahānā ariyā jarāmaraṇā jarāmaraṇato vippamuccanti.

Because it must be said, 'Is it only this much?' it is said, 'Having done meritorious deeds,' etc. Having done meritorious deeds, persons who have made merit go from a heavenly world to a heavenly world. The noble ones, by abandoning the fetters, are freed from aging and death.

“Tattha sutte katamena katamo dassito”ti vattabbattā “puññāni karitvāna, saggā saggaṃ vajanti katapuññā’ti vāsanā, ‘saṃyojanappahānā, jarāmaraṇā vippamuccantī’ti nibbedho”ti vuttaṃ.

Because it must be said, 'Therein, in the sutta, which is shown by which?', it is stated: '“Having done meritorious deeds, those who have made merit go from a heavenly world to a heavenly world”—this is accumulation; “through the abandonment of the fetters, they are freed from aging and death”—this is penetration.'

“Ettakamevā”ti [M 0.0316] vattabbattā “dvemānī”tiādi vuttaṃ. “Katamena katamo dassito”ti vattabbattā “tattha yo…pe… ayaṃ nibbedho”ti vuttaṃ.

Because it must be said, 'Is it only this much?' it is said, 'These two,' etc. Because it must be said, 'By which is which shown?' it is said, 'Therein, that which ...pe... this is penetration.'

Nānāvidhaṃ vāsanābhāgiyañca nibbedhabhāgiyañca suttaṃ ācariyena niddhāritaṃ, amhehi ca ñātaṃ[V 0.0434], “katamaṃ taṇhāsaṃkilesabhāgiyaṃ sutta”nti pucchitabbattā “tattha taṇhāsaṃkilesabhāgiya”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Tatthāti tesu soḷasasu saṃkilesabhāgiyādīsu suttesu taṇhāsaṃkilesabhāgiyaṃ suttaṃ taṇhāpakkheneva niddisitabbaṃ, bahuvisayattā niyametvāna niddhāressāmīti vuttaṃ hoti. “Kena pakārena niddisitabba”nti vattabbattā “tīhi taṇhāhī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Bhavataṇhāyāti rūpabhavataṇhāya. Vibhavataṇhāyāti arūpabhavataṇhāya. Yena yena vā pana vatthunā taṇhāpabhedaucchedādivatthunā ajjhositā bhavataṇhādivasena ajjhositā, tena tena pakārena taṇhādinā vā taṇhāpabhedaucchedādivatthunā vā taṇhāsaṃkilesabhāgiyaṃ suttaṃ niddisitabbaṃ.

The various suttas pertaining to accumulation and pertaining to penetration have been determined by the teacher, and have been understood by us. Because it must be asked, 'Which is the sutta pertaining to the defilement of craving?' it is said, 'Therein, pertaining to the defilement of craving,' etc. 'Therein' means: among those sixteen suttas pertaining to defilement and so on, the sutta pertaining to the defilement of craving should be indicated only from the side of craving. Because its subject matter is extensive, the meaning is: 'having defined it, I will specify it.' Because it must be said, 'In what way should it be indicated?' it is said, 'By the three cravings,' etc. 'By craving for being' means by craving for being in the form realm. 'By craving for non-being' means by craving for being in the formless realm. Or by whatever subject matter—such as the divisions of craving or annihilationism—one clings, clinging by way of craving for being and so on, by that manner, by craving and so on, or by the subject matter of the divisions of craving, annihilationism, and so on, the sutta pertaining to the defilement of craving should be indicated.

Taṇhāsaṃkilesabhāgiyaṃ suttaṃ taṇhāpakkheneva niddisitabbanti ācariyena vuttaṃ, amhehi ca lakkhitaṃ, “diṭṭhisaṃkilesabhāgiyaṃ suttaṃ kena pakkhena niddisitabba”nti vattabbattā “tattha diṭṭhisaṃkilesabhāgiya”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Yena yena vā pana vatthunāti diṭṭhippabhedaamarāvikkhepādivatthunā.

It has been said by the teacher, and noted by us, that the sutta pertaining to the defilement of craving should be indicated only from the side of craving. Because it must be said, 'From what side should the sutta pertaining to the defilement of views be indicated?' it is said, 'Therein, pertaining to the defilement of views,' etc. 'Or by whatever subject matter' means by the subject matter of things such as the divisions of views and eel-wriggling.

Diṭṭhisaṃkilesabhāgiyaṃ suttaṃ diṭṭhipakkheneva niddisitabbanti ācariyena vuttaṃ, amhehi ca lakkhitaṃ, “duccaritasaṃkilesabhāgiyaṃ suttaṃ kena pakārena niddisitabba”nti vattabbattā “tattha duccaritasaṃkilesabhāgiya”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Tatheva vattabbattā “tattha taṇhāvodānabhāgiya”ntiādi vuttaṃ, “diṭṭhivodānabhāgiya”ntiādi vuttaṃ, “duccaritavodānabhāgiya”ntiādi vuttaṃ.

It has been said by the teacher, and noted by us, that the sutta pertaining to the defilement of views should be indicated only from the side of views. Because it must be said, 'In what way should the sutta pertaining to the defilement of misconduct be indicated?' it is said, 'Therein, pertaining to the defilement of misconduct,' etc. Because it must be said in the same way, it is said, 'Therein, pertaining to the cleansing from craving,' etc.; 'pertaining to the cleansing from views,' etc.; and 'pertaining to the cleansing from misconduct,' etc.

112. Yasmiṃ sāsanapaṭṭhāne aṭṭhārasa mūlapadā daṭṭhabbā, taṃ sāsanapaṭṭhānaṃ soḷasahi saṃkilesabhāgiyādīhi suttehi ekadesaniddhāraṇavasena vibhajitaṃ, amhehi ca ñātaṃ, “kiṃ pana taṃ sāsanapaṭṭhānaṃ tehi soḷasahi eva saṃkilesabhāgiyādīhi vibhajitabbaṃ, udāhu aññehi suttehipi vibhajitabba”nti vattabbattā aññehi aṭṭhavīsasuttehipi vibhajituṃ “tattha katame aṭṭhārasa mūlapadā? Lokiyaṃ lokuttara”ntiādi vuttaṃ[M 0.0317]. “Yadi aññehipi aṭṭhavīsasuttehi vibhajitabbaṃ, evaṃ sati ‘lokiya’ntiādivacanameva vattabbaṃ, kasmā ‘tattha katame aṭṭhārasa mūlapadā’ti vuttā”ti ce? Tassa sāsanapaṭṭhānavibhāgo aṭṭhārasahi mūlapadehi saṅgahito, aṭṭhārasa mūlapadāpi vibhajite sāsanapaṭṭhāne daṭṭhabbā, tasmā mūlapadā vibhattāyeva. Tāni mūlapadāni vibhajituṃ “tattha katame aṭṭhārasa mūlapadā”ti vuttaṃ. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ (netti. aṭṭha. 112) pana –

112. That foundation of the teaching in which the eighteen root terms are to be seen has been analyzed by way of specifying a portion through the sixteen suttas pertaining to defilement and so on, and this has been understood by us. Because it must be asked, 'Now, should that foundation of the teaching be analyzed only by those sixteen suttas pertaining to defilement and so on, or should it also be analyzed by other suttas?' in order to analyze it by twenty-eight other suttas, it is said: 'Therein, what are the eighteen root terms? Mundane and supramundane,' etc. If it is said: 'If it is to be analyzed by twenty-eight other suttas, then only the words “mundane,” etc., should be stated. Why is it said, “Therein, what are the eighteen root terms?”' The reply is: The analysis of the foundation of the teaching is comprised by the eighteen root terms, and the eighteen root terms are to be seen in the analyzed foundation of the teaching. Therefore, the root terms are indeed analyzed. To analyze those root terms, it is said, 'Therein, what are the eighteen root terms?' But in the Commentary (Netti-aṭṭha. 112):

“Evaṃ [V 0.0435] soḷasavidhena sāsanapaṭṭhānaṃ nānāsuttehi udāharaṇavasena vibhajitvā idāni aṭṭhavīsatividhena sāsanapaṭṭhānaṃ dassentena yasmā ayampi paṭṭhānavibhāgo mūlapadehi saṅgahito, na imassāpi tehi asaṅgahito padeso atthi, tasmā mūlapadaṃ, vibhajitabbatañca dassetuṃ ‘tattha katame aṭṭhārasa mūlapadā’ti pucchāya vasena mūlapadāni uddharitvā ‘lokiyaṃ lokuttara’ntiādinā nava tikā, thavo cāti aṭṭhavīsatividhaṃ sāsanapaṭṭhānaṃ uddiṭṭha”nti –

“Having thus analyzed the foundation of the teaching in sixteen ways by means of various suttas as examples, now, as one is showing the foundation of the teaching in twenty-eight ways, since this analysis of the foundation is also comprised by the root terms and there is no part of it not comprised by them, therefore, to show the root terms and their analyzability, having extracted the root terms by way of the question, 'Therein, what are the eighteen root terms?' the twenty-eight-fold foundation of the teaching—nine triads and praise—has been set forth by means of 'mundane, supramundane,' etc.”

Vuttaṃ. Tatthāti tesu soḷasahārapañcakanayaaṭṭhārasamūlapadesu katamāni padāni mūlapadāni hontīti pucchati. Loke niyutto sabhāvadhammoti lokiyo, loke vā vidūhi vidito sabhāvotipi lokiyo, lokiyo sabhāvadhammo assa visesasuttassa atthīti taṃ visesasuttaṃ lokiyaṃ nāma. Esa nayo “lokuttara”ntiādīsupi veditabbo. Jānātīti ñāṇaṃ, ñāṇaṃ assa visesasuttassa atthīti ñāṇaṃ. Ñātabbāti ñeyyā, ñeyyā assa visesasuttassa atthīti ñeyyaṃ. Eseva nayo – “ñāṇañca ñeyyañcā”ti etthāpi veditabbo. Nibbānaṃ paṭhamaṃ passatīti dassanaṃ, paṭhamamaggañāṇaṃ, dassanaṃ assa visesasuttassa atthīti dassanaṃ. Bhāvanā assa visesasuttassa pāḷiyā atthīti bhāvanā. “Dassanañca bhāvanā cā”ti etthāpi esa nayo veditabbo. Sassa attano vacananti sakaṃ, sakaṃ vacanaṃ sakavacanaṃ, bhagavato vacananti attho. Parassa vacanaṃ paravacanaṃ. Vissajjanīyo assa visesasuttassa atthīti vissajjanīyaṃ. Natthi vissajjanīyo assa visesasuttassāti avissajjanīyaṃ. Kammaṃ assa visesasuttassa atthīti kammaṃ. Vipāko assa pāṭhassa atthīti vipāko[M 0.0318]. Sesesupi assatthiattho gahetabbo. Atha vā lokiyādiattho mukhyattho, taṃvācakasuttampi ṭhānyūpacārena vuttaṃ. Buddhādīnaṃ guṇe abhitthavati etena suttappadesenāti thavo, suttappadeso.

It is said. 'Therein'—he asks which terms among these sixteen modes of conveyance, five methods, and eighteen root terms are the root terms. 'A natural phenomenon connected with the world' is worldly (lokiya). Or, 'a natural phenomenon known by the wise in the world' is worldly. Because that particular sutta has a worldly nature, that particular sutta is called 'worldly.' This method should be understood similarly for 'supramundane,' etc. 'One knows,' thus it is knowledge (ñāṇa). Because that particular sutta has knowledge, it is 'knowledge.' 'To be known,' thus it is the knowable (ñeyya). Because that particular sutta has the knowable, it is 'the knowable.' This same method should be understood here too in 'knowledge and the knowable.' 'One sees Nibbāna first,' thus it is seeing (dassana), that is, the knowledge of the first path. Because that particular sutta has seeing, it is 'seeing.' Because the text of that particular sutta has development (bhāvanā), it is 'development.' Here too, in 'seeing and development,' this method should be understood. 'One's own word' is one's own (sakaṃ). One's own word (sakavacanaṃ) means the word of the Blessed One. Another's word is paravacanaṃ. Because that particular sutta has what is to be explained (vissajjanīyo), it is 'to be explained' (vissajjanīyaṃ). Because that particular sutta has nothing to be explained, it is 'not to be explained' (avissajjanīyaṃ). Because that particular sutta has kamma, it is 'kamma.' Because this passage has result (vipāko), it is 'result.' In the remaining cases too, the meaning 'it has' should be understood. Or else, the primary meaning is 'worldly,' etc., and the sutta that expresses it is also spoken of by a metaphor of location. 'One praises the qualities of the Buddha and others with this portion of a sutta,' thus it is praise (thavo), a portion of a sutta.

“Tesu aṭṭhavīsatividhesu lokiyādīsu sāsanapaṭṭhānasuttesu katamaṃ suttaṃ lokiyaṃ sutta”nti pucchitabbattā “tattha katamaṃ lokiya”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Tatthāti tesu aṭṭhavīsatividhesu lokiyādīsu sāsanapaṭṭhānasuttesu katamaṃ suttaṃ lokiyaṃ sāsanapaṭṭhānaṃ suttanti pucchati.

Because it must be asked, 'Among those twenty-eight kinds of suttas on the foundation of the teaching, such as the worldly, which sutta is the worldly sutta?' it is said, 'Therein, which is the worldly?' etc. 'Therein'—he asks: 'Among those twenty-eight kinds of suttas on the foundation of the teaching, such as the worldly, which sutta is the worldly sutta that is a foundation of the teaching?'

Bhikkhave, dhenuyā thanehi nikkhantaṃ sajjukhīraṃ nikkhantakkhaṇe na muccati na pariṇamati khīrabhāvaṃ pajahitvā dadhibhāvaṃ na pāpuṇāti, takkādiambilasamāyogato pacchā khīrabhāvaṃ pajahati dadhibhāvaṃ pāpuṇāti iva, evaṃ yena bālena pāpaṃ yaṃ kammaṃ kataṃ, taṃ kammaṃ karaṇakkhaṇe [V 0.0436] tassa bālassa apāyadukkhādinibbattāpanavasena na vipaccati. Dutiye pana vā tatiyādimhi vā attabhāve vipaccati. Bhasmacchanno chārikāya paṭicchanno pāvako aggi akkantaṃ janaṃ akkamanakkhaṇe na ḍahati. Chārikaṃ pana tāpetvā kālantare ḍahati iva, evaṃ yena bālena pāpaṃ yaṃ kammaṃ kataṃ, taṃ kammaṃ karaṇakkhaṇe taṃ bālaṃ apāyadukkhādinibbattāpanavasena ḍahāpentaṃ hutvā na anveti. Dutiye vā tatiyādimhi vā attabhāve apāyadukkhādinibbattāpanavasena ḍahāpentaṃ hutvā ḍahantaṃ taṃ bālaṃ taṃ anvetīti yojanā. Idaṃ “na hi…pe… pāvako”ti suttaṃ lokiye atthe vācakañāpakabhāvena pavattanato lokiyaṃ nāma.

Just as, monks, fresh milk drawn from a cow's udder does not curdle or change at that very moment; it does not give up its nature as milk and acquire the nature of curds, but does so later through contact with buttermilk or some other souring agent; so too, whatever evil kamma has been done by a fool, that kamma does not ripen at the moment it is done by way of producing suffering in the plane of misery for that fool. But it ripens in a second, third, or subsequent existence. Just as a fire covered with ash, concealed by embers, does not burn a person who steps on it at the moment of stepping, but after heating the embers, it burns him after some time; so too, whatever evil kamma has been done by a fool, that kamma does not follow him at the moment it is done, causing him to be burned by way of producing suffering in the plane of misery. But in a second, third, or subsequent existence, it follows that fool, burning him and causing him to be burned by way of producing suffering in the plane of misery. This is the construction. This sutta, 'For not ...pe... a fire,' is called 'worldly' because it proceeds by way of expressing and indicating a worldly meaning.

“Ettakameva lokiya”nti vattabbattā “cattārimānī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Attho pākaṭo. Idaṃ “cattārimāni…pe… kāḷapakkheva candimā”ti suttaṃ lokiye atthe vācakañāpakabhāvena pavattanato lokiyaṃ nāma.

Because it can be said, 'Only this much is worldly,' the passage beginning 'these four' was stated. The meaning is clear. This sutta, 'these four... like the moon in the dark fortnight,' is called 'worldly' because it functions by way of expressing and indicating a worldly meaning.

“Evaṃ duvidhaṃyeva lokiya”nti vattabbattā “aṭṭhime, bhikkhave, lokadhammā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Attho pākaṭo. Idaṃ “aṭṭhime”tiādikaṃ suttaṃ lokiyesu aṭṭhavidhesu atthesu vācakañāpakabhāvena pavattanato lokiyaṃ nāma.

Because it can be said, 'Thus the worldly is just twofold,' the passage beginning 'Bhikkhus, there are these eight worldly conditions' was stated. The meaning is clear. This discourse beginning with 'There are these eight' is called 'worldly' because it functions by way of expressing and indicating the eight kinds of worldly meanings.

Nānāvidhaṃ lokiyaṃ ācariyena niddhāritaṃ, amhehi ca ñātaṃ, “katamaṃ suttaṃ lokuttara”nti vattabbattā “tattha katamaṃ lokuttara”ntiādi vuttaṃ[M 0.0319]. Ito paresupi esa nayo veditabbo. Tatthāti tesu aṭṭhavīsatividhesu lokiyādīsu suttesu.

The various kinds of worldly teachings have been determined by the teacher, and they are known by us. Because it should be said, 'Which sutta is supramundane?' the passage beginning 'Therein, what is supramundane?' was stated. Hereafter, this same method should be understood. Therein means: among those twenty-eight kinds of suttas, the worldly and so on.

Chekena sārathinā sudantā assā samathaṅgatā yathā, evaṃ pahīnamānassa pahīnanavavidhamānassa yassa anāsavassa bhikkhuno indriyāni chabbidhāni cakkhundriyādīni samathaṅgatāni. Tādino tādilakkhaṇena samannāgatassa anāsavassa tassa bhikkhuno devāpi manussāpi pihayantīti yojanā. Idaṃ “yassindriyānī”tiādikaṃ suttaṃ lokuttare atthe vācakañāpakabhāvena pavattanato lokuttaraṃ nāma.

Just as horses well-tamed by a skilled charioteer have become calm, so the sixfold faculties—the eye-faculty and so on—of a bhikkhu who has abandoned conceit, who has abandoned the ninefold conceit, who is taintless, have become calm. Even gods and humans yearn for that taintless bhikkhu who is Such, endowed with the characteristic of being Such. This is the syntactical connection. This discourse beginning with 'whose faculties,' because it functions by way of expressing and indicating a supramundane meaning, is called 'supramundane.'

“Ettakamevā”ti vattabbattā “pañcimāni bhikkhave indriyānī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Idaṃ “pañcimānī”tiādikaṃ suttampi lokuttare atthe vācakañāpakabhāvena pavattanato lokuttaraṃ nāma. (1)

Because it should be said, 'Only this much,' the passage beginning 'Bhikkhus, there are these five faculties' was stated. This sutta beginning with 'these five' is also called 'supramundane' because it functions by way of expressing and indicating a supramundane meaning. (1)

“Laddhāna [V 0.0437] mānusattaṃ dve, kiccaṃ akiccameva cā”tiādikā dve gāthā vuttā. Iha gāthāsu “sukiccaṃ ceva puññānī”ti yaṃ gāthāpadañca “puññāni karitvāna, saggā saggaṃ vajanti katapuññā”ti yaṃ gāthāpadañca vuttaṃ, idaṃ gāthāpadaṃ lokiye atthe vācakañāpakabhāvena pavattanato lokiyaṃ nāma.

The two verses beginning, "Having obtained a human state, two things, what should be done and what should not be done," were stated. Here, in the verses, the line of verse "what is well done and meritorious deeds" and the line of verse "having done meritorious deeds, those who have made merit go from heaven to heaven" were stated. This line of verse is called 'worldly' because it functions by way of expressing and indicating a worldly meaning.

Iha gāthāsu “saṃyojanavippahānaṃ vā”ti yaṃ gāthāpadañca “saṃyojanavippahānā, jarāmaraṇā vippamuccantī”ti yaṃ gāthāpadañca vuttaṃ, idaṃ gāthāpadaṃ vuttanayena lokuttaraṃ nāma. Idaṃ “laddhānā”tiādikaṃ vuttappakārena lokiyañca lokuttarañca.

Here, in the verses, the line of verse "or the abandoning of the fetters" and the line of verse "through the abandoning of the fetters, they are freed from aging and death" were stated. This line of verse, in the way stated, is called 'supramundane.' This passage beginning with "having obtained," in the manner stated, is both worldly and supramundane.

Bhikkhave, viññāṇe āhāre āhārapaṭibaddhe chandarāge sati nāmarūpassa avakkanti hoti. “Viññāṇe…pe… hotī”ti idaṃ vuttanayena lokiyaṃ nāma. “Viññāṇe…pe… nirodho”ti idaṃ suttaṃ lokuttaraṃ nāma. Idaṃ “viññāṇe ce bhikkhave”tiādikaṃ suttaṃ lokiye atthe ca lokuttare atthe ca ekadesavasena vācakañāpakavasena pavattanato lokiyañca lokuttarañca. (2)

Bhikkhus, when there is desire and lust for consciousness as nutriment, for what is connected with nutriment, there is the descent of name-and-form. The passage 'Consciousness... there is'—this, in the way stated, is called 'worldly.' The sutta 'Consciousness... cessation'—this is called 'supramundane.' This sutta beginning with 'Bhikkhus, if in consciousness' is both worldly and supramundane because it functions partially by way of expressing and indicating in both a worldly sense and a supramundane sense. (2)

113. Sattaloke sabbā disā anuparigamma kvaci disāyaṃ cetasā attanā attato piyataraṃ aññaṃ neva ajjhagā, attāva piyataro yathā[M 0.0320], evaṃ paresaṃ sattānaṃ puthu visuṃ visuṃ attāva piyo piyataro, tasmā attanova piyatarattā attakāmo attano hitakāmo paṇḍito sattaloko attānaṃ upamaṃ katvā paraṃ na hiṃse na hiṃseyyāti yojanā. Idaṃ “sabbā disā”tiādikaṃ suttaṃ sattesu vācakañāpakabhāvena pavattanato sattādhiṭṭhānaṃ nāma.

113. Having traversed all directions with one's mind in the world of beings, one finds no one anywhere dearer than oneself. Just as oneself is dearest, so for other beings, each one separately, oneself is dear, very dear. Therefore, since oneself is so dear, one who loves oneself, who desires one's own welfare, a wise person, having made oneself the example, should not harm another. This is the syntactical connection. This sutta beginning with 'all directions' is called 'founded on beings' because it functions by way of expressing and indicating with regard to beings.

Ye keci khīṇāsavā puggalā bhūtāva na bhavissanti, sabbe te khīṇāsavā puggalā dehaṃ attabhāvaṃ pahāya nibbānaṃ gamissanti. Ye ca puthujjanādayo sattā punabbhavesu bhavissanti, sabbe te puthujjanādayo sattā dehaṃ attabhāvaṃ pahāya paralokaṃ gamissanti, taṃ sabbajāniṃ sabbassa sattassa hāniṃ maraṇaṃ, vināsaṃ vā kusalo yo puggalo vijānāti, so kusalo puggalo taṃ sabbajāniṃ viditvā ātāpiyo brahmacariyaṃ careyyāti yojanā. Idaṃ “ye kecī”tiādikaṃ vuttanayena sattādhiṭṭhānaṃ.

Whatever persons whose taints are destroyed have come to be will not be reborn. All those persons whose taints are destroyed, having abandoned the body and their personal existence, will go to Nibbāna. And whatever worldlings and other beings will be reborn in future existences, all those worldlings and other beings, having abandoned the body and their personal existence, will go to the next world. A skilled person who understands that universal decay, the loss of all beings, death, or destruction—that skilled person, having understood this universal decay, should live the holy life ardently. This is the syntactical connection. This passage beginning with "whatever" is, in the way stated, founded on beings.

Sattahi aṅgehi samannāgataṃ kalyāṇamittaṃ yāvajīvaṃ kusalena puggalena na vijahitabbaṃ. Katamehi sattahi? Parisuddhasīlasampattiparisuddhadiṭṭhisampattīhi samannāgatattā piyo ca piyāyitabbo [V 0.0438] ca hoti, pāsāṇachattaṃ viya garu ca hoti, sambhāvetabbatāya bhāvanīyo ca hoti, “kālena vadāmi, no akālenā”tiādike pañcadhamme attani upaṭṭhāpetvā sabrahmacārīnaṃ vā sissānaṃ vā vinicchayaullumpanaovādadānabhāve ṭhatvā vattā ca hoti, sabrahmacārīhi vā sissādīhi vā vuccamāno suvaco hutvā tesaṃ vacanakkhamo ca hoti, saccapaṭiccasamuppādādigambhīraṃ vā aññaṃ gambhīraṃ vā kathaṃ kattā ca hoti, dhammavinayādivaseneva dīpanato aṭṭhāne ca na niyojako hoti. Imehi sattahi aṅgehi samannāgataṃ kalyāṇamittaṃ yāvajīvaṃ na vijahitabbaṃ. Idaṃ “sattahī”tiādivacanaṃ bhagavā avoca. Idaṃ “sattahī”tiādikaṃ vacanaṃ sugato vatvā athāparaṃ etaṃ gāthāvacanaṃ satthā avoca. Kiṃ avoca?

A spiritual friend endowed with seven factors should not be abandoned for life by a skilled person. With what seven? Because they are endowed with purity of virtue and purity of view, they are dear and to be held dear; they are venerable like a stone umbrella; they are to be revered because they are worthy of esteem; having established in themselves the five qualities—'I speak at the right time, not at the wrong time,' etc.—they are a speaker who stands in the position of giving judgment, dispelling doubt, and giving advice to their companions in the holy life or to their disciples; when spoken to by their companions in the holy life or their disciples, they are easy to speak to and patient of their words; they are a speaker of profound talk, such as on the truth of dependent origination or other profound matters; and by explaining in accordance with the Dhamma and Vinaya, they do not engage one in what is improper. A spiritual friend endowed with these seven factors should not be abandoned for life. The Blessed One spoke this statement beginning 'With seven.' Having spoken this statement, the Sugata, the Teacher, then spoke this further utterance in verse. What did he say?

“Piyo garu bhāvanīyo, vattā ca vacanakkhamo;

Gambhīrañca kathaṃ kattā, na caṭṭhāne niyojako;

Taṃ mittaṃ mittakāmena, yāvajīvampi seviya”nti. –

"Dear, venerable, and to be revered, a speaker and patient of speech, a speaker of profound talk, who does not engage one in what is improper. One who desires a friend should associate with such a friend even for one's whole life."

Etaṃ [M 0.0321] gāthāvacanaṃ satthā avocāti yojanā. “Na ca aṭṭhānayojako”ti pāṭho atthi. Idaṃ “sattahī”tiādikaṃ vacanaṃ sattādhiṭṭhānaṃ.

The syntactical connection is: 'The Teacher spoke this utterance in verse.' There is the variant reading: 'And not one who engages in what is improper.' This statement beginning with 'With seven' is founded on beings.

Loke yaṃ kāmasukhañca yaṃ idaṃ diviyaṃ sukhañca atthi, ete kāmasukhadiviyasukhā taṇhākkhayasukhassa soḷasiṃ kalaṃ na agghantīti yojanā. Idaṃ “yañcā”tiādikaṃ suttaṃ dhammādhiṭṭhānaṃ.

The syntactical connection is as follows: Whatever sensual pleasure and whatever divine pleasure there is in the world, these sensual and divine pleasures are not worth a sixteenth part of the happiness of the destruction of craving. This sutta beginning with 'Whatever' is founded on the Dhamma.

Yattha nibbāne dukkhaṃ nirujjhati, sammāsambuddhadesitaṃ asokaṃ virajaṃ khemaṃ taṃ nibbānaṃ susukhaṃ vatāti yojanā. Idaṃ “susukha”ntiādikaṃ suttampi dhammādhiṭṭhānaṃ. (3)

The syntactical connection is as follows: That Nibbāna wherein suffering ceases—taught by the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, sorrowless, dustless, and secure—is truly a great happiness indeed. This sutta beginning with 'A great happiness' is also founded on the Dhamma. (3)

Tīsu bhavesu sattānaṃ jananato taṇhāsaṅkhātaṃ mātarañca, pitaraṃ nissāya mānassa uppajjanato mānasaṅkhātaṃ pitarañca, raṭṭhe loko raṭṭhissaraṃ rājānaṃ bhajati viya dvinnaṃ sassatucchedadiṭṭhīnaṃ sabbadiṭṭhigatehi bhajanīyattā sassatucchedadiṭṭhisaṅkhāte khattiye dve rājāno ca, āyasādhako puriso raṭṭhe atthaṃ anucarati iva nandirāgassa dvādasāyatane anucaraṇato nandirāgasaṅkhātena anucaraṇena saha pavattanaṭṭhānaṃ dvādasāyatanasaṅkhātaṃ raṭṭhañca khīṇāsavo yo brāhmaṇo hanati, so brāhmaṇo hantvā anīgho niddukkho hutvā yātīti yojanā. Iha “mātara”ntiādigāthāyaṃ [V 0.0439] “mātaraṃ…pe… hantvā”ti idaṃ gāthāvacanaṃ dhammādhiṭṭhānaṃ. “Anīgho yāti brāhmaṇo”ti idaṃ gāthāvacanaṃ sattādhiṭṭhānaṃ. Idaṃ “mātara”ntiādikaṃ suttaṃ sattādhiṭṭhānañca dhammādhiṭṭhānañca.

The syntactical connection is as follows: Whatever brahmin, one whose taints are destroyed, slays craving, designated as mother because it generates beings in the three kinds of existence; and conceit, designated as father because conceit arises in dependence on a father; and the two khattiya kings, designated as the two views of eternalism and annihilationism, because they are to be followed by all who hold views just as the people in a country follow the king of the country; and the country, designated as the twelve sense bases, which is the place where one fares together with the attendant designated as delight and lust, because delight and lust follow upon the twelve sense bases just as a man seeking revenue fares about a country—that brahmin, having slain them, goes untroubled and free from suffering. Here, in the verse beginning 'mother,' the utterance 'having slain mother...' is founded on the Dhamma. The utterance 'the brahmin goes untroubled' is founded on beings. This sutta beginning with 'mother' is founded on both beings and the Dhamma.

“Cattārome bhikkhave iddhipādā”ti idaṃ suttappadesavacanaṃ dhammādhiṭṭhānaṃ. So catūhi iddhipādehi samannāgato puggalo kāyepi karajakāyepi cittaṃ pādakajjhānacittaṃ samodahati pakkhipati, so puggalo dissamānakāyena gantukāmo karajakāyagatikaṃ pādakajjhānacittaṃ adhiṭṭhahati. Cittepi pādakajjhānacittepi kāyaṃ karajakāyaṃ samodahati pakkhipati, so puggalo sīghaṃ aññaṃ gantukāmo pādakajjhānacittagatikaṃ karajakāyaṃ adhiṭṭhahati. Kāye karajakāye sukhasaññañca sukhavihārasaññañca lahusaññañca lahugamanasaññañca okkamitvā aññaṃ gamaneyyaṃ icchitaṭṭhānaṃ ekacittakkhaṇeneva ca gantvā upasampajja viharati. Idaṃ “so”tiādikaṃ suttappadesavacanaṃ sattādhiṭṭhānaṃ. Idaṃ “cattārome”tiādikaṃ suttaṃ sattādhiṭṭhānañca dhammādhiṭṭhānañca. (4)

"Bhikkhus, there are these four bases of spiritual power." This utterance, a passage from a sutta, is founded on the Dhamma. A person endowed with the four bases of spiritual power places and inserts the mind—the mind of the basic jhāna—into the physical body. That person, desiring to go with the visible body, resolves upon the mind of the basic jhāna, which pertains to the movement of the physical body. They also place and insert the physical body into the mind—the mind of the basic jhāna. That person, desiring to go elsewhere swiftly, resolves upon the physical body, which pertains to the movement of the mind of the basic jhāna. Having entered upon the perception of pleasure, the perception of a pleasant dwelling, the perception of lightness, and the perception of light travel in the physical body, they go to a desired destination in a single mind-moment and dwell there, having attained it. This utterance, a passage from a sutta beginning with 'That person,' is founded on beings. This sutta beginning with 'These four' is founded on both beings and the Dhamma. (4)

114. Yaṃ [M 0.0322] sabbaññutañāṇaṃ lokuttaraṃ lokaṃ uttaritvā abhibhavitvā ṭhitaṃ, yena sabbaññutaññāṇena bhagavā “sabbaññū”ti vuccati, tassa sabbaññutaññāṇassa parihānaṃ natthi, taṃ sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ sabbakāle jānituṃ āvajjanakāle pavattatīti yojanā. Idaṃ “yaṃ ta”ntiādikaṃ ñāṇe atthe vācakañāpakabhāvenapi pavattanato ñāṇaṃ nāma.

114. The knowledge of omniscience is supramundane, established by having transcended and overcome the world. By this knowledge of omniscience the Blessed One is called 'the Omniscient One.' There is no decline of that knowledge of omniscience; that knowledge of omniscience arises at the time of adverting in order to know at all times—this is the construction. This, beginning with 'that which,' is called 'knowledge' because it proceeds by way of indicating and making known the meaning in the domain of knowledge.

Yāya nibbānagāminiyā maggapaññāya jātimaraṇasaṅkhayaṃ pajānāti, sā nibbānagāminī maggapaññā sabbāhi lokiyāhi paññāhi seṭṭhā pasatthāti yojanā. Idaṃ “paññā hī”tiādikaṃ vuttanayena ñāṇaṃ nāma.

By means of that path-wisdom leading to Nibbāna one understands the destruction of birth and death; that path-wisdom leading to Nibbāna is the best and most praiseworthy of all mundane kinds of wisdom—this is the construction. This, beginning with 'wisdom indeed,' is called 'knowledge' in the aforesaid manner.

“Dhotaka, vo tumhākaṃ santiṃ ahaṃ kittayissāmī”ti bhagavā avoca. “Diṭṭhe dhamme dukkhādidhamme vā attabhāve vā sato aniccānupassanādisatisampanno hutvā caraṃ caranto yogāvacaro anītihaṃ yaṃ santiṃ yaṃ nibbānaṃ ariyamaggena viditvā loke saṃsāraloke visattikaṃ visappakaṃ taṇhaṃ tare tareyyā”ti bhagavā avoca.

'Dhotaka, I will proclaim peace to you,' said the Blessed One. 'Faring mindfully, endowed with mindfulness of such things as the contemplation of impermanence in regard to phenomena such as suffering or in one's own existence in this very life, the practitioner, having known not by hearsay that peace, that Nibbāna, by means of the noble path, would cross over craving—that which clings and spreads—in the world, in the world of saṃsāra.' Thus spoke the Blessed One.

Dhotako bhagavantaṃ vadati “mahesi mahante sīlakkhandhādī esanasīla, gotama, sato ‘sabbe saṅkhārā aniccā’tiādisaraṇasampanno hutvā caraṃ caranto yogāvacaro uttamaṃ yaṃ santiṃ yaṃ [V 0.0440] nibbānaṃ ariyamaggena viditvā loke saṃsāraloke visattikaṃ taṇhaṃ tare tareyyāti tañca vacanaṃ tañca santiṃ nibbānaṃ ahaṃ abhinandāmi abhipatthayāmi, mahesi tvaṃ, yañca sampajānāsī”ti dhotako bhagavantaṃ vadati.

Dhotaka said to the Blessed One: 'O great sage, Gotama, you who are of a seeking nature for the great aggregates of virtue and so on! The practitioner, faring along mindfully, endowed with the recollection of such things as "all formations are impermanent," having known by the noble path that supreme peace, that Nibbāna, would cross over craving, which is attachment, in the world, in the world of saṃsāra. I rejoice in and long for that statement and that peace, Nibbāna. O great sage, you are one who fully understands this.' Thus said Dhotaka to the Blessed One.

“Dhotakā”ti ālapitvā bhagavā dhotakaṃ avoca. “Uddhaṃ anāgataṃ upari adho atītaṃ heṭṭhā ca tiriyañcāpi majjhe paccuppannaṃ parito ca loke saṃsāraloke etaṃ taṇhaṃ bhavābhavāya khuddakabhavamahantabhavatthāya saṅgo laggoti viditvā vicaranto tvaṃ taṇhaṃ mākāsi mā akāsī”ti bhagavā dhotakaṃ avocāti yojanā. Idaṃ “kittayissāmī”tiādikaṃ ñeyye visaye atthe vācakañāpakabhāvena pavattanato ñeyyaṃ nāma.

'O Dhotaka,' the Blessed One said, addressing Dhotaka. 'Above in the future, below in the past, and across in the present, all around in the world, in the world of saṃsāra—having known that this craving is an attachment and a bond for existence and non-existence, for the sake of minor existence and great existence, you who are faring along should not create this craving, do not make it.' Thus the Blessed One spoke to Dhotaka—this is the construction. This, beginning with 'I will proclaim,' is called 'the knowable' because it proceeds by way of indicating and making known the meaning in the domain of the knowable.

“Ettakamevā”ti vattabbattā “catunnaṃ bhikkhave”tiādi vuttaṃ. Bhikkhave, catunnaṃ ariyasaccānaṃ ariyabhāvakarānaṃ saccānaṃ ananubodhā abujjhanena appaṭivedhā appaṭivijjhanena evaṃ iminā kāraṇena mamañceva tumhākañca dīghamaddhānaṃ idaṃ sandhāvitaṃ sandhāvanaṃ, idaṃ saṃsaritaṃ saṃsaraṇaṃ ahosīti, bhikkhave, ajja [M 0.0323] tayidaṃ taṃ idaṃ dukkhaṃ ariyasaccaṃ mayā anubuddhaṃ paṭividdhaṃ…pe… tayidaṃ taṃ idaṃ dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadā ariyasaccaṃ mayā anubuddhaṃ paṭividdhaṃ, mama bhavataṇhā ucchinnā, bhavanetti taṇhā khīṇā, idāni mama punabbhavo natthi, iti idaṃ “catunna”ntiādikaṃ bhagavā avoca, sugato idaṃ “catunna”ntiādikaṃ vatvā athāparaṃ etaṃ “catunna”ntiādigāthāvacanaṃ satthā avocāti yojetvā gāthāyañca tatheva yojanā kātabbā. Idaṃ “catunna”ntiādikaṃ vuttanayena ñeyyaṃ nāma. (5)

Because it should be said 'just this much,' the passage beginning 'Bhikkhus, of the four' was spoken. 'Bhikkhus, it is through not awakening to, not understanding, not penetrating the four noble truths—the truths that make one noble—that for a long time this running on, this transmigrating, has occurred for both me and for you. Bhikkhus, today this noble truth of suffering has been awakened to by me, has been penetrated... this noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering has been awakened to by me, has been penetrated. My craving for existence has been uprooted, the guide to existence is destroyed, now there is no more renewed existence for me.' Thus the Blessed One spoke this, beginning with 'the four.' The Sugata, having spoken thus, then the Teacher spoke this verse beginning with 'the four'—thus it should be connected, and in the verse, too, the connection should be made in the same way. This, beginning with 'the four,' is 'the knowable' in the aforesaid manner. (5)

“Rūpaṃ aniccaṃ…pe… viññāṇaṃ anicca”nti idaṃ suttaṃ ñeyye rūpādidhamme vācakañāpakabhāvena pavattanato ñeyyaṃ nāma.

'Form is impermanent... consciousness is impermanent'—this discourse is called 'the knowable' because it proceeds by way of indicating and making known the meaning in regard to knowable phenomena such as form.

Evaṃ “rūpaṃ anicca”ntiādinā pakārena jānaṃ jānanto evaṃ “rūpaṃ anicca”ntiādinā pakārena passaṃ passanto ariyasāvako ariyassa bhagavato sāvako “idaṃ rūpaṃ anicca”nti rūpaṃ passati, “ayaṃ vedanā aniccā”ti vedanaṃ passati, “ayaṃ saññā aniccā”ti saññaṃ passati, “ime saṅkhārā aniccā”ti saṅkhāre passati, “idaṃ viññāṇaṃ anicca”nti viññāṇaṃ passati. Iti idaṃ suttaṃ rūpādipassane ñāṇe vācakañāpakabhāvena pavattanato ñāṇaṃ nāma.

Thus, knowing in this way—'form is impermanent,' etc.—and seeing in this way—'form is impermanent,' etc.—the noble disciple, a disciple of the Blessed One, sees: 'This form is impermanent'; he sees: 'This feeling is impermanent'; he sees: 'This perception is impermanent'; he sees: 'These formations are impermanent'; he sees: 'This consciousness is impermanent.' Thus, this discourse is called 'knowledge' because it proceeds by way of indicating and making known the knowledge in the seeing of form and so on.

So [V 0.0441] “rūpaṃ anicca”ntiādinā pakārena passanto ariyasāvako rūpena rūparāgena parimuccati…pe… viññāṇamhā viññāṇarāgamhā parimuccatīti dukkhasmā parimuccatīti ahaṃ vadāmīti yojanā. Idaṃ “so parimuccatī”tiādikaṃ suttaṃ ñāṇe ca ñeyye ca vācakañāpakabhāvena pavattanato ñāṇañca ñeyyañca hoti.

Seeing in this way—'form is impermanent,' etc.—the noble disciple is liberated from form, from lust for form... is liberated from consciousness, from lust for consciousness. 'He is liberated from suffering,' I say—this is the construction. This discourse, beginning with 'he is liberated,' is both knowledge and the knowable because it proceeds by way of indicating and making known the meaning in regard to both knowledge and the knowable.

Sabbe pañcakkhandhā paccayehi saṅkharitattā saṅkhārā ādiantavantabhāvato, aniccantikabhāvato, tāvakālikabhāvato ca khaṇaparittabhāvato aniccā bhavanti. Idaṃ “sabbe saṅkhārā aniccā”ti suttappadesavacanaṃ vuttanayena ñeyyaṃ nāma. Yadā vipassanākaraṇakāle paññāya vipassanāpaññāya passati aniccatādikaṃ passati. Idaṃ “yadā paññāya passatī”ti suttappadesavacanaṃ ñāṇaṃ nāma. Atha passanakkhaṇe dukkhe pañcakkhandhe vipassako nibbindati, nibbindanto puggalo dukkhādijānanādivasena cattāri saccāni paṭivijjhati, eso catusaccapaṭivedho visuddhiyā visuddhatthāya maggoti. Idaṃ “athā”tiādikaṃ suttappadesavacanaṃ ñāṇañca ñeyyañca hoti.

All five aggregates are formations because they are formed by conditions. They are impermanent because they have a beginning and an end, because of their impermanent nature, their temporary nature, and their momentary nature. This passage from the discourse, 'All formations are impermanent,' is 'the knowable' in the aforesaid manner. When, at the time of practicing insight, one sees with wisdom, with insight-wisdom, one sees impermanence and so on. This passage from the discourse, 'When one sees with wisdom,' is 'knowledge.' Then, at the moment of seeing, the insight meditator becomes disenchanted with the five aggregates, which are suffering. Becoming disenchanted, the person penetrates the four truths by way of knowing suffering and so on. This penetration of the four truths is the path for purification, for the sake of purity. This passage from the discourse beginning with 'Then' is both knowledge and the knowable.

Soṇāti [M 0.0324] soṇaṃ ālapati. Samaṇā bāhirakasamaṇā brāhmaṇā jātibrāhmaṇā aniccena rūpena, dukkhena rūpena, vipariṇāmadhammena rūpena “ahaṃ parehi seyyo uttamo asmī”ti vā samanupassanti, “ahaṃ parena sadiso samāno asmī”ti vā samanupassanti, “ahaṃ parato hīno lāmako asmī”ti vā samanupassanti, yathābhūtassa adassanā aññatra vajjetvā aññaṃ kiṃ nāma kāraṇaṃ siyā, yathābhūtaṃ adassanato tāva samanupassanassa aññaṃ kāraṇaṃ natthi, yathābhūtaṃ adassanameva kāraṇanti veditabbaṃ. “Aniccāya vedanāyā”tiādīsupi iminā vuttanayena vuttanayānusārena yojanā kātabbā. Idaṃ “ye hi kecī”tiādikaṃ suttappadesavacanaṃ ñeyyaṃ nāma. “Ye ca kho kecī”tiādiko sukkapakkho pana vuttavipariyāyena veditabbo. Idaṃ “ye ca kho”tiādikaṃ suttappadesavacanaṃ ñāṇaṃ nāma. Idaṃ “ye hi kecī”tiādikaṃ suttaṃ ñāṇe ca ñeyye ca atthe vācakañāpakabhāvena pavattanato ñāṇañca ñeyyañca hoti. (6)

'Soṇa!'—he addresses Soṇa. Ascetics, non-Buddhist ascetics, brahmins, and brahmins by birth who, with regard to impermanent form, suffering form, and form subject to change, conceive 'I am better than others, supreme,' or 'I am equal to another,' or 'I am inferior to another, base'—what other reason could there be for this apart from not seeing things as they really are? Indeed, for such conceiving there is no other reason than not seeing things as they really are; it should be understood that not seeing things as they really are is the only reason. In the case of 'impermanent feeling,' and so on, the application should be made in accordance with the method stated here. This passage from the discourse beginning 'Whatever ascetics or brahmins...' is 'the knowable.' The bright-side portion beginning 'But whatever ascetics or brahmins...' should be understood in the opposite way. This passage from the discourse beginning 'But whatever...' is 'knowledge.' This discourse beginning 'Whatever ascetics or brahmins...' is both knowledge and the knowable because it proceeds by way of indicating and making known the meaning in regard to both knowledge and the knowable. (6)

Nānāvidhaṃ ñāṇañca ñeyyañca sāsanapaṭṭhānasuttaṃ ācariyena niddhāritaṃ, amhehi ca ñātaṃ, “katamaṃ dassana”nti pucchitabbattā “tattha katamaṃ dassana”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Tatthāti tesu lokiyādīsu aṭṭhavīsatividhesu sāsanapaṭṭhānesu suttesu katamaṃ suttaṃ dassanaṃ nāmāti pucchati.

The Discourse on the Foundations of the Teaching, comprising various kinds of knowledge and the knowable, has been determined by the teacher and understood by us. Because the question 'What is seeing?' should be asked, the passage beginning 'Therein, what is seeing?' was stated. 'Therein' means: among those twenty-eight kinds of foundations of the teaching in the discourses—mundane and so on—which discourse, he asks, is called 'seeing'?

115. Gambhīrapaññena [V 0.0442] sabbaññubuddhena sudesitāni saṅkhepavitthārādīhi tehi tehi nayehi suṭṭhu desitāni ariyasaccāni ye bhāvitabhāvanā ariyapuggalā paññāobhāsena vibhāvayanti, te bhāvitabhāvanā ariyapuggalā devarajjacakkavattirajjādipamādaṭṭhānaṃ āgamma bhusaṃ pamattā kiñcāpi honti, tathāpi te bhāvitabhāvanā ariyapuggalā sotāpattimaggañāṇena abhisaṅkhāraviññāṇassa nirodhena aṭṭhamabhavādīsu uppajjanārahānaṃ nāmarūpānaṃ niruddhattā aṭṭhamakkhattuvasena aṭṭhamaṃ bhavaṃ na ādiyantīti yojanā. Idaṃ “ye ariyasaccānī”tiādikaṃ suttaṃ dassane paṭhamamaggañāṇe vācakañāpakabhāvena pavattanato dassanaṃ nāma.

115. Those noble persons whose development is developed illuminate with the light of wisdom the noble truths that were well taught by the omniscient Buddha of profound wisdom, excellently expounded by various methods such as in brief and in detail. Although those noble persons whose development is developed might become very heedless, having encountered grounds for heedlessness such as divine kingship or universal sovereignty, still, through the knowledge of the path of stream-entry, with the cessation of formational consciousness and because name-and-form fit to arise in an eighth existence has ceased, they do not take up an eighth existence for the eighth time. This is the construction. This discourse, beginning 'Those noble truths…,' is called 'seeing' because it proceeds by way of indicating and making known the first path-knowledge, which is 'seeing'.

Nagaradvārabāhathirakaraṇatthaṃ ummārabbhantare pathaviyaṃ aṭṭhahatthadasahatthappamāṇaṃ āvāṭaṃ khaṇitvā tasmiṃ āvāṭe ussāpitattā pathavissito pathavinissito antopathavinissito indakhīlo sāradārumayo thambho [M 0.0325] catubbhi catūhi disāhi āgatehi vātehi mahāvātehi asampakampiyo sampakampituṃ asakkuṇeyyo siyā yathā, yo sappuriso ariyasaccāni avecca passati, taṃ sappurisaṃ sabbatitthiyavādavātehi asampakampiyattā tathūpamaṃ ahaṃ vadāmīti yojanā. Idaṃ “yathindakhīlo”tiādikaṃ suttaṃ vuttanayena dassanaṃ nāma.

Just as an Inda-pillar, a post of heartwood for making a city gate-post firm, set up in a pit dug eight or ten cubits deep in the earth within the threshold, rests on the earth, is based in the earth, and has gone deep into the earth, and would be unshakable, unable to be shaken, by winds and great winds coming from the four directions; even so, I declare, is the likeness of that good person who has understood and seen the Noble Truths, being unshakable by the winds of all sectarian doctrines. This is the construction. This discourse beginning, 'Just as an Inda-pillar...' is called 'seeing' in the manner described.

Bhikkhave, catūhi sotāpattiyaṅgehi samannāgato ariyasāvako ariyassa bhagavato sammāsambuddhassa sāvako ācikkhituṃ ākaṅkhamāno hutvā attanāva sayameva attānaṃ byākareyya “bho, mama atta ahaṃ idāni khīṇanirayo amhi, khīṇatiracchānayoni amhi…pe…. dukkhassantaṃ karissāmī”ti byākareyya. Caturaṅgasarūpaṃ dassetuṃ “katamehi catūhī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Idaṃ “catūhī”tiādikaṃ dassanaṃ nāma.

Monks, a noble disciple endowed with the four factors of stream-entry, a disciple of the noble Blessed One, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, if he wishes to declare it, can by himself declare of himself: 'Sirs, I am now one for whom hell is destroyed, for whom the animal realm is destroyed... I will make an end of suffering.' To show the fourfold nature, the passage beginning, 'By which four?' was stated. This discourse beginning with 'By four...' is called 'seeing'.

Nānāvidhaṃ dassanaṃ niddhāritaṃ, “katamā bhāvanā”ti pucchitabbattā “tattha katamā bhāvanā”tiādi vuttaṃ.

Various kinds of seeing have been determined. Since the question 'What is development?' should be asked, the passage beginning, 'Therein, what is development?' was stated.

Idha sāsane yassa ariyasāvakassa ajjhattaṃ kāmabhave nibbattāpakānaṃ orambhāgiyasaṃyojanānaṃ pajahanavasena ca bahiddhā rūpārūpabhavesu nibbattāpakānaṃ uddhambhāgiyasaṃyojanānaṃ pajahanavasena ca indriyāni saddhindriyādīni indriyāni subhāvitāni ariyamaggabhāvanāvasena suṭṭhu bhāvitāni bhavanti, bhāvito bhāvitamaggo sa danto so ariyasāvako imaṃ lokañca paraṃ lokañca nibbijjha nibbijjhitvā paṭivijjhitvā kālaṃ maraṇakāle[V 0.0443], kālaṃkiriyaṃ vā kaṅkhati patthetīti yojanā. Ayaṃ “yassindriyānī”tiādikā pāḷi bhāvanāya vācakañāpakabhāvena pavattanato bhāvanā nāma.

Here in this Dispensation, for whichever noble disciple the faculties, beginning with the faculty of faith, are well developed by means of the cultivation of the noble path—both by abandoning internally the lower fetters that cause rebirth in the sensual realm, and by abandoning externally the higher fetters that cause rebirth in the form and formless realms—that noble disciple, developed, with a developed path, tamed, having become thoroughly disenchanted with and having penetrated this world and the next, awaits his time, that is, desires the making of an end at the time of death. This is the construction. This passage beginning with 'whose faculties' is called 'development' because it functions as an indicator and revealer of development.

Dhammapadāni jhānavipassanāmaggaphalanibbānadhammakoṭṭhāsāni. Anabhijjhā dhammapadaṃ anabhijjhāsīsena adhigatajhānavipassanāmagganibbānadhammapadaṃ koṭṭhāsaṃ. Esa nayo sesesupi. Ayaṃ “cattārimānī”tiādikā pāḷi vuttanayena bhāvanā nāma. (7)

The Dhamma-sayings are sections of the Dhamma comprising jhāna, insight, path, fruition, and Nibbāna. Non-covetousness is a Dhamma-saying, a section of the Dhamma-saying of jhāna, insight, path, and Nibbāna, attained by means of non-covetousness. This method applies to the rest as well. This passage beginning with 'these four' is called 'development' in the manner stated. (7)

Devaputta chindanto puggalo pañca orambhāgiyasaṃyojanāni heṭṭhā maggattayena chinde chindeyya, pajahanto puggalo pañca uddhambhāgiyasaṃyojanāni arahattamaggena jahe pajaheyya, bhāvayanto puggalo pañca [M 0.0326] saddhindriyādīni ca uttari bhāvaye bhāveyya. Pañcasaṅgātigo rāgasaṅgadosasaṅgamohasaṅgamānasaṅgadiṭṭhisaṅgātigo bhikkhu oghatiṇṇoti kāmoghabhavoghadiṭṭhoghaavijjoghatiṇṇoti vuccati kathīyatīti yojanā. “Pañca chinde pañca jahe”ti idaṃ vacanaṃ dassanaṃ nāma. “Pañca cuttari…pe… vuccatī”ti ayaṃ pāḷi bhāvanā nāma. Idaṃ “pañcā”tiādikaṃ suttaṃ dassanañca bhāvanā ca hoti.

O son of a deva, a person in the process of cutting off should cut off the five lower fetters by means of the three lower paths; a person in the process of abandoning should abandon the five higher fetters by means of the path of arahantship; a person in the process of developing should further develop the five faculties beginning with faith. A bhikkhu who has gone beyond the five attachments—the attachment of lust, the attachment of hate, the attachment of delusion, the attachment of conceit, and the attachment of views—is called one who has crossed the floods: the flood of sensual desire, the flood of becoming, the flood of views, and the flood of ignorance. This is the construction. The statement 'cut off five, abandon five' is called 'seeing.' The passage 'develop five further... is called' is called 'development.' This sutta beginning with 'five' is both seeing and development.

“Tīṇimāni, bhikkhave”tiādīsu yojanā pākaṭā. (8)

In the passages beginning with 'These three, monks,' the construction is clear. (8)

116. “Sabbapāpassa akaraṇaṃ…pe… buddhāna sāsana”nti idaṃ suttaṃ sammāsambuddhassa vacanabhāvato sakavacanaṃ nāma. Attho heṭṭhā vuttova.

116. 'The non-doing of all evil...this is the teaching of the Buddhas' — this sutta is called 'one's own words' because it is the speech of the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One. The meaning is as stated above.

Bhikkhave, bālassa bālalakkhaṇāni bālaupalakkhaṇakāraṇāni bālanimittāni “ayaṃ bālo”ti gahaṇakāraṇāni bālāpadānāni bālassa apadānāni porāṇāni viruḷhāni kammāni yehi bālalakkhaṇādīhi bālaṃ “bālo”ti pare paṇḍitā sañjānanti, imāni bālalakkhaṇāni mayā vuccamānāni tīṇi. Katamāni tīṇi? Bhikkhave, bālo duccintitacintī ca duccintitaṃ abhijjhābyāpādamicchādassanaṃ cintī ca hoti, dubbhāsitabhāsī dubbhāsitaṃ musāvādādiṃ bhāsī ca hoti. dukkaṭakammakārī ca dukkaṭaṃ pāṇātipātādikammaṃ kārī ca hoti. Bhikkhave, bālassa…pe… bālāpadānāni iminā mayā vuttāni tīṇi kho bhavanti. Sukkapakkho pana vuttavipariyāyena veditabbo. Idaṃ “tīṇimāni bhikkhave”tiādikaṃ vacanaṃ sammāsambuddhassa vacanabhāvato sakavacanaṃ nāma.

Monks, the characteristics of a fool, the reasons for recognizing a fool, the signs of a fool, the reasons for grasping that 'this is a fool,' the deeds of a fool—the ancient, established actions of a fool by which others, the wise, recognize a fool as 'a fool'—these characteristics of a fool spoken by me are three. What three? Monks, a fool thinks ill thoughts, that is, he thinks thoughts of covetousness, ill will, and wrong view; he speaks ill speech, that is, he speaks speech such as falsehood; and he does ill deeds, that is, he does deeds such as killing living beings. Monks, these three characteristics of a fool... these deeds of a fool, spoken by me, are indeed three. The bright side, however, should be understood as the opposite of what was stated. This statement beginning with 'These three, monks' is called 'one's own words' because it is the speech of the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One.

Pathavīsamo [V 0.0444] vitthato sambodho nāma natthi. Pātaṃ vuṭṭhaṃ udakaṃ ābhuso lābhi gaṇhātīti pātālo, pātālena samo pātālasamo ninno na vijjati. Merusamo unnato natthi, cakkavattisadiso poriso natthīti yojanā. Idaṃ “pathavīsamo”tiādikaṃ vacanaṃ parassa devassa vacanabhāvato paravacanaṃ hoti.

There is no enlightenment as extensive as the earth. Water that has fallen, friend, the receiver takes, hence it is called 'pātāla' (abyss); there is no depth equal to the abyss. There is nothing as elevated as Mount Meru, and there is no person like a wheel-turning monarch. This is the construction. This statement beginning with 'as extensive as the earth' is called 'another's words' because it is the speech of another, a deva.

“Devānaṃ inda, tava subhāsitena jayo hotī”ti vatvā “vepacitti, tava subhāsitena jayo hotū”ti vatvā “vepacitti, tvaṃ gāthaṃ bhaṇa bhaṇāhī”ti avoca. Bhikkhave, atha kho asurindo vepacitti imaṃ vuccamānaṃ gāthaṃ abhāsi “te paṭisedhako no ce assa no ce bhaveyya[M 0.0327], evaṃ sati bālā bhiyyo pakujjheyyuṃ, tasmā dhīro paṇḍito bhusena daṇḍena bālaṃ nisedhaye”ti.

'Indra, lord of devas, victory is yours through your well-spoken words,' he said, then said, 'Vepacitti, victory is yours through your well-spoken words! Vepacitti, speak a verse, speak!' Monks, then the lord of the asuras, Vepacitti, recited this verse that was being spoken: 'If there were no one to restrain them, if there were none, fools would grow even more enraged. Therefore, the wise and intelligent one should restrain a fool with a harsh punishment.'

Gāthāya, bhikkhave, asurindena vepacittinā bhāsitāya asurā anumodiṃsu, devā tuṇhī ahesuṃ. Bhikkhave, atha kho asurindo vepacitti devānaṃ indaṃ sakkaṃ etaṃ vacanaṃ avoca “devānaminda, tvaṃ gāthaṃ bhaṇa bhaṇāhī”ti etaṃ vacanaṃ avoca. Bhikkhave, atha kho devānamindo sakko imaṃ gāthaṃ abhāsi “bālassa paṭisedhanaṃ paraṃ paccatthikaṃ saṅkupitaṃ ñatvā sato satimā yo paṇḍito kodhato upasammati, tassa paṇḍitassa etadeva upasamaṃ varanti ahaṃ maññe”ti.

Monks, when the verse was spoken by Vepacitti, the lord of the asuras, the asuras applauded, but the devas remained silent. Monks, then Vepacitti, the lord of the asuras, said this to Sakka, the lord of the devas: 'Lord of the devas, speak a verse, speak!' Monks, then Sakka, the lord of the devas, spoke this verse: 'Knowing that to restrain a fool is a further hostile provocation, the wise and mindful one, when angered, grows calm. For that wise one, this very pacification is best, I think.'

Gāthāya, bhikkhave, devānamindena sakkena bhāsitāya devā anumodiṃsu, asurā tuṇhī ahesuṃ. Bhikkhave, atha kho devānamindo sakko asurindaṃ vepacittiṃ etaṃ vacanaṃ avoca “vepacitti, tvaṃ gāthaṃ bhaṇāhī”ti etaṃ vacanaṃ avoca. Bhikkhave, atha kho asurindo vepacitti imaṃ gāthaṃ abhāsi “vāsava yadā titikkhati, tadā naṃ titikkhantaṃ puggalaṃ bālo “ayaṃ me bhayā titikkhatī”ti maññati, titikkhāya etadeva vajjaṃ ahaṃ passāmi. Vāsava gogaṇo palāyinaṃ gavaṃ ajjhottharati iva, evaṃ dummedho khamantaṃ bhiyyo ajjhāruhati ajjhottharati.

Monks, when the verse was spoken by Sakka, the lord of devas, the devas rejoiced, but the asuras remained silent. Monks, then Sakka, the lord of devas, said this to Vepacitti, the lord of asuras: 'Vepacitti, recite a verse!' Monks, then the lord of the asuras, Vepacitti, spoke this verse: 'Vāsava, when one endures, the fool thinks of the enduring person, "This one endures out of fear of me." I see this very fault in endurance. Vāsava, just as a herd of cattle overwhelms the fleeing cow, so the foolish one further oppresses and overwhelms the patient one.'

Gāthāya, bhikkhave, asurindena vepacittinā bhāsitāya asurā anumodiṃsu, devā tuṇhī ahesuṃ. Jāyamāne ca goyuddhe paṭhamaṃ dveyeva goṇā yujjhanti, gogaṇo pana yāva eko goṇo na palāyati, tāva olokentova tiṭṭhati. Yadā ca eko goṇo palāyati[V 0.0445], tadā sabbo goṇo taṃ palāyinaṃ gavaṃ bhiyyo ajjhottharatīti goyuddhasabhāvo veditabbo. “Atha kho”tiādīnaṃ yojanattho pākaṭo.

Monks, when the verse was spoken by Vepacitti, the lord of the asuras, the asuras applauded, but the devas remained silent. And when a cattle fight arises, at first only two bulls fight, but the herd stands watching until one bull flees. And when one bull flees, then the entire herd overwhelms that fleeing bull even more—the nature of a cattle fight should be understood in this way. The meaning of 'Then' and so forth is clear.

Vepacitti, yo puggalo titikkhati, taṃ khamantaṃ puggalaṃ “ayaṃ me bhayā titikkhatī”ti kāmaṃ maññatu vā, mā maññatu vā, taṃ maññanaṃ nipphalameva. Atthā sadatthaparamā bhavanti. Khantyā khantito bhiyyo sadattho nāma na vijjati.

Vepacitti, as for the person who endures, let them think of that patient person as they wish, 'This one endures out of fear of me,' or let them not think so—that thought is indeed fruitless. One's own welfare is the highest welfare. There is no welfare for oneself greater than patience.

Yo balavā santo dubbalassa have titikkhatīti tassa balavantassa taṃ titikkhanaṃ paramaṃ khantinti sappurisā āhu, dubbalo niccaṃ khamati eva.

Whoever, being strong, endures the weak—the good people say that such endurance of the strong one is the highest patience. The weak one always endures.

Yassa [M 0.0328] bālassa bālabalaṃ atthi, tassa bālassa bālabalaṃ “abala”nti sappurisā āhu, yassa dhammaguttassa yaṃ balaṃ atthi, tassa dhammaguttassa tassa balassa paṭivattā paṭippharitvā vattā na vijjati.

The fool who has the strength of a fool—the good people call that strength of a fool 'weakness.' But for one guarded by the Dhamma, whatever strength they possess, there is no one who can turn back or oppose that strength.

Vepacitti, yo puggalo kuddhaṃ paṭhamaṃ kujjhantassa paṭikujjhati, so paṭikujjhanto puggalo tena paṭikujjhanena tassa paṭhamaṃ kujjhantassa pāpapuggalassa pāpapuggalato pāpiyo eva pāpataro hīnataro eva bhave.

Vepacitti, whoever gets angry in return at one who is first angry, that person who gets angry in return, by that very act, becomes more evil, worse, and lower than that first angry, evil person.

Vepacitti, yo sappuriso sato satimā paraṃ saṅkupitaṃ ñatvā paṭhamaṃ kujjhantassa appaṭikujjhantova bhave, so sappuriso dujjayaṃ saṅgāmaṃ jeti nāma, attano ca parassa ca ubhinnaṃ atthaṃ carati nāma.

Vepacitti, the good person who is mindful and aware, knowing that another is provoked, does not get angry in return at one who is first angry. That good person indeed wins a battle difficult to win, and indeed acts for the welfare of both—oneself and the other.

Attano ca parassa ca tikicchantānaṃ ubhinnaṃ kodho upasammati, ye janā dhammassa khantidhammassa atthe, catusaccadhamme vā akovidā bhavanti, te janā khamantaṃ sappurisaṃ “ayaṃ bālo”ti maññanti, tesaṃ akovidānaṃ janānaṃ taṃ maññanaṃ nipphalanti.

He is a healer for both himself and the other; the anger of both subsides. Those people who are unskilled in the meaning of the Dhamma—the teaching of patience or the teaching of the Four Noble Truths—consider the patient good person to be 'a fool.' That thought of those unskilled people is fruitless.

Gāthāsu, bhikkhave, devānamindena sakkena bhāsitāsu devā anumodiṃsu, asurā tuṇhī ahesunti yojanā. Idaṃ “bhiyyo bālā”tiādikaṃ vacanaṃ sakkavepacittīnaṃ vacanabhāvato paravacanaṃ nāma. (9)

Monks, when the verses were spoken by Sakka, the lord of devas, the devas applauded, but the asuras remained silent—this is the explanation. This statement, beginning with 'More foolishly,' is called 'another's words' because it is the speech of Sakka and Vepacitti. (9)

117. Pattaṃ [V 0.0446] etarahi adhigataṃ yañca kāmūpakaraṇaṃ, āyatiṃ pattabbaṃ adhigataṃ yañca kāmūpakaraṇaṃ atthi, etaṃ ubhayaṃ rajānukiṇṇaṃ rāgarajādikiṇṇaṃ iti āturassa āturānaṃyeva puggalānaṃ santike anusikkhato anusikkhantassa sikkhāsārā hutvā upaṭṭhahanti, sīlaṃ vataṃ jīvitaṃ brahmacariyaṃ ime sikkhāsārā hutvā upaṭṭhahantīti ye upaṭṭhānasārā puggalā sārato gahetvā ṭhitā. Ettha sīlaṃ nāma “na karomī”ti oramaṇaṃ. Vataṃ nāma bhojanakiccakaraṇādi. Jīvitaṃ nāma ājīvo. Brahmacariyaṃ nāma methunavirativisesabhāvo veditabbo. Tesaṃ upaṭṭhānasārānaṃ puggalānaṃ ayaṃ vādo eko paṭhamo anto lāmako. Ye ca puggalā “kāmesu doso natthī”ti evaṃvādino evaṃdiṭṭhino hutvā ṭhitā, tesaṃ puggalānaṃ ayaṃ vādo eko dutiyo anto [M 0.0329] lāmako. Iccete ubho antā antavādā puggalā kaṭasivaḍḍhanā kaṭasiyo diṭṭhiṃ vaḍḍhenti. Ete ubho ante attakilamathānuyoge kāmasukhallikānuyoge eke puggalā anabhiññāya olīyanti, eke puggalā atidhāvantīti yojanā. Idaṃ “yañca patta”ntiādikaṃ vacanaṃ paresaṃ puggalānaṃ vacanabhāvato paravacanaṃ nāma.

117. What has been attained now as an instrument of sensual pleasure, and what is to be attained in the future as an instrument of sensual pleasure—both are strewn with defilement, strewn with the dust of lust and so on. Thus, for an afflicted person training in the presence of only afflicted persons, these things present themselves as the essence of the training. Virtue, observances, livelihood, and the holy life—these present themselves as the essence of the training for those who stand firm, having grasped them as essential, upholding them as the essence. Here, virtue means restraint with 'I will not do.' Observances refer to duties such as those concerning eating. Livelihood means one’s means of living. The holy life should be understood as the special state of abstaining from sexual intercourse. For those individuals who uphold these as the essence, this view is one low, initial extreme. And those individuals who hold the view and declare, 'There is no fault in sensual pleasures,' for them, this view is another low extreme. Thus, these two extremes, the holders of these extreme views, increase the charnel ground; they increase views of the charnel ground. Not directly knowing these two extremes—the pursuit of self-mortification and the pursuit of indulgence in sensual pleasure—some people fall short, while others overshoot. This is the explanation. This statement, beginning with 'What has been attained,' is called the speech of others, as it comes from the words of other individuals.

Ye ca sammādiṭṭhipuggalā te ubho ante attakilamathānuyogakāmasukhallikānuyoge abhiññāya tatra ca ante na ahesuṃ. Tena ca abhijānanena te ubho ante na amaññiṃsu, tesaṃ sammādiṭṭhipuggalānaṃ vaṭṭaṃ tividhaṃ vaṭṭaṃ paññāpanāya natthi. Iti evaṃ idaṃ “ye cā”tiādikaṃ vacanaṃ bhagavato vacanabhāvato sakavacanaṃ nāma. Ayaṃ udāno “yañca pattaṃ…pe… paññāpanāyā”ti ayaṃ udāno vuttanayena sakavacanañca paravacanañca hoti.

But those individuals with right view, having directly known these two extremes—the pursuit of self-mortification and the pursuit of indulgence in sensual pleasure—did not exist in those extremes. And through that direct knowing, they did not conceive of those two extremes. For those individuals with right view, there is no designation of the threefold round of existence. Thus, this statement, beginning with 'And those,' is called the Blessed One's own word because it is the Blessed One's word. This utterance, from 'What has been attained...to...for designation,' is both the Blessed One's own word and the word of others, according to what has been said.

Pasenadi nāma kosalo kosalissaro rājā bhagavantaṃ etaṃ “idha mayhaṃ…pe… tesaṃ piyo attā”ti vacanaṃ avoca. Bhante, idha rahogatassa paṭisallīnassa mayhaṃ mama cetaso cittassa evaṃ parivitakko udapādi, kesaṃ sattānaṃ attā piyo nu kho, kesaṃ sattānaṃ attā appiyo nu kho iti etaṃ parivitakkanaṃ udapādi. Bhante, tassa mayhaṃ etaṃ parivitakkanaṃ ahosi, ye ca keci sattā kāyena duccaritaṃ caranti kho…pe… manasā duccaritaṃ caranti kho, tesaṃ sattānaṃ attā appiyo kho. Te duccaritaṃ carantā sattā “no attā piyo”ti evaṃ kiñcāpi vadeyyuṃ, atha kho tesaṃ duccaritaṃ carantānaṃ sattānaṃ attā appiyova. Taṃ kissa hetu? Appiyo appiyassa anatthāya yaṃ duccaritaṃ kareyya, taṃ duccaritaṃ te duccaritaṃ carantā sattā attanāva. sayameva. Attano anatthāya hi yasmā karonti, tasmā tesaṃ duccaritaṃ carantānaṃ sattānaṃ attā appiyovāti etaṃ parivitakkanaṃ ahosi.

King Pasenadi of Kosala, the ruler of the Kosalans, addressed the Blessed One with these words: 'Venerable sir, while I was alone in seclusion, this reflection arose in my mind: 'To which beings is the self dear? To which beings is the self not dear?' This consideration occurred to me. Venerable sir, this consideration occurred to me: 'Whatever beings engage in misconduct by body, speech, or mind, to those beings the self is not dear. Though those beings who engage in misconduct might say, "The self is dear to us," yet for those beings who engage in misconduct, the self is indeed not dear. For what reason? Whatever harm an enemy might inflict upon an enemy, these beings who engage in misconduct inflict that very harm upon themselves, by their own selves. Since they act for their own harm, therefore, for those beings who engage in misconduct, the self is not dear.' This was my consideration.

Bhante[V 0.0447], ye ca keci sattā kāyena sucaritaṃ caranti kho…pe… manasā sucaritaṃ caranti kho, tesaṃ sucaritaṃ carantānaṃ sattānaṃ attā piyo kho, te sucaritaṃ carantā sattā “no attā appiyo”ti evaṃ kiñcāpi vadeyyuṃ, atha kho tesaṃ sucaritaṃ carantānaṃ sattānaṃ attā piyova. Taṃ kissa hetu? Piyo piyassa atthāya yaṃ sucaritaṃ careyya, taṃ sucaritaṃ te sucaritaṃ carantā sattā attanāva sayameva attano atthāya hi yasmā karonti[M 0.0330], tasmā tesaṃ sucaritaṃ carantānaṃ sattānaṃ attā piyovāti etaṃ parivitakkanaṃ ahosi. Etaṃ vacanaṃ avocāti yojanā.

Venerable sir, whatever beings engage in good conduct by body, speech, or mind, for those beings who engage in good conduct, the self is dear. Though those beings who engage in good conduct might say, 'The self is not dear to us,' yet for those beings who engage in good conduct, the self is indeed dear. For what reason? Whatever benefit a friend might bring to a friend, these beings who engage in good conduct bring that very benefit to themselves, by their own selves. Since they act for their own welfare, therefore, for those beings who engage in good conduct, the self is dear.' This was my consideration. He spoke this statement—this is the connection.

“Evametaṃ mahārājā”ti vacanaṃ paṭhamaṃ vatvā “ye hi kecī”tiādike bhagavato vuttavacanepi yojanā tatheva kātabbā.

Having first spoken the words, 'So it is, great king,' the connection should be made in the same way also to the words spoken by the Blessed One, beginning with 'For whoever...'

Gāthāsu pana yo paṇḍito attānaṃ “piya”nti ce jaññā, evaṃ sati so paṇḍito naṃ attānaṃ pāpena kammena na saṃyuje na saṃyojeyya, taṃ vacanaṃ hi saccaṃ piyaṃ attānaṃ sulabhaṃ na hoti, dukkaṭakārinā sukhaṃ sulabhaṃ na hoti.

In the verses, however: if a wise person should know the self to be 'dear,' this being so, that wise person would not yoke that self to an evil deed. For this saying is true: a dear self is not easily obtained; for a wrongdoer, happiness is not easily obtained.

Antakena maccunā adhipannassa mānusaṃ bhavaṃ jahato pajahantassa tassa maraṇamukhe ṭhitassa sattassa kiṃ sakaṃ hoti, maraṇamukhe ṭhito so satto kiñca ādāya paralokaṃ gacchati, chāyā gacchantaṃ sattaṃ anapāyinī iva, evaṃ assa paralokagatassa sattassa kiñca anugaṃ hoti.

When a being is overpowered by the Ender, by Death, and is abandoning human existence, for that being standing at the mouth of death, what is their own? Standing at the mouth of death, what do they take when they go to the next world? Like a shadow that never leaves a moving being, what follows that being who has gone to the next world?

Iti bhagavā evaṃ pucchati, pucchitvā “ubho”tiādivissajjanavacanañca āha. Idha loke yo macco yaṃ puññañca yaṃ pāpañca ubho kamme kurute karoti, tassa paralokagatassa maccassa taṃ puññapāpadvayaṃ sakaṃ hoti. Paralokaṃ gato macco taṃva puññapāpadvayaṃ ādāya paralokaṃ gacchati, chāyā gacchantaṃ sattaṃ anapāyinī iva, evaṃ assa paralokagatassa maccassa taṃva puññapāpadvayaṃ anugaṃ hoti.

Thus the Blessed One asks, and having asked, he also spoke the words of explanation beginning with 'both.' Here in this world, whatever merit and evil a mortal does—both these deeds are their own when that mortal has gone to the next world. The mortal who has gone to the next world goes taking that very pair of merit and evil. Just as a shadow never leaves a moving being, so for that mortal who has gone to the next world, that very pair of merit and evil follows them.

Tasmā paṇḍito samparāyikaṃ samparāye phalanibbattāpakaṃ kalyāṇaṃ nicayaṃ nicayanto hutvā kareyya. Pāṇinaṃ paralokasmiṃ puññāni patiṭṭhā honti, iti bhagavā āhāti yojanā kātabbā. Idaṃ “rājā pasenadī”tiādikaṃ suttaṃ kosalarañño vacanabhāvato paravacanaṃ hoti. “Evametaṃ[V 0.0448], mahārāja, evametaṃ mahārājā”tiādikā anugīti bhagavato vacanabhāvato sakavacanaṃ hoti. Idaṃ dvayaṃ vacanaṃ sakavacanañca paravacanañca hoti. (10)

Therefore, a wise person should do good, accumulating a store that is for the future life and produces fruit therein. For beings in the next world, merits are their support—thus the Blessed One declared; this is how the connection should be made. This discourse, beginning with 'King Pasenadi,' being the words of the king of Kosala, is the speech of another. The response, beginning with 'So it is, great king, so it is, great king,' being the words of the Blessed One, is his own speech.
