This is a pair of speeches: one's own speech and the speech of another. (10)

118. Pañhe pucchite idaṃ dukkhasaccaṃ abhiññeyyaṃ, idaṃ samudayasaccaṃ pahātabbaṃ, idaṃ maggasaccaṃ bhāvetabbaṃ, idaṃ nirodhasaccaṃ, phalaṃ vā sacchikātabbaṃ, ime kusalākusalā dhammā evaṃ kusalākusalabhāvena gahitā anavajjasāvajjabhāvena vā gahitā sukhavipākadukkhavipākabhāvena vā gahitā[M 0.0331], idaṃ iṭṭhavipākaṃ idaṃ aniṭṭhavipākaṃ phalaṃ nibbattayaiti evaṃgahitānaṃ tesaṃ kusalākusaladhammānaṃ ayaṃ vuḍḍhi attho, ayaṃ hāni atthoti. Iti idaṃ “pañhe pucchite”tiādikaṃ suttaṃ vissajjanīye atthe vācakañāpakabhāvena pavattanato vissajjanīyaṃ nāma.

118. When a question is asked: this is the truth of suffering to be fully understood, this is the truth of the origin to be abandoned, this is the truth of the path to be developed, this is the truth of cessation, or the fruit, to be realized. These wholesome and unwholesome qualities are thus grasped as wholesome or unwholesome, as blameless or blameworthy, or as resulting in happiness or suffering. They produce this desirable result and this undesirable result as fruit. Thus, of these wholesome and unwholesome qualities so grasped, this is the meaning of growth, and this is the meaning of decline. Therefore, this discourse, beginning with 'When a question is asked,' is called 'An Explanation' because it proceeds by way of expressing and making known a matter to be explained.

“Uḷāro buddho bhagavā”ti iminā padena buddhauḷārataṃ ekaṃseneva ekakoṭṭhāseneva niddise. “Svākkhāto dhammo”ti iminā padena dhammasvākkhātataṃ ekaṃseneva ekakoṭṭhāseneva niddise. “Suppaṭipanno saṅgho”ti iminā padena saṅghasuppaṭipattiṃ ekaṃseneva ekakoṭṭhāseneva niddise “sabbe saṅkhārā aniccā”ti iminā padena saṅkhārāniccataṃ ekaṃseneva niddise. “Sabbe saṅkhārā dukkhā”ti iminā padena saṅkhāradukkhataṃ ekaṃseneva niddise. “Sabbe dhammā anattā”ti iminā padena dhammānattataṃ ekaṃseneva niddise. “Sabbe saṅkhārā anattā”ti avatvā “sabbe dhammā anattā”ti vuttena iminā padena saṅkhārehi aññaṃ yaṃ vā pana maggaphalanirodhasamāpattidhammajātaṃ atthi, taṃ maggaphalanirodhasamāpattidhammajātampi evaṃjātiyaṃ evaṃ ekaṃsabyākaraṇīyanti maggaphalanirodhasamāpattidhammajātassāpi anattataṃ ekaṃseneva niddiseti yojanā. Idaṃ “uḷāro”tiādikaṃ suttaṃ vissajjanīye buddhauḷāratādike vācakañāpakabhāvena pavattanato vissajjanīyaṃ nāma.

'The Buddha, the Blessed One, is sublime'—by this phrase, the sublimity of the Buddha is indicated categorically, as a single part. 'The Dhamma is well-proclaimed'—by this phrase, the well-proclaimed nature of the Dhamma is indicated categorically, as a single part. 'The Sangha is practicing well'—by this phrase, the good practice of the Sangha is indicated categorically, as a single part. 'All conditioned things are impermanent'—by this phrase, the impermanence of conditioned things is indicated categorically. 'All conditioned things are suffering'—by this phrase, the suffering of conditioned things is indicated categorically. 'All phenomena are not-self'—by this phrase, the not-self nature of phenomena is indicated categorically. By this phrase, which says 'All phenomena are not-self' instead of 'All conditioned things are not-self,' it is indicated that whatever other class of phenomena exists apart from conditioned things—namely, the class of phenomena that is path, fruition, cessation, and attainment—even that class of phenomena is to be declared categorically as being of such a nature. Thus, the not-self nature of the class of phenomena that is path, fruition, cessation, and attainment is also indicated categorically—this is the connection. This discourse, beginning with 'Sublime,' is called 'An Explanation' because it proceeds by way of expressing and making known the matters to be explained, such as the sublimity of the Buddha.

Naradammasārathi ākaṅkhato te bhagavato manasā sabbaññutaññāṇasahitādimanasā vicintitaṃ ñeyyadhammaṃ devā manussā sabbe pāṇino na jaññā na jāneyyuṃ. Santaṃ araṇaṃ samādhiṃ nisevato te bhagavato manasā vicintitā kasiṇāpi sabbe pāṇino na jaññā na jāneyyuṃ. Kasiṇāpi vā kasiṇārammaṇāya paññāyapi na jaññā na jāneyyuṃ. Kasiṇāpīti ettha ca “kasiṇāyapī”ti vattabbepi ya-kāra lopavasena “kasiṇāpī”ti vuttaṃ. Atha vā “yaṃ ākaṅkhati yaṃ ākaṅkhanaṃ karoti, taṃ ākaṅkhanaṃ kiṃ katama”nti pucchitaṃ pañhaṃ aññesaṃ avisayattā [V 0.0449] avissajjanīyaṃ hotīti yojanā. Idaṃ “ākaṅkhato”tiādikaṃ suttaṃ avissajjanīye visaye vācakañāpakabhāvena pavattanato avissajjanīyaṃ nāma.

The knowable phenomena contemplated by the mind—a mind endowed with omniscience and so forth—of that Blessed One, the charioteer of trainable men, as he desires, neither gods, nor humans, nor any beings would know. Even the kasinas contemplated by the mind of that Blessed One as he cultivates peaceful, passionless concentration, no beings would know. Or, they would not know even with the wisdom that has the kasina as its object. Here, 'kasiṇāpi' is stated due to the elision of the 'ya' sound, when 'kasiṇāyapi' should be said. Alternatively, the question asked, 'What does he desire? What is this desiring? What is that?' is unanswerable because it is not the domain of others—this is the connection. This discourse, beginning with 'As he desires,' is called 'The Unanswerable' because it proceeds by way of expressing and making known a matter that is unanswerable.

Bhagavā sīlakkhandhe sīlakkhandhahetu ettako etaparimāṇo, bhagavā samādhikkhandhe samādhikkhandhahetu ettako etaparimāṇo, bhagavā paññākkhandhe [M 0.0332] paññākkhandhahetu ettako etaparimāṇo, bhagavā vimuttikkhandhe vimuttikkhandhahetu ettako etaparimāṇo, bhagavā vimuttiñāṇadassanakkhandhe vimuttiñāṇadassanakkhandhahetu ettako etaparimāṇo, bhagavā iriyāyaṃ kāyavacīsamācāre kāyavacīsamācārahetu ettako etaparimāṇo, bhagavā pabhāve ānubhāvahetu ettako etaparimāṇo, bhagavā hitesitāyaṃ mettāhetu ettako etaparimāṇo, bhagavā karuṇāyaṃ karuṇāhetu ettako etaparimāṇo, bhagavā iddhiyaṃ iddhividhahetu ettako etaparimāṇoti avissajjanīyoti yojanā. Idaṃ “ettako”tiādikaṃ suttaṃ avissajjanīye visaye vācakañāpakabhāvena pavattanato avissajjanīyaṃ nāma.

The Blessed One, in the aggregate of virtue, because of the aggregate of virtue, is of such an extent and such a measure. The Blessed One, in the aggregate of concentration, because of the aggregate of concentration, is of such an extent and such a measure. The Blessed One, in the aggregate of wisdom, because of the aggregate of wisdom, is of such an extent and such a measure. The Blessed One, in the aggregate of liberation, because of the aggregate of liberation, is of such an extent and such a measure. The Blessed One, in the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation, because of the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation, is of such an extent and such a measure. The Blessed One, in deportment, in bodily and verbal conduct, because of bodily and verbal conduct, is of such an extent and such a measure. The Blessed One, in his radiance, because of his power, is of such an extent and such a measure. The Blessed One, in his desire for the welfare of others, because of loving-kindness, is of such an extent and such a measure. The Blessed One, in his compassion, because of compassion, is of such an extent and such a measure. The Blessed One, in his psychic power, because of the kinds of psychic power, is of such an extent and such a measure—this is the connection: it is unanswerable. This discourse beginning with 'ettako' is called 'unanswerable' because it functions as a declarer and an indicator concerning an unanswerable matter.

Bhikkhave, arahato sammāsambuddhassa tathāgatassa loke uppādā uppādahetu tiṇṇaṃ ratanānaṃ uppādo sambhavati, āyatiṃ buddharatanassa uppādo sambhavati, ekassa buddharatanassa dharamānakkhaṇena hi aññassa buddharatanassa anuppajjanato āyatinti vuttaṃ, dhammaratanassa uppādo sambhavati, saṅgharatanassa uppādo sambhavatīti tīṇi ratanāni. “Tāni tīṇi ratanāni guṇato kiṃpamāṇānī”ti pucchite sati tāni tīṇi ratanāni guṇato etaparimāṇānīti na vissajjitabbānīti yojanā. Idaṃ “tathāgatassā”tiādikaṃ suttaṃ avissajjanīye visaye vācakañāpakabhāvena pavattanato avissajjanīyaṃ nāma.

Monks, because of the arising in the world of a Tathāgata, an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One, the arising of the three gems occurs. In the future, the arising of the Buddha-gem occurs. For while one Buddha-gem is present, another Buddha-gem does not arise; thus it is said 'in the future'. The arising of the Dhamma-gem occurs. The arising of the Sangha-gem occurs—these are the three gems. If asked, 'What is the measure of these three gems in terms of their qualities?', one should not answer that these three gems are of such a measure in terms of their qualities. This is the connection. This discourse beginning with 'tathāgatassa' is called 'unanswerable' because it functions as a declarer and an indicator concerning an unanswerable matter.

Buddhavisayo puggalaparo puggalapadhāno pañho avissajjanīyo, buddhavisayāva puggalaparoparaññutā avissajjanīyā. Bhikkhave, avijjānīvaraṇānaṃ sattānaṃ pubbā koṭi na paññāyati taṇhāsaṃyojanānaṃ, sakiṃ nirayaṃ sandhāvataṃ saṃsarataṃ sattānaṃ, sakiṃ tiracchānayoniṃ sandhāvataṃ saṃsarataṃ sattānaṃ, sakiṃ pettivisayaṃ sandhāvataṃ saṃsarataṃ sattānaṃ, sakiṃ asurayoniṃ sandhāvataṃ saṃsarataṃ sattānaṃ, sakiṃ deve sandhāvataṃ saṃsarataṃ sattānaṃ, sakiṃ manusse sandhāvataṃ saṃsarataṃ sattānaṃ pubbā koṭi na paññāyati na dissati na upalabbhatīti. “Sā pubbā koṭi katamā”ti kenaci kataṃ pucchanaṃ avissajjanīyaṃ saṃsārassa pubbakoṭiyā abhāvato avissajjanīyaṃ hoti. “Na paññāyatī”ti desanā sāvakānaṃ ñāṇavekallena katā, na attano ñāṇavekallena. “Na paññāyatī”ti desanā attano ceva sāvakānañca ñāṇavekallena kātabbā [V 0.0450][M 0.0333] siyāti codanaṃ manasi katvā “duvidhā buddhānaṃ bhagavantānaṃ desanā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Attā upanetabbo etissā desanāyāti attūpanāyikā. Paro upanetabbo etissā desanāyāti parūpanāyikā. “Katamā attūpanāyikā desanā, katamā parūpanāyikā desanā”ti pucchitabbattā niyametvā dassetuṃ “na paññāyatī”tiādi vuttaṃ. “Na paññāyatī”ti desanā sāvakānaṃ netabbānaṃ vasena desitattā parūpanāyikā desanā nāma, “natthi buddhānaṃ bhagavantānaṃ avijānanā”ti desanā attano netabbassa vasena desitattā attūpanāyikā desanā nāma. “Natthi buddhānaṃ bhagavantānaṃ avijānanā”ti vuttattā pubbāya koṭiyā abhāvato eva na paññāyatīti viññāyati, bhagavato ñāṇassa paññāpanaṃ kātuṃ asamatthattā na paññāyatīti na viññāyati tena aṭṭhakathāyaṃ “natthi buddhānaṃ bhagavantānaṃ avijānanāti etena purimāya koṭiyā abhāvato eva na paññāyati, na tattha ñāṇassa paṭighātoti dassetī”ti (netti. aṭṭha. 118) vuttaṃ.

A question concerning the Buddha's domain, pertaining to individuals, having individuals as its primary subject, is unanswerable; the knowledge of others' minds, pertaining to individuals within the Buddha's domain, is also unanswerable. Monks, the prior end of beings shrouded in ignorance and fettered by craving is not discerned—of beings who have wandered and transmigrated through hell, through the animal realm, through the realm of ghosts, through the realm of demons, through the realm of gods, or through the human realm. The prior end is not discerned, not seen, not found. The question, 'What is that prior end?' asked by someone, is unanswerable, for there is no prior end to the cycle of existence. The teaching 'It is not discerned' was given due to the deficiency in the knowledge of the disciples, not due to a deficiency in his own knowledge. Having considered the objection that the teaching 'It is not discerned' might be given due to a deficiency in the knowledge of both oneself and the disciples, it is said, 'There are two kinds of teachings of the Blessed Buddhas,' and so on. The self is to be led by this teaching—this is called self-referential. Another is to be led by this teaching—this is called other-referential. Because it should be asked, 'What is self-referential teaching? What is other-referential teaching?', to define and show this, 'It is not discerned,' and so on, was said. The teaching 'It is not discerned' is called other-referential teaching because it is taught according to the disciples who are to be led. The teaching 'There is no non-knowing in the Blessed Buddhas' is called self-referential teaching because it is taught according to what is to be led in oneself. Since it is said, 'There is no non-knowing in the Blessed Buddhas,' it is understood that the prior end is not discerned precisely because of its absence, not because the Blessed One's knowledge is incapable of making it known. Thus, in the commentary, it is said: 'By this, it is shown that the prior end is not discerned precisely because of its absence, and there is no obstruction to knowledge there' (Netti. Aṭṭha. 118).

“Kathaṃ pana buddhānaṃ bhagavantānaṃ avijānanāya natthibhāvovijānitabbo”ti vattabbattā avijānanāya natthibhāvaṃ jānāpetuṃ “yathā bhagavā kokālikaṃ bhikkhu”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana – “yaṃ pana atthi, taṃ aññesaṃ appameyyampi bhagavato na appameyyanti bhagavato sabbattha appaṭihatañāṇataṃ dassetuṃ ‘yathā bhagavā kokālikaṃ bhikkhuṃ ārabbhā’tiādimāhā”ti vuttaṃ. Bhagavā kokālikaṃ bhikkhuṃ ārabbha “kīva dīghaṃ nu kho, bhante, padume niraye āyuppamāṇa”nti pañhaṃ pucchitvā nisinnaṃ aññataraṃ bhikkhuṃ yathā yena pakārena “seyyathāpi…pe… āghātetvā”ti evamāha. Tato tena pakārena avijānanāya natthibhāvo vijānitabboti attho gahetabbo.

Because it must be said, 'But how is the non-existence of non-knowing to be understood for the Blessed Buddhas?', to make known the non-existence of non-knowing, 'as the Blessed One [spoke about] the monk Kokālika,' and so on, was said. In the commentary, however, it is said: 'That which exists, even if immeasurable to others, is not immeasurable to the Blessed One'—to show the unimpeded knowledge of the Blessed One everywhere, 'as the Blessed One, concerning the monk Kokālika,' and so forth, was said. The Blessed One, concerning the monk Kokālika, spoke to a certain monk who was sitting after asking the question, 'How long, venerable sir, is the lifespan in Paduma hell?' in the way that he said, 'Suppose... having harbored ill will...' Thus, the meaning to be taken is that the non-existence of non-knowing is to be understood in that manner.

Bhikkhu, tvaṃ sallakkhehi, kokāliko vīsatikhāriko kosalako tilavāho rāsiṃ katvā ṭhapito, tato tilato puriso vassasatassa vassasatassa accayena ekamekaṃ tilaṃ uddhareyya, so vīsatikhāriko kosalako tilavāho iminā uddharānupakkamena khippataraṃ parikkhayaṃ pariyādānaṃ seyyathāpi gaccheyya, eko abbudo nirayo parikkhayaṃ pariyādānaṃ na tveva gaccheyya. Vīsati abbudā nirayā tattake kāle [M 0.0334] parikkhayaṃ pariyādānaṃ seyyathāpi gaccheyyuṃ, evameva eko nirabbudo nirayo tattake kāle parikkhayaṃ pariyādānaṃ na tveva gaccheyya. Esa nayo sesesupi. Sāriputtamoggallānesu cittaṃ āghātetvā padumaṃ nirayaṃ kokāliko bhikkhu upapanno kho, bhikkhu, tvaṃ evaṃ sallakkhehīti bhagavā āhāti yojanā. Bhagavā “ayaṃ appameyyo ayaṃ asaṅkhyeyyo”ti vā na kiñci āha. “Tasmiṃ appameyye [V 0.0451] katamo appameyyo, tasmiṃ asaṅkhyeyye katamo asaṅkhyeyyo”ti kenaci kataṃ pucchanaṃ buddhavisayattā avissajjanīyaṃ. Idaṃ appameyyaasaṅkhyeyyasuttaṃ vuttanayena avissajjanīyaṃ. (11)

Monk, consider this: Suppose there were a Kosalan sesame seed heap of twenty khāris, piled up. From that heap, a person were to remove a single sesame seed at the passing of every hundred years. That Kosalan sesame seed heap of twenty khāris would, by this method of removal, be more quickly exhausted and used up. Yet, one Abbuda hell would not be exhausted or used up in that time. Twenty Abbuda hells would be exhausted and used up in that same time, but even one Nirabbuda hell would not be exhausted or used up in that time. This is the method for the rest as well. Having harbored ill will toward Sāriputta and Moggallāna, the monk Kokālika was reborn in the Paduma hell. Monk, consider it thus—so said the Blessed One. This is the connection. The Blessed One did not say anything such as, 'This is immeasurable, this is incalculable.' The question, 'In that immeasurable, what is immeasurable? In that incalculable, what is incalculable?' asked by someone, is unanswerable because it pertains to the Buddha's domain. This Appameyya-Asaṅkhyeyya Sutta is unanswerable according to the method stated.

119. “Yadā so upako”tiādīsu yojanā pākaṭā.

119. The connection in 'When that Upaka,' and so on, is clear.

“Kathaṃ kena pakārena jino”ti upakena kataṃ pucchanaṃ “kilesappahānapakārena jino”ti vissajjanīyattā vissajjanīyaṃ. “Kena pakārena jino”ti upakena kataṃ pucchanaṃ “pāpakānaṃ dhammānaṃ jitattā jino”ti vissajjanīyattā vissajjanīyaṃ. “Katamo jino”ti kataṃ pucchanaṃ “rūpādiko jino”ti vā “rūpādikaṃ muñcitvā añño jino”ti vā vissajjetuṃ asakkuṇeyyattā avissajjanīyaṃ. “Katamo āsavakkhayo, katamo rāgakkhayo, katamo dosakkhayo, katamo mohakkhayo”ti kataṃ pucchanaṃ “nibbānaṃ āsavakkhayo”ti vā “arahattamaggo āsavakkhayo”ti vā “arahattaphalaṃ rāgakkhayo”ti vā iti evamādinā vissajjanīyattā vissajjanīyaṃ. “Kittako āsavakkhayo, kittako rāgakkhayo, kittako dosakkhayo, kittako mohakkhayo”ti kataṃ pucchanaṃ “ettako etaparimāṇo āsavakkhayo”ti evamādinā avissajjanīyattā avissajjanīyaṃ. Idaṃ vuttappakāraṃ suttaṃ vuttanayena vissajjanīyañca avissajjanīyañca hoti. (12)

‘How, in what way, is one a victor?’ is a question posed by Upaka. It is answerable because it can be answered by stating, ‘One is a victor by way of abandoning defilements.’ ‘In what way is one a victor?’ is a question posed by Upaka. It is answerable because it can be answered by stating, ‘One is a victor by conquering evil qualities.’ ‘Who is the victor?’ is a question. It is unanswerable because it cannot be answered by stating, ‘The victor is form, etc.,’ or ‘The victor is another apart from form, etc.’ ‘What is the destruction of the taints? What is the destruction of lust? What is the destruction of hatred? What is the destruction of delusion?’ is a question. It is answerable because it can be answered by stating, ‘Nibbāna is the destruction of the taints,’ or ‘The path to arahantship is the destruction of the taints,’ or ‘The fruit of arahantship is the destruction of lust,’ and so on. ‘What is the measure of the destruction of the taints? What is the measure of the destruction of lust? What is the measure of the destruction of hatred? What is the measure of the destruction of delusion?’ is a question. It is unanswerable because it cannot be answered by stating, ‘The destruction of the taints is of such and such a measure,’ and so on. This discourse, as described, is both answerable and unanswerable in the manner stated. (12)

“Tathāgato satto atthī”ti pucchanaṃ “pañcakkhandhe upādāya paññāpetabbo sattabhūto atthī”ti vissajjanīyattā vissajjanīyaṃ. “Atthi rūpa”nti kataṃ pucchanaṃ rūpassa vissajjamānattā “āmantā”ti vissajjanīyattā vissajjanīyaṃ, “rūpaṃ tathāgato”ti kataṃ pucchanaṃ tathābhāvato alabbhanato avissajjanīyattā avissajjanīyaṃ. “Rūpavā tathāgato”tiādīsupi esa nayo [M 0.0335] yathāsambhavaṃ yojetabbo. Idaṃ vuttappakāraṃ suttaṃ vuttanayena vissajjanīyañca avissajjanīyañca hoti.

‘Is the Tathāgata a being?’—this question is answerable because it can be answered by stating that ‘a being is designated in dependence on the five aggregates.’ ‘Does form exist?’—this question is answerable because, as form can be specified, it can be answered with ‘Yes.’ ‘Is form the Tathāgata?’—this question is unanswerable because such a state is unobtainable. This method should be applied as appropriate in cases such as ‘Does the Tathāgata possess form?’ and so on. This discourse, as described, is both answerable and unanswerable in the manner stated.

“Passati bhagavā dibbena cakkhunā…pe… yathākammūpage satte pajānātī”ti kataṃ pucchanaṃ “passati bhagavā”ti vā…pe… “pajānāti bhagavā”ti vā vissajjanīyattā vissajjanīyaṃ. “Katame sattā, katamo tathāgato”ti kataṃ pucchanaṃ paramatthato alabbhanato avissajjanīyattā avissajjanīyaṃ.

‘Does the Blessed One see with the divine eye... and understand beings according to their deeds?’—this question is answerable because it can be answered by stating, ‘The Blessed One sees,’ or... ‘The Blessed One understands.’ ‘Who are the beings? Who is the Tathāgata?’—this question is unanswerable because, in the ultimate sense, they are unobtainable and thus the question cannot be answered.

“Atthi [V 0.0452] tathāgato”ti kataṃ pucchanaṃ heṭṭhā vuttanayena vissajjanīyaṃ. “Atthi tathāgato paraṃ maraṇā”ti kataṃ pucchanaṃ “atthi tathāgato paraṃ maraṇā”ti vissajjamāne sati ca idhaloko eva paralokoti āpajjati, “natthi tathāgato paraṃ maraṇā”ti vissajjamāne sati ca idhalokato añño paralokoti āpajjati, tasmā avissajjanīyattā avissajjanīyaṃ. Idaṃ vuttappakāraṃ suttaṃ vissajjanīye visaye ca avissajjanīye visaye ca vācakañāpakabhāvena pavattanato vissajjanīyañca avissajjanīyañca hoti.

‘Does the Tathāgata exist?’—this question is answerable in the manner explained above. ‘Does the Tathāgata exist after death?’—if this were answered by stating, ‘The Tathāgata exists after death,’ it would follow that this world is the same as the next world. If it were answered by stating, ‘The Tathāgata does not exist after death,’ it would follow that the next world is different from this world. Therefore, it is unanswerable. This discourse, as described, is both answerable and unanswerable because it functions as an explainer and indicator of both answerable and unanswerable topics.

120. Nānāvidhaṃ vissajjanīyāvissajjanīyasuttaṃ ācariyena niddhāritaṃ, amhehi ca ñātaṃ, “katamaṃ suttaṃ kamma”nti pucchitabbattā “tattha katamaṃ kamma”ntiādi vuttaṃ.

120. The various kinds of answerable and unanswerable discourses have been determined by the teacher, and understood by us. Because the question ‘Which discourse is kamma?’ was to be asked, it was said, ‘Therein, what is kamma?’ and so on.

“Antakenādhipannassā”tiādīsu attho heṭṭhā vuttanayattā pākaṭo “maraṇenābhibhūtassa…pe… chāyāva anapāyinī”ti idaṃ suttaṃ puññakammapāpakammadvaye vācakañāpakabhāvena pavattanato kammaṃ nāma.

In the passage beginning ‘To one overcome by the End-maker,’ and so on, the meaning is clear according to the method explained above. This discourse, ‘Overcome by death... like a shadow that never departs,’ is called ‘kamma’ because it functions as an explainer and indicator of the pair of meritorious and demeritorious kamma.

Bhikkhave, tumhe puna caparaṃ kammaṃ sallakkhetha. (Anuṭṭhānagilānaṃ) anuṭṭhānagilānassa pīṭhasamāruḷhaṃ pīṭhasamāruḷhassa bālaṃ bālassa vā mañcasamāruḷhaṃ mañcasamāruḷhassa bālaṃ bālassa vā chamāyaṃ bhūmiyaṃ semānaṃ semānassa sayantassa bālaṃ bālassa vā kāyena duccaritāni vācāya duccaritāni manasā duccaritāni pāpakāni yāni kammāni pubbe pubbakāle vā atīte anekakappakoṭisatasahasse vā assa bālena katāni, tāni pāpakāni kammāni tamhi pīṭhasamāruḷhādisamaye olambanti viya upaṭṭhahanti ajjholambanti viya upaṭṭhahanti abhippalambanti viya upaṭṭhahanti. Bhikkhave[M 0.0336], mahataṃ mahantānaṃ pabbatakūṭānaṃ chāyā sāyanhasamayaṃ pathaviyaṃ seyyathāpi olambanti ajjholambanti abhippalambanti yathā, bhikkhave, evameva bālaṃ…pe… abhippalambanti. Bhikkhave, tatra tasmiṃ upaṭṭhānākāre upaṭṭhānākārahetu bālassa katapāpassa evaṃ parivitakko hoti “me mayā kalyāṇaṃ akataṃ vata, me mayā kusalaṃ akataṃ vata, bhīruttāṇaṃ kataṃ vata, me mayā pāpaṃ kataṃ vata, me mayā luddaṃ kataṃ vata, me mayā kibbisaṃ kataṃ vata, bho agilāna sappurisa akatakalyāṇānaṃ akatakusalānaṃ akatabhīruttāṇānaṃ katapāpānaṃ kataluddānaṃ katakibbisānaṃ yāvatā gati duggati atthi, taṃ gatiṃ ahaṃ pecca gacchāmī”ti evaṃ parivitakko hoti. Evaṃ vitakkento so bālo socati kilamati paridevati, urattāḷiṃ kandati sammohaṃ āpajjatīti yojanā.

Monks, you should further discern kamma. (Concerning the sick person unable to rise) For the fool who is sick and unable to rise, whether mounted on a seat, mounted on a bed, or lying on the ground—the bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, mental misconduct, and whatever evil deeds were done by that fool in the past, in previous times, over many hundreds of thousands of crores of aeons—those evil deeds appear as if hanging down upon them, as if hanging over them, as if pressing down upon them. Monks, just as the shadows of great mountain peaks in the evening hang down upon the earth, hang over it, and press down upon it, even so, monks, do they... press down upon the fool. Monks, on that occasion, because of the way those deeds appear, this reflection arises in the fool who has done evil: ‘Alas, good has not been done by me. Alas, the wholesome has not been done by me. Alas, a refuge for the fearful has not been made by me. Alas, evil has been done by me. Alas, cruelty has been done by me. Alas, wickedness has been done by me. For those who have not done good, not done the wholesome, not made a refuge for the fearful, but have done evil, cruelty, and wickedness—whatever woeful destination there is, to that destination I shall go after death.’ Reflecting thus, that fool grieves, is afflicted, laments, beats his breast and weeps, and falls into confusion. This is the explanation.

Pabbatakūṭānaṃ [V 0.0453] chāyā nāma sūriyuggamanakālepi pathaviyā olambantīpi chāyā hāyanavasena olambanti. Sāyanhasamayaṃ pana chāyā vaḍḍhanavasena olambanti, tatheva kammānipi tasmiṃ kāle vaḍḍhanavasena upaṭṭhahanti, tasmā tameva vaḍḍhanupaṭṭhānaṃ sandhāya “sāyanhasamaya”nti vuttaṃ. Sukkapakkhepi yojanā kaṇhapakkhe yojanānusārena kātabbā. Idaṃ “puna capara”ntiādikaṃ suttadvayaṃ kusalakammaakusalakammesu vācakañāpakabhāvena pavattanato kammaṃ nāma.

The shadows of mountain peaks, even at the time of sunrise, hang down upon the earth, but they diminish in length. In the evening, however, the shadows hang down by way of increasing, and similarly, deeds also appear at that time by way of increasing. Therefore, ‘evening time’ is said with reference to this increasing appearance. The explanation for the bright fortnight should also be made in accordance with the explanation for the dark fortnight. These two discourses, beginning with ‘Furthermore,’ and so on, are called ‘kamma’ because they function as explainers and indicators of wholesome and unwholesome kamma.

Nānāvidhaṃ kammaṃ ācariyena niddhāritaṃ, amhehi ca ñātaṃ, “katamo vipāko”ti pucchitabbattā tattha katamo vipāko”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha tesu aṭṭhavīsatividhesu lokiyādīsu sāsanapaṭṭhānesu katamo vipākoti pucchati. Bhikkhave, vo tumhehi ye manussattasaddhāpaṭilābhādayo paṭiladdhā, te manussattasaddhāpaṭilābhādayo vo tumhākaṃ lābhā bhavanti. Tumhehi pabbajitvā yaṃ catupārisuddhisīlādisampādanaṃ laddhaṃ, taṃ catupārisuddhisīlādisampādanaṃ vo tumhākaṃ suladdhaṃ bhavati. Bhikkhave, yo buddhuppādo navamo khaṇo tumhehi laddho, so buddhuppādo navamo khaṇo vo tumhākaṃ brahmacariyavāsāya paṭiladdho bhavati.

Various kinds of kamma have been determined by the teacher, and we have understood them. Since it was to be asked, "What is the result?", therefore "Therein, what is the result?" and so on, was said. Therein, among those twenty-eight kinds of mundane and other establishments of the Dispensation, the question is asked, "What is the result?" "Monks, those attainments of human existence, faith, and so on that you have gained—those attainments of human existence, faith, and so on are gains for you. Whatever accomplishment of the fourfold purity of morality and so on you have obtained by going forth—that accomplishment of the fourfold purity of morality and so on is a great gain for you. Monks, the ninth moment, the arising of a Buddha, that you have obtained—that ninth moment, the arising of a Buddha, is an attainment for you for living the holy life."

Bhikkhave, mayā chaphassāyatanikā nāma nirayā diṭṭhā, tattha tesu diṭṭhesu chaphassāyatanikesu nāma nirayesu yaṃ kiñci rūpaṃ cakkhunā passati, taṃ aniṭṭharūpaṃyeva passati, no iṭṭharūpaṃ. Akantarūpaṃyeva passati, no kantarūpaṃ. Amanāparūpaṃyeva passati, no manāparūpaṃ.

Monks, I have seen hells called 'Of the Six Spheres of Contact.' There, in those hells called 'Of the Six Spheres of Contact,' whatever form one sees with the eye, one sees only disagreeable form, not agreeable form; only unlovely form, not lovely form; only unpleasant form, not pleasant form.

Yaṃ [M 0.0337] kiñci saddaṃ sotena…pe… ghānena…pe… jivhāya…pe… kāyena…pe… yaṃ kiñci dhammaṃ manasā vijānāti, taṃ aniṭṭhadhammaṃyeva vijānāti, no iṭṭhadhammaṃ. Akantadhammaṃyeva vijānāti, no kantadhammaṃ. Amanāpadhammaṃyeva vijānāti, no manāpadhammanti pāṭho yutto. “Aniṭṭharūpaṃyeva vijānāti, no iṭṭharūpa”ntiādipāṭho ayutto, katthaci pāḷiyaṃ ayuttapāṭho diṭṭho. Sukkapakkhe vuttanayavipariyāyena yojanā kātabbā. Ayaṃ vuttappakārā “lābhā vo, bhikkhave”tiādiko pāṭho vipāke vācakañāpakabhāveneva pavattanato vipāko nāma.

Whatever sound is heard by the ear... whatever odor is smelled by the nose... whatever taste is tasted by the tongue... whatever touch is felt by the body... whatever mental phenomenon is cognized by the mind, one cognizes only disagreeable phenomena, not agreeable phenomena; only unlovely phenomena, not lovely phenomena; only unpleasant phenomena, not pleasant phenomena—this reading is correct. The reading 'one cognizes only disagreeable form, not agreeable form,' and so on, is incorrect; such an incorrect reading is found in some Pāli texts. The explanation for the bright fortnight should be made in the reverse order of the explanation for the dark fortnight. This passage, as described, beginning 'It is a gain for you, monks,' and so on, is called 'result' because it functions as an explainer and indicator of the result.

Mārisā niraye paccamānānaṃ amhākaṃ sabbaso nimujjanaummujjanavasena saṭṭhivassasahassāni paripuṇṇāni, nirayassa anto pariyosānaṃ kadā kasmiṃ kāle bhavissati.

Sirs, for us who are being cooked in hell, sixty thousand years have been completed by way of continually sinking and emerging. When and at what time will there be an end, a conclusion, to hell?

Nirayassa [V 0.0454] anto pariyosānaṃ natthi. Nirayassa anto pariyosānaṃ kuto atthi? Nirayassa anto pariyosānaṃ amhākaṃ na paṭidissati. Mārisā, yadā tumhe ca ahañca seṭṭhiputtā jātā, tadā tuyhaṃ tumhākañca mayhaṃ mama ca pāpaṃ hi yasmā pakataṃ pakārehi kataṃ, tasmā nirayassa anto pariyosānaṃ amhākaṃ na dissatīti ayaṃ pāṭho vipāke vācakañāpakabhāvena pavattanato vipāko nāma. (13)

There is no end to hell. How could there be an end to hell? The end of hell is not visible to us. Sirs, when you and I were born as sons of wealthy men, because the evil done by you and yours, and by me and mine, was thoroughly committed, therefore the end of hell is not seen by us. This passage is called 'vipāka' because it indicates and makes known the result. (13)

121. Adhammacārī naro kusaladhammesu pamatto hi yasmā hoti, tasmā so adhammacārī pamatto naro yahiṃ yahiṃ yaṃ yaṃ duggatiṃ gacchati, taṃ taṃ gacchantaṃ adhammacāriṃ naṃ naraṃ attanā carito so dhammova hanati. Kimiva hanati? Sayaṃ attanā gahito kaṇhasappo gaṇhantaṃ janaṃ hanati yathā, evaṃ attanā carito adhammo adhammacāriṃ naṃ hanati. “Na hi dhammo adhammo cā”tiādigāthāya attho pākaṭo. Idaṃ suttadvayaṃ kamme ca vipāke ca vācakañāpakabhāvena pavattanato kammañca vipāko ca hoti.

121. A person who behaves unrighteously and is negligent in wholesome qualities, because of that, such a negligent and unrighteous person, wherever he goes, to whatever unfortunate state he goes, that very unrighteous conduct destroys him. How does it destroy him? Just as a black serpent, seized by oneself, kills the one who grasps it, so too does unrighteous conduct destroy the unrighteous person. The meaning of the verse beginning 'For neither Dhamma nor Adhamma...' is clear. These two suttas are both kamma and vipāka because they proceed in the mode of indicating and making known kamma and vipāka.

Bhikkhave, tumhe puññānaṃ mā bhāyittha; bhikkhave, yadidaṃ yaṃ idaṃ “puññānī”ti adhivacanaṃ pavattaṃ; etaṃ “puññānī”ti adhivacanaṃ iṭṭhassa kantassa piyassa manāpassa sukhassa sukhavipākajanakassa kammassa adhivacanaṃ hoti. Bhikkhave, ahaṃ dīgharattaṃ katānaṃ puññānaṃ dīgharattaṃ paccanubhūtaṃ iṭṭhaṃ kantaṃ piyaṃ manāpaṃ abhijānāmi kho. “Kathaṃ abhijānāmī”ti ce puccheyya[M 0.0338], pubbe satta vassāni mettacittaṃ mettāya sahitaṃ dutiyajjhānacittaṃ bhāvetvā satta saṃvaṭṭavivaṭṭakappe imaṃ lokaṃ manussalokaṃ puna na āgamāsiṃ. Satta saṃvaṭṭavivaṭṭakappeti cettha saṃvaṭṭaggahaṇena saṃvaṭṭaṭṭhāyī, vivaṭṭaggahaṇena vivaṭṭaṭṭhāyīpi gahitāti veditabbā. Sesesupi evameva gahetabbo. Bhikkhave, saṃvaṭṭamāne kappe ahaṃ ābhassarūpago homi, vivaṭṭakappe suññaṃ brahmavimānaṃ upapajjāmi. Bhikkhave, tatra brahmavimāne tatra upapajjamāne upapajjamānahetu ahaṃ brahmā homi, aññe mahānubhāvena abhibhavanato abhibhū, aññehi anabhibhavanato anabhibhūto mahābrahmā homi, aññadatthu ekaṃsena daso ahaṃ vasavattī homi.

Monks, do not be afraid of merit. Monks, what is called 'merit' is a term for actions that are desirable, pleasing, agreeable, and productive of happiness, actions that generate happy results. Monks, I recall having experienced for a long time the desirable, pleasing, and agreeable results of merit accumulated over a long time. If you should ask, 'How do you recall?'—for seven years I cultivated a mind of loving-kindness, a mind of the second jhāna accompanied by loving-kindness, and for seven cycles of contraction and expansion, I did not return to this human world. Here, it should be understood that the phrase 'seven cycles of contraction and expansion' includes both the periods when the world remains in contraction and the periods when the world remains in expansion. The same should be understood in the remaining instances. Monks, during the contraction of the world-cycle, I go to the realm of radiant beings. During the expansion, I arise in an empty Brahmā mansion. Monks, there in that Brahmā mansion, because of arising there, I become Brahmā, the Great Brahmā, the Overcomer because I overcome others with my great power, the Unovercome because I am not overcome by others, and indeed, the ten-fold Wielder of Power.

Bhikkhave, ahaṃ devānamindo sakko chattiṃsakkhattuṃ ahosiṃ kho, dhammiko dhammarājā cāturanto vijitāvī janapadatthāvariyappatto cakkaratanādisattaratanasamannāgato cakkavattirājā anekasatakkhattuṃ ahosiṃ, padesarajjassa rājabhāve ko pana vādo.

Monks, I was Sakka, the king of the devas, thirty-six times. I was a righteous king, a king who ruled by Dhamma, victorious in the four quarters, who had attained stability in the territories, possessed of the seven treasures including the wheel treasure—a wheel-turning monarch many hundreds of times. What need is there to speak of being a regional king?

Bhikkhave, tassa cakkavattirājabhūtassa mayhaṃ etaṃ parivitakkanaṃ ahosi “yena phalena yena [V 0.0455] vipākena ahaṃ etarahi evaṃmahiddhiko evaṃmahānubhāvo amhi, taṃ idaṃ phalaṃ kissa kammassa phalaṃ nu kho, so ayaṃ vipāko kissa kammassa vipāko nu kho”ti etaṃ parivitakkanaṃ ahosi. Bhikkhave, tassa vitakkentassa mayhaṃ etaṃ parivitakkanaṃ ahosi “yena phalena yena vipākena ahaṃ etarahi evaṃmahiddhiko evaṃmahānubhāvo amhi, me pavattaṃ taṃ idaṃ phalaṃ tiṇṇaṃ kammānaṃ phalaṃ kho, so ayaṃ vipāko tiṇṇaṃ kammānaṃ vipāko kho, seyyathidaṃ katamesaṃ tiṇṇaṃ kammānaṃ phalaṃ vipāko? Dānassa damassa saṃyamassāti tiṇṇaṃ kammānaṃ phalaṃ vipāko”ti etaṃ parivitakkanaṃ ahosīti avocāti yojanā.

Monks, when I was a wheel-turning monarch, this thought occurred to me: 'By what fruit, by what result am I now so powerful and mighty? This fruit, what action's fruit is it? This result, what action's result is it?' This thought occurred to me. Monks, as I reflected, this consideration occurred to me: 'By what fruit, by what result am I now so powerful and mighty? This fruit that has arisen for me is the fruit of three actions; that result is the result of three actions. Namely, of which three actions is it the fruit and result? It is the fruit and result of generosity, taming, and restraint.' This thought occurred to me, he said—this is the explanation.

Tattha tasmiṃ “mā, bhikkhave, puññānaṃ bhāyitthā”tiādike sutte yañca dānaṃ, yo ca damo, yo ca saṃyamo atthi, idaṃ dānādittayaṃ kammaṃ, taṃvācakañāpakaṃ suttampi kammaṃ nāma. Tappaccayo taṃkammapaccayo paccayuppannabhūto paccanubhūto yo vipāko atthi, etaṃ vipāke phalampi pakkhipitabbaṃ, ayaṃ vipāko taṃvācakañāpako pāṭhopi vipāko nāma. Cūḷakammavibhaṅgo cūḷakammavipākaputhuttavibhāgo tathā vattabbo.

Therein, in the sutta beginning with 'Monks, do not be afraid of merit,' the generosity, taming, and restraint that exist—this triad beginning with generosity is kamma, and the sutta that indicates and makes known that kamma is also called kamma. The result that is dependent on that, that has arisen as a condition from that kamma, that has been experienced—whatever result there is, the fruit should also be included in this result; this result, and the passage that indicates and makes it known, is also called vipāka. The Cūḷakammavibhaṅga, the Exposition of the Diversity of the Results of Kamma, should be spoken of thus.

Todeyyaputtassa [M 0.0339] subhassa māṇavassa yaṃ suttaṃ bhagavatā desitaṃ, tattha sutte vuttā ye pāṇātipātādayo dhammā appāyukadīghāyukatāya saṃvattanti, ye hiṃsanādayo dhammā bahvābādhaappābādhatāya saṃvattanti, ye usūyanādayo dhammā appesakkhamahesakkhatāya saṃvattanti, ye kodhādayo dhammā dubbaṇṇasuvaṇṇatāya saṃvattanti, ye agāravādayo dhammā nīcakulikauccakulikatāya saṃvattanti, ye maccherādayo dhammā appabhogamahābhogatāya saṃvattanti, ye asallakkhaṇādayo dhammā duppaññapaññavantatāya saṃvattanti. Idaṃ pāṇātipātasattayugaṃ kammaṃ, taṃvācakañāpakaṃ suttampi kammaṃ nāma. Tattha subhasutte yā appāyukadīghāyukatā vuttā…pe… yā duppaññapaññavantatā vuttā, so ayaṃ appāyukadīghāyukatādiko vipāko, taṃvācakañāpakapāṭhopi vipāko. Idaṃ subhasuttaṃ kusalākusalakamme ceva vipāke ca vācakañāpakabhāvena pavattanato kammañca vipāko ca hoti. (14)

In the sutta taught by the Blessed One to the young brahmin Subha, son of Todeyya, the deeds mentioned therein, such as killing living beings, lead to short or long life; deeds such as violence lead to many or few ailments; deeds such as envy lead to insignificance or prominence; deeds such as anger lead to ugliness or beauty; deeds such as disrespect lead to low or high birth; deeds such as stinginess lead to poverty or wealth; and deeds such as lack of discernment lead to foolishness or wisdom. This sevenfold group beginning with killing living beings is kamma, and the sutta that indicates and makes known that kamma is also called kamma. In the Subha Sutta, the short or long life that is mentioned...and so on...the foolishness or wisdom that is mentioned—this result beginning with short or long life, and the passage that indicates and makes it known, is also vipāka. This Subha Sutta is both kamma and vipāka because it proceeds in the mode of indicating and making known both wholesome and unwholesome kamma and their vipāka. (14)

122. Yo puggalo vacīduccaritaparivajjanena vācānurakkhī bhaveyya, abhijjhādianuppādanena manasā saṃvuto bhaveyya, pāṇātipātādipajahanena kāyena akusalaṃ na kayirā, iti tayo ete kammapathe visodhaye, so puggalo isippaveditaṃ maggaṃ ariyaṃ aṭṭhaṅgikaṃ maggaṃ ārādhaye ārādhayeyyāti yojanā. Idaṃ “vācānurakkhī”tiādikaṃ suttaṃ kusale vācakañāpakabhāvena pavattanato kusalaṃ nāma.

122. A person who avoids verbal misconduct and guards their speech, restrains the mind by preventing the arising of greed and other defilements, and abstains from unwholesome actions with the body by abandoning killing and other such deeds—thus purifying these three paths of kamma—that person would realize the noble eightfold path proclaimed by the sages. This sutta, beginning with 'one who guards their speech,' is called wholesome because it proceeds in the mode of indicating and making known the wholesome.

Yassa [V 0.0456] puggalassa kāyena dukkaṭaṃ duggatisaṃvattaniyakammaṃ natthi, vācāya dukkaṭakammaṃ natthi, manasā dukkaṭakammaṃ natthi, tīhi ṭhānehi uppajjanaṭṭhānehi saṃvutaṃ taṃ puggalaṃ “brāhmaṇa”nti ahaṃ vadāmīti yojanā. Idaṃ gāthāvacanaṃ vuttanayena kusalaṃ nāma.

A person who has no bodily misconduct leading to a bad destination, no verbal misconduct, and no mental misconduct, who is restrained in these three sources of arising—that person I call a "brahmin." This verse, explained in the manner stated, is called wholesome.

“Tīṇimāni, bhikkhave…pe… kusalamūlānī”ti idaṃ vacanaṃ vuttanayena kusalaṃ. Bhikkhave, kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ samāpattiyā vijjā pubbaṅgamā hoti, hirī ca ottappañca anudevāti yojanā. Idaṃ vacanaṃ vuttanayena kusalaṃ nāma.

"Monks, these three... are the roots of the wholesome." This statement, as explained, is wholesome. Monks, for the attainment of wholesome qualities, wisdom comes first, followed by moral shame and moral dread. This statement, as explained, is called wholesome.

Māluvā sālaṃ rukkhaṃ onataṃ bhūmiyaṃ patanaṃ karoti iva, tathā yassa janassa accantaṃ dvīsu tīsu bhavesu dussīlyaṃ atthi, so jano attānaṃ onataṃ [M 0.0340] apāyesu pākaṭaṃ karoti. Anatthakāmo jano yathā anatthaṃ icchati, tathā anatthaṃ karoti yathā, tathā īdiso dussīlo naṃ attānaṃ anatthaṃ karotīti yojanā. Idaṃ “yassā”tiādikaṃ vacanaṃ vuttanayena akusalaṃ.

Just as the Māluvā creeper bends the Sāla tree, causing it to fall to the ground, so too for a person who is exceedingly immoral in two or three existences—such a person clearly brings themselves downward into the realms of misery. Just as a person who desires harm wishes for harm and acts accordingly, so too does such an immoral person bring harm upon themselves. This statement, beginning with 'for whom,' is called unwholesome by the stated method.

Asmamayaṃ asmasaṅkhātaṃ pāsāṇamaṇimayaṃ vajiraṃ vajirassa uṭṭhānasaṅkhātaṃ pāsāṇamaṇiṃ abhimatthati vidhaṃseti iva, tathā attanā hi sayameva kataṃ attajaṃ attasambhavaṃ pāpaṃ dummedhaṃ pāpaṃ karontaṃ janaṃ abhimatthatīti yojanā. Idaṃ “attanā hī”tiādikaṃ vacanaṃ vuttanayena akusalaṃ.

Just as a diamond, a gem made of stone, crushes the very stone-gem from which it originates, so too does the evil done by oneself—self-made, self-originated—crush the foolish person who commits evil. This statement, beginning with 'by oneself,' is called unwholesome by the stated method.

Devate kusalehi vivajjitā akusalā dasa kammapathe niseviya katvā garahā gārayhā bhavanti, bālamatī mandabuddhino nirayesu paccareti yojanā. Idaṃ “dasa kammapathe”tiādikaṃ suttaṃ vuttanayena akusalaṃ.

O deity, those devoid of wholesome qualities who indulge in the ten unwholesome courses of action become blameworthy and deserving of censure. Fools of weak intellect and dull understanding are roasted in the hells. This sutta, beginning with 'the ten courses of action,' is called unwholesome by the stated method.

“Tīṇimāni, bhikkhave…pe… akusalamūlānī”ti idaṃ vacanaṃ vuttanayena akusalaṃ. (15)

"Monks, these three... are roots of unwholesomeness." This statement, explained in the manner stated, is unwholesome. (15)

Yādisaṃ yaṃ bījaṃ vapate, taṃ bījaṃ tādisaṃ phalaṃ harate iva, tathā kalyāṇakārī paṇḍito kalyāṇaṃ phalaṃ harate, pāpakārī bālo ca pāpakaṃ phalaṃ harateti yojanā. Tattha “yādisa”ntiādike sutte “kalyāṇakārī kalyāṇa”nti yaṃ vacanaṃ āha, idaṃ vacanaṃ kusalaṃ. “Pāpakārī ca pāpaka”nti yaṃ vacanaṃ āha, idaṃ vacanaṃ akusalaṃ. Idaṃ dvivacanaṃ vuttanayena kusalañca akusalañca hoti.

Whatever kind of seed one sows, one reaps a corresponding fruit; so too, the wise doer of good reaps good fruit, and the foolish doer of evil reaps evil fruit—this is the explanation. Here, in the discourse beginning with 'Whatever kind,' the statement 'the doer of good reaps good' is wholesome. The statement 'and the doer of evil reaps evil' is unwholesome. These two statements, by the stated method, are both wholesome and unwholesome.

Kalyāṇakārī [V 0.0457] sappurisā subhena kammena suggatiṃ vajanti gacchanti, pāpakārī kāpurisā asubhena kammunā apāyabhūmiṃ vajanti gacchanti, kammassa abhisaṅkhāraviññāṇasahagatakammassa khayā khayanato vimuttacetasā samucchedavimuttipaṭippassaddhivimutticittā te sappurisā asubhe nibbanti. Kimiva nibbanti? Indhanakkhayā joti nibbāti iva, tathā te sappurisā kammassa khayā anavasesakhayanato nibbantīti yojanā. Tattha tasmiṃ “subhenā”tiādigāthāvacane “subhena…pe… suggati”nti yaṃ vacanaṃ āha, idaṃ “subhena…pe…suggati”nti vacanaṃ kusale vācakañāpakabhāvena pavattanato kusalaṃ nāma. “Apāyabhūmiṃ asubhena kammunā”ti yaṃ vacanaṃ āha[M 0.0341], idaṃ “apāya…pe… kammunā”ti vacanaṃ akusale vācakañāpakabhāvena pavattanato akusalaṃ nāma. Idaṃ “subhenā”tiādikaṃ gāthāvacanaṃ vuttanayena kusalañca akusalañca hoti. (16)

Good people, doers of good, go to a happy destination through wholesome deeds. Evil people, doers of evil, go to the realms of suffering through unwholesome deeds. With the exhaustion of kamma—kamma accompanied by volitional formations and consciousness—those good people, with minds liberated by eradication, tranquilization, and release, attain Nibbāna from unwholesome things. How are they extinguished? Just as a flame is extinguished when its fuel is exhausted, so too are those good people extinguished with the complete exhaustion of kamma—this is the explanation. Here, in that verse beginning with 'through the wholesome,' the statement 'through the wholesome... to a happy destination' is called wholesome, as it functions by expressing and indicating wholesome things. The statement 'to the realms of suffering through unwholesome kamma' is called unwholesome, as it functions by expressing and indicating unwholesome things. This verse beginning with 'through the wholesome,' in the manner explained, is both wholesome and unwholesome. (16)

123. “Yathāpi bhamaro pupphaṃ…pe… munī care”ti idaṃ gāthāvacanaṃ anuññāte caraṇe vācakañāpakabhāvena pavattanato anuññātaṃ nāma.

123. "Just as a bee extracts nectar from a flower... so should the sage wander." This verse is called 'permitted' because it functions by expressing and indicating permitted conduct.

Bhamaro nāma puppharasapivanagahaṇavasena caraṇako madhukarādiko bhamaro. So puppharasaṃ gaṇhanto mandavego hutvā pupphañca vaṇṇañca gandhañca avināsetvā yāvadatthaṃ puppharasaṃ pivitvā madhukaraṇatthāya ca puppharasaṃ gahetvā madhukaraṇaṭṭhānaṃ vanasaṇḍaṃ paleti. Pupphavaṇṇagandhā pākatikāva honti. Evameva piṇḍāya gāmaṃ pavisanto muni pasādajanakaṃ ālokanavilokanagamanatiṭṭhanādikaṃ janetvā pītisomanassasahitaṃ pasādaṃ janetvā saddhādeyyaṃ piṇḍapātaṃ yāpanamattaṃ paṭiggahetvā gāmato nikkhamitvā udakaphāsukaṭṭhāne vane bhesajjaṃ limpanto viya, kantāre puttamaṃsaṃ khādanto viya, piṇḍapātaṃ paccavekkhitvā paribhuñjitvā bhamaro vane madhuṃ karoti viya, kammaṭṭhānānurūpaṃ vanasaṇḍaṃ pavisitvā jhānamaggaphalanibbattanatthāya samaṇadhammakaraṇatthāya gāme care careyyāti adhippāyo veditabbo.

The bee (bhamaro) is so called because it is a wanderer that gathers and drinks flower nectar, like a honey-maker. While gathering flower nectar, it moves gently, without destroying the flower's color or fragrance, and having drunk as much nectar as needed, it takes the nectar to make honey and returns to the forest grove where honey is made. The flower's color and fragrance remain natural. Similarly, when a sage enters a village for alms, he generates faith through his pleasing way of looking, observing, walking, and standing, arousing joy and gladness, and having accepted almsfood given in faith, only enough for sustenance, he leaves the village. Like one applying medicine in a comfortable place with water in the forest, or like one eating the flesh of his own child in a desolate place, he reflects upon the almsfood before consuming it. After eating, like a bee making honey in the forest, he enters a forest grove suitable for his meditation subject, in order to produce jhāna, the path, and the fruits, performing the duties of a monk. The intention to be understood is that he should wander in the village in this way.

“Tīṇimāni, bhikkhave, bhikkhūnaṃ karaṇīyāni…pe… imāni kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhūnaṃ tīṇi karaṇīyānī”ti idaṃ suttaṃ bhagavatā anuññāte ācāre atthe vācakañāpakabhāvena pavattanato anuññātaṃ nāma. Tasmiṃ sutte yo bhikkhu sīlaṃ pāti rakkhati, iti rakkhaṇato so bhikkhu pāti nāma. Yaṃ sīlaṃ taṃ pātiṃ bhikkhuṃ apāyādidukkhato moceti, iti mocanato taṃ sīlaṃ pātimokkhaṃ nāma. Yena sīlena bhikkhu saṃvaritabbacakkhundriyādikaṃ saṃvarati, iti saṃvaraṇakaraṇato taṃ sīlaṃ saṃvaraṃ nāma, pātimokkhaṃ eva [V 0.0458] saṃvaraṃ pātimokkhasaṃvaraṃ, pātimokkhasaṃvarena saṃvuto samannāgato hutvā saṃvuṇanato catuiriyāpathesu cārako hoti, iti saṃvuṇanato bhikkhu pātimokkhasaṃvarasaṃvuto nāma. Viharati catuiriyāpathe pavatteti. Vārittacāraṃ vajjetvā cārittasīlaṃ ādāya caraṇaṃ ācāro, agocare vajjetvā gocare [M 0.0342] caraṇaṃ gocaroti. Attho vuccamāno ativitthāro bhavissati, tasmā kiñcimattaṃ kathetvā sāsanapaṭṭhānasuttabhāvaṃ kathessāma.

"Monks, there are these three duties for monks… these, monks, are the three duties for monks." This discourse, declared by the Blessed One regarding permitted conduct, is called 'permitted' because it functions by expressing and indicating the meaning. In this discourse, a monk who guards and protects morality is called 'one who protects.' That morality which frees the monk from suffering such as the lower realms is called 'Pātimokkha' because it liberates. By that morality, the monk restrains the eye-faculty and so forth, thus it is called 'restraint.' The Pātimokkha itself is the restraint, hence 'Pātimokkha-restraint.' Being endowed with and restrained by the Pātimokkha-restraint, having restrained himself, he walks in the four modes of deportment, thus he is called 'one restrained by the Pātimokkha-restraint.' He dwells, he maintains the four modes of deportment. Avoiding prohibited conduct and undertaking prescribed morality is 'conduct.' Avoiding unsuitable resorts and frequenting suitable resorts is 'resort.' Explaining the meaning in detail would be too lengthy, therefore, having spoken briefly, we will declare the discourse's foundation.

“Ettakameva suttaṃ ‘anuññāta’nti niddhāritabba”nti vattabbattā “dasayime, bhikkhave, dhammā pabbajitena abhiṇhaṃ paccavekkhitabbā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Idaṃ “dasā”tiādikaṃ suttampi anuññāte dasavidhe paccavekkhitabbe dhamme vācakañāpakabhāvena pavattanato anuññātaṃ nāma. “Tīṇimāni…pe… karaṇīyānī”ti idaṃ suttampi anuññāte tividhe sucarite vācakañāpakabhāvena pavattanato anuññātaṃ nāma.

“Because it should be said, ‘Only this much of the discourse should be determined as “permitted,”’ therefore, ‘These ten things, monks, should be frequently reflected upon by one who has gone forth,’ and so on, was said. This discourse beginning with ‘these ten’ is also called ‘permitted’ because it proceeds by way of being a verbal indicator for the ten permitted things to be frequently reflected upon. Similarly, the discourse ‘These three... should be done’ is also called ‘permitted’ because it proceeds by way of being a verbal indicator for the threefold permitted good conduct.

Nānāvidhaṃ anuññātaṃ suttaṃ ācariyena niddhāritaṃ, amhehi ca ñātaṃ, “katamaṃ suttaṃ paṭikkhitta”nti pucchitabbattā “tattha katamaṃ paṭikkhitta”ntiādi vuttaṃ.

Various permitted discourses have been determined by the teacher, and known by us. Because the question, ‘Which discourse is rejected?’ should be asked, therefore it was said, ‘Therein, which is rejected?’ and so on.

“Natthi puttasamaṃ pemaṃ, natthi gosamitaṃ dhanaṃ;

Natthi sūriyasamā ābhā, samuddaparamā sarā”ti. –

“There is no love equal to that for a son, no wealth equal to cattle; there is no light equal to the sun, the ocean is the supreme reservoir.”

Idaṃ devaputtavacanaṃ paṭikkhipanto bhagavā –

Rejecting these words of the devaputta, the Blessed One said:

“Natthi attasamaṃ pemaṃ, natthi dhaññasamaṃ dhanaṃ;

Natthi paññāsamā ābhā, vuṭṭhi ve paramā sarā”ti. –

“There is no love equal to that for oneself, no wealth equal to grain; there is no light equal to wisdom, and rain is indeed the supreme reservoir.”

Gāthaṃ āha. Ettha etasmiṃ gāthādvaye yaṃ “natthi puttasamaṃ pema”ntiādikaṃ purimakaṃ hoti. Idaṃ “natthi puttasamaṃ pema”ntiādikaṃ devaputtavacanaṃ bhagavatā paṭikkhittattā, paṭikkhitte atthe pavattanato ca paṭikkhittaṃ nāma.

He spoke the verse. Here, in this pair of verses, the former is that which begins, ‘There is no love equal to a son,’ and so on. This statement of the devaputta, beginning with ‘There is no love equal to a son,’ is called ‘rejected’ because it was rejected by the Blessed One and because it pertains to a rejected meaning.

Dubbhikkhakāle vā kantāre vā mātāpitaro puttadhītaro ghātetvāpi attānameva posenti, tasmā “natthi attasamaṃ pema”nti vuttaṃ. Dubbhikkhakālādīsu hiraññasuvaṇṇasārādīni, gomahiṃsādīnipi dhaññagahaṇatthāya dhaññassāmikānaṃ datvā dhaññameva gaṇhanti, tasmā “natthi dhaññasamaṃ [V 0.0459] dhana”nti vuttaṃ. Sūriyādīnaṃ ābhā paccuppannatamaṃ ekadesaṃva vinodeti, paññā pana dasasahassilokadhātumpi ekapajjotaṃ ekobhāsaṃ kātuṃ samatthā, atītānāgatapaccuppannadhammakoṭṭhāsesupi paṭicchādakaṃ kilesatamampi vidhamati, tasmā “natthi paññāsamā ābhā”ti vuttaṃ. Samuddo bhūmiyā [M 0.0343] ca ekadeseyeva tiṭṭhati, so ca deve avuṭṭhe sati khayanasabhāvo bhaveyya, vuṭṭhi pana koṭisatasahassacakkavāḷesupi yāva ābhassarā brahmalokāpi pūrā bhavati, tasmā “vuṭṭhi ve paramāsarā”ti vuttaṃ.

In times of famine or in the wilderness, parents may even kill their sons and daughters to sustain themselves—thus, ‘There is no love equal to that for oneself’ was said. During times of famine and so on, even gold, silver, and other valuables, or cattle and buffaloes, are given to the owners of grain in exchange for grain—thus, ‘There is no wealth equal to grain’ was said. The light of the sun and so on dispels only the present darkness in one region, but wisdom is capable of making even the ten-thousandfold world-system a single lamp, a single radiance, and it dispels the darkness of defilements covering all portions of past, future, and present phenomena—thus, ‘There is no light equal to wisdom’ was said. The ocean remains only in one part of the earth, and if it does not rain, it would be subject to depletion, but rain fills even hundreds of thousands of millions of world-systems, up to the Ābhassara Brahmā world—thus, ‘Rain is indeed the supreme reservoir’ was said.

“Idameva paṭikkhittaṃ niddhāritabba”nti vattabbattā “tīṇimāni bhikkhave”tiādi vuttaṃ. Idaṃ “tīṇimānī”tiādikaṃ suttampi paṭikkhitte duccarite vācakañāpakabhāvena pavattanato paṭikkhittaṃ nāma. (17)

“Because it should be said, ‘This alone should be determined as “rejected,”’ therefore, ‘These three, monks,’ and so on, was stated. This discourse beginning with ‘these three’ is also called ‘rejected’ because it proceeds by way of being a verbal indicator for rejected misconduct. (17)

124. Nānāvidhaṃ paṭikkhittaṃ ācariyena niddhāritaṃ, amhehi ca ñātaṃ, “katamaṃ anuññātañca paṭikkhittañcā”ti pucchitabbattā “tattha katamaṃ anuññātañcā”tiādi vuttaṃ.

124. Various rejected things have been determined by the teacher, and we have understood them. Because the question should be asked, ‘What is permitted and what is rejected?’ therefore it was said, ‘Therein, what is permitted?’ and so on.

Bhūripaññabhūripaññavanta gotama, taṃ bhūripaññaṃ gotamaṃ ahaṃ pucchāmi. Idha loke anekā yā janatā bhītā, sā janatā kiṃsu katamā bhave. Yo ca maggo anekāyatano iti pavutto, so ca maggo kiṃsu katamo bhave. Kismiṃ dhamme ṭhito jano paralokaṃ na bhāye na bhāyeyyāti pucchatīti yojanā.

“O Gotama of vast wisdom, possessor of vast wisdom, I ask you, Gotama of vast wisdom. Here in this world, the many people who are afraid—what kind of people might they be? And the path that is said to be of many bases—what kind of path might that be? Established in what principle does a person not fear the next world, would not fear? Thus he asks. This is the construal.

Devaputta yo jano sammāvācañca paṇidhāya, sammāmanañca paṇidhāya, kāyena pāpāni akubbamāno ca bhave, ayaṃ eko. Bahvannapānaṃ gharaṃ āvasanto ca bhave, ayaṃ eko. Saddho saddhāsampanno cittamudubhāvena mudu ca bhave, ayaṃ eko. Vadaññū yācakānaṃ yācanavasena vuttavacanaññū hutvā saṃvibhāgī ca bhave, ayaṃ eko. Iti etesu catūsu dhammesu ṭhito jano dhammesu ṭhito hutvā paralokaṃ na bhāye na bhāyeyyāti yojanā.

“O devaputta, a person who, having directed right speech and right mind, does no evil with the body—this is one. A person who dwells in a house with much food and drink—this is one. A person who is faithful, endowed with faith, and gentle through gentleness of mind—this is one. A person who is generous, being one who knows the words spoken by beggars according to their requests, and is a sharer—this is one. Thus, a person established in these four principles, having been established in these principles, does not fear the next world, would not fear. This is the construal.

“Tasmiṃ sutte katamaṃ anuññātaṃ, katamaṃ paṭikkhittaṃ nāmā”ti pucchitabbattā “tattha yaṃ āhā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha tasmiṃ “kiṃsūdhā”tiādipañhāya vissajjane “vācaṃ manañcā”tiādivacane “vācaṃ manañca paṇidhāya sammā”ti yaṃ vacanaṃ bhagavā āha, idaṃ “vācaṃ…pe… sammā”ti vacanaṃ anuññāte vacanīyādike atthe vācakañāpakabhāvena pavattanato anuññātaṃ nāma. “Kāyena pāpāni akubbamāno”ti yaṃ vacanaṃ āha, idaṃ “kāyena [V 0.0460] …pe… māno”ti vacanaṃ pāpakubbena paṭikkhitte vuttanayena pavattanato paṭikkhittaṃ nāma. “Bahvanna…pe… na bhāye”ti yaṃ vacanaṃ āha, idaṃ “bahvanna…pe… na [M 0.0344] bhāye”ti vacanaṃ vuttanayena anuññātaṃ nāma. Idaṃ “vāca”ntiādikaṃ vacanaṃ vuttanayadvayena anuññātañca paṭikkhittañca hoti.

Because the question, ‘In that discourse, what is called permitted and what is rejected?’ should be asked, therefore it was said, ‘Therein, what he said…’ and so on. Therein, in the answer to the question beginning ‘What here?’, in the statement beginning ‘speech and mind,’ the words ‘having rightly directed speech and mind’ which the Blessed One spoke—this statement ‘speech… rightly’ is called permitted because it proceeds by way of being a verbal indicator for the permitted meaning of things to be spoken, etc. The statement he spoke, ‘not doing evil deeds with the body’—this statement ‘with the body… doing’ is called rejected because it proceeds in the aforesaid manner concerning the rejection of evil-doing. The statement he spoke, ‘much food… not fear’—this statement ‘much food… not fear’ is called permitted in the aforesaid manner. This statement beginning ‘speech’ is both permitted and rejected by the two aforesaid methods.

“Sabbapāpassa akaraṇa”ntiādiko vuttatthova. “Tasmiṃ sabbapāpassātiādike katamaṃ anuññātaṃ, katamaṃ paṭikkhitta”nti vattabbabhāvato “tattha ya”ntiādi vuttaṃ.

That which begins ‘The non-doing of all evil’ has the meaning already stated. Because it should be stated, “Therein, in that which begins ‘of all evil,’ what is permitted and what is rejected?”, therefore “therein, what…” and so on, was said.

Devānaminda, ahaṃ kāyasamācārampi duvidhena vadāmi – sevitabbaṃ anavajjaṃ kāyasamācārampi vadāmi, asevitabbaṃ sāvajjaṃ kāyasamācārampi ahaṃ vadāmi. Vacīsamācārādīsupi vuttanayānusārena yojanā kātabbā.

“O Lord of the Devas, I speak of bodily conduct in two ways: I speak of blameless bodily conduct that is to be cultivated, and I speak of blameworthy bodily conduct that is not to be cultivated. The construal should be made for verbal conduct and so on according to the aforesaid method.”

“Kiñca vaḍḍhanahāyanaṃ āgamma kāyasamācārādikaṃ sevitabbāsevitabbabhedena vutta”nti vattabbabhāvato “kiñcetaṃ paṭiccā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Akusaladhammavaḍḍhanaṃ, kusaladhammahāyanañca paṭicca kāyasamācārādayo na sevitabbā, kusaladhammavaḍḍhanaṃ, akusaladhammahāyanañca paṭicca kāyasamācārādayo sevitabbāti sallakkhetabbā. (18)

Because it should be explained on the basis of what increase and decrease bodily conduct and so on has been spoken of with the distinction of ‘to be cultivated’ and ‘not to be cultivated’, therefore it was said, ‘And depending on what is this?’ and so on. Bodily conduct and the like should not be cultivated if they depend on the increase of unwholesome qualities and the decrease of wholesome qualities; it should be noted that they should be cultivated if they depend on the increase of wholesome qualities and the decrease of unwholesome qualities. (18)

125. Nānāvidhaṃ anuññātañca paṭikkhittañca ācariyena niddhāritaṃ, amhehi ca ñātaṃ, “katamo suttaviseso thavo”ti pucchitabbattā tathā pucchitvā ayaṃ suttaviseso thavo nāmāti viññāpetuṃ “tattha katamo thavo”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha tatthāti tesu aṭṭhavīsatividhesu lokiyādīsu sāsanapaṭṭhānasuttesu katamo suttaviseso thavo nāmāti pucchati.

125. The various kinds of what is permitted and what is rejected have been determined by the teacher, and known by us. Because the question, “Which special discourse is a praise?” should be asked, and having asked thus, in order to make it known that “this special discourse is a praise,” therefore “Therein, what is the praise?” and so on, was said. Therein, ‘therein’ means: among those twenty-eight kinds of discourses on the establishment of the teaching, beginning with the mundane, he asks: “Which special discourse is called a praise?”

Maggānaṃ jaṅghamaggadiṭṭhimaggādīnaṃ aṭṭhaṅgiko sammādiṭṭhimaggaṅgādiaṭṭhaṅgiko maggo seṭṭho uttamo. Saccānaṃ vacīsaccakhattiyādisammutisaccaparamatthasaccānaṃ caturo dukkhasamudayanirodhanirodhagāminipaṭipadāvasena caturo ariyasaccā padā seṭṭhā uttamā. Dhammānaṃ sabbasaṅkhatasappaccayadhammānaṃ virāgo asaṅkhatanibbānasaṅkhāto virāgo dhammo seṭṭho uttamo. Dvipadānaṃ sabbadevamanussādīnaṃ dvipadānaṃ cakkhumā pañcavidhacakkhumā bhagavā seṭṭho uttamoti yojanā. Ayaṃ “maggānaṭṭhaṅgiko”tiādisuttaviseso thave atthe vācakañāpakabhāvena pavattanato thavo nāma.

Among paths—such as footpaths and paths of wrong view—the eightfold path, consisting of the eight factors beginning with right view, is the best and supreme. Among truths—such as truth in speech, conventional truths like 'khattiya', and ultimate truths—the four Noble Truths, namely suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path leading to its cessation, are the best and supreme statements. Among phenomena—all conditioned and causally arisen phenomena—dispassion, known as the unconditioned Nibbāna, is the best and supreme phenomenon. Among two-footed beings—all two-footed beings such as devas and humans—the Blessed One, endowed with the fivefold eye, is the best and supreme. This special discourse beginning with “the eightfold among paths” is called “praise” because it proceeds by way of indicating and making known the meaning of praise.

“Ayameva [V 0.0461] suttaviseso thavo”ti vattabbattā “tīṇimāni bhikkhave”tiādi vuttaṃ. Apadā ahimacchādayo vā, dvipadā manussasakuṇapakkhijātikādayo vā, catuppadā hatthiassagomahiṃsādayo vā, bahuppadā [M 0.0345] satapadiādayo vā, rūpino kāmarūpasattā vā, arūpino arūpasattā vā, saññino sattaviññāṇaṭṭhitisattā vā, asaññino asaññasattā vā, nevasaññīnāsaññino bhavagge nibbattasattā vā yāvatā yattakā sattā saṃvijjanti, tesaṃ tattakānaṃ apadādīnaṃ sattānaṃ yadidaṃ yo ayaṃ arahaṃ sammāsambuddho tathāgato uppanno, so ayaṃ arahaṃ sammāsambuddho tathāgato aggaṃ aggoti akkhāyati, seṭṭhaṃ seṭṭhoti akkhāyati, pavaraṃ pavaroti akkhāyati, ayaṃ paṭhamo aggo.

Because it should be said, “This special discourse is indeed ‘Praise’,” the passage beginning “These three, O monks,” was spoken. However many beings there are—whether footless, such as snakes and fish; or two-footed, such as humans, birds, and winged creatures; or four-footed, such as elephants, horses, cattle, and buffaloes; or many-footed, such as centipedes; whether they have form, like beings in the desire and form realms; or are formless, like beings in the formless realms; whether they are percipient, like beings in the seven abodes of consciousness; or non-percipient, like beings in the realm of non-perception; or have neither perception nor non-perception, like beings born at the peak of existence—of all those beings, the one who has arisen, the Arahant, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, the Tathāgata, is declared the chief, the best, and the most excellent. This is the first chief.

Saṅkhatānaṃ dhammānaṃ vā sappaccayasabhāvānaṃ vā, asaṅkhatānaṃ paccayehi asaṅkharitānaṃ paṇṇattimattabhūtānaṃ dhammānaṃ vā yāvatā yattakā paṇṇattī voharīyanti, tattakehi paṇṇattīhi paññapetabbānaṃ tesaṃ saṅkhatāsaṅkhatānaṃ dhammānaṃ yadidaṃ yo ayaṃ madanimmadano…pe… yo ayaṃ nirodho, yaṃ idaṃ nibbānamaggaphalānamālambaṇaṃ bhavati, so ayaṃ madanimmadanādiko dhammo aggaṃ aggoti akkhāyati…pe… akkhāyati, ayaṃ dutiyo aggo.

Of conditioned phenomena, that is, those with a nature dependent on causes, or of unconditioned phenomena, that is, those not formed by conditions and existing as mere designations—however many designations are in use, among those conditioned and unconditioned phenomena to be designated by just those designations, that which is the subduer of intoxication… and so on… that which is cessation, which becomes the object for the path and fruit of Nibbāna—this phenomenon, beginning with the subduer of intoxication, is declared the chief… and so on… is declared. This is the second chief.

Saṅghānaṃ yāvatā paṇṇatti, gaṇānaṃ yāvatā paṇṇatti, mahājanasannipātānaṃ yāvatā paṇṇatti voharīyanti, tattakehi paṇṇattīhi paññapetabbānaṃ tesaṃ saṅghagaṇādīnaṃ yāni imāni cattāri puggalāni purisayugāni, ye ime aṭṭha purisapuggalā…pe… lokassa yaṃ idaṃ puññakkhettaṃ saṃvijjati, so ayaṃ catupurisayugādiko tathāgatasāvakasaṅgho aggaṃ aggoti akkhāyati…pe… akkhāyati, ayaṃ tatiyo aggo. Imāni tīṇi tathāgatanibbānaariyasaṅgharatanāni aggāni bhavanti.

However many designations are in use for communities, for groups, or for great assemblies of people—among those communities, groups, and so on, that are to be designated by just those designations—that which is the Sangha of the Tathāgata’s disciples, namely, these four pairs of persons, these eight individuals… and so on… which exists as a field of merit for the world, is declared the chief… and so on… is declared. This is the third chief. These three jewels—the Tathāgata, Nibbāna, and the Noble Sangha—are the chief ones.

Sabbalokuttaro apadādisabbasattalokato uttaro satthā ca, kusalapakkhato kusalaanavajjapakkhabhāvato uttaro dhammo ca, narasīhassa satthuno gaṇo ca iti tīṇi satthudhammagaṇaratanāni aggāni, tāni tīṇi satthudhammagaṇaratanāni visissare guṇavasena visissanti.

The Teacher, who is supramundane and superior to the world of all beings, beginning with the footless; the Dhamma, which is superior by being on the side of the wholesome, on the side of what is wholesome and blameless; and the assembly of the Teacher, the lion of men—these three jewels of the Teacher, the Dhamma, and the Assembly are chief. These three jewels of the Teacher, the Dhamma, and the Assembly are distinguished; they are distinguished by virtue of their qualities.

Samaṇapadumasañcayo sare ruhamānaṃ padumaṃ sobhanaṃ iva sāsane sobhanasamaṇapadumasamūho gaṇo ca, dhammavaro ca, vidūnaṃ sakkato naravaradamako [M 0.0346] naravarānaṃ brahmadevamanussarājarājamahāmaccādīnaṃ [V 0.0462] damako anudamako cakkhumā sambuddho ca iti tīṇi gaṇadhammabuddharatanāni lokassa uttari bhavanti.

The assembly, a beautiful collection of ascetic-lotuses in the Dispensation, like a beautiful lotus growing in a lake, a cluster of lotuses; the excellent Dhamma; and the Self-Awakened One, the one with vision, honored by the wise, the tamer of the best of men, the tamer and gentle tamer of the best of men such as Brahmās, devas, human kings, and great ministers—these three jewels of the Assembly, the Dhamma, and the Buddha are supreme in the world.

Appaṭisamo satthā ca, nirupadāho niggataupadāho, sabbo dhammo ca ariyo gaṇavaro ca iti yāni tīṇi buddhadhammagaṇaratanāni aggāni, tāni tīṇi…pe… nāni khalu ekaṃsena visissare visissanti.

The Teacher, who is matchless; the entire Dhamma, which is without affliction, from which affliction has departed; and the excellent noble Assembly—these three jewels of the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Assembly are chief. These three… and so on… are indeed definitively distinguished.

Saccanāmo avitathasaccadesanato saccanāmo khemo sabbābhibhū sabbe manussadevādike anabhibhavamānopi guṇātirekavasena abhibhavamāno viya pavattanato sabbābhibhū jino ca, saccadhammo avitathasabhāvato saccadhammo ca, tassa saccadhammassa uttari uttamo añño dhammo natthi, viññūnaṃ niccaṃ pūjito pūjāraho ariyasaṅgho ca iti tīṇi lokassa uttari uttamāni bhavanti.

The Victor, named ‘Truth’ from teaching the unfailing truth; who is secure, the all-conqueror—proceeding as if conquering through an abundance of virtues, though not overpowering all humans, devas, and so on; the true Dhamma, so called because of its unfailing nature, than which there is no other Dhamma higher or more supreme; and the noble Sangha, always honored by the wise and worthy of honor—these three are supreme and highest in the world.

Ekāyanapadassa vacanattho aṭṭhakathāyaṃ (netti. aṭṭha. 170) bahudhā vutto. Jātikhayantadassī hitānukampī bhagavā ekāyanaṃ maggaṃ pajānāti. “Yaṃ ekāyanaṃ maggaṃ pajānāti, tena maggena kiṃ taratī”ti vattabbabhāvato “etena maggenā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Yaṃ maggaṃ bhagavā jānāti, etena maggena pubbe atītamaddhānaṃ buddhādayo ariyā oghaṃ saṃsāroghaṃ tariṃsu, anāgatamaddhānaṃ tarissanti, ye cāpi buddhādayo paccuppanne uppajjanti, te cāpi buddhādayo paccuppanne taranti, visuddhipekkhā visuddhiṃ apekkhamānā sattā devamanussaseṭṭhaṃ tādisaṃ yathāvuttaguṇaṃ taṃ sammāsambuddhaṃ namassanti, iti ayaṃ nānāvidhasuttavisesopi thave ratanattaye, ratanattayaguṇe ca vācakañāpakabhāvena pavattanato thavo nāma. Iccetaṃ sāsanapaṭṭhānasuttavisesadassako saṃvaṇṇanāvisesopi sāsanapaṭṭhānaṃ nāmāti veditabbo.

The meaning of the term ‘ekāyana’ has been explained in various ways in the commentary (Netti. Aṭṭha. 170). The Blessed One, who sees the destruction of birth and is compassionate for the welfare of others, understands the one-way path. Because it can be asked, “By what path does one cross, knowing the one-way path?”, the passage beginning “by this path” was spoken. The path that the Blessed One knows is the one by which noble ones of the past, such as the Buddhas, crossed the flood, the flood of saṃsāra; by which they will cross in the future; and by which those who arise in the present, such as the Buddhas, are also crossing. Beings seeking purity, desiring purity, pay homage to that Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, who is such, endowed with the aforementioned qualities, the foremost among gods and humans. Thus, this diverse collection of special suttas is also called ‘praise’ (thava) because it proceeds by way of indicating and making known praise for the Triple Gem and its qualities. Therefore, this special exposition, which reveals the special suttas that are the foundation of the teaching, should also be understood as ‘the foundation of the teaching’.

Amhākācariya tumhehi amhākācariyehi soḷasappabhedasaṃkilesabhāgiyādisāsanapaṭṭhānasuttañceva aṭṭhavīsatividhaṃ lokiyādisāsanapaṭṭhānasuttañca niddhāritaṃ, amhehi ca ñātaṃ, “tesu saṃkilesabhāgiyādīsu sāsanapaṭṭhānasuttavisesesu katamaṃ suttavisesaṃ katamena suttavisesena saṃsanditvā niddisitabba”nti vattabbattā “tattha lokiyaṃ [M 0.0347] sutta”ntiādi āraddhaṃ. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana – “evaṃ duvidhampi sāsanapaṭṭhānaṃ nānāsuttapadāni udāharantena vibhajitvā idāni saṃkilesabhāgiyādīhi saṃsanditvā dassetuṃ puna ‘lokiyaṃ sutta’ntiādi āraddha”nti (netti. aṭṭha. 170) vuttaṃ.

O our teacher, by you the suttas on the foundation of the teaching—namely, the sixteen kinds beginning with those partaking of defilement, and the twenty-eight kinds beginning with the mundane—have been determined, and this is known by us. Because it should be asked, ‘Among those special suttas on the foundation of the teaching, such as those partaking of defilement, which special sutta should be explained by correlating it with which other special sutta?’, the passage beginning, ‘Therein, the mundane sutta,’ was commenced. In the commentary, however, it is said: ‘Having thus divided the twofold foundation of the teaching by citing various sutta passages, now, to show their connection with those partaking of defilement and so on, it begins again with, “the mundane sutta,” and so on’ (Netti. Aṭṭha. 170).

Tattha [V 0.0463] tatthāti tesu soḷasavidhesu saṃkilesabhāgiyādīsu sāsanapaṭṭhānasuttavisesesu ceva aṭṭhavīsatividhesu lokiyādīsu sāsanapaṭṭhānasuttavisesesu ca akusalapakkhe pavattaṃ lokiyaṃ suttaṃ saṃkilesabhāgiyasuttena samānatthabhāvena saṃsandati, kusalapakkhe pavattaṃ lokiyaṃ suttaṃ vāsanābhāgiyasuttena samānatthabhāvena saṃsandati, tasmā lokiyaṃ suttaṃ ekavidhampi saṃkilesabhāgiyena ca vāsanābhāgiyena ca dvīhi suttehi niddisitabbaṃ. Dassanapakkhe pavattaṃ lokuttaraṃ suttaṃ dassanabhāgiyena samānatthabhāvena saṃsandati, bhāvanāpakkhe pavattaṃ lokuttaraṃ suttaṃ bhāvanābhāgiyena samānatthabhāvena saṃsandati, asekkhapakkhe pavattaṃ lokuttaraṃ suttaṃ asekkhabhāgiyena samānatthabhāvena saṃsandati, tasmā lokuttarampi suttaṃ dassanabhāgiyena ca bhāvanābhāgiyena ca asekkhabhāgiyena ca tīhi suttehi niddisitabbaṃ. Vuttanayānusārena sesesupi saṃsandanayojanā kātabbā.

In this regard, among those sixteen kinds of specific suttas of the foundation of the Dispensation, such as those partaking of defilement, and among the twenty-eight kinds of specific suttas of the Dispensation, such as the mundane ones: a mundane sutta that occurs on the side of the unwholesome correlates with a sutta partaking of defilement by having the same meaning. A mundane sutta that occurs on the side of the wholesome correlates with a sutta partaking of proficiency by having the same meaning. Therefore, even a single kind of mundane sutta should be explained by two suttas: one partaking of defilement and one partaking of proficiency. A supramundane sutta that occurs on the side of vision correlates with a sutta partaking of vision by having the same meaning. A supramundane sutta that occurs on the side of development correlates with a sutta partaking of development by having the same meaning. A supramundane sutta that occurs on the side of the non-learner correlates with a sutta partaking of the non-learner by having the same meaning. Therefore, even a supramundane sutta should be explained by three suttas: one partaking of vision, one partaking of development, and one partaking of the non-learner. Following the method stated, the remaining correlations should also be made.

Amhākācariya tumhehi amhākācariyehi nayadassanavasena suttavisesasaṃsandanaṃ dassitaṃ, amhehi ca ñātaṃ, “kimatthāya saṃkilesabhāgiyādibhedena vibhajitvā bhagavatā vutta”nti vattabbattā “vāsanābhāgiyaṃ suttaṃ saṃkilesabhāgiyassa suttassa nigghātāyā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Ettha ca suttavasena suttatthā gahitā.

O our teachers, by you, our teachers, the correlation of specific suttas has been shown by way of the method of exposition, and this is known by us. Since it should be asked, 'For what purpose did the Blessed One speak, having divided them by way of those partaking of defilement, etc.?', therefore it was stated, 'A sutta partaking of proficiency is for the elimination of a sutta partaking of defilement,' etc. And here, the meanings of the suttas are understood by way of the suttas themselves.

“Yaṃ sattādhiṭṭhānaṃ ācariyena niddhāritaṃ, taṃ sattādhiṭṭhānaṃ kittakehi suttehi vibhajitvā niddisitabba”nti vattabbattā “lokuttaraṃ suttaṃ sattādhiṭṭhānaṃ chabbisatiyā puggalehi niddisitabba”nti vuttaṃ. “Te chabbīsati puggalā katihi suttehi samanvesitabbā”ti vattabbattā “te tīhī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Dassanabhāgiyena sattādhiṭṭhānena, bhāvanābhāgiyena sattādhiṭṭhānena, asekkhabhāgiyena sattādhiṭṭhānena cāti tīhi suttehi te chabbīsati puggalā samanvesitabbā.

Since it should be stated, 'The sevenfold foundation that has been determined by the teacher—by how many suttas should that sevenfold foundation be explained, having been divided?', therefore it was stated, 'The supramundane sutta, as the sevenfold foundation, should be explained by twenty-six individuals.' Since it should be stated, 'By how many suttas should those twenty-six individuals be investigated?', therefore 'By three,' etc., was stated. Those twenty-six individuals should be investigated by these three suttas: the sevenfold foundation partaking of vision, the sevenfold foundation partaking of development, and the sevenfold foundation partaking of the non-learner.

“Katamehi [M 0.0348] katamehi katamaṃ katamaṃ suttaṃ niddisitabba”nti vattabbattā “tattha dassanabhāgiya”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha tatthāti tesu tīsu dassanabhāgiyādīsu suttesu. Tatthāti vā tesu chabbīsatiyā puggalesu. Sattādhiṭṭhānekadesaṃ dassanabhāgiyaṃ suttaṃ ekabījinā puggalena ca niddisitabbaṃ…pe… dhammānusārinā puggalena ca niddisitabbaṃ, iti imehi pañcahi puggalehi sattādhiṭṭhānekadesaṃ dassanabhāgiyaṃ suttaṃ niddisitabbaṃ. Ettha ca dassanaggahaṇena sotāpattiphalaṭṭhāpi gahitā, tasmā ekabījikolaṃkolasattakkhattuparamā phalaṭṭhāpi gahitā.

Since it should be stated, 'By which individuals should which sutta be explained?', therefore 'There, the sutta partaking of vision,' etc., was stated. 'There, there' means among those three suttas, such as those partaking of vision. Or 'there' means among those twenty-six individuals. A sutta partaking of vision, which is a portion of the sevenfold foundation, should be explained by the one-seeder individual... and also by the Dhamma-follower individual. Thus, by these five individuals, a sutta partaking of vision, which is a portion of the sevenfold foundation, should be explained. And here, by the inclusion of 'vision,' those established in the fruit of stream-entry are also included; therefore, the one-seeder, clan-to-clan, and seven-times-at-most fruit-attainers are also included.

Saddhānusārī [V 0.0464] pana yo vipassanākkhaṇe saddhaṃ dhuraṃ katvā sotāpattimaggaṃ nibbatteti, so puggalo nibbattetabbasotāpattimaggakkhaṇe saddhānusārī nāma, saddhāya samāpattiṃ anussarati, iti saddhāya samāpattiyā anussaraṇato sotāpattimaggaṭṭho puggalo saddhānusārī nāma. So puggalo sotāpattiphalakkhaṇe saddhāya vimuttattā saddhāvimutto hutvā ekabījikolaṃkolasattakkhattuparamo bhavati. Yo pana puggalo vipassanākkhaṇe paññaṃ dhuraṃ katvā sotāpattimaggaṃ nibbatteti, so puggalo nibbattetabbasotāpattimaggakkhaṇe dhammānusārī nāma, dhammena paññāya samāpattiṃ anussarati, iti dhammena paññāya samāpattiyā anussaraṇato dhammānusārī nāma. So puggalo phalakkhaṇe diṭṭhiyā paññāya nirodhaṃ pattattā diṭṭhipatto hutvā ekabīji…pe… paramo bhavati. Dhammoti cettha paññā gahitā. Iti pabhedato dve maggaṭṭhā, cha phalaṭṭhāti aṭṭhahi ariyapuggalehi, sampiṇḍite pana pañcahi ariyapuggalehi sattādhiṭṭhānekadesaṃ dassanabhāgiyaṃ suttaṃ niddisitabbaṃ.

However, the faith-follower is one who, at the moment of insight, having made faith the dominant factor, generates the path of stream-entry. That person, at the moment of generating the path of stream-entry, is called a faith-follower. He recollects the attainment by faith; thus, because of recollecting the attainment by faith, the person established in the path of stream-entry is called a faith-follower. That person, at the moment of stream-entry fruition, being liberated by faith, becomes faith-liberated, becoming a one-seeder, a clan-to-clan goer, or a seven-times-at-most. However, the person who, at the moment of insight, having made wisdom the dominant factor, generates the path of stream-entry, that person, at the moment of generating the path of stream-entry, is called a Dhamma-follower. He recollects the attainment by Dhamma, by wisdom; thus, because of recollecting the attainment by Dhamma, by wisdom, he is called a Dhamma-follower. That person, at the moment of fruition, having attained cessation by view, by wisdom, becomes one attained to view, becoming a one-seeder... or at most. And here, 'Dhamma' is taken to mean wisdom. Thus, by distinction, it is by eight noble individuals—two established in the path and six established in the fruit—or, when grouped together, by five noble individuals, that a sutta partaking of vision, which is a portion of the sevenfold foundation, should be explained.
